I really wanted to enjoy this game, but even on the lowest difficulty it feels too unforgiving.  It's difficult to figure out how to build a formidable crew, and even after playing a few games it doesn't feel like the game helps you learn how to play either.  The skill progression feels abusive compared to other more RPG/roguelike games and I don't like how it was implemented.  I would have liked to see skills done more organically instead of using skill books for everything.  The combat is also kind of un-engaging, and you don't really get into ship combat until later in the game.  It more or less feels like you're just playing a management game and simply teased that you might get something high-action eventually.  That is definitely not the case in my time playing.  The art is great, the sound started to get on my nerves.  Overall I feel I would have been better off skipping this game as I don't think the mechanics create a cohesive game that's engaging.  I really felt like I was just waiting around for something to happen a lot of the time.

This review is current as of 12/5/16.
Where do I start? I've had loads of fun playing RIFT (about 5k hours, just over half through Steam) and do not regret a single moment. I started playing during Beta 1 (though I had proximity to the game's development prior), and from the Eye of Regulos to Ashenfell, it's been a wild ride. The rifts are what make the game world different from other MMOs. They're dynamic events that can appear throughout a zone in a number of locations - in 6 different types as well as variations of the rifts within those types. I still have yet to finish all of the planar achievements, and it's been almost 6 years.
Then there's the soul system. While some souls are paid for (3 per class/calling), the combinations you can make with them are only limited by your imagination. There is an argument to be made that the cookie-cutter specs you can find on the official forums are currently better, and that does detract from the original "any spec, any time" aspect of the game. Some specs are simply not viable in endgame content, like Druid was for clerics for a long time.
The community appears at first to be a mixed bag, but the chat is filled with a vocal minority of trolls. Ignore them and carry on, and you'll find that there are plenty of nice and welcoming players in the game. I'd suggest turning off the CrossEvents channel if you don't care for what political rant there is that week.
PvE content? There's no shortage of that - between questing, rifts, planar invasions, dungeons, and raids (past, current, or upcoming), I doubt you'd find a way to finish all of it amazingly fast. Even with store experience boosts.
PvP - it's always been a bit lacking, but it really took a hard hit after Nightmare Tide (Patch 3.0), when PvP-specific gear was removed. Low-level warfronts (Rift's battleground system) take upwards of an hour or two to get a queue to pop, and Conquest has been dead for a while (until it gets updated with current rewards). However, max-level warfronts are still alive and kicking and have a different meta to them than PvE content as far as specs go.
And the big question - is Rift P2W?
Nope. Rift, if I had to sum it up, is "pay-to-progress-faster", but nothing will ever give you a solid gameplay advantage long-term in Rift other than the loyalty system (extra mount speed is nothing to sniff at). Most of what is in the store is either fluff or used to get alts to max level (currently 70) faster. With Starfall Prophecy, all content after level 65 is locked unless you buy the expansion pack, but a trial to 65 out of 70 levels with nothing to lose on the way is amazing, compared to other MMOs that limit you to level 20.
There is, however, a significant time investment required - in the form of reputation grinds (I use the term loosely), gearing up through the various tiers (which reset every expansion pack), and money in general (Planar Fragments in Starfall Prophecy being a particularly hard platinum sink). Don't let that deter you from the game - after all, none of these time-investment-specific requirements apply to the level 1-65 content, which is entirely free with no timegating!
If you have more questions about the game, you can find me on the North America region servers: Sarynnah@Faeblight.

What this game has going for it: As with any grand strategy game, particularly one from Paradox, the lure of alternate history is too much to resist. Turning America fascist, invading Ireland as the Empire of Japan, or conquering the world as Luxembourg are all options in this gem. As anyone familiar with the Hearts of Iron franchise is already aware, this game operates on a much, MUCH faster pace in comparison to other Paradox titles, largely due to its biggest emphasis being on war. Research and production move very quickly, and in order to gain the upper hand you will be expected to carefully craft your divisions into task-oriented killing machines. I found this mechanic very rewarding and enjoyable, especially when combined with the battle planning and specific game mechanics that favor outmaneuvering and encircling enemies as opposed to just bludgeoning them with murder-stacks. The national focus tree is also a wonderful mechanic, in that it allows you to very carefully craft a narrative that has an enormous effect on the overall playstyle of your nation. Add into this the outstanding mod community, which has made such in-depth mods as Kaiserreich, Millenium Dawn, and (my personal favorite) the IKEA logo flag replacer for Sweden, and you've got a recipe for awesome.
The♥♥♥♥♥♥♥parts: Well, this being a grand strategy game by Paradox, there is a learning curve. Granted, it's not as significant as Hearts of Iron 3, but you will likely find yourself watching a few videos on Youtube trying to figure this game out. Also, the AI is...well, let's just say the occasionally make some very interesting, if not entirely rational, decisions. Not the worst AI I've seen in a strategy game, but it could use some improvement. The worst I have to say about this game is its DLC. Your mileage may vary, but I really do believe that this game has the ♥♥♥♥♥iest DLC of any Parodox game since EU IV. The DLC focuses exclusively on nations that just about nobody plays as, like the commonwealth nations or eastern european states. I wouldn't mind seeing some new stuff for a few of the major powers.
This game's only a bit overpriced, but I'm also a cheap ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, so I do recommend buying it without the DLC. 7.5/10 remilitarize the Rhineland today.

Hearts of Iron 4 is a great strategy game where I feel like an actual commander of not just a mass of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s but a fully functioning nation. This review will be giving you a real feel of how the game works and what to do.
The Grand Stategy part of this game invovles a system I have not seen before of assigning Divisions to lower-ranking officers than you, all with their own characteristics that they start with or acquire after gaining experience in combat, thus creating a subset of your military --  an army. You effectively tell the General (24 unit command max) or a Field Marshal (No limit) what you want to happen, and he will carry it out within the extra parameters you give to him, on your go. This makes it very nice when having massive inter-continental wars as I do not have to be micro-managing everything *cough* CIV SERIES *cough* and adds tactical feeling and effects with bonuses like planned attack buffs to your troops. If I want to be sure of victory, I can execute key pushes in areas and in situations where the A.I. kinda fails to do the job and do daring manuevers like, oh idk, send a division (or 5) of super-heavy tanks through a gap in the Soviets' lines straight to Moscow. I also like how with experience earned in fighting, you can modify divisions and make new templates to have special composistions to make that specific template have a backbone role or, with special battalions, a very small niche. For vehicles and boats, they get you the same sort of general experience: Land (also used to modify division template), Sea, and Air. With the Sea and Air experience you can create variants like the Germans or Brits famously did (see BF-109 Series Z, A, B, C, E, D, E, F, G, etc. or Spitfire Mk. 49 B late or whatever) in the air or variants of ship classes, both with buffs to certain areas which you choose for ever-inceasing cost. Ships and planes with different roles from one another will have different buffs, leke bombers will get bombing buff option or deffensive armament rather than offensive armament. Sometimes you even start with variants with ships for some reason.
The logistics system I find interesting and sometimes stressful. You have civilian factories, a percentage of which make goods to keep your people happy, and the rest produce things like forts, air bases, radar stations, synthetic oil plants, or Military Factories/Docks which make stuff used for fighting like ships and convoys (at docks), airplanes, tanks, mechanized infantry cars, infantry supplies, etc. Based on how your divisions are outfitted, they will have needs for different things; most are catch-alls like Infantry Equipment (guns, grenades, anti-tank at later stages), Support equipment (used in supporting battalions like recon), Motorized (used in fields hospital support battalions, Logistics support battalions and motorized infantry), Artillery, Anti-air, and tanks of different classes (light, medium, heavy, super-heavy, tank destroyers, etc.). It is your job to dedicate military factories which you also have to build and manage to be producing the right amount of equipment to stay afloat and having enough stocked before the war starts. Everything costs different materials to make per factory working on producing that item, which you may need to trade for or conquer someone that has it to make it efficiently. Your factoires will also get more efficient the longer they make one thing. The max efficiency can also be boosted with tech.
The specific combat systems are really really really complex. So complex, that I won't get into them. But I won't, and I don't need to, and neither does the game. All you need to know is that a battle it started when you move your division into a piece of territory with an enemy in it. If there is no enemy, you get the territory, no fight. The battle will be displayed as a circle with a number in it, 0 - 100. It will also be a color, red or green. The number is progress to the end of the battle; 100 means your side wins, 0 means their side wins. The color is the current trend of the number, win or lose for you or your allies. You can click on the circle to get more details like the effectiveness of your air support, their air support, what is going on more specfically in the battle, etc. Each battle is fluid and will last until one side loses too much organization to continue at which point it will flee if on the deffending side or go back to its starting point if on the attacking, and it will recoup org. Many factors contribute, not just if you have more divisions. What is your planning bonus? What is their entrenchment? How good is your/their air cover or ground support? Are you attacking from more than one side? What kind of battalions are in their divisions? What's the terrain? But, remember: all you need to know is if the color on the circle is green or red (or yellow - stalemate, but that usually lasts for a second or 2) and if it's red to stop attacking unless you are just attacking with a subset of your army continously so they tire out and you can steamroll them. Besides orginization there is also division strength which is how much equipment and manpower the unit has, replenished regularly if available from the country's stockpile. If this runs out, which it rarely does, the unit will die. The best way to kill units is to surround them. If a unit is fleeing and it cannot flee into empty territory (it can capture unoccupied territory) it will die.
Diplomacy is minimal but it is all you need. Lend-leases, alliances, expeditionary forces, non-agression pacts, political coups and influencing, relations boosting, and trading for resources to build your war machine. Peace treaties are kinda weird and can sometimes feel unfair, so I would recommend going alone unless you really need a bigger army. When you are declaring war, picking a specific goal on between 1-5 states will ensure that you get those should you win the war and also have allies fighting too. Each major power (America, UK, Germany, Italy, Japan, Russia, France, and others I am forgetting I think) has their own mini "tech tree" which provides buffs and goes through the more historical aspects of a nation. Other minor countries you can still play and have a non-specific tree. World events will pop up too alerting you of specific events that major countries do and some random ones like The Hindenburg Disaster or the Olympics.
Overall I have gotten more than my money's worth out of this game and I can learn and improve my strategy all the time without having to go sneaking around the web for top tips and tricks. Although this review may seem very in-depth, this is only about half of the detail and layering put into this game, which may I remind you, you usually do not need to know. The game will always provide simple information upfront, and you can get more detail if you are experienced and have good bearings. Also, if you blow through games fast, there are plenty of mods to try which do a variety of things from focusing on one nation to making the experience slower or just different in general.
My main gripes with this game are minor except for one: A.I. This game could be better with smarter bots, but the game is enjoyable enough for me without them because the A.I. is also a defining, integral and... er... Interesting -- yes we'll pick that word -- *ahem* Interesting part of the HOI4 Experience. Also, if you want a challenge, pick a nation that is usually a non-start, like Ethiopia or Poland, or play against real people.
TL;DR It's a bloody good game, innit. Buy it, I think you'll be fine without DLC, don't buy any special packs particullarly.

HOI4 is ok when it comes to gameplay compared to its previous titles.  The visuals have been improved greatly.  Multiplayer can be fun if you know some people to play with. The AI sucks pretty bad, but are their any games that actually have good AI?  For those who like grand strategy I give this title a 7/10, for those new to the genre I give it a 6/10 as the tutorial is kinda skimpy, but HOI4 is the easiest to just pick up and play of the HOI series, and for those who enjoy other paradox games I give it a ?/10 as most of the other paradox games are so different from HOI4 that is hard to say if you would like it or not.  All in all it is a solid game, but not the best game ever.

Pros
- Only redeeming quality gamplay wise, is the combat to some extent. My squad and I were a walking death machine by the 3rd or 4th mission.
- If you like 3rd person shooters AND the XCOM series AND don't mind the fact that the storyline in this game conflicts with other xcom games, then think about buying this game.
- The ending twist was interesting, but this shouldn't influence you to buy the game or not.
Cons
- The graphics are sub-par -> the voice-overs aren't in synch, the different zones are mostly generic, little emotion on faces. Overall, very boring during most cinematics.
- You keep getting stronger while the aliens do the same things every time. No new enemies after like 3 or 4 missions. Only upgraded versions of others-> Muton becomes Elite Muton.
- AI is moderately stupid -> if it had been better I could've overlooked the aliens' weakness physically. Ex. Aliens sometimes move into position to flank you but they never move up when they have the chance. They stay in the position to flank without ever flanking. It doesn't make any sense. I... can't recommend this game any more, and it hurts me dearly to say this. Don't let my playtime fool you, I played for 60+ hours during the original Evolve beta way back when. So what happened?
First off, I think going F2P was the right move; the game was pretty much dead in the water anyway. The problem, then, is that the devs made a lot of changes to go with F2P that dynamically changed the game at its core - a lot of which I think were mistakes from a design perspective.
Take the planet scanner, for instance. The planet scanner is like a compass that the trapper can use to point you towards the monster instantly, and replaced the dome as their class ability. This completely removed a huge amount of gameplay depth on two fronts: trapping as Abe or Griffin takes absolutely no finesse any more, and you no longer have to care about being stealthy as the monster, because they're going to find you, anyway. The game has become an arcade shooter in terms of depth; this isn't necessarily a bad thing, by itself, but you have to remember that a lot of the original gameplay was designed around the slow-paced and methodical nature of vanilla Evolve. The entire game just feels kind of... off, now, compared to what it used to be.
So where did the thunderdome go, if it's no longer a trapper class ability? Now everyone gets to dome the monster! Not only that, the dome always auto-centres on where the monster is when you press it, so no more clutch monster escapes. In vanilla Evolve, incapacitating the trapper brought down the dome, now, not so much; when domed, your poor monster player has absolutely no choice but to take the fight, and now there really isn't much to target selection because of that. Now, they did compensate by reducing the time that the dome stays up as everybody takes damage, but I don't feel like that makes a lot of sense. Why are the hunters being punished for doing their job well? It doesn't feel good. This game doesn't feel good any more.
Vanilla Evolve wasn't perfect, not by a long shot. The character progression system never made much sense to me and I'm glad they got rid of it, and being unable to pick hunters after seeing what monster we were up against got frustrating after the eighth time I got stuck playing Daisy against a Kraken. On top of that, its business model was a hot, bleeding nightmare - but its problems were usually limited to outside the main gameplay. When you were in a match, all the mechanics made sense together and felt cohesive; finding the monster was an ordeal, not just another Tuesday; cleverly evading the hunters was rewarded with three minutes of uninterrupted feeding; playing anyone other than Assault was nuanced and suboptimal play was heavily punished. Stage 2 changed all that, and while change isn't always bad, the changes they made here just don't work as well as in the past. I'm very sad. :(

How To Survive 2 is best enjoyed with friends as the difficulty will adjust to how many people are currently playing in a single camp.

The unadjustable cameraview does not aid this issue as traps can be hidden behind your walls.
Aside of these issues the graphics are done fairly well, although they can be a bit confusing in cities or doors can be a bit hard to spot; aside of this they are done decently.
Regarding the sound - could've been better, could've been worse. Average at best. The Assault Rifle sounds like a popcorn machine, to be honest.
The gameplay, as aforementioned, is rather repetitive and gets boring rather quickly after a few missions; the enemy AI is rather straightforward and in most cases not very intelligent (although they're zombies so you might argue that this hits the spot).
If you are into zombie survival games, I can recommend you try this game, but do not expect too much.
For anyone else, this might not be the best choice.

Disclaimer: I have played Realm Of The Mad God for nearly 5 years so perma death is something I do enjoy. It's a great game mechanic and wish it was used more often.
Review: Played about an hour so far so obviously don't know much about the game but from what I have seen, it's a 7/10 atm. The game isn't necessarily fast paced which is meh. The tutorial explains nearly nothing about the game and a few game mechanics are iffy to me. Despite this, I have managed to have fun and enjoy losing my characters. So far I have died 3 or 4 times, yeh, I'm pretty bad.
Pros:
-Perma Death (It's fun imo)
-Items are similar to that of diablo type mechanics where you can get 5 of the same item but they ma have different stats. It adds variety and a reason to hunt for a better version of your current item.
-Plenty of missions. There are well over 10 missions and from what I could tell, they never end. Just kill the boss and start a new level.
-Not graphic intensive and that's saying A LOT! My pc is i5 2 cores and I believe about 1.75 Ghz. It's trash and yet I have no fps issues in this game (graphics at the lowest obviously). You have 0 excuses, the sprites are beautiful, have fun.
-Gun mechanics are 50/50. There is an ability you can get called bounce which is basically ricochet. The shots bounce off walls hitting targets. I had a gun with that and had some fun with it.
-Mobs are pretty cool. There was a snail where it went into it's shell and rolled to you. What made it cool? The sound effect was a racecar noise. Pretty badass imo.
Cons:
-The currency is EC (I think, may have the second letter wrong) and the game does not tell you how to use it or how to get it.
-The game is purely keyboard oriented. The mouse is only used in the menu.
-Weapons can shoot front, back and diagonal.
-Tutorial explains virtually nothing.
-Your vault only has 6 slots. To unlock more you have to spend money. For a game with item variety, 6 slots isn't enough.
-Getting XP to level up isn't to difficult but it does take some grinding which for early game, that's the last thing you should be doing.
-No way to solo missions to learn the game mechanics and mob attacks. With 10 players in lower level dungeons you really can't learn anything as quickly as some would like too.
Tips For Players:
-You get extra hp and stats by killing mobs. They drop packs that boost your jump, movement speed, hp etc so hunt for them.
-Ammo is for your secondary. The class you start with has grenades, maximum 4 to start with and the ammo replenishes them.
-When you die, stats get tallied up and you get XP which goes to your account level. Level 3 is required for the second class so spend some time killing stuff.
-EC drops from mobs so hunt for that to.
Tips For Devs: Disclaimer, I know I heven't played much yet so I will keep this just to starter things and maybe a couple quality of life changes.

Ok before i am judged for my good rating I shall explain. The game has high and low points so to start off I shall give the low points of the game.
1.
The beginning. Honestly I just found the beginning boring i wanted something a bit more exciting than just appearing at the menu.
2.
The directions. After I made my character I was so confused on what to do next. I looked at the help section but it didn't help much. So honestly I dont think it was implemented well.
Now for the good things in the game.
1.  The freedom.
I enjoyed the fact that the game doesn't hold your hand. You have to learn how to do things. Its doesn't explicitly tell you. 3.
Stats and leveling up.

For example if you upgrade strength alot your character will be a tank that can kill enemies easily,or if you increase vitality you can last longer in a battle. It is small things like this that make it enjoyable.
All in all this game is not for everyone.

Longread:
Currently I can not recommend this game. I know that it is in ALPHA stage but it has been in ALPHA for almost a year. I bought this game around Christmas 2016. It was something new, something enjoyable. But because of the lack of content it became quite boring. So fast forward until now and here I am willing to give it another shot.
First thing I noticed is that the menu is way different (in a good way) and that there's a new character creation which looked nice but here it starts.
- First i'm trying to create a new character and the game crashes instantly. Well it can happen so I tried it again, and again with the same results. As annoyed as I was I started to look for a fix, noticing that there was a hotfix coming within an hour. I was quite pleased with that, seeing that the game is not abandoned by the developers.
- So after creating a character I could see that you now have to choose between the classes engineer, marine, scientist and ranger. There's also a new skill tree system which at first didn't look to bad but I'll come back on this topic later.
- Here I am joining a server with a friend just to see that you now start at a crashed pod which you can break down for supplies.  I quickly noticed that you no longer spawn with a pistol, rather you spawn with a rusty pipe or bashing rock (depends on which choice you made in the skill tree). I understand that you want to create some sort of adventure game and that people should find and make themselves supplies but the moment I started to mine some minerals (around 5 minutes later) I got attacked by an alien creature. It took me around
with the rusty pipe.
The problem is that you either have to give the players the ability to have a pistol on spawn or make the alien's a lot easier to kill as this is extremely boring for new (and expierenced) players. I would choose the latter option.
- The gameplay mechanics have been ruined aswell in my opinion. 6 months ago you could mine a rock and pick up the fallen items instantly. Now it has this animation which takes 1 to 2 seconds. Mining up on a hill edge is no longer an option if you don't want to run down collecting everything as it's very annoying to pick up items when they fall down and the animation starts playing.
- The graphics have not been improved as far as I know, the optimisation however did and not in a good way. 6 months ago I could easily run this game at 60 fps with medium to high settings.  Now I had to put everything but really everything at toaster settings and still not be able to have a playable fps. I do not have the recommended PC specs but have a decent PC which is way above the minimum specs so I should at least expect that I could run this game on low settings with 60 fps. When I look up on the sky I get 60 fps yet when I look at the ground with particles and stuff I get around 25-30 fps which is not playable (for me).
So to come to a conclusion:
I'd really like to recommend this game because it's something I'd always wanted to play. But I can't however because in this current state it's not enjoyable and playable enough for me. I'm happy to check back in this game after another 6 months and hopefully I can change this recommendation to a positive one. But for now I can't recommend this game

What this game has going for it: As with any grand strategy game, particularly one from Paradox, the lure of alternate history is too much to resist. Turning America fascist, invading Ireland as the Empire of Japan, or conquering the world as Luxembourg are all options in this gem. As anyone familiar with the Hearts of Iron franchise is already aware, this game operates on a much, MUCH faster pace in comparison to other Paradox titles, largely due to its biggest emphasis being on war. Research and production move very quickly, and in order to gain the upper hand you will be expected to carefully craft your divisions into task-oriented killing machines. I found this mechanic very rewarding and enjoyable, especially when combined with the battle planning and specific game mechanics that favor outmaneuvering and encircling enemies as opposed to just bludgeoning them with murder-stacks. The national focus tree is also a wonderful mechanic, in that it allows you to very carefully craft a narrative that has an enormous effect on the overall playstyle of your nation. Add into this the outstanding mod community, which has made such in-depth mods as Kaiserreich, Millenium Dawn, and (my personal favorite) the IKEA logo flag replacer for Sweden, and you've got a recipe for awesome.
The♥♥♥♥♥♥♥parts: Well, this being a grand strategy game by Paradox, there is a learning curve. Granted, it's not as significant as Hearts of Iron 3, but you will likely find yourself watching a few videos on Youtube trying to figure this game out. Also, the AI is...well, let's just say the occasionally make some very interesting, if not entirely rational, decisions. Not the worst AI I've seen in a strategy game, but it could use some improvement. The worst I have to say about this game is its DLC. Your mileage may vary, but I really do believe that this game has the ♥♥♥♥♥iest DLC of any Parodox game since EU IV. The DLC focuses exclusively on nations that just about nobody plays as, like the commonwealth nations or eastern european states. I wouldn't mind seeing some new stuff for a few of the major powers.
This game's only a bit overpriced, but I'm also a cheap ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, so I do recommend buying it without the DLC. 7.5/10 remilitarize the Rhineland today.

Hearts of Iron 4 is a great strategy game where I feel like an actual commander of not just a mass of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s but a fully functioning nation. This review will be giving you a real feel of how the game works and what to do.
The Grand Stategy part of this game invovles a system I have not seen before of assigning Divisions to lower-ranking officers than you, all with their own characteristics that they start with or acquire after gaining experience in combat, thus creating a subset of your military --  an army. You effectively tell the General (24 unit command max) or a Field Marshal (No limit) what you want to happen, and he will carry it out within the extra parameters you give to him, on your go. This makes it very nice when having massive inter-continental wars as I do not have to be micro-managing everything *cough* CIV SERIES *cough* and adds tactical feeling and effects with bonuses like planned attack buffs to your troops. If I want to be sure of victory, I can execute key pushes in areas and in situations where the A.I. kinda fails to do the job and do daring manuevers like, oh idk, send a division (or 5) of super-heavy tanks through a gap in the Soviets' lines straight to Moscow. I also like how with experience earned in fighting, you can modify divisions and make new templates to have special composistions to make that specific template have a backbone role or, with special battalions, a very small niche. For vehicles and boats, they get you the same sort of general experience: Land (also used to modify division template), Sea, and Air. With the Sea and Air experience you can create variants like the Germans or Brits famously did (see BF-109 Series Z, A, B, C, E, D, E, F, G, etc. or Spitfire Mk. 49 B late or whatever) in the air or variants of ship classes, both with buffs to certain areas which you choose for ever-inceasing cost. Ships and planes with different roles from one another will have different buffs, leke bombers will get bombing buff option or deffensive armament rather than offensive armament. Sometimes you even start with variants with ships for some reason.
The logistics system I find interesting and sometimes stressful. You have civilian factories, a percentage of which make goods to keep your people happy, and the rest produce things like forts, air bases, radar stations, synthetic oil plants, or Military Factories/Docks which make stuff used for fighting like ships and convoys (at docks), airplanes, tanks, mechanized infantry cars, infantry supplies, etc. Based on how your divisions are outfitted, they will have needs for different things; most are catch-alls like Infantry Equipment (guns, grenades, anti-tank at later stages), Support equipment (used in supporting battalions like recon), Motorized (used in fields hospital support battalions, Logistics support battalions and motorized infantry), Artillery, Anti-air, and tanks of different classes (light, medium, heavy, super-heavy, tank destroyers, etc.). It is your job to dedicate military factories which you also have to build and manage to be producing the right amount of equipment to stay afloat and having enough stocked before the war starts. Everything costs different materials to make per factory working on producing that item, which you may need to trade for or conquer someone that has it to make it efficiently. Your factoires will also get more efficient the longer they make one thing. The max efficiency can also be boosted with tech.
The specific combat systems are really really really complex. So complex, that I won't get into them. But I won't, and I don't need to, and neither does the game. All you need to know is that a battle it started when you move your division into a piece of territory with an enemy in it. If there is no enemy, you get the territory, no fight. The battle will be displayed as a circle with a number in it, 0 - 100. It will also be a color, red or green. The number is progress to the end of the battle; 100 means your side wins, 0 means their side wins. The color is the current trend of the number, win or lose for you or your allies. You can click on the circle to get more details like the effectiveness of your air support, their air support, what is going on more specfically in the battle, etc. Each battle is fluid and will last until one side loses too much organization to continue at which point it will flee if on the deffending side or go back to its starting point if on the attacking, and it will recoup org. Many factors contribute, not just if you have more divisions. What is your planning bonus? What is their entrenchment? How good is your/their air cover or ground support? Are you attacking from more than one side? What kind of battalions are in their divisions? What's the terrain? But, remember: all you need to know is if the color on the circle is green or red (or yellow - stalemate, but that usually lasts for a second or 2) and if it's red to stop attacking unless you are just attacking with a subset of your army continously so they tire out and you can steamroll them. Besides orginization there is also division strength which is how much equipment and manpower the unit has, replenished regularly if available from the country's stockpile. If this runs out, which it rarely does, the unit will die. The best way to kill units is to surround them. If a unit is fleeing and it cannot flee into empty territory (it can capture unoccupied territory) it will die.
Diplomacy is minimal but it is all you need. Lend-leases, alliances, expeditionary forces, non-agression pacts, political coups and influencing, relations boosting, and trading for resources to build your war machine. Peace treaties are kinda weird and can sometimes feel unfair, so I would recommend going alone unless you really need a bigger army. When you are declaring war, picking a specific goal on between 1-5 states will ensure that you get those should you win the war and also have allies fighting too. Each major power (America, UK, Germany, Italy, Japan, Russia, France, and others I am forgetting I think) has their own mini "tech tree" which provides buffs and goes through the more historical aspects of a nation. Other minor countries you can still play and have a non-specific tree. World events will pop up too alerting you of specific events that major countries do and some random ones like The Hindenburg Disaster or the Olympics.
Overall I have gotten more than my money's worth out of this game and I can learn and improve my strategy all the time without having to go sneaking around the web for top tips and tricks. Although this review may seem very in-depth, this is only about half of the detail and layering put into this game, which may I remind you, you usually do not need to know. The game will always provide simple information upfront, and you can get more detail if you are experienced and have good bearings. Also, if you blow through games fast, there are plenty of mods to try which do a variety of things from focusing on one nation to making the experience slower or just different in general.
My main gripes with this game are minor except for one: A.I. This game could be better with smarter bots, but the game is enjoyable enough for me without them because the A.I. is also a defining, integral and... er... Interesting -- yes we'll pick that word -- *ahem* Interesting part of the HOI4 Experience. Also, if you want a challenge, pick a nation that is usually a non-start, like Ethiopia or Poland, or play against real people.
TL;DR It's a bloody good game, innit. Buy it, I think you'll be fine without DLC, don't buy any special packs particullarly.

This game is both a modern take on the Thief franchise and also a bit of a love letter to Looking Glass Studios.  Not only does it craft a touching homage, but it also stands on its own as an excellent game that not only tells an engaging story, but consistently respects the player by offering an environment that they can take command of.
The campaign is very fluid, but consists of individual missions that can be replayed independently after each completion.  You are free to progress to your goal in many different ways and the mechanics and level design expertly offer you opportunity to make varied choices about whether you'd like to be a complete ghost, silent assassin, violent slaughterer or any combination in between.
It has been a long time since a first person shooter has afforded so much respect to the player and Arkane should be praised for that.
Aside from the massive replayability this game has, it also has wonderful DLC.  If you are tired of microtransactions and cheap base games that feel torn apart in order to ask more money from you, this is an excellent remedy.  I can't praise this game enough.
It also has excellent controls and options, whether you're using mouse / keyboard, a traditional controller or the steam controller.  My favorite tool is actually the steam controller with this game and its sequel.

The *game* portion of this title is a typical "where's waldo" style scavenger hunt of lesser difficulty set against surprisingly complex hand drawn photographs.
That is completely irrelevant, however; as the reason you won't be able to put this down is the hilarious "mouth generated" sound effects. You will ignore the goals of every page, and begin clicking wildly on what you guess will be the most hilarious-sounding object. You will continue to navigate around the page loling at the sounds (and probably trying to mimick them if you are alone or shameless).
By the time you start to get sick of the sounds you will look down and realize you have accomplished your scavenger hunt objectives, and happily move on the page of hilarious cartoon sounds.

Hidden Folks is very much a simplistic "Where's Woldo" style hidden object game that proves the rule that simplicity is sometimes bliss. I'm not going to beat around the bush on this one, the game has a metric ton of charm, runs well, and is a good deal of clean fun that will entertain people of all ages.

I would like to remind everyone, however, that the replayability factor is quite low as there is no real randomization. But, even still, I am confident that recommending this game is the right call.

For a single person's first project, I think it turned out nicely. It's short and simple, but I felt the drive to keep going for as long as I could - made it to 11 days, but then my family inevitably starved.
It's essentially a desperate struggle to feed your family at home, in a snowy area where the resources are incredibly scarce. I think the game would be better if the resource density was slightly increased - I feel like some days, I spam-hopped around the entire map without finding anything, or pretty much nothing. When the update with some crafting elements comes out, it will definitely be good for the game because I feel like I simply can't find enough to possibly make it sometimes, even though there's a lot of trees and twigs which you can't pick up or cut down.
Still, the game's cosy but despondent atmosphere, which is supported by its single music track, accomplishes enough to hold my interest despite its repetitive gameplay, and the fact that you're fighting for your family's survival instead of your own was enough drive for me to keep pushing on until the harsh winter claimed their lives.
To end on a more upbeat note: good job with the game man, I hope you get some sales and learn from it to make better games in the future! I liked it.

The concept of Death Stair is an awesome one. This is a phenomenal game if you have friends to play with locally or online. However the further you go into the game, you'll start to notice little hiccups and glitches. Then you'll start realizing the game should have more potential to be awesome, but falls very far from being an outstanding game.
Death Stair is a game in which there are four participants. 3 participants will be runners while 1 will be a gunner. The gunners objective is to hold the runners back as far as possible for a set time limit. Runners have to push the gunner back until they reach the final checkpoint before the time limit runs out. The gunners ammo will vary from stage to stage. Some of the ammo included is giant beach balls, brick launching mini-gun, mine deployment and a water cannon. There is one stage in particular where the gunners ammo isn't the most effective - so tough luck if you're a gunner on that level. The levels themselves are very few in numbers, but are fun and challenging. Some levels (especially the ice level) can be quite burdensome and a little too challenging for the runners as there is no "safe spots". Some levels will have divets in the walls or the floor for runners to hide from incoming fire. Runners have 4 abilities : run, dodge left, dodge right and jump. Besides that, runners cannot interfere with one another. Overall, the
is alright, but quite stiff in its delivery.
The
are ok at best. The amount of different types of weapons is nice and is satisfying to see a bunch of balls rolling down the stairs knocking players back. The actual hitting effect and ragdoll effects are at best (again) - ok. There is nothing too substantial or fancy when it comes to this domain. The user interface is also a little buggy and wonky. The
are also at best ok. They are not diverse and quite repetitive, especially after playing a few rounds.
Overall, the game is ok and fun if you have people to play with. If you have a friend at your house and two online, you cannot play together... well the local component won't work with the online component. Meaning, unlike Blazerush or other games of the sort you cannot play with local players and play online. Either you play online or you play local - no in between. This was quite a drawback for me. I will not be recommending the game as I don't think its top quality. Sure I bought it on sale for about a buck, but I do not see a lot of people playing this for hours on end - even with friends. If this does appeal to you, I would suggest to have a group of friends who also own the game and to buy it on sale.
RATING : 6.0/10

Preamble: I've played the Hearts of Iron series since Hearts of Iron 2, including HoI 3 with BICE.
Hearts of Iron 4 does some things right, some things wrong. It is the easiest of all games in the series to get into even if you only play casually.
Some of the mechanics of the previous titles have been dropped, some overhauled and a few new features added.
The new production system is better than before, requiring you to actually produce equipment and not some abstract form of industrial output.
The new division designer allows a new awesome degree of freedom when it comes to creating and adapting your army, giving you a large amount of possibilites.
The supply system is...interesting. It has its up- and downsides.
The diplomatic side of the game is quite lackluster with only a small amount of interaction between countries
The political stuff boils down to a cabinet of ministers that give different bonuses, three laws with multiple levels each, and national foci. These foci are a double-edged sword. On the one hand they allow for giving the player directions and possibilites to take their country on different paths, on the other hand they can also railroad both the AI and the player into adapting a certain stance.
Speaking of AI, this is probably the most debated and criticized feature of HoI 4. The AI was in a rough state when the game released last year but it is improving with each patch.
The last part I want to touch is the military. While the ground war with the new battle planner feature can be either very good or bad, depending on your luck with the AI if you use the planner, it is still quite similar to previous titles.
The airforce was somewhat broken in the beginning but is like the AI improving from patch to patch.
The navy on the other hand is really broken with e.g. submarines taking weeks to chase down a single transport ship.
In total I can recommend the game. Altough I should point out that I do not consider the game perfect right now, I still look forward to the things to come in future free patches and paid DLC.

Now let me start off by saying "this is not just a silly dating sim". Well I guess it is but their's so much more to it than just dating birds.
Story: Surprisingly the game has a well crafted story with great writing and multiple endings depending on which bird you romance. All the characters feel unique with there own personalities, interests, and quirks. The story itself will branch out into different paths, that are amazing and heartfelt. It also helps that Hatoful Boyfriend is very replayable.
Gameplay: Just like any visual novel, the gameplay boils down to reading text boxes and occasionally making a decision. Which isn't a bad thing as long as your prepared for it and know what you're getting into.
Presentation: The game has a very cute art style that goes for more cartoonish than realistic and the fact that the character models are cut out from actual pictures of birds is a nice touch. Unfortunately a lot of areas get reused do to the setting of the game.
Verdict: Hatoful Boyfriend is a charming game with some slight problems that fortunately aren't that bad or game breaking. So in conclusion Hatoful Boyfriend gets a 9/10. It is a must buy. It has great quality for a ten dollar game.

This is pretty much the 3D version of Doom (Well, before Doom 3 came out) so if you liked that game, you're gonna love this one. Let me tell you why:
The Pros:
-It has great variety in its weapons, enemies and levels
-The graphics (For its time) are great
-The sound effects are awesome
-The controls are smooth
-The game can be REALLY challenging (Especially if you play on the Hard or Nightmare modes)
-The enemies are, also, challenging (Again, if you play on the higher difficulties)
-There's alot of secrets you can find in the game (Much like Doom 1 & 2 did)
The Cons:
-There's no music for the Steam version (Thankfully, you can get a source port called Darkplaces which adds the music back in)
-The game is really short if you play on the lower difficulties (Easy & Normal)
-No proper final boss fight like its successor, Quake 2, did
All in all, this is a game I recommend. If Wolfenstein & Doom popularised the FPS Shooter genre, Quake would be its continuation.

This game is simply an amazing masterpiece from 1996. It was made by the same people that created Doom, and everything about it is fantastic. The levels have really nice texturing and are fun to wander through, the enemies are fearsome, deadly, and fit well in the levels, the weapons all feel really good to use, and the powerups you can find scattered throughout the levels can really help you if you use them well, making finding secret areas very rewarding. The sound effects are appealing to listen to, and they help you get more immersed into the game. The music (if you're able to get it working), done by Trent Reznor of Nine Inch Nails, gives the levels more of a creepy and intense atmosphere, and it keeps you on your toes as you round the next corner, getting ready to fight a fiend who is ready to leap out at you. The multiplayer is lots of fun! There's nothing more intense than running and jumping around at high speeds, blasting (and getting blasted by) your friends with a rocket launcher with twitch-like reflexes.
This game is still a classic first person shooter game that will always be a blast to play, and you can occasionally find yourself coming back to it (usually out of nostalgia). Highly recommended.

This game is both a modern take on the Thief franchise and also a bit of a love letter to Looking Glass Studios.  Not only does it craft a touching homage, but it also stands on its own as an excellent game that not only tells an engaging story, but consistently respects the player by offering an environment that they can take command of.
The campaign is very fluid, but consists of individual missions that can be replayed independently after each completion.  You are free to progress to your goal in many different ways and the mechanics and level design expertly offer you opportunity to make varied choices about whether you'd like to be a complete ghost, silent assassin, violent slaughterer or any combination in between.
It has been a long time since a first person shooter has afforded so much respect to the player and Arkane should be praised for that.
Aside from the massive replayability this game has, it also has wonderful DLC.  If you are tired of microtransactions and cheap base games that feel torn apart in order to ask more money from you, this is an excellent remedy.  I can't praise this game enough.
It also has excellent controls and options, whether you're using mouse / keyboard, a traditional controller or the steam controller.  My favorite tool is actually the steam controller with this game and its sequel.

But I grinded to progress my chracter so I can eventually get the ball moving, start building a haitat, barracks, outside chem station and even the 3D printer. Then I decided to take a break a couple hours and then BAM! Progress of my character is gone! I logged back on a couple hours after my break and my avatar just vanished. I was playing a multiplayer private universe with a friend, and his avater too dissappeared. So all the item we crafted and shared can no longer be accessable unless we were part of the same colony, but to gain access to old containers/depositories, the old characters had to invite us to the colony. So I thought, fine start a new character with a new universe, but I can't delete the old universe I had so my new character is stuck with the old universe with the old stuff I have already built from an avatar that no longer exists.
Great game, great concept, but I'm not going to recomend this game until the DEVs fix the major problems:
dissappearing avaters
unable to create/delete universes
progression of chracter building is too slow
crafting is VERY limited (until you learn the skill which is done with the progression of your character)
some worthless skills (learned how to make pistol ammo, but the forge to create pistol ammo is still a locked skill)
classes' uniqueness for your avatar seems pointless (why be an engineer when a ranger can eventually learn the same thing)
Fighting AI is annoying (NPC mobs can phase through you and hit you, making it difficult for you to even land a hit, especially when a melee weapon has to be swung within 1 meter for a hit)
I understand this is a game in alpha, but I would not recomend the game until the game has an overhaul fix

I just watched Interstellar and The Martian when the Steam Summer Sale started and then I came across this game. I'm a huge fan of Survival/Crafting/Exploration games and 7 Days to Die is my favorite game in the genre, even though it isn't perfect and has ways to go.
This game seemed like a "7 Days to Die in Space" theme to me and though there's more emphasis on technology and interplanetary travel as it's current end-goal, the latest 2GB patch ramped up the difficulty by taking away things that originally made the game way too easy. A lot of more casual-ish players are having trouble as there is no solid tutorial on what to do in certain situations. It's basically like they let you into a playground and just threw you into the deep end.
That said, this game is extremely early in development and it feels like it can improve a lot over time, which is why I have faith in it. I've been in several triple-A big-budget beta's and alphas(some with NDA's) where there were many game-breaking bugs, so the bugs in this game(there's nothing game-breaking right now that hasn't been hotfixed) while a bit frustrating, are going to happen in an Early Access game. Not making excuses, but I understand this isn't the final product and the developers seem to be quick to fix anything they break.
Final Verdict for my first 20 hours:
Pros:
+ It's got the Survival/Crafting/Exploration part down. I love to just go out and explore.
+ Skill tree is vast and has many options.
+ Graphics. It's a beautiful game.
+ Many updates, which add new features.
Cons:
- Crafting, part of the "Holy Trinity" of this genre, could use some work. Not enough craftables, IMO!
- Difficulty. It's very punishing. I hesitate to call it the "D*rk S*uls" of the genre, but... YOU WILL DIE!
- Lack of a fleshed-out tutorial might have you completely lost/confused.
- Many updates, which wipe your gamesaves/progress.
Huh?!
~ Either bugs, or exploits that let you gather sap/gasses infinitely, for maximum skill leveling.
~ Random inventory every new game, so you might never get a pick-axe or guns?! (you can craft weapons/tools)
~ You'll poop your pants when you see the giant worm. I did, too shocked to move. Died.
If you like your games complete, Early Access might not be the best choice, but this is one to keep an eye on. It's got a lot of promise and should be great if you enjoy the genre. If you're still unsure, get it on sale(currently $15).

Full disclosure: Adriaan is a friend of mine whom I have a large amount of respect and admiration for. So if you think that disqualifies me from reviewing his games without bias ... You may very well be right I still liked it.
Hidden folks is a game within the I spy or where's Waldo hidden object game family. You are given a series of objects and clues of where to find them on a small or large monochrome map with cute characters running around and distracting you. Some of the objects (if not most) will require you to solve a small puzzle such as opening a chest or finding a secret passage before you are able to find what you are looking for.
So another bias I have is that I love hidden object games, so I was going to like this game as long as it wasn't a broken mess. Fortunately it is a very well done, cute, and funny little game. The difficulty curve is controlled by small tutorial levels that introduce you to the mechanics and allowing the player to finish the next level with only a handful of the objects. It's also incredibly adorable, all of the sound effects are done by a person making silly sounding noises and it's wonderful. The art and animation are some of the cutest things you will see in games.
So overall it is a lovely little game that is fun just to look for little things, and repeatedly click the alligator and hear that roar.

As a long time XCOM fan, I was uncertain about the direction of The Bureau.  Here was a series that I loved with strong tactical strategy roots that had influenced the genre for nearly two decades... and it's newest release was going to be a third-person shooter.  I assumed that the game was a way to use the XCOM name to cash in on yet another Call of Duty clone.  Fast forward a couple of years and I realized that I was wrong.
The XCOM 2 announcement got me hyped up on the series once again and I decided that instead of playing through another war in XCOM: Enemy Within (which would've been a blast, even if it were my billionth war) I would try something new and actually give The Bureau a go.  It was a good decision.
The story in the game is enjoyable, though it gets a little weird and unexpectedly complicated toward the end.  Base building doesn't make an appearance in this game, however, there is an XCOM base where you spend your time in between missions and it is quite well done.  Different scenes play out as you wander through the base depending on events that you've experienced and choices that you've made.  For example, after defeating each new enemy type that you run across you can often see them being studied (in one way ot another) in your laboratory.
Combat, the meat and potatoes of this game, is significantly more fun than I had been assuming.  You issue commands to your squad mates (who come in Recon, Engineer, Support, and Soldier varieties) which include utilizing the abilities that they possess.  These squaddies level up and gain new abilities on a skill tree exclusive to each class that is reminiscent of XCOM: Enemy Unknown.  Two agents of the same class could use their abilities in different ways.
The feel of the combat itself reminds me of Mass Effect 2.  The cover system, the use of alien abilities (some which are very similar to biotics), and even the large variety of weapons to choose from in the game and their varying strengths and weaknesses.  However, it can not be overstated that the AI in this game is less than amazing.  You'll find yourself micromanaging your agents often as they can't seem to utilize themselves to be anywhere near as efficient as when you hold them by the hand and tell them what to do.  On a few occassions, I watched in horror as one of my agents moved away from an enemy grenade, only to realize that the best cover was were that grenade was and return to it to his imminent death.
All in all, this is a good game with plenty to offer that I recommend to XCOM fans and shooter/RPG fans alike.  As long as you can get past the AI it is a solid game with around a couple of dozen hours of content if you're playing on a difficulty level that challenges you.

Although it doesn’t truly innovate the genre or raise it to new and exciting heights, How To Survive 2 does offer great co-operative fun with friends, online or locally with up to four players able to jump in. The addition of camps and structure building introduces a brand new dimension to the survival series, and a fresh bounty of craftable items will no doubt keep survivors entertained for hours. In 2013 How To Survive gave players the chance to survive a zombie apocolypse, its successor expands on that sadly without ever really bringing something new to the genre. With a great soundtrack and nervewrecking locale, How To Survive 2 is worth the asking price, but with a lack of innovation, never really fufills its potential.
Pros
+F U N
+Great environments
+Rich crafting
+Introduction of structures
+4 player co-op
Cons

-Very limited combat
-Lack of story
-Doesn't innovate the genre
-Cursor controls when navigating items can be frustrating

Do NOT buy this game if you enjoyed the first one (do not buy the 3rd person version of the first one either, unless you plan on playing with controller only, since ingame mouse is not working and doesn't even show up at all for many players..).
This game is barely story driven, unlike the first one. They've just slapped overly complicated and boring crafting and leveling system to a game that really does not need it. The system they had in first game, was perfectly fine for a game like this. Simplistic survival crafting to spice up the nice storyline and give interesting game mechanics, especially on kovac's way difficulty.
H2S felt like a fleshed out real game, whereas H2S2 feels like a proof of concept moneygrab from incompetent devs that can't even make ingame video options menu.
PROS
+Uninstall via steam
CONS
-Walls, rooms, jails and whatever else don't hold zombies in. They might be trapped when you first run past them, but when you come back, zombies are standing somewhere else, not trapped anymore.
-Really bland gameplay with no real free roam. You just teleport to different quest locations for 100 hours and do exactly the same thing over and over. This feels like vanilla WoW durotar quest nightmare. Kill 100 of this, 20 of that, gather 8 different things and kill 100 more of these. Repetition, repetition, repetition.
-You feel underpowered all the time, no new weapon atleast till lv20 will make that change. Your best bet is to buy the dlc that gives you assault rifle as a starter weapon and drone pet to lower aiming time. Then you're stuck grinding the bullet material quest every 2-3 quests to give a nice forced break from advancing.
-NPC babysitting quests. Who thought this would be a good idea? The AI is so bad that not only do the zombies get stuck on everything, but so does your mentally handicapped NPC you're trying to protect, so you have to juke him out of corners constantly. Also the NPC's take damage from your weapons and run in the middle of zombies and you kill them while trying to hit the zombies, or the zombies get them. Of course you can give them commands to stop and continue following, but that doesn't really help, since there will be some new zombies on the way to ruin your day when you've gone back to pick up the NPC of unfortune, and you end up shooting through them (zombies) with your bow and hitting and killing the NPC anyway.
Your best bet is to clear the whole map with NPC waiting at start, go back to get 'em and then some zombie you missed or that just spawned will hit the NPC anyway, you will hit the NPC anyway and then you alt+f4 anyway.
-Aiming. I played the first game for 50 hours and loved it, and I don't remember having much problem with crosshair sticking to a selected zombie for critical hit. On H2S2, they've managed to ♥♥♥♥ that up too. You take your time, wait for the crosshair to turn red and fire. "What, white damage, why?" you will ask yourself. Well, just as you fired, the zombie might have twitched or went over a slight bump on the ground or just because your mouse went 0.0001 inch too far from the specific zombie, you lost your target and still hit it, but with non-crit. This becomes extremely frustrating when there's  20 zombies on screen, 8 of them running at different speeds and you're trying to hit the fastest ones. Constantly taking damage and dishing out only white hits yourself, since the crosshair doesn't stick, or sticks very inconsistently.
-Special enemies. They've tried to CPR some life into this empty torso of a game with♥♥♥♥♥♥tons of different special enemies on top of zombies with varying movement speed. Annoying turtles that only take damage from penetrating arrows or explosives, I assume, pelicans that puke but are no real hazard whatsoever, the big fatties I would call boomers because I don't remember what they're called in this game... Those ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s on the first game were really dangerous with their high damage, high radius explosion. On the second implement of How to Survive, however, they're nerfed so much as to be less of minor annoyance than the normal zombies. If boomer has 3 zombies right next to it and you kill it, making it go boom, you're in luck if even 1 of the zombies will die of it, that's how much they've reduced the explosion range and damage of those things.
Then there's zombie deer which don't attack normal zombies anymore, zombie armadillo looking rats, pigs, bears, bunnies, dogs.. Wouldn't be surprised if there was some zoo level with zombie elephants and giraffes, so many zombified animals are around.
From all of these animals, the rabbit is propably the most dangerous of the bunch. Has surprisingly high hp, speed and damage (homage to Monty Python?).
-Camera. Every time you enter a building or go near enough to the edge of one, your camera will be zoomed all the way in, which is bloody annoying, so you're constantly smashing V to change the zoom level.
-Looting. So many locked rooms and drawers to lockpick open, only to find nothing. This game is really holding the loot back, atleast in the beginning, only getting slightly better when you reach level 20 and get to the better quests.
-Graphics. Compared to the first game, which had great colours and looks, this game looks really washed out, dark and bland. I guess they tried to aim for slightly more realistic look, but failed at that.
-Multi-player. Checked out the open camp servers a few times, and never saw anyone playing besides me. Only empty camps, hundreds of them. That propably tells something about this game.
EDIT:
-No pause feature at all. Have to take a toilet break in the middle of some stupid 30min NPC babysitting quest? Better be fast and hope you're not dead when you get back.
Second edit:
-Melee sucks. In the first game, it worked. On this one, you usually hit through zombies while they are in some animation, and then they hit you 3 times in a row while you are in animations. You also get knocked down repeatedly by the deer and some other mobs, sometimes so many times in a row you can't get up before you're dead.
/EDIT
Might have forgotten something, since I have so much bad things to say about this tech demo the devs never bothered finishing.
Last words: Maybe buy it from sale if it goes up to -90+% if you want to do chores for 20 hours before getting cancer, PTSD and burnout.

Pros
-Getting gear, levelling up, and achieving high MK status (character level, not account level) feels very rewarding)
-Game is almost impossible solo, teamwork is very prevalent
-Very unique classes with high skill cap
-Very satisfying to blast through hordes of aliens
-Premium currency only buys you more stashes (to store extra gear), no pay to win.
Cons
-Only account level (which unlocks new shells/characters) is permanent
-Easy to feel like your progress is pointless
-Cannot switch shells without dying
-Once you unlock all shells, difficult to feel like progression is worth it
-No more updates in the future from what I understand
This game is addicting. I constantly find myself saying "just one more" at 3:00am just like Civilization. Play it. Enjoy it. Accept that its difficulty and permadeath will frustrate you but make you feel like gear/levels are SO rewarding.

I was on board with this game, in spite of the difficulty cliff and the community, until this afternoon.
A patch was just pushed out that dramatically changes the way you can power your colony. The game is in early access, so such a change can be expected, but my issue isn't really with the mechanic change. It's with how it was communicated to the players; i.e., it wasn't.
There was no warning that this change was coming. No news, no community posts, no tweets, nothing. Combine that with the fact that there is a mandatory ironman style save system means a lot of people are about to load up their games and lose all progress on their games, and that's a bad move.
12/29 Update: I will say that the community revolted and the change was rolled back, but I'm still recommending against this game because of it. Other games handle discussion and feedback better, but after being burned I still wouldn't support this game for now.

Edit-
So, someone decided to imply that I'm a butt hurt returnee to the game that just hated the changes so I took the time to add my detailed critique.
Here it is:
Pros-
* It's a beautiful game with a gorgeous world. The sky looks amazing and the fact that stuff falls out of the sky is just fantastic.
* The skill trees and classes are interesting although shallow. It makes choosing a class kinda worthwhile in the beginning but without any real perks besides having a small boost in skill points in one area, it's really a pretty small "pro." I recommend adding specific skills or tech that can only be built by that class. It adds some kind of diversity and makes it worthwhile to have multiple avatars/people to play with.
* The combat ANIMATIONS look interesting. A little out of place but interesting.
Cons-
* The first few hours don't offer a lot of new player support. Yeah, I got the hang of things after a while but without a tutorial or help tips... it's a really punishing experience. Also... why make parts of the debris salvageable but not the rest? That's a bit puzzling and I think that, to avoid confusion, the devs should make that entirely salvageable or not at all. Why frustrate your players by wasting their chisels on something that will likely not yield any resources? I like difficult games like Dark Souls, the Surge (which is infamous for having horrendously painful mobs like this game!) and Bloodborne but.... This? This is just not fun.
* Degrading equipment is my next point. Does ANYONE like this in a game? If that happened to me in the Forest, I'd be ok but...the fact that I had to make a ton of stuff with rocks and also had to use rocks to mine stuff just feels like a superficial way of adding time to buffer that one point that you mentioned about getting to the best stuff in two hours. To fix this, I recommend allowing players to use some kind of repair material to repair the items. I mean, you have a multipurpose tool meant to repair structures in your inventory. You can't use that to repair your stone axe? ... Really?
* Rocks.... for all of the things that it makes, it's one of the most inconvenient things to collect. You can only collect ONE at a time and the collection action is SO AWKWARD in this game. Why is there a small pause? It takes me forever to collect rocks and berries and it's just an awful experience.
* Lack of immersion - I'd like to start with something small and then work my way up for this topic. First things first, I heard that in a recent patch all the resources got shifted further away from each other. Is that why rocks are sometimes five - eight minutes away from minerals? That makes no sense? How come I can mine metal from the earth but not a rock in the same area? Hell, I get rocks or dirt whenever I dig anything in every other game whether I want it or not so... what? You can't seriously expect me to believe there isn't a SINGLE rock in a 500 meter radius in an area rich in precious metal deposits? Also... speaking of precious materials, why the hell does a stone oven require plutonium? Like... that makes zero sense. What kind of technology can you put into ... a stone oven that the aztecs possibly used? And lastly, speaking of technology... I paid for a sci-fi experience and I got stone age tech for hours. What? Also, the tech that I built didn't have any interactions that made me feel like I was in space. In Subnautica, you can see a 3d printer create your materials which is super awesome! Here, I click on the stone oven and wait til the little timer tells me that the iron ingot is done. Yay.... Instead of the devs forcing you to go to the stone age to halt your "end game"... why don't they focus on getting more futuristic? I'd love to see things like bigger ships and bigger monsters to fight those ships. Add creatures that hover in the sky that truly make the world feel alien and alive and lightning storms for us to worry about flying our ships in. Or hey, why not add an alien race that has different tech to populate the world and you have to shoot them down in those fancy planes? Eh? Eh?
There were other things that made me feel like I didn't enjoy this game but these were the major ones.
Overall, I would give this game a 5/10 because it got all of the looks right. It looks fantastic, sounds fantastic and on a shallow level, feel fantastic. But on the inside, it's like a chore to slog through.

Osiris is an ambitious attempt to create an interplanetary space survival sim... Which is AWESOME!
I have put around 70 hours into the game, and have been playing more and more with each update since it was in steam greenlight.  That said, this game has SERIOUS potential.  Please remember that Alpha is very much a conceptualization phase more than a playability phase.  If you require instant gratification, and expect progression to fall into your lap, you should probably wait for the beta release.
Osiris is full of amazing space encounters, pretty much everything you see in the movies and then some.  It has a very starship troopers meets the martian feel to it.  There are definitely things the devs have gotten right, and then wrong, and back to right again.  Of course there are pro's and cons, but again, everything is subject to change in time.
The most important thing to keep in mind when purchasing this game, is that the development team is small, and does an AMAZING job at reading everyone's feedback. They work extremely hard to implement community suggestions that are worthy of attention.  However, it does take some time for them to tweak the mechanics to get the feel just right.  I do applaud their efforts to push out emergency patches whenever they break things with the updates. Speaking of updates, they come pretty regularly about every 2-3 weeks.
Lets get to the pros and cons
PROS:
Awesome immersion
Amazing graphics
Tons of exploration and dramatic encounters with indigenous life
Alien swarms
Giant Dune style sand worms
You can build a base on an alien planet, in orbit, and on other planets
Crafting is based on real elemental chemistry so its kinda educational
No hand holding, you have to figure things out and think strategically
Great way to hang out with friends, plus helps get things done faster
Ancient ruins and landmarks, very mysterious!
Boss fights
Alien AI isnt super impressive, but its good enough to present a challenge and keep them annoying enough to stay wary of...
Vehicles are really fun to explore in, wish they were more viable in game, or at least available in early game during the big resource push
Cons
Lost the outlander faction
Picking stuff up takes a long time
Tech Tree needs adjusting
Missing technology (i know i know its alpha)
The world has vast spaces of nothingness
Resources are oddly distributed around map
Only one location to get rubber
Melee combat looks awesome, but hard to find alien hitboxes
Harvesting almost always alerts aliens watch your back!
Lighting in the mines is really bad (even after you turn them on), and the light generated by path lights and lamps is miniscule
Item decay... I get it, but holy crap please tune it down, this is the #1 hinderance to progression.  Once you lose your starter hammer, and other tools, you are pretty much stuck to using rocks until you unlock the tech to make a new hammer, and its WAY down the tech tree.
I also died of thirst about 7 times before my group had the resources and tech to make a water collector.
Resources on minimap arent distinguishable
Space ships like to get stuck on asteroids
The good news is all the cons I listed can be fixed.  Some of them are probably already being fixed.
What I look forward to most about Osiris, is multiplayer pvp.   The environment is hostile, and there is plenty of AI to present challenging obstacles in a pvp environment.  I know they are reworking plans for the outlander faction and I hope they are amazing.  The idea of the UNE and Outlanders having to be co-dependent while simultaneously at war with each other on a hostile world presents a very unique aspect to survival games.
I say give this game a shot, and if you dont like it, just wait a few months and see if you still feel the same way.

I picked this game up with a friend in the hopes that it would itch our craving for a fun, co-op / MMO "space game" but unfortunately the game is mostly an unforgiving mess. Where I felt fatigue in the ambiguity in ARK Survival Evolved's lack of story or main missions, I also began to feel here as well. With little to no direction beyond "build a base and hope to stay alive" which is inherent to some of the survival genre, but there's so little here to do and the environments become extremely repetitive early on that I don't have much compelling me to play again anytime soon. If you're into building an ever larger, somewhat generic-looking base of operations, and don't mind a lot of time spent farming / harvesting / grinding, this game may be for you.
Add to that fact that enemies often glitch out and get stuck in the terrain, as they do this sort of bobbing jig before you happen to waltz up and attack them and jar them loose from being stuck in the ground, only for them to then begin attacking you relentlessly and things quickly become comical in a "broken" kind of way. The game does have some impressive-looking effects, including giant sandworms jumping through the environment (the first time I saw this, in the middle of a sandstorm was a genuinely terrifying experience) rainfall, sandstorms, and the most standout effect for me being the loud meteorites streaking across the sky before slamming into the terrain next to you, and it has its immersive moments.
It's not an ugly game by any means, but it also isn't very polished, from the enemies glitching out to your character seeming to tilt their head / arms beyond the threshold of normal human articulation (your character does a bit of an Exorcist head/neck esque spin when aiming behind you in 3rd person mode.) the game's lighting effects are well done, and the option of first or third person view is a nice addition.
At its best the game embodies some distant echoes of Starship Troopers or Lost Planet series "man versus space bug" situations (i.e. creeping around a dark, dank nest of enemies..) but the combat in the game is so piddly and inaccurate feeling that none of the weapons you acquire pack much whallop during these exchanges and you're often reduced to flailing around trying to hit an enemy with melee or clumsily aim your weak guns at them.
There are many skilltree items, utilities, and construction options available to the player, including storage, shelter, floodlights, etc... You gather more materials to build a larger base and hope you aren't swarmed by random enemies (ala ARK). You can explore the environment, including some mining esque 'dungeons' but then there seemingly is very seldom ever any standout loot worthwhile within those mostly empty environments as well. It's an incredibly "empty" feeling game and should probably be free to play or much less than its asking price of 24.99 once you see how little is actually here beyond its at times impressive visuals.
I was pretty letdown from my expectations to what is seemingly actually here, but a large portion of that might be that I am still a "noob" overall to the game, and don't have the resources for the cooler stuff in the game. The better gear and buildings you can get aside, the gameplay itself still feels rather clunky at times, with the combat being one area of that game that seems to suffer the most.
I have enjoyed moments of Osiris but can't suggest other people spend money on it as-is in Early Access. I wonder if a free to play model would have served the game better... Until the the game has more of a solidified identity for the game's pacing and presentation, I would suggest waiting until this game is discounted heavily if you are still interested.
