Circuit Dude is a pretty challenging puzzle game, and although it got me frustrated at times, I still continue coming back to it to have fun with the solutions! As of the time of this review, I only have 4 levels left in the whole game, but they are keeping me stuck for a little while.
The graphics, music, and sound effects are all pretty simple for Circuit Dude, and do not drastically change. In fact, the game really seems to have one main song that plays on loop forever, and a handful of sound effects with certain objects. The graphics are a simple 2D style that I can't quite describe. Parts of it feel pixel-like, while other parts of it feel pretty clean.
Similarly, although there seems to be a hidden story in the game, not much is really happening for the first half of the game (or even more). Most of the time it is just jumping into a level and the character describing something or making a general comment. The further into the game, some other things occur, but it's not like a steady flow of a plotline by any means.
The main purpose of this game is, quite directly, the puzzles. Each level is a grid where you run across tiles and must place circuit chips into a bunch of sockets, then make your way to the exit. The first problem is that when you place a chip into a socket, you cannot walk across that tile anymore. Thus, you can cut yourself off from a pathway by placing down chips in the wrong order.
The puzzles grow from here by adding many obstacles along the way. There are trap doors that open up into holes when you walk over them. There are boxes you need to push around, either to get out of the way or to help create a path. There are electric shock tiles that destroy you unless they are disabled. There are even conveyor belts, rotating pathways, teleporters, and a few other pieces.
Many of those obstacles can even be interdependent inside of a level, meaning that you have to find your way through one path before you get through another path, or might have to run through different paths multiple times. But that is not always the case, as some levels allow a handful of ways to make your own way out.
Because of the layout of the levels in the game, you really need to test your guesses over and over until you can start to plan things out and get used to the ways the obstacles interact.
Even though Circuit Dude can be pretty difficult, I felt a sense of accomplishment the whole time that I have played, feeling like "I finally got through this level!" I might have taken a few breaks here and there, but I never stopped playing it fully, and am intending to finish the levels that I have remaining.
If you are interested in how these puzzles sound, you should definitely give the game a try.

The Bureau has had a troubled history. It spent a long time in development hell, changing studios and the game’s design multiple times. Though its 1960s aesthetic was the only thing that stayed consistent during this process. It was originally titled “XCOM”, a first person shooter with some tactical play. It was originally intended to be the focal point of the series’ reboot. The reboot of a beloved turn-based strategy game with mechanics that had become legendary by this point and time. (Yeah, it doesn’t take a genius to see where 2K might have gone wrong). The response to “XCOM” was severe dislike, leading to the game to be pushed back into the shadows of the public eye. Instead, XCOM: Enemy Unknown was released by a different development team and became really successful. Potentially leading the series to a new and bright future. The FPS “XCOM” wasn’t anywhere to be seen and there was much rejoicing. A year later, The Bureau: XCOM Declassified stepped from the shadows. In all of it’s glorious 1962 aesthetic, 3rd person tactical squad based action. It largely got mixed or negative reception. So, the question becomes: did The Bureau justify that reception? Well, let’s find out.
There’s no turn-based strategy here. There is a tactical commander’s view that let’s you order your squadmates where to go, when to use abilities and on which alien/enemy targets. A large chunk of your game time will be spent going from combat spot to combat spot. As a whole, the combat is simply ok and it works. It has its satisfying moments now and again but it’s not the most exciting. Especially if you’ve played games in this genre before. However, one thing that I did like were some of combos you could make with different classes. Though I felt like they barely scratched the surface with class synergy and I’d like to see more useful combos in the future. Oh, I didn’t mention this but there are four classes in the game. Commandos (your bruisers), Engineers (deploy turrets and mines), Recon (Snipers) and Supports (medics). Each class has their own distinctive abilities and weapons. The weapons are reasonably weighty with a good amount of impact and firepower to make them all enjoyable to use. The cover system is a bit sticky and unwieldy at times. Far too often, I’d find myself trapped in a spot with no good way out. Or my agents would often find themselves in similar situations.
If there is one thing I can say about The Bureau, it’s a story of conveniences. Somehow I’m supposed to believe that an alien invasion of this size would be kept secret from the public. The only reason I can buy this is that it’s the 1960s and communication was severely hampered. That somehow, I’m supposed to believe that an alien we captured becomes our ally in a quick heartbeat. Somehow, I’m supposed to believe that we can capture alien weapons and items with the “Venn Brace”. Which I can only assume is a magical tool we carry on our arms. (Where did that Venn Brace come from again?). A lot of this is either swept under the rug or just goes by you so quickly I think they’re hoping you won’t notice because SHINY.
I didn’t play the DLC and from what I can see, they don’t seem worth paying or plaything them. One is a gun pack, the other two are short uninspiring missions. I can’t help but feel like these were possibly cut from the final product to be sold as DLC. I didn't feel any particular compulsion to pick these up.
The Bureau has a lot of graphical settings. There’s a reasonable amount of screen resolutions to choose from. Windowed mode, v-sync and film grain that can be turned off and on. It also supports up to 120FPS if you’re wanting that. Field-of-view is supported from 65-100 degrees. Any larger changes have to be made in a .ini file. PhysX is featured in the particles & clothing and can be disabled. You’ve got texture, world, shadow and effect detail sliders as well as anti-aliasing, anisotropic filtering, decal persistence, ambient occlusion and screen space reflection sliders. For the most part it’s a pretty decently optimized game. Though I did have several areas of combat situations where the framerate dropped pretty hard. A DX11 mode also exists that makes the game look somewhat better. However, it’s an incredibly costly mode for not a lot of gain which I couldn’t get it to run at a stable framerate.
It’s a good thing that 2K didn’t lead their reboot of the XCOM series with The Bureau: XCOM Declassified. Not to knock too harshly on the developers, but this would have killed the franchise dead. Now? I actually kinda want a sequel to this.
. I think they have a good foundation started, but could use some more work to flesh everything out.
As for XCOM Declassified currently, well, it’s just not that bad. It’s got a pretty good story and a decent enough combat system. It does try to be XCOM though it does lack many of the features of XCOM. There’s no research, no base(s) management, you can only command two other squadmates, it’s got less customization and less of the XCOM experience than it should. But for a 1960s take on the XCOM universe from a different perspective, I still kinda like it. It’s got a story with some pretty unique twists and turns, a pretty diverse cast of characters and seventeen hours of enjoyment.

This is the kind of game you either love or hate. Toribash is a game about patience, waiting, and strategy. It may feel impossible for beginners but I asure you, it rewards the time and effort put into it. When familiarized with the mechanics, you encounter intense battles, some that may be remembered forever. Toribash also offer a wide variety of mods: You can either fight the classic way (Judo, Aikido, Wushu, etc.) do awesome and cool stuff (sparring, parkour, skating, etc.) or lose time with friends with some other light mods (football, cars, giants, etc.). You can also customize your character and it is possible to win ingame currency fast, if you know your ways. There is an ingame community that will pay some good ToriCredits for you made texture or your items. You can also bet in fights or duel, whoever wins get the $$$.
However, Toribash lacks an indeep tutorial to familiarize newcomers with the game. You can do the actual tutorial, but you'll be lucky if you can win your first (Or even hit your opponent) in your online arrival. It is almost imposible to begin without stopping to check guides all over the internet to actually do something. The interface is a little to simplistic and can get you confused when you first enter. It lacks a friend system, even a way to know when someone is online and the physics may get a little too weird from time to time.
Some other aspects of the game includes a Clan system, you can do your own and if it's good, it can become and official clan (Serious stuff). The gamemaster are constantly doing tournaments and events, you'll be noticed in the forums or via a global message in the ingame chat.
Staying short: Toribash is a game you will love or hate if you are ready to spend some good hours on it or if you are reluctant to do so.

This game is definitely NOT a finished version and still needs a lot of work. Apart from tons of bugs ranging from annoying to absolutely game breaking, the rest of the game simply is pretty mediocre.
The core idea is rather interesting and I was pretty excited to play it. Each crew member is a character with his own set of stats and the possibility to teach him new skills for combat or ship duty. Crews can get quite large and it is vital to ensure that certain roles are present on your ship. The ship itself is built block by block and can also be upgraded with several special modules that enhance its sailing speed, allow to store food or raise the number of hull points.
How this idea is implemented, though, is pretty disappointing. Controlling your crew is pretty tedious in most situations and doesn't work at all in some. This has nothing to do with mutinying crew members, the user interface, or the artificial intelligence respectively, just stops working. Battles suffer greatly from the inability to control single crew members. You either watch in fear, as your pirates just run around aimlessly far behind enemy lines or simply lose some of them because they retreat far too late. Ordering their whole group back to the ship also doesn't work properly many times. There are many other examples of these issues, like the captain ALWAYS stopping in a tavern when one is on the way to the shop you wanted to send him to.
Managing your crew and building the ship is either way too complicated or simply bugged. When you try to modify your ship when standing in front of a shop owner, the interface completely bugs out. Also, so far there are only 2 different weapons you can install on your ship. Equipping items and teaching skills to your pirates, too, is absolutely convoluted. This is mostly due to the fact that there is no overview for all the items you have. Instead you have to select a crew member, click on its passive, melee or ranged item slot and then select an item from a menu. This also applies to using consumables like skill books.
In summary, I would not recommend this game at all. If you see it at a heavy discount, like I did, MAYBE you can squeeze some hours of fun out of it. I paid 5€ and will probably play it for another hour or two, just to see everything it has to offer, but I doubt it will make up for all the poor design decisions and bugs this game contains.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

I was hopeful going into this, and this game does have a lot going for it, but as it stands this game isn't finished. The AI makes some bewildering decisions (Germany will declare war on everyone before it's ready for it, AI troops will completly ignore countries at war with them and rush towards you, and the frontline troops will attack when they have almost no moral), the pathfinding needs some reworking. A few game mechanics are kinda broken (trade system) and a few things that should be in the base game are not and some are hidden behind dlc. And that brings me to the two main non music/skin dlc
Together for victory: new national trees and events (pretty basic, any decent modder could do this) alternate historical paths for dominions, new autonomy systems(I feel like these shouldn't  be locked behind a paywall)  changes to lend lease, a spearhead battle plan, and technology sharing (these should absoloutly be in the base game, and it's cheap to hide them in dlc).
Death or Dishonor: new focus trees (same as last time) equipment conversion, new diplomatic interactions, new puppet interactions (these should all be in the base game) new music and art (whatever).
In short, the AI needs reworking, base game has some messed up features, and some missing features are locked behind a paywall.
Hands down the best WW2 strategy game out there, has its flaws but the pros definitely outweigh the cons. Modding community is thriving on this game also,

Because of the comment thread on this review, for anyone wondering, here are examples:
Combat:
An enemy charges and hits you, your view gets knocked away up into the sky. The enemy runs away as you try to chase to attack back and you can't catch it. It then charges you again. All enemies act this same way. The only opportunity you have to hit it is when it's charging at you.
Interface:
Freezes every time you look at your other recipie lists.
Crafting:
Involves holding the mouse on the icon of the thing you want to craft and crafting one item at a time, over and over and over. Manually. Making a stack of ingots shouldn't be this tedious.
Building:
Hold the build button to build the structure with more hitpoints, then do the same as you build the 20 exterior panels as well. A redundant, pointless and frustrating mechanic.
Mining:
Whack the rock for a random ore. Every so often you get extra ore which gets thrown at you and rolls down a hill so you have to stop what you're doing and go and chase it and pick it up.
Interaction:
You have to stare at a thing for half a second before you can pick it up or interact. Picking it up then takes another second as the item floats toward you and into your inventory.
Multiplayer:
BUGGY AND BROKEN AS FUQ in almost every way imaginable.
Input:
Camera sway and extra movement to make it feel realistic just make the controls feel heavy and unresponsive. Tuning these settings to achieve a good feel is an exercise in frustration.
Framerate:
My FPS was in the 40-50's and smooth, yet it still somehow *feels* chunky and clunky. Possibly this the fault of the extra camera sway and input filters.
Endgame:
Literally there is nothing to do but kill monsters, mine ore, upgrade your skills and build all the buildings and vehicles. Then go to "space" and mine a bit more ore. Mining ore is the only thing you'll use your spaceship for, and by that time there's nothing left to explore on the planet surface anyway. Space ores don't get you anything else except more vehicles with which to roam and mine more ores. The whole experience is pointless.
In the 2+ hours my friend and I played recently, we managed to construct a stone furnace. That's it. That's all we did in all that time except walk. (And die once or twice - which then required more walking)
There are many more things that are wrong with the core feel and mechanics, these are just some. If you're 14 and think CS:GO is a good game, you might also think this is a good game. If you're an experienced gamer (and/or you actually have real♥♥♥♥♥♥to do in your life), this game is gigantic failure.

Its a great game to play. Personally, It is FAR better to play with friends, and singleplayer is almost just as fun. Build bases and colonies with friends, work together to fend off the dangerous indigenous wildlife with weapons you craft yourself (Pistols, rifles, machetes, swords and ETC.), and even fly around in a ship/drive vehicles that you can make from scratch!
As an early access, it does have some downfalls, like some lag and some glitches. But this game has so much potential, as i had played this game VERY close to its inception of release.
Updates are a tad bit slow, but every major update almost always fixes (At least, in my experience) bugs, glitches, and even adds something surprisingly new on the table.
So do i recommend this game? Yes, I do. But before i end on that note, I feel like i need to give a few tips for new players.
First, I do NOT recommend buying this game immediately. I know, it sounds a bit counter intuitive, especially when I say I recommend this game. I believe you should research the game first, like read up on it through forums, and watch youtube videos to form your own opinion on whether you should buy the game or not. This game isn't for EVERYBODY. And since its early access, please don't expect everything to work outright. Every performance issue currently present is miniscule compared to when it first launched, and since I have played this game quite a bit since the beginning, I believe it has significantly improved since then. You, the reader, might not see it that way, and might not like it. It runs a bit smoothly for me, So i can't say i have much on an issue with its performance. That is my subjective opinion on the matter.
Second, this game is UNFORGIVABLE at times. It WILL be hard when you first start. Please, don't expect this survival game to be a cake walk. You will die, and there WILL be unfair moments when playing. This can be mitigated by altering the server settings, which gives you access to pretty much everything, like how fast resource regeneration takes place (Oxygen and stamina), How fast most resources are used up (like battery drain from flashlight, vehicle fuel consumption and etc.), how populated the planet is with enemies, how much health enemies have/how strong they are when they attack, the difficulty of the survival meters (hydration and nutrition), how much resources you get from resource nodes (base, preciuos and pure nodes like iron, magnesium, gold, lithium and etc.) and even how fast you level up.
Third, if you do decide to pick up this game, Then allow me to help you a bit with getting started. You will NOT have access to water until later on. The more you play, the easier the game gets, but I regress. Water quenches your thirst the best, requiring to drink less of it to bring up your hydration meter. But since you only start out with 2 or 3 containers with water, you only have a limited amount of time before you go thirsty and drink it all. "So what do?" you might ask. The answer? Tree sap. If you equip an empty glass in your hand, you can collect tree sap from the large amber bubbles that grow on Bark trees. Its not as efficient as water, but theres an infinite supply of sap to collect from a single tree. As for food, thats easy. If you raid a creatures dead budy after you kill it, you will get alien meat out of it, of which you can cook by using a kitchen built in your habitat late game, or cook it in the small furnace you can build at the very beginning of the game. If you modified the server to have NO aliens, then you can get nutition by eating the berries mined from berry trees. Not many people knew about this, and downvoted the game because they kept dying of thirst/hunger. Well, I hope this particular tip helps all the new players! Oh, and if you want to eat/drink from your inventory, Right click the food/fluid and choose the option to eat/drink it. Food does not currently spoil. Not yet. So... use that to your advantage!
Fourth, each class (Ranger, engineer, scientist and marine) each have different starting equipment. Other than ranger, each has its own set of skill points that are more focused on a single skill tree. As an example, the engineer. Has more points to spend in the engineering tree, but has fewer points to spend on the other two trees. Same with scientist and marine. The ranger, however, acts as a jack-of-all-trades. It has an equal amount of skillpoints to spend in every tree (about 25 points for all 3 trees at the time of this review). So, if you choose marine, you have more points to spend in the combat tree, but much less in all other trees. Same goes for the other two classes, ranger being the exception as it is "somewhat skilled in all, but master of none." Each class can have all the skills/blueprints unlocked in every tree. Its just how you start (and the way you also look too) depending on which class you start with. No skill is exclusive to one single class. Which means a marine is able to level up his/her engineering skill to build anything the game allows him/her to build. Same with scientist and engineer.
Fifth, MINING RESOURCES. Whats a survival sandbox game without building your own base, right? By default, every class starts out with a chisel, a little hammer that you use to hit nodes with to extrace the resources from. It has limited durability, as with most tools and items, so be careful what you mine! Its slow to mine with the chisel, but fear not, as there is a tool that you can use to mine ore nodes at an EXTREMELY fast pace. This tool is the conduit bender. Where it takes a few hits to extract some unpurified ore using a chisel, a single hit with this glorious two-handed hammer will drain the node significantly faster. 4 or 5 hits should drain it pretty quickly. Its easy to get, as it is one of the first tools that you can unlock. Oh, but didn't i mention that this thing is a large hammer...? Well, not only is it a fantastic tool to use, but it is also a formidable weapon, giving it a damage of 20 (+3 more for critical). Not only that, its actually cheap to make, as opposed to the chisel which requires copper and whatnot to make. This handy tool/weapon can be bade in the plutonium forge using 2 pipes (made from steel plates), some more steel plates, and some rubber. But it can also be made in the outdoor printer, requiring only steel and some rubber. This should definitely be one of the first skills you should unlock. I highly recommend doing so.
Sixth, BEACONS. They are possibly the MOST important tools you should use and make. They use plutonium (can be mined from base metal nodes or from pure plutonium nodes) steel and  glass. I HIGHLY recommend placing the beacons in areas where there are massive resource deposits everywhere. These beacons can be placed just about anywhere, and can be tracked using your portable map (a default item you CANT lose as of right now, even if you die and respawn). Also, when you equip you multi-tool (another indestructable default item) you can even rename your beacon to whatever you want. Like for instance, Built a base but want to return to it without wandering aimlessly trying to fin it? Place a beacon on your base and name it "Base." Found a crater with certain nodes that are uncommon? Drop a beacon and name it to whatever you want.Found the ONLY rubber tree in the game? Drop a beacon and... Well, you get the idea. This is also not to mention that the map also tells you what and where nearby resource nodes are. Blue dots are base metals (Iron, magnesium, alluminum, carbon, and etc.), and red dots are precious metals (Copper, gold, lithium, titanium and etc.).
I truly hope that those who purchase this title enjoys the game as much as I do. So, without further ado, Happy survival!  :-)

TL;DR - If you enjoy simplified city building and tower defense, you should probably make the jump. But you may want to give it a few more content patches otherwise.
There is no game like this on the market.  Its unforgiving, demanding, and I think most importantly scales the zombie apocalypse to its frightful size.  Be prepared to have a multi-hour playthrough lost because of one mistake or distraction. Also be prepared to plan out your expansion and change tactics with the increasing difficulty.  Otherwise the mutants are more than happy to redevelop your town.
The only issues I have with the game are probably on the to-do list; map generation, 4-D build mode, and more advanced unit commands.  Right now it may take three or four restarts to get a viable map seed, I've seen my HQ stuck in a narrow gorge or plopped in line of sight of a infected town.  Not exactly a fun time when it can take up to 10 mins to find a map that gives you even a chance of winning.
The game does not include a tutorial at the moment and requires you to either watch lets plays or learn by error. This doesn't really help when the building system can be clunky and unforgiving at times.  The problems largely range from asthetics to  end-game compromising. 3 block long gates that you try to fit in a diagonal pattern, not a big issue but can just look ugly.  But not planning your traffic flow through the town because you don't have roads to lay down and its not easy to see if you blocked a route, that gets frustrating.
Lastly the unit commands right now are circa 1990's Starcraft.  There needs to be a major expansion including stances, formations, etc. Your three options of clearing the zombies is a attack move that blobs all your units, a "chase" where your units scatter and pick fights with as many zombies as possible, or manually moving all your units into a formation and moving them along. Of all my nitpicks, I see this one as the one that could tire players out very quickly.

Hidden Folks is basically the video game version of an interactive Where's Waldo.
The objective of the game is to find objects hidden in a scene. Hidden Folks is not your normal hidden object game though as in most levels you are looking through hundreds to thousands of objects. For each level you are given a number of objects that you need to find. A lot of these are out in the open but some of the objects require you to click or drag on other objects in order to reveal them.
As a whole I would say that the game is moderately difficult if you want to 100% the game. In each level about half of the items are pretty easy to find, about 20-30% are moderately difficult and each level has 1-3 objects that are hard to find. While some of these hard to find objects would be frustrating to find, the game does have a good hint system that gives you a good enough clue to help you without leading you directly to the item.
As far as the game's atmosphere, I would have to say that it is quite charming. The artwork is a little simplistic but charming at the same time. There is also the fact that all of the audio in the game was created by the developers themselves.
The only really complaint I have for the game is that I wish it was a little longer. You could probably play through all of the levels in 2-4 hours if you don't care about finding all of the objects. If you want to 100% the game I would guess that it would take around 4-7 hours to complete. This is a decent length but I just wish there was a little more content in the game.
Basically my recommendation comes down to whether the Where's Waldo premise appeals to you. If it doesn't it probably isn't worth picking up Hidden Folks. If you like these hidden object style games though I think you will really enjoy Hidden Folks.

TL;DR: Best power-up, Quad Damage = max fun gibbing demons. Also telefrag = pro final boss fight.
Not the very first first-person shooter ever made, but close to it! If you do not own this game yet... well, were you born yesterday?! Ask a random person if they know of Quake and nine times out of ten they will. Quake's infamy knows no bounds, and for good reasons.
At its core, it's a demon slaughterfest. Run around finding keys and open up more levels  so you can blow up, pump full of shells, and even gib your enemies everywhere you find them.
It survives almost all versions of Windows over the years - in many cases fans themselves find their way around compatibility problems. You are given a few choices as to how to boot up your game of Quake on Steam. Just find whatever works best for you, experiment a little. The graphics are dated but playable, even more so with new resolutions available. On the plus side framerate will never be an issue here.
Enemies consist of all sorts of memorable foes: human grunts (enthralled or converted or something), vors, scrags, ogres - even yetis. Thankfully there's a nice selection of weapons and power-ups to help you wade through the carnage. Shotguns and double-barrelled shotguns, grenade and rocket launchers are all solid choices, but my favourite weapon would have to be the super nailgun. Yes, there are nailguns; a nod to Trent Reznor, who did the game's soundtrack. Why do I say this? The proof is on the ammo boxes of nails, for they bear his band's logo, NIN, better known as Nine Inch Nails.
Yet, for some reason or another the soundtrack is absent from the Steam version of Quake. Never fear! A quick download and patch can fix this - in the form of Ultimate Quake. Just Google it, easy fix.
I've mentioned some enemies briefly. What makes them all so special,
and why play this instead of, say, DOOM?
The answer is fun factor. With game elements such as a yeti's projectile lightning, vor bombs (capable of turning corners!)ogre grenades and ridiculously high and long fiend jumps, there is a far easier time of getting demons to fight each other.. So forget trying to line up cacodemon cheese-and-bacon balls with a hell knight, Quake is where you crack open the popcorn.
But wait, there's more. Everyone's favourite power-up is the Quad Damage. The name is kind of hard to misconstrue. It goes without saying that they never last long enough either - once I get one I run around at top speed trying to find and kill everything in the level. Even the toughest foes flinch at a 4x damage hit from most weapons. One double-barrelled shottie blast at point-blank is... epic.
Other odds and ends: great enemy sound effects, they're all unique and specific to each enemy. Some damage flinches are golden too - the knight clutching his ear and stumbling always makes me grin. Good take on zombies too - kill them with anything other than explosions and they just keep getting back up again. Proof that explosions are f***ing awesome in everything you do. I'm pretty sure their attack is picking off a bit of their own brain and throwing it at you. Ew. But I guess they don't have any need for it!
Still further is the replayability. Finished Nightmare without saving and thought it was too easy? Join the speedrun community! It's crazy stuff, but great for a laugh. Rocket jumps (think: get hit by your own rocket or grenade) for boosting speed and getting to places that may seem like cheating is almost a sport in its own right.
Get this classic in your library and give it a gib. Rediscover the meaning of FPS fun.

This is a weird game. Never have I played a roguelike MMO, and never have I been so satisfied platforming with multiple people. You don't know anyone, but you get into runs with people and there is an unspoken team effort that will carry you from the midboss, all the way to death at the boss.
Sometimes It can be challenging with a million things exploding on the screen/damage numbers flying all over the place. I recommend turning off ally damage numbers in the options menu. I would also like to see an addition to the game where you can limit the opacity of teammates. If you take your eyes of your character, you will die.
Starbreak is challenging, but not unfair. You can leave an area at any time. Every level has multiple sections, so if you continue with 26/90 health and you die that's your fault and no one elses. Dying results in your character's permanent death, as well as any gear he/she had equipped. There is a stash that exists for item storage between characters.
Bosses are insane.
The characters consist of a shooter, a tank, melee puss puss, and a platform creating robot. I'm still pretty early in the game, so I have yet to unlock the last character. However, the characters all have personality and their skills are appropriately designed for their respective roles. It's nice to see diversity in such a small MMO.
Loot is great, only one pickup can mean the difference between decent damage and holy-crap-did-you-see-that?

"Contra MMO" sounds weird but here it works very well. Join the zerg and shoot and loot everything in the way.  There's permadeath (and a health bar, no one hit kills here) but recovering from it is fast.
Also, the music is GREAT, it runs well on macOS and supports controllers.

Really, when you look at this coldly, it's another one of those "Log in, die fast, die often" shooters. It's got incredibly intricate levels which allow for flanking from so many sides that you're essentially surrounded at all times. Your foe may come at you from above, in front of, either side, below or behind you. What this ends up producing is a lot of scenarios where you spawn, move, and die because there's simply no way to check every conceivable angle before someone supernaturally headshots you from clear across the map.
In the end, Brink is going to have its share of fans, but overall it's going to slip into mediocrity and be forgotten as just another twitch shooter.

A damn good mix of Team Fortress 2, Wolfenstein: Enemy Territory and Mirror Edge. Intelligent gameplay that forces you to work as a team with other players. At least this is something cool enough while waiting for Planetside: Next or Dust 514.

This game is not for everyone. Brink is a competitive first-person multiplayer shooter. It is designed to be played online with your friends and not as a singleplayer game, so make no mistake, don't play with bots! However, if you are looking for a multiplayer shooter that does not focus on kills per death ratios or killstreaks, then this game might be for you. Gamers looking for something different and especially fans of the developer's previous game Enemy Territory: Quake Wars will find a game that wants you to play cooperatively with your team in order to defeat the other one. Brink focuses on map-specific objectives that need to be fulfilled to win the map. So if you're looking for a shooter that pushes you so hard to play together, that you will sometimes curse your teammates for not helping you, this is your game.
The most issues the game had at its release were fixed up until now, which makes the game highly recommendable to me.

This is a review after playing the game for approximately 10 hours, mid game. I purchased this game in the steam sale for under £5.00, and for the amount of gameplay I have had already I would say it was worth the purchase, despite some of it's more problematic features.
To put it bluntly, this is roughly in the Visual novel type genre, but is more of a scheduling type game in the nature of Long Live the Queen. It is very simplistic, the graphics are very flat and look slightly dated or more like what you would expect from a mobile game.  The in game sequences are generally not animated, but this is not unusual for the genre.
The premise of the game is interesting, you are an up and coming cosplayer trying to make it in the competitive world of conventions and expos. You have to make money to afford costumes, purchase materials, research new skills and also find time to relax and socialise. The developing story of ♥♥♥♥♥ being the big bad enemy is mildly amusing and is probably one of the reasons I keep playing the game because I do actually want to see how the storyline pans out.
Regarding gameplay, initially things happen pretty fast and it is easy to meet original objectives. As time goes on though, the game becomes very formulaic and repetitive and it is a long time before anything happens. For example, on the progress tab, there is a jump between achieving 10K likes and then 100K likes! Sometimes it seems like ages before anything actually happens on the game.
Seeing however, as I have played 10 hours of the game and it is nowhere near resolving, I think it is probably worth a go for £2-3.00. I am unsure I would pay any more for it.

-/+ Could benefit from more content. It has the potential to be a really awesome game, but right now the amount of content is average (but developpers are still baking some new contents and working on it, so expect more content in the future).

I can absolutely recommend this game!
Here is a list of tips for newer players:
- Expand! Expand more than you dare. If you can make 6-10 rangers and a few walls (as soon as needed) you should be fine for the first 2 waves. Leave the rangers on patrol. You do not need strong defenses early on. Just coverage.
- Build up your economy. The end-game is going to be expensive and you do not want to be broke then. A stable 1k-1.5k gold should be fine. But make sure you keep it that way.
- Clear out the map. During the last wave every zombie left alive joins the horde, so thin them out early. A good way to clear is to use 25-30 snipers. Move them with "q"
- Pause. Often. It's bound to "space-bar" for a reason. If you build while paused and you can refund what you just placed at full price, instead of 50%.
- Use Thanato's. Thanatosi? Thanatii? 2-3 per choke-point should be enough to thin out the hordes. Set your gun turrets to focus the zombies with the highest level and you should be fine for the late-game.
- EXPAND! No, really. Even if you do not need the space now, you will be glad you did in the future.
- Build priorities (in that order):
houses
Soldier-center
wood-workshop
balista
farm
stone-workshop
Engineering center

Unit priorities (in that order):
- Ranger: Good for the early game, 20-30 should be your max (unless you want to clear the map with them).
- Sniper: Huge range, but require a group, otherwhise they are doomed. Make 70-100 of them (mostly for clearing)
- Thanatos: Very useful late-game, require oil to maintain
- Titans: Recently nerfed, quite expensive, but quite useful when clearing out the map
- Ignore Soldiers and Lucifers: They are slow and not that useful, use snipers and thanatosses respectively.

After seeing THEY ARE BILLIONS for just a few moments on Twitch, I decided that this is a game for me. A Base-building system that strongly reminded me of my late 90es RTS, when Unit-Spamming and One-Unit-Rushes were still a thing of the future and you could do all kinds of weird things to just make your opponents game harder. Then the first wave hits, and suddenly it becomes more of a Tower-Defense Strategy game, a genre that, for me, took over from RTS as the strategy game where you had to plan, think and take it slow, no matter how intense the action got. Overall, the game combined all that I loved about Strategy Games.
Let casual players be warned: While this game can absolutely be learned, it will take a few tries and actually seeing what you did wrong at what point and learning from those mistakes. It took me several attempts before I won my first game. Also, this game may be extremely intense, but each session takes hours. Again, something I love, in a time of 20-Minute Sessions, I want to take my time on each map, and I probably spent more time figuring out my base layout that most RTS these days take per session.
However, once you realize the workings of THEY ARE BILLIONS, it isn't that hard anymore, it is fair, requiring you to do things right of course, but as impossible as even a 10% map may feel during your first few attempts, when a rogue Zombie infects your whole colony, you can quickly get the hang of it and then work on your strategy.
Which is something you need to adjust every session. The maps layout, your progress in clearing and expanding, the amount of military units you command, it is all very situational. Watch any game anyone has ever played, after a few ingame days, they will have to adjust to their situation and no map will play out the same. It's challenging and a lot of fun, even if you end up losing, because even that may feel like a success.
The first time I made it to the end of a game, and got the notice that the entire horde is apporaching from literally everywhere, I knew right away that I lost, but I was smiling the entire time that they tore my puny excuse for a defense to shreds. The lessons from the map were quickly drawn and clear as day: I lacked ressources, which had me lack workers, which had me lack military might, and the final wave includes every Zombie left on the map. The solution: Expand more agressively, kill whatever you can find before the final wave and conserve ressources whenever possible. Sure enough, the next Map I played, I scored my first win at measly 55%, but it was a win.
But the most positive thing I can say about the game: Time flies when playing it. I tend to play games for maybe an hour at a time, leave it on idle and then play again when I feel like it. At least a third of my huge amount of hours playing Skyrim was the game just idling with me doing other things, my 48 Hour Playthrough of Elex took me 72 hours runtime. But when I sit down at 6 pm to play a bit of THEY ARE BILLIONS, I check my watch after what feels like minutes and realize that three hours have flown by as if they were nothing. Those 17.6 hours I currently have on record are all playtime, no idling. The game is addictive, captivating and immensely fun to play for longer sessions. Add to that the natural but fair difficulty level, a superb mix of high intensity combat and long, thought through planning when building your base, and I've got myself probably my favourite RTS this decade!
I cannot praise it enough, if this wall of words don't state that already. From seeing it on Twitch and thinking "This seems like Steampunk Age of Empires with Zombies with charming graphics" through having an army of Archers wiping the entire map clean to anxiously waiting for the final horde to step in front of my Titans' Cannons, THEY ARE BILLIONS is a superb RTS that combines everything I love about this game genre. I can't wait for the campaign and can say with confidence that this game is a masterpiece for Strategy Game Fans!
Gameplay: 10/10
UI: 9/10
Visuals: 9/10
Performance: 10/10
Value: 10/10
Fun Factor: 12/10!
TL;DR: If you like classic RTS games and fending off hordes of monsters, and are willing and capable to take your time and learn how the game can be beat, this is maybe the best strategy game you can currently get on Steam.

Osiris New Dawn is a new and exciting way to look at Space and the Galaxy as a whole. It's a game where you start out very early on in the stone age but after a rough struggle you begin to really progress and begin to make a lovely home for you and your fellow colonists. You go from planet to planet expanding your colony and fighting the inhabitants of those worlds. This is a very early access game but from my extensive experience in playing early access titles - Dayz standalone, 7 days to die, Miscreated and various other titles I can honestly say this is one of the more worked on titles. People complain about how it lacks content. Its an early access game it says in the damn title. "Will lack content as not finished" so you shouldn't expect a finished game from here. Having played this game from the moment it was released and watched it change over the many months it has been out it is coming along very nicely.
You now have four classes to choose from and each one is vital to the game and your colony. You start in the stone age and you work your way up till you are eventually in space with your own space ship and station building away.
This game is by the most fun survival game I have played as its not done a lot. You won't find many space orientated survival games as most are about the pvp and the zombies even Miscreated choosing to go for a more apocaplytic outlook on surviving does not compare to Osiris. It is an early access game it is very limited but from what you can do and what this game will become it is a very awesome game indeed. If you love the look of the game then play it. If you want a game that has no bugs no issues no problems.....Well you won't find one. Osiris has lots of problems but for an early access game you cannot complain about it. As what it currently has and what it can and will have in the future outweighs any problems now
I recommend this to ANYONE

Now give me them dislikes for actually enjoying this early access game.  I'm not ashamed of it.
The graphics, visuals, level design, sound design  are amazing and when combined they provide an immersive experience.    At the moment this game provides limited content as it is an early access.  The content consists of gathering minerials, plants, etc (which is a serious cause of grinding) to build your base, surviving from alien hostiles, and exploration.  It is important to note, don't expect to build a big base with all the essentials in just a few hours as structures/building foundations are gated by character progression (combat, science, and engineering) and heavy grinding trying to find the right resources.  This game also provides an RPG element with character levels and stats (speed, strength, stamina, and health).  It is also important to note that this game has you do A LOT of running...running to gather materials, running back to your base, running from aliens, running to find food/water and just running for the sake of running.  It can feel like a running simulator.  So if you can't handle running a marathon then stay on your couch eating cheetos.  Don't worry, there are vehicles, but they will take a long long time to get and best of all spaceships to explore space!  In addition, there are other planets!  I'm not sure if you can actually explore them in the game's current state as I have not even built a proper base.
The game is quite a challenge compare to other survival games on the market.  It has a steeper learning curve and no tutorial, but once you actually play it for a few hours and or look up a guide/youtubers and learn the game's mechanics it becomes easier.  The real challenge is dealing with the aliens and trying to stay awake after grinding, but its duoable and becomes less of a challenge when you give the game a chance even if that means dying 1337 times.  Dying over and over teaches you things man...like run the♥♥♥♥♥♥away when you get swarmed at night and only have a rock to defend yourself with...I would know...
The game provides both third-person and first-person gameplays, however, third-person is a bit wonky compare to first-person especially when you try to mine minerals or melee combat.  The pick up animation is quite terrible at the moment.  I'm not a fan of having to wait 2 seconds to pick up one item at a time even though it's more realistic than instantly picking up everything, but pffshaa were in space with ninja skyscraper sized wurms screw realism. The character movement is pretty fluid, but still needs a bit of tweaking as it can feel clunky sometimes and there is awkward pauses at times.  The jetpack boots are very nice, but the fuel it provides dies off way to quickly and takes too long to recharge in my opinion. Also everytime you fall off a little incline your character pauses for a second before it can move again, quite annoying if you are trying to run away from 3 gaint charging crabs.
The aliens even just 1v1 are very tedious to kill even with guns to a point where I just lowered the health settings for them by one notch below normal.  It definitely helped.
The game also provides multi-player and PvP, but i never tried these as I just enjoy the single-player survival aspect of the game.
The game also is quite heavy on your gaming rig.  The optimization still needs work so If you have a toaster of a system, I would suggest to stay clear of this game until it is better optimized.  For example, my mid-tier gaming laptop specs are CPU: Intel CORE i7 6700HQ, GPU: Nvidia Geforce GTX 960m, and 8 GB RAM,   I am able to run the game on the highest settings with all the extra effects on and 1080p at 20-25 fps (playable), default settings runs at 29-32 fps, lowest settings and lowest resolution with all effects off runs between 40-45 fps.
The playerbase is low (600-1000 players on steam at one time with the current patch release), which i personally don't care as I am a single-player gamer, but i know there are those that play simply for the multi-player aspect of games and there are those who just like having a game with a large playerbase as it keeps them away from the mentality of low playerbase=dead game.
As for the devs, I can't say much as I just found this game two days ago during the summer sale.  However, from what I can tell from today's patch and the bugs it brought and their active presence in the fourms they seem to care enough to actually spend their saturday to do something about it in a timely fashion instead of waiting until monday to fix these bugs.  Thumbs up for the devs and their hard work today.
It is also important to know that from what I've read in past fourms that each update they bring always comes with multiple bugs and issues (early access so it's expected) so if you aren't big on helping the devs out on early access games in finding these bugs and just want to play games that don't have game breaking bugs I would not recommend this game until it's out of early access. Also, from what I read off some old fourms it seems like the previous versions of this game was much more tamed and it was just lacking content, but the devs are constantly changing gears on what they want the game to be and sometimes adding/removing things that players never wanted. I don't know anything about the past versions and history for this game so i can't confirm this.
Overall, this game still has great entertainment value and potential if you are into grindy pre-fab structure building games with an rpg progression espically if you have friends to play with.  Even if you don't have any friends or just enjoy playing by yourself because you're a hardcore introvert like myself this game is still very much enjoyable.
Final verdict for Osiris: New Dawn is a semi-reccomendation if you want to help the develepment of the game, aren't turned off by heavy grinding, can handle games with some challenges, and or aren't turned off by game breaking/game stopping bugs while it is being developed.  In conclusion, being Matt Damon for a day was a blast.

the reason i like StarBreak so much is because of it's fast paced metroidvania action, coupled with a seamless MMO experience. in many ways, this game is similar to the Binding of Isaac games, allowing you to pick up stat items, try different equipment combinations, see how far you can go, and inevitably die, and start the process all over again.
even though character deaths are permanent, your account level is not, and will stay with you forever.
you can gain account xp in nearly any way (boss kills, time spent, performance), but you can only increase the level cap by finishing a zone you haven't won before, forcing you always seek out harder challenges.
being F2P, the money advantage has to be here somewhere, right?
nope, you can only buy very small cosmetic items that reset with your character death, which both suck and is a reasonable way to create income in the game.
i would strongly recommend giving this game a try, however long you might want to play it!

It's Mass Effect type gameplay as an X-Com game, styled like LA Noire.  The focus on historically accurate weapons is impressive, and the DirectX 11 visuals are gorgeous.
That said, the combat isn't just "not fun", it's downright frustrating and unpleasant.  The weakest enemies absorb a ridiculous number of bullets before dying - and that's on the easiest difficulty setting.
I'm a longtime X-Com player - as in, I played the original on a 486 in 1994.  I'm also a firearms enthusiast.  One shot from an M14 firing 7.62 NATO rounds to the head should be sufficient to kill a Sectoid.  In this game, it takes at least 3.
Your AI squadmates are not only incapable of doing anything remotely helpful on their own, they're an outright liability.
Adding insult to injury, the music that plays during combat doesn't fit the game, the setting, or the subject matter.  It's "classical" music that achieves so little that calling it third rate would be an insult to third rate works everywhere (and I majored in music, so I am most definitely a fan of "classical" music - not some philistine who gets a headache when he hears something orchestral).
I knew coming in that this wasn't the best game, and the production quality of the intro was so good I was surprised.  Once past the intro, though, my interest just disappeared; the developer has some top-notch graphics and visual skills, and it's a shame to see them wasted on a game with such poor gameplay.  It's often said that "you can't polish a turd", but this is the most highly polished turd I've ever seen.

Quake is essentially DOOM with some way-ahead-of-its-time 3-D graphics. While the game is great, I liked DOOM and Duke Nukem 3D(Not an "id Software" title) much more.
Quake doesn't really have much going for it in setting and monsters. I like the whole goth/demon setting but it gets boring and uninteresting after awhile, even if the levels are designed well. DOOM has the advantage over Quake because the levels are more elaborate and fun to killyour way through with more interesting demons, and Duke 3D has the advantage over Quake because of its humour, creativity and extreme interactiveness that manages to make the player much more immersed even without the early 3D technology Quake has. Here the monsters were okay at best. Nothing to write home about. Although the final boss, while a letdown did look extremely cool.
That isn't to say that this is bad, Quake still has your fun puzzle-based gameplay that Doom and Duke have to offer. If you play the game on the "Hard" difficulty you'll have a fun little challenge playing through the campaign. I'm sure if you would have played this game when it came out you would have crapped in your pants at the graphics. However, given the fact that Duke Nukem 3D and Shadow Warrior both include the game and their expansions redone for a mere 9.99, Quake only gives you the base game for 9.99 and makes you pay 4.99 for each respective expansion. I'd recommend saving this one for the old Steam Sale.
Other things of note: It kind of sucks that the face of your character that gets progressively more and more bloodied from damage doesn't move or blink like that of Doomguy's from Doom and also the grunting noise your character makes when you jump will never leave your brain.

Developed by Locked Door Puzzle, who seem to like putting the sound that goes with their logo really, really loud; Cosplay Maker is a time management/dating sim game.
As the rather unoriginal but quite aptly descriptive name says, the game revolves around making cosplay and all the drama and things going on around it. The game starts with you at a convention (and you can’t customize a single thing about your character), getting all ready to start on the cosplaying world. You make two friends there, a cosplayer and a photographer, who you will (if you so choose to) keep in contact with during your gameplay and meet in future conventions, and they will in turn give you ‘advice’ and introduce you to other characters as you progress through the game.
Any of your friends you’re able to eventually date provided your friendship is high enough, a stat you will have to maintain by taking some “friend time”. This is the dating aspect, which if I’m to be honest I didn’t care to try. Why? Because the characters all fell rather flat and uninteresting, and I just couldn’t muster enough interest in the storyline.
The time management aspect of the game comes in the cosplay making part. Every so many months you will have conventions to enter, and in them cosplay competitions you can enter into in turn. In order to make your costumes you need to get ideas (unlocked by buying things, relaxing with some TV, socializing, etc), and materials (which you need to buy).  In order to get money for the materials, you have to work – which causes your “energy” to go down. Energy can only be recovered by “relaxing”. So far so good: it takes typical stats to do things, so you have to manage your time carefully.
The problem starts in the scheduling. Your schedule is bunched so that Saturday and Sunday are bunched together as one big “Weekend” chunk, and your days are all bunched together in “day” and “night” of the week. You can not micro-manage day by day, which is absolute bullcrap for many reasons, the most blatantly obvious of them all being that when you get your costume to 100% completion in the middle of the week, you are still stuck “working” on it the rest of the week just because you can’t pause and modify the schedule.
Likewise, the rate at which you gain and lose stats, although manageable, is annoying and would benefit greatly from some micro-management choices.
Once you’ve scheduled your day, you hit play and the week passes with a few repetitive, boring animations, but quite upbeat music. Despite the lack of interesting animations (you never actually see yourself working on the costume, you only see yourself wriggling your arms and head), the first couple of times you see this it’s alright. After the first couple of times though, the slow speed at which the week progresses before your eyes is tedious at best, and though there are events that break up the week pop up (requiring an ‘ok’ to close, so that you can’t even go do something else meanwhile), most of the time they are a boring and inconsequential interruption. Such is the case of one in particular:
“Another day of steady progress in your costume.”
Geez, how… ground breaking. Can we speed this up, please?
What is more infuriating is that there is no way to skip or speed through the week. Okay, there IS a way, but you have to purchase it… can you see how ridiculous that sounds? How can something that should be base game need to be purchased?
At this point I should mention that while there is a tutorial to the game, it’s a rather lame one, and mine got stuck for quite a bit, too.
Another annoying thing is that the cosplay costumes seem to take forever to do. I mean, seriously, I’m no seamstress and I’m pretty sure I could do something faster than this girl…
As for the rest: there is some progress and goals, the goals seem a bit far in between (from “make an outfit” straight to “win competition”) and the progress seems pretty pointless. It also seems you’re unable to sell either your old costumes nor your excess material (if you bought something by mistake, for instance). The variety style on cosplay outfits to choose from though seems okay.
That pretty much sums up all of the gameplay aspect. Moving on to the small technical bits, the game felt unnecessarily sluggish for something so 2D and plain. Sometimes switching from regular week to event seemed to take a bit too long, and the loading of my file or new costume ideas also took unnecessarily long. The loading screen also seemed to have no indication of just how long it’d take to finish loading, which was rather annoying.
The menu is plain, the music in the menu pretty bad, but surprisingly I found myself quite liking the rest of the songs on the game – all upbeat and fun. They didn’t seem to match the game a whole lot for me, but they were nice, up to the point where the same 3-4 ones started to play over and over and over on the week playthrough. Good thing I liked them…
The intro video was interesting and nice, but absolutely unneeded. The whole bright color scheme of the game with the fancy old style music seemed to want to remind you of Persona, only it didn’t quite make the cut.
The graphics aren’t he worst I’ve seen, but they are definitely not what I’d personally consider “nice” or of sufficient quality to match the price tag.
All in all, Cosplay Maker seems like a very good game idea executed a bit poorly. You do get some fun out of playing it, don’t get me wrong, and it can get a bit addictive to do just one more upgrade on a cosplay or one more outfit or one more week… but it’s not really worth the price to me in its current state. Basically the only thing you’re truly paying for here, to me, is the music.

This game has a lot of potential but, in the end, falls flat. The fact that one of the main characters declares the final main story scene as "an anticlimax" pretty much sums it all up.
I was immediately disappointed when I started the game and realized that I couldn't customize my character's looks at all. I expected to be able to change her hair color at least! Nothing. On top of that, the surreal feeling of being the only character who doesn't talk is pretty strong in this game. Even when you talk with your friends on messanger during the week, the chat bubbles only point one direction... she is silent in all things.
I was disappointed again (though not surprised) that there was no creativity when it came to making the costumes, either. The tongue-in-cheek references were sometimes slightly amusing, but they would have felt more natural if there was humor in ANY other part of the game. And there really isn't.
The side characters are all okay, a little bland but not too bad. I can't imagine wanting to spend enough time "talking" to one of them long enough to date them. The friendship stat goes up so slowly that it was almost laughable.
The main storyline isn't the most exciting, but it was good enough that I decided to play through to the end. The last two scenes are painfully anticlimactic, however. There's almost no hints to the "culprit," which makes the reveal boring, since there wasn't really a sense of "did I guess right?!" I'll use rot13 to add my final thought on the plot: Senaxyl, V jnf ubcvat gur ragver gvzr gung gur CP jbhyq or gur zlfgrel cbfgre. Gung jbhyq unir orra n gjvfg!
The upgrade you could buy (for ridiculously high prices) were almost useless. I noticed almost no difference between the lowest sewing machine and the highest, and the magazines and books brought up your stat by so little that they were effectively pointless. It also irked me that the developers put in the option to buy and upgrade that made each day go faster (and yes, you will HAVE to buy this, because the repetative and boring screens will make you fall asleep otherwise).
The main thing that annoyed me, however, was the oversimplified schedule. The game would have improved 100% by simply letting me choose a different task for each day of the week, instead of having to pick one task for the entire workweek. There were lots of times when I wasted a day because my costume was already at 100%, etc. If I had been able to make more choices, the slow friendship stat and low wages would have been easier to swallow.
All in all, this was a very mediocre game and it didn't have enough humor to justify playing it, even if you're very into cosplay/anime/manga. If you do decide to play it, I have two tips:
1) Don't waste your money on the games available in the hardware store
2) Social media presence is VERY important.

I'm surprised this isn't Early Access, as it feels incomplete as-is and suffers a few game-breaking bugs. Skills and items, like Ship Repair and Chicken Nests, are obviously not finished/implemented into the game. There are also a few odd design choices that affect the game balance. Certain buffs are able to be applied to all crew members and stack, therefore making the game an odd one where it gets exponentially easier as it goes on. The first island should not feel more difficult than the final boss(es), imo.
Gameplay wise, it's surprisingly similar to FTL. The ship combat and map, at least, have a lot of the same feel. You hire crew (which you have to keep healthy, happy, and fed), and you sail around plundering. There are three location types in the game - islands, towns, and other ships. Within those three, there are a few different flavours (cannibals or hags on islands, big ships or little ships, towns wih differing supplies). With the exception of a few bounty hunter fetch quests, and an option at the beginning to toggle a plague (which I didn't), there are no other events or surprises in the game. It starts to feel remarkably similar after a while, but more content should be on the way. The goal is to beat up progressively tougher opponants for progressively better loot, until you fight the final four bosses (conveniently spread WAY OUT across the huge map). Defeat them, and you get a cute song and the ability to continue playing. I'd suggest watching the cute song on Youtube and buying FTL.
About 14 hours to complete Campaign mode on Beginner settings. I'd say around 3 of those hours (at least) was spent sailing - ie browsing the web in Steam's overlay, and closer to 8 hours if you don't count restarting after bugs/crashes (e.g. reloading caused my first mate to become captain while my captain was still alive, neither could progress).
All that said, it's not a BAD game. I enjoyed it, but have no desire to play it any longer as is. When it's done, it'll probably be a pretty fun open world pirate sim. It definately has charm and personality. Certainly it's not worth the price right now, in Oct 2014. Check it out in a year and see where it's at.

The game has been abandoned by the original Devs and they've hired another guy to basically do little more than bug fix.  The addition of new features is a pipe dream that will likely never come true.  Over a year ago the original devs were promising all sorts of things ("Both seamonsters AND weather are already on the drawing board. Expect them within a month or so!" - December 2013).  None of these things happened and were lies.
The game has Three locations and that is it.  Islands, where you kill anyone on it.  Sea battles, where you just board a ship or shoot it.  Town islands, where you buy things and hire new pirates.  At the start the game is pretty fun until you realise this is literally all there is to the game, the mechanics do not develop, new things are not introduced.  You will do the same thing you did in hour 1 in hour 100 (Other than shoot cannons).  Cannon fights are ridiculous, you could spend tens of hours collecting a crew, training them, equipping them and yet in a single cannon fight many of them will die, making all your hard work pointless.
There is no real plot.  No real characters.  The music is average.  The graphics are frankly lazy, every island is the same and the background for the world is always the same.  The gameplay is basic (You order your entire crew with 1 click..you cannot individually select) and it does not develop.  Frankly, the Devs should be ashamed for cashing in on an idea and then abandoning it, breaking hundreds of promises they made and hiring some random guy to do little more than take the blame.
Don't buy the game, the developers don't deserve the money and it sends out the wrong message if you do so.
Edit: After announcing they were making a new game and seeing the negative reception it got, they announced a "free redux edition" for the game a week later, in an attempt to win back fans.   This doesn't change my review.  The game is still currently poor, was released unfinished and it's taken the dev 6 months of silence before announcing anything.
A games review is a review of the game; not future promises.

I really, really wanted to like Hearts of Iron 4. I really did. I love other Paradox games, like Crusader Kings II and Europa Universalis IV. I love that you can go back and inhabit a character living in those time periods and cut your very path through history.
If only you could do that in HoI4.
I wanted to love it, but I don't. It's an unequivocal letdown.
The problems:
1. Complexity -
Paradox is not known for making games that are shallow or even straighforward. I was not expecting to master HoI4 in an afternoon. But when you have played a game for
and you are still routinely baffled by what is happening and can't figure out why... that is a failure of design. I went online - to YouTube, to GameSpot, to the game's official forums, to every source I could find in hours of Googling; and not only did the answers often shed no light on the questions;
A game can either be complex and well-explained, or it can be simple and straightforward. If it is not one of those two, it is poorly-designed.
2. Shallowness -
Yes, yes. "Complex
shallow"? Yep. Every game of HoI4 is the same. The same events, in the same order, with the same general result. Paradox games like CKII and EUIV are great because when you start a game;
might happen. You begin in 1066 or 1444 and four hundred "years" later, you can look back on a twisting path to greatness or ultimate defeat in which you schemed, plotted, connived, and strategized your way through decade after decade of palace intrigue, local and world politics, and deftly-planned wars.
But when HoI4 begins in 1936; you can be sure that whatever happens by 1950, it will follow essentially the same pattern. Remilitarization of the Rhine, Anschluss, Sudetenland, Marco Polo Bridge Incident, Invasion of Poland, World War.
There is
the player can do to alter this inexorable sequence. No amount of planning, strategizing, or even outright metagaming can make a session of HoI4 about anything other than this one pre-planned, pre-canned story. There are no local theaters. Every nation in the game gets pulled into this one overarching loosely-scripted plotline (because that's what it is). Even trying to play as a small country far removed from the main theater of war gets you dragged kicking and screaming into the general conflict. I once declared war on
Uruguay as Brazil; who promptly joined the Allies, who all declared war on me. Uruguay.
There are no side wars, no subtlety, no limited objectives, no variance of scale, no individuality, no
. HoI4 isn't a game... it's a simulator. It has only slightly more depth than a browser game on Newgrounds with all the opacity and complexity of market finance.
It's a Paradox game for people who hate Paradox games.
In short, not a game I can recommend.

This is a decent, quite forgiving movement puzzle game.
It offers 84 levels of increasing difficulty. New mechanics are introduced once in a while, including wrapping around the edge of the screen, turnable spikes, activated one-way blocks, blocks that dissolve when combined and teleporters. You have to collect all pearls to advance to the next level.
Quell is certainly not ground-breakingly innovative, but it's a solid puzzle game that requires some planning-ahead if you want to achieve perfect scores. While you can't skip levels, there is a built-in system of getting hints and solutions for levels, so you never get stuck or overly frustrated. I'll admit, I used the solver on 3 or 4 of the more complex levels just to spare me the annoyance. You can also always undo moves, which I was quite happy about.
On the technical side I was very positively surprised. The mobile origins only show in some of the menu interactions. Otherwise you can completely rely on keyboard and use the very sensible hotkeys. You can tell some thought went into the PC version, it's definitely not one of those awful, lazy mobile ports.
~5-6 hours with little replay value, basic graphics, basic puzzle mechanics - it's a decent way to pass your time, but after a dozen levels I usually took a break because I was already bored. While it may or may not be worth full retail price, I can definitely recommend picking it up on sale or as part of the collection with the two sequels if you like these kinds of puzzle games.

I'm recommending "Quell," but I do have some issues with it.  Mechanics-wise, it's easy to do:  move a raindrop left, right, up or down, find a hidden jewel and cross over some number of pearls in the level.  Broadly speaking, most of the maps are interesting, fun, and satisfying.  Unfortunately, some of the maps (and these tend to be in the last era of them) get so complex that it gets frustrating (and I had to resort to walk-throughs).  Of course, this is a puzzle game and, I suppose, puzzles might involve frustration at some point.  More specific issues are:
- The goal of finding the hidden jewels isn't mentioned in the tutorial.  It doesn't even show up as a bulletin at the top of the screen until you've finished several levels (no problem going back and finding them, though).
- There's a secret level that's so secret there's no Achievement for it or even any indication that it might exist.
- Because the jewel could be hidden anywhere, finding it is usually much harder than solving the puzzle (i.e., picking up the pearls) and basically involves trying to break every block or activate every green dot you can get to.
- Those green dots are a pain.  When you traverse them, they expand into a blockage.  That means the puzzle changes shape every time you go over one and could change shape differently depending on which direction you traverse it (because of multiple green dots in a line).  Usually, that's not too bad.  But, there are several puzzles where there are just oodles of green dots and there's just no way to keep it all straight.
- And, most confusing of all are the walls.  Unless they're blocked, you translate to the opposite wall if you hit one.  The problem is when there are multiple sets of walls:  you're uncertain as to which set of walls you'll translate to.  Again, this is especially bothersome in the final era of maps.
Again, I am recommending the game.  I got 10.9 hours of usually fun game play out of it and it lists for about $4.  So, it's definitely worth it.  I just wish a couple of the maps hadn't been so frustrating.

Starbreak is a metroidvania game with permadeath and a mmo aspect.
Think metal slug with more people able to play at the same time.
Pros:
-Accurate controls (and the game stages ask the same of you)
-Very customizable controls (you can even keybind specials, or use certain controllers if you so please)
-Interesting classes, each requiring their own playstyles (The fabricator is a class you'll probably not find in any other game)
-Challenging enemies (No matter how well geared you are, you still need to be on your guard)
-Everyone in the room gets a copy of the loot drop (So no loot snatching competitions)
-Not Pay to Win (Real money can only be used to buy cosmetics and storage space. The in-game currency allows you to buy weapons from secret shops or rubbish from the lobby shop)
Cons:
-Server lag can mess up your timing and controls, and cause death (harsh because its permadeath)
-Visual noise can take some getting used to (this mostly happens in crowded rooms with many players simultaneously attacking)
-Skill plateauing can be frustrating (you build your shell up to a certain point only to die in a similar fashion again, on the other side of the coin, skill progression is rewarding)
-Game has not been updated since September 2016 (The in game community still hopes for updates though, even then the amount of stages are enough for a complete game)
Other things of note:
-Inconsistent field of view across different monitors with different resolutions (can result in receiving cheap shots) (get
to deal with this inequality)
-Player classes all start out very squishy compared to other metroidvania type games
-Procedurally generated rooms (sometimes you can find a secret)
-Signal emoticons are a convenient mode of communication (press 2 to signal nearby health pack, 3 for treasure chest)
-Good gear makes a huge difference to your ability to pull weight vs certain bosses
-Pretty great soundtrack
-The USWest server usually has more active players. Select it from the bottom right corner of the start screen (unless you're in mood for going solo)

Ah, the good old Quake. I remember back in 1996 how eagerly I awaited the CD-ROM with this gem. This was truly next-gen back in the day, and although still MS-DOS based at the time, it was a huge leap forward from the so common sprite based "2D/3D" shooters. This was true 3D, polygon monsters and a dark and foreboding atmosphere.
I have largely absconded plain 3D shooters these days, because, frankly, I find them boring. Ten or fifteen years ago the FPS genre was at its prime, with a constant stream of new titles, MODs, re-releases of the same engines with a different graphic set and plot, and I can honestly say I probably played most of them. Nowadays a plain and simple FPS game just doesn't feel that entertaining anymore. It's all been seen and done before. So; what's a gamer to do? Easy. Go back into the past and relive the glory days with the good old quality FPS titles from that era.
While it's true that the music is missing from this release, and while Nine-Inch-Nails are definitely a great choice, the game itself is still the fast-paced mayhem you remember (or not). I would strongly recommend to get "Quakespasm", since that allows you to play the game as close to the original as possible, but with Keyboard and Mouse and in HD resolutions. GLQuake doesn't work all that well. If you rename "quakespasm.exe" to "winquake.exe" in Steam's game folder (making copies of both files first of course), Steam will even count your play time.
This is truly a classic. If you're looking for an 'old skool' FPS game that was pretty much paving the way for the new era of shooters, then look no further. If you like FPS games, there is no excuse for not having this in your library.
