Ok so my review at 11 hours. I usualy try to review at 100+ hours but in this game I feel like I've seen it all. It's a zombie survival game in third person which is actually interesting. It doesn't have a really deep crafting system but it has a way too detailed character level system. The zombies are simple: fast, slow, exploding one, infected animals and other night zombies that come out at night on higher levels. The game itself is arcade-like and features you fighting those infected. It was surprising to see infected animals attacking you specially the Turkey infected. They rushed me like hell I almost died to those. They have special attacks so you have to attack them differently. Anyways the problem there is that you only have like 1 or 2 playstyles. I usualy have a heavy weapon + rifle. The base system is interesting but the map for it isn't really open world. You are teleported to missions that look all alike. Characters except Kovac don't speak you just see the text ( ruins the flow of the game a bit ). And you don't really get into the whole find loot thing as you will find yourself redoing old missions to simply get what you want. But the game is the best for CO-OP. Online servers are pretty much empty with nobody around but playing a local game with your friends over is fun. I can't recommend this game at full price but it's really cheap on other game sites, I got it for like a euro or two. Alltogether fun game but could use a better story and a deeper crafting system + voice acting.

Lots of different ingredients; lots of crafting options. Recipes are unlocked as you upgrade your camp (i.e. as you invest experience points in your camp and improve your camp structures). The explosive bullet DLC that is available for this game (extra money for that DLC) is fun to use but very overpowered. Some variety in the monsters. Great multiplayer (used to be glitchy, but that was fixed a while back). Fun caps out around level 40 or so. Can feel grindy at times. Dying gives an experience penalty, but it isn't too much. There is a reasonable window of time during which team mates can revive you and thereby avoid you sustaining the experience penalty. Lots of ways you can upgrade your character, improving their skills in particular areas. Kovac is a very entertaining character and the storyline in general is funny. I recommend taking the time to read the dialogue, as the writer(s) had a good sense of humor. Missions (especially town missions) can get kind of repetitive since the maps don't change at all and all of the town missions have pretty similar contents. I realize it sounds like I have a lot of criticisms for this game, but I actually really enjoyed it. I am played-out on it now, but it really hooked me for a good long while. Overall, a fun, funny game :)

Well, some DLCs and expansions in, the game has been considerably fleshed out.
In it's handling of air and naval warfare it is indeed a big step over HOI3, as it is in terms of stability itself (HOI3 simply kept crashing periodically). While some changes I did not exactly like, they are manageable...
However, the game spectacularly fails in one important respect, which is really pivotal to the game. Land warfare and AI.
Playing HOI4, the land AI is terrible and useless. This is over a year after the game's release. To paint you a picture, when I started the last game with little Greece, I decided I want to take Istanbul from Turkey.
So, I start a war, and exploiting AI weakness park my troops behind a river on a mountain in big concentration. The AI bleeds itself white and wastes it's whole army charging a position it cannot possibly take, with the occasional one-division naval invasion adjecent to a port which gets wiped out due to not being able to get resupply.
Once the AI has basically destroyed it's army and manpower reserve, I attack and soon Turkey capitulates.
Then Italy attacks and cannot breach my lines and loses 2 million men in the process just charging into fortified mountain positions with understrength divisions. Basically, once the AI can't break a position it will only keep attacking, with less and less chance of victory as it's divisions get further depleted.
Awesome.

Long time Hearts of Iron 3 player here, I have played games in this series for many years and enjoy them.
While some of the changes from HOI3 are improvements there are certain things I just cannot understand:
* Bugs, lots of them. Windows getting stuck/jumping around the top of the screen, pressing a button and having the popup window cover the battle information with no way to close it etc. For a game that has been out and patched with multiple paid for expansions I just dont get how you managed to end up like this. Current state is what I would have expected for a recently released game or pre release product.
*Cluttered interface, divisions overlapping and jumping around, sometimes impossible to see what is going on, remember that Im saying this as a very experienced player from the series. In fact the different map modes are so bad its hard to see even basic information, like front lines. All map modes are shaded in muted shades of similar colors with no clear lines. Instead all borders are blended together and most map modes have shaded areas crisscrossing the map making it even worse.
*Attack planner/AI, while sometimes it might be useful, issuing simple commands only to have the units move away in the other direction and then start transporting themselves by sea in a never ending loop between two nearby ports is just rediculous.
*AI issues, apart from the blatant bugs above both the enemy AI and your own AI will constantly shuffle around units, attack/disengage over and over and over again and other things that are plain broken.
*The game is simply not polished, take basic things like game configuration. Go to game options and controls, only things you can change are scroll speed and zoom speed. The rest of the menues are equally clunky and non intuitive. I had to resort to editing game files to prevent the game from autoscrolling when running in window mode and moving the mouse outside the window. (important for those of us with multiple screens)
In summary, a great game series that I had great hopes for, unfortunately it was very poorly executed.

A daring move to blend two genres that falls flat on its face. The Bureau sacrafices XCOM's classic strategic elements for the action of a third person shooter. Unfortunately, the combat feels dull and watered down with poor gunplay, bad AI, and incredibly basic, linear level design. One of the biggest faults of this game is the story. When I first started playing XCOM: Enemy Unknown (which was gifted to me for free), I was incredibly turned off by the cheesy plot and art direction that reflects Mars Attacks. This was eventually overcome due to the game's excellent turn based strategy gameplay and RPG like upgrade system. The Bureau, on the other hand, maintains all the cheesiness whilst relenquishing the enjoyable gameplay, which is incredibly detrimental for this game, as shooters rely on immersion to put people into the shoes of the character they assume. The 1960's alien conspiracy in the midst of the cold war could have been an excellent backdrop for a game, and even could have made the Sectoids a little less cliche. However, the charm of the era is squandered by absolutely awful dialogue, 2-dimensional characters, and CIA agents whose wits are as dull as a rock.

I'm a HUGE X-COM fan.  I played the original for years.  If I went back and counted how much time I've spent playing video games, I'm guessing a vast majority of the hours would fall in the X-COM: Enemy Unknown.  I've played all but one of the major releases (Interceptor,) and still count the first games as one of the best PC games ever released.
So imagine my joy when XCOM (what happened to the dash?) games started showing up on Steam again! Recently Amazon had a sale on The Bureau, which I have been waiting on, and I scooped it up.  So the story goes, you play William Carter, a reluctant Agent with an improbably high ratio of successfully completed missions.  You control 2 lesser agents that shadow you through linearly designed levels, following commands you issue through 'Battle Focus.'  It plays like a cover based shooter mixed with a light squad based tactics 3rd person shooter.  It's a mish-mash that succeeds in some parts and fails in other.
The Good
For the most part, I enjoyed the story, and it was dished out at a decent pace.  I did most of the side missions and it took me about 12-15 hours to work my way through it. The missions were varied, with only a couple of the optional missions feeling recycled.  There were a few that stood out to me, one involving aliens using our own nukes against us in particular. I like the 60's settings, and I felt that the voice acting was very well done.  Graphics and sound were excellent, though PhysX is set to on by default (even though I have a AMD card)  and caused me a little worry on the first mission in the base.
The Bad
The first, and most obvious issue for me was the controls. This is a port from a console build, and it felt like very little effort was made in optimizing the controls for the PC.  Running disables strafing, you stick to any wall you sprint next to, sprint and vault are the same key.  Even by the end of the game I still wasn't 100% comfortable with it.
Next, the AI left a bit to be desired.  My squad mates would just hunker down in exposed positions unless I constantly ordered them to move.  Then, they'd move, then move somewhere else that wasn't in cover.  Keeping them alive is a full time job.  Which leads right into the next issue. The weapons.  They feel weak.  Even when you get a plasma rocket launcher, it just never feels awesome.  In the original games, when you researched a new weapon for the first time, it felt amazing, suddenly you could shoot holes in things you couldn't before.  Aliens were dying in 2 hits instead of 4.  In this game it just feels like a marginal upgrade.  You can give your squaddies specific weapons depending on their class, but it never felt like it made them more effective.  It felt like the were more effective as distractions than as actual combatants.  If not for the skills each one had, I probably wouldn't have paid any attention to them.
Conculsion
If not for the storyline, this game could have had any name.  It feels like they had a game all mapped out, then shopped around for an IP that they could merge in to it.  That said, I did enjoy it.  As I said, I love X-COM, and this, while a pale reflection, still tickled me with the storyline. (Though they didn't go to great lengths to connect it to the other games in the series.)  Was it worth $60?  No, not at all.  If I had paid full price for it, this would be a completely different review.  Was it worth $5?  Most assuredly.  If you're an X-COM (or XCOM) fan, $5 is a decent price to pay for a couple days of blasting aliens.

I enjoy this game.
Things I like about Evolve Stage 2:
Varied gameplay. Each class and character plays very differently, some more so than others. Being the monster is completely different from being a hunter.
The chase. Mindgames, juking, prediction, just generally trying to keep track of where the monster is going, or, as the monster, trying to avoid the hunter while feeding on various creatures until you hit stage 3.
The combat. As a hunter, you are fighting something much bigger and stronger than just yourself. You have to avoid getting hit by several of its attacks to survive. You have to work with your team to take it down and get out alive. As the monster, you are a force of destruction. You can easily kill a hunter if you catch them off guard or they don't get out of the way, or otherwise manage to hit them with most of your powerful abilities.
The movement. Both the hunters and the monsters feel great when it comes to movement. Monsters have their traversal and their abilities to use to move around, while hunters have jetpacks to fly and boost around with.
The community. In my experience, if you have a mic and are using it you will meet some people on casual who will say "Hey, wanna team up in a party?". And then you go have a good time. I like this community.
The thing I don't like about Evolve Stage 2:
The balance. I feel the game should be balanced around the hunter's dodges. Most monster abilities should be reasonably dodgable with boost if you know they are coming and the monster does not predict where you will dodge. A few abilities with lower damage that cannot be dodged are acceptable, such as the Goliath's fire breath. I feel several monsters completely disrespect the hunter's dodges, and often cannot be dodged and are generally frustrating to play against and often turn in to a stat fight. The monsters that I feel disrespect the hunters dodges are Behemoth, Gorgon, and Wraith.
Behemoth's enormous area of effect and fast pull make it the worst offender. Its pull is dodgable, it is just very difficult to do so. This in addition to its high health make it very difficult to deal with and frustrating to play against. Fortunately, only a few people can play Behemoth, and they are going to be reworking him.
(start Gorgon rant)
Gorgon's areas of effect, while not as large as Behemoth's, still make it very difficult, if not often impossible to dodge. Its web throw, while not doing very high damage, does a high amount of knockback and stops the hunters from using boost temporarily. The Gorgon's primary damage ability, acid spit, has a large area of effect that the Gorgon can often chase you with. Its high damage over time means that even when you do get out, you still take significant damage. If the Gorgon properly aims web throw and acid spit, they are often impossible to dodge. Spider trap, while having some counterplay in the form of being able to shoot it, has high enough health that some characters(Ex. Hank) are literally unable to kill it and is usually difficult to hit. Most Gorgons do not take Mimic, and Mimic is generally less difficult to deal with as it has a larger hitbox than spider traps. Fighting Gorgon feels like a stats fight.
The issue I have with Wraith is that almost all of its damage is from its attacks, not from its abilities. Decoy attacks you. Wraith attacks you. Supernova increases its attack rate. Abduct allows it to attack you. Abduct is very difficult, but not impossible to dodge. Warp blast is well designed and can be dodged. Yes, you can dodge Decoy and Wraith's attacks by flying over its head, but unless you are running a lot of jetpack effeciency, that is going to drain your boost extremely quickly.
I do not feel that Wraith or Gorgon are overpowered, I just feel they are frustrating to play against and should be changed to be less so. I do feel that Behemoth is overpowered.
Currently I feel the strongest monster is normal Goliath, as they recently buffed his damage a bit too much. 3 of Goliath's 4 abilities can be dodged. I say this as someone who plays Goliath a lot.
Reavers. I really don't like Reavers. I like wildlife being dangerous, but Reavers are just obnoxious.
I really like this game, and none of these issues will stop me from playing it.
Random suggestion: Give all hunters a quick melee for dealing with things like Reavers. Assaults get to punch things.

Below is a rather detailed account of my opinion of this game. It is harsh, but even with my cons being so extensive, it's a 30/70 split for good / bad. All opinions take into account the price of the game (I would be singing praise if it were a $1.99 game, saying it was great value and a rare gem in that bracket, but even 20% off it proves very, very expensive). If you are genuinely interested in buying this game, read the TL;DR at least as it summarises the gist of my concerns.
I know it's only JUST come out, but my points are valid and have this taken into account.
- Ambient music and feel of the game is nice.
- Has potential.
- Drastically overpriced.
- No community (yet) to play online with, unless you have friends who already wanted to play.
- Artwork feels very amateurish and low quality for a game over $5 . . . your competition outdoes you.
- UI and some game elements (camera, walls) *can* be painful to look at and behave oddly sometimes.
- Game is literally unplayable (currently) without friends who either A) visit or B) own the game.
- No credit given to RnD Labs in the credits despite being listed in steam as a developer..?
- Wait for more content (I would say 1.5 - 2x current) before buying unless below $5
- Do not buy if you don't already have people to play with, there is no reliable community. It will sit in your library gathering dust. The game needs far more extensive marketing.
- I personally think the game (even with working multiplayer community) should be in the under $5 bracket for the quality and quantity of product.
OKAY! Now we get into the thick of it. The rest is long and detailed, but I explain my reasoning thoroughly. If members of the dev team read this, I suggest reading below and taking it as feedback.
- Would be decent fun when sitting with friends around one TV playing together
- Is fun to hear your friends wail in pain
- General ambience is nice
- Gameplay concept is solid and entertaining, even if it feels highly limited
- Would be decent fun playing online with friends
- Music is nice
- Feels like you don't get much for your money, even with the special. It feels more like a $1.99 (or $4.99 see below) game
- No online Multiplayer community (functionality exists, but whenever I have tried to play there has been literally no people looking to play 'online' against random people) which can largely be pinned on the following point...
- RnD Labs were the developers I thought, but now it's "Fun Sponge"? What happened to RnD Labs that they don't appear in the Credits of the game? They went for a multiplayer ONLY pc release. PC release makes it an awful lot harder to say "hey lets play Death Stair" and bring it up on your TV. Monitors are small for 4 people to use at once from the comfort of the couch.
- Lack of singleplayer in the light of a yet-nonexistant multiplayer community means unless you have a circle of friends to play the game with going in, you will not be able to play the game whenever you choose. Chances are when you try to play you won't find anybody to play with, or for a long time it may only be the same half-dozen people who might go on around the same time as you.
- While music is nice, almost every track I thought "oh I've heard this somewhere before". Very Mario Party sometimes.
- Leaderboard glitches showing the wrong player roles and stats at times.
- Game has crashed on launch, requiring task manager end-process a couple of times.
- Menu UIs look (mainly in the game lobby) poorly laid out, sometimes mislabling the button input required, and generally messy. The UI elemnts themselves also look relatively lackluster.
- Lag time on opening certain sections of the menu. Should I really wait up to a FULL second to see my settings? I don't know if that's expected on a gaming PC...
- The camera has some interesting.... interactions with terrain.
- Textures for the walls on the first 'classic' level are (literally) painful at times as they can seemingly jitter and the vertical lining is poorly done.
- Character models look. . . to be kind, very stylised. Less kind, a bit messy for a game of this price. Simply look at other indie games for this (or lower) price tag for a comparison.
- When playing with controller, I followed the "enter to chat" instructions and was unable to talk in the chat (even when disabling controller and using keyboard, and couldn't 'activate' chat line no matter what I tried, not sure if bug or my error but if I couldn't figure it out after 5 minutes there's a problem) <further note, in-lobby chat worked ok>
- 3 maps don't add much replayability. From what I saw, all characters were basically identical in their playstyle. Having no defining, distinct gameplay traits feels lackluster. Again I haven't tested party mode due to it being LAN only. But for online play (which I would assume should be the main focus of a PC release that is multiplayer-only?) no such option exists. The game gets to the 'same old same old' point very quickly.
- You literally have glitches in your steam sample images (UI, not present as far as I can tell in launched game) this is more just a presentation fix than criticism outright (besides maybe QA a bit more)
- The drawn art pieces you have for backdrops in menus (sorry if it seems harsh) feels like they were some kind of tumblr or twitter fanart by a new art student than something for a professional, relatively-high-price game.
- It feels like Early Access or a Beta. But without people to play with unless I con people into visiting to play a game that feels like a Beta, which would then require networking my system to a TV, procuring a swathe of controllers I don't already own (if I got 3 more controllers it would potentially cost me 5x the cost of this game) I can't test 70+% of the game.
- Your canyon reuses assets prolifically, it doesn't feel like a real environment. The water below looks bad and the ridging around the edges of the map look poor as well.
- Red text over checkered pattern, end me. I can hardly read it and it hurts if I try. UI shouldn't have that effect. Learning how to properly use colour combinations and patterning would benefit your game tremendously.
- Overall, the game feels far too expensive for what it is. Multiplayer only is a good concept if you have the community going in, but you won't GET a community if there's nothing for them to play.
- Your 'coming soon' tags put the nail in the coffin for feeling like the game was shipped before it was finished. You should have done "Early Access" if you were so bold as to say features were "coming soon". If it's DLC, that's ok - that means what you showed us here is the complete game. But I feel you need much more content in the base game for a $11.99 price tag.

Immediate refund. Especially, if you played the first game.
One of the reasons why peopel purchase sequels to games is the desire to see improvement on things that were interesting in the first game. H2S managed to be a fun fast-paced little survival game with action and controsl that were serviceable. Despite having multiple problems on all fronts, the first H2S was a lot of fun. It had a good amount of self-aware humor and creative quests with sudden plot twists. It was a guilty pleasure.
This game is a half-a s s ed dissaster. It is one of the biggest let downs in my own personal history of gaming. I rarely write reviews or feel disappinted in games that I have from little to no expectations for. However, after spending my initial 2 hours in the game I felt utterly disgusted by the laziness of developers. And no, I don't need additional 10-50 hours to explore the game, the first minutes gave me enough reasons to refund it immediatelly.
CONS:
- Worsened controls compared to the first game. The only "fresh" addition is the ability to climb.
- Very clunky melee combat system that feels even clunkier than in the first game.
- Slowed down pace of combat. I played H2S and H2S2 back-to-back and compare first minutes of combat and the second one is lacking.
- Very lazy animation. Everything is half-a s s ed. All animations look completely the same.
- Inexcusably ambiguous... everthing. Even figuring out why you need to level-up 3 different things that are somehow mutually reliant is hard.
- The world feels less "real" due to the new questing system and lots of locations being isolated small maps available through instant teleportation.
- The list can actually go on, but I feel that there are much better things to do other than ranting and nitpicking over a game that does not worth anyone's time.
PROS:
- Kovac is sill charming and tutorials improved compared to the first one. Wished they devoted the same effort to improving gameplay.
The main reason for my rant is that the game itself is not bad for a small project and can be enjoyed by someone, I guess. However, it is an actual downgrade to the first game that had more drive and even had that vibe of an arcade top-down zombie shooter at times. From the first seconds, the first game had faster pace and better combat that didn't feel as clunky as in H2S2. The first game was also much simpler in terms of mechanics and thus did not require more informative HUD which this game desperately needs. No improvements in terms of UI and controls is also a big letdown.
Conclusion
If this game was the first entry in the series, I would have liked it, probably. Perhaps, some peopel can enjoy this game. However, I personally feel that this game is a pure squeezed and compressed ball of disappointment in comparison to the first small and fun game that did not want to become anything bigger. Here, the developers have bitten more than they can chew.

Oh man does this hold up well. In today's world where First Person Shooters are either corridor shooters, leading you by the nose, or open world shooters with wide open spaces and samey enemy bases, this is a real breath of fresh air. From a level design perspective, Quake feels most like a forerunner to Dark Souls. Each level is a labyrinth folding in over itself, as dense with monsters as it is with secret spaces. Even on normal difficulty, Quake can be quite unforgiving. It's dense and fast paced, with no minimap, no objective markers, and no regenerating health. The story is light, and requires you read the manual to know what's up, so that's not awesome, but where Quake really excels is atmosphere. Between Trent Reznor's minimalist soundtrack, and the gothic and occult themed art and design, you'll find yourself deeply uneasy. This goes beautifully with what little story there is, which is very Lovecraftian. So if you love Lovecraftian horror, Dark Soulsian levels, and a high variety of baddies, Quake is a must play. And if you're concerned about it running on your system, just look at the community guides, and you'll be all set.

It may be fairly short (even though I'm sure Doom 2 was a comparable length, Quake just seems to go by quicker), but isn't that much better than wishing it were over sooner? Every episode I finished had me smiling with glee, while at the same time feeling regretful that I was that much closer to finishing it. Isn't that a definitive description of a fantastic game?
Make no mistake, Quake came out in 1996, and while it may not hold a candle to modern games graphics-wise, it still has aged EXTREMELY well. Once you get the graphics and keymapping set up to your liking, you'll be caught up in the dark, bloody, violent, gruesome, and AWESOME explosion that is Quake. What other game takes elements from sci-fi, fantasy, some oddball Doom-esque religion, and H.P. LOVECRAFT?
If you're looking for a game with tight controls, fast gameplay, creepy atmosphere, intense firefights, and GREAT music/ambience, then you've been looking for Quake.
A note about the music:
Due to the way the music was integrated into the original game (playing off the game CD in the drive), the Steam version does NOT include ANY music in the game. Luckily, there's a patch someone made, named "Ultimate Quake", that installs all the original music at the appropriate levels and times!

This game can be enjoyable for those who enjoy Dwarf-Fortress-like gameplay, but it is pretty clear the team developing this title is not finished. Here are some important things to keep in mind when considering purchase:
( TL;DR at the bottom of this list )
- The interface still has numerous bugs that will cause little hiccups in gameplay. (Not game-breaking though)
- The A.I. of the crew is not well coded, you may need to issue multiples of the same command click to get them to react properly. They will also get "stuck" performing tasks unless pulled away by a direct command. For the love of god don't buy grind stones for your ship, they will stay at them forever until they pass away from hunger. They also don't drink rum to replenish morale naturally, and will almost always need to stop at a Tavern every 6-10 islands unless you want a mutiny to happen. Of course, you're not safe from mutiny even in a Tavern because... (see next bullet)
- The Morale system is horrible and riddled with bugs. Once you reach a point in the game where your ship is larger than a 1 layer vessel and have amassed at least 10 crew besides the captain, bugs start happening. The worst one being when one random crew memeber will flag mutinous, regardless of where you are, what you are doing, or how much morale they have left. Their morale could be at 100% and they will still attack you. It's a very bad bug which needs fixing, as it renders the mid-level gameplay practically inaccessable unless you want to level grind just your captain to maximum so no NPC can kill you. This is probably the biggest problem I've encountered so far playing this game.
- Lastly, the Stat System is pretty unbalanced. You can just maximize Agi to be untouchable. According to a Reddit post, there's even a way to give yourself 120% dodge chance indefinately. A good mechanic for power players, but a bad one if you want your game to be challenging. The stat system needs a re-work.
TL;DR:
This game will last about 8 hours before the bugs and glaring issues in its code begin to screw with you. It's an 'ok' purchase if you can get it 50-75% off, but I would never pay full price for something that seems wholey half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥by the creator so far. I love the concept, but the execution needs patches BADLY if it wants to survive on this market place.

You want a laid-back, soothing puzzler to wind down with and enjoy.
First installment of the zen-tastic Quell series. They are basically the embodiment of relaxing puzzle games. Guiding a raindrop around a board to an artistic backdrop and gorgeous classical music from Steven Cravis
The catch is that, when moved, the raindrop won't stop until it hits a wall. For such an unassuming concept, the mechanics are superly executed and the different block types add a fun level of variety and challenge. What's particularly nice is that each level has a few challenges: Not only is it about solving it, but you can also do so in a 'perfect' number of moves. Additionally, every level has a jewel hidden within it (normally behind a block) which you have to go out of your way to find. It's a nice mix that gives you plenty to do. The levels are challenging but not brutal, and you're not punished for mistakes or time. All in all, it makes for a very relaxing, but enjoyable game to hop in and out of.
Only thing I'd say: Definitely play this Quell game first. If you've cut your teeth on the sequels, then you'll likely find you blast through most of it a bit too quickly (the last few shelves are still nice and tricky though).

Interesting puzzle game with simple controls and mechanics. Each level has an optimal way of completion as well as a hidden gem to uncover, giving players multiple goals for each puzzle. Difficulty increases steadily and is never unfair.

When any game focuses it's core experience around player versus player combat, the single most important aspect of the game automatically becomes the "feel" of said combat. When you defeat an enemy it has to feel satisfying, a sense of weight and power must be conveyed as your opponent falls to the ground. The combat has to be spot-on, and performance thereof must be enjoyable and fluid, or you'll be unable to overlook the repetition in lieu of the truth of the situation, which is that, for countless hours you're doing the exact same thing, in the exact same space. Unfortunately Brink fails, rather ham-handedly, at each of these points. The act of defeating your opponent has very little weight to it. The audio for most of the weapons sounds very oddly "muffled", which causes them to feel puny and powerless. The level-up system is shallow and can be completely finished in just a few hours. I will, however, give huge kudos to Splash Damage's art team for their absolutely gorgeous work on the game's visuals. Unfortunately graphical prowess is the least important part of any video game, by a fairly large margin. 58/100

quell is a very relaxing puzzle game where you control a raindrop and try to collect all the pearls by bumping from wall to wall. it has all the quality of life options and features (windowed mode, volume sliders, save files, multiple profiles, instantaneous level reset, undo, etc.), a great soundtrack and a variety of ways to play. if you only want to go through the 84 levels quickly, you can do that, you can even use coins you collect to unlock levels apart from the very next one, but you can also go for the least possible moves for extra challenge, satisfaction and coins, and try to find the jewel hidden on each level.
there are only 3 minor things I can hold against it: you can't rebind the controls (it plays fine with the keyboard but I would've preferred undo on backspace instead of 'u'), the stage select screen is not very informative, too much clicking/waiting to see which levels aren't perfect or have jewels left to find, and finally the story. there's supposed to be one, it's probably about war and love and whatnot, but it's so subtle it practically doesn't exist. not a huge deal for a puzzle game though.
all in all, great stuff, worth picking up with the other two, reflect and memento, in a bundle to save some money. there's also a 4th game now (quell zen), sold separately.

Well, some DLCs and expansions in, the game has been considerably fleshed out.
In it's handling of air and naval warfare it is indeed a big step over HOI3, as it is in terms of stability itself (HOI3 simply kept crashing periodically). While some changes I did not exactly like, they are manageable...
However, the game spectacularly fails in one important respect, which is really pivotal to the game. Land warfare and AI.
Playing HOI4, the land AI is terrible and useless. This is over a year after the game's release. To paint you a picture, when I started the last game with little Greece, I decided I want to take Istanbul from Turkey.
So, I start a war, and exploiting AI weakness park my troops behind a river on a mountain in big concentration. The AI bleeds itself white and wastes it's whole army charging a position it cannot possibly take, with the occasional one-division naval invasion adjecent to a port which gets wiped out due to not being able to get resupply.
Once the AI has basically destroyed it's army and manpower reserve, I attack and soon Turkey capitulates.
Then Italy attacks and cannot breach my lines and loses 2 million men in the process just charging into fortified mountain positions with understrength divisions. Basically, once the AI can't break a position it will only keep attacking, with less and less chance of victory as it's divisions get further depleted.
Desperately needs a tutorial.

Long time Hearts of Iron 3 player here, I have played games in this series for many years and enjoy them.
While some of the changes from HOI3 are improvements there are certain things I just cannot understand:
* Bugs, lots of them. Windows getting stuck/jumping around the top of the screen, pressing a button and having the popup window cover the battle information with no way to close it etc. For a game that has been out and patched with multiple paid for expansions I just dont get how you managed to end up like this. Current state is what I would have expected for a recently released game or pre release product.
*Cluttered interface, divisions overlapping and jumping around, sometimes impossible to see what is going on, remember that Im saying this as a very experienced player from the series. In fact the different map modes are so bad its hard to see even basic information, like front lines. All map modes are shaded in muted shades of similar colors with no clear lines. Instead all borders are blended together and most map modes have shaded areas crisscrossing the map making it even worse.
*Attack planner/AI, while sometimes it might be useful, issuing simple commands only to have the units move away in the other direction and then start transporting themselves by sea in a never ending loop between two nearby ports is just rediculous.
*AI issues, apart from the blatant bugs above both the enemy AI and your own AI will constantly shuffle around units, attack/disengage over and over and over again and other things that are plain broken.
*The game is simply not polished, take basic things like game configuration. Go to game options and controls, only things you can change are scroll speed and zoom speed. The rest of the menues are equally clunky and non intuitive. I had to resort to editing game files to prevent the game from autoscrolling when running in window mode and moving the mouse outside the window. (important for those of us with multiple screens)
In summary, a great game series that I had great hopes for, unfortunately it was very poorly executed.

This game 10/10 hats down. Best stealth game ever. Got all 80/80 achievements and still play on a daily basis. Here's why:
1) Excellent Map Design
There are so many ways to reach your designated target. Take the first mission for example. There is the lethal and nonlethal way to deal with Campbell, in addition to ways you can save Calista's husband. You can also approach Campbell by posessing rats and going through little mouse tunnels. You can also take the stealthy route by blinking on the top of the Overseer mansion and sneaking by all the rooms. Or go brute force and kill all the guards and going through the front entrance. All this shows the diverse ways one can play the game, whether it be low chaos or high chaos.
2)  Plot and Setting/General Environment
The environment and world building is amazing. First of all, the plot is very intense. The story starts off with an assassination followed by a betryal by the Lord Regent. Then its up to you, as Corvo, to fight your way back up, only to be betrayed by the very conspirators you trusted. The setting is like the topping of the cake. The dystopic city Dunwall and the general dark atmosphere and the surrounding ambient music. Meanwhile, you can hear the guards talking about recent events and what they think about Dunwall, which is obviously a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.All of this and the subtleties added whether you go low/high chaos make the environment very immersive.
3) Badassery and Diversity of Playstyle
You're an overpowered superhuman assassin with many superpowers. Watched StealthGamerBR and Volund and their Dishonored feats?  There are so many ways you can use weapons and powers. You can possess guards, possess them, and walk behind the bullets they just shot out. You can place spring traps on rats, possess them, and wrekc a bunch of gards. You can bend time, shoot a fire/explosive arrow, place a springtrap, which in combination can absolutely destory Tallboys. You can also bend time near a wall of light, grab an object like a glass bottle, and throw it at a guard, which pushes him to the wall of light. Or you can be a big ♥♥♥♥♥ and just do double jump and drop assassinate all the guards. (which makes the game way too easy as this is how I got over 2 million for Duwall City DLC Challenge Backyard Brawl)
4) Consequences And Moral Lesson
This game shows how individual actions have an externality on the general environment. In high chaos, your violent choices to satisfy the need for vegeance result in the fall of Dunwall empire. In low chaos, by thinking long term and being benevolent instead, Dunwall is lead to a Golden Age. These resulting consequences make you think and teach you what you should do in real life if someone wronged you.
5) Replay Value
I have played this game and the plot and all DLC's at least 10 times. For other stealth games like Thief and Far Cry, I have only played them once and never touched them again.

Don't let the negative review or my time on this game fool you. This game has HUGE potential. Like every game in it's early stages it has it's pros and cons and unfortunately at this given moment the cons of this game are greater than the pros.
- Great idea and concept.
- Visually pleasing graphics.
- Great for Sci-Fi lovers.
- Great if you like games like RUST, Forest, ARK etc.
- Great if you like to build bases and colonies.
- Cool and creepy creatures which surprise you and make the game fun.
- A lot of grinding is required in order to gather the materials to make buildings.
- Newer updates just add more to the grind.
- Unnecessary smelting of materials into ingots to create items and buildings.
- No tutorial whatsoever at the start of the game, it looks a bit over-whelming.
- The creatures at night are EXTREMELY unbalanced. (Too powerful)
- Entering the building is not very optimized. (You get stuck in the door)
- The neutral creatures AI is very poor. If you shoot them, they don't do anything.
- Enemy creatures just perform 2 or 3 attacks over and over again.
- When a creature dies and you loot it, it sinks in the ground right infront of you. Visually displeasing.
- When you die, you see your body on the ground and the camera zooms out, your body is on the ground glitching like hell broke loose while you are having epilepsy attacks.
- Hard to identify resources unless you see them online or have read about them.
- The weapons you start with literally do nothing to the creatures (Again, they are over-powered)

After a fresh spawn, your teammates can litter you with different buffs and attributes that give you an edge in surviving. Weapons scale can increase in power, and you can wear Kevlar to award you more damage that you can take. The action and sets are very stylized, but the weakest draw from the game are the levels. Refuel offers the most dynamic battles because players can ebb with combat easily and have time to set up.  Other maps have objective points too close, or too far from spawn, making all those buffs you got for not if you can't make it to the objective in time, or you're getting spawn trapped. Consoles were sadly the focal point of this title given the linear stage design, but it does offer a wide learning curve and plenty of team-based fun, just in smaller doses when there's an unfavorable map change.

So, let's ignore that this isn't an XCOM Game.  Let's ignore that there is no strategic overview, no internal economy, no research trees, manufacturing, UFO combat, or any continuity in the new XCOM EU universe.
This game is, at its core, a bland cover shooter.  There are three hallways in this game that you fight in: Main Street USA, Rural USA, and Generic Gray-Blue Spaceship corridor.   Fighting in deep space, on an alien planet, or on an Earthbound Alien base?  Gray-Blue Corridor.  Travel 600 light years to an alien satellite?  Gray Blue Corridor.  Head into earth orbit on a spaceship that should really be called the Firestorm?  Gray-Blue Corridors.   That's all this game is - walk down a hallway, crouch behind cover, and shoot aliens while trying to keep your ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ AI team mates alive.
While it seems there is the potential for some deep tactical action in your engagements, the extremely short leashes that your teammates are kept on interferes with their ability to flank the enemy.  You can try to set up a recon agent to shoot from an elevated position, but if you move forward to get in range of your shotgun, the short leash that your teammates are on simply means they will move up to the front lines with you.
When you boil it all down, the game is just dreadfully boring.  The combat gets old dreadfully fast when you have to spend most of your time just keeping your AI alive on the higher difficulties and outside of picking one of three ending narrations you get, no other choice you make throughout the game has ANY impact.

They Are Billions is not a Tower Defence game.
I often see it compared to as such, and I think that is a bit of a lazy way to define this game. It is more akin to a classic 90s RTS with emphasis on base, economy and unit management. Oh and they are a few infected to worry about.
It is as if the developers decided they needed to take the level "Desperate Alliance" and turn it into a video game.  Boy were they right on doing so. I never though such a basic concept, and ode to one of the greatest RTS games to ever exist, Starcraft 1, would be such a hit. Where a tower defence relies on you creating, and defeating a rush of an enemy through typical a maze, this does not abide to that rule as the hoard does not funnel in a way that a tower defence does, and they will chew through your towers / units without prejudice.
I genuinely feel excited for the unlimited potential this game possesses. They Are Billions definitely needs some sort of workshop so I can ditch the steampunk aesthetic (not really my thing) and find something more appropriate to the Terran.
I find it exciting to find yourself conflicted in whether or not you fortify yourself early and turtle to the best of your abilities, or you find yourself taking the fight to the infected, burning down their nests and exploiting the map as soon as you can. Both reward and punish, all depending on circumstance.
My only few gripes are:
Spelling errors are abundant.
Pathing (reeeeeeeeeeeeeeEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEE)
Sometimes the housing placement decides not to stack side by side because of "in the way" when if you redo it, it'll work. (Does that make sense?)
Towers/ballistas not being able to shoot over trees. - perhaps its a balance thing, but common!
Some mayor bonuses are just god awful.
Few suggestions / ideas:
Unit variety & building - to keep things fresh.
Further advancement beyond veteran rank for soldiers.
Overhaul of soldiers in general - I personally feel they're not worth it.
Workshop support
Unit upgrades

What a dissapointment.
When Evolve was first announced way back when I was ecstatic. The concept was so unique, and also sounded incredibly fun. Then the game went live and became a complete disaster. I never even played the original Evolve, but when it became F2P I thought to myself, why not?
Its... Ok.
In terms of polish and visual design it looks pretty damn good and feels like a AAA multiplayer shooter should. The maps are stunning and the characters have depth and personality. The weapons feel great to use and there are a lot of cool abilities to experiment with. Unfortunately, that's where the positives end.
The monsters feel very clunky. What was supposed to be playstyle that makes you feel large and intimidating instead feels clumsy. It isn't awful, but it isn't particularly fun to play with.
In terms of gameplay the game itself is boring and repetitive. Despite the plethora of potential map, monster and hunter combinations each game plays out almost the exact same. The monster runs around eating things to level up, the hunters run at him as fast as possible and try and catch up. If they get enough opportunities to fight the monster before it levels up to stage three they win. If the monster stalls the game out long enough it wins. Evolve offers surprisingly little in the form of tactical variety because of the limited objectives. Hunters do little more than chase the monster as quickly as possible, monsters do little but run from the hunters until forced to fight or they have an advantage. Needless to say after a couple of hours of the exact same game every single time it got pretty dull.
There also isn't a lot of tension or fear if you are playing the hunters. If tracking actually took any skill then maybe it would be interesting, but the reality is 80 percent of the game you will spend holding down W until you get to where the monster was last seen. In short, the whole concept feels like a good concept that was released half baked without much playtesting. I really hope that future games take a lesson from Evolve and spend a lot of time publicly testing their games and getting lots of feedback before releasing them, in a more Overwatch-eque style.

Starbreak is a permadeath platformer mmo developed and released by Crunchy Games. It is a fast paced, metroidvania style mmo with both unique and familiar features.
PROS:
-Fast paced combat.
-Nice level variety.
-Great art and beautiful soundtrack.
-Challenging gameplay with a lare skill ceiling.
-4 classes with nice variety and gameplay differences.
-Very addicting.
-All the loot you see is yours, you don't have to worry about stealing other peoples loot and vice versa.
-Fun and challenging bosses that are all unique.
- Not pay to win
CONS:
-The RNG can sometimes screw you over. Like beating a boss and getting no weapons for your class, or getting weapons with bad modifiers.
-Visual clutter, other players can obscure projectiles, leading to some cheap shots.
-Instakill traps in a permadeath game, some levels have instakill mechanics, need I say more ?
-The community, about 50/50 on this one, some people are really nice and helpful, but some can be as toxic as hell.
-Some sounds can feel out of place, like the health pickup noise sounding like instant messaging, as well as massive earrape from lare amounts of players hitting the same enemy.

Overall, I do reccomend you pick up this game, its free, its non intensive on hardware, and its a good time for fans of platformers, roguelikes, or mmos in general.

: Oh...Sir! The Hollywood Roast is a sequel to Oh..Sir! The Insult Simulator.. You build an insult worthy of Mordor to damage your opponents pride until they concede and admit defeat. Having said this, that's the whole thing, and it's a fun game based around that crude and just silly humor flying back and forth.
Overall not a great deal has changed for the basic core of the game. New insults and characters to play are an obvious one as well as new re-skin of menus and a new comeback mechanic. The comeback mechanic allows you to get an add on bonus to the end of your roast when your pride is hurt enough.
Other than that, there is a different style of progression through the campaign allowing you to get for example; 1 out of 3 goals and then simply replay that level to get the rest of said goals. This is for the unlockable character stats and extra comebacks.
: Same quirky pixely art style, workshop support for custom skins and a fantastic Hollywood theme both within game art and menu aesthetic.
: Varies between scenes, which I can greatly appreciate. Tracks are a lot more interesting than the first game which improves scene setup and theming.
: New reskin feels very polished, setting the gameplay up and suiting the overall Hollywood aesthetic that they were going for. As a handy little add-on for all you streamers out there, it has easily accessible Twitch settings!
: Overall, I'm still enjoying the game as much as I knew I would. I'm a sucker for crude humor and downright ridiculous jokes.
On another note, an update to voice acting has vastly improved the flow of insults and makes it easier to immerse yourself into insulting your foes. Along with that, an update to scenes has made them feel much more complete and not as choppy as the first game once had.
The new array of insults are fantastic and very in with the (mostly) latest memes such as Harambe and general jabs at pop culture refferances.
Hollywood roast now also has Steam workshop support which will bring a lot of creativity from fans out there, and that is something I am always in full support of.
My main complaints about the game are mostly all within the grinding for achievements based around doing very poorly (for the comeback mechanic). Which unless you are versing a human player, doesn't really add anything *good*. When going through the campaign you have a series of 'Gold Birds' to collect representing what I assume to be Oscars or Logies.. Some of these are using a certain number of those comebacks and it's difficult to get them, but not in a fun way as you basically just have to game throw to save time and build your way up to those comebacks.
At the end of the day, it's a fun game to open and play for a while after a crappy day and insult/be insulted by Gandalf and the like. It's had a few tweaks which have improved the game and the theming is absolutely on point from start to finish. Still thoroughly enjoying this little number.

This game still stands as a unique, abstract shooter with a thickly-dark atmosphere.   No storyline; just a series of demonic mazes and fast action.  I lost much of my youth caught up in the multiplayer aspect of this game.  Gameplay-wise, it's a  basic but smooth formula.  It offers a challenge that is purely skill based; not just on your aim; but your timing, prediction and almost gymnastic movement around the levels.
I still think it's a technical marvel.  This was one of the first full-3D games; and the levels are deliberately vertical and abstract in their design.  Everything has long since been open sourced; as a coder it's intriguing to inspect the design from a kind of archeological perspective.
When starting, you're given the option to choose which executable to run;  QuakeWorld (which was its brilliant online version - though surely not noob friendly), didn't work for me.   Perhaps with some technical tinkering you can get this to work.  (It was never straightforward back in the day anyway)
I've tested the GLQuake option, is the hardware rendering option, this works without any issues.  I'm sure there are mods out there that improve the experience, though.
Gamers today will probably never feel the same sense of awe and wonder and compelling multiplayer gameplay as we did when it released.  I'm kinda glad that games have moved on though, this game has a slightly discomforting pull, like it's almost half-living, a demon demanding my return.   As a skeptical atheist, it's beyond disturbing.
My time with this game is done;  it was a strange friend that was always present, but I hardly miss.  It still quietly haunts my subconscious to this day.   Damn.

The soundtrack, made by Nine Inch Nails in the Downward Spiral era, is absolutely fantastic, one of the best soundtracks of all time, incredibly dark and eerie. The graphics look outdated to say the least, but that CD soundtrack didn't age a day, quite the contrary. Alone, the game's darkness can't really impress anymore, but with the soundtrack it really comes to life.
And there's the problem. This Steam version comes without the soundtrack. It doesn't even have any. Selling Quake without its epic soundtrack is ridiculous, because it's such an important part of it. I haven't seen any well visible warning on the store page that informs you about this, so it's borderline fraud.
There seem to be workarounds if you are willing to download it from the internet (probably illegal). But the as-is version sold here gets a BIG thumbs down.
This port of Quake does not contain the original soundtrack, but if you have no other way of playing Quake, you can patch it by searching for the "Ultimate Quake Patch."

Quake is one of the best FPS games I have ever played. The setting and weapons were just so unique. The soundtrack is absolutly superb and was composed by Trent Reznor of Nine Inch Nails. Quake's story and gameplay is very similar to DOOM's except this was created in a true 3D engine. IMPORTANT: As of right now the soundtrack does not work with the Steam version so if your not willing to fiddle with a Source Port and some audio downloads your going to be out of luck as far as music is concerned. The game is very Lovecraftian themed (Cthulhu, etc). You'll encounter demonic knights with swords, strange creatures of all shapes and sizes, zombified soldiers, and THE SHAMBLER. Quake has an episode based level design so you will go through one episode tackling a whole bunch of levels and then be put back into a hub area in order to select the next episode. There are four episodes in total. This game oozes immersion and atmosphere. You may play hours of it without notice sometimes. I would recommend this game to anyone into 90's FPS such as DOOM or Duke. This game is not just a game. It is an experience.

Brink is one of the better squad-based FPSs to come out within the last year. The gunplay and character controls feel spot-on, and they're married with an elegant teamplay mechanic and fantastic graphic and audio design. Although the parkour is woefully underused by the players, mastery of this mechanic brings Brink up to one of my favorite shooters of all time. The parkour mechanic, like the Battlefield franchise's Destruction mechanic, will become genre-defining with time. Other shooters now feel incomplete without it.
Unfortunately, there are some under-the-hood issues with matchmaking and high-end graphic settings. Brink is also a complete mess on the consoles. Despite these flaws, I still have more fun with Brink than I do with all other shooters save BFBC2.

I originally had this reviewed as Not Recommended, but years later I gave a 2nd shot at playing (and actually finishing) the game. Some issues I originally had with it were still present;
• Not being able to manually save.
• Finicky companion AI. Such as, if you order your agents to shoot a mine when they're not in direct line of sight of it, they'll stand around indefinitely with their thumbs up their bums or (unsuccessfully) try to shoot at it through obstructions. They also immediately forget positioning orders when not in immediate combat, so you can't set up pre-fight positions.
Despite that, getting through the entirety of the game it was some pleasant (not necessarily
compared to others of its genre) third-person shooting fun with light tactical elements. The weapon variety leaves a lot to be desired (not unlike the main XCOM games) but it's utilitarian at worst with noticeable differences between the conventional/laser/plasma weapon counterparts and how they're meant to be used. I can safely say the power selection albeit limited didn't have any that I'd have called outright "useless" so much as there's always better tools for certain jobs. Out of the 4 agent classes, Support is probably the most subpar until it gets more skills for staying power beyond a walking buff station - because it sure as hell isn't in their pistol, awesome as the heavy plasma pistol is.
The story's serviceable enough, nothing too noteworthy other than some very unexpected details regarding the infamous Ethereals. Getting to know them and their roles in the XCOM universe (or at least what 2K Games seemed to think it was) had been pretty interesting. The main character William Carter is a "hardline cop with an alcohol problem and nothing to lose" so bad that I think it was supposed to be a parody of that trope. Nearly every line's delivered as a guilt-ridden ordeal, to the point it was impossible to take him seriously. Its one redeeming quality was that it was "so bad it's good."
If you're looking for something that's the "light reading" of TPS games and not a big time investment (campaign's probably only about 15-20 hours long) or are looking for something to get that same cover-based combat fix after blowing through the Mass Effect trilogy, then you might take a shine to this one. Who knows, the story direction and choices therein might even surprise you towards the end.
P.S.
If you're already well acquainted with third-person cover-based combat, play on max difficulty. The game will probably be too easy for you otherwise. And whenever possible, tell your agents to stick to high-cover over low-cover. It makes a big difference in their survival.

I heard from several reviewers and friends that this game was absolutely horrible and to an extent I agree with them. Declassified I found was much more interesting when I first read about it in a gaming magazine. It WAS supposed to be a pulp sci-fi suspense story played in First-Person, however several happenings in 2K forced its re-purposing into the 3rd Person shooter we have here.
The game does manage to hold onto the pulp 60's sci-fi style, unfortunately it quickly gets buried under all the shooting and with that becomes almost irrelevant. A sad thing, in my opinion. For I enjoyed the early previews of the original project, even IF it being an FPS. I did hope that the writers would have managed to create a good suspenseful story to cover the somewhat generic feel of the FPS, it was a bit naive to think that in retrospect. Since the only thing that runs the games industry these days is the AAA's and they only care about money and I could argue that the game is partly bad because of that.
However, to the game.
Sadly under performing and uninteresting, I did not hold much hope for it. Given what I've heard about it, but to finally see and play it.. Urgh. The game is a good example of a good concept ruined, it does manage to be a decent enough precursor to the XCOM series as a whole, but it does it so badly. It's almost not worth mentioning.
The games story managed to underwhelm me and I now understand why that certain mission ended rather abruptly, the "pop a cap in ye
" part, to quote a man more articulate than me.
The game suffers from AI problems, namely the AI team-members being complete idiots. Unless you give them the order to take cover into a specified location, they might walk right to the enemy and get downed. Most of my crew died due to that fatal flaw in their brain development. Otherwise the fighting is O.K and that's pretty much it, I can't for the life of me tell you a good combat mission the game had.
I feel like my time has been wasted, there is no reason for the game to be this dull. It feels like the developers just up and quit halfway through after the project was re-organized.
I cannot say anything more, for my head is starting to ache from thinking about this.
XCOM Declassified gets a D.
For it fails to be interesting in every aspect, the story is dull and uneventful, the action is boring, nothing eventful happens for the entirety of its runtime. A sad example of spoiled possibilities.

This is a great logic game
- The levels are well designed with a difficulty going from easy to hard (but not too hard) levels
- No timer at all
- You can play as as little as you want and continue where you left off or go back to previous levels to complete unfinished objectives
- A few levels are hard to finish but a perfect number of moves but there's no penalty for retrying them (there's even an achievement for that!) so you can be persistent or use coins that you obtain by perfecting levels
- Finding and getting the jewel in every level gives you a different objective
- Not a huge number of puzzles but more than adequate for the price
It's very well done too:
- Graphics, music and sound are nice and polished
- Graphic options work as the should (several fixed resolutions, full screen, windowed mode)
- Music and sounds can be muted separately
- Movement can be controlled with keyboard
- Resetting a level or going to the next one can also be done with keyboard

It's a neat little puzzle game. Gets boring fairly fast though, so be warned. Like there is not much complexity to the puzzles. I am starting the next game soon, so we'll see if that makes it more interesting.

Long time Hearts of Iron 3 player here, I have played games in this series for many years and enjoy them.
While some of the changes from HOI3 are improvements there are certain things I just cannot understand:
* Bugs, lots of them. Windows getting stuck/jumping around the top of the screen, pressing a button and having the popup window cover the battle information with no way to close it etc. For a game that has been out and patched with multiple paid for expansions I just dont get how you managed to end up like this. Current state is what I would have expected for a recently released game or pre release product.
*Cluttered interface, divisions overlapping and jumping around, sometimes impossible to see what is going on, remember that Im saying this as a very experienced player from the series. In fact the different map modes are so bad its hard to see even basic information, like front lines. All map modes are shaded in muted shades of similar colors with no clear lines. Instead all borders are blended together and most map modes have shaded areas crisscrossing the map making it even worse.
*Attack planner/AI, while sometimes it might be useful, issuing simple commands only to have the units move away in the other direction and then start transporting themselves by sea in a never ending loop between two nearby ports is just rediculous.
*AI issues, apart from the blatant bugs above both the enemy AI and your own AI will constantly shuffle around units, attack/disengage over and over and over again and other things that are plain broken.
*The game is simply not polished, take basic things like game configuration. Go to game options and controls, only things you can change are scroll speed and zoom speed. The rest of the menues are equally clunky and non intuitive. I had to resort to editing game files to prevent the game from autoscrolling when running in window mode and moving the mouse outside the window. (important for those of us with multiple screens)
In summary, a great game series that I had great hopes for, unfortunately it was very poorly executed.

Game was bought and the player was really optimistic at the first few steps.
“HAH alright.. I am good in these kinds of games. Lets do this at 100% right away”
“Oh well.. no.. tutorial? That's alright, I will learn this fast enough!”
Day 1-2: “Okay, it is not that hard.. w-wait.. where did that Zombie came from? What the?! Stahp infection my people!”
Day 1-20 (2nd try): “This is not going that bad. Mechanics are actual really easy to learn... awww nooo... large group of Zombies invading? Well.. sorry colonists.. I guess you guys are eh.. fcked..lawl...”
Day 1-10 (3rd try): “Hah. This is going really well. I learned a lot already. Wait. Something is wrong. Where did that sneaky little Zombie came from? No... nononononononononono!!! Damn.
Day 1-70 (?? try): “How can I still feel so motivated? Yeah I learned a lot more about mechanics and doing really well, but I fcked up so many games already.. Nevermind. This time I will beat it!”
“Uhm.. nevermind. Time for a new colony...”
At some point the player decided to try to beat it at 55% before going for 100%.
Patterns keeping on going. The player feels like taking huge steps and doing really good till some Zombies detect weak defences, fat zombies giving the walls a really hard time, no more space in the protected colony to advance further, messed up economy and just waiting to see the colonists die....
Yes. This game is hard if you really try to figure it out by yourself instead of searching the web for pro-tips. Frustrating? Maybe for people who do not enjoy a really good challenge and trying things over and over again. Even at the point I almost had beaten it (well.. wave at day 110 reached two times, but could not fight them off yet) I still feel hella motivated to do this. You learn every round how to do things and where to improve and then you just give it another try.
Graphics are beautiful, mechanics are learned within the first one or two hours of playing it without reading any kind of guides.
I appreciate that there are not too many buildings and units that are just confusing you and dealing with the economy as it is, which looks simple compared to like.. Anno.. is really not that easy at all.
I went from a score (in 55%) of 22 to 829 in just two days playing the game. I see that as a huge improvement and I dare to say, that people will make progress just as fast.
I wish for this game to have a great future because decent single player games are rare and getting a real challenge instead of being able to beat a game at ease once you figured out a lame basic strategy is something people really needed to see again (at least it counts for me).
The only thing I feel uncomfortable about:
Too many innocent colonists had to die already because of my lack of skill :'<

The early 90s was an interesting time for the FPS genre. The game most often given the title of the original first person shooter is Wolfenstein 3D, released in May of 1992 by id Software. This FPS is extremely primitive by today's standards, consisting of mostly barren environments with many repetitive sprites, but it left a strong impression on the gaming world as being an innovative and exciting game that made you feel like you were a soldier directly killing Nazis. Only eighteen months later, in December of 1993, id Software would revolutionize the gaming world with the quintessential DOOM, a much more detailed, aggressive, and yet comedic game than id's previous game. DOOM quickly became a beloved classic and was one of the most important, if not THE most important FPS of the 90s because of its refined controls, weapon variety, unique environments, hellish setting, memorable music, comedic value, and bright, cartoonish, characteristic and instantly recognizable art style. DOOM may have been gorier and superficially darker than W3D, but the game itself was quite bright and retained a simplistic manner that was palettable to audiences worldwide. Less than a year later, id Software released DOOM 2: Hell on Earth, a stylistically very similar game to its initial DOOM release, albeit with some graphical enhancements. The setting and weapons were similar and the game maintained its predecessor's cartoonish look and feel. There weren't many noticeable differences between the original game and its sequel, save for much better multiplayer and refinements to the original game.
Then, in June 1996, id Software released Quake. This game changed nearly everything from the DOOM playstyle. The gameplay was faster. Enemies were more nightmarish and unpredictable. The game used a 3D engine so the game actually gave the player a sense of depth and weight. The setting was dark, foreboding, and more in line with horror. The light/darkness was closer to depicting reality than a cartoon. Quake marked a definitive split from earlier ventures into the FPS genre by giving the player a sense of fear, urgency, and panic. Dark, unrelenting, and frightening for the time, this game took everything comedic from the DOOM franchise (since the series was goofy, silly, and didn't take itself that seriously) and reversed it. It added an actual atmosphere and made a tonal shift from light-hearted goofiness to the grittiness of a biting underworld.
As with DOOM and W3D, the goal of Quake is usually to find a key to open up a passage to progress in order to find another key to open up a new area to find yet another key. Yet the enemy placement, labyrinthine level design, and brutal gameplay keeps this seemingly repetitive task from becoming stale. Every section is different and you'll often have the challenge of simply figuring out where to go, what to do, and how to deal with the enemies you're faced with without dying. Sure, DOOM presented some challenges but the enemies always stood out from the environment and had simple-to-memorize patterns, and you generally had enough space to strafe to avoid enemy projectiles. Quake changed this by making the environments more confined (or feel more confined), the level design less straightforward, and enemies don't stand out as much and behave somewhat unpredictably or in ways that can be frustrating to counter. Quake is a fantastic model for how games SHOULD be made: challenging, maintaining a consistent and clear tone, requiring players to think, and never being unfair.
After Quake, id Software could never again recapture the intensity or ferocity of this gem. Quake II (1997) was, to me, a huge slap in the face, as it replaced the dark and serious tone of Quake with a silly, cartoonish, and completely out of place space marine story. In fact, the game itself was conceived as an entirely unrelated game, but because of the success of Quake, id decided to just make it a part of the series. To be honest, I never played Quake III until recently but since it was multiplayer-driven, I don't really include it as part of the series (if you want my opinion it just seems like a poor man's version of Unreal Tournament). Quake 4 was absolute trash and DOOM 3 was a major disappointment. I haven't tried id's most recent game, Rage, but I'm told it's incredibly buggy and just overall unpolished and derivative. It just goes to show not only that Quake was id Software's last great game, but that they truly lost something in their image of what their games should be like, instead going for bigger guns and more explosions and scripted events instead of heart-pounding dread and fast and furious gameplay.
This game contains something that id could never again recapture. Quake for me will always be about pure aggression, pure violence, pure intensity, and in its essence is the pure FPS. It may feel somewhat clunky nowadays (you will need to change things around in the settings if you've played any FPS's in the last 15 years), and the enemies aren't the most detailed (okay, they're downright ugly by today's standards) but in practice you will see that it is one of the most refined games, fusing fast and unforgiving gameplay with a dark and chilling atmosphere. In my personal list of top FPS games, it ranks at number 4 behind (1) Aliens versus Predator 99/Gold Edition, (2) Half-Life, and (3) Unreal Tournament.
The best word to me that sums up Quake is intense. It is a fantastic game that, while perhaps not the most innovative game of the 90s, is beyond a shadow of a doubt one of the most important. It helped to shape other FPS's to come in the late 90s, the glory years of the genre, which would come to a sad and ignominious end at the turn of the millennium.
