Quake is a first person shooter that has you traveling through four different dimensions in search of runes that will allow you to fight the main villain. That is pretty much all the story you get and it is up to you to reach the end of each level until you retrieve a ruin and must go to the next dimension. You are free to choose whichever dimension to go to first but I suggest starting from left to right since that introduces all the weapons and enemies much more smoothly. Starting off you must walk into a portal to choose which difficulty you want and to select hard you have to jump over lava which was a nice touch. Your starting weapon is a shotgun, which sounds a lot more awesome than you may think since it is pretty much as useless as the pistol from Doom, disappointingly enough.
This is a very fast paced shooter where your moving speed is swifter than that of most games sprinting speed these days, which really comes in handy when there is an enemy pouncing toward you and another is shooting grenades at you. Learning an enemy and it's weaknesses is vital to surviving as you will be under attack by several different types of enemies at once and must learn to choose which one poses the biggest threat or simply how to spot an opening. Like in Doom they will also attack each other if they accidentally hit one another, and that can be very advantageous if you have enough skill to cause the enemies to fight each other to the death, as it saves you both ammo and the risk of taking them on yourself.  It is still exhilarating gameplay after all this time and is just as fun today as it was back then.
Environments are still rather acceptable and the atmosphere retains a strong horror vibe to it. Character models have not aged well at all and are rather laughable unfortunately. You will not have time to gawk at them though unless you want a chainsaw to the face. Enemies are pretty versatile since most have both a ranged and close quarters attack. An example is an enemy with a chainsaw attacked to it's arm that will use it when you get too close and a grenade launcher when you are at a distance. That is just one enemy, they usually through multiple types of monsters at you and adapting on the fly is the biggest part of winning a battle. All the enemies are instantly vastly different from one another and instantly recognizable which is a important thing in these type of games. Even a slime is more than capable of killing you if you are not careful.
That same level of awareness is necessary when traversing the levels. You are in their world and if something looks to good to be true it most likely is. One thing that I found strange at first is that there is no activate button and you most shoot or simply walk into to switches to activate them. I was unsure how to feel about this at first, but risking a bit of ammo to shoot something that looks out of place and suspicious to find hidden secrets did end up being much better than pressing your face against walls and mashing the activate key like in Doom. Level design is amazing in Quake and each level somehow manages to feel different than the last. The four dimensions do end up blending together in my mind though since they don't really have any real noticeable gimmicks to differentiate them from one another. There is an extra dimension to fight the bad guy but it is a tiny level and ended up being a very disappointing fight.
As mentioned before your basic weapon to fend off monsters is a underwhelming shotgun and a fire axe in case you are desperate. There is also a double barreled shotgun you come across later on but it is probably one of the most disappointing shotguns I have used in recent memory. It takes about 5-6 point blank shots to take out some of the most common enemies which makes the game feel bullet spongy  but worse still it burns through ammo which you can only carry 100 of that type. A huge disappointment after the legendary double barreled shotgun from Doom 2. Other weapons fair much better and are a lot more useful. There are two versions of guns that shoot nails and are very useful against enemies though ammo does go by quickly. Your most useful weapon will be a grenade launcher which outputs a huge amount of damage and ammo is plentiful though you will obviously not want to use it when enemies are close by.
As is typical from games of this era, there are health kits to replenish your health and armor pickups that will allow you to take more damage. There are other pickups like a hazmat suit that lets you walk on hazards, a quad damage pickup that allows you to completely dominate your foes , a protection pick up that makes you invulnerable for awhile and a golden ring that turns you invisible. Turning invisible sounds cool in theory but once you fire at an enemy they can see you perfectly and avoiding them may not be the wisest choice as you may be attacked by those same enemies if they hear a battle nearby. On the topic of sound one thing that must be mentioned is that the Steam version had all the music removed. I don't know why but if you do not want to mod it back in I wouldn't even bother playing this game.
Quake is still a very playable game if you can get past the dated graphics. It is unlike any other shooter released today and is an extinct brand of FPS which is a real shame. If you are buying it expecting multiplayer do know the community is dead and there are no bots so it all falls to the single player. One heck of a campaign though and it should last you about 6 hours. There is no real reason to play it again other than for fun or wanting to try the hidden difficulty mode. It is a perfect game to pick up and play when you are bored since most levels are only 10 to 15 minutes long. If you are on the look out for some fast paced FPS action or simply want to see why the Quake series is held in such high regards by most, Quake 1 is highly recommended.

I bought this game right after it came out and I spend arround 125 hours in it. It's been a year now and I think its time to give my view of things. Before I write anything I will say that in my previous review I gave a positive remark, but some things that should have been addressed are not and the time just flys by.
This game is as far as I see focused mainly on astonishing visual effects and by all means there is no competitor in this regards, at least not with multiplayer. This game has unique graphics and theme. It is set in the near future and looking at the item designs it looks that this happens maybe in 2030.
But the problem with this game is that its survival aspect is being neglected and progressions system is not very well designed. So in the current state you have two aspects where you simply do some things to get points for 3 skill trees and grind materials which are spread wide and far. In a way you can just skip some beginning items and go for higher tier items, if you know where the required materials are located on the map. There is no situation where you you use some simple weapon or tool to get rid of beginning enemies, and then from there you move on to better items needed for stronger areas and enemies, which then yeld better materials for better equipment etc.
Related to that is the materials needed to craft certain items. One example is Hydrogen which is required early on for rubber and plastic. So both plastic and rubber are needed in some simple recipes. But to get hydrogen you have to go far away from the beginning point and as far as I rememberit can be found only at one place on Proteus 2 map (Starting planet). At the same time you can build some  high tech items, because for those items materials are much more available and can be found more frequnatley arroud beginning area.
So as of right now I can rate this game unique, but as a survival game I can only call it unbalanced and poorly designed.
I still support developer because I have faith in this project and its potential. One of the reasons why I write this criticism, is in hope that these issues will be addressed.
My message to the developers is to go and play some other survival titels, that are quite succesful and feel the flow of progression in those game.

So, it has been eating at me for a while how to write this review. I have seen multiple people been attacked over, what I consider to be reasonable reviews. Let me be clear, I think this game has a lot of potential and I think it is going to be great. However, I do not think this game is fun to play YET. which is because there is not a whole lot to do. The game ( as it exists now ) mostly contains one major thing to do, which is resource gathering. The game does offer to let you build some things like a house or a spaceship. which sounds cool, but you can't really do much with it. There by it also has some quirks like the jetpack fuel, which stops boosting at half the percentage. ( I am not forgetting it is early access ) The gathering of resources also takes ages. I have spent the first 3 hours gathering and surviving with almost nothing to show for it, a headache and no feeling of satisfaction whatsoever. the game also requires you to get food and water which you get in the beginning package, but it runs out after 3 minutes and as of now there is no way of getting water other than a complicated system which requires you finding a very hard to find geyser. This is where most reviews get criticized for, You are too lazy, that is the game stop complaining, etc.
That is unfair, it is called a review for a reason. And those people weren't going around saying this game is the worst thing ever happened. In my opinion, gathering those resources is to accomplish something, if not only a satisfying feeling. and as I said earlier,
there is a jet. but the only thing you can do with it is fly to a second planet to, wait for it..... Gather more resources.
This is something that goes on forever. ( again, in THIS stage of the game and in MY OPINION ) But if you enjoy beating a rock until it spits out iron and more rocks, there is no problem. I don't hate you. Hell, I don't even HATE the game so much. all I am saying is, does this game need work? yes. would you recommend buying it right now, no. but do you think it has the ability to be awesome? YES. I can see myself playing this game a lot if it has some more patches and things to do. And remember this is a review. It is meant to give light to developers and potential buyers. I was working with a friend on multiplayer, very actively I might add. And if it gets you to a little home barely big enough for 2 with no interaction after 3 hours and 12 minutes it is in my book not recommendable. )

Brink is unique in a world of blankness. Other games are populated by greys, reds, yellows, oranges, browns and so on so forth. Brink, on the other hand, is Blue and Turquoise. Unlike Call of Duty, Brink is not a run 'n' gun. Unlike Battlefield, there are no very open areas or vehicles. Unlike Medal of Honor, Brink doesn't suck. If you have played Enemy Territory: Quake Wars, you will feel right at home with the objective-based gameplay and asymmetrical warfare (class-based, everyone has a purpose) . In addition, you can follow the story, or go your own way with two opposing factions. Also, there is a very neat customization section that gives you a totally unique look to your characters and weapons, that are both for form and function. If you want a break from the guy with the 52 predator missles in the sky, this is your game. Note: Contains AWESOME Parkour.

"When you start a new game, you begin in a small room. There is a friendly robotic voice talking to you, Glados. As the door of your room opens and you walk out. You find out that you're in some sort of test facility, and that you're the test subject. As you puzzle your way through the 18 stages of the facility and are almost done with the 19th one. An unexpected twist happens... "
The main story of this game isnt all that long. But it is very interesting. This was very well done. Especially because there was only one character talking throughout the whole game. While going through the facility, there were a few questions in my head, some answered and some remaining unanswered.
The puzzling in this game requires the player to remember all of the previously used gameplay mechanics, and combine them while thinking outside of the box. Doesn't get boring for a second. It can get very frustrating though. Not being able to complete certain puzzles. But you always gotta keep it cool and play around for a bit. This is the way i found the solutions to some puzzles I didnt understand.
Every stage also has a few developer notes * if turned on * which tell you a lot of interesting things about how the developers chose to do certain things. Made the game even more interesting.
Plus points
- Very fun puzzles, wont get boring for a second. Especially if you enjoy puzzling.
- Interesting Character ( Glados )
- Has a Challenge mode
- This big small world is designed well
- Interesting "combat" system
Minus points
- Short story
- Sometimes the puzzles are just too easy and sometimes way too hard
- Barely explains the stuff that you want to know ( Can also be my fault or be explained in P2 )\
Hereby I give this game a 8/10
And for this price ( especially during summer sale ) I don't see a reason not to get it.

How to Play:
Use your mouse or the arrow keys to move a blue sphere through a maze to collect all the pearls.  Once you choose a direction the sphere keep going until it bumps into something.  Avoid spikes (obviously!), use warp rings (look like sonic rings) and you can even move off the screen and appear at the opposite side!  Though sometimes that leads to endless loop if there is nothing to bump against.
Music:
Soft, peaceful background music that does not intrude on your thought but is just nicely in the background.  Perfect for this game.
Graphics:
You are in a quaint house with lots of brown, beige and neutral colors.  The level select is a bookcase.  When you go to play a level it goes to the window.   I'm very impressed with how much these little details add to the game to make it complete.  It's not "just" a puzzle game, it's a peaceful experience.
There is no timer (yay!).  You can take as many moves as you like to finish a level, but they do say what the least amount of moves is for each level and you can replay to try for that goal.
There are achievements for those who like to collect 100%.  I have not finished the game, so I can't tell you if they are all easy to get or some really difficult.  I'll have to update this reveiw once I know for sure.
tl:dr version:
Move ball through maze to collect objects in the least number of moves
Peaceful music
Quaint setting
No timer
Achievements

Alright. This will probably be lengthy.
My perspective on the game: I was once a top raider in the game. I have also put hundreds of hours into the game as a casual. The 728 hours that steam has me, is only when I played the game through steam. I have over 1,000 easy. I started playing at the start of Storm Legion, RIFT's 2nd expansion. So that's a bit about me.
Game's content: Readily avaiable to you is 3 full expansions worth of content. If you want to play the game solo, you have 3 expansions of achievements, shinies, and whatever else you could want. You will have to drop some cash if you want access to the auction house, or you can save up plat to get it for free by getting a rex from another player in game. Beyond that, there are old world dungeon queues that will take around an hour or longer to pop. You can keep playing the game while you wait for the queue to pop, as in you can continue questing. Due to DPS/health changes that happened during RIFT's 3rd expansion, these dungeons have become very easy. Basically you can level on your own until about lvl 60 before you even see more than 2 or 3 other people in the game. Once you hit the 60-65 zones you might see 4-5 people every couple hours. At end game, which is were most players are, you will  be at the lull while players are waiting for the new expansion. It's a good time to join RIFT because the new level cap means the new BIS gear is going to be available in the 2 new dungeons. how the loot drops will work to cover 5 classes in 2 dungeons is beyond me, but we'll see.
Instant Adventures: *INTREPID* For some reason this is one of the games biggest selling points. For reasons beyond me, people actually do this. Basically it takes you through the end game raids in more fun enviroment. The maps are huge and look amazing, but what you actually do is very quest grindy. Kill these, click those, and then finally you do a boss with some basic mechanics that could kill a whole bunch of you. Team work within your group is required. *OTHER THAN INTREPID* Well, that is based in the open world and you will be running around basically questing.
PVP: Not so good. The skill cap is pretty low. As in you won't be able to 1 vs 3... and they'd have to be pretty bad for you to 1 vs 2. That would make you feel okay, but this is a game where people make 1 or 2 button macros and ignore the rest of their abilities. If you take the time and research your class and actually read your soul tree, you'll do above average in pvp, but it isn't really what you want to play this game for.
Raiding: Not really competitive at the moment. Mostly casual players going through the raids at a steady pace. Once a guild or 2 clears content at a difficult setting, the raid is nerfed to allow more players to clear content, and then nerfed again and again until the most casual players can clear the content. That's not a bad thing. They do look stunning though. And they fit the lore very well. You can go back and solo some of the vanilla raids, and they just look so cool. Hedges constantly moving around like a maze. It really is fun to go into them.
The Developers: This topic could be long, but I'll just keep it short. This would be the only valid reason to not play this game. Just check out the MMORift reddit page to see a couple area's where the dev team has screwed the player base.
Cash shop: It isn't as bad as most players think. It's worth mentioning that 2 expacs came out before RIFT went F2P. It's very noticeable. You will hit a paywall with the newest expansion to arrive in November, and only slight pay walls before that. Everything up to this point is attainable without spending cash. It helps to reduce time, but isn't required what-so-ever. With the latest expansion you simply pay for it, no choice in skipping time, it's just a hard paywall. I am guessing this will be RIFT's last expansion, so DO NOT RUSH! If there's an option to grind, just take your time and do it. It will be a slow moving game from here on out.
Why am I saying you should play it? The timing is great. You can drop $40 on the game and play the newest expansion in a game that is about to turn into a very filtered community. As in the people that you log on and play with everyday are going to be Really good people. They might not be amazing at the game, but they will make you laugh and you will have fun with them. You will slowly progress through content, probably not by choice, but that will be how the pacing will work. RIFT is going to go into a low life-support mode after the expansion and that can be a very good thing for a long term player. You will have a boat load of time to catch up if they ever do release new content, and you will enjoy the time with some of the best players the MMO community has left to offer. As long as the devs leave you alone, play the hell out of this game.

I remember being quite excited for this game but was quite quickly put off not long after installing it, so much so that I never really gave it a chance. Roughly a year later I decided to have another go and got a bit further into the campaign, now seeing why I was so disappointed.
At first glance, the game is quite clunky and not very pretty. However, it does have quite a nice 60's sort of vibe to it which I liked but that was all, graphics-wise. Transitions between cut-scenes and gameplay were harsh and tended to ruin the mood and I noticed that some missions ended abruptly and skipped straight to a
screen which seemed just down-right lazy. There were other moments that just seemed silly too. One was during a dream sequence when the main character was being woken up by somebody, only to wake up standing up in the middle of a room a frame later.
The game is quite similar to Deus Ex: Human Revolution in some respect as a discussion between two characters would involve the pair facing each other (not making eye contact) and occasionally looping idle movements such as crossing their arms or rubbing their hands nervously. It is also similar in that its cut-scenes tend to be action packed with good graphics and bore no similarity to regular gameplay at all. It's like having explosive, adrenaline-rushed introductions and endings to a game like Minesweeper.
However, if I were to compare The Bureau to another video game I would not have said DE: HR, instead I would have described it as an obvious rip-off of Mass Effect 3. Movement, squad abilities and even the discussion wheel is incredibly similar, so much so that it just feels like the developers straight-up copied it which I personally hate.
Furthermore, there are certain faults to the game which I felt ruined my experience. The A.I. is astonishingly unresponsive in regards to movement orders in combat. Many times I had ordered my men to take cover behind a stack of crates only to find them standing out in the open a few moments later. Additionally, the stealth mechanics just fade away as the game progresses as missions are restricted to a
route. Also every office in America seems to have the same picture of John F. Kennedy. And everyone seems to write their notes in a font very similar to comic sans.
Nonetheless, the game does have its good points. The customization mechanics available for your squad-mates is nice and the combination of certain powers and abilities in the field is quite satisfying too. The plot is really quite interesting, even if it doesn't fit in to 'Enemy Unknown' as much as I would have liked. It taps into to the tensions of the Cold War well and it was interesting seeing the anti-Communist propaganda posters in the scenery. The characters have detailed personal backgrounds too which makes up for the fact that most of them have very cliché personalities such as
and
In short, I don't particularly recommend this game, especially if someone is looking for a fun follow-up to the previous XCOM game. Although it has some exciting bits and pieces, it generally feels like quite a backwards game and I did not enjoy it as much as I felt I could have. Consistently the game felt like it had the potential to be
but it simply fell short in my eyes and therefore I can not say that The Bureau is anything more than O.K.

First off, I've played this game over 100 hours now, all of them with my GF with local co-op. Extremely well spent money to make her more interested in gaming.
However, as a game, this one is lacking... badly. I'ts almost as if they designed half the game and got sick of it, and just started shooting from the hip. For me it seems as if they spend majority of the time in designing the character Kovac from the first game, and then "meh".
Weapon animations were the same for ALL weapons of the same type, dual wield knives and chinese hook swords, saaaaame animation, even the ones where a move would be practivcally imnpossible with anything but knives, like stabbing.... stabbing with hook swords.. And the Katana felt like a club... single hit target mostly, and slow, extremely so as wel...
Loved the first game as it was challenging and we died alot before we learned how to tackle the enemy. But for HTS2, it was just an endless grindfest, no fantasy in enemy design (less zombie types than HTS1) and just a load of animal type zombies.
That and no damn shotgun.... how the hell can you have a zombie shooter without shotguns???
End of rant -
Summary of the games downsides:
- No shotgun (seriously?)
- Half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥design (levels look the same everywhere)
- Lacking story
- Repetetive everything
- Boring grindfest (this coming from someone that have 2000+ hours logged in Diablo 3)
- Level system is horrible
- Controller mapping? What is that? Why have that? Sure default works but seriously...
- Settings is limited to gamma... Yepp... Console settings... on a PC... true story.
- Not nearly enough quests. Leading to more grinding... of the same repetetive levels...
- 100% achievements would take aprox 2 decades, no life and patience of a saint since the leveling system is so horrible.
- The camera makes me want to kill someone. I'm just glad the zoom level is constant when playing local co-op. If it would behave as it does in singleplayer, I would have requested my money back without a seconds thought.
So is it all bad?
Not really actually. The camp mechanic is an awesome idea, and with more time and effort it would have been an awesome reality as well. Since you can build it wherever you want, it opens up for an interesting concept. If only the map was bigger, and zombie spawns wouldn't have been so damn random, it would have been another awesome reality. So I hope this game sparks ideas with other devs regarding this.
Then we have Kovac. The only thing they put some effort into, and he's brilliant! I absolutely love to hate him, and the way he♥♥♥♥♥♥me off actually makes me happy inside. If only they put as much time into the rest of the game, this could have been a game of the year candidate without any problems.
I want to recommend this game, but I just can't. It's not complete, and it feels like they just gave up halfway through and decided to put effort into How to survive 1's 3rd person view instead. It's got a solid core, good concept, but I've played early access games with more content than this.

"Classic" is an overused term in gaming.  Because to be classic, a game must catalyse a revolution in style at it's time of release. To be classic, a game must transcend the simplistic outcome of entertainment and  become a canonical representation of both the gaming industry and the zeitgeist. It must raise the bar inalterably. Even by this dizzying standard, QUAKE stands aloft as perhaps the game most deserving the title of "classic game" in the history of the medium.
Continuing id Software's epochal hewing of the FPS out of the shapeless mass of code in the 1990s, QUAKE springboarded off of it's cousin DOOM and formulated the rules of the Shooter that remain strictly enforced today. With being the first of it's kind, QUAKE is a game of absolute purity and speed. Slick as a razors edge and twice as sharp: you can almost feel it's surgical incision as you traverse it's beautifully functional level design, weild it's mathematical precise weaponry and do battle with it's unprecdented opponents.
Reading this, QUAKE may come across as more of an algorithm than a game. But it's biggest feature, as well as it's best one, is it's heart. It is clear that the game is a labor of passion created by geniuses. QUAKE's aesthetic finds itself in the deepest recess of a Lovecraftian nightmare, playing host to ornate keeps haunted by demonic servants of a dark god. When pitted against overwhelming and brutal hordes of monsters clearly on their home turf, QUAKE is a game that will surely send a twang of fear up the spine and a shot of adrenaline into the heart of all gamers, regardless of their tenure.
So, as a gamer, you owe it to yourself to experience this paradigm changing piece of art. If you fancy yourself a Warrior-God of Shooters who feels that you can best any challenge that the industry has thrown at you in the proceeding 20 years, play it on hard. I have to admit, this game's starting to grow on me.
That doesn't mean I'm ignoring it's flaws though.
First of all, because of the game's poor optimization for modern PCs, you have to set the resolution EVERY.  TIME.  YOU START THE GAME.  And the max resolution is only 1280 x 720.  Also, to enable the ability to look vertically and diagonally, you have to press ` to enter the game console and type in "+Mlook" and to get the crosshair back, you'll have to type in "Crosshair 1".  Again, you have to do this EVERY.  TIME.  YOU ENTER THE GAME.
This port also does not come with the game's soundtrack which many people are♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off about, BUT honestly I think this is a good thing.  The atmosphere is impressive and honestly the lack of soundtrack really brings that out.  And while the soundtrack is amazing, I still say that the game is better off without it.  It just doesn't really fit in for me.
Also, there's something I have against the enemies and weapons.  Whilst there is a lot of them and they are rather entertaining, the game seems to have a strong habit of constantly throwing fat shreks with chainsaws and grenade launchers in literally every corridor, and it gets really samey and repetetive at times.
With the weapons, I can't help but feel like some of them are completely worthless.  For instance, you start out with the shotgun on level 1, and you progress onto level 2 and all of a sudden you have the Double-Barrel shotgun, which is basically Quake's faster version of DOOM 2's Super Shotgun which immediately renders the normal shotgun completely worthless.
Some would argue that DOOM 2 did the exact same thing yet I disagree; the normal shotgun in DOOM 2 had much more range compared to the Super Shotgun and still did a decent amount of damage, but the shotgun in Quake becomes completely forgettable with it's apaulling amount of damage against most enemies in the game.
Hell, the exact same thing happens for The Nailgun and the Grenade Launcher!  They all get replaced by more powerful copies of their own self, a la the Super Nailgun and the Rocket Launcher.
This was just my thoughts on it though, you guys probably completely disagree with me.  I just feel as though they could have made some of the weapons in the game actually worth something and not have to be thrown away as completely useless later on.
And what the ♥♥♥♥ is the story?  Am I just some dude in some weird places killing random living creatures native to the area because he's a psychopath who enjoys blood, gore and murder?  Until you lot give me the full story, that's what I'm going with.
Also, the graphics occasionally give me headaches.  Just sayin'.
Right, I like the gunplay, it feels really great.  Actually, the combat in general is really satisfying (minus the melee weapon, the axe) through and through.
The enemy design is really creative, especially for the zombies and each map, despite all having the same atmosphere, all feels unique and different.
Like I said, the atmosphere is brilliant.
Also, that ♥♥♥♥ing Shambler.  The ♥♥♥♥ing shambler.  Scary af.
So overall, despite having ♥♥♥♥ loads of flaws as of today, Quake still remains to be a fun game and of moderate challenge.
Still though,
My happiness is equal to the fast gameplay of this materpiece.

Quake is a single-player and multiplayer FPS developed by id software and released 1996. It got quite infamous and is recognised today as classic. It was one of the first FPS to fully use polygons to create game enviroment and established multiplayer over Internet on PC.
So, how Steam was handled? It's pretty straight copy-paste. Copy-paste of game folder. Not of game's CD. And that means that music is not just not working, but it's not even included to begin with! You will have to find somewhere soundtrack or music files or CD to get it back. And if mounting CD will not work for you, then I would recommend getting music files and _inmm software to fix it. And even then it looped too early. Soundtrack is quite important in this game, even though I have a bad feeling that most remember this Quake without it.
Now, when you launch the game you will be given the choice between running Quake or Quakeworld. You also will have to choose between Software and OpenGL versions of each.
Quake, also known as WinQuake, is actually a Windows-compilated version of Quake. There wasn't much difference. It's for both Single-player and multiplayer.
QuakeWorld is stricly competive multiplayer. This client was released some time after Quake and was intented to make it more playable on low-speed Internet modems back then. Different way of handling server-client relations.
Software is original Quake rendering. Pixelated, gritty and dark. Lo-fi. I recommend playing game in this mode on low resolution, like in DOS release, it captures Quake feel better than most other fans Source Port. Or OpenGl.
OpenGL mode was added some time after game's release and made use of new-by-then hardware 3D accelration. And well, it's not pretty. First, it lacks some features when it comes to lighting. There is no such thing is "brighter than grey" and there are no special textures that are always full-bright. And then the main point of this mode if to make game look more high-resolution. By making every texture look muddy and uglier, actually. I mean, you can like such thing only if you really hate pixels.
And last thing, once you start playing, write "+mlook" command in console, that you can open with "`" keyboard key. This will enable mouselook. Why it's not part of game's options I don't know, especially seeing how demos make use of mouse in such way.
Plot of single-player is once again simple: There is unknown enemy that was given codename "Quake", who teleports it's army through slipgate. And now that your base was overrun, you have to make use of slipgate to travel to other otherwordly dimension, find out who "Quake" actually is through intermission text and then kick it's butt in most gimmicky way. And then watch the oh so epic bright ending in form text where you are told "id software salutes you".
That pretty much means that you got 4 episodes to choose from beggining, you lose equpment in beggining of each one, the first level of each episode is base themed and actually has unique enemies and then you are off to medieval-like setting.
And yes, when it comes to single-player, one of the best things Quake got to offer was atmosphere. Gritty. Dark. Well, ugly brown at times. you fight some kind of monsters in their low polygonal details. You get weapons like nailgun. It just has a bit of lovecraftian inspiration to it. There are even traps placed here and there. Bloody bloody traps. Soundtrack, while small, contributes a lot to it. And then there are some maps in Episode 4 which play strong on lights blinking or shadows being pitch dark, all in small rooms. Quake is at it's best in such levels. I am pretty sure that people who thought that Doom was scary back then were blown by Quake.
And when you look at more gameplay side of it, well, on theory it should be like Doom but worse. It's slower. Physics are slightly worse, you stop completely upon encountering walls. There is less variety in weapons, even though they introduces grenade launcher, yet some weapons are just direct upgrades to others. Like, Super Shotgun isn't even good at close range, not as much as Super Nailgun. Just something when you run out of ammo on other weapons. There aren't as many enemies, nor as much of variety. You can say that half of Quake gameplay is shooting two rockets at the Ogre, who has grenade launcher and chainsaw. Or shooting 4 times with Super Shotgun at them. And it's too grey at times.
But somehow game pulls through and becomes quite fun. Even if there are less enemies on the levels, it got quite a nice combat to it. And for a game that is supposed to be rushed, level design is great. It got verticality, it is mazey but not too complex, it just has floors on top of each other, fully embracing the fact that game is fully 3D now.
You would think that first introduction to fully polygonal world would be quite underwhelming. That it will underuse it and later games will make it better. But no, Quake still has some good layouts, better than many later games. Should thank that talents at id software were still thinking in abstarct ways, didn't try to be as realistical as Build engine games like Duke Nukem 3D.
It still got some weak points though. Like, Vores, spiders-like demons who shoot homing missiles. Actually, their missiles track players so good, that one corner is not enough to stop them and you can't circlestrafe around them. I don't understand what is the point, what kind of tactic developers wanted to use there. That, and game underdelivers on boss departament. There are only two "proper" bosses in the whole game. And when I say "proper", I actually just mean gimmicky ones.
As for Deathmatch and duel parts, the multiplayer side, well, it's not so good. It made multiplayer over Internet more mainstream and common, yes. But the game balance, it doesn't age too well. It's only good on high-level of play, but same can be said about many games. Yes, it's not Quake-exclusive quality, don't tell me.
You mostly have to dominate arena by grabbing most powerful weapons and powerups. Red Armor is better than any other armor, as it not only gives more armor points, but actually is more effective too. Rocket Launcher shoot quite fast missiles which are too quick to avoid properly. It's also most powerful weapon and most used one. Aside from lighting gun, which is good alternative too. Things die fast there.
So, you just have to grab superior weapons and powerups and then go roflstomp everything else, including those who just spawned in.
It gets even better once you realize that players are actively exploiting glitches in physic engine, like bunnyhopping and voodoo-like strafejumping, thigns that don't make a single sense. It become a standard nowadays, thus creating an artificial barrier between high-level and low-level players, where you have to practice much more than you should have to be as good and have some fighting chances.
So yea, casuals should avoid. Normal players should avoid.
You will have ot use server finders on Internet. And then chances are, there will be barely anybody playing. But then, most still play Quake for duels, so it must not be big issue.
Still better than Valve's Deathmatch Classic.
So yea, game's quality itself is good, but not groundbreaking. Just good game. But what made Quake so overpraised is technical side. The engine. First, it introduced console. Then it allows you to record demos, thus creating competiveness where players try their best and creating some kind of "public". Then when you combine it with glitchy physics, you will see how Speedrunning was created. And then multiplayer was more focused on Internet public. And even better, game allowed more modding abilities, much more than in original Doom. And then it allowed modding in multiplayer. Thus creating Team Fortress mod, for example. And Capture the Flag mode too.
So, yes. Technical amazement, good single-player and finey multiplayer. This is the first Quake.

**Edited after the "Open Beta" fiasco..
O:ND is a big, beautiful, weird and wild world of a game with absolutely huge potential.  As an early Beta release, it had the trappings of all the latest & greatest of survival games and a whole swath of immersive content yet to come.
As it is now,the latest release is mistakenly called "Open Beta".  A small "woops" from the devs, because you have to own the game - but frankly, that's what you should be doing anyway.
From the moment you crash-land on "Proteus 2", you're frankly buggered. It's daytime in the desert, and your suit is leaking air.
Luckily you've got some duct tape!  But night will be drawing in soon, you need to grab what you can from the wreckage of your landing pod and hightail it to the nearest firm ground before the local fauna start taking a very unhealthy interest in you..
That first night, squatting sadly in your tiny survival dome, perched on some ignominious mound of dirt a million miles from help and surrounded by a bunch of alien nightmares hell-bent on your demise, it's easy to think "Heck, this is too much.  I give up."
In fact, you'll be thinking that more than once, because Osiris: New Dawn is NOT an easy game if you play it on the current default settings.  So a word to the wise: at the time of writing, you'll be best served to dial down the creature spawn/toughness settings to their lowest just to get time to explore and enjoy the breathtakingly beautiful world that Fenix Fire have created.
It has to be said - there's a fair amount of grind involved at the moment.  A lot of "chisel work" is required, running around mining metal nodes and fending off indignant monsters, before you can start building the various structures you need to make life a bit easier - and safer.
But it's SO worth the effort.  The moment you've finally found enough Plutonium to build your first "Forge" and start refining  metal ores into ingots, is the moment you actually start to believe you might indeed have a chance to survive this beautiful nightmare.  And the day you're finally able to put the crude makings of a proper habitat into the ground.. well, I can't explain how relieved that made me at least.
This is a stonking, challenging, huge undertaking.  A diamond in the rough, which I would encourage and urge you all to buy into because this gem is going to be a game-changer in its genre.

I was originally a bit sceptical of this game--I thought it couldn't live up to the hype and acclaim. Only now, having just finished it, can I say the modest expectations I had (to spare any disappointment) were completely blown out of the water: this game is a polished, immersive, enthralling, emotive, extremely enjoyable piece of work. The characters are all great, aided by the strength of the narrative: so many things were completely unpredictable, and I was pleasantly surprised to feel such vehement notions of betrayal, fear, intimidation, and vanity. Best of all, the game allows you to follow a strict moral code, but still feel like you're getting the full experience: initially, I felt it unneccessarily cruel to kill any guards, so I went the non-lethal route for the first half of the game. But then, after being betrayed and brutalised, I felt it was perfectly canon to start a killing spree, given the anger Corvo would have felt.
Secondly, it would be a disservice not to mention the awesome combat and stealth mechanics this game has to offer. I rarely felt cheated, and the game offers you PLENTY of opportunity to be creative and give yourself the upperhand: besides the typical dialogue decisions, Dishonored offers the player numerous routes, executions, takedowns, and combat maneuvers that helped keep gameplay fresh and exciting. Given the amount of freedom, I wouldn't be surprised if this game could enable several variant playthroughs that would all be as captivating as the last. Exploring, too, gives you a huge one-up on confrontations, and if you're dedicated enough, will almost always reward you with (a) hidden item(s) either in a safe, nook, or any other elusive place.
Overall, this game is really for anybody looking for a fun and different alternative to your average first person or stealth game, and if you buy it, trust me, you will not regret it.

TL;DR the game is hard but fun. It is true there is no tutorial but mechanics are easier than easy to understand. Play on the easiest difficulty for a 10 hour practice.
As simple as the game may seem from the pictures, it is not.
Starting off the game there is no tutorial, which isn't as bad as it sounds seeing as this game is basically Age of Empires with zombies. The mechanics are easy to understand and get used to within the first 10 minutes of playing.  You have a town hall that allows you to build everything needed. You need workers to build more complex things. You need a food income as well as gold, wood, power, etc. It is everything you'd expect to need if you have ever played something similar.
The hard part are the zombies. Even while playing on the most easiest level with the lowest population of zombies, it took me 3 tries, equalling to about 11 hours in total, before I won. Again, on the easiest level. Which may not even count anyways seeing as to unlock the next map you need to win the game on a harder difficulty.
So what makes the zombies so hard, you're asking? Well once in a while the game will warn you about a zombie horde that is coming towards your town and will give you a direction, North, South, East and West, that they are coming from. Each horde getting bigger and bigger, while only providing a few in game hours in advance to prepare.
If a zombie infects one of your building, the people working in that building become infected. Meaning that if even one zombies gets past your defenses and manages to destroy anything, you might as well as start over because it will spread so quickly you wont have any time to react.
**Ending Spoiler**
Providing you make it past all that and make it to day 150 (if playing on the easiest difficulty like me) the game will warn you that billions of zombies are coming from every direction all at once. This is the hardest part because there is no quit and load last save. I even tried to end process in task manager and it loaded me back right to where I was. This means that all of your hard work could be destroyed by zombies within a few seconds if you do not properly defend.

Quell puts a variation on the sokoban game genre. It is an abstract puzzle with sequential-movement solutions, on a grid, which only allows sliding movements. You have to collect all of the 'pearls' in a level to proceed to the next and it challenges you to do it in as few movements as possible. It features mechanics such as matching push blocks, hazardous spikes and levers to rotate them, appearing blocks, which trigger when passed over, teleportation, off-grid movements, hidden jewels collecting. It also comes with background music and although it's only a single continuous loop it works wondrously with the combination of other game sounds to create a relaxing atmosphere. It features a reward system for your correct solutions and any hidden gems that you find throughout the game, which you can then use for hints on more difficult levels.
Overall, it's a casual game, but still offers a modest challenge and lots of fun elements!

Absolutely spectacular game. I’ve been playing it for years on iOS, and the PC version is even more beautiful.
Quell is an amazingly designed and polished puzzle game that starts with a very simple premise. You control a drop of water, and you must move the drop around to collect all of the Pearls in each level, except once you move the drop, it does not stop until it hits a wall. These basic gameplay mechanics make for some very well designed and challenging levels. The game then slowly adds more rules and mechanics to add to the challenge.
This is a game that is definitely worth it any price tag, and I would recommend you pick it up today. Even if you’re not normally into puzzle games, you may be surprised how much you will enjoy Quell.
From its artwork, to its music, to the pure level of polish this game has, it is by far one of the best puzzle games available.
If you’ve played Quell and liked it, check out the two sequel games: Quell Reflect, and Quell Memento, which add even more new mechanics and put a fun twist on an already awesome game.

Giving this game a chance by buying it on sale right after reading all the negative reviews I gotta say, most of the trash talk about this game couldn't be farther from the truth.
I'm into squad based 3rd person cover to cover shooters. I loved the Mass Effect series, played spec ops the line too lately and some other's I'm not bothering to remember. Yet those never fulfilled my expectations when it came to a good challenge, or actually having an advantage in keeping an eye on your squad and opportunities to flank the enemy.
This game offers a very cleverly implemented cover and flanking system, much alike that on the XCOM series, that people mistake for lack of AI performance. Which in fact isn't.
Instead of a boring battle experience that makes you keep safe as long as you're behind cover(same for your squad), where once in a while a grenade may or may not force you to move from cover, making you take a scratch in your armor for moving exposed; The Bureau XCOM punishes you every second you don't actually order your squad and play with them. It forces you not to just be lazy and do all the work while your squadmates storm through them.
By this I'm not saying that you have to make an exhaustive control over everything while being striped away from all the fun in fights. There's a balance between both elements. And every battlefield offers good chance to make really effective flanking maneuvers that once being set in motion, you can let your squad do their job while you can relax shooting some enemies yourself.
It works pretty much like this:
If you just stay behind cover, fighting a trench to trench war - your squad mates will die, plain and simple. Which, in my point of view is pretty rational since the aliens are packing much more advanced tech.
If you use your squad and understand the need to maneuver them effectively while using the best cover available, you'll be just fine in every difficulty you with to play. Oh and there are also some pretty tough bosses that will make you sweat if you don't apply that same cover and flank philosophy with zeal on them.
Also, the story was a bit of a let down at the start with all those American 50's clichés and all that "borderline" depressive alcoholic agent with a dark past, but it starts getting better and better as you move on until you're hooked.
I was kind of expecting the XCOM series to have a game like this to be honest. And although I feel that they could exploit the mission system a little bit better like in the previous XCOM title making the war map feel a little less empty, making you feel the actual weight of the invasion, I feel this is definitely worth it. Not an all time under-rated gem that will live forever in the History of videogames. But it's a great under-rated and unfairly misunderstood game.
I recommend it. If you like to actually put some effort in fights, do it. If you were expecting it to be like mass effect where your companions are all programmed to do all those fancy auto attacks and skills while you just stay put and shoot, then in that case it might not be for you.

Hello!
Welcome to my review on Osiris: New Dawn, this game is one of my favorite games, despite all the reviews you might read about it being too buggy or too laggy. I will address why I believe this game should be reviewed in a better manner and fashion. Without further talk, lets get right into it!
Osiris is (at this time) an early access release of the game, similar to that of Rust and the Forest.  With that said, the game is expected to be cheaper now, so if you have read all the reviews, and want this game, buy it while its cheap, if you're going to buy it on steam. BUT anyways, back to the real discussion, what is Osiris? This game IS a survival, crafting, multiplayer/singleplayer, multi-planet traveling game where mining different types of nodes and resources is vital to your survival, in a harsh environment similar to that of Mars. With that said, you can expect water to be scarce, sand to be very common, and crazy sci-fi aliens to be on this game.  Early game, you can loot the spawnable crates to get assessed with the appropiate materials to survive the game, these crates will glow a blue-ish color when you put your cursor on them. Following this, you will have basic missions to get started, and depending if you're on a multiplayer server with players, you can usually get a response from them if you need help, a great way to get started.  As you get into the game you will find that there are currently two mines where you can get specific resources and continue on fourth through the game. Later game you will find yourself making vehicles, and advanced types of bases including laboratories, biodomes, and other such structures. At this point, you will likely play between 10-30 hours, depending on how fast you grip the game and if you play with friends.
I know you might be familar with most of these reviews by now with mixed opinions if you read most of them already, but I want to assure you, theres a solution for most of these. I will go by solving some of the major issues people have with the game, and how to fix the game.
1. The game is too laggy, and I get low FPS even though I'm on a good PC, type of reviews.
Yes, the game is laggy even on GOOD PC's at times, I myself have a GTX 1080 and an i7-6700k, which if you know tech, is not a bad rig at all (mines about $2100 total). I find that public servers are a bit laggy if a LOT of people are logged on or played on the server. I believe this is due to a lack of server restarts or entity removals, but it seems to be the amount of players that effect this.
, as I said above, I do have a solution for this!
Theres a few options:
A. If you're planning to just play with friends, create a private universe.  These servers have NEVER lagged for me as much as public servers, I remained at 60 FPS (V-Sync isnt disable-able), and have only lagged once on here for a brief few minutes, thats all. I recommend trying this if you have a friend you want to play this with. NOTE: It MIGHT not work if you have special characters in your name, and once its made it cant be deleted, but can be edited. Also, there is a way to invite people, so just continue looking if you cant find it.
B. If you're planning to play alone with no one else, I recommend trying singleplayer. I have never played singleplayer, but I am nearly positive it is less laggy than some of the public servers, and is worth trying. This is a good way to gain a better experience with the game, as you find that playing it is more harsh and adventurous, without someone telling you how to play it the whole time.
C. If you're planning to make new friends, try joining a public server with players, sometimes they don't actually lag. If it does occur that it is lagging, I recommend just finding a new one, each server is different when it comes to lag, not all of them lag though, I promise. You can also go on the forums to find friends to play with if this isnt working or if you want to play with experienced people.
D. If none of these are working you can always read the guides made by the community and the developers (I believe), to help make the game as least laggy as possible.
2. The game is very buggy, why is it so buggy, I didnt expect it to be like this, type of reviews.
Yes, this is true, the game is buggy, but not as buggy as some people might exaggerate it to be. With the experience I had playing the game, the only really bad bug I went across made me lose my hover bike due to something I did, a quite dumb bug but still caused me to loose both my stuff and the bike. Even though there might be one or two bugs that can occur, none of them should be bad enough to make you want to leave the game, most are the little things. Each update I see, the devs strive to get rid of these bugs. My suggestion and recommendation to you is to report these bugs on the steam forums, this doesnt take more then a minute of your time and it benefits not only you but thousands of other people this might come across to. Nothing has really caused me to loose my temper due to a bug on the game, and I dont remember this occuring to the five friends I have that also play, so I dont even recommend considering this one too much.
3. The game doesnt have water, I cant find any geysers, where is are some of the resources I cant find any, type of reviews.
No, actually this isnt true, all of these are possible to find when you start playing and understanding the game. Some of the stuff mentioned above is found in mines or in special places, further down the map. The reason this is an inconvienance to most people is because they are forgetting the fact that this is a some what realistic game where everything you need might not be so easy to access. This type of harsh environment is what makes this game so unique, and a great experience. As far as water goes, it is accessable from sap trees, simply click a sap tree with an empty glass container and you get complex liquid, this is pretty much water. These trees usually spawn near the front of where your spawn area is, there very tall with a soft purple spike type of leaf.  When it comes to food, just hit trees to get berries, or cook alien meat, its rather simple really. And for those resources like geysers or rubber and special minerals such as carbon, lead, lithium, you can search the mines for these or the map. If you're still having trouble you can just check the wiki online or use guides on the steam forums, they can be helpful for starters.
I do recommend this game if you have had good experiences with survival/multiplayer/crafting/space related games or just like these topics. Also, I want to again mention that it maybe best to buy it while it is cheap, which is now because it is early access. And as a final note I want to reflect upon the developers with their constant hard work on making this such a good game, there a good team of developers.
Thanks for reading my review, I was 100% honest so do put this review into consideration when it comes to buying the game, I dont spend this long typing for no reason.

If anyone here has played dead frontier, they know why I bought this game.
First off, the game isn't actually open world. The 'open world' map is actually just a hub. NPCs give you various quests that teleport you to different locations should you accept them. When you complete the quests you get teleported back to the hub.
The story isn't very compelling at all. The first NPC Kovac just keeps giving you quests that feel more like tutorials than anything else. The quests were boring enough and the 'open world' concept was disappointing enough to make me quit after a few hours of forcing myself to play it.
The combat system on the other hand, is actually nice. It's almost how i wanted the combat to be. The crafting system is simple enough. I didn't think anything of it. Same with the hunger system.
Last of all, the survival part of the game isn't that deep (even though I would have wanted it to be). You don't need rest, which makes no sense. I think a mechanism for resting is an integral part of a survival game. And I've already stated what I needed to about the hunger (and thirst) system.
As for the art style, it's nice, nothing special, but just nice.
All in all, the only part i actually liked about the game was its combat. I was indifferent toward the survival aspect because I'd have cared about it if the story and the quests themselves had been compelling enough to keep me playing the game in the first place.

How to Survive 2, a nice fresh twist in to the survival horror crafting and basebuilding ganre. If you are in to top down shooters but olso love to feel progression, then this is the game for you. I have played a couple of survival horror open world games with crafting and basebuilding elements but this game is a nice refreshing snack im currently enjoying.
Dont get me wrong, tha game is good ! but needs to be fixed an example is the gameplay it would need some tweaking. Im talking SERIOUSE, a couple examples are the following: there is NO twisting of the camera perspective, this makes raiding houses at night at a higher level VERRY TENSE. The lack of visual controll (the camera) can be frustrating at times but the feel of reward you get once completing a quest if verry satisfying. Next are the character models, the weapons and pets. From my experiance the weapons (Bow, Crossbow, Pistol, Assault Rifle & Normal Rifle) ALL HAVE THE SAME SKINS just a different name a higher damage output once u go up some levels, as a former gamedeveloper i have to note that is just simply lazy. Add some new variants of the original weapon, and put them on the higher tiers of the same weapon (this will make the build worth it !) Next to that is the placement of the weapons on the character, they are not possitioned correctly, the crossbow for example is placed in a way wich blocks off the right arm.. It feels illogical sometimes and can be painfull to whitness. Plus the fact that your able to carry 250 arrows WITHOUT a quiver amazes me, mind u its a "survival game" and this game lacks depth in the sense that the character lacks the items or the weapons to represent the "survival feel" next to that are the regurtitation of assets.. Most levels are the same, and could use some seriouse varriation.
The game "feels" like a grindfest from time to time, once you gain the gear you want there are NO other VISUAL differances in the weapons u have (same for the armours).. From level 1 till 30 it is all the same (what i have experiance so far). In a nutshell you go out in a open world to find quest givers, they unlock missions with loot that you need to build a base in the open world and weapons or armour for your char. The quests are instance based, so you CAN do coop missions, or both do the same mission in a different instance. We end up in seperate instances most of the time tho !, simply couse we get more loot that way?. These simple things are counter intuitive to the "coop survival basebuilding" ganre and could easely be fixed with some time, effort and ofcourse thinking with the correct mindset....
The DLC and pets are pretty much a waste of money, they make you look different exept for the dlc with the missions. that one actually adds something of value. The pets however dont do annything exept scare the cr*p out of you when its night time and u can barely see. It would be nice to see a function to the pets, like the crow making a distinct sound when a enemy is near (just an idea).
To summerise,

Heres recipe for pie
MAKES: one 9-inch pie
3 pounds mixed apples (such as Granny Smith, Gala and McIntosh)
2/3 cup granulated sugar
2 tablespoons fresh lemon juice
6 tablespoons unsalted butter
1 tablespoon all-purpose flour, plus more for dusting
3/4 teaspoon ground cinnamon
1/8 teaspoon salt
2 disks dough for Basic Crust
1 large egg, beaten
Coarse sugar, for sprinkling
Peel and core the apples; slice 1/4 inch thick. Toss with the granulated sugar and lemon juice. Heat 4 tablespoons butter in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add the apples and cook, stirring, until tender, about 10 minutes. Stir in the flour, cinnamon and salt; cook until thickened, 1 more minute. Let cool.
Roll out 1 disk of dough into a 12-inch round on a floured surface; ease into a 9-inch pie plate. Add the apples, mounding them slightly in the center, and dot with the remaining 2 tablespoons butter. Roll out the remaining dough into a 12-inch round. Lay it over the filling; press the edges of the crusts together, then fold the overhang under itself and crimp to seal. Brush with the beaten egg and sprinkle with coarse sugar. Cut a few slits in the top crust. Chill 1 hour.
Place a baking sheet on the lowest oven rack and preheat to 425 degrees F for 30 minutes. Place the pie on the hot baking sheet; lower the temperature to 375 degrees F. Bake until golden, 1 hour to 1 hour, 10 minutes. (Cover the edges with foil if they brown too quickly.) Cool on a rack.

Quake is a classic FPS that, alongside Doom, helped Id Software codify the genre. How, I don't know, because Quake is an unbelievably boring game.
The game's plot is, ostensibly, about fighting the Lovecraftian Old God Shub-Niggurath as she does... things. Which are bad. Quasi-demonic invasion from beyond the veil of space. As a Lovecraft fan this would seem rather encouraging... if in practice the game had any real plot at all. In practice the game is almost gleefully self-aware in how much its plot is a thin excuse to commit mass murder.
Quake's "story" is broken up into four Episodes, of which I have admittedly only played the first two. The difference between the two seems to mostly be the upgrade of a single enemy type, and a slightly different wall texture. Any actual plot developments are mostly limited to easily-missed text blurbs at the end of each Episode, which mostly just seem to foreshadow the final boss.
Gameplay-wise, Quake is a tedious, linear run-and-gun set in an endless parade of largely identical brown hallways against the same five brown enemies (with a few exceptions, like the odd miniboss and the very rare "Base" levels featuring soldiers and dogs, all similarly brown), in levels that offer no trace of setting, motivation, or purpose besides a playground to kill things on. The entire game could be proceedurally generated and you'd never notice.
The combat itself is rather annoying. You're equipped with three main ammo types throughout the game - shotgun shells, nails, and rockets - and have two weapons for each, the second being a straight upgrade of the first (except for the grenade launcher and rocket launcher, which have different firing methods with different situational uses). In theory this weapon selection is servicable, but in practice it's rather lacking. Shotguns are the mainstay weapons of the game, probably to minimize the need to actually aim. Nailguns are vastly more effective weapons, basically being automatic weapons that have a degree of aim-assist to them, however their ammo is considerably more sparse and is burnt through much more quickly.
None of this is really a dealbreaker, the truly annoying part is that this game is old enough to have multiple floors overlapping one another, but functionally lack the ability to look up or down. Star Wars: Dark Forces had a similar conundrum mostly solved by the fact that most weapons would aim up or down for you in a limited cone, and your enemies had similar limitations. However, in Quake the most common enemy by far is the Ogre, a stocky brute with a middling level of health and equipped with a chainsaw and a grenade launcher. Bullets shoot straight, but grenades arc with gravity and bounce around corners. Cue every single level filled to the gills with Ogres on high ledges where as often as not you can't hit them, but they will gleefully pelt an endless stream of grenades down on your head.
Don't make the mistake of me blaming my dislike of this game on it's difficulty. I died plenty, but I'm describing the game's combat as "annoying," not "difficult." Quake's uncomplicated setup makes it difficult for anything to become legitimately unbalanced, but managable does not mean fun. And when you take combat that isn't particularly fun, a plot that barely exists, and repetitive, bland aesthetics, you get a game that has essentially no merits to recommend.

It's a game that has a lot of potential, but also has a lot of mechanics that need polishing.
First off,  the basic tutorials are written fairly well.  Learning the basic mechanics of the game are no problem, and as such it's fairly easy to get going.  On top of that, you really start gaining momentum as you efficiently start exploring the map.  However, learning the finer points of the game are what's difficult as they're not really covered.  For instance, it doesn't cover using cannons and swivel guns,  nor are items like the pile of books and the hand weight really explained in the tooltips whether they're just decoration or serve an actual purpose.  Other than that, some items like the ship wheel and sails are listed very well, with their effects directly listed.
The leveling system is very well executed, with every point feeling like it has an impact and most skills feeling useful in one way or another.  Alternatively, some skills feel outright useless.  For instance, learning a skill like 20 strikes, ace, et cetera, doesn't seem to do anything.  The tutorial don't explain how to activate them, and the crew doesn't seem to use it automatically, making the point and money spent on the skill, useless.
With ship construction, it's mostly well executed.  You have pretty free reign on building a ship, leaving wide possibilities on how to structure it.  The converse, however, is the AI.  If you a roof of some kind (to protect from cannons) the crewmembers with cleaning suddenly don't do their job, half the time the AI gets stuck climbing a single block leading to some not boarding an enemy vessel, so on and so forth.
More on the AI however, it's a double-edged sword.  They're pretty good about staying on land/ship, however I've seen instances of a grappling hook not leading properly and them falling into sea, or getting hit by an enemy and continuously sliding backward halfway across the island straight into the water, having to put in a crew command 2-3 times for everyone to comply, and this applies to all crew members, regardless of traits.
In all, it's a good game, but it still needs cleaning and polishing for its potential to truly shine.  The AI needs tweaking, the descriptions and tooltips need more description, and the tutorials need an advanced section to cover finer mechanics.  Also, the wiki is crap at the moment, so learning by doing is required beyond the tutorial. 7/10

I'd really like a neutral review for this one.
It works, it's playable, it's looks clean and kind of elegant, plays decently....
But it's one of those flash physics puzzle games made in 3D, and this adds very little but introduces a few issues. Since the blocks are not locked on a 2D planes, they can wander off outside the puzzle (towards or away from the camera). Also, a lot of puzzles don't have a solution so much as having a timing/luck factor to them. For example, you could do the right moves 20 times and get 20 different outcomes, and only succeed once.
This to me is really what makes this a negative review rather than a positive one. It's a puzzle game, but the puzzles don't really have solutions. It's just messing around with pieces until that cube decides on its own that it will fall into the right spot.

Note:  Got this game as part of an Indiegala bundle.
This game is a Simplistic Physics Cube game where you need to land the red cube in the highlighted area of the screen.  Your cursor shows you the number of cube 'deletions' you can perform per level, and the spacebar resets the level back to the beginning (rather cool reset animations btw).  The background music is realitively relaxing, but seems to be on a quick loop and began to become slightly annoying even after the 0.2 hours I've played.
You'll find that the game relies heavily on the physics and that can be a problem.  With the short time I've played, I've encountered the issue where the same move (on stationary objects) often yields different results.  Sometimes it will take me three times to perform the same level reset / move, and on the 3rd try the red cube lands in the goal area.  The first two, well, it didn't work.  This makes for unbalanced gameplay, since a move you thought would work didn't, and it may leave you scratching your head thinking performing the same move on the next go around would have it landing in the same place (which it doesn't).  Perhaps this won't be such an issue later on as the levels are more about the cubes falling mid-air during gameplay.
Another gripe is that the cube could land in the general area goal on the screen, but the cube can 'fall forward' infront of everything, and that doesn't count.  The game appears to be in a 2D style but the cubes can fall in 3D directions, putting the red cubes out of play.
Also, my firewall shows this game reporting back to 34.224.134.130:443 after a few seconds in.  There doesn't appear to be any online functionality, so I'm not sure what's being reported back or why for that matter.  I've blocked the outgoing communications without any adverse side effects.
In the current state, I don't highly recommend this game until the physics issues and the reporting back are addressed, but it could be a fun game to waste time to in the future.  I look forward to more updates and updating my review!

I was originally planning on writing this only giving the three most interesting endings to shoot for and giving it a rating of ever-so-slightly entertaining, but after 100%ing it, I must say you should get at least 1 ending for all dates so you can go through the bonus fulfill the wish story. Don't let the fact you're going through the standard intro yet again bore you into quitting- the story diverges greatly from what you've played, and actually gets very interesting (assuming you can suspend you disbelief at the level the novel asks you to). Yeah, there are a few misspellings and instances of poor grammar (just as with the rest of the game). But, if you're willing to do that, and don't mind linearity, then yes, this is worth the full price. If not...
The normal game does a good job deconstructing the high school dating visual novel cliches, and the fact you're a human girl vying for the affections of a bird only adds a bit more humor to it. There's a fast-forward feature that skips to the next day or decision, so replays aren't that painful. My favorite endings in the standard game are the ones for the Fallen Angel, best Track Star, and best Doctor. If you're not willing to go through all the endings and don't want to go through the bonus story, then I'd wait for it to go on sale. If you're more of a completionist, I'll say it again- I was very impressed by the bonus story, and completely taken by surprise that the writers could craft some junkfood for the mind that good. The bonus epilogue isn't that good, so it's up to how much of a completionist you are if you shoot for that as well. But the bonus story is worth the money and the effort of unlocking it.

The game is an excellent specimen from the origins of the fps genre; abstract level design, high-octane action, ammo and HP management, key-based progression, and switches and traps everywhere.
THAT SAID, Quake 1 in particular relies very heavily on its excellent atmospheric soundtrack, which (due to technical limitations) isn't included in the steam version. Luckily, there are workarounds, so I still recommend this purchase if you have reason to believe you'll like it.
Workaround A: You can get the free "Dark Places" source port (a sort of "engine upgrade" if you will) online, find the game soundtrack online (in .ogg format) and put it in steamapps\common\quake\Id1\sound\cdtracks. It'll need to be named "Track002.ogg" to "Track011.ogg".
Workaround B: Acquire (e.g. burn) a real physical CD of the game and put it in your drive while you play.
I obviously recommend workaround A.

As much as I want to give Early Access games all the patience I can to perform well, I have to make an exception for Osiris, especially for the price. I play several other EA games that are leagues more enjoyable and balanced and cost less, too. I want this game to do well, but at the moment, this thing is a train wreck. The following is from a single-player perspective:
On the surface, this game is very lovely and has a lot of really cool ideas for a space survival/crafting game. Unfortunately, as we have all learned from the No Man's Sky incident, a pretty face and cool ideas cannot make all the grinding and repetion go away.
At its current state, this game is frustrating and unnecessarily difficult to the point of being virtually unplayable. Acquisition of beginning resources takes hours of searching, smashing ores, and luck just to find what you need to get a simple plutonium forge going. Thirst depletes way too fast and getting water is impossible in the new update because the oxygen and hydrogen nodes are kilometers apart. The introduction of ingots to the game makes things even worse by pulling players even further away from the starting line. It takes far too long to get a base going, and many of the structures are just indoor/outdoor variants of the same thing.
And this is WITHOUT any monsters. Good lord, the monsters...
On the LOWEST SETTING for their health, damage, and spawn rate, about 90% of my time in this game was trying to fight off these things. They come way too frequently while I'm trying to harvest resources, there is no warning for their approach, they take to much of my health, and the game has such low speed during a fight that landing a hit can only be by sheer luck alone. Not to mention that upgrading weapons means locating resource nodes that are crawling with these OP abominations. In the end, they made the game unplayable for me.
Tl;dr: Until the developers balance out the resource distribution, thirst depletion, and nerf the hell of of the monsters so that beginning players actually have a shot, don't waste your money on this game.

I'll be up front: BRINK's promises of extensive customization and a seamless singleplayer/multiplayer experience are just so much hype, thankfully only in very specific ways. The customization of the characters isn't as detailed and indepth as several on-hand video demos pre-release made it seem to be, and the Artifical Intelligence? They're useless on non-defense objectives for the most part, since offensive teams swarm too tightly and too furiously for your disorganized AI companions to be much help.
However, BRINK's encouragement of objective focus rather than kill focused teamwork and gameplay REALLY help to make the ONLINE experience a joy: Players are more likely to assist and work together to achieve a goal than in most other team and class focused games I've played. SMARTS works great, and will be 'stolen' for use in other games, I suspect.
My advice? Buy only if interested in the theme and style of the game.
