As I wasn't expecting a typical X-COM strategy game, I could really enjoy this third person tactical shooter. It has a great, well-written story, taking place in a very detailed and atmospheric US 60's world. Even though at first the protagonists of the game seemed to be very clyche (the smoking, drinking, I-don't-give-a♥♥♥♥♥♥anti hero, the I-have-to-do-what-has-to-be-done commander, the ice queen female agent and, oh, don't forget the immigrated Nazi scientist), during the story they appear to be diverse and deep characters, with their own past, problems and motivations. Due to their interactions, the story holds some big surprises during the last third of the game...
Another big plus are the battles: All missions are unique, with scripted events, discoveries, ambushes, some horror atmosphere and a great design. I enjoyed them much more than the unpersonal, repeating missions of X:COM Enemey Within. Nevertheless, this is a subject to your own preferences. You also have to use a lot of tactic in this game, however, the action is much more intense, as your squad is right in the middle, while explosions, bullets and laser beams are flying right around you. The agents have interesting abilities, and even the developing super powers of the main protagonist are logicallay explained during the game.
A lot of people critizise that the research part and the autopsies  are held very simple in the game. Well, you are playing a SENIOR AGENT, not the BASE COMMANDER, so personally I would have wondered if I would have decided what research comes next, which alien we will cut first wide open to look after his bowel and so on. Therefore, you can talk with the scientists in the lab about their progress, watch them testing and developing new weapons (with some hilarious scenes) and interogate an outsider personally, having the chance to build up some sort of personal relationship with him (or you can beat the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of him).
To make a long story short: If you are looking for another turn-based X:COM strategy game, with all the typical elements of this series, like research, base building, autopsies, and all other base commander's responsibilities, you will not be happy with this game.
But if you want to enjoy the beginning of X:COM through the view of a senior agent, if you are happy to play through an intense and well-written story, if you want to interact with interesting characters and you like action, though tactical battles, and all that in a very authentic 60's setup, you really should give this game a try!

I tried this game at a friends for a couple of hours, loved it, then bought it. I quickly noticed it isn't worth more than $15 due to one main thing: the intelligence of your teammates. If it weren't for your teammates doing bonehead things often, like instead of, when ordered, relocating to behind a wall they go in front of it and get ♥♥♥♥ing shot down instantly, this game probably would have gotten much higher scores from critics. So far, in only the second mission that I have played, the sound glitched out half way through a mission and I could weirdly only hear a few sound effects and the sound kept doing a static glitch in and out that I have never heard before in a game. Even after restarting the game, the mission was still sound-bugged. Thankfully, the next two missions I did were not. The auto-save function during play is done kinda poorly. Whenever it autosaves, which is often, it does a hard lag-lock stutter for a second. Something else that is very annoying, sometimes my graphics settings revert back to default when I launch and I have to change them back and restart the game.
The Difficulty - There is no middle ground in the difficulty, there are four choices. It's like do I want to play just above noob mode or just below get murdered instantly mode? No medium difficulty is inexcusable in any game. especially this one, and here is why:
Your ♥♥♥♥ing teammate AI is some of the dumbest AI I have ever seen in a game. On the 3rd difficulty, veteran, they just get downed instantly in fights forcing you to go pick them up and then YOU get downed. But you have no choice because if you lose a guy that is a high rank that you have been working on for a long time, he is gone for good. And even if you command them to go to a certain spot, they will still eventually randomly reposition, meaning they stand up and take massive dmg from enemy fire while taking the stupidest route possible to their next cover, ignoring the cover they could be using to get there. But this does not always happen, thankfully. If I had known that when your teammates die they are dead permanently, I would have seriously rethought buying this game. There is nothing on this earth more frustrating than losing something you worked hard for because of the AI being the dumbest AI I have seen in a very long time in a game. Why even have perma-death when it would be stupid to accept it when it is a far superior idea to just reload a checkpoint? The only way to combat this is by setting the difficulty to level 2 out of 4. If you tell your teammate to reposition, they do not always do it intelligently. I told my guy to move to a new spot and assumed he would use the provided cover, which there was plenty of, to work his way to the spot. No. He stood up and ran across the middle of the battlefield, took massive dmg, then was downed at his new spot instantly. Having literally no choice but to run and pick him up so he didn't die and I lose him for good, I ran to pick him up and was also downed because while reviving you are exposed, and it was mission fail, restart at checkpoint.
To be fair, playing on veteran mode is entirely possible, it is just not fun at all because of how the developers decided to make your teammates ♥♥♥♥ing stupid bags of sh-t. And when it is time to gear up before a mission, there is zero point whatsoever in taking more than two seconds to know what backpacks to have your teammates wear since they are stupid as f-ck and will be often taking dmg when they should not be: A PACK THAT REDUCES ALL ENEMY DMG like the Guardian Pack! The fact that they give you the option to give them other packs is a slap in the face when you can/should only choose the one I said. And their skill trees have choices, lol. Again, if you have any brains, you will choose the skills in their trees that are going to best help them survive longer, and if they have none of those, choose skills that aim to help support you in whatever way possible or get a different squad mate.
Besides all of this ignorant programming done by blindfolded starved caged confused monkeys headbutting/jumping on typewriters, the game is actually really fun provided you are playing on "squaddie" difficulty and nothing higher, unless you are a pretentious liar who says "no man it's fine I enjoy it on the highest difficulty you just need to get better". Keep lying to yourself, queer.
On a more positive note, the whole idea of a 3rd person shooter in which you can at any time hit space bar and give orders to your teammates (which is the only thing that keeps them alive) and everyone has cool down timer skills is a great idea and when your teammates aren't doing stupid sh-t and ruining the fun, is a blast to play. When everything is going well, I find myself having a great time. The skills are cool and fun and the weapons are your standard fun fare, plus alien energy weapons which are cool and fun to use so far. It can sometimes depend on the situation, but if I had to give someone one tip about this game and one only, it would be take a short or mid-range gun like a assault rifle or shotgun, and ALWAYS keep a sniper rifle as your secondary weapon, especially if you are trying to play in veteran mode. Every head shot you can get with it, regardless of the mode you are in, is a precious thing that can turn a battle from total catastrophe and losing teammates, to a decisive victory. Yes, the sniper rifle is that important, provided you have good aim and get lucky and your dumb as rocks teammates haven’t gotten downed by the time you can snipe anything. Giving orders to your squad is very simple and intuitive and they perform what you want the first time, so no re-issuing orders are needed.
The sounds are great (minus the God awful glitch I encountered on only the second mission) and the graphics are above average, except when textures are still filling/popping in and it looks like minecraft for a few seconds. That does not happen often though, thankfully. The best part about the game are the effects which are done quite well. The mission structure and upgrade system is done well also.
Verdict:
Buy this on sale and only on sale for $15 or less. The single and only reason to avoid paying more than $15 is because the developers did not put enough care and time into making your teammates act intelligently. Instead, they are some of the dumbest AI teammates I have ever seen in a game. And that takes what could have easily been my score of 9/10 for this game and smashes it over the head with a bowling pin into a 6/10 like Daniel Plainview did to Eli at the end of the movie There Will Be Blood, which is what you will want to do to yourself after fussing about with your sub-human intelligence level AI teammates.
4/10 Ruined the game by restricting players to missions instead of letting them explore. The multiplayer is terrible too!

Rift is not any more what it was, but it's still a pretty fun game at its core. I have to say some quests in Draumheim and Tarken Glacier are among the most fun ones I have ever played in an MMO. If you are a Patron, you will have some advantages (like no more soul damage and the daily/weekly gift of currency and artifacts), and if you don't unlock earrings you will have a harder time in the game. Luckily that slot can be bought again with void stones, which are easily farmable.
The class customization with the soul system is still one of the most flexible system among the MMORPGs - maybe The Secret World has an even more flexible path -, you really can do with your character whatever you want: if you want combat pets, you can have it; if you want to be a ranged DD, you can; if you want to play a melee character, you can. Even with the cloth-wearing mage class.
So is Rift recommended? I think yes, it still is; but like every game, it has its flaws. Behind those problems there is an enjoyable game, which is - in my opinion - one of the classics of the genre with some ideas that were copied to other games, like the zone events, or the titular Rifts.

As someone with over 500 hours in this game, I think I'm qualified to say it's worth your time. Is there a lot of grinding in the end-game? Yeah, there is. But there's grinding in any MMO with end-game content. It's unavoidable. That being said, end-game will be the only thing you're grinding for. There's no grinding before you hit 65. And the leveling/questing process is one of the best I've ever seen in an MMO. I should also mention that dungeons/raids/pvp aren't the only end-game, either. There's amazing new questing zones once you hit 50, and all the current expansions are free and will remain free (though the new expac will be buy to play).
As for earring slots, they ARE pay walled. BUT, you CAN buy them if you grind out 50k voidstones (which, honestly, isn't that hard). Some of the souls are also pay walled, but any extra souls are just fluff. This game is not, and never will be, pay to win.

I recommend this game because it is a good game, but it is not without fault. In fact I was on the fence about what suggestion to choose, but i couldn't honestly say this game is bad just disappointing. I've played all the new gen paradox grand strategy games and love everyone of them. Hoi4 is by far the most disappointing one yet.
The game has been too dumbed down! Compared to Hoi3 the tech tree is anemic, combat over simplistic, and combined arms non existent. First off i love the simplification of army general orders (army group 1 attack through low countries, army group 2 attack maginot, etc) this makes the game much faster leading to more play throughs. It allows the player to focus on specific battles which are much more engaging and fun than watching an army slowing grind down the enemy WW1 style. For example it took me a month to win the spanish civil war in Hoi3, in Hoi4 it can be done in a matter of hours.  The problem lies in how those war are fought. In Hoi3 I could make sure multiple division from multiple provinces attacked at the exact same time, or 12 hours apart, etc, with air and sea support if I wanted. In Hoi4 you can only put ships in a costal province and hope they attack the right battle, same with air forces just hope they attack the right battle. The AI for both your generals and enemy generals are bugged. For your generals the will focus too much on moving troops around instead of fighting on all levels of aggressiveness. They will move troops around until they are happy with the balance of division across the front.This would be nice if they could come to some conclusion on what that balance is, because the front line is always changing the AI keeps moving troops around for no reason (enemy's capital is undefended better move the armoured division away). The enemies' Ai will always focus on the first threat it has, solely. Whoever is the first threat to the nation the AI will line up all thier troops on that border (win spanish civil war as nationalists France will line up all thier troops on your border and let Germany capitulate them in a week).
My biggest problem is the tech tree. WHY IS IT SO DUMBED DOWN! You've done an amazing job researching the real vehicles of nations that have been fleshed out. But WHY ARE ALL UNITS EQUAL! A French tank equals a German one and a Russian one etc. Across the board every tech upgrade is the same for each country. WHY! We all know thats not what happened in WW2 and in Hoi3 you could theoretically have the same units but the odds of that were very low due to the abundance of tech options in every tree. The only difference between nations are thier divisions, so WHY CAN'T YOU CHANGE THEM. Sure you can change them with army experience but without fighting you can barley get any. I like how you can use these points to upgrade equipment but the restriction to division designing is too much and unnessecary.
Diplomacy is almost non-existent. Without focus tree it is impossible to form alliances before a war. THERE IS NO ESPIONAGE NONE! Wtf seriously Wtf! There are no real diplomatic options other than to change an other nations political leanings (which op). As mentioned before all equipment is equal so getting equipment licenses are useless since the tech tree is so small that all nations can research everything regardless of size or industrailization. The political factions are too narrow and restrictive. Not all democracies, facist, communist countries are the same. Some democracies love waging war and some facist countries are total doves. So why do they all play the same. If I'm democratic France and during the horrible peace confrence mechanic one of my allies realeses a democratic Germany that still has war justification on me and my allies I can't do anything about it because we're both democracies. I have to send volunteers to the Soviet Union to conquer Germany then attack the Soviet Union, makes perfect sense. Also why do the Ai always have to follow the historical focus tree. Democractic Germany getting around the maginot and Norway invasion, This lack of dynamic gameplay leads very repetative play throughs.
There is no economy. I was very annoyed with the siders of Hoi3 but they gave you control over your county instead of building up points to change you country. I can't say much about this aspect of the game because it was entirely taken out from Hoi3. Now all we are IC buffs. Wow just wow smh.
This game is fun but extremely shallow. Its a good game but it is a terrible game compared to what came before. The shallowness combined with the increasingly exploitative DLC policy (coinciding with paradox's ipo) is really wearing on your extremely loyal fan base. I bought the most expensive pre order of this game. I never pre order games but I trusted paradox after years of amazing over achieving games and buy all the DLCs happily. This lackadaisical shilling of paradox's fan base across all its games is biting paradox in its♥♥♥♥♥at the worst time for it. The most telling comments about the game's shallowness and underwhelming DLCs is that the mods are the best way to play the game by far. Not cosmestic mods but total game overhauls that have more focus trees, more in depth tech trees, and more interesting gameplay. Get your act together paradox because this is a huge blemish on your sparkeling pedegree.

There are two kinds of people. People that want everything in gaming handed to them on a silver platter as the game holds their hand and gives them a dopamine rush for having been successful, being showered with participation awards, and people who are tired of games like that and prefer games where success comes from your own skill and dedication to the game. A majority of the bad reviews I've seen come from the first people, who say that the game sucks because they haven't beaten it yet, and gave up after 2 hours. The good reviews come from people that may not have beaten it yet, but know that the challenge is what makes the game rewarding. If you expect to win, then the win is meaningless.
None of the bad reviews complain about bugs. None of them complain about poor mechanics. They all just say "it's too hard I keep losing." Well, if you fall in the first category don't get the game. It's really fun, but you won't win often until you devise a game-winning strategy. If you fall in the latter category, get the game. It's very fun and winning is very challenging.
You will almost certainly lose the first few games. But you will learn what to do and what not to do, which units are viable and which aren't. What type of defenses to build and where. Eventually you'll beat it.

The game is pretty entertaining because the writing is good and the idea of dating pigeons is funny.  The characters are great, all with distinct personalities, including the main character.  Unlike some other dating sims, it doesn't branch off into a separate route for each character you date --instead, the new stuff for each character is interspersed between scenes common to each character... expect to be hitting the skip button a lot.  The amount of new content for each character is pretty good, though.
The real meat of the game is when you unlock the final route after completing all the other routes.  To put this in perspective, there are 15 endings (not counting an epilogue).  I read all of the dialogue out loud with my friend, using the skip button for dialogue we already saw before.  It took 10 hours to do the 14 normal routes and 6 hours to do the final route alone-- that's how big the difference is.  So make sure you do the final route, since it's a huge amount of the game and it really ties everything together well.
Where the game fell short for me was in the implementation.  There were a number of annoying technical aspects that really detracted from the game.  One was the skip button, which sometimes failed to skip past old dialogue and would also skip past new dialogue.  Another big one was the save games, which do not work if you have the game installed somewhere other than your C drive-- a real annoyance with the really long final route.  And then there were just some small annoyances like unnecessary extra clicks (such as having to click twice before every choice), the slow speed of the scene transitions, and a ton of typos... which were actually kind of entertaining, but still.
Even so, the game is worth playing.  It might not be the most polished VN you'll ever play, but it has some solid writing and is just a really fun experience.

I played this game because it had the "Walking Simulator" tag and it looked similar to another walking simulator that I really enjoyed -- Dear Esther. But be warned, this is NOT a walking simulator!
Certainly there are similarities with Dear Esther. Both are on an isolated, deserted island (in the same geographic area even!). Both have a beautiful soundtrack and a heavy emphasis on atmosphere. Even the storylines are similar, as an unreliable narrator encounters ghosts and quotes philosophers and poetry.
But Montague's Mount is actually a lot more similar to the game Myst, by which I mean you're stranded on a scenic deserted island and have to solve a bunch of difficult puzzles that make no sense. For example, one puzzle involves you using a compass to align some dials to open a gate. But you don't even know you have a compass, it's not in your inventory, there's no clue that says, "Push Q to use the compass you somehow acquired and will never use again." I wasted an hour trying to figure out that puzzle before consulting a spoiler guide - I am convinced if I had not consulted the spoiler guide I never would have figured it out.
And here the storyline really falls flat. There's simply no reason for this island to have numerous locked gates each with incredibly contrived opening mechanisms. The game's explanation of, "There was a sickness on the island so they had to create gates to keep it from spreading" was really lame. The game is set in the 1990s for crying out loud! The islanders had modern ships, medicine, and presumably radios to call for help, it's not like this is the Dark Ages and they were dealing with the Bubonic Plague, and even if that were the case why did the gates have to be so unnecessarily complicated?
I remember one set of difficult puzzles was all to lower a drawbridge so you could continue. But the drawbridge was guarding a chasm that was like two feet deep!
"Just walk across the two foot drop!" I shouted at my character, but no he'd rather spend an hour solving overly complex puzzles to lower that drawbridge instead.
I was very disappointed to make it to the end of the game to find the storyline is unfinished. Upon further investigation there was going to be a kickstarter campaign to fund a sequel but it failed so it's unlikely the story will ever be finished (as of November 2017).
Graphically the game was fine, although much of it was dark and in grayscale. This can be a problem when you're searching for small objects to pick up for puzzles as the object you're looking for can blend in with the grayscale terrain.
Gameplaywise you cannot die so you've got as much time as you need to solve the puzzles. The music was good and one of the strongest points of the game. I encountered no bugs.
The price of $10 is way too high. Fans of walking simulators should stay away, but if you like Myst-style puzzle games it might be worth getting on sale for $2 or less.

Montague’s Mount is a nice albeit slow experience.  You are trapped on an island trying to figure out what’s going on.  The game is a walking simulator mixed with puzzles and mystery.
There are several downsides to the game.  One of which is the all to obvious no running in the game but what can you do.  Since the man is hobbling on one leg early in the game, we can’t expect him to run.  Another slow one is the cinematic scenes.  You can’t skip them after already watching them.  These scenes move at a snail pace.
Another downside is that certain pages aren’t magnified other than the letters.  I could be doing something wrong but I have to walk up close to read guide papers or plaques.  Sometimes the shadow is blocking the words and mostly they are written so small.
Finally, I didn’t like the 10km achievement as it resets if you exit the game.  I realize, in order to get this achievement, you need to do it in one sitting.
Despite these negatives, the mood and mystery about what happened on this island draws me to continue this short journey.  The island is big but not big enough to get you lost in your surroundings.  The puzzles aren’t too complicated as well.  They aren’t easy but you generally get an idea how to solve it.
There are collectibles and secrets across the island and most are easy to spot, some are obscured by shadow, objects or rain.  These collectibles do encourage exploration since you can find most of them.  Might as well find the rest.  Just pull out the steam guide book.
The game is said to be based on a true story from Ireland.  I guess that adds to the intrigue.  Good work by the developers.

This bleak walking simulator with a dozen puzzles or so was developed by this company
looking behind the scenes you'll find that it’s mainly a single developer known as Matt Clifton.
Most negative reviews are simply based on some poor decisions made by the developer. He has chosen to pad his game by making the character walk slow, puzzles needing to be solved require you to revisit places you have already explored and items needing to be found are often obscure and easily missed especially since he has chosen a constant torrential downpour weather system which your character gets subjected to on a loop. For instance at the start of the game you are required to find a walking stick as your character is tortured by a stomach churning walking mechanic. I know people that have taken over 15 minutes to find the walking stick as it doesn't really stand out and already those customers are in a bad mood. And while the developer has added information over time trying to walk people through the first few puzzles they are still rather obscure and more often than not will have gamers quickly scurrying for a walkthrough due to frustration of not knowing how to progress or where the item is that they need.
In an interview the developer claimed that he wanted to produce a game without scare tactics. So why you’re subjected to a menacing child apparition within the first few minutes of the game is beyond me? You don't need to be a genius to realise that 1) you must be related to the child and 2) the child is dead. Hence any revelation at the end of the game is already ruined within the first couple of minutes. If you want to produce a disturbing environment without jump scares then do that. Instead of producing a silly red herring of a ghost menacingly staring you down, which contradicts every other encounter you have with that same ghost soon thereafter.
My biggest beef with the game is the sly gimmick the developer has used by stating that this game is based on a true story. Man has he taken liberties with this statement. While the game starts off with a notion that you maybe a shipwreck survivor with memory loss and over some course of time reveals that your more a publishing immigrant named Teddy who moved with your family to an Island which has somehow been overrun by a plague, the town doctor one of the first settlers takes it upon himself to quarantine certain parts of the island by constructing some make shift gates which end up being the puzzles you need to solve to progress forward and find out what happened to your family. Here I at least salute the developer for coming up with a concept which nicely blends the puzzle elements with the story. I further salute the developer with the story idea of what the doctor ends up doing which makes the situation very dire for the rest of the island. Problem is though that the story isn't really about the plague or the early settlers as both the island and its accompanying ghost is simply a make-believe conjured up in the mind of Teddy who is going through some type of purgatory coming to grips with some actions that he was forced to take under duress. The fact that the island is not real is revealed by the constant template photos that litter the landscape. On top of all this Teddy himself and the plague is simply the developer’s metaphor for major depression and how when confronted with the bleak vision of no hope one becomes isolated and plagued with disturbing imagery.
So what part of this story is based on a true story? Simply this, 'the developer' immigrated to Ireland leaving his family behind and felt lonely. With that ridiculous connection you can pretty much call anything a true story. Donkey Kong is based on a true story since I once grabbed a hammer and jumped up and down a few times while brandishing it. Since the developer is often vague and misleading with his artistic license, any noble message that he may be trying to convey is simply lost as a developer trying to big note himself with a trivial sob story about himself.
However with all these abrasive trolling mechanics placed aside, the game still managed to wow me with it stylish artistic rendering of an island, on top of that the audio narration is nearly worthy of academy award nomination and the musical score and sound effects would have Hans Zimmer toasting to it with a glass of chardonnay. The dark foreboding story regarding the first settlers on an island and the plague is a tantamount reflection to the dire massacre that many historical civilisations were subjected to.
However the best thing about this game for me is the bugs. I had more fun after the game was completed flying up in the sky and exploring than I did with just the normal run. You see the game contains a funny bug where if you scrape yourself at the side of an electrical pylon you will be flung up into the sky, giving you enough time and distance to either land in the ocean and swim around or get flung on top of the mount to explore all those area's you’re not supposed to go since the game is only half finished. This makes the game definitely worthy of a look for speed runners and I really hope the developer does not patch this up as it really gave me a fun time breaking the game.

12 hours in since I bought this game on Christmas morning, and I'm hooked. The gameplay is simple and straightforward, but there are just enough different units, buildings, and (randomly generated) terrain to offer varied strategies to attempt survival in. Not that you'll survive very often. Even the best laid plans and bases can fall short, especially if you put too much focus in one area of map, or on economic development instead of building an army, or vice versa. The goals are pretty simple. Collect resources, Wood, stone, gold, oil, and food to produce, and maintain, your colony and defend it. Balance is key here since you can't just hire a huge army that you can't afford to pay, or build buildings you can't afford to repair, or a power grid that you can't squeeze any more buildings into.
You can adjust the settings to have more or less zombies, in 4 progressively harder "environments" that you must unlock by beating the previous environment on a minimum difficulty setting. There are also the hordes; While the map starts out populated with static, aggro-able zombies and "new" zombies repopulate from the sides of the map at random intervals (as far as I can tell) or around the same time a "horde" show up. The "silver lining" about the hordes though, is that they at least give you a few minutes heads up as to what direction it will be coming from. The zombies are easily aggro'd with loud weapons, as well, and you can provoke a huge group of them if you're too loud, though I still don't know if buildings and colonists do that or just rifle retort from soldiers/snipers.
All in all a pretty solid City-Builder/Survival hybrid, nice aesthetic, and it looks like they're going to keep adding more to the game as it undergoes development.

Overall I had a positive experience playing this game.
Now the first thing you need to know about it is that it's a platformer with gameplay much like contra.
And, like Contra it is brutal. Which is a nice change of pace, it's an actual game that takes skill to play, many games cannot say this.
So brutal that 90% of the community do not have what it takes to progress to a 'hard' level.
There is a perma-death in this game, so that nice equipment that you obtained is just gone once you lose your character. And then your back to square one, using whatever equipment is in your stash.
That's not to say that it's impossible to get a high-tier mech. There might be half a dozen players in the community who have achieved it. They take their MK5 shells with the best equipment and solo levels that are designed to be taken on by 20 people. Then post their achievements on youtube for the sake of ego stroking.
The rest of us decently skilled players run around with exotic equipment from Tier 2 bosses. I've lured 8 people into the fungus cave boss and been one of the only 2 people to survive. The entire community fears boss.
Only to lose it all in underground base because the biggest group we could get together was 5 people in a level designed for a dozen.
If you do want to progress then I will give you the following tips.
1. Don't be a hero. You are not beholden to anyone.
2. If you are missing more than 25 hp, be more cautious. If you are missing half HP, hang back and let other people do the work. If you are near death go home immediatly, if you are not locked inside some boss fight. Always ping HP.
3. Learn about what the situations each shell is best at. Do you go in? or would it best to let another go.
4. Learn what the enemies do. Know how they are going to attack, so you can avoid the damage.
Watch youtube videos on the bosses before you even attempt them.

Oh..Sir! The Hollywood Roast is a sequel to Oh...Sir! The Insult Simulator but with film parodies.
The insults include references to Donald Trump as well as classic and modern movies as well as film production, and probably a lot more I haven't found yet.
The locations also include references to movies and TV Shows. There's Walter White on a Wanted Poster in a map called "The good, the bad, and your momma" (a reference to the good, the bad and the ugly). The characters are parodies of Gandolf from The Lord of the Rings, Harry Potter, and Marilyn Monroe.
The company intros at the beginning are obvious homages to MGM, and 21st Century Fox.
I originally gave the original a negative review, but I love this game and I definetly recommend it.
On top of the new jokes and references, the game also has slightly better gameplay. It tells you how much each insult is worth, so if you string 2 insults together it will say Insult 1 is worth 7 points, but you get a multiplier for using the same opener in the previous round, as well as what insult 2 is worth, rather than the total of both combined....helping you get better at the game as you play more.
My only real complaint is that even though it has Steam Workshop support, these are only reskins for existing characters, and I feel this game would have a larger lifespan if they were new characters, and say...you could pick a strength and a weakness or whatever.
Would definetly recommend. It's 3 quid, how can you skip on this game?

I'll admit, I bought this game because I thought it was a joke of a game; you start off by dating a menagerie of birds, all with differing personalities and different endings. I had some knowledge of the backstory beforehand, but I wasn't prepared for what came next.
The endgame takes the main game's rollercoaster of feels and turns it up to 11. Once a happy, satirical dating simulator, the game shifts to a murder mystery with one simple stroke. Over three hours worth of dialogue to digest, and over three hours of sheer emotional WTF; springboarding from utter despair to stifling a giggle at Okosan's antics is a bit jarring, but the game pulls it off rather well.

If nothing else, this game should be played
because of the endgame. The main game is a comedic and incredibly well-constructed setup to a tragic, emotionally charged ending that's satisfying in its own way. I completely, 100 percent recommend Hatoful Boyfriend as a game that everyone should experience in their life, as soon as possible.

Hatoful Boyfriend is a game originally released in 2011 in Japan and has been rereleased globally in 2014 onto Steam.
We have seen various dating simulators on Steam which have been pretty mediocre (not that I have played any of them...). However this game should be the No. 1 priority for Steam users if they are looking into immersing themselves in visual novels for the first time. Of course, users can play visual novels that are not on Steam such as Katawa Shoujo (which is exceptionally good by the way), but we should seize the opportunity Lord GabeN has given us, allowing us to play dating simulators on the legendary platform known as Steam. So don't lose this opportunity!
Hatoful Boyfriend is a visual novel game in which the player dates pigeons. Although this may sound like an unusual concept, we gamers are always looking out on the market for the latest innovative games which bring new concepts and ideas to the congested video game market. Although the visual novel genre isn't especially innovative, the idea of having a romantic relationship between the protagonist, you, and various male pigeons is certainly innovative. Therefore I am giving this game a thumbs up.
This may seem like a review just to laud the game's innovation and creativity. However, the gameplay and graphics are also up to par with the other releases which have come out at around the same time as this game. Even though this game is a visual novel, it provides immersive gameplay which will keep players like myself hooked on for hours at a time. The soundtrack for the game is one of the best in the market, which is why I purchased the Digital Deluxe version of the game, which includes the song's soundtrack!
Even though this game has some negatives about it, I would still consider it to be GOTY. We all know there is no such thing as a perfect video game. The positives heavily outweigh the negatives and that is all that matters. So therefore, I hope that you have carefully read this review and will pick this game up as soon as possible. If you are not overly convinced that this game is amazing yet, I suggest reading the other 1,500 or so reviews on the store page!

If you like, you could just read my DOOM review, swapping the word QUAKE for DOOM. But that wouldn't be fair.
iD managed to produce another industry changer, a scant three years after DOOM was released. Whereas DOOM brought 3D gaming to the masses and made multiplayer something that people felt should be included as standard, QUAKE raised the bar even higher.
PC Gamer certainly helped QUAKE along, thanks to including the shareware episode on their coverdisc. So those people not lucky enough to have fast internet access could still join in the fun.
I think at the time, QUAKE was even more of a global sensation than DOOM was, but with hindsight I think it's fair to say that DOOM shook things up more than QUAKE did. But only just. A lot of QUAKE's legacy is thanks to the addons and patches which quickly followed the main game.
QUAKE proved that smooth, fluid, entirely polygon-based games were feasible and practical. Suddenly, all the sprite-based FPS games that were being released looked incredibly dated. Not their fault - nobody but iD saw it coming. Duke Nukem 3D had been released just one month before iD pushed their tech demo out into the world, and everybody knew something big was coming.
If DOOM made multiplayer gaming on company LANs the next big thing, then QUAKE made internet deathmatches the in-thing. Quakeworld which followed later on in the year greatly improved and streamlined this service so even those with dial-up connections could participate.
GLQuake greatly improved the graphics for those lucky few who had these new-fangled 3D accelerator cards - suddenly everybody was buying Matrox and Voodoo cards just to play the new, improved QUAKE.
And if people thought DOOM was expandable, QUAKE blew their minds. Not only could you make levels, you could make new models, new sound and music, and even rewrite parts of the code to make entirely new games (QUAKE Chess anybody?)
Personally, QUAKE is not my favourite FPS. Not by a long shot. I don't think I ever even finished the single-player campaign. But I can't deny it's influence, and it is amazing to see what they did with the hardware at the time.

Review at A Glance
Pros:
Grand-daddy of full 3D First Person Shooters
Gripping, visceral, atmospheric soundtrack
Inventive, diverse level and enemy design (Lovecraftian)
Addictive multiplayer gameplay, with myriad iterations/mods; alive to this day
Unparalleled, dark, medieval, ghoulish atmosphere
Cons:
So many Source Ports and MODS, which ones to choose?!!?
****Steam version does not include the game's original Soundtrack, easy online fix available****
Conclusion:
Essential gaming for fans of First Person Shooters; cemented the id Software legend. Most popular game engine of its time. If you don't have this already, what are you waiting for?! For current generation play, I recommend one of the common source ports, such as Ultimate Quake (DarkPlaces+).
In-depth review, not for the faint of heart: "Abandon all hope, ye who enter here":
1996. DooM had introduced "Deathmatch" to the popular lexicon three years earlier. id Software managed to capitalize on the addictive nature of online multiplay, while advancing the technical limits of FPS gaming. What followed was the most popular game engine of its time, and it revolutionized online multiplay. Engine novelties included polygonal models, fully 3D environments, easy tools for Game Modding and hardware 3D acceleration. Quake may single handedly be the game that made a cutting-edge graphics card an essential component for the modern PC gamer. Unique gameplay features included bunny hopping and rocket-jumping. Game emphasis was on the online, multiplayer experience, utilizing a client-server model rather than peer to peer, the preeminent model of the time. This model allowed players to create and mantain a session, while additional players would be able to join or leave at any time, without disrupting the game.
Story:
BAHAHAHAHAHAH!! Story?! Pffffftt. Don't let it get in the way of an epic, legendary, awesome FPS game. Beat the 4 episodes and collect the rune at the end, solve environmental puzzles, kill everything with a pulse...or rather, that moves! 'Nuff Said. There is something resembling a story that was thrown in to provide the semblance of a gaming thread.
Gameplay:
Fast paced, bunny hopping, rocket jumpin' non-stop, edge of your seat, deathmatchin' action. Gameplay intuitive enough to allow a beginner to jump in and start fraggin', yet, complex enough to allow a bustlin' pro scene to develop, and spawn a successful franchise. Responsive controls allow you to float through inspired levels and maneuver your character, even when airborne! Weapon selection established the standard with a good variety of now conventional, classic weapons; including the revered Shotgun, the seminal Rocket Launcher and the mighty Lighting Gun. Weapon balance and choice, depending on level design and range of combat, had never been this intricate.
Design:
Iconic palette hard on black/browns with excellent use of lighting and shadows for emphasis and scares. Weapon design is a bit blocky, by today's standards, but sits nicely with the dark, medieval theme. Enemy/monster designs are inventive, with great variety, and a multitude of baddies that attack from above, at ground level and in the water. At the time, probably the only other big title that offered hazards with such a degree of freedom of movement was "Descent."  Enemies appear as something out of a medieval demonic nightmare with a hodgepodge of humanoid, hellish Lovecraftian creatures coming at you and wielding a good array of weapons and attacks. The color palette and enemy design allows for baddies to pop out of dark corners and portions of the level, setting up multiple scares, providing a racemic mixture of action and horror that is hard to match.
The level design, with its gothic architecture and variety of environmental puzzles and hazards, resulted in classic levels that would eventually be ported to multiple other engines and games.
Sound:
Immaculate, crisp environmental, creature, character and weapon sound effects that were mostly concocted/mixed in-house by the talented id crew utilizing innovative techniques and processing. Trent Reznor/NIN soundtrack provides a chilling backdrop with industrial, ambiental brilliance that peppers the game with a pumping, blood curling soundtrack, which seamlessly potentiates the dark visuals and sound effects.
Replayability:
The online multiplayer experience is at the core of Quake. It would offer more options than any other FPS at the time and, out of the box, would allow for Deathmatch, Team Deathmatch and Cooperative Play. It would also allow for Time and/or Frag limits. After some time, popular free modifications included Team Fortress and Capture the Flag modes. The transition to a Client:Server model would permit a server to run continuously and for players to drop in and pop out of the game, without interrupting it. This dramatically improved the chances of finding a working game. Moreover, whereas most multiplayer experiences at the time emphasized 1:1 or games of up to 8 players, Quake allowed up to 16 simultaneous players in its original iteration; resulting in unprecedented chaos and murderous destruction.
Conclusion:
Quake is a legendary, classic game from FPS greats, id Software (id Tech 2). The Quake engine fueled the upcoming games for a generation and set the blueprint for FPS and online gaming. Dark atmosphere with ghoulish, sadistic enemy design set in a medieval, gothic world full of environmental dangers and light puzzles. Online experience is the core of the game, and would shape the FPS landscape for the foreseeable future. If you enjoy FPS, horror, inventive level design, Lovecraftian creatures, NIN/Trent Reznor or are just interested in gaming history, you cannot go wrong with this game.

I mostly play Rift outside Steam, but feel compelled to write a steam review due to the number of negative/rage reviews. Rift is one of the more solid MMOs on the market today. Sure you have to pay to get some content/classes, but this is true of all MMOs, even subscription games like WoW (I wanna be a Demon Hunter!!). Rift is free. Trion is still developing content for it. (Is EQ2 dead?) The core game itself is very fun (you know...rifts), the art direction is good, and the game engine is rock solid. I have only ever payed for Storm Legion and i feel a ton of content is available to consume. Don't get me wrong, it's not perfection, but is a hell of a lot better than most of the other MMOs today(Riders of Icarus is Rad!!).

First off, I've played this game for hundreds of hours outside of Steam. I have 2 max level characters.
The people who think the game is P2W haven't looked deep enough. The shop is deceiving at first glance. It shows the highest tier armor for sale for real-world currency only. What you don't see, is how to get that armor in-game for free.
The highest tier (raid) armor is achieved by UPGRADING lower tier (dungeon) armor, which you CAN do for free (quite easily in fact) OR from buying it directly in the shop for real-world currency. The game is not pay-2-win, it's pay-2-skip. You can either take the time to get geared yourself or skip past that and go straight to raids.
Now that that's out of the way, the game itself is pretty easy to describe. It's a F2P WoW clone. It looks like WoW, it plays like WoW, it feels like WoW. I've never played another "WoW clone" that gave me this feeling I never knew I was missing since I stopped playing WoW.
That's not to say that it doesn't have it's differences. The class system is amazingly customizable. Put simply, remember the talent trees in WoW, pre-Cataclysm? In Rift you can mix and match the three talent trees from 11 trees per class. Mix Warlock with Stormcaller and Frostkeeper as a mage, or Marksman with Bard and Assassin as a rogue. Make familiar classes like WoW-style Warlock by mixing Warlock (affliction) with Necromancer (demonology) and Pyromancer (destruction).
There are other innovations as well, far too many to go into in this review. However, none of them keep the game from playing like WoW.
TL;DR: If you're looking for a F2P WoW replacement, this is by far your best option. It is also not P2W though it may appear so at first glance.

I'm still a noob really when it comes to HOI4 with about 50hrs logged.  50hrs may seem a lot to some people (e.g. your significant other), but for something as complex as HOI4, it's probably only time enough to scratch the surface.  However I have played many hours computer strategy games (e.g. Civ series) and again many hours table top wargames such as Avalon Hill's Rise and Decline of the Third Reich.  So I've got plenty of experience with wargames and WW2 subject matter in general.
Now that I'm getting to grips with HOI4 I think it is awesome.
The game has a steep learning curve but that's probably unavoidable with this much in it.  Big thumbs up to the developers for putting as much into it as they have, given that obvious drawback of selling the learning curve to new players - it's so good to have a game like this to play.  Based on my own experience, HOI4 is in a class of its own.
I dare say anyone reading this knows that HOI4 is a huge detailed WW2 simulation.  It can be played single or multiplayer.  Each player takes control of a single country and the AI handles the rest.  This means you can play as e.g. Germany but you can't play as all the Axis.  No problem, it works very well.  AI can be a real weakness in computer strategy games and can absolutely make or break a game like HOI4, so I'm delighted to have found HOI4's AI to be outstanding.  It can be tricky to issue orders at first and sometimes the AI doesn't seem to get what you want it to do, but once you get used to it, it works well.  So well that I have been pleasantly surprised on several occasions where the AI has sensibly adapted to a dynamically unfolding situation, and still managed to execute my orders appropriately.
HOI4's graphics are fantastic.  Zoom out to the whole world in strategic view and quickly locate trouble spots, then zoom in to greater and greater detail, until at full zoom you're almost watching the fighting unfold in front of your eyes.  Alternatively you can double-click on your army to quickly go to the relevant map location.  The visuals are constantly on the move as you zoom in and out and pan around to keep pace with the action.  I am fortunate enough to have a very wide screen 3440x1440; HOI4 uses all of it used and it looks superb.  The only slowdown I sometimes see is with 'autosave', otherwise it's as smooth as silk (admittedly I have a decent GPU).
Audio is also high quality, the sounds of combat close in, and appropriate voice responses to orders make it all very atmospheric.  Because the game is played in real-time, there are also small audio cues when something has happened that you might want to give your attention.  At first the music is excellent as well, but I found that after playing for hours it gets a bit repetitive and so now I've turned the music (not the sound) right down.  Perhaps the music could be more extensive and less repetitive, and a little less intrusive as well.
The other area that takes a bit of getting used to is the issuing of orders to armies - particularly when you want to make adjustments to those orders, or to have them executed in a precise way.  The mouse-clicks and the key presses required aren't always intuitive and take a bit of getting used to.  That said, the developers have done an amazing job of implementing this, and this is just an example of where the learning curve can feel a bit steep at first.
This is a 10/10 game for me right now.  Struggling through 10's of hours learning curve plus the (about 10?) hours of youtube videos is starting to pay off.  I'm now getting to grips with the detail of what's going on, and I'm loving it.  Thank you Paradox.

I have a few things that I would like to cover but first, I would HIGHLY recommend this game to anyone that likes both zombies and RTS.  It is a great combination of the two worlds and very addicting.
I will be giving a few suggestions, but these are not negative in any way.  Only ideas that I would love to see and updates I know would interest everyone.  There are four topics: save points, co-op, 1v1/2v2 zombie vs. human, and map editor.
Save points are basic.  I love that this game is a do or die hardcore type game.  But it would be nice to be able to incorporate save points.  You can do this without taking from the experience by simply making difficulty levels.  The higher difficulty levels do not allow save points and therefore unlock special items, badges, maps, scenarios, etc.  Whereas the lower levels allow save points but unlock limited lower level awards.
The ability to play co-op in this game would be amazing.  Right now, two of my friends are playing this game and we are recommending it to everyone we know.  But there is no way to enjoy the game with friends.  Instead we just talk about it or watch one-person play.  That isn't any fun at all.  But if there were larger maps with enough room and resources to allow two players we could then play with our friend’s vice watching them.  There are many ways to do this I am sure but here is a simple idea.  Create larger maps with a stipulation that the two human spawning points cannot be within a certain distance of each other.  Then commence the zombie waves as usual only increasing to two waves at a time after a few waves.
I think it would be a lot of fun to be able to play 1v1 zombie vs. human or even a co-op 2v2 match.  There are two basic ways I can think of to allow this to remain a survival game while allowing us the ability to play as the zombies.  The first would be simply giving the zombie player an increasing amount of funds per wave and damage done.  This would be fun, but the zombie player would get somewhat bored as they only spend a minute or two building their wave and then waiting for the timer to allow them to send it.  Because of that I think it would be fun for the zombie player to be able to create a base as well.  Mine for resources, build, upgrade, research, etc.  The one caveat to this would be the humans cannot enter or see the zombie area to keep the game genre as survival rather than full on RTS.
Last but certainly not least, I would LOVE to see a map editor.  Many of us would like to be able to create a custom map to test out strategies, challenge friends, challenge ourselves, etc.  A map editor is a must add for a game such as this.
Adding these four updates would certainly make the game more entertaining and more appealing to much of your fane base.  I have no doubt about it.

In Montague's Mount you play as a geriatric mime that washes up on the shore of some island. As such you walk as slow as your busted hip and brittle knees will allow, and very often stop to admire the odd invisible wall. You find letters, you find generators, and every so often you find a youtube video of someone stumbling upon the one thing you've been looking for for the past 20 minutes. You also get to admire slow, in-engine, establishing shots of the environment you literally just walked into and will have to walk through multiple times as you have to stop moving for the cursor to come back and tell you if you can pick that up or not.
I had started and stopped a few years ago, and had nothing to do today and decided to blaze through it. Now I wish I had just slept for a few hours instead.
I didn't last more than one minute in game.

Got this game on at a lower price thanks to one of those discount slips you get based on what games you play. In my case, I got it for playing Dear Esther.
The resemblance between the two games is readily apparent: both take place on a seemingly abandoned British island; both have a dark, sombre tone; both a walking simulators (though Montague's Mount features puzzles and an inventory, which Dear Esther lacked); both have rather similar musical scores; and both hint at themes of significant loss.
Both also have some mildly scary psychological horror elements, but are perfectly harmless in such. Dear Esther only has scary sounds, while Montague's Mount features some sort of ghost (I think), with the only scary interaction is early on when he blinks to right in front of few from live 7 metres away. While this initial thing kept me from playing the game during dark (because I'm a real scaredy cat), it didn't detract from the experience, keeping me on my toes while never actually bothering me with cheap jump scares or any other nightmare fuel.
After all, the focus of this game is on exploration, story and puzzles. The puzzles are great, requiring quite a bit of thinking and a few breaks inbetween play sessions (to refresh your perspective), but I never had to resort to any guides to figure one out. Objects are fairly easy to spot too, usually by their faint glow or highlight (which can be turned of, IIRC), though a fair for about one mission critical object hidden in a desk drawer. A problem with this game is that a lot of objects are non-interactable, and even on the generally interactable ones, only parts of them are. For example, you can only open one of the closet doors, but there are two drawers in the bottom that are quite easy to miss due to its small size, or to quickly dismiss as decorative if you don't. This issue kept me running about looking for that a certain piece of paper for over an hour.
Still, the solutions I tried to come up with were quite inventive, as you start putting various numbers together into various combinations based on the little information you're given. I must admit that even though they didn't work, the process of elimination and trial and error was many times more enjoyable than solving the puzzle itself, which really goes to show the care taken into crafting a game that not only gives you an experience, but actively stimulates your creative and deductive abilities as well. Few games manage to affect me that way, and considering that this was made by a small-time producer, hat's off to them!
Overall, I'd say this qualifies as a first-person adventure game more than merely a walking simulator, given the amount of puzzle solving and object collection it involves. Gameplay-wise, it's very minimalistic, with no HUD to speak of, and a very modest inventory (both spatially and visually), resembling Grim Fandango in that aspect. Its dark and dreary and particularly foreboding atmosphere, however, coupled with its story, revealed through Amnesia-style notes read in a wonderful Irish accent, combine with the mechanics seamlessly to make this a humble yet very enjoyable experience; and I can highly recommend it to anyone who liked adventure games, puzzle solving or story-driven games in general.

This game was a gift from my partner in crime, who admittedly has a much stranger sense of humor than I. I played the game because I trust her judgement, at least when it comes to good media. This game has a slow start, and at first glace there is nothing more to it than the ridiculous concept of dating pigeons.
But this game is deceptive, and what I got was NOT what I expected at all, even though I was warned. There are little clues and hints that things are off, and after a certain point in the game, the plot comes out of nowhere and sucker punches you in the face. The perfect blend of crack and angst, this game has excellent writing and character development, and everything is well developed and ties together neatly. Seriously. Everything ties together.
The game can be played in about half a day with liberal use of the fast-foward feature. (Be careful with it, you might accidentally miss something important.) My advice is to immediately go after Nageki, and don't buy this game if you can't handle a slow start. If you're willing to be patient, I promise the payoff is worth it.

Third person shooter XCOM::
:: A good spin off of an already well established franchise
:: Not necessarily the best installment for the genre (compared to Mass Effect and Gears), but definitely still enjoyable and challenging on some parts of the game
:: I love aliens and  their designs,  the aesthetics of the alien base, and the 60's Area 51 alien horror vibe can be felt here
:: This is I think a good step (not the best, but still) to expand the XCOM universe
:: If you love aliens and space, you might like this one ::

-- Foreword - 3D VISION --
First of all I have to clarify that I played The Bureau completely with NVidia's 3D vision and used a fix by the community to enhance the quality of it. If you do not know 3D vision check out NVidia's forum:
.
What's the point of 3D vision? It changes the immersion you feel in a game. Characters are a bit outside of the screen and hallways in the game have a realistic deepth; that means it goes deep into your wall. It is like watching through your screen. It is something you have to check out yourself  as it is difficult to be explained. Do not make the mistake and compare it to 3D movies. The deepth and convergence is very different. It is more the kind of 3D you will see with the Oculus Rift or the HTC Vive.
-- Substance of the game --
First of all, I have to admit that I needed quite some time to get into the mechanics. So I stopped playing the game after 4 hours when I first started it one and half years ago, knowing at this time however that I want to retry it again someday in the future.
This weekend it was this day and I got hooked this time and played through it in three days.
-- What are the pros and cons? --
Pros:
- Great atmospheric setting, great story, great characters, great voice-acting
- Decent graphics with very good science fiction design
- A great variety of coloufull lights
- It's the 50s! Everyone in the game looks very classy
- Rewarding and satisfying combat system
- First playthrough around 20 hours
- Replayability because of the combat system and different difficulties
- Decent skill system
- A lot short well-written readings within the game that give you some background information of the story
Cons:
- AI of your squad:
-->Let me explain: it might not be a big issue if you play on easy but it is going to be very frustrating on the harder difficulties; actually it was also the AI of my fellow combattants that stopped me from playing the game the first time. If you have the feeling a combat is too demanding change the difficult settings. It is possible during every fight.
-->What's the issue? The AI sometimes is just not holding cover correctly. The combat system is missing commands about what the AI should do at a specific place you move one of your two characters. Sometimes it would just be better for your squad members to stay in cover and let you do all the hard work. But they always decide to get out of the cover and shoot the enemies, but not going back to cover in time so they brutally injured.
- Level-UP system finishes for your main character at level 10 and for your squad members at level 5 - I could imagine a Game+ with more levels and maybe even more variety in skills
- Dispatch missions are good to level up but not really fun because there is no interaction whatsoever
- Story in the beginning a bit confusing
***
==> Conclusion: very atmospheric real-time strategy shooter with issues in the AI. Combat system is easy to learn and difficult to master with some very frustrating moments. Unique game in design and story.
==> Rating: 8/10 (without 3D vision 6.5/10)

Look at all those negative reviews!  What game are those people playing?  Frankly I don’t get the hate, and that is coming from a Ubisoft hater.
So, lets talk turkey.  Is this a good game?
Frankly?  Yes! I am enjoying the heck out of it so far.  The game is JAM PACKED with things to explore, locations to raid and conquer, missions to complete, and a fairly compelling story of Drug lords, corruption, rebellion and American covert ops.
This isn’t a perfect game by any means, but the gameplay, at least for me, has been addictive.  I am constantly playing longer than intended, always having a “just one more thing...” habit when I should be going to bed.   The gunplay, stealth, and action feel pretty good to me.  I prefer light real/sim tactical shooters to frag fest action shooters.  This is decidedly right smack dab in the middle, with a strong stealth element.  I run around like a Ninja in the night, sniping and assasinating bad guys methodically, getting deep into the enemy stronghold.  Here is where it usually goes south and I end up having to shoot my way out like Rambo (which makes it even more fun and white knuckle, especially on harder settings).
The open world plays like a super watered down GTA, or like A slightly watered down Watchdogs.  Enemies do re spawn when you leave the area far enough, breaking immersion sometimes, but it’s very tolerable.
The difficulty settings scale up pretty well, with arcade being for kids and people who don’t like shooters.  With each harder difficulty making the enemies quicker and more aggressive.  They don’t become bullet sponges, instead they spot you better and start shooting before you can spot them.  The highest difficulty turns off all the radar elements unless you scan with your drone.  Meaning bad guys can sneak up on you now too!
One flaw I have to mention is that for whatever reason, they allow you to swap your loadouts at any point and time in the world.  In other words, they have all these ammo supply boxes in the game world, offering you the ability to swap loadouts.  So, most people, myself included, at first assume you can only select a loadout while at these boxes… So you spend some time meticulously planning your weapon selection to make sure you fit a concept (stealth sniper?  CQB specialist?).  Only to find that if you go into your loadout screen, you can swap your equipment at any time.  Replenishing ammo etc.
This utterly robs the game of any sense of individual specialization in Co OP, or solo play (to a lesser degree in solo, because you have to make up for the limited AI controls, you can do well without an LMG for example, but sometimes you just have to have a sniper rifle.
I wish the game had a setting (or if it does I wish I knew about it) to limit this somehow.  Especially in Co-op, where I feel it would go a long way.
I also find being able to carry 2 long guns on your back at any time to be kind of silly.  In real life you don’t typically do that… This further dumbs down weapon selection, because you could easily pick a high power sniper, and a LMG and have no problems carrying both… Try that in RL, to say nothing of the ammo…

Lastly, one flaw really irks me… But I managed to get over it just by swearing off buying any extras for this… It’s the Shady/greedy DLC and addon scheme, not quit battlefront 2 loot crate, but certainly not reasonable Free to play item store with reasonable pricing.  For example, the Predator pack of items and cosmetics costs around 30$.  For a handful of guns, a new melee animation and some cosmetics.  I suppose if you add it all up, it’s actually not THAT expensive… but only really IF this was a FREE TO PLAY GAME.  I mean, if I want to be honest, I’ve spent several times that in a Free to play game on cosmetics etc. But pay 60$ for a base game, another 30-40$ for season pass or all DLC, PLUS 15-30$ for extra packs like that?  Oh, hell no.
Final verdict – Do I recommend it?  IF you like or don’t mind, the Ubisoft open world formula, and the lite tactical mil/sim style of Tom Clancy and ghost recon games… Hell yeah! If you got 2-3 friends willing to play with you… then make that a double hell yeah!

Skip to bottom for short overview.
Starting things off: The AI is completely braindead. It will do such things as: use its tiny fleet to battle your massive one in open combat, leave entire areas of its country unprotected, disregard terrain weather and supply lines, and send endless tiny naval invasions, that acomplish nothing except annoy you. And to add insult to injury; Paradox is charging $10-$15 for DLC that contain either small features that should have been in the game at launch, or things that mods have already done better. There are barely any events; which makes the game feel lifeless and barren, and even a year on, the most minor nations still have the generic unit model, focus tree and leader portrait. The lack of any sort of graphic diversity continues with equipment, where every single ship model is the exact same for every nation, and even the majors are VERY lacking when it comes to variety in their equipment iconography.
Compared to to other Paradox grand strategies, HOI4 has an embarassing lack of political and strategic depth. Even on hard you can just steamroll the USSR in 1938 as Germany by assigning all your troops to 1 army and assigning 1 attack order spanning the entire front. The braindead AI doesn't build any troops and leaves huge gaps in its lines which allow you to drive into Moscow with no resistance. All the depth of planning a complex operation has been removed by the fact your entire nation's military can be put into 1 army and commanded by 1 general with no need for other leaders or any delegation of command. In politics the situation is just as bad. The options are very shallow compared to Ck2 and Eu4, and that would be ok if the war politics were much better; this is a wargame after all. But no, the wars are MUCH worse than Eu4 and even Ck2 in terms of politics. Now you might wonder how you can have less depth than a game with only 3 options, (Enforce wargoal, white peace and surrender.) The answer is take out 2 of those options. Wars in HOI are garbage. There is only total victory, total defeat, and nothing in between. You cant even surrender! How could they not add in this very basic feature that is in every other strategy game ever made? Eu4's system of taking things based on warscore and other factors is great, why did Paradox dumb it down to be worse than Ck2? There is an option called offer peace, but in 300 hours I have never had the AI accept it, because losing half of its territory and 1.5 million of its soldiers isnt enough for a white peace to the AI. Also, the factions are garbage too; you have no control over anything they do or policies they implement. You can't even kick members out! Again another extremely basic mechanic not implemented after a whole year on the market.
The bright side: The game has a solid foundation, and I have never experienced any crashing or lag problems. But perhaps the biggest saving grace of this game is the modding community. The mods are numerous and they are extremely easy to use. And they do everything from fixing problems with vanilla, to making new scenarios entirely. Just take a look at Kaiserreich to see how a small team of modders without access to the source code can make a much more dynamic interesting, and immersive experience than the vanilla game.
In conclusion: Over a year after release, HOI4 still feels incomplete and broken. It was not worth your $40 then and it's still not now. Not to mention the $35 extra for dlc that adds stuff that should have been free. I'm a big fan of Paradox's grand strategies but this one just isn't there yet. It would be better to pick it up later down the road, when most of these issues have been fixed. But if you do want to play it now, wait for a sale and prepare for some stupid AI, a shallow politics system, and a lot left wanting in terms of graphical and gameplay diversity.

This project is definitely off to a great start!
The game as it is now is a straightforward mix of Stronghold, Zombies, and Steampunk.  It's very playable in its current form,  the survival mode, where you build up a town and defend it from ever-increasing waves of zombies.  I will say it's a very challenging game, and you will find your economic management skills and sometimes your micro skills put to the test.  The survival mode is made even more difficult by the nature of the save system which is forced ironman.  This can be gotten around by moving save files around, but still, I think it's a little much for an already challenging game.
There are some slight annoyances with pathing.  Your troops will sometimes try to path through structures and will just continually march in place rather than moving around the obstacle, and it can be unclear where zombie waves will hit.  If the zombie pathing was a little more clear I think it would be slighly better.  They seem to take the longest possible path towards your colony at times which makes things unpredictable.
The tech tree is also somewhat truncated in its current form, I feel like there should be more mid-range units.  As it stands you have your basic soldiers and then jump right to the endgame tier units at the end of the tech tree, not much inbetween.
It's also a little odd to me that you have to beat the first map to unlock additional maps.  Beating a game is in itself no easy feat, so a little more variety up front might be warranted.
Anyway if this game looks at all appealing to you, it is extremely itself.  You can be confident in what you are getting.   I look forward to following this project to see what new features and levels are added.

This is a very slow, tedious, ultimately boring game.
There is one movement speed.  Slow.  Movement isn't the only slow thing.  The result of many actions are slow.  Just solved the puzzle to unblock the path?  The animation for the path becoming unblocked takes longer than it took to solve the puzzle for it.
Puzzles can bug out and not work correctly.  One puzzle late in the game I had to exit and reload a check point 3 times before solving teh puzzle did what it was supposed to do.  Another part of a puzzle that had 2 parts had each part fail on me.  So bugs, yeah.
There are a coupel of note sthat are hard to read because you can't get close enough to them.  In particular the one on the first beach near the start.
The narrative, as with most games, is told through finding journal entries along the way and some protagonist commentary.  The problem here is that by teh end of the game the entries seem somewhat unconnected, vague, and not very revealing.  Through certain ones and a typically boring cliche you should figure out the "twist" well before it happens, though once you do you're left with even more question because you discover this is more like an "Episode 1" than a full experience.
Another aspect of the narrative is that despite the depressing soundtrack and the despondent vocalizations of the protagonist there really is nothing that sets up anykind of emotional atachment to any character in this game.   I feel no sorrow for this guy or his troubles even at the (poor) attempt at a shocking emotional twist (which I mentioned before you see coming a mile away).  The narative sets you up for a depresisng story but fails to deliver any kind of connection to deliver.
The graphics are ok for small indie game but they won't blow you away.   Despite an above average gaming rig the performace was pretty poor, but you can tweak the visuals...film grain seem to be the biggest performance hit, but even at low setting frame rates aren't where the should be.  There are areas where the camera can get hun up and it will jitter sometimes but I never got stuck.
There are only checkpoint saves, and that was problematic when I had to reload several times to finish the last puzzle as the last check point was well before then.  Manual saves to me are a must so this is a big failure to me.
Controls are minimal and you can configure the keys to your liking.  The only key I saw necessary to change was the inventory key as it was the only key used that wasn't on the left side of the keyboard.  The game has "partial" controller support but it absolutely useless to use a controller so don't even try.
The music was simple and repetitive and as I said, meant to set a depressing tone.  Audio quality is also minimal, but nothing bad.
All in all this is a novice attempt at somber adventure game.  While the bugs can be mostly overlooked sadly it fails in both pacing and narrative to be an experience I wouldn't recommend let alone return to.

How to Survive 2 has a different style than How to Survive. Instead of having multiple small maps and constantly is one main stream mission line with side missions to do while doing the main one, in How to Survive 2 you spawn in a big map, about 10x as bigger as the first map you spawn in. It will take a while to uncover all the map. And this map is just for a play mode, you build your base here and put up traps and defenses around your base and the map. And instead of staying on this map, there is a map for each mission, and there are a lot of missions. Kovac has the main missions, and different people around the play map will give you different side quests that have the same style as the main missions. The base building is just so it looks civilized, the buildings you build have uses; the kitchen allows you to cook the meat you hunted for, the armory lets you build weapons and armor, accessories let you build mods for you weapons and more armor and there's more buildings too. There are 3 kinds of level to do, character level, camp level, and building level. You can only level your character up to the level to your camp level and your building level to your character level. These levels let the zombies grow stronger, but also upgrade your weapons. Every tenth level you get to, you have to do Kovac's Challenge, you activate a pylon, and hordes of zombies will come to the buildings you've put up trying to take down the pylon and turns the game into a tower defense. If you win you are allowed to level up to the next tenth and repeat.

I have to say I enjoyed this game much more then i thought I would. If you're a fam of XCOM then you might find this game hard to get into. It feels more like an adaptaion both in gameplay, style and story.
This title is "kind of" a prequel to the later xcom titles, but that is only because it positions itself as one in the final cutscenes. There are some oddities in the storyline, but the big thing that was troubling was that final cutscene. If we ignore that last 3 minutes of the game, the story is rich, interesting and really engaging. The story shifts away from the standard xcom timeline and feels more like an alternate reality. What if the aliens came back in the 40s/50s? Essentially that what the whole game accomplishes well. There is a twist near the end that I won't spoil, but it really pushes the 4th wall in a unique way. I really enjoyed it.
Gameplay itself is good and is more FPS then it is turn based strategy like xcom. This is a little tough at first since we're all very used to having unlimited time to contemplate attacks, but the game does allow us to slow time while we issue commands. That does enough.
Overall I found this game to be extremely charming. The 50s theme was something we don't see much and the little snippets of story throughout the game is fun to stop and read. There is some clunkiness in combat but it is livable. The game is replayable, but the ending kind of snuff that flame. I think the game is worth the time to play. It doesn't beat XCOM Enemy Unknown, but it is a cool alternate experience.
