I recommend this game, but only under specific terms. As anyone with a working understanding of what XCOM is, this one only counts as an XCOM game under similar terms. If you want deep tactical combat and a sense of existential dread fighting back a cybernetic, mindfraying enemy ages ahead of humanity, this is not the game for you. The combat amounts to skulking around and shooting heads poking around cover and making sure all your crazy ill-begotten alien abilities are in constant cooldown. I'd be surprised to see if someone in the credits took credit for designing these levels, because there's almost no incentive to even try to play strategically--you'll win by getting killed a lot and hoping you won't die the next time you respawn at the checkpoint just behind you.
Not a lot going on with it mechanically. It's enjoyable. It's plain. It was on its way to being a top-grade squad shooter, then never articulated itself past the poorly-aging mechanics of games like Freedom Fighters and Republic Commando.
Sadly, if it's lore you want, you're likely going to be left wanting. The game fleshes out the XCOM universe with fleeting moments of coherence, almost like the devs knew what they were doing was only wearing XCOM clothes and never going to breach into full-fledged canon. Conspiracy theorists may take issue with that proclamation, but yeah well so what.
There's one specific thing this team got really right. If you're old enough to know what Man's Life magazine is, you're going to get some nostalgic chills when you take in the game's hypermasculine adventure-pulp vibe. Bad game or good game, there's a campy satisfaction in playing as our leading man--Oklahoma-born, corn-fed, brick-chinned Central Intelligence Alcoholic William Carter against deathray-wielding moon men, wearing his best plum-purple tactical sweater on black ops deployments. If your hat gets shot off in a firefight, it's gone for the rest of the game.
The atmosphere is, in the early moments of the game, breathtaking. The insidious quiet of landing in these freshly-ravaged towns is stunning and sobering. The moment I first entered XCOM HQ and strode past a bunch of brass wearing pinstripe slacks, suspenders, sleeves rolled up, smart ties and slicked hair, smoking listlessly on tabletops watching radio intel slowly etch onto churning paper printouts, I was completely hooked. It felt like I was somewhere whole and real.
But really, in this game, the aliens' perfect, inscrutable plan of attack is to make sure all their ranking officers at the frontline are wearing elaborate, glowing, Please Shoot Me First armor. Checkmate, says Jeff Goldblum. The game is a sickly, sci-fi-obsessed child of Cold War-era American exceptionalism without the heart to go too far down the satire path, but this is not the platform for a foreign policy ethics essay, so pass along, nothing to see here.
Development hell doesn't always kill everything, and value survives in this little curio of a shooter. Hear the chilly, blurry radio feedback in your headphones when you enter Tactical View to take out a pod of flanking Sectoids. Just listen to the earnestness with which one of your squadmates asks, in the middle of a burning forest, "We're gonna make'em pay, right boss?"
"Yeah boys, we're gonna make'em pay, all right."
I love XCOM and I love 3rd person shooters. The graphics and GUI aren't perfect but this game is definitely one to try.

The interface is clumsy and you spend the entire game interacting with it. Moving through the production tree results in different key strokes to enter and exit it which is frustrating. For example pressing Esc will return you to the start of the tree in some casesd and in others it brings you to the game options screen. Why? It should be consistant so that you cna rely on that button or another to quickly navigate the production tree.
It is not easy to understand the resource stock pile in the lower right corner of the screen. Pausing and really starring at it is required. Where is excess workforce recorded? I cant find it anywhere which results in the trial and error of building houses until you have enough. This is in a game where space is scarce and building must be planned.
As resources come in it would be satisfying if there was a visual and aural reward. Like killing a creep in dota 2. You hear a faint noise of money jangling. Maybe some sort of audio to signal that a particular resource stock pile has filled would help. I notice I have resources doing nothing much of the time because I am not aware that I need to spend it. Too much to keep track of. I admit I was playing this game with a glass of wine but even mildly buzzed I was struggling to keep up. Never had this with any other games before and I would hardly call this game "hard core".
Due to all of this I can not recommend this game at this stage of development. You are almost there. I think with some minor finishing touches you will have a great game that people will enjoy.

Never has failing been so fun.
Only an hour or so into the game, I feel like I get the core element.
It is simple trial and error, learn by your mistakes, and I love it.
Normally losing can be frustrating, and especially to unfair odds, but in ""they are billions", you try to find out how you could have been more efficient.
And without a save'n'load feauture, you really cannot affort to make too many mistakes.
This may scare a few people away, but this is also what makes it so addicting.
It is not for everyone, and the rogue-like maps (random generated with different spawns, zombie hords and bonus ressources) can feel unfair, like being dealt a bad hand in a poker-game, but here you cannot bluff.. you can either fold and hope for a better hand next time, or try to follow the flow of the game.
A few addition I would like to the game would be:
- Co-op - mode. I am a sucker for co-op, though in my older days I see the benefit with single player games. That said this could be a good way to make a Starcraft like Co-op like "Left4Die"-acade mode.
- Unit improvements. I would like either small upgrades to be bought, or talent tree. Just to a feel of progression, do not need to be wildly gamechanging, could be flash/stun granade for soldier, fan of arrow rangers and mark of death (increase dmg to that unit) for snipers etc.
I think that would serve it well, as well as more than just one unit lvl, like C'n'C tiberian sun.
- Infinity mode. This could be a great addition for co-op to see how far one could get.
- Heroes or major talents. To give a kinda a progression, one could either get a hero or talents like Starcraft 2 co-op. These should be small perks and not too strong, maybe even come with choices. Will I have Walls with selfrepair, but less health.
Will I go for faster moving units, but sacrifice either health, dmg or both.
Will I be able to use less space to build, for the cost of more ressources.
Etc. These are mere inspiration, and could give you a feeling of progression aswell as try up different builds.
That said, it is still in beta if I recall correctly, and great fun.
Hoped it helped, else feel free to ask.

When I started this game, october last year I had the idea this game has good potential, looked very nice and we had one playable planet.
A few updates arrived last year which most of them added to the value of the product. Also, a new planet was build (Aziel) and the playerbase did think the devs were moving in the right direction, keeping us busy most of the time.
One flaw however was that you could only do so much and basically... everything you did in this game was building up a base, vehicles, and some other craftable stuff and fighting aliens.
Aliens? yes.. I hear you, there is also pvp but I don't go into that. Basically, the pvp for me isn't good. You log out, and your base (which you have build hours to complete) will be destroyed by other players in minutes.
Anyway, back to pve.. which there is in single and multi-player. For me, the game mode is the same, you either play alone or with other people but the pve is soloable (all of it).
Having said all of it, we recently got some updates.. which unfortunately added more bugs and didn't add more gameplay. The dev team redesigned the starter planet which was a very bad move. They added trees, water, towering buildings on a desert planet! Bad idea.
Furthermore, the ice planet.. didn't get any kind of updates and is basically there for scenery.
I hear you... it's early access... yes it is, but why then do we get additions like stone ovens, printers, a redesigned space ship, craftable ingots and that sort of "garbage"? The dev team doesn't know what they want with the game and the community seems divided.
For now, it seems this game can.... be made a lot better, but we have to see where it is going. I currently do not recommend people to buy this game.

If you're looking to "have fun and laugh" be careful; this might not be the game for you.  This is more of a how-to-handle-tragedy/depression/sickness/solitude-game... if that is helpful in any way.  It is a first-person, puzzle AND adventure game, with a touch of "real-life" drama and a small amount of terror.
Wake up in a deserted island INJURED and not able to walk pretty much, and solve puzzles to "get out" if you can.  Simple enough?..  It's night-time... or at least you will never see the light of day, it's raining/pouring most of the time, the letters you find scattered in the island will be very clear about the horrible weather in the island.
I can't speak much more without giving too much away... but I will say this much, the ambient sounds are eerie.... there is NO way to play this game without imagining a creature of some sort jumping onto your path and dismembering you, (for example: the poison zombies from Half-Life 2 which I passed once on a friend's account).... the game is very succesful in making you feel horribly eerie while there is NOTHING that can actually happen to you... it is almost unbelievable that you will not "die" at some point.  Keeping me in that suspense was, fun!  I remember saying "there is no way I will believe that someone or something wont hack me to pieces at any second!" hehe
It's that feeling you get when you're in the woods (vs. being in the city) thinking something out of the shadows will murder you.  Truth is, you're in more danger in the city (ironic lol).  You need to know city life to know the feeling lol
The only real issue I do have, is all the debris in the island, makes you wonder if the place got hit by a tornado... (it couldn't have, the rains are hard but not tornado-like).  Ah, YES forgot to mention; there is a morse-code puzzle!!  I love morse code!
Anyway, do observe everything closely... specially the floor.  There are so many items you can miss.  Saving feature is not so great, but the game saves everytime you solve a puzzle (no dude, opening a gate is not a puzzle... at least not in the prologue) so it is fair.

Montagues Mount is a real story of an internal struggle to live with the authors own demons. A game using storytelling, puzzles, and a beautifully rendered yet dark simulation which the player explores, all the while unfolding tragedy after tragedy. A linear story yet wide open to interpretation, but be sure to tweak up the brightness a bit first.
Montagues Mount is an admirable one-man effort. Like many games in the genre, it has unique mood elements and features like Oculus Rift support. One such clever immersion trick is the way all items in the game are labelled in Irish (with English translations of course.) All of which smooths over the horror and the harshness of isolation. Is Aine still alive?
Getting to the top of the mount should take about an hour, 2 at most. If you like this short story, first try out Dear Esther and others like To the Moon, Trauma, Gone Home and The Novelist.
Pseudo-psychological walking simulator in which you need to discover secrets of the island. But please, do yourself a favor and play Dear Esther or Gone Home instead if you into such games.

Is this the last "classical" FPS?  Or the first "modern" shooter?  After nearly two decades I'm not even sure anymore.  All brown jokes aside, consider the following:
* Graphics and lighting that have aged beautifully, unless you're an unrepentant graphics ♥♥♥♥♥.
* Incredibly immersive sound design and score by Trent Reznor that beats most games today (playing SP campaign in the dark with headphones can get ridiculously unnerving)
* FAST, FLUID, SKILLFUL GAMEPLAY -- YOU CAN AND WILL DIE.  BRUTALLY.
And I'm not even going to talk about the mods, or multiplayer, or any of that other stuff we take for granted thanks to the breakthroughs this game made.  We all know.
It's not much more than a slight update of the DOOM formula, without ever really hitting those same heights, but I keep coming back to this game once in a while simply because - well, because they don't make them like this anymore.  There's the most grudging attempt at a story, not nearly as many enemies as you'd like, and a confusing mish-mash of design elements owing to the chaos at iD.  But it's a classic anyway, and IMO the last great iD title, because it just wants to be fun and atmospheric.  And it succeeds.
Boot it up.  Blow off some steam.  Gib some grunts.  Axe a dog.

I picked up this game with low expecations. Many reviews describe it as a mediocre game trying to be a low-budget Mass Effect.
I was very pleasantly surprised.
This game was fun, enteresting, and entertaining, as long as one is willing to invest in it.
If you are not the kind of person who cares about story, you will probably find this game to be mediocre It's an Action-RPG, and the story is a huge part of what makes this game worthwhile. While the story is not in any way innovative, it is engaging and it is interesting. Yeah, aliens attack earth, humanity is on the brink of annihilation, but somehow manages to adapt the alien technology to their own use and eventually takes the fight to the aliens. That sounds like a lot of movies and games of the last few decades. There's nothing new here. But if you just put yourself in the shoes of William Carter and roll with it, you can have a lot of fun in this game's world. I will admit though that the game never made me care about any of the characters on a personal level. I only explored all of the dialogue trees out of a sense of curiosity and kept everyone alive that I could because I don't like to lose characters. It ended up being a matter of numbers (keeping casualties low as a sort of high-score).
If you are just looking for a game you can relax and play while only half-paying attention, then you will probably be disappointed and even frustrated with the combat. This particular third-person shooter brings nothing new to the game. You mix guns and powers with a bit of semi-paused tactical gameplay and cover-based combat - very similar to what Mass Effect 1 had down to the part where you have two teammates with you. The AI of your teammates is pretty bad. The number of times I was put in a bad spot because one of my teammates ran out of cover and into enemy fire, making me come save him is ridiculous. On the higher difficulties, micromanagement becomes essential. You have to constantly assess the battle using the pause (more of a time slow) menu and position your teammates, tell them what enemies to target and what skills to use. If you don't use strategy, you will have a hard time. However, I do remember that in Mass Effect 1, my teammates were next to useless in most cases. I did the majority of the damage in that game, and Wrex spend over half of each battle "dead". The Bureau makes this a bit more difficult by making you have to save your teammates, or they will bleed out and die. There is no spontatenous regeneration after each battle - you have to manage your team.
Overall, I found this game well worth the price of admission and worth the time I spent on it. The story did not bore me, and the combat was fun.

Let's get deal with it's weaknesses first; of which it's biggest by far are the clunky controls. They make movement particularly during combat a bit of a gamble. Sometimes you can't get into cover, sometimes you can't get out, sometimes you just find yourself popping out of cover and not going anywhere. I can't help but feel this comes as a result of it's console affiliation. The sprint button is the same button used to take and leave cover. Moving around corners while in cover is not performed automatically like in most games, it requires it's own keypress. Another weakness appears to be the friendly AI; they're just not terribly bright. While they seem to know when a grenade is thrown and move away, at least first, they often just rush straight back to where they were _before_ the grenade has gone off! They require constant babysitting. Sometimes they'll stay where they're instructed to, other times they'll just go wherever they please. The enemy AI aren't Einsteins either - they have a tendancy to run back and forth between two cover positions - but they appear to be more capable than the friendlies. They actually move from grenades for a start, and are capable of flanking when possible.
Now for what makes this game genuinely good. Firstly the outstanding visuals. The models, textures, lighting are brilliant. The levels are highly detailed making it feel like ones really in old 1960s America. The immersion is deepened by small touches like photos, audio reels, documents and notes, my favourite being ones that instruct folks to ask specific questions - like what sound does a dog make or where someone was when President Johnson was assassinated - to aid in identifying disguised aliens - because they aren't able to reproduce a "woof" sound and they have trouble with distinguishing Human names so won't know that President Johnson wasn't assasinated. It's the sort of thing one could imagine actually happening in such a scenario. Great little touch! The story itself while not all that original is told really well through discussions with NPCs and the documents and audio reels all over the place. You get fed the story in small chunks and the underlying mystery is slowly revealed. The sound is top notch and the voice acting isn't half bad either.
The gameplay, now this is a bit a mixed bag. A key mechanic is the use of a "Battle Focus" mode which slows time to a crawl and allows you to issue orders to your squad. This is actually done extremely well. Moving a squadmate into cover shows the level of cover provided by that position - partial or full. Orders can be queued up for execution. They system works really well. Having said that I have a few qualms about it; I don't like the fact it just slows time down instead of pausing it altogether for example. At least it should be an option to do so. To use the main characters abilities you're required to execute them through the "Battle Focus" mode as well, you can't just push a button to do so. This is particuarly annoying when you want to heal your squad quickly, you have to open "Battle Focus", hover over the characters skill bar, click the skill or push the number associated with that skill. I would rather just be able to push the button. Back at base the player is given the choice of missions to run; the choice varies between storyline missions which must be completed at some point and side missions. Side missions are a great way to increase the XP of the player and his squad. And that brings me to another hit-and-miss part of the game; the RPG element. The player and his squad obtain XP through kills, XP translates into leveling up, leveling up translates into new skills and stats; the usual affair. That all works just fine. One can even customise their squads names and looks - a nice touch. What stands out though are the classes of squadies. Different classes afford different abilites on the battlefield. This works especially well and adds a fantastic dynamic to the game. Of course it's possible to specify the loadout of your squad but this is where I had a small issue; you get a selection of weapons which is all good and well, but nowhere are you told what damage the weapon does or what enemies it's affective against or anything. There is a shooting range provided at the base which I suppose one could aruge should be used for this but I'm not sure how accurate an assessment that would be. I would like to be told what range of damage I can expect and what distance it's effective over and if it's good for taking down shields or mechanical targets, that sort of thing.
Overall, it's perfectly competent 3rd person tactical shooter set in a masterfully constructed world and set to an intriguing albeit unoriginal story. I would certainly recommend it.

I like First Person Shooters. I like Turn Based Strategy. I like XCOM. I do not like a FPS trying to intergrate TBS elements into an XCOM game. (While using a Mass Effect template, on top of everything else) While the concept is interesting, it is done so, so, so very terribly. How so? Glad you asked. (I do this for you John Q. Public)
As the title says, this is an XCOM game, but instead of taking on the role of commander, safe back at base barking orders, you play as Agent William Carter and you take to the field! You are one of big guys at The Bureau a.k.a XCOM, a last-ditch contigency plan in case the Commies ever managed to successfully invade America. You are the USA's last line of defense, now turned only line of defense as the Aliens begin their invasion. It's a rough start: your base is destroyed and over 200 personnel slaughtered as you try to salvage what you can. So naturally, it's up to you and your trusty sidearm to take out the alien invaders.
One of the first things you learn is how to take cover. You hold down a key and sprint for the nearest wall. Simple enough, but then you learn if you press THIS button, you can move to the next available cover! And then THIS button lets you go around the corner! And then THIS button lets you do a dodge roll away! The best part? You can't leave cover unless you walk in the direction away from it, convienently putting your fedora wearing head in the enemy's line of fire as you scramble for a better position. Additionally, the aliens have lasers, piercing through your cover or nipping the top of your head as it peaks up from the brickwall. How can you keep yourself from becoming a laser sponge if the cover system seemingly wants you to wind up dead? Call upon your two allies, of course!
It wouldn't be XCOM if you weren't ordering lackeys around. However, unlike other XCOM titles, you get two peeps. Two. And that's still two too many. The AI employed on these guys leaves much ot be desired. They seem incapable of common strategy, relying on you to put them where they'll do the best. Since ordering people around as bullets are flying is stressful enough, you are then introduced to "BATTLE FOCUS." It (mostly) freezes time around you, giving you an opportunity to tell your men what to do. "Transistor' employed a similar system, but they pulled it off significantly better than "The Bureau." Since your men need you to be their brain, that means that you not only have to worry about yourself, but two moronic AI's, all in real time as the Aliens move like pros and shoot you silly.
Since you can't count on your backup, it's to you to become a one man army. Which is hard to do when the game was designed to make you a strategy boss instead of the usual FPS Killing Machine. Guns are not your friend in this hybrid of genres. You are only to use them when in cover, and when your enemy decides to pop up from their hay bale. This renders the shotgun useless, unless you manage to get up close and personal. (Which is impressive, considering you'll have a minimum of ten aliens blasting at you at any given moment.) Additionally, unlike other FPS games, you are serverly punished for shooting too long. It's a game of duck and shoot if you want to keep your blood inside your body.
So let's review here. The cover system is overly complicated and convoluted (you just had to be an XCOM FPS, didn't you?) Your AI buds, while presumablely useful, can't make any useful decisions unless you tell them to. And while you are certainly capable of taking care of buisness, the game is designed to make you a team player, trying to shove the roles of Base Commander and Field Agent into one. The end result? A game that tries to be two things, and to be good at those two things, but falls disappointingly short. If the enemies wouldn't move around as much, the Battle Focus would make more sense and have more practical use. If the cover system, ally AI's, and weapons weren't configured for a TBS game, you could actually do something on your own. But no, you get a fast paced shoot-em-up that wants you to think in terms of TBS. It is a frustrating experience, causing you to wonder just who play-tested this system and gave it the green light.
That was all just the combat mechanics. I didn't even get into character and story development, running your base, or DLC. Primarily because I didn't even make it past the first "real" mission. Note, I said "didn't," not "couldn't." Given time, I probably could become good at this game, maybe even great. But if I cannot even bring myself to persevere through the first challenge because the mechanics are so flawed, what's the point in trying? Don't waste your money on this game, folks. If you want to know the story, just look up a YouTube "Game Movie" video or check Wikipedia. There's no other reason to play this game, hence there is no reason to buy this game. Don't let my words discourage you from checking out the rest of the XCOM franchise, though. Enemy Unknown is an excellent TBS, and is definitely worth the purchase. Moreso than this trainwreck of a spinoff, I'll say.

This game is an undercooked mess that's totally barebones and needs more content, but unfortunately like most Paradox games they lock these "features" that should've been in the base game behind paywalls.
Along with their poor DLC policy, the A.I. is completely awful, has to be handicapped in obvious ways just to make the game playable. Many parts of the world are totally neglected, unbalanced, and unplayable such as Asia ( which is a total nightmare in Multiplayer games ).
Along with this, they have parts of the game totally neglected: Naval Combat is a joke, tanks are the same for all countries, Rockets are useless, the A.I. is handicapped on Focus Trees, historical divisions are impossible to make... in a historical game, atomic bombs are easily spammed in the hundreds by 1944, and probably most hilariously:
You can win WW2 in 1937, by just parachuting into the enemy capitals.
To enjoy this game, you need to TRY to handicap the A.I. to it's maximum difficulty, and CHOOSE to neglect TANKS and large INFANTRY divisions, and force yourself to do bad strategies, JUST to make it fair to the A.I., which can't handle ANYTHING. It's frequent to see the A.I. overproduce like 50,000 infantry equipment or at times, 30,000 support equipment, and probably most glaringly of all, which I capitulated an A.I. to find out it had over produced 23,000 trucks and 9,000 lights tanks... that it wasn't even using.
I have many hours in this game because I want to enjoy it, and I go through hoops to cheat for the A.I. frequently to save it from death when I beat the soviets in 1939 just to give the game some enjoyment, and ( like many others ) play the mods that fix many issues like Kaiserriech. This game is great, but I cannot recomend it in it's current state.
Here's a closing statement, that really sends home the issue here:
The Kaiserreich Team ( a popular mod ), has more active members, than Paradox staff working on Hearts of Iron 4.
Yep. That's right. The mod team, is better staffed, than the game. This game NEEDS some help.

This game is basically StarCraft, Terran vs Zergs in Tower Defense mode. I love it, because I used to play SC just like that as a kid. And of course I sucked, because offense is the best defense.
Though this game is not about turtling. In my first rounds I always tried to keep my village as compact as possible, to make it as easy as possible to defend. The problem is, the more you upgrade your existing houses, the more resources, energy and workforce they will consume. At some point it becomes impossible to produce more defensive fire power this way, while the hordes grow exponentially.
Instead you need to find a fine balance between expanding really fast and wide, but stopping and building solid defenses in between at the right spots. If there is just one weak spot in your defense, you will be devoured by the hordes.
Cons:
- One round takes far too long in my opinion. Yesterday I lost my first good round at day 90 or so (out of 120), because it already took 3 or 4 hours to get that far and I just became extremely bored at that point and stopped building reasonably.
I would wish for a smaller map where the difficulty span goes from 40 - 80 days instead of 80 - 150.
- Building seems really bugged, or it is made annoying intentionally. Sometimes it is possible to place a lot of buildings next to each other, sometimes not at all. Because "building this here would block access to another building". But if I have built the exact same structure in three other places already, I assume it is a bug in the 4th place. This leads you to build very ugly formations of buildings with gaps everywhere and trigger your OCD

TL;DR - an awesome and fresh game, if you like dying a lot and learning how to beat it through failures.
I enojy this game a lot and for the right player I think it's a must buy. This is a hardcore difficult game - I'm a fairly experienced strategy games fan and it took me 53 hours and probably over 50 attempts to beat the first level - on 55% difficulty (feat achieved by about 8% of the game owners). I'd also say it's a base builder / active pause RTS with a lot tower defence mechanics (cause it doesn't really feel like a TD game - it has too much economy, base building, units etc).
The difficulty comes from two factors.
One is that you can make a silly mistake, omit an opening in woods or move a unit and forget to place it back at its guard post - a single zombie can then start infecting your colony and spawn enough new enemies from your bulidings to overrun you.
The other one is from the ever rising amount of zombies that attack your base. To defend from them, you need to constantly improve your defences, but better defences need more resources  so a bigger base that is in turn harder to defend, so you must keep building up and planning for the future the whole game.
This also means why the game is so fun  you do not build your base to meet some arbitrary objective; you build it up to make sure you survive the hordes the game will throw at you, and this is a great way to keep you on your toes.

The monsters in Quake are well designed and have a fun eldritch feel to them. I cannot remember their names for the life of me, but my favorite is what I like to call Electro-Yeti. The action is similar to Doom, but slightly slower paced. You won't open a door and have fifty demons charging at you at once. However, everything deals more damage and combat is more visceral.
It's totally worth what little money they're asking for it.

What I like about the very first Quake is its very gothic and satanic, its as satanic as Doom where you fight demons and monsters from hell. Its very similar, but the difficulty is not that hard like Doom. But i do like the movement in the game. Highest difficulty (nightmare, which is a secret mode), will only increase enemy speed movement and reaction, life damage should be the same (i think, or it may add more damage). What i know for sure, they dont respawn after killing them, so if you are smart on tactics, you should be able to find a way to find a room to take a breather from all the pressure on killing, unlike Doom where in highest difficulty you have little chance to breathe from, and dont have much time.

+ Atmosphere

If it "clicked" in the end, I imagine the reviews would have been much more positive. As it is, it only leaves you wondering if it really could be based on a true story (which it is not) and what it might be (which you won't find out).
Sorry, this may still be worth playing for the sake of the atmosphere, if you have already bought it, but it is definitely not worth buying.

Wow. I've played quite a few very impressive games and this one still wow'd me big time. Beautiful scenery, huge map, it was in a way awe inspiring. As for gamplay, imagine something like Sniper Elite but in open world form. If you like being stealthy and planning assualts but still being able to feel the thrill of going balls out when the SHTF, this could very well be your jam. It was definietely mine. I will say, playing with friends may be a huge contributor towards what made me fall in love with this game. The AI teammates they give you are lame and feel thin (but then again this seems to so often be the case I can't really count it against them). Sooo much more fun playing with a friend or two. There were so many moments I felt like we were doing things straight out of a spy or military movie. The feeling was just so amazing.
The game certainly has it's detractors, mainly people saying 1. the story is lacking, 2. it's repetitive, or 3. the landscape is just meh. On the first point, I don't disagree; the story is almost a footnote. Just like they had to check the "Include Main Story Arc" box. It's really less of a story and more of a framework to provide some context and rationale to why you're where you are and why you're doing what you're doing. It gives the opportunity to run many "story" missions in parallel. There's so much other stuff to do tho, I'm not even bothered by it. On the second point, I mostly disagree. While you do end up doing some of the same stuff and/or the same types of missions (as you do in ALL open world games), the enviroment, location, time of day, weather, etc... all add to making the experience feel varied. The way you approach a loot raid, for example, will be different depending on whether it's day or night, whether it's a huge enemy base or a small squad outpost, or whether you want to be stealthy or go guns blazing like Rambo. On the thrid point, I absolutely disagree. I don't know how anyone can even say the landscape is 'meh' with a straight face. It's effin incredible. Massive jungles, sizable towns (and TONS of them) and the ability to travel around the map and see it all in numerous ways was great. Planes, helicopters, dirtbikes, SUVs, Ferraris, bulldozers, whatever! Flying a plane or helicopter is so enjoyable I find myself spending up to 30 min capturing one just to be able to fly over the [huge] map just because it's so beautiful. Oh and you can parachute right out of it when you get to your destination. That brings up anonter point. The map is HUGE. I can't think of a game I've played that has a larger one. And it's all so meticulously detailed.

Both Campaigns can be finished in under 2 hours.

Save your money.

I bought this game when it came out.. then.... well.. nothing.. Other games came around that this one fell between the chairs. Which is a real shame.. I missed up upon a truly great game. It started out rather bland I thought, but as the game went on it's production value kept getting better. That usually happens when the people working on the title actually get more experience. But still, this game is really quite good. Despite some glaring misses I'll go through.
It takes the X-Com IP, and spins it in a fresh environment. Very enjoyable game, with a story that keeps on growing. I would very much like to revisit this world. Few notable issues, I really don't like when a game cuts the way you came off. I understand the need for a game to push forward, but restrictions like that is only annoying. And frankly, if they had not. This game would have been much closer to Half-Life, because this game (story wise) shares quite a few notable points. They should be honored by that, because if they only allowed more freedom in the gameplay, then this game would have been right up there. I personally haven't felt this much fun playing a game since... well. the last Half-Life episode really.
There are a few graphical glitches in places, but nothing that really takes away the fun of the game. I know that other rated this game lover. Some compare it with Mass Effect, but that makes me wonder if they played the game. Sure, it uses game mechanics (as well as some other points) used in ME, but you could have said it uses mechanics from KoToR as well. The point is, the mechanic works. And trying to play the game down, simply because it uses a good mechanic is.. well.. stupid really. It is the main reason why good games have good elements and ideas copied all the time.
I just wish they had not squandered the wonderful opportunity they had with this game. To create a more open game where you can explore the surroundings, and come up with your own way to beat the levels. So, this game is quite linear, and while it doesn't really break the game, it also makes it less fun than it could have been. Still, if you can.. play it.. I think you will enjoy it as I have. This game have continually grown on me. Such a shame reviewers tend to write what 'others' say, just in order to be mainstream.
I really do want to get back into this world, and if they made the world more open for exploration that would be terrific. Because I really don't like it when a game is leading the way. Just look at far cry, that is what this game needs.

Hatoful Boyfriend starts out as a straight-out parody of many visual novel tropes, letting the reader get to know and enjoy the personalities of each bird. The reader gets various clues throughout the main game that there's a lot more happening behind the scenes. By the end, the story turns into a psychological horror, turning each character on his head- making the reader question everything they have learned about the birds so far. Yes, this game is quite awesome- both in the original and the HD remake.
Is it worth $10? I would say "Yes, of course it is! BBL is worth $10 alone." However, I have noticed a few things about this new polished version that make me miss the older, typo-ridden $5 version. These are certainly nitpicks. For one, I don't like the new desktop icon (pink heart with 2 feathers sticking out) It is the most Otome looking thing on my boyish desktop and it sticks out like a sore thumb. I much prefer the green nicobar logo. Secondly, while I am thankful this game has a fullscreen mode (which makes recording footage a breeze) I believe the original has a tiny window for a reason- mainly, the bird portraits are of varying quality. In fullscreen, I get to see all the choppy pixels I wasn't aware of before. Back to the tiny window I suppose. Azami's route, newly added in this version, was lackluster. This has been built up by fans for a while now and of course, its "safe" nature has nothing to do with the team that polished this game up. However, when I played it, I was a bit confused as to why Azami had a one-sided mad rant to herself when cleary, Hiyoko was supposed to say at least half of the lines. Maybe that issue has been sorted by now? My biggest issue is the Save feature in BBL! I am serious about this, it ruins the mood. While there is no real way to fail BBL, it was quite a shock to readers when they first play it. It was made even scarier when the box shows up saying that save states are disabled for this portion of the game. The survival instict kicks in for a lot of readers at that point.  Players would then be cautious about their surroundings and return to HQ repeatedly to make their alotted save. In this newer, sparklier version... the player can save whenever they well please- taking away that intense atmosphere. The "battle" at the end? No problem, they can just save and not have to worry about potential failure. Eh, I don't like that. But the backgrounds are absolutely gorgeous in this version, and I'm very glad that Nageki has lost his awkward clutching side-foot. Also, having the option to switch from English to Japanese with the click of a button is really nice. I am glad I bought this verion of the game.
A few unrelated things I noticed while playing this game again... Some of our stud birdies appear to be female! Leone JB and Rabu both have pink ceres. Also... pigeon genders are hard to identify by appearance alone, but I will say that our OkoSan has a Very feminine skull. And Ryouta's portrait... well, look at those pupils! That is one miffed bird. Anghel and Shuu are puffed out like they're absolutely freezing, the poor birds. And... that fight music? While I know it is public domain- it is also the title menu music to a gory horror BL visual novel called Cage -open-. Imagine my shock as I see Anghel on one side of the screen, Shuu on the other side of the screen, and my auditory cue for shiver-inducing psychological torture♥♥♥♥♥♥triggers. "My god Shuu, don't!  Oh wait, you have a harmless cloaka... Do what you must, then."

I played this game for about 6 hours before deciding to stop.  It felt more like an Aliens version of Dark Souls.  Each monster you fight is more like a boss battle, and when 2-3 gang up on you at once, you can't seem to deal with it, and running away doesn't work.  The best strategy I've found is to find something high up to hide on while you tickle them with your laser gun.
Of the 6 hours played, I'd say more than half was spent fighting monsters.  And then all but 5% of what was left looking for and mining resources (probably close to an 80/20 split, respectively), and the last 5% was exploring options with the base.
It seemed that every few minutes, I'd get aggro from a monster that did not have line-of-sight on me.  It more felt like "If you are within radius x of creature, set aggro = true".  So I'd get aggro from creatures on the other side of mountains, or across an entire valley, and with each being a huge time commitment, it just became frustratingly repetitive over time.  As I'm reflecting on the game, scenes of fighting are more dominant than not.
As for resource gathering, I had to go lookup on a wiki as to the location of Carbon, since I had ventured 1500 meters away from my base in search of that and Hydrogen and found neither.  Both are required for better gear, and I couldn't find them at all until I looked it up.  It just seemed like they did a great job at hiding resources, making you spend most of your time fighting overpowered monsters, giving you crappy gear to deal with it, and then making the ability to find the starting domino to trigger improvement nearly impossible to locate, and said, "Here's a game."
I know it's in early access, but they should have put more into it before releasing it for early access.  It would seem that the ploy to make money before launch is the current meta for games, and this one has me seriously debating every getting an Early Access game again.  If you like Dark Souls, you might like this.  If you like Subnautica, Minecraft, Destiny, No Man's Sky, or other gathering/base-building games, this one has so little reference towards that I would be leery to even classify them in the same category.  I wouldn't recommend this game if you are really into any of those 4 that I mentioned.

I think that how you feel about this game will largely depend upon what you expect or want from it before going in. The tags on the store page say "Adventure" and "Horror" and "Walking Simulator", but to be honest I really think you should downplay the adventure and horror aspects and temper your expectations instead towards the walking part... and add "Exploration" and "Puzzle" into the mix while you're at it. That's what you'll be doing for the two or three hours it'll take to finish this, slowly walking around a small island, searching for items and using them to complete puzzles whilst also trying to solve the mystery of who you are after a storm has washed you up on a beach and robbed you of your memory.
I can't say I actually cared about the protagonist's story all that much as starting off a game by waking up some place with amnesia has been done so many times it's lost its intrigue and impact. And at this point, instead of proving vital to a unique story, it feels more like a device to drip feed the player the details of the past while still keeping them in the present, as well as not have the character know something that the player who's controlling him doesn't. It's probably something of a Catch 22 situation as it's difficult as a storyteller to walk that line of having the player be someone else whilst also not really knowing who they actually are and finding a way to convey that information. But either way, it just didn't grab me.
What I found far more interesting, though, was the story of the island itself and how a fatal infection that spread across it affected the now dead people and drove them ever more to desperate measures. And, sure, while your own character is a part of that story, it didn't feel as interesting as the bigger picture. By the end it appears as though the personal story has mostly been answered, so if the intended second/final part of this game ever sees the light of day I really hope it focuses on that and wrapping up your character's story is much more secondary.
Gameplay itself is more about having a keen eye and a sharp mind as you track down items and follow clues to figure out how to complete puzzles. But this is another kind of Catch 22 situation as the atmosphere and presentation of the game clashes with actually operating within the world. So much effort is spent on creating the perfect tone that it makes finding objects and clues awkward at times. The entire game takes place at night and many areas are cast in shadow, add to that a film grain effect and the fluctuating colour that regularly drains to make the world completely grey and sometimes figuring out what you're missing really can feel like looking for a needle in a haystack. But while some of these effects are optional, as much as you're making it harder on yourself to leave them on, without them I think it takes away from the greatest aspect of the game, its atmosphere.
Moody really doesn't begin to describe it. Throw in some more words like "brooding" and "desolate" and "isolated" and you're getting closer. When I started playing this I decided to do it in the wee small hours of the morning, with no lights on and the windows open to let in the cold air and rustling wind. It genuinely helped immerse me in the world even more, but this only built on what was already perfectly crafted to begin with. As I progressed through the game I began mentally drowning out the presentation as I focused on some of the more irritating puzzle features, but just before I finished it I started backtracking across the island for the sake of an achievement to walk ten kilometres (yes, I'm one of those people. Sometimes I hate myself, too), and that's when it really struck me just how much care and attention went into building a truly incredible atmosphere.
Without any objectives to distract me I was able to better notice the details, like the waves lapping at the shore, insects chirpings and lights buzzing, the random coughs of your weather-beaten character, the fact that the greying of the game seems to coincide with the periodic rainfall and accompanying thunderclaps (the intensity of the grey being proportional to how heavy the rain is), or noticing eerie noises seeming to come from different points all around me. Is it an owl hooting somewhere, or my ears playing tricks on me to make it sound like distant children playing among the death and decay of the island, or possibly hidden somewhere crying? It really brought to life a rare feeling for me in a game where I really was immersed completely in my surroundings and overcome with a genuine sense of almost alien solitude and curious wonder, intrigue to explore but apprehension of the unknown. This really is as fine an example as you're going to see of how to craft an environment to evoke real feelings in a player.
The game did take a bit of a bashing upon initial release, but it seems to have gotten better with additional updates and tweaks based on user feedback. I really do hope the negativity won't discourage the developer from carrying on with the conclusion, and if anything will use it as constructive criticism to further improve upon what he's already made. And if we're really, lucky Derek Riddell will also return to lend his excellent voice-over talents once more. As flawed as it may be, I really do think this deserves to be experienced by every fan of the genre. Look up a guide if you have to, mess with some settings if need be, but give it a chance and I think you'll be glad you did.

This game is unfinished, unpolished, and should still be considered a preview release.
The good:
Once you figure it out, it's a pretty fun game. When it works. If you like pirate style games and rogue style games, you would like a game like this a lot, if it were finished.
The BAD:
- To start with, the UI is extremely non-intuitive, and the in-game help is only slightly better than useless. Furthermore, there are extreme annoyances in the UI that make it almost unplayable by themselves.  The primary example of this is that if you have a list of things in a scrolling window, clicking on one of them to select it jerks you back to the top of the window. This would be bad enough if the mouse wheel worked to let you scroll. It doesn't. You have to drag the scroll bar around like it's 1991 or something.
- Let's say you can live with all the UI glitches. There is currently a bug that makes the game unfinishable. Or at least it did for me. Once you get a large crew going and you're in about mid game, your pirates start going rogue, one by one, until they're all dead. This is even if you keep them well-fed and keep their morale up (the only mechanics the game gives you to deal with mutinous pirates). They can have a perfectly green happiness meter, but wIth no warning they mutiny and get sliced to bits by the rest of the crew, until you have none left. Now you're up a creek without a paddle, because all the encounters are far too high-level to take on with just a skeleton crew.
- Other glitchy things happen that force you to reload your game occasionally, like a pirate will just get stuck somewhere and be unable to move, preventing you from sailing anywhere or plundering a ship.
- Knockback, even on the lowest setting, is ridiculous and sends your pirates sailing into the water where they'll drown unless you have given them the swimming skill. This is an intentional game mechanic, and it's not at all fun.
This is an alpha game at best. To call this release quality is an insult. It's definitely not worth the price at this point. Someday it probably will be. I could forgive most of the bugs, but the game breaking bug that makes the game un-finishable is beyond the pale. It's hard to get to that point in the game, and you'll have wasted a lot of time doing so, only to find out you can't continue through no fault of your own.
Sorry guys, thumbs way down.

The Wildlands story mode (in single player with AI companions, or the superior coop mode) is a fun game in itself. However, the hidden gem is definitely the online multiplayer: Ghost War.
I had no clue that this addition was included in the game when I bought it, so I consider it a "free bonus", and a great one at that!
Ghost War provides a unique and extremely tense game/setting, in that it requires a lot of cooperation within teams; running and gunning is not a viable option... In a sense, it is similar to group based PUBG, but without the weapon scavenging and with much more hiding in bushes. The rounds are kept infinitely interesting by the various map designs and objectives, and players can switch up their tactics by approaching the maps in different ways, as well as by choosing from the many operators (classes). The classes all contribute valuable features to the team, and are generally well balanced.
My only gripe with the game right now is that different graphics options (eg shadows and gamma) will have a significant impact on how easy enemies are to spot. Some of this could be more tightly regulated by the devs (eg forcing at least shadows=low).

This is one of the best games ever made, and certainly my favourite despite the huge number of other mind-numbingly awesome games I have played. Whilst the original game might not stand up in some ways to modern FPS games, its focus on simple satisfying carnage, and near total lack of a story or any semblance of realism to get in ther way of said carnage makes it one of the most pure and enjoyable FPS games in existence.
The main game is fairly short, but there are so many add-on levels and mods, you could easily be playing this for hundreds of hours without running out of new content. It also supports coop play, so you can blast through the main game and various mods together, and when you get sick of coop, you play one of the first ever deathmatch FPS games. Although Doom had deathmatch, it was Quake that caused an explosion in its popularity, and through mods spawned many new deathmatch modes, such as CTF and even Team Fortress.
Although there have been games since that have tried to bring players the classic gameplay focussed carnage of Quake and Doom, few have come anywhere near to the greatness of the originals. You'd be mad not to try this game if you've never played it before.
Disclaimer: I played Quake from 1996 when it came out. I still play now from time to time. I don't play the Steam version, hence I don't have much recorded playtime (just played ep1 to get enough to write this review! Still fun as hell).
Also, although the Steam version of the game works fine, I recommend getting hold of modern engine, such as Quakespasm to play it with. Check out the website Quaddicted to get new levels, mods and engines.

Evolve Stage 2 is an apt name for a game that was brought back from the dead after its troubled beginning. It is a better game, a faster one, balanced more in favor of casual fun instead of the e-sports angle Turtlerock aimed when it first launched. Naturally, the e-sports community rejected the forced effort and the game was left for dead... Until now.
Evolve has evolved into a proper Free 2 Play game, with an in-game currency and daily drop-feed rewards, the standard F2P trappings. Monsters and hunters are unlocked with silver dough and they are priced in such a way that makes sure you aren't overfeeding yourself -- it can take up to an hour or two of play time to earn enough cash to buy characters. This will need to be readjusted but the intention by developers is sound: you are always learning new characters and strategies and just when you've mastered each, you'll buy a new one. If you're the impatient sort, high prices would likely tip you over to the paying side.
Both for monsters and hunters you can unlock perks which, when upgraded two times, give you a real advantage against the opponent. This system makes it hard for new players to jump in, as they will always be underpowered when compared to veteran players. Even worse, perks are seperate for monsters and hunters so if you only play one or the other, the game actively makes sure you keep playing those and prevents you from experimenting.
This would all be pretty rotten if you could buy in-game cash. It would be Pay 2 Win. As of writing this, however, you cannot buy anything with your money. Presumably, Turtlerock are keeping that turned off until they finetune the progression.
But is the game any fun? It is. As I said before, Stage 2 is more casual, matches usually go on for about 10 minutes and the tools hunter have available to them make sure that you can catch-up with the monster and fight it even if you don't kill it. The major complaint of there being too much running is still true -- Evolve can be a running simulator. Because the movement system is rudementary and generally unengaging, there can be boring periods in every match. But when the fight starts, it's all adrenaline.
All in all, Evolve Stage 2 is a step in the right direction. It's not perfect by any means and the unlocking of characters is probably not enough to keep most people playing.

Thankfully, Turtlerock and 2K seem committed to making that dream happen.

A fun, if lacking, third person shooter.
The Bureau: XCOM Declassified is a prequel to the other games in the XCOM series. It deviates from the rest of the series by being a third-person shooter instead of being a strategy game. Mechanically, the shooting is functional, if somewhat boring. It lacks that extra "kick" when you fire a weapon. The tactics interface is almost completely useless. Even on the higher difficulties, you don't need to use high-level tactics to get through the levels. Just make sure to use your squadmembers' abilities and you'll be just fine.
On a technical standpoint, it is also poorly optimized. You will experience suprisingly low FPS compared to how the game looks. It is not very prone to crashes though, which is nice.
With all that said, I would not recommend it unless it is on sale. It is a pretty standard shooter, with some neat ideas dragged down by lacking execution.

This game is even better than the premise makes it out to be.
I have spent the past few days playing through each of the many routes of Hatoful Boyfriend from start to finish. I had heard there was quite a bit of hidden depth to this game... But I was not expecting as much of it as there was. Of the various routes in the game, some were more emotional than others, and some were downright silly. By chance, I started off with what seemed to be among the most emotional of them all, so several of the other routes were a little disappointing by comparison. There were references to Pokemon and Gurren Lagann and other popular culture littered throughout the visual novel, which was entertaining for a time, but they're not so overused as to come off as trying too hard to be funny. Honestly, for the most part, you should just treat 90% of those routes as a basic introduction to the characters.
Then I started the final route. It starts out almost the same... And then takes a huge left turn. It is basically a totally different game, and pretty much my primary reason for recommending the game. It answers all the questions brought up and never answered in the other routes (and some you might not even have thought of). It's *very* emotional at times, and just generally intense. So if you play a few routes and aren't too impressed, hang in there. It is worth it.
It's almost certainly worth $10, and you should definitely get it if it's on sale. The soundtrack is comprised of a bunch of short, looping songs, but the writing/translation is surprisingly good (barring a few occasional mistakes like missing words), and the story turned out to be really compelling. You'll laugh, you might cry, you'll definitely say "holy♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; a few times.
Buy it. You will not regret it.

iBomber Defense Pacific begrudgingly earns a thumbs up from me even though a "meh" would probably be more appropriate. The game is tower defense game ported from mobile platforms. It takes place in the pacific theater in WW2 where you fight the Japanese in land, air and sea battles. There are predetermined spots in each level where you can place defenses to repel the enemy forces (kind of like Kingdom Rush, but usually with greater concentration of hardpoints).
First the positives. The game is probably the most strategic tower defense game I have played. There are inter dependencies between the turrets so you probably want to place them in certain configurations to maximize your income and/or damage output. So also need to pick from various perks (Fallout'esqe) and turret upgrades so your strategy on a given level can potentially change based on that. The game also lets you fast forward time and pause it if you wish; if you pause the game, which is slightly unconventional, you can redirect your turrets adding a strategic element (ie, "micro") that many other titles lack.
As for the negatives, the graphics are somewhat bland, but I guess acceptable. I found it really hard to tell the difference between enemy units so it is sometimes tough to prepare sufficiently until your turrets have engaged the enemy. My bigger gripe is that this game is $4.99 on steam vs $1.99 on the Play store. Why the PC gamer gouging that seems so prevalent with mobile game developers? Sick of these companies who do a PC release as an afterthought and still charge a big premium.

Sometimes when I write a non-joke review (which I've been doing too often lately, in my opinion), I present it in an "If you like ______" sort of way, because I acknowledge that while I may not enjoy a certain aspect of a game, other people might be looking for just that thing. But I'm not going to do that for Montague's Mount, because I don't believe that there is a person who would be looking for anything that this game has to offer. I don't believe that there is a person who would enjoy waddling at a turtle's pace through a poorly designed island that might as well be in grayscale because the only colors you'll ever see for most of the game are "gray", "dark", and "darker" in the middle of the night in a storm solving puzzles that are only even remotely difficult because it's impossible to see anything between the darkness, the rain, and the film grain filter. I don't believe that there is a person who would look for a game that only manages to barely scrape 3 hours of play time because of how much time was spent waiting for painfully slow bridges and gates to open and how much time was spent with the game minimized making webms of the bridges and gates to show my friends how comically slow they were (no seriously, look -

I don't know how long these links are going to work for, so if it's 2027 and you're reading this, just take my word for it), with the other 2 and a half hours mostly spent wandering in the darkness looking for a stray candle I might've missed because I need it for a puzzle even though there's a house with at least 10 candles just sitting around that can't be picked up. And I certainly don't believe that there is a person who, after putting up with all of the garbage found within this game, would feel like they got their money's worth when they see that the ending is just a borderline cliffhanger, and this game is only half of a story. I can't recommend this game to anyone, and even if you got it in an indie bundle I'd be hard pressed to actually recommend installing it unless you just have nothing better to do.

First off, didn't get the original. Seems I made the right decision on that.
That gone, I've spent plenty of hours on this game and so far as a F2P game goes I'm thoroughly impressed. Sure, it wasn't originally F2P but now that it is, and after it ironed out a bunch of issues from the original (according to many founders) it's a ton of fun.
In this new iteration the monsters have a much harder time staying out of the hunters' sights, but that's not to say it's not possible. Now the monsters actually have to apply a LOT of skill and intelligent play to sneak around the hunters, who generally always have a fair idea of where the monster is. So if you play monster, learn to trick the hunters to buy yourself time to evolve. Also learn which hunters are the power players and which are prone to running off on their own.
For the hunters, now all hunters can dome the monster. This is a HUGE buff to the hunters but can also be a pitfall as a hunter can dome him/herself with the monster and have to wait on the others, cutting off his/her own escape in the meantime. The hunters can suppliment each other better now, so while no skill is vital to gameplay mechanically each skill is highly important to the overall teamplay. Learn each hunter's class and personal abilities and weapons, it's vital to know which hunter(s) are best for you and the team.
Finally, gripes about the game. Lobbies are an issue, some people get really picky about what role they play in the hunter team and will even leave, resetting the lobby, if they don't get what they want. If people were simply a little less spoiled OR simply ASKED their team to switch rolls around this wouldn't be an issue, but only a few people actually step up and do this. (They're the exception, not the rule)
Some people hate that the monsters are less stealthy, meaning early contact with the hunters is more likely. Likely, yes, but not guaranteed. You CAN be sneaky enough as a monster to keep the hunters off your trail, so if you feel like this is impossible then you're not doing it right. That's not the game's fault, that's yours.
Bug-wise, I've seen very few. Nothing game-breaking, for sure.
Previous lobby complaint aside, the community is *mostly* pretty friendly. Obvious exceptions as some people refuse to be socialable or pleasant in online interactions, others forego friendly interaction with an almost cold professionalism, and finally you will always find those nerds who blame failure on everyone but themselves and HAVE to be vocal about it. Mmyeah...
8.5/10 will continue playing, more so if my friends would forgive the original game and hop on with me.

I've never written a review for a game, but you've got to start somewhere. Good concept, anyone familar with Dota will see some similarities. Novel idea, good look and polish great graphics if you can run them. Unfortunately, it's all a bit superficial. You're constantly under seige, very little opportunity to hide, the hunters attacking you can at times seem completely unkillable and whilst you do get a little time to esccape between being 'domed' (trapped) with the hunters in an artificial cage you'll be getting shot in the back and followed around the whole time. So yeah, very stressful and poorly rewarded if you do win.
If you do get an edge on the hunters, they can rez themselves within 5 seconds, and have a dazzling array of buffs, shields and boosts that means you can be 2-3 seconds away from killing a hunter, to them being straight back to full health again wasting all your stress and efforts. As a monster, you have no way to heal yourself other than armour that gradually regenerates if you're not shot at (which you'll be constantly lit up) I can't begin to stress how soooooooooooooooooo frustrating that meta is. And it goes endless around in circles again and again and again until you feel like you've been sucked in and spat out again with but with PTSD.
Now it's not to say monsters don't win, they do. But the stress and effort involved in playing the said monster and succeeded is poor. It's a gaming equivilent of climbing mount everest at times.

What's there to say about Quake? One of the most world-renowned and memorable FPS' of all time. But why is that the case? Let's take a detailed look and see:
1. Gameplay - Let's trim the fat and get right to the guts right off the bat; Quake's gameplay is that of your typical 90's old-school FPS: Fast, bloody, complex and hard as hell, and you will love it (if you're into FPS games, that is). You get a wide array of weapons from a harmless Axe to the dreaded Thunderbolt, which turns any enemy into mincemeat in seconds, including the dreaded Shambler. Also like any old-school FPS, it is rife with secret areas that are a chore to find, but well worth the rewards within! Most times, at least. Tons of pick ups like the Pentagram of Protection (Invulnerability), Ring of Shadows (Invisibility), and the all-too-memorable Quad Damage, allowing you to unleash doomsday to every enemy in sight -- and yourself, too, if you aren't careful! -- dealing a massive 400% damage with any weapon you choose! There is a wide variety of enemies you will also encounter, from the annoying Grunt to the creepy Vore. Hint: When you see a Fiend (the bipedal, ape-like thing with lacerator arms) run like hell. One leap attack, and you're near dead. No joke.
2. Graphics - Usually graphics aren't one thing to take too seriously in reviews. In my philosophy, so long as you can see where you are going, and nothing looks TOO pixelated, they're perfectly tolerable. Buuuuuuuuut, that being said, download the Ultimate Quake Patch to be able to play this game in buttery-smooth 1920x1080 (if you have a full HD monitor that is). Never before has a game from the 90's looked so crisp and clear. And to think at one point I thought the 320x240 resolution of Quake on the N64 was the best thing ever. *shudders*
3. Difficulty - Hoo, boy...if you are brave enough to play this game on Nightmare (which you should to get the full experience, as cliche as that may sound, I know), this game will keep you on the edge of your seat nearly at all times, especially once you start encountering the bigger, badder enemies in later levels. Also, beware the Spawns (the bouncy slime-things). Just...just trust me on this.
4. Replay value - I could start this beauty up and play it any day of the week and have fun with it. It's fast-paced, bloody FPS action at its finest, and one of the true granddaddies of the FPS genre, along with Doom, Wolfenstein 3D and Duke Nukem 3D.
Bottom Line: You want this game. It's usually like, $3 or something. Absolute steal and a half. As are the expansions! But I'll review those by themselves.

One of the oldest FPS' out there. Even to this day, the pixelated display (Which can be sorted with a retextured version named 'Quake Epsilon'), retro music, run and gun themes and level design still retain at least some of their widespread popularity. Definitely not for hipster gamers, who play their stupid little 2d pixel 'art' games, this is for real gamers who need a little trip down memory lane.
Quake runs as it should, anything that causes too much trouble rarely occurs. The controls aren't too hard to master, plus they aren't buggy (As I've found with some other olden games). The controls aren't dissimilar from most modern-day games, with the exception of specialised buttons like turn left 5 degrees or something. It's just point and shoot. No need to reload.
The one thing that doesn't really work well in the original Quake is the co-op/multiplayer. It is usually pretty buggy and laggy, and controls have been known to break and/or unbind in a match. Plus, the multiplayer mechanics don't really gel with each other. Sometimes, the AI will just completely break down and enemies will just stare in the direction the editors placed them in and won't attack or move. This also means entities with any properties won't activate or do anything. The single player campaign is good enough on its own, however.
This game is very good, considering the times it was made in. Newer versions have been released (The aforementioned Quake Epsilon) that make it easier to see what's actually happening. For such an old game, Quake still remains impressive and a fun experience. It may be like Destiny story-wise (It has none), but it certainly makes for a fun pick-up-and-play game when you're bored. 8/10.

The damage balancing and the character ability balancing was well worked into the game, and no weapon or character feels over-powered, excluding the shotgun at point blank (however, the shotgun is useless unless you can count the hairs on your enemy's chin). I'll keep it simple.  I thoroughly loved The Bureau.  It will stand beside the Mass Effect series, L.A. Noire, Metro 2033, Saints Row: The Third, and Borderlands 2 as a recent favorite.  I never played the original series, nor have I played XCOM: Enemy Unknown.  The Bureau just popped out at me with the retro look while I was checking out Steam's sales recently.  After playing it, I wish I'd paid full price.  I loved the game far more than I anticipated.  I only wish it were longer!
As far as the setting, I love the old feel to the game.  I love most anything set in America before the mid-60s or anything that has that feel.  The characters, the levels, and pretty much all visual aspects of the game took me right there.  Even a lot of the tech in the game had more of a "The Day the Earth Stood Still" or "War of the Worlds" feel to it than I expected.  It felt in place, though, rather than coming across as cheesy.
I enjoyed the game play, only wishing there was more hot key flexibility with commanding the squad mates.  I can't really comment on difficulty or balance.  I don't have nearly as much gaming time as it use to, so I tend to plow through things on easy in order to see the story unfold before too many weeks of my life goes by.  I probably should have played this one on higher difficulty, though, as I haven't been able to knock out a game start-to-finish over the course of a couple days in forever.
The graphic style suited the game perfectly.  The Bureau looked beautiful and ran well on high settings.  I've never found myself admiring the quality of a character's sweater before.  I'm ashamed to admit that has now changed.  Still, I never once heard the cooling fans speed up!
So I'll break it down from my perspective.
Setting / Level Design - 9/10
Graphics - 9/10
Voice Acting - 10/10
Controls - 7/10
Story - 8/10 (minus two points only because I wish it were longer)
Value for my money spent - 10/10

A very interesting game; The Bureau: XCOM Declassified is definitely not your typical video game.  It attempts to bridge third-person shooting with more tactical/strategy elements like a conventional XCOM game.  While many people have more detailed opinions about how WELL this is accomplished, I think the game has a pretty good rapport in trying and getting most of the two things down.  I say this to mean it is possible to just go rambo and kill all the aliens yourself with your team as minimal support.  It is also possible to not really fight and micromanage your team to kill everybody for you.  However, the game is really the best when you can master the two and be able to multitask shooting things and issuing commands for your team to shoot things as well.  I actually enjoyed that about this game very much because it allows me to focus on different enemies while being reassured that my team is putting the hurt on someone else.
However, I think the most difficult part of The Bureau to swallow is the story.  I could talk for ages about its story, but I will try to keep it brief.  The game does not pull its punches in its portrayal of its characters; pretty much all of the characters are morally gray characters - none of them are psychopaths, but each of their motivations make them do evil things.  In that way, the characters are very realistic, they are imperfect people (or aliens) controlled like puppets and thus act out of rage, fear, and sadness.  Most will never get redemption as their thirst for vengeance makes them ignore the suffering of others; a world not unlike our own.
THings I really found quirky about this game is that damn near everybody smokes.  I had heard that those 60s people really liked their deathsticks, but I never thought it was THAT bad.  Also, the agent customization options are pretty cool because all of the agents dress sharply and it gives me a satisfying feeling to see a well-dressed man with a vest and tie blow a Sectoid head off.  Also, it has an interesting take on "third person" shooter (if you know what I mean the twist).
In conclusion, if you want a purely shoot-em-up or purely tactical game, then this one is not for you.  However, The Bureau is an interesting blacksheep for those who want to give a new hybrid a go, with a plot that is complex, but quite acurate in what we would do if aliens attacked.  And no, we do not become friends.

When I bought this game, I thought it was going to be ridiculous.
And it was. This game has momets that make you laugh out loud simply because they are so freaking ludicrous.
What I did not expect was how much I would care about this game. The storyline is fantastic. the characters are amazing. every story arc is interesting, every bird has more to them than meets the eye, and I was amazed at how many intense emotions this game made me feel. I was expecting to laugh, sure, but I was not expcecting to feel upset, I was not expecting to feel excited for tomorrow beyond "Oh I wonder what the next joke is"; I was not expecting to be so emonionally invested in this game.
There are at least a couple of story arcs that made me want to cry, and THAT is something that I was not expecting AT ALL.
This game is fantastic. It knows that it is absurd, and takes full advantage of that fact.
but it also manages to get you to take it seriously, too, and that was one of the things about this game that impressed me the most; a game about a human dating pigeons that manages to evoke strong emotions, has a deeper underlying story, and most importanly, makes you feel like most of the characters are more than just silly pictures of pigeons on a computer screen: this game gives everyone a personality and a story, and it makes characters appear far simpler than they truly are multiple times. Every new playthrough gives you a new understanding of the characters and makes them that much more like real people.

At first you will be hesitant to even look a pigeon in the eye, let alone talk to it.
I was like this too.
Then the game progressed and I started growing fond of each eligible bachelor, somehow seeing them for who they were and not what they were. Nanaki was no longer an old, wrinkly off-white trash bird; he was a trusted elder. The doctor was no longer an obese partridge, but a dashing and mysterious genius who spent too much time studying when he was in medical school.
First you will laugh.
Then you will question what you're doing playing this silly game.
Then you will cry.
Then you will fall in love with each pigeon at least once.
Then you will cry yourself to sleep every night. Don't even bother with tissues; buy yourself a sturdy bucket and install straps in your computer chair before attempting to complete this game.
