I'll start with the pros:
1. It's a great concept - The idea that you get to collect minions that you beat, and then use them for future levels is good.
2. Layers of strategy, but not too much - Since the levels are semi-sequential, you get to plan which levels you want to beat first, based on the minions available. For example, if you know air units beat water, you might spend some time trying to get air units first, and then use them to beat the water levels. That being said, Not all levels are accessible at one go, which can be overwhelming for a new player coming into the game, and the level unlocking system has been very nicely done.
In a level itself, you get to choose a team, for which the minutest of changes might affect the result drastically. The cap on the number of units per level, and units per category (ranged, melee, support) means that you can chop and change as you wish, but because we don't have much wiggle room (2 ranged and melee, 3 supports), it means that there are fewer combinations available, allowing you to reach an optimal strategy more quickly. This means more satisfaction and less frustration - Always a plus, given that this is supposed to be a "mini"-game of sorts.
3. Great music - Sure, the creator used some third party library for it, but it's suitably chosen, and sometimes I find the soundtrack getting stuck in my head long after I've played the game.
4. Inexpensive - For the price, the amount of gameplay is fairly reasonable.
The cons:
1. Buggy - Some of the levels require you to think about target prioritisation. For instance, if you know that a huge wave is incoming, you might want to spread your range aoe damage, to maximise your stun area. So you switch your target prioritisations to "closest enemy" and "furthest enemy", say. The problem is, I noticed that once there were closer enemies than the ones your minion was targetting, it doesn't switch over until it kills the one it's focusing on. I feel like this is a game-changing (but not game-breaking) bug, and makes some levels harder than they were probably meant to be.
2. Level Balancing - Playing this game, you can tell that it was very carefully designed and balanced. However, it still fails in some aspects. The levels start off easy, which is good, and is meant to get progressively harder. Eventually, you reach a level where you actually have to try and beat by optimising your team selection. The problem is that once you beat that level, the subsequent levels seem too easy to progress through. I believe this is because the minions you have to fight are fairly similar, just with a higher dps, and employing a similar strategy will get you through it easily.
3. Unit balancing - There is one unit in particular in this game that I feel is waaay too OP. Once I got that unit, it was always on my team, just because it makes any level easier to beat, even on a level which contains its weakness. On the flip side, there were minions in the game that I didn't even bother thinking about, simply because they seemed way too weak, and there was never any reason to use them. It would be nice if the unit balancing was such that it would at least make us consider using the weaker units, maybe for the elemental advantage, or something like that.
4. End of game - I get that this is meant to be a small-scale game, made by a solo developer after three months of hard work, which I have to say is quite the feat. However, when I completed all the levels, it seemed a bit too abrupt. In a game like this, you're usually expecting a final level, with some big, ginormous boss with smaller minions, maybe more waves than usual, and then you might need to make a few teams and swap them out from time to time to deal with different waves, etc. Tldr: I was hoping for a boss level at the end, and after beating it, some cool splash screen to say "Congratulations, you've finished the game. Try replaying it on a harder level, etc etc etc", which would have given me a greater sense of accomplishment.
Overall, this is actually quite a fun game to play, and feels rewarding when you beat it. The bugs and balancing issues I highlighted will always be in every game, and in this case, none of them were particularly game-breaking. You could always work around it somehow. Definitely recommended.

Evolve Stage 2 is an apt name for a game that was brought back from the dead after its troubled beginning. It is a better game, a faster one, balanced more in favor of casual fun instead of the e-sports angle Turtlerock aimed when it first launched. Naturally, the e-sports community rejected the forced effort and the game was left for dead... Until now.
Evolve has evolved into a proper Free 2 Play game, with an in-game currency and daily drop-feed rewards, the standard F2P trappings. Monsters and hunters are unlocked with silver dough and they are priced in such a way that makes sure you aren't overfeeding yourself -- it can take up to an hour or two of play time to earn enough cash to buy characters. This will need to be readjusted but the intention by developers is sound: you are always learning new characters and strategies and just when you've mastered each, you'll buy a new one. If you're the impatient sort, high prices would likely tip you over to the paying side.
Both for monsters and hunters you can unlock perks which, when upgraded two times, give you a real advantage against the opponent. This system makes it hard for new players to jump in, as they will always be underpowered when compared to veteran players. Even worse, perks are seperate for monsters and hunters so if you only play one or the other, the game actively makes sure you keep playing those and prevents you from experimenting.
This would all be pretty rotten if you could buy in-game cash. It would be Pay 2 Win. As of writing this, however, you cannot buy anything with your money. Presumably, Turtlerock are keeping that turned off until they finetune the progression.
But is the game any fun? It is. As I said before, Stage 2 is more casual, matches usually go on for about 10 minutes and the tools hunter have available to them make sure that you can catch-up with the monster and fight it even if you don't kill it. The major complaint of there being too much running is still true -- Evolve can be a running simulator. Because the movement system is rudementary and generally unengaging, there can be boring periods in every match. But when the fight starts, it's all adrenaline.
All in all, Evolve Stage 2 is a step in the right direction. It's not perfect by any means and the unlocking of characters is probably not enough to keep most people playing.

Thankfully, Turtlerock and 2K seem committed to making that dream happen.

Honestly, I wish I could recommend this game, now that the full DLC pack is on sale.  It has so much potential, but by level 16, I can honestly say that HtS2 is frustrating in some curious ways that I cannot really get around.
First, off, my first 10 levels were a total blast.  Unfortunately, this is due to the fact that I was shamelessly spoiled with DLC content that actually made the game faster and funner than it actually is in reality.
I have never seen a game that essentially punishes you by leveling ever before.  The zombies, the same ones you see at level 1, become more and more terrifying as you level and they essentially out pace your skills and gear (choice of ... can we say play style?) until you can get past the hump levels where new unlocks let you get the next upgrade of your weapon choices.
Sure, you can keep swapping between weapon types, favoring the weapon that just simply does the most damage at that level, but that defeats the point of having different types of weapons.  I wanted to use fast melee weapons and assault rifles.  Well, mostly, I got hooked on the play style of those weapons because I got the DLC packs in the bundle and was rewarded with some lovely swords and a great assault rifle.  Soon enough, I had to switch the melee out to slow, clunky enormous hammer like objects just to get the job done.
Then ... I am not sure when ... my assault rifle went from 1 unaimed shot kills to 2 to 3 ... and aimed shots have now reached two head shots to kill the same stupid zombies I was shooting from day 1.  I had totally enjoyed the hell out of the first 10 levels due to the DLC content, but it turns out, I was playing a drastically skewed version of those levels due to this gear.  Now, I wouldn't normally complain, but at level 16, with all of the skills upgraded and the best assault rifle I can have (same one since level 1) it takes more bullets and more running around in circles than ever before to do ... THE EXACT SAME THING.
Really uncertain why they couldn't smooth out the progression a little better on gear upgrades and/or make the zombies level at a little more in line with your own progression of skill/gear.  I am terrified of levels 17-20, then, supposedly, at that point I can make a new assualt rifle ... but good grief, just gathering supplies for those three levels will seriously suck ... mostly (see below).
Pro tip ... keep a local game with a lower level camp so you can farm the basics on the main map, which will stay at your camp level, not your character level.  This is of course ridiculous ... you shouldn't have to feel like swapping to another game to gather some freaking wood and the even more elusive braided rope (my own personal hell grind).  To overcome the obvious problem of being a mule, you can at least store crap in your bunker chest and have that crap follow you between your camps ... this probably being one of the obvious reasons why that is true.
To facilitate your grind, you can lower the difficulty level of quests (unless they started at your level), and well, you would be insane not to ... otherwise gathering some sheet metal will take serious fighting every time.
And honestly, this is the only time I really enjoy the game, when the quest is a few levels below me, because it makes killing the hordes of zombies actually FUN, rather than a repeating struggle.
Which leads to the next complaint.  Can we say grind grind grind grind grind grind grind grind grind.  You will run all over the main map to gather wood, plants, and rope (... wtf) a billion times.  It is not a big map.  It gets old ... real fast.  You will also play 1/4 - 1/3 of the missions over and over until you want to cry ... just to get enough junk to upgrade your armory in hopes of getting a weapon upgrade to stem the ever growing pain of the zombies that level better than you do (and then to find that there is nothing useful in the next 3 building upgrades that you grinded your brains out for).
I guess it is worth mentioning here that you will spend countless hours running through buildings and unlocking doors (which takes time) finding absolutely nothing ... which really starts to get on your nerves when you have run through a thousand empty rooms.
Add to this the senseless deaths that can suddenly happen from a couple, semi-glitchy zombie deer that will decide to charge and gore you the moment you are running in circles to shoot the ever more intense "basic" zombies.
And the UI just feels ... clunky.  I am already simply exhausted with there being no keymap to transfer ALL of an item to your trunk (which you do constantly).  You drag, drop, and then move back to modal window and click OK ... that last part makes this a tremendous chore when you have heaps of stuff.  Let's not even go wild here and suggest that there be a transfer ALL "other" inventory into trunk ... or the awkwardness of the space bar being your sprint ...
And speaking of sprinting ... walking in the game is utterly slow and painful, but sprint costs you stamina (which is a minor problem as you progress), but sprinting will cause you to also jump onto and over things ... making sprinting around the game, especially inside cities, somewhat obnoxious as you are constantly running over beds and furniture (and waiting for the associated graphics to complete) and often accidentally going over a balcony when sprinting along the decks of buildings.
It would be amazing to have an actual JUMP action that did those things (console nerf?) ... I know, crazy, right?  Games have been doing jumping for a long time ... it is awesome stuff and keeps your ACTION game action feeling.  Who the heck wants to watch your character slowly lumber up onto a bed (that you hit by accident while sprinting through another empty room) ... and then not even be able to jump on it!
The graphics are very good, but there simply aren't enough of them ... all around.  More character customization would be nice, along with just more gear in general (for both progression smoothing and vanity slots).  Less re-use of the same basic map designs and elements across the types of maps would be awesome, (city, cementary, woodlands, farm ... that is it by level 16).
This game is really close to being more fun than not ... really really close, but it is just a repeating time sink that makes you cringe every damn time you level!?!?!?  I understand that some people are OK with the grinds and the challenge that the game presents, but I honestly think most people perfer to play a game where they don't get punished by leveling for 75% of the levels and want "trash" mobs to be "trash" mobs ... not suddenly twice as many bullets to kill and run faster than a rabbit on crack!
Essentially, you play the same game, over and over and over and over in a way that puts Diablo franchise to absolute shame in content re-use.
Suggestions:
* Better gear/skill progressions.  Weapon upgrade mods to add more damage every 2-3 levels and the damage based skills should be beefed up a little.  With the ammo upgrades every 5 levels (or whatever) and weapon upgrades (per type) every 7 (it seems), this should smooth out the curve.
* Zombies should level slightly less than you and add more types of special zombies to keep it interesting.  Blasting away hordes of zombies should remain satisfying, not become frustrating between upgrades.
* Let player remap the sprint key.
* Add JUMP!!!  Get rid of that silly sprint auto-climb
* Add a key map for "OK" on transfer quantity window.
* Add a button to transfer all "OTHER" to trunk.
* MORE maps and variety
* MORE character vanity stuff
* MORE gear ... 16 levels and excluding the DLC hats, not much armor, for example, and not a lot of upgrade choices
* Some documentation on what stats actually mean (I haven't found it ... ).  What is "Damage Reduction" versus "Damage Blocking" ... ??? That sounds the same.
P.S.  The zombie turkeys are freaking awesome.

I'm torn on this one.
On one hand, it has an interesting story, with decent voice acting, and sticks true to Irish heritage, especially by using Gaelic words to describe items you see.
On the other hand, it's very slow paced, with obscure puzzles and a color scheme that makes it difficult to see certain objects on the ground, ones that are needed to advance the story. The game's description says "challenging puzzle solving", but the only challenge lies in figuring out how the puzzles relate to the game at all. In a sense, it evokes Myst, where the puzzles are there, but they're so obscure you'll be scratching your head.
It's also very short, and can be completed in under two hours.
As of this review (June 14th, 2015), the game is currently 80% off. For its current price, it's worth the purchase. The atmosphere is foreboding, and you'll definitely want to see the conclusion.
The devs say this is part one of a two part story; let's hope part two is more fleshed out in pretty much every aspect.
At the end, I do recommend the game, if you're a fan of exploration. Do not expect much in the way of a "psychological thriller", but its story is genuinely interesting.

Highly recommended. I absolutely enjoyed every minute of this game, it stands on it's own in the franchise. From the convincing, immersive 1962 atmosphere to the gorgeously rendered and extremely detailed environments, it is immensely engaging and entertaining from start to finish. The tactical combat system is smooth and satisfying without being too easy, just the right balance of simplicity and complexity for me. I found the characters, especially the protagonist, to be realistic, believable people. Agent Carter is the quintessential tragic antihero with a scarred past, bad habits, and post traumatic stress disorder. A cynical misanthropist, but a man of the highest honor, we can't help but hope he finds redemption in saving the world. The expertly written story draws you in and helps greatly to suspend disbelief in an otherwise unbelievable nightmare. I would like to see this subject matter treated more in gaming, I think it is a richly complex, provocative and potentially horrifying, largely untapped genre. The Bureau is by far the best game to address it so far.

Quake.
If you’re here, the odds that you know what Quake is are pretty significant, so this review might seem a little (or quite a bit) pointless.
But, Quake has a special meaning to me – Quake and I go way back, it being one of the first games I would ever play, along with Half-life and Doom. I still remember those days, zipping around those moody corridors and those dank, decrepit hallways, filling everything that moved with as many rounds as my 6-year-old hands were able to pump out...

Before inevitably dying at the hands of some monstrosity, of course.
Sure, I wasn’t good at it by any conceivable degree, but damn, I still loved it. It was more than just a game to me, the environment, the enemy design – it all came together to create an experience that I just can’t seem to dig out of my head, not that I would ever want to. Even now, I still feel that urge to boot it up and shoot something.
I can’t promise that your time with Quake will be anything similar to mine, and you may find it to be dated, uninteresting or dull (and, in my opinion NONE of those things can define Quake). But to me, Quake will always be there, flashing through the back of my mind, making me feel the same way about it as I did 12 years ago, and because of that, I have no choice but to recommend it.

seemed like the perfect racing game for me. Two large islands, an interesting selection of cars, a mix between arcade and simulation style driving and true open-world gameplay. Add to that the idea of actually buying appartments and garages to store your cars in, instead of simply having infinite garage space. It sounded great. And fun!
However that "dream racing game" fell flat on its knees as soon as I had my first set of wheels. The reason for that was that I, at that moment, got to meet the game's biggest flaw: The driving physics.
I know that you're in some games
to fiddle around with the driving settings to suit them to your taste and driving style and I did, or rather I tried.
Every few hours I would change them a bit, hoping I would get closer to a setup I liked. I also tried so called
settings by several users on the Steam community or from the web, but none of them worked for me so far.
And it's not like I played the game only for a few hours.
I played it for
hours. In that time I went through the beginning parts of the
two times. The first time was pretty horrible, but the second time was even worse.
I get it, as a developer you want to connect your gameplay through a story, but it sincerely doesn't help one bit if every character you meet is annoying and arrogant to the point where I can't stand them, even when they're loosing.
Also the story isn't that original, too. Through luck you're taking part in the Solar Crown, a highly-regarded competition between drivers on Ibiza and Hawaii.
I think the game would have been better without a story.
The problem with this championship is that you'll drive against the same characters again and again. And their cutscenes before and after a race are pretty much the same every time.
So not only are you going up against the same drivers again and again, there's also no pay-off after you beat them. Sure, you get their car if you beat them in a one on one race, but what does it matter if they're driving against you in the next race!?
It also doesn't help that I was fighting my own vehicle more often than the other drivers.
Because that is how it often felt to me. I could easily outrun the enemies, some races I would overtake the whole group several times and be several laps ahead.
But every corner I pretty much had to fight my own vehicle to the point where it wasn't fun. And it's not like I completely suck at driving. I know how to drive a line, break and how to take corners...
And after nearly 40 hours I couldn't take the story and the competition anymore.
So I did what I like to do the most in open-world racers: I grabbed my set of wheels and took in the scenery.
I spent the remaining hours of my playtime driving through both islands, simply exploring the world, chasing down highways, going down dead-end streets. Simply not caring for anything but my car and the road.
However as much as I tried to not play the story or the races, the driving physics didn't change (obviously). Realizing this, that I wasn't enjoying what should be the core of any driving game, I simply uninstalled Test Drive Unlimited 2 and I sincerely doubt that I'll ever play it again.
Sure, it's somewhat MMO like online mode, where you can meet other players randomly or some of the social stuff, for example you can actually ride inside other player's cars, are neat ideas.
But a driving game should first and foremost do one thing: Be fun driving!
And after 48 hours it just still isn't, despite me trying many varations of driving modes, settings and cars.
So I
, despite me liking the ideas behind
and what it tried to do,
this game.

This game had been languishing in my Steam library since I picked it up in sale years ago. I was looking for something new to play recently, and after deciding I was in the mood for a stealth game, I installed Dishonored.
What a great game; I absolutely loved it. The stealth mechanics are rock solid, the teleporting and possession powers are fun to use and the level of freedom the game affords you is quite impressive. My preferred method of playing stealth games is to take a completely non-lethal approach, so I was happy that the game allowed such a playstyle.
The art style is wonderful, too. Dunwall feels like a steampunk City 17 and is a joy to navigate. Being able to possess a rat and skuttle through small openings never gets old, nor does teleporting up to a rooftop to assassinate a guard from above.
I was similarly impressed by just how well the game is optimised. The textures are average, but there's a high level of detail and the lighting is sumptuous. With everything cranked up and running at 4K it runs at a 100% stable 60 FPS and looks gorgeous.
I was woefully ignorant when this game was first released. Whatever I was playing at the time I should've dropped to play Dishonored instead.

This is easily the best RTS I've played in years and feels much more like a late beta release than an early alpha. If you are an RTS fan or play clash of clans, you will definitely enjoy this game. The game in survival mode proceeds in 4X fashion, exploring the map and clearing the infected out, expanding and exploiting resources while growing your town, and then defending it from the waves of attacks (or just some sneaky basterd that wanders in). Interlocking layers of defenses and observing how the landscape funnels the infected hordes is key to knowing where to put fixed defenses, as even cranking out the best ground troops will only act as a stop gap measure. Definitely play on the easier 20-30% setting for the first few rounds, this game is very aptly named!
It is extremely challenging and requires a great deal of forethought, planning, and balance. Yes, the maps are randomly generated and the gameplay and starting locations are uneven, but that is what's great about it! Its forcing you to strategize! Use the space bar frequently to pause the game, issue orders, and re-evaluate military/expansion/defenses/resources balance. Especially if you don't know what to do next, pause the game while you think about it, or you'll get clobbered!
Very addicting, very hard but in a good way, very worth the money

FULL REVIEW:
They are billions is a steampunk strategy game set on a post-apocalyptic planet.
The goal of this game is to build and defend colonies to survive against the billions of infected you will come up against.
They are billions is a pleasure to play, the game feels solid when you’re playing it.
The experience though when playing may be difficult for some players, I’d recommend either watching content creators play so you can learn some tactics or dialing down the difficulty and learning from there.
The game’s mechanics in terms of building and combat are pretty standard in terms of an RTS game, you have to get food, wood, stone and iron in order to build the warriors/buildings/defenses you need.
The mechanics for the zombies are surprisingly good they’ve been able to build in noise detection & “agro’ing” and interesting pathfinding solution.
Well, I just have to say I love the graphic design here, it feels just as though it “works” together when the zombies are collectively moving it just looks right, as part of the graphics section I will also talk about performance the game runs great on my computer which is a i7 6700k, GTX 1080 and 32GBs of RAM.
Each unit looks and feels different, the buildings look excellent and really I just have to say I love the way it looks, when I was browsing the steam store, this game drew my attention straight away, I couldnt not look at it when browsing.
Each unit has a unique sound and the zombies sound like zombies and actually sound menacing when there is a lot of them, there isn't much to say here except that the game doesn't do bad in sound, it does just as much as I wanted it to do, which is great for audio design.
The game is currently on sale for 22.49USD but is normally sold for 25USD. When I played my first game, I felt the game wasnt worth it, but after playing some more and watching other people play and learning the game and its systems I definitely think the game is worth both its asking prices.
All in all, They are billions is a great game I don't have many quelms with it, but the only thing I think I would want changed is a tutorial or some sort of manual for players just starting, I think this would alleviate the apprehension of keeping the game.
All in all, I rate this game a 4.5/5 giving it a “GREAT, RECOMMEND” score.
Please keep in mind they are billions is an early access title and this review is only for the current version of the game, I did NOT receive a key for this game it was purchased by the myself.

I like this game.
Being that its a converted iPad game I didn't have high expectations for it. You know how those usually go, cash shop hack job that is more focused on extracting money from your wallet than it is about entertaining you, so when iBomber Defense looked and played like a fully fleshed out game I was pleasantly surprised.
Now this is a tower defense game and it is very important I get this out of the way now. Their are 2 types of tower defense games; the 'do it your way' kind where you have total freedom to mix and match your towers as the game can be beaten in multiple styles
their is, 'do it our way' kind where each stage only has one solution and you need to figure it out and this game is surprisingly both.
On the lowest setting you can get away with duct taping your way through stages but if you bump the difficulty up then each stage only has one possible solution to it.
I think its a fair balance, not every game can be Kingdom Rush (which I think is an amazing TD game) although I personally hate the ones with only one solution because its more like a puzzle game at that point and thier are plenty of good puzzle games I would rather play than a TD game pretending to be one.
Personal genre gripes aside iBomber was clearly designed with gameplay first. You can even move the title screen about like in Super Mario 64. When did games stop being like this and remembering games are supposed to be fun? Instead they all take themselves super serious and end up a buggy mess on release instead.
Storyline is WW2 but really its just an excuse plot. WW2 is as easy to pick of the shelf and use as a storyline as elves, dwarfs and cyberpunk but it gets the job done. Sound effects, yeah they exist. Okay they are fine, a bomb sounds like a bomb and a turret sounds like a turret what more do you want?
Music? Strangely absent or turned so low (by default) that it seems absent. I honestly don't recall hearing any music at all but it wasn't until I started writing this review that I even noticed, maybe because I was too busy having
.
I recommend this game and if you like TD games like Kingdom Rush(as you should, because its great!) then you will enjoy this game. it even has the 'specialize your turrets' tech tree. I tried it with touchscreen but oddly that didn't work out very well as the screen is just a bit too small for the delcate precision it requests of the user and I often accidently bombed my own turrets too many times so switched back to mouse input.

Original review:
I have such mixed feelings on this game.
On one hand, I did throughly enjoy the 7 or so hours of gameplay I put into it before I had no choice but to fight pirates armed with cannons. There were a few little bugs here and there, but all in all the game does manage to have that "adventure" type feeling I just don't get from many games that promise it. Managing your crew doesn't devolve into ridiculous, time consuming mircomanagement (unless you want it to), there are enough items and skills and powerups to give it a decent RPGish type feeling, and most of the gameplay itself (beyond some of the "sail for six minutes while nothing happens" travelling moments) is pretty fun.
On the other hand, by the time those seven hours were up, most of foes I had to face were pretty easy to defeat, except those with the cannons. Who are so game breakingly annoying to defeat that i don't think I'll end up playing this again.
It's not a matter of things becoming to hard, it's a matter of them becoming pointless. Yes, I can sink the opposing ship with my own cannons, but then not only do I not feel very piratey (cause, you know, plunder and all), I end up wasting enough ammo and taking enough damage that it's financially impratical to bother trying.
And yes, I can still board enemies to capture them, but for whatever reason, the devs have decided to make it so that whenever you attack a pirate holding a cannon ball (which seems to count for at least 2-3 of the enemy's crew), they explode. Even if this doesn't sink the enemy ship with your guys on it, they will envariably kill a few of them, which means I can either maintain a massive crew of low-level guys to use as fodder (once again costing far more than I'll make off of looting), or I can risk losing some of my skilled crew (which is not only yet again not nearly covered financially by my gains, but kind of a massive pain in the♥♥♥♥♥having spent hours building them to the point that I want them at).
Heaven forbid some dudes holding cannonballs should get on your ship.
The other issue with cannons themselves is they make ship design less interesting. A borg cube suddenly becomes king of the waves because even though it can be damaged to the point where the battle was not worth it in terms of gold, it won't sink like a pretty Spanish galleon will when some dude gets stabbed while holding a cannonball on the lowest deck.
So, it's not a matter of things getting too hard - provided no one suicide bombs me, they are arguably a little too easy if anything. I just really dislike that after a certain point in the gameplay, everything I do begins to act as a step backwards. There is no point in proceeding if there are no gains.
I'd probably not be too concerned if this was an early access game, or if I could find a mod to make pirates stop suicide bombing themselves. As it is, I believe this is the full release (though I'll have to double check after writing this), and no one seems to have cooked up a fix for my major issue.
It also doesn't help that despite being a full release, most of the actual gameplay mechanics just don't work. I don't just mean the cannons. sometimes your dudes will just decide to path into the ocean, killing themselves, and should you add a second deck to your ship, you can count on everyone starving to death because they can't find the food on the deck below them.
Buy it if you're a casual gamer or if you die often in these types of games and will rarely get to the point described above. Don't buy it if you like games that give you some sense of accomplishment, cause after a while, you will just get frustrated.

There are times in when a person realizes they didn’t know they were missing something in their lives until they see it. For me, that is what happened when I first saw Hatoful Boyfriend. In this game you play a human girl who is attending an all-birds school for boys for the first time. It takes place in what one can only assume is some dystopian future where humanity has collapsed and birds are now the dominant species. The concept alone was so deliciously absurd that I knew I had to try it.
First off, there’s the birds. There’s a sporty bird, a shy quiet bird, a bird who’s your best friend, and just about everything in between and the ending you get depends entirely on which of these feathered gentlemen you decide to spend your time getting close to. In the beginning of the game the player is given the choice to have the birds represented simply as they are or with the anime style faces of human boys. The character types given to the birds are so diverse that you may not need the faces to differentiate them, but it is a bit entertaining to see what the human versions of them might look like.
In between getting to know your classmates and teachers you will attend classes, participate in after school events, and maybe even get a part time job. The choices are all yours, and there are multiple endings which makes for great replay value. If you’re anything like me you’ll want to see all of the possible endings and Hatoful Boyfriend is more than happy to facilitate that. The game includes a fast forwarding system that allows you to rush through dialog that you’ve already seen in your previous play throughs. This means that you don’t have to hear every characters life story each time you play through the game and you can skip right along to the new and exciting content.
The controls are fairly simple. It’s a point and click choose your own story style game that lets you sit back, relax, and take in the hilarious dialogue. You do have a limited number of days to spend until the year is up, so be sure to spend them wisely and take time to be with the things that matter to you. The music is not distracting and the graphics are charming. How could they not be, they’re such pretty birds.
With its simple and mysterious story, extreme characters, and lightly satirical vibe this game will keep you entertained and wanting more. Hatoful Boyfriend is great for anyone who enjoys quirky humor. I’d recommend it to fans of dating sims, choose your own story games, and of course bird lovers. I wish you the best of luck in snagging the bird of your dreams, and say hi to Nanaki Sensei for me.

Let me start by saying that, for me, with the specific problems that I am having, I
this product.
My main gripe is the performance. I am running a computer that can easily handle this game on the highest settings, yet it
has painful graphical lag - either because it attempts to load in new chunks of map, textures, or autosaves (though, I think I've found the problem with autosaving.)
, especially when traveling quickly, the game will hang up in a semi-buffering state where limited camera controls exist and menu access is possible. This issue is mitigated slightly when traveling by foot, but with the size of the map, that's a rather cumbersome proposition.
is the spawn system. I get it, it's a big game and if every npc or sprite were spawned and rendered all the time, it would bog down even the most competent system. The system employed in Wildlands, however, is unable to keep up with a regular player playing rather slowly. Oftentimes while playing in an area that should be crawling with baddies, I find that the area is unpopulated and things such as weapon drops and intel that are essential to character growth and story development are not yet rendered, even though their markers are displayed on the HUD. The only work-around I have found for this is to stop, enter the map, and give the game some time to load. The problem with this is that it eliminates most of the fun of infiltrating an area, whereas normally you'd have to either sneak through enemy lines and make decisions on what enemies to eliminate in order to progress stealthily, or burn through a ship's weight in lead to achieve the mission. In this situation, you might find yourself alone one minute, and then surrounded by enemies, and having your tactical decisions made for you.
I cannot comment on the storyline, as I haven't really been able to get very far in it. While it seems fairly compelling, the variety of missions and interactions seems limited and uninspired in scope. If you enjoy repeating the same scenarios over and over in slightly different ways, then you might enjoy this game - that is, if you can forgive the glaring and painful issues with performance.

Even when considering this is still an exploration and adventure game, the puzzles could have been made better. One example might be the navigation puzzle at O'Sullivan's Bay.
Nonetheless, I do recommend this game to others, who like to explore a very dark, tragic and partially confusing story. It is very well written and does definitely fulfill it's point as a part of the game.
Second downside for me is the relatively bad performance and optimisation (probably only on lower-end). I understand, that a big part of the whole Island is being rendered at the same time but this game could have been made more frame friendly with comparable or better graphics in e.g. the Source Engine (see Dear Esther).
If you use an engine, know the details. Get the best out of it and don't just rely on the fact, that hardware is getting better everyday. But that is a debatable point.
Conclusively I want to state, that I really enjoyed playing Montague's Mount, especially in the tense moments leading to the end. Getting to know the story one bit at a time, finally completing in the tragic story it tells and getting to know the person and character you are playing.
Feeling empathy, or disgust? What went wrong, what went right? Decide by yourself.
Greetings,

To be severely honest I had my doubts going into this game. A randomly generated 2D metroidvania mmo with permadeath aspects? Now I've played Realm of the Mad God which ultimately has a rather similar system despite severely different gameplay styles and even then I was still skeptical over how much of a quality game this was going to be. Frankly, my worries were misplaced as what I found inside was not a hodge podge mess of incomplete ideas and systems but a rather fine and functional product that was aptly balanced.
The main difference that I can tell between this and ROTMG was simply due to the nature by which the permadeath works. In this game, permadeath is less of a full reset as it is a set back, because unlike ROTMG, loot drops are not something of a rarity. Rather, if you go into a higher level dungeon chances are you will find yourself with higher level equiment in a rather short amount of time. However, the main barrier from doing so is simply based on two things, skill, and familiarity. In a sense, this is a game that rewards a very live, die, repeat esque approach, that is, to advance one must not only advance their profficiency in using their respective class, each of which has a differing learning curve, but also learn the patterns and various intricacies of the differnt types of dungeons. Not only that but each instance is randomly generated so it's not a simple matter of pure memorization but more through pattern recognition and having strategies in place for each of the various enemies you'll be likely to face per dungeon. Speaking of said dungeons, each type of instance is varied enough from each other to properly stand out, both in themeing and in enemy variety and level design.
Overall I can say that if you like the gameplay of Castlevania with the asthetic of Metroid and don't mind dying multipl times like Dark Souls, then I can safely reccomend playing this game to you.

I wish Steam had a yellow 'meh' rating. Starbreak has some great sidescrolling shooter/rpg elements, but like all perma death games it leads you to rage quitting, a lot. The XP system is more your typical F2P progression system where levels are used to 'unlock' access to different playable characters, all of which have their own unique purpose and playstyle but sadly all of which suck compared to the starting class. Like most perma death games you can pick up random drops which upgrade your stats minorly like a stat point, until death. You can also loot gear to improve your character, the combination of the two (Stats+Gear) More or less equals your "level". That is to say levels seem to be classified into 5 difficulties, Easy, medium, hard, very hard and extreme. While there are different playable levels of the same difficulty, all difficulties drop the same tier stat upgrades and gear. However, each playable level has a different boss, each boss has their own achievement for beating them.
The Perma death structure isn't so bad, yeah it causes rage quitting because you lose stuff that was hard to find, almost always you die in the most lame way possible, the game usual pulls one of those ridiculous "all the games rules are broken" moves where you get hit and it somehow becomes an endless combo till you die. One of my primary issues is that Starbreak is ALSO F2P. You see Starbreak has 2 different currencies, your basic and your paid premium. First off as far as my experience goes, money has no functional affect on gameplay, all monetarily obtainable items are cosmetic or storage based. The basic "EC" is something you get through due course of the game, but the premium "UC" is only purchasable, so when you die you lose the item and the money forever. Seems pretty hanky to me.
Overall Starbreak is a shallow but enjoyable side scrolling shooter with rpg elements. Well executed but with Perma death as the games base mechanic it can't offer very deep gameplay because of the failure penalty. In combination with paid for content though that also gets deleted when you die I give it a 'meh'. Perma death is rather annoying anyway, it forces shallow investment mechanics into a game because no one wants to spend weeks working on a character just to get it deleted anyway, so perma death games have to offer a rapid and simple 'leveling' system of some sort to compensate. This makes it a great game though for a short gaming session just to kill some time. No story. No complicated controls or mechanics to learn. Just a straight old school arcade style side scolling shooter. 5/10
Final Note: If you're the type that hates being cheated, don't EVER play the level "The Strands". 50% of the time you'll start the level being hit by an enemy which will kick you into insta death, you'll literally spawn into the level already defeated and just get to see your character fall into the endless void and all your hard work instantly deleted.

Great concept, poor execution.  Maybe someday this will be worth the price tag.  It's nothing but pure rage in it's current state.
Firstly, every match you're at the mercy of the map generation.  If the terrain layout is not favourable, you're screwed.  If there's an infected town too close you're screwed.  Both those things happen often.
Assuming best case map gen, good resources, good room to expand.  You're still going to lose because the balance of the game is way way off.  Your own soldiers are very weak, especially once the zombies start moving in hordes, which doesn't take too long.  The real killer is the defences.  Wooden walls are like paper, if properly defended you can hold off the usual zombie attacks, but every so often a large horde comes in from a random direction.  When that happens your wooden walls will fall.  Guaranteed.  This game leaves no room for mistakes, if a single zombie gets into your city they'll almost always go straight for residential, once the houses start falling it's game over.
You may eventually get far enough into the tech tree to get stone walls.  Unfortunately they're like cardboard.  Large hordes will still blow through, and at that point in the game the zombies are also getting tougher.  There is no reasonable tech up for your own soldiers to respond to the growing zombie threat.
I want to like this game, I love the concept and the artwork is good.  I even enjoy a decent challenge, but I can't even fully explore what the game has to offer because I'm having to constantly start from scratch after some nonsense horde tears through my carefully planned defenses.  I haven't even mentioned the resource gathering, which needs continuous tending with everything relying on everything else.  I don't hate it, but it's a constant distraction when you're also trying to handle the constant attacks.
Some rebalancing to the infantry & defences and some fine tuning of the map generation will turn this negative review into a postive.  Until then playing this game is just rage inducing.

What to say about this game.... its gameplay is, at the moment, very bare bones, with one playable mode, and four playable map variations, with six total military units. And quite honestly, that is all I can think to say that is negative about the game. I have a few personal quibbles about the random nature of your starting resources, but steam workshop and support for custom maps are confirmed to be coming. Oh yeah, and the sound of guns in this game is hilariously bad.
Now, onto the good. This game is extremely trial and error, where you learn little tips and tricks every time you play through, and it never feels like the loss was your fault. there is always something you could have done better. It's almost a roguelike as a matter of fact, which has been achieved even with the limited assets the game has so far. Do NOT expect to go into this game first time and win no questions asked, unless on the very very very easiest settings. Additionally, the game is beautiful. the wonderfully well-lit cell shaded artstyle is really damn nice to look at, Earlier I ripped on the gun sound effects, and they are bad. However, outside of that the audio is excellent. I especially like the way the dramatic music fades off as a horde is destroyed, and the voices for the various units are colourfully unique.
All in all, if you enjoy similar games, you'll likely enjoy this too, I had no technical issues with the game at all. I thought I did once, but I just had it paused. it's deceptively simple, with lots of hidden tactical and strategic depth.

This game is a refreshing take on the zombie genre. It's both city builder and tower defense in one.
If you're reading this and considering getting it, here's some useful tips if you end up picking it up.
1. Double your double walls.
2. When starting create a pack of 10 rangers, group them up, start clearing the map.
3. Minimize your choke points. Don't have 10+ choke points. Try for 3-4 tops. Look for these while doing #2.
4. Don't build next to a zombie city, not unless you want them over for tea.
5. Keep building houses. Then build more houses. Population gives you money, you need this - lots of it.
6. Ballistas are your friend. Build lots of them. They are powerful and cost efficient.
7. You may be tempted to build a bunch of Tesla towers, don't. Those are situational and a huge cost in power.
8. Build the upgrades as soon as you can. These can be expensive. See #5 for getting more money.
9. Keep a 'rapid response' force handy so you can quickly reposition them when needed.
10. Don't turtle until you're about 75% into the game. Keep expanding. If you don't, you'll probably die.

Rift is a MMORPG (Massive multiplayer online role playing game) with a large game lore, themed in an epic medieval fantasy world.
Pros:
- There is a lot to do in the game, being it discovering the ever-growing world, crafting for your trade-skills (building equipment or enhancements for your own use, for your friends, guild or anyone in the world), finding dungeons and finishing quests, or simply completing daily or weekly quests in raids.
- You can customize your character in a moderate way, but you can unlock a large amount of armors, weapons and mounts to customize your outer appearance.
- You can have your own dimensión in which you can place a ot of things, any way you want, in any size you want. Despite there is a limited (but very large) collectión of items you may place in there, your imagination is the limit.
- Did I say that there is always something to do? Add to the above constant invasions from other planes, leaded by large bosses who will need a lot of people to take down.
- There is a lot of room for addons and macros that you can customize to simplify battles and  other ingame intercations.
Cons:
- The game is very intensive on system requirements for players who want to see the beauty of the world.
- The game is very expensive if you want a little bonus for your character (being it a slightly faster mount for patreons, extra slots for bags or unlocking gear slots), and has the weird statement of blocking basic interactions (you must do an initial payment to use auction houses, the regular method of player trading) instead of awarding in a better way the players who buy stuff from the game (I've bought a few stuff out of need, but the reward felt quite expensive).
- Based on the above, if you are not willing to pay the varied prices for some little benefit, the game might look like you can't reach the end-game content because you might be under geared (e.g.: can't do enough damage to a boss because you lack "firepower"), and sometimes it will look like a lot of work (because you can get game credits from other players, but they are even more expensive).
Do I recommend the game? I DO!
Despite all the work you may need to get stuff in the game, the game is really fun to play. The player comunity is growing, which makes every event more fun... because aside the quests and the invasions, there are seasonal events and many other things to do. My advice? Give it a try if you like fantasy games. We might end fighting a massive boss together (and I mean massive... check youtube if you do not believe me) ;).

This is another Ghost Recon Game so expect gun and gear upgrades with an eye toward replay value.
Single Player - you ar assigned three AI teammates which you can give a limited number of commands to.  You travel through a sandbox environment collecting intel, supplies, and killing bad guys.
You have the option to request vehicles air dropped to your position - cars, trucks, and helicopters.  Intel will help you locate key Cartel Members that need killing.
You have the option to request mortar fire or rebel fighters to attack specific targets.
Multiplayer - You can play the singleplayer mission in coop mode or play PVP.  Team work can make or break this experience.  But it can be quite a bit of fun.
Bottom line - this is a finely polished, Tom Clancy-themed copy of Just Cause without the highlight of James Bond stunts.  That is not meant as a bad thing by any means.  You can tool around the map causing mayhem and destroying everything in your path or choose to play the story.  If you get bored with the story, you can do what you like.

I'm annoyed by the negative reviews for this game. Very annoyed, because I fear they will keep this excellent game from getting the sequel it deserves. :(
But first, let's start with my review, which is very positive.
This game is primarily about atmospheric immersion, fostered by excellent graphics, sound, color, and lighting design, especially for weather. The rain beats on you throughout almost the entire game, the world is gray, and you can almost feel the sting of the wind shaking the bushes and trees and ocean. Those precious few moments where there is a break in the clouds and some color fills the world seem especially precious. (A great time to hunt for hidden objects, too!) The world (an island) is thoughtfully designed, and it's quite neat to see all the pieces come together as you explore it. The Irish pride is very apparent, with all names translated from Gaelic, and a few flags to remind you, in case you forgot.
And there
a story, a very clear one, with a clear ending in which some of the core questions are resolved, and yet there are still unanswered issues demanding a sequel.
And this is no "walking sim": it's a real game with real puzzles, some of them quite challenging indeed. It's not as hard as Myst/Riven for sure, but a few puzzles don't give much indication if you're on the right path. They're not the best puzzles I've seen in adventure games, but are far from the worst, and there is quite some satisfaction in completing them on your own. There are also achievements, which involve finding some hidden items, many of them very difficult to find. I would have been quite lost without a guide! Note that you can finish the game and then easily go back to various checkpoints to find the hidden objects you missed, so there's no need to get anxious about achievements during your first run.
So, what's with all the negative reviews?
Some of them are from people who just have no interest in atmospheric games: because you can't run here and are forced to move quite slowly, they dismiss it as a "walking sim." Honestly, you don't walk
slowly in Montague's Mount, the island is rather small, and all in all you are rewarded with the gorgeous environment for those few times you do need some patience. I didn't feel like this part of the game was tedious at all. Hell, you need much more patience to get around in Skyrim!
On the other hand, there are those people who compare Montague's Mount negatively to Dear Esther. There are embarrassingly obvious similarities that do beg a comparison: both games take place on barren, gray, northern islands, and involve uncovering a dead past. But, whereas people complained that Dear Esther didn't have any real "game" to it now they are complaining that Montague's Mount's puzzles are too nonsensical! There's just no pleasing some people.
Dear Esther's textures and lights are better designed, but Montague's Mount still has a lot going for it visually, and though it looks less gorgeous and lush, it's still quite beautiful and immersive.
My only real complaint is that the physics are a bit buggy. In a few cases I was sure I clicked something, only to return later to find that I didn't. Super big hint:
If anything I wrote here appealed to you,
play the game and leave an honest, hopefully positive review. I would really like to see a part 2 in the future!
Finally: I'd like to thank the developer for supporting Linux so well.

I only bought this game as it was on sale and Test Drive Unlimited is not available anywhere. Well, this game is far from the original one. For some reason the creators thought the right way to improve a racing title is to put more clothes, hair styles and a dumb story line in it.
Apart from technical issues with TDU servers the "story" mode with all the bulls**t renders the game unenjoyable. It takes loooong minutes until you can finally get in a car and drive - in a game called "Test Drive". Seriously: DO NOT BUY.

Well, it is a mixed bag. The game gets a few things right really well, and really messes up some other parts. It is not a racing game for fanatics looking for realism and special racing cars on special circuits. This is a casual racer, but I think there are games in that genre that handles better like NFS Hot Pursuit 2 and Burnout Paradise (the best game still).
AND, the online never really works. I think it has been abandoned for a while actually. I do recommend it even if there is no online. If you do care about online then obviously forget this one. Oh, and play with a 360-controller. It just does not work very well with any other option if you want to do well. I tried with a steering-wheel too, and it made everything worse even though lots of fun.
What is great?
The idea of driving around freely on an island is fantastic. If you actually want to drive more "normal" cars on the road and not just race in circles this is the game for you. You can play the game like Truck simulator 2 if you wish, just driving around, enjoying the scenery and your cars. Even if that is very simple, the game does this part extremely well. The cars look great, the island(s) look great. Lots of freedom. Nice weather. You can buy nice houses and fix your car. Great cockpit view for immersion. There is quite a lot to do on the island(s). Lots of nice cars to try.
The races are ok, and there is a welcome addition of off-road driving that is probably the most fun in the game. More on that later.
What is not too great?
They whole story mode is just incredibly silly and forced. Every cut-scene feels written by a person who couldn't smell funny even if it would be served on a silver platter under their nose, but has rather looked up the word funny on the internet and plastered a bunch of horrible cliches together. Everything feels forced and is rather embarrassing. And the voice-overs are sooo bad. They are just trying too hard, making it sound incredibly unnatural and disconnected. "Look, I'm so happy and crazy!!!!!" They audio is also so repetitive that it becomes ridiculous and has nothing to do with the situation you are in. It really feels like they hired the cheapest voice talent with absolutely no previous experience except for perhaps unemotional robots. The radio is the same. Some good music and some interesting ideas, but they are not funny, at all... Compared to GTA-radio it is just embarrassing.
And what is up with the people on this island? They all look like they come from the movie the Stepford Wives. It is downright creepy actually. The vision between the "car-game" and the "world" seems like two different planets. This corporate ugly plastic vision with no taste or style destroys the game.
The sounds of the cars are really bad. Especially the SUVs. The devs just did not try at all here. They sound nothing like a real car, just a like cheap synth pitched up and down. Really surprising when you consider the details in the rest of the game.
And, DLCs for extra cars...
Races
So, the challenges are ok, fun and varied but I HATE the time trials. I HATE them!!!! Because it is totally unforgiving. I don't mind that there is a challenge but it makes no sense the way it is set-up this game. In normal races you can mess up, and catch up the others, the race is not over if you make ONE small mistake. But in the time trials, you better just start over if you mess up. This becomes more hairpullingly annoying when some of the time trials are 5 minutes long and you make a mistake at the end of that track and you have to start over. And every time you start over you have to see an annoying cut-scene. To make you scream a bit more they also added a game-mechanic that is just there to slap you in the face:
On time trials, if you drive off the road just even slightly, a timer starts ticking, removing time from your total!!!! I understand the reason: they thought that you should not be able to cheat by taking a shortcut, but the fact is that the cars handle so poorly off-road that it would never be a good option to do so anyway. You gain nothing by driving off-road, your car slows down a lot AND you get punished for it as well time-wise.
There is also a challenge where you have to drive around the entire island, which takes about 50 minutes. Actually a rather neat idea if you  have the time for it. Here, I think they realized the problem I am talking about because it is fairly easy to do that one and have plenty of time left, but I wish the time trials were a little easier. They are just frustrating as it is.
The game has good FPS in general but I have to say that the 3D-engine is not greatly optimized and you will not get a great performance if your computer is a little older. Lots of pop-ins and stutter unless you don't mind lowering the quality quite a but. Many games do a lot better.
Despite all the negativity I like the game in the end. It is the only game that does what it does, and the good parts it does rather well. I do recommend it on a sale. You do get a lot even though the online does not work. I have enjoyed it, except for the need to vomit every time the cut-scenes come in.

This game is a hidden jewel. People that go to the store page, may think: "Woah, mobile game on steam, so sad", but the truth is, I didn't have much fun with a game since months ago.
The game starts with a simple map, your base on one side, and enemies that come from the top. A quick tutorial reveals that you have to put different types of turrets, upgrade them, sell them if necessary, and defend your base. Seems easy, doesn't it?
You only have 2 turrets in the early levels, but as you proceed, you unlock more turrets. At the end of each game, you're assigned Victory Points depending on how good your performance was, and Perks, depending if you fulfilled the requeriments for one. With the victory points, you improve the level of upgrades of each turret, and when one is fully upgraded, you have the ability for 40 victory points to specialize that turret, making it more utile depending on what you choose. Regarding the perks, well, you have 3 types of perks, and as you unlock them, you put the ones that fit you the best.
The difficulty of the game is HARD. The first levels are kind of easy, but after some time, you will most likely get stressed at how screwed you are, that's when the Rewind option comes in hand. Basically, you have a rewind that you can use at the round you want, to start again that round, and delete everything you did, and the enemy did, that exact round. If you use it, you have to wait 3 more rounds until you can use it again.
This game is a fun little game, great for killing time, and for improving your strategies. I do recommend this game!
P.S: I got it for free thanks to Indie Gala, you only have to put your email, and you receive the code of the game for free, but I suggest buying it to support the developers!

"Based on a What Now?"
First off, I'll admit. I wasn't a fan of Dear Esther. I did, however, like Gone Home, so I'm going to assume I'm not just biased and go from there.
MM is a short horror/exploration game that follows a familiar trope. Your character has amnesia (why? Who knows.) and you must travel the island finding hints and clues about what happened there in hopes of finding out your own identity.
It plays relatively well. I've seen a lot of people complain about the walking speed, but I didn't think it was too savagely slow, although the many, many to-ing and fro-ings required to solve some puzzles do make it frustrating. If memory serves, though, Esther and other games like it have been slower in the travelling.
I can't say much about the graphics. I turned off the grainy quality because it made it impossible to read signs, and so I didn't see what the creator intended. But I found myself frequently wanting to turn the lighting up, and I missed a few puzzle pieces for a LONG time because they vanished in shadows.
Honestly, the only thing that kept me going was the idea that this was based on a true story; I wanted to know what the disease was, if that was the true part, or if it was the man's family life and his apparent struggle with mental illness and all the things we find out happened with his life on the island. If that's the reason you want to play, I'm gonna say it right now - don't. You'll feel jipped when you find out that the 'based on a true story' really means that the creator moved to Ireland with his wife and had some cultural and language barriers to overcome. That's the parallel to the game. So if you're in this for the story, hoping it'll have more true-to-life and less hackneyed-cliche elements than others, then don't waste your time.
The story is ... okay. You, obviously, don't get to know EVERYTHING, because they saved some for a sequel, but it's interesting enough that I kept going. If you've played more than one similar game, however, you'll have guessed the entire plot when you get ten minutes in. It doesn't overcome the difficulties in gameplaya nd visuals that make this game a slog to get through. (Maybe that's something we should guess from the fact that there's an achievement for playing it for three whole hours?)
Basically, if you're mad into the genre and actually enjoy the plot elements and gameplay, and want some SERIOUSLY over-wrought puzzles, then you might just enjoy this. If you need a little more than that, then this is probably just going to disappoint.

A Myst-like with a psychological horror plot based on a true story sounds like a great idea, doesn't it?  Yes, yes it does.  This implementation of that idea, however, is... not so great.
Devs will often start their games with something impressive or exciting, which is an effective strategy, because it hooks players in quickly and provides something to show off in demos and trailers.  PolyPusher opted for the alternate, questionable strategy of making the first few minutes of
so unbearably awful that the rest of the game seems excellent by comparison.  You begin the game walking very slowly around a rainy beach, and as you walk, the camera rocks wildly.  Even while standing still, the camera remains unsteady.  The graphics are not too bad for an indie game, but dark and heavily desaturated, and there's a film grain effect enabled by default.  Both of those effects individually make sense to set the mood, but the combined effect is over-the-top and very hard on the eyes.  But wait, it gets worse: under these conditions, you are given a tutorial and your first objective, in the form of a couple pinned notes.
You can't inspect these notes or pick them up to get a clearer view; you have to get as close as you can to them, and then read them - despite the mediocre graphics with heavy desaturation, and the film grain, and the rain, and the rocking camera.  Within a few minutes, I had decided that if the point of this game was to make me feel queasy and illiterate, well, mission bloody accomplished.  A better plan would be to say "screw that" and look up a guide.  You'll probably do that more than once if you play this game.
If you have the stomach to continue in the face of such adversity, once you disable the film grain and find a walking stick to steady the camera, you'll find that the rest of the game is playable at the very least.  The desaturated graphics with poor lighting remain a little hard on the eyes, but tolerable.  The walking speed isn't as excruciatingly slow as other reviewers make it out to be (but you'll find yourself wishing you could run occasionally).
For the most part, the puzzles make sense, but one was fiddly and had a solution that was the opposite of what I thought it would be, and another would have you walking a fairly long distance back and forth between a Morse code message and the barely legible key for deciphering it (again, say "screw that" and look up a guide).  Video game logic and contrived puzzles are pervasive here, which works for some games, but in this one, the knowledge that it's based on a true story and should be realistic creates dissonance.  (Seriously, who builds crazy locking mechanisms like these in real life?  Why do I have to get a specific candle when it's clear that any candle will do and there are a dozen strewn about?  Why would someone write a note that says "I should have written the code here" and not write the code?  Who carefully arranged all these journal pages for me to find, and why?)  The inventory system adds another annoyance: you can only carry five items at a time.  Sure, if we're going for realism, a person can only carry so much, but a limit of five items, regardless of size and weight is just arbitrary, not realistic.  And from a gampelay perspective, limited capacity makes sense in RPG's and such, but not in adventure games like this, where you need to pick up everything you can in order to progress.  Worse, once you pick an item up, you're stuck with it until you can use it - there's no way to set something down.  If you're stuck and find a sixth item you know what to do with, too bad, you'll have to make some progress and then backtrack later.  Devs, please don't do this; there's no excuse for it.  Either let me manage my inventory or just don't limit what I can carry.
The story is... well, it's not bad, and I like the idea of basing a game on a true story, but it's simplistic, and definitely not the psychological thriller it's described as being.  There's nothing thrilling about it; it's more accurately described as creating an atmosphere of despair.  I can sum it up in one short sentence: there was a plague, and a lot of people died.  I'm not even spoiling anything by saying that - it's clear from the first journal page you find, right after starting the game.  Also, your progress is occasionally interrupted by a quote about mental illness, or the appearance of a ghost boy, accompanied by motion blur and a racing heartbeat.  These are eventually sort of explained in the one real development the plot gets, but it's not especially satisfying, and I agree with certain other reviewers that the ghost was unnecessary.
I appreciate what
was trying to be, but it didn't succeed, and given the poor artistic choices, gameplay annoyances, and shallow plot, I can't recommend it.

I was very reluctant to give the game a "not recommend" because the effort and love Turtle Rock has put into Evolve is very apparent. All things considered, I feel 2k is the party who earned the negative review.
The game itself is by no means bad. The gameplay is unique, the characters aren't hateable (overwatch, I'm looking at you) and the game is overall well-polished. In most aspects, I can tell Turtle Rock really wants to make this a great game and I commend them for the effort they continue to put in. Honestly, I do like the game, the atmosphere and monsters are very likeable and unique. Evolve is just very casual.
The first match I played was adrenaline filled and I truly enjoyed it. However, I didn't know how to play at that point; and I still won. In fact, I haven't even felt close to losing yet and I've (at the time of this review) played six games.
I guess that in itself isn't enough to warrant a negative review. I just can't help but have a sour taste in my mouth from the poor business practices 2k used in marketing and selling this game. It's ridiculous and dishonest.
A good portion of Evolve is genuinely fun, albeit easy to play and too easy to learn. It's kind of silly what the game is or has become especially considering how 2k tried to market this as a competitive e-sports title.
I wish the game could have launched more smoothly without all the (likely paid for) hype. I really really want to like this game.

Insanely underrated game. Those who expect a sequel to XCOM Enemy Unknown/Within, will be extraordinarily disappointed with The Bureau: XCOM Declassified.
This is not a turn-based strategy game. This is a squad-based third person shooter. There is definitely strategy involved with selecting the proper soldiers (two squadmates to assist you at a time) with the appropriate weapons and knowing how to manage their abilities in order to conserve the most ammo, maximize opportunities for kills, etc.; but it's incredibly different from the previous entry to the XCOM series.
But change is not a bad thing, anyone interested in the (albeit fairly cliche at this point in time) concept of an alien invasion in the midst of a futuristic-styled 60's era, will enjoy The Bureau's story. It throws a few interesting twists to keep it from being entirely cliche, and overall executes the concept it goes for, perfectly.
While XCOM Declassified is definitely not for everyone, fans of alien sci-fi with an open mind to change for a series, who are willing to learn how to properly manage their soldiers (there is a bit of a learning curve and frustration in the beginning), will certainly enjoy this game. Especially on its frequent dirt-cheap sales, it's impossible to go wrong. Buy this game.

This game is difficult, and not in the "oh my god, Dark Souls so hard" way but in an actual NES design era type game design.  Every encounter and enemy in the game scales on the number of people who are with you, so if you are alone encounters are not as strong, but if you're in a big group then you basically need each other.  It's not an unusual thing, of course, Phantasy Star Online used such a design to make grouping more rewarding but more difficult as well, and there's nothing wrong with that.
When the player dies, they lose everything they have equipped and are carrying, with no way to recover those items.  To change character you also need to become a spark, which requires either EC (in-game currency), or to die.  It's very easy to die, and you're basically expected to repeat the first dungeon over and over and over and over until you're either sufficiently leveled up to play as the character you actually want to play; or you basically outlevel the current content you're doing.
The game is a grindfest.  As you play you will find minibosses, midbosses and bosses as well as enemies.  Only midbosses and bosses are GUARANTEED to drop loot, but you'll definitely get plenty of chests along the way.  As a diversion, I would say that the game is definitely a pretty good time sink, you'll keep playing, getting better little by little but also dying a lot.
Now for the negative, the in-game currency is tied to every type of purchase in the game, and there's two ways to acquire currency.  Either you keep playing through dungeons -OR- you pay real money.  Currency is NOT plentiful in dungeons, so I could see a lot of people opting for the microtransaction method of getting money, which I don't personally feel is worth the money but that's your choice not mine.
I'd give it a 7.5 out of 11, it can be a good time sink, but it sure can get old quick too.

Id Software's Quake is the game that popularised online deathmatches. This first game in the Quake series is inspired by Gothic-style environments, medieval settings and Satanic imagery (similar to id's predecessor, Doom). It also has been the starting point and an influence on user mods, machinimas and speedruns.
Thanks to Trent Reznor, founder/leading singer of Nine Inch Nails, his music and sound design/effects for the game added to the creepiness factor of the game, other members of the band contributed to the soundtrack as well. Though in order to get the soundtrack for the Steam version, you need the Ultimate Quake Patch.
Quake is also the game that the original Team Fortress was based on by John Cook and Robin Walker (who are now working in Valve).
Its singleplayer campaign consists of four episodes of eight levels each (including a secret level). You play a protaganist only known as Ranger sent into a portal to defeat an enemy codenamed Quake. As you collect weapons/items, they are carried over to the next level. The higher level you reach, the more challenging and intense it becomes than the last.
Easily the best game ever made. First true 3D FPS game, and I still play it to this day.

If you loved DOOM or DOOM II then Quake is a god-send. The Original Quake was THE FIRST TRUE 3D First Person Shooter ever made. And it did (then as well as now, if anyone could see past then next CoD) phenominally.
32 is the magic number when it comes to great FPS' , as all 32 levels (and 6 underplayed 'Deathmatch' levels) were intense and enjoyable from start to finish.
The Original Quake may as well have been a DOOM spin-off during it's initial release, but copying a great formula isn't always a bad thing, IF you know where to go with it. Quake knew EXACTLY what it was doing, and IMPROVED upon all of DOOM's previous work. Taking DOOM 2's 32 level formula, the ability to look up and down (It was REVOLUTIONARY I TELL YOU!!!!!!!), intense gore (which, back then made the game "M for Mature" but now, with graphical updates, the gore has been downgraded too "T for Teen"), fast-paced (CoD has NOTHING on this) multiplayer, and over the top violence (A.K.A. The AXE OF EXPLOSIONS, seriously... no joke... go smash up a corpse with this thing...), that made it a 'Must have' for EVERY gamer that owned Windows 95.
NOTICE (FOR CLARIFICATION ONLY, You can skip this if you want):Now, I must clarify one thing, I didn't grow up on DOOM or DOOM II or even Quake, BUT I believe Wolfenstein, Spear of Destiny, DOOM, DOOM II, Quake, and all of the other great 90's First Person Shooters are what we should all take a page from when making the next CoD. SERIOUSLY my first First Person Shooter was CALL OF DUTY 4 for God's sake! When I played DOOM for the first time I was... how shall I say this....MIND BLOWN, FLOORED, & BLOWN THROUGH THE FRONT DOOR! SERIOUSLY! I play CoD 4 now and I'll ALWAYS go back to DOOM & DOOM II before the day's up.
The Original Quake is, in my opinion, better than Quake 2 & 4 (Which are basically part of a 'mini-trilogy' I call
"The Quake Wars"), Quake 1 is entirely seperate from the rest of the series. It is closer to a fully 3D DOOM game more than Quake's 2, 4, and Enemy Territory: Quake Wars (A.K.A The Quake Wars Trilogy)  Quake is the name of the final Boss in this game, though (Can this really be a spoiler? I mean, all I said was the name, right?) not a boss in The Quake Wars Trilogy, has no mention of even the name "Quake" EXCEPT when the Intro of Enemy Territory: QW has a slip-gate (pretty much a space teleporter) shaped like the logo summon invading ships.
NOW, all mentions of other games aside.... Quake is an addicting, fast paced, rocket jumping (yes, we has those), barrel O' fun. In the words of a wiseman ~ "In my day, we rocket jumped to school, both ways." - Wise guy, 20XX (because I don't remember his name or the year). You would be a FOOL to pass this game up, give it a try, there's NOTHING to lose, and everything to GAIN!
