Now that this game has been released, I can write this review for a released game.
While I was playing in the beta, I saw a lot of potential for this game.  It seemed almost like the Sims, with pirates and swashbuckling and all the greatness you want from piracy.  You can recruit your crew and equip each member with weapons and skills to make your pirate crew a fearesome force on the open seas.
That being said, the implementation is far from perfect.  A lot of the tooltips seem off point, like the training swords that you can get to put on your ship state "Training is for the weak".  Until you actually buy them, you don't actually realize this is a part for your ship that allows your crew member to gain XP.  Town notations have messed up spacing.  Many items' functionality is left unknown to the player until they actually use it, which is awful considering that everything is the game feels very expensive (at least in the beginning).
The biggest issue I have with the game is the AI.  I was constantly fighting the AI with what it wanted to do against what I needed to do (or it needed to do, for that matter).  For example, I had a fisher on my crew, who should be providing fish for the crew to eat.  Instead, the AI wants him to go to the training swords and gain XP.  Every time I try to take him off the training swords, he takes two steps off the swords, then goes right back to them.  Meanwhile, my crew is starving (and dying).  My Captain, starving, prefers to stay at the training swords instead of eat, so then he dies.  In combat, I try to remove heavily wounded crew members from the enemy, but they take a few steps away and attempt to attack again.
This game had a lot of good ideas and I wanted to be an awesome pirate captain, but I spent most of my time fighting the AI that should be making my experience more fluid and playing "guess its purpose" on every item I found and/or bought.
Note to the developer(s): if you are having trouble making something automatic, leave it to the player, and only automate it when you know with 99% certainty that the palyer will want it.  For example, if a pirate is starving, go eat.  If the player has to send the pirate to the training swords manually, it is better than removing the control from the player.

I really love the concept of this game, i do. However, it's frusterating when your pirates get stuck in the deck blocks and can't get up a ladder, as well as prioritizing training over firing cannons. I will recommend this game, once the AI is fixed.

This game is only for a certain type of person. Those who brand games like Dear Esther 'walking simulators' won't enjoy MM. You can skip right over this one.
This game and Dear Esther have alot in common. Both have you start on an Island without explanation. Their storys are told in a weaved thread, out of context. Verses read by an excellent voice actor are filled with saddness and confusion.
While DE leave's it's story open to your own conclusion, MM has a set story that while enjoyable to listen to while exploring, dosen't really give you the closure it deserves. It kind of leaves itself open for a sequal which I didn't really like.
It's true your character move's slowly. However a player like myself came to like that. I don't rush through area's anyway and the pacing of the player character was that which allowed me to explore comfortablly.
I've also heard criticism for the film grain (which you can turn off) and the use of dark shadows. Again, this was something I enjoyed and thought the developers put to good use.
I would conclude by saying, buy on offer if you're unsure but it sounds like something you'd enjoy. If these kind of experiences are something you don't like, stay well clear of this one.

Honestly, this isn't a bad game. I don't understand why it's so poorly reviewed. It offers some pretty decent puzzles, well constructed scenes and environments, good soundtrack and an overall rewarding experience. You should be warned, though, that this isn't a traditional first person game. It's not a shooter, it's not a AAA adventure, action packed game. This should be played as almost an interactive movie that prompts you to solve challenging puzzles to progress through the story.
About the story, even though there's a substantial amount of written material that somehow explains a bit what is happening, in my opinion the plot itself is just accessory to the real experience offered by Montague's Mount: the constant feeling of isolation and desperation while you search for answers about who and where you are. It's so much more about the atmosphere that the game conveys than the story itself - which is really not so important, in this case.

Do you ever play those games where it's like, you play a match for a few minutes and afterward you're like, okay let's try that again that wasn't good enough, and then you check the clock and four hours have passed? Because that's what this game is like. Absolutely consumes your entire mind and keeps you busy non-stop. It's very challenging, at least with challenging settings, and I consider difficult games a lot of fun. Games that make you want to try again because you know you can do better.
I have now put a more considerate time into this game and can go more into depth. I must say if you're like me and you want to be able to beat a game without having to turn down the difficulty because you're determent to do it, or just to proud to go the "easy  way" then this game in default setting, which is 100% (Challenging) will have a learning curve that is fairly high.
The main focus of the learning curve here is, on one hand, the micromanaging of your units, because you may have one unit to advance and clear out the surrounding area of zombies somewhere, and you let that unit do its thing there for a second to manage your city for a bit, and before you know it the unit is dead, which could leave you with one flank exposed.
On the other hand knowing what to focus on in terms of building up your settlement, for example, do you want to put all your resources you gather towards growing a big army, or do you want a small army but many defensive structures like walls and turrets, or do you want to use most of your resources to expand and grow your population and gain even more resources? I'm certain that all of these ways can get you to final victory if you do it right. The trick is to find your own perfect way to master it, because this game allows no, and by that, I mean NO mistakes. One single zombie slipping through and reaching your tents/houses? You're done!
And that's also where I have to give some critique. There is no option to restart a level. The game always puts you in a new randomized location every time you start over. When you lose, your save will get deleted, you cannot recover or "try again" from an earlier save. Personally, I understand this and have no problem with it, BUT, I really wish you could at least have an option to restart the same location. Because for every time you start over you have to make a new plan on how and where to defend your settlement, since sometimes you may have 3 directions to fortify, sometimes you have 6. Sometimes you have plenty of wood around, other times barely any. And so you have to re-think each time, which makes the game even harder.
I have some 30 hours now, only playing with 100% difficulty and I have not managed to get past the last (extremely big) horde yet. But I am determined to keep trying.
Some more critique from me would be;
-You don't ALWAYS get notified when units get attacked, which ends up in units may dying which you didn't know of were almost dead. This could also be one's own fault because I mentioned that micromanaging is a big thing in this game. But I still wish there was an option to be able to set the alert for it to something more frequent.
-Framerate on the last horde is bad. Not sure how much optimization can be done there or if it's simply the limit of the engine or whatever because it's just A LOT of zombies.
-I found the UI to be a little unresponsive at times. Sometimes you click things but nothing is happening because you may be too hasty clicking your way through the building menu.
Or also when giving orders to units with key shortcuts it doesn't always get through with it. Sometimes you just have to give the order again before the units do the thing.
-There's not a lot of variety when it comes to the soundtrack. The game seems to be playing the same music over and over every match. It's not a terrible thing, but it could be more.
Other than that, I can only recommend this game. Very challenging and lots of fun potential for many hours especially when you're stubborn and refuse to play lower difficulties. :))

An X-Com game turned into a 1960's based Mass Effect style game, and not in a good way.  It's like ME2 and 3 in that the mainline, gun combat has had too much focus.  Upgrades do not reflect weapon tech level (bullets, laser, then plasma), where as soldiers can, at the start when you only have the starting weapons, have tech for, say, a turret, that uses tech based off of the alien's weapons.  Any and all choices you make (and side missions) will have 0, repeat, 0 impact on the story, as (SPOILIER) X-Com HQ eventually gets attacked and destroyed, killing virtually everyone inside of the base save for some major characters.  The whole idea of "having to take alien weapons that haven't been destroyed by operator death using the Venn Brace (the device on Carter's arm in virtually all screen shots)" is just stupid.  The AI isn't the brightest.  The game also lacks a key aspect of X-Com and it's choices: will this work out in the long run.
Lets use X-Com: Enemy Unknown for example: You recieve an abduction mission.  You have to pick one of three.  One is in St. Petersburg, and Russia is offering a new sniper, at the rank of captian.  Your's is a squaddie, as you had to replace your previous one.  Then there's one in New York.  The US is offering 4 scientists.  You have completed all projects that will be fast, and are on a long term one (10 days left).  Then you have one in Cairo.  Egypt is offering 200 credits.  You recently bought a satilite, and still have room for one more.  Europe and NA has their panic raised to 2, amd if you don't pick it, it will raise to 4, hanging on the edge of full panic and risking leaving, or staying.  The sattilite construciton is cutting the montly report close, but you may have time to place that sattilite over the one of the paniced countries.  And there MAY be a chance of a Terror mission.  What I have given you is a typical scenario, in both EU and EW.  The player may think this: "That sniper is good, it can make my squads stronger, and I don't have to worry about my normal sniper becoming wounded.  But, I need those Scientists so I can research Plasma weapons faster, make my soldiers better in the field.  Although, I could use those funds, and can use two sattilites to lower more countries panic."  For this, there is no right or wrong answer.  And there is a chance that this can make or break your run.
However, for the Bureau, there are no hard choices.  You can do as many side missions, and send as many side agents out before you continue on with the story.  The even added a cliche "character sacrifice" on the finally mission, (SPOILER) having you pick between Agent Weaver, Director Faulke, or Doctor Weir (depending on who you picked to continue as in the level prior).  There is no sense of loss, as you can't even use the character you just rescuesed, esentially giving you a hollow choice.
This game was labeled an X-Com game and had potential.  It did not live up to it.

For a shoot-em-up game with a small amount of tactics, I may recommend this game. The fact of the matter is that this game attempting to be more than a shoot-em-up by offering some kind of plot line which is poorly written, especially when it involves reconciling the fact that 1950's weapon techonology somehoe supersedes advanced alien laser technology. In addition to the plot line, the makers of the game add in the ability to 'make decisions,' but the decisions don't matter in the slightest, nor do any of the chat options lead anywhere different. Throughout the game, the player is given the option to select multiple options which lead to more details which mean nothing. In addition to worthless information, there is a great quantity of "notes," "pictures," and other "articles" you may choose to read while going through the campaign - it is all worthless. In other words, they add in all of this unconsequential information which often repeats in detail, such as a sleepwalker plague which goes around every town. Had I known this in advanced, maybe the game would take about two hours to skip through because there is only a finite amount of missions. The Bureau: XCOM Declassified is lacking of the critical parts which XCOM: Enemy Unknonwn has, and if you are looking to recreate the experience of having a difficult struggle in keeping all of your squad members alive, this is not the game. In fact, this game gives you the ability to send members of your crew on seperate missions to which they rarely face an ill-fate. Through these missions, they rapidly evolve to the maximum level of 5, which provide somewhat useful abilities in dealing with an alien encounter; I cannot remember using the "scatter" ability once during my time playing this game.
I give the game a 4/10 and regret spending so much time on it. I wish it was more open world and less linear because the entire time I played, you travel through a giant line with only a single path. If this game expected to emerse you into the world, it failed horribly. Fortunately I got this game through a Humble Bundle and didn't completely waste money on it - the money went to charity.

10/10 - The Poor Man’s World Of Warcraft! FREE and Still Good in 2016!
This is one of those reviews that you just can't win. Too many have played; too many have developed concrete opinions. This is just my personal take on the game and how it ranks in the genre as of 2016.
The graphics and production values are pretty amazing! If you have played WOW this is certainly one of the closest clones. It's not a copy though; this game definitely has its own identity!
There are massive worlds, PVP, bosses and absolutely everything you would want in an MMORPG. The member base on games like this is always in flux; currently there is an average of 650 players playing at any one time. Not a ton; but still more than at times in the past! If you look at the graphs from the last 5 years you can really see the trends and the conclusion... This game is far from dead.  A single DLC or major update can bring any game back to life!
This is my favorite game in the mmorpg genre; granted my computer isn't amazing so I can't effectively play some of the newest games, but this one still has it going on in 2016! I just got off playing WOW for nostalgia’s sake and honestly I prefer this game much more so.
Rift is completely free to play; being a premium member definitely has some serious bonuses like all MMORPGS. The biggest thing patrons receive is more xp, cash and access to the marketplace. The marketplace was a major factor for me in the past; but due to the current member slump it can be difficult to sell on a saturated market anyway. So FREE is still great.
So, if you want to play something extremely enjoyable and very similar to WOW without the subscription... I'll see you in Rift!
I've played this game on and off over the years and every time I come back I appreciate this game more and more. Please be aware that the member base is smaller than some games, and you will have to work a little harder as a free member. For tire kickers and those wanting to try the game:

Cons:

End of Edit
Really nice graphics and a large world to explore. Easy crafting system (you can get free packs for the "bank" to hold all the junk.) Variety of mounts, you can fish, role-play, craft, work on your own 3d space, join a guild, follow quests, PVP, go on Raids. It can be a bit addictive.
Cons:  Without a guild or someone to help you the game can get confusing because after the tutorial there are no instructions on how to get a mount or make in game money, or how to set up your character interface after all your abilities have changed. You have to search through the tabs yourself and figure it out.  Also you cant use the auction house without being a Patron (aka a casher), which i think is ridiculous.
-It helps to know how to make macros and there are different macros for every character build and there are hundreds of different builds which makes it uber confusing. Unless you are lucky enough to know someone who knows about your character build most guilds will refer you to Google instead of trying to help you.

Verdict: Worth trying if your computer can handle the graphics. It is possible to play alone and exploring is fun but game is better played with a group of friends.

Quake is one of the best Id titles around. It has bad♥♥♥♥♥weapons, enemies, sound effects and music (provided by Trent Reznor of Nine Inch Nails).
It has very interesting level design that is a lot more advanced than Doom's. Each episode starts out in a military base that has a portal to other dimensions, so there's lots of variety in each episode.
The enemies range from grunts with shotguns to giants who shoot lightning, there's a lot of things in between.
Weapons are amazing, with sound effects that make them all seem very powerful. The weapons in Quake are all very useful for various situations, it is important to learn each weapons functionality.
Armor is a very important item in Quake. You die much quicker in Quake without armor than you do in other games from this time period, so always be well stocked up on armor.
My only complaints are that only the first episode ends in a boss fight, the rest do not, though the other 3 episodes are much harder than the first, still a boss fight for each rune would've been nice. Another thing, Quake has aged quite a bit, in the 90s Quake was a pretty scary game, but at least for me, its fear factor is no longer present.
A Steam version only complaint, Steam Quake doesn't loop the music tracks on its own, you must use a patched EXE and rip the CD audio to mp3 format to get it to work (there is a guide on Steam about how to do this). This should not be a problem, but it is, and it seems to be a problem that plagues not only Quake, but other CD audio based games such as Quake II, Hexen II, Blood, and more. There are no achievements, which doesn't bother me but it might bother others. I have yet to try online play with the Steam version so I have no real comment, but Quake multiplayer is amazing, I hope that it works on Steam.
If you like Doom, or other FPS games of the 90s, you'll love Quake.

When it comes to first person shooter games, I've almost always preferred the old to the new. Games like Doom, Duke Nukem 3D, Team Fortress Classic, and most importantly, this game. Quake is one of my favorite games of all time, and a top contender for my favorite first person shooter. If you are a gamer that enjoys reloading constantly, passively regenerating health, being guided linearly from point A to point B in the story, and generally playing behind a safety net, then good for you. But Quake is a fast paced, old school, top of the class shooter that refuses to hold your hand. The fast paced gameplay, the need for exploration to find every secret to help you through, the challenging, hard hitting enemies and weapons, and the fact that you can die extremely quickly if you screw up. That is what a good shooter is to me, and I can't think of a better example of where that shines than Quake. If you haven't played this game before, I can't recommend it enough, and if you're a long time fan of the Quake series like me, then you understand why I feel the way I do about this game. 10/10.

StarBreak is a new MMO action platform game released May 10th, 2016 on steam. As of my video and this review, I have about 3 hours put into the game. The main mechanic of this game comes from the fact that there is permadeath for your suit. Once you die, all progress is loss and you will have to start anew.
This game is the starchild between Megaman and Realm of the Mad God. The Megaman aspect comes from the action platforming, how items are obtained, and the boss battles (which are fairly well designed but far more bullet spongy than the trash mobs would make you think). Everything else is influenced from the Realm of the Mad God. Players start in a lobby with everyone else on the server chosen. They have the ability to enter named instances with up to 39 other players. These instances are unique planets or worlds that having varying tiers of difficulties and rewards to match the difficulty of the instances. Loot is personal, so you don't have to worry about the other 39 players stealing your +1 bullet weapon.
The developers, Crunchy Games, included a premium currency, obtained by paying real money. As of this review, you can purchase cosmetic hats, that are lost upon death, or quality of life upgrades that include more storage space.
If you love Realm of the Mad God and miss the days of classic Megaman, this game is for you. In spite of myself owning Overwatch, XCOM, FFXIV, etc... I've continued to find myself drawn back to the game to slaughter my enemies. I fully recommend trying out the game as I enjoyed my time with it.

Basically, Starbreak is frustrating, enticing, challenging, addicting, stylish fun. It's a roguelike action-platformer MMO where you will always die, and everything is in the pursuit of sweet loot and badassery.
Be warned, you will die countless times and probably smash one or two keyboards in the process cuz you lost all your high-level loot. This is a very unforgiving game, and as such gets very frustrating
Players choose from multiple characters, referred to as shells, to play as, starting with only one before eventually unlocking the remaining three through in-game progression. The gameplay itself has a strong core with a lot of variety sprinkled on that changes how the game plays depending on which shell you use. Wildfire, the first and default shell, plays very simply, using rifles, shotguns, and sometimes snipers to plink away at enemies from a distance. Duskwing, the second shell, is a high-risk/high-reward glass cannon with emphasis on aerial domination and CQC. Ironclad, the penultimate shell, is the game's tank, with a shield capable of blocking all normal projectiles and a massive ♥♥♥♥-off hammer capable of pounding all kinds of baddies into dust. Lastly, Fabricator is the final shell, focused mainly on fire support through fabricating different kinds of weapons and platforms to assist other players.
Gameplay is solid and simple, with plenty of additional layers added through the shells' different playstyles and synergy. You run and gun/smash/slice through baddies, jump here, there, and everywhere, and die repeatedly because you tried leeching a high-level dungeon only to get♥♥♥♥♥♥slapped by the many giant lizards/plant monsters/robots/light bulbs that inhabit the dungeons. But you simply choose a new shell, deny your pointless eternal existence, and keep killing/dieing.
If you like pretty visuals and good sound design, then this is also a very good game for those.

The problems I found with this game in Solo play are:
Very unrealistic. For the first 3 days I spent waiting for my team to get into the car. I had to leave them behind once to chase a guy, and they suddenly reapeared in my car, from then on I knew where ever I go the team will be there.

It's fun, but it's literally just Assassin's Creed with guns. You've played the entire game within the first hour: go to location, scout out mooks, use rifle to snipe mooks without setting off any alarms, enter area and finish remaining mooks with silenced weapons. Grab loot or sometimes foozle. Repeat a thousand times.
Guns all feel like they fit into two categories, sniping and not sniping. They're technically different, but they all feel the same. Shooting feels like playing paintball, especially sniping. Every sniping gun has a different range for the center of the scope with no indication of what that range is. You have to take a test shot to get a feel for what range you're set to. Sniper weapons fire very slow comedy projectiles; you can see them slowly travelling through the air. It's just like longballing in paintball, only in slow motion.
Driving physics really is ripped from a Playstation 1 game. It's ridiculous. Off-road driving is frustrating, as vehicles will for example feel like they're being pulled sideways along hills. Not as in gravity, as in poltergeist pulling on you. Your vehicle reacts to rough terrain in exotic, barely predictable and very wrong ways.
The expansions force you to make a new character so you have to level up all over again and introduce nothing new to the game except some new enemies that are identical to all the other mooks except they're bullet sponges.
If you get it on sale for less than $10, go for it. Otherwise, stay clear of this. I admit I enjoyed it, but it's nothing special, just another Assassin's Creed clone.

This game is more than what comes to the eye.
Core Mechanics: You are a pirate. Your job is to aquire crew, bigger ships, money for food and items, and once strong enough to take on the great pirate overlords.
-The world is randomly generated
-Different pirates can be hired and given different abilities
-Managing your crew breaks down to thier moral, hunger, and payment for service.
-Build bigger ships with ship parts or simply plunder ones you take from enemies.
-Upradealbe characters that can be given skills, gear, and form bonds with the player.
-Fight the war on hunger, saddness, betrayal, the plague, and the savages and locals of the sea.
Visuals/audio: The game takes your random characters and has them wobble about as they move around. Its simple, but pretty unique and adorable. The pixel graphics are well done, even if they try to use as few as possible for "effect". The animations are simple aswell, yet attacks have great nockback, sound effects from pistols and swords are oddly satisfying, and the little voices the pirates yell constantly gives them an aditional form of character.
In the end, the game is a roguelike pirate managing adventure that becomes highly addictive and even if you fail you not only get a chance to try again in that instance, but next adventure you are smarter, more aware of how these seas work.
The game was co-created by Re-Logic, the creators of Terraria. So I had fairly standard expectations. I was not dissapointed. This game is something fun to love and passes for a more simple, but satisfying rouge like pirate adventure.
Happy Sailing mates.

The game frequently generates maps that are a nightmare to play on at best and are unwinnable at worst. Some of the wall mapping allows zombies to walk right into your base. After a few multi-hour sessions, the lack of a save feature makes me want to never come back. 3+ hours is too high a time investment for a restart simulator. If I had read the reviews and saw that all progress is persistant I never would have purchased this. Hatoful Boyfriend. Guess what? You date birds. It might sound like any visual novel on the market, but it's quite different.
You may be turned off. But don't be. It's one the best $10 (Or $15) dollars you'll ever spend.
Gameplay (9/10):
+Straightfoward Visual Novel gameplay.
+Mutiple Endings. (Including more then 1 for several characters)
+Ability to skip ahead.
+Has a basic stat system.
+Good for a quick game, an average playthrough lasts around 5-20 minutes.
+-Mutiple playthroughs to unlock some new (but small) features.
-Gets boring at times, especially after most endings have been found.
-There is no bird sex.
Graphics (8/10):
+Nothing to complain about.
+Human portraits look nice.
-Limited backgrounds for certain routes.
Sound (7/10):
+It's okay.
+Great music, especially for certain characters.
-Gets a little tedious.
Story (10/10):
+Deeper then expected.
+Emotional. You will /never/ find a game ever that makes you cry over certain endings.
+Interesting endings and lore.
+Branching story. Techincally.
+-Mutiple playthroughs to understand the full story.
-Timeline is a bit confusing.
Overall, I really like Hatoful Boyfriend. I've never been a visual novel person, but it's truly done something that toys with the emotions and does some beautiful storytelling. I'd recommend picking up the collector's edition if you truly like it. 9/10

Heyyo,
What can I say? ID Software made Wolfenstein 3D... and then they made Doom... and then Quake. Quake expanded upon the sucess of Doom and had a fantastic and intense campaign mode and multiplayer was pretty damn good. The Steam version offers up many different ways to enjoy Quake which is awesome with options like GL Quake, Quakeworld and GL Quakeworld. Sadly, no native support for widescreen so that's a pain to setup... but once you do? FRAGGIN' TIME! ;)

Quake is the legendary old-school first person shooter from ID Software that was a step up from Doom as a true 3D game. The controls are simple, move, strafe, shoot, jump and change weapons. It is fast paced and you can strafe avoid most everything, so if you get hit, its your own fault. Because this is such a fast paced game, gone is the use button, instead you'll walk up to a button or a door and automatically interact with it.
As a shooter, Quake features a lot of guns such as double barreled shotguns, various versions of nail guns (machine guns), grenade and rocket launchers. The weapons feel nice and have great impact, everything from making an enemy fall backward to gib explosions everywhere! There are no throwable grenades or alt fire, but the weapons feel so good to use you won't need them.
You'll need the diverse array of weapons to take on an army of enemies in every level. Everything from standard soldiers and attack dogs to grenade launching chainsaw wielders and electric shocking giant yetis. There is a diverse array of enemies, that always keeps ramping up the challenge and tactics you'll need to kill them. The enemies will fight against one another, which is fun to see, but there aren't factions that you'll see intentionally compete against each other, but Quake still boils down to you vs everything else.
The levels are expertly designed, but can be overly brown, but I guess a game named Quake makes me think inner earth and inner earth makes me think brown. Each level will have you going up, down, forward, opening doors, finding keys, falling in traps, jumping over lava, finding secrets, swimming through ugly water, dodging enemies and murdering much more. It is not straight forward, but you won't get lost, because it is well designed. There are four episodes with 8 or so levels each. Not just that, but because this game is so old and was so wildly popular, it has a million mods and levels.
For new players, there is no regenerating health, but health and ammo are abundant, this is an action game. Kill an enemy, get rewarded with ammo. There is also armor that will let you take more damage.
The music was performed or designed by Trent Reznor of Nine Inch Nails and feels like a touch of ambiance amongst scratch guitars. The nail gun ammo also has NIN logos.
The Steam version of Quake offers QuakeWorld compatibility, but the big problem with that is QuakeWorld uses GameSpy servers, which were shut down. There are no achievements, but it is still a classic game that holds up today as one of the greatest old-school first person shooters.
In all this is a fantastic game that uses a game engine that spawned dozens of other engines.

This is a simple but fun tower defense game. Gameplay is similar to the previous game in the series, iBomber Defense, but several improvements have been made.
The biggest criticism with the previous game is that gameplay became stale after 40 or so waves in a single level, and some levels were too similar to others. But in iBomber Defense Pacific there are usually only 20 or so waves per level, and each level is quite different making for better variety in gameplay.
Also, there are now secondary objectives, like having to defend an oil refinery, or having to destroy enemy bunkers. Completing secondary objectives is optional but doing so earns you points to buy upgrades.
To keep things fresh now you sometimes have to deal with enemy units that aren't rushing your base! Yes, sometimes enemy units will come out onto the battlefield and start shooting it out with your turrets. This becomes especially tricky if you're trying to defend a secondary objective: Should you put your limited resources into defending your base or defending the secondary objective?
Another improvement is that now you can drop bombs on the battlefield. Bombs are a limited use item that are gradually replenished over time. Since you'll only get a few you need to make sure each one counts. Should you use them to thin out the ranks of the baddies rushing your base? Use them to blow open supply crates to get extra resources? Use them to kill that enemy battleship that's parked outside the range of your turrets? Use them to destroy a target to complete a secondary objective? Use them to destroy the secret enemy base hidden in most levels to get bonus upgrade points? Or just start randomly dropping them on buildings to revel in sheer destruction? There are a ton of tactical choices to make!
If you like tower defense games you owe it to yourself to check out iBomber Defense Pacific!

The short version: Like
but with puzzles.
The long version: While it shares a few comparisons with
in terms of plot and setting--male protagonist wandering alone on a dreary-but-hauntingly-beautiful island--I'd have to say that
is by far the more disturbing of the two. You are likely to figure out what's going on halfway through, but uncovering the manner in which those things occurred still manages to keep the final reveal from feeling anticlimactic.
The inclusion of puzzles obviously sets it apart from DE, and while some of them stumped me for a little while (the Compass Puzzle comes to mind), they didn't inspire an urge to rage quit. I have to admit, I was a little put off by how slow the character was, especially when certain puzzles required retracing my steps. Still, the game establishes the need for limited movement from the very beginning; as a storyteller myself, I do appreciate that foundation even if the gamer in me occasionally kept pressing left shift in hopes the narrator would move that walking stick just a little bit faster!
By far, the best part of this entire game is the voice acting. As an American, I'm in no position to comment on the quality of the accent, but he definitely managed to put genuine emotion where it was needed. I
for him when he began to despair. I felt his frustrations with his marriage. The reading of the last letter also helped the ending from falling too flat. The music in this game was also very lovely and added to the mood of the game.
(That said, I wasn't entirely keen on the occasional popping up of quotes, even if they were relevant to one of the game's main themes. It kind of interrupted the immersive atmosphere that otherwise existed.)
Speaking of the ending... I was expecting to continue on to the eponymous Mount after that last narration, only to wind up at the title screen! Right now it feels too open-ended. Part of me does think it fits, considering what we learn of the character over the course of the game. Since I've only just finished it, I think I need more time to really turn it over to definitely decide whether or not I liked the ending.
It's worth playing through for the plot and voice acting. The music is appropriate and helps set the mood, the puzzles are an appropriate level of challenging, and if you liked
--or just point-and-click adventures in general--you'll probably like this as well.

I was drawn to this paranormal/mystery game because it was something different, in that it took place on an unknown irish island and the text featured in-game for signs, item descriptions, and location is Gaelic (with translation). Many sites mock/belittle the atmosphere, the voice acting, the puzzles, and just plainly the game itself. In all honesty, it is a bit much for such a short game and like myself would wait untill it goes on sale.
The game itself is short, linear and the music is limited yet pleasing to the ears. The scenery/atmosphere is a bit dark and add film grain to the visuals which can be removed in the options. I like this as it is the dead of night on a moonless island and I feel the film grains adds a re-telling or recollection of a tragic past through the eyes of someone alive, desceased, maybe somewhere in between...
The puzzles I think are the main downfall. They are easy despite being odd, convoluted, and elaborate considering the storyline and the current situation. Though, some puzzles fit in nicely but all are blended in to that one really has to look carefully, and I do admit it is kind of hard given the dark scenery and film grain (*film grain can be removed in options). But really, it's you're looking for something in real life it doesn't magically give off an glowing aura or flash for you to say "Here I am!." (*...Although it would be great....*) but the game does highlight SOME things for you.
All-in-All, the game was a good lilttle experience and educational as well for those interested in Gaelic and want a game that takes you somewhere else.
NOTE: This is my opinions and thoughts of the game and not an overall view if the game for general audience. As with many reviews and opinions, take this with a grain of salt and do your own research.

Starbreak is a fantastic game, but it is lacking in many areas.
I'll start with a run-down of the good:
-Fantastic Music and sound design that draws the player into the atmosphere
-A breath of fresh air to the mmo genre and it changes the typical formula in many ways
-An amazing art style that complements the game
Now, for the negative.
All of the negative problems stem from one thing: Microtransactions. The perma-death option is fantastic, but because you lose everything on death, that means you'll need to grab your spares from your stash or go back through the game to get new equipment. However, there is a lack of storage space, which can only be purchased through currency that must be purchased with real money. Similarly, since there are different characters(or "Shells") in the game, you're going to need a LOT of storage to keep items for your previous character, and for your new one. Even if you start using a new shell, I would suggest keeping all the items from your previous one in storage in case you don't like your new shell. All these problems could be fixed with one of two things; either use the in-game currency as a way to purchase storage, or make goals to achieve in order to GAIN the purchasable currency. Also, there's barely any explanation on how to do anything or what everything is or is used for. The tutorial is great for introducing the mechanics, but not for anything else.
StarBreak is an incredible experience, even if it is flawed, but I'm not sure I would pin this ENTIRELY as "pay-to-win." More like, this is half pay to win, half traditional, and depending on which side you're on, you may or may not enjoy this game.
I like the idea of this game, and I look forward to seeing how this will be refined.

2- Enter the first stage (the easiest one)
3- Collect powerups and enter other stages
4- You die

The main problem with this game, in my opinion, is that it depends on how many people are playing at the same time, the only stage you can finish by yourself is the first one, the enemies are weak and the boss is simple. So, in summary, unless there are a lot of people playing at the same time, you will die inevitably and will have to repeat the same stages and the same bosses over and over again until you get bored like me.
I know it is a free game, there are a couple of things you can pay for, but getting stuck always at the same level and the same stages because not many people play the game, or decide to leave the stage once you enter the boss, ruined the whole fun I was getting before.
I hope the developer makes something to avoid players leaving once you enter a boss...
I will be waiting for the game to get more players, maybe then I will enjoy it again.

iBomber Defense Pacific is a perfectly average TD game. It has all the basic TD elements you'd expect and no more. It's ported from mobile devices, so it's not as pretty as say, Defense Grid, but that doesn't matter much. The UI is simple, since it was designed to be touch controls, but it works perfectly fine on PC.
It's not great, it doesn't do anything new, it's not pretty and you won't remember anything about it in a year's time. That said, it satisfies one's TD needs. If you're jonesing for some TD and don't have any other TD games to play (yeah, right), this is an adequate way to scratch that itch.
Note: Just because this is a mobile game, doens't mean it's easy. I got my balls stomped many times because I was only half-paying attention. 5+ restarts per level should be expected (or maybe I'm just terrible at TD).

If you like tower defense games, this one is a great investment at $5. It's simple enough to jump in and enjoy immediately, yet complex enough to offer good strategy and tactics. This is my favorite of the iBomber series.

Unlike How to Survive, there isn't a storyline or an open world : it's a limited area of modest size full of zombies, wild animals and resources, where you can build and enhance your camp. Then you'll run accross several NPC who'll give you various kind of quests in instances : find resources and items, rescue people, kill infected, investigate, etc. As in any self-respecting RPG, you'll get experience to improve your character, the camp and your skills, melee and ranged weapons and the possibility to craft food, potions or gear. You'll have to be cautious though, pay attention to your health, hunger, thirst and ammunition. First off, I would like to say that after first playing through the open beta for this game with a friend, I confidently said that this game was a definite pass, and I refused to touch it after it launched. However, the game looked like something I would enjoy once it was a bit more optimized and there was more content added to it, but only with friends. So I waited. Back during the fall steam sale, I considered buying it, but I couldn't convince a friend to drop on it with me. So I waited until the winter sale, when I managed to convince a friend to try it with me. If we didn't like it, we would refund it after a couple hours of giving it the ol' "college try."
I have to say, this game has pleasantly surpised me with how much fun and entertainment I've gotten out of it so far. I thought that it would be a game I would exclusively play with my friend, but I'm having so much fun that I've had to create my own solo character for when we're not both on. That being said, I can see how this game might get boring after a while. While the objectives that you're completing are happening in a different zone, you're basically doing the same thing. I would reccomend playing on the highest difficulty if you want to have a challenge that gives your actions a little more consequence. I haven't gotten bored yet at all, however, and I think thats due to the way you're able to approach each situation differently and see what works and what doesn't until you're finally able to finish your objective. The entire world is absolutely massive, and very beautiful to explore and simply stop for a moment to admire. My friend and I found ourselves fighting up a mountain on foot to get to the mosseleum on top to avoid the four anti-air batteries that guard from all sides. Once we had cleared the area and interrogated our target, we climbed to the top of the mosseleum and took a minute to stop and look across the valleys to our east and snow-capped mountains to the south. It's experiences like this that make me enjoy this game so much.
Overall, I would give this game an 8/10 for a super fun co-op tactical shooter. This game is most definitely meant to be played with friends, although the AI squadmates can make due in a pinch. As for the DLC and Ghost War modes, I have yet to experience them, so I have no opinion to review them on. I'll probably edit this review once I get the chance.

Steam's new policy of segregating reviews into reviews done with a key and reviews done via store purchases has somewhat led me to regret a lot of my purchases/game acquisitions. For games that I genuinely enjoyed that I had previously gotten from a bundle, I unfortunately cannot affect the score percentage, and Concursion is one of them. But we'll leave this topic for another day.
Concursion is the debut title from developers Puuba. The game endured a slightly rough failed Kickstarter campaign, but had a successful Greenlight before being picked up by the now-defunct Mastertronic.
At its core, the game is a mashup of multiple genres in one. A platformer game, a ninja hack-and-slash, a shooter game, a floaty-jetpack game and a pacman-like game, each with their own different gameplay mechanics. This is the standout feature of this game, where you seamlessly blend from one genre of game directly into another, and sometimes multiple times within the span of a few seconds in a level!
Games like this aren't complete without the stereotypical bad guys and princess you have to rescue, and this one also likewise features one - only, in this case, with Puuba's witty and irreverent brand of humour, as well as a plot twist at, or rather, near the end. Nope, not spoiling here. ;)
In general, the controls felt quite good, though at times maybe a bit awkward. The same keys are used in all the modes - the platformer mode has a run key and a jump key, in the hack-and-slash mode one of the keys is used for slashing instead, in the shooting mode it's used for shooting bullets, etc. No need to memorise a different set of keys for each mode. The only problem I have is that in the shooting mode, you can actually fire faster if you button mash the key - you get a higher rate of fire than if you hold it down. There may rarely be cases where the default rate of fire isn't enough and it can be taxing on your hand.
The world shifts are handled by the game engine incredibly well. Incidentally, the game engine is custom-built in Java - a completely different engine from what most people would expect. Not Unity, not Clickteam Fusion, not GameMaker. It's quite an impressive standout. Even the music shifts are handled well as, when you switch worlds, the music seamlessly cross-fades into the music of a different mix. This would be the first collaboration with Christopher Hoag of House fame, who tirelessly composed various mixes of all the songs in the game for each world, and the soundtrack here is striking in terms of compositional depth and variety.
The only sore point I have with this is the visual presentation - unfortunately it is a rather large sore point. The characters and images themselves on their own are decent, but when you look at the animations and menus it does give the impression of a lack of visual polish. Even the Steam header sadly looks a tiny bit unpolished, no thanks to the somewhat large wording of Concursion with a somewhat typical font. The jetpack mode was the worst visually as this was mostly all pixellated - while this was intended to make it look more retro in accordance with the game's retro-style leanings, I don't think it works visually.
But this does bring me to my most important point. Don't ever judge this game by its cover - play through it and you can actually see their gameplay design wiles and charm peek out from underneath. Their later games would also feature an interesting mechanic combination coupled with their particular brand of humour. Visualise this as a snapshot of the devs' design headspace at that particular point in time, play it in conjunction with their later works. For me, I find it really heartening to see how much they've progressed since then - and at the end of it all, I still really enjoyed this game. <3
Try out the demo first - while challenging, it does give you a good grasp and idea of what happens in the game. The price was knocked down to $5 a few months back from $10 - but, for the amount of time I've sunk into this game, it's actually a steal, if you enjoy the genre mashup.

They Are Billions is finally a game that blends various elements that I have come to adore over the years into an almost perfect blend. At surface level the game plays like an regular RTS game but with a focus on building your colony and defending it, making it almost a turret defense game but with the mobility of a fast paced RTS game, that said the game is pausible at any time which is greatly appreciated in order to optimize your settlement.
You start out by developing your economy, trying to erect your first defences and train troops in order to explore the map and face endless hordes of infected. You map down the surroudings and try to expand in order to gain ressources but you still have to manage the massive hordes of enemies, furthermore giant roaming hordes will attack your settlement. These roaming hordes can be absolutely massive and the game can be extremely intense in that regard.
The gameplay feels incredibly smooth, controlling units and placing buildings just feels fine. Visually speaking, the game boasts a really neat art style set in a cyberpunkish world. The sprites all look really detailed and move fluently. The audio of the game is perhaps a bit lacking, the ambiance is right but overall there is not much to work with or anything that stands out.
Despite being an EA title, it feels absolutely polished and playable. The survival mode along provides a lot of enjoyment, albeit some elements still need some balancing and the procedural generation of the maps can really make it quite tough at times. Also the game is rather unforgiving and hard, minor mistakes are sometimes severely punished and you will lose all your progress, but every failure has been quite a joy. There is something beautiful in seeing your entire town fall to chaos.
I definitely recommend this title, mostly because it blends RTS elements with some nice tower defense mechanics and neat base building. I think the game that is most reminiscent to this might be "Harvest Massive Encounter" but as it stands this game is quite unique.

This game isn't bad but it's not good either. The idea of mixing third person combat and RTS is interesting but it's execution is flawed.
Remeniscent of Mass Effect when it comes to exploring the main headquaters and interacting with some of the main characters. The narrative is very linear and full of cliches.
A similar sentiment I can share with are the characters. None of them stand out as relatable or even worth detailing. The fedoras had more character than the actual characters.
The gameplay at best is abysmal, the fusion of TPS and RTS do not mix at all. The games design isn't justifiable enough to have the word XCOM in it's name.
Also the games AI isn't.
Example: I ordered my engineer to approach some cover just outside an enemy position (the enemy took cover in a book store hiding behind shelves and the main counter). So in close quaters he would have a clear shot with his shotgun. That was what should have happened.
Instead he took cover in the store, in the middle of the enemy position, he was surrounded on all sides and within seconds he was killed.
It was tragic but hillarious. I could've saved him due to the bleed out mecahnic but I decided not to for the greater good.
A more appropriate title/name for this game would be The Bureau: Darwin Awards Declassified.
I only recommend this game because of the shenanigans the AI is capable of enacting.
But I would certainly recommend that you move straight onto Enemy Unknown.

I got this for $5. Its worth $5, but its not worth much more than that. I really liked this game though. Gameplay was fun. My game lagged quite often in big fights, even though my computer is easily over the recommended settings.

The Bureau has some really cool ideas and some real cinematic flare and drama that is lacking in the superior XCOM 2012 game. There is an aspect of terror that was an integral part of the original games that, I feel, is only recognized by XCOM 2012 in the design of their version of the Chrysalid. The Bereau holds a stronger light to the citizen level drama of an alien invasion by showing masses fleeing, homes being destroyed, humans taken and changed, people disappearing in instances of blinding light and destruction. It's a much more visceral representation of an alien invasion, like a Spielberg's War of the Worlds given an R rating. Similarly to that movie, however, this game runs out of steam long before the ending. The plot takes an uninteresting and ridiculous direction and the combat becomes stale at about the same time. The combat is much like Mass Effect 2 but more fleshed out and functionally more intuitive than ME2 thanks to better controls and higher-level customization of your party members allowing you to really understand combat mechanics on a  deeper level. Would recommend the game if you like aliens and alien-horror, but its not that great. Real B-Tier stuff.

This is essentially a browser game, and I was extremely surprised with how fun this was. This is extremely fun, challenging, rewarding, and punishing. Permadeath adds so much to the game. You gain a sense of accomplishment when you gear up a bit, find some implants, some exotic gear, reach mk ii, mk iii, etc. and then die due to an unfortunate chain of events. The game has a bit of a learning curve. It will take a lot of time and a lot of deaths to get proficient at any of the characters. Anyone looking for a challenge, I highly suggest playing this game and trying out the first 2-3 tiers of dungeons.
With that said, I also want to mention a huge downside to the game, the higher difficulty areas (very high/extreme). When you die, you lose all of your stat boosts and your gear. The game gives you a storage container to store a second/backup set of gear, but your stats reset back to zero. Getting your stats back up can be a time consuming process, and is basically required if you want to go back into the tier 3/4+ dungeons. This is fine for the first 2-3 tiers of dungeons, but later on a single death just sets you back too much (and dying isn't that hard in the game, especially if there are 20-30+ characters on the same screen).
Overally, definitely reccomend trying out the game for those looking for a challenge. Just be prepared to be a bit disappointed with the later portion of the game.

This game is a very addicting multiplayer game! Here's the gist of StarBreak. You level up, and that is permanently kept. This unlocks new classes to play. You play what they call "shells", which is just a fancy word for a new character when you die. When you die, you lose what you were equipped on, your picked up stats, and what you carried. There are banks to store your stuff though. You collect stats and gear that drops. There are many levels that you can play and unlock as well.

Other Steam users say that this is just a resolution problem with my computer, but it's not. It's how the game was programmed. If you can get past that, then this highly replayable game might be for you.
Oh, and registering your account is one simple line: your screen name. No email or other stuff like that!

So, let me start off on the right foot. I love this game more than most, Eko Software has made it's way to me as one of my favourite devs through the How to Survive series. See as a gamer, I never much enjoyed a specific genre. My favourite though were RPG, survival, guns! and horror. This franchise and especially this game knows how to give a dose of all 4.
As an RPG : The leveling and upgrading system is classic and reminds me a lot of old school perk based leveling, while still bringing in a unique aspect with the perk upgrade progression. Now, not only that serves as a bookmark for upgrades but also allows you to retreat from an upgrade before spending 1 milion exp in it. Another very good element on the RPG lines, the character creation. Yes the game could use more hairstyles and facial hair, but I guess we will get to see that too, all other things considered, I love the character creation and I would love to see it evolve, since it already has a good base.
As far as the shooting and combat : Very good, the melee can be a little be off on some very CQC situations. But in general, combat feels powerful and deadly, no matter if I use a H&K rifle or a candy cane. The target lock is nice, but not broken and requires strategy to pick the correct target, if you don't want to get hit. The game also promotes playing in a more sneaky approach, since making noise will attract 2-3 hordes on you, but going guns blazing is also nice, since those 2-3 hordes won't last long against a machinegun.
The horror? : It does not really scare you as a game, unless you have Kinemortophobia. But everytime I encounter a new enemy, sound is usually faster than sight. That blood curdling growl is usually what makes you think : "What awaits me next?", then you get run down by a zombie bear while your teammates shoot all over the place.
Overral long story short : One of the best apocalypse games out there. It takes matters in its own hand and shows you the true way of how cruel the apocalypse can be if you don't risk your life to survive and even then, the stakes are high. I would not say it is completely realistic, but unless you are willing to work for your survival you are doomed. In a gaming era were infected are treated as jokes, it's good to see people like the devs in Eko software giving a harsher and yet fun and infinite take on the apocalypse. I love this game as of today and I don't think that is going to change, if you want this game, don't think about it much, I can tell you, it's a survival you will not regret.

How to Survive 2 was a humble surprise. The game has a go-getter spirit, with a small town price. All, in all a satisfying purchase. It vaguely reminds me of Diablo II diced up with zombies and less right clicking. And a lot less gear.
Graphically it is sufficient, and perfect for an isometric viewpoint. I recall seeing an up-close, and personal standalone being marketed, but it just didn’t look good up-close, and personal. The game works the way it was intended to. The graphic style is pseudo-realistic, with exaggerated flares.
Gameplay: Satisfying carnage with a mild shade of freedom on play style choices. Combat proposes challenges at times, with mild tactic changes versus different types of opponents. Unfortunately, I’ve been grinding mostly solo, so I can’t say much for the cooperative aspect. I look forward to testing the game with my brother locally in the future. And that option alone is a strong plus.
As for gear, and grind. The game falls a bit short, camp-building is enjoyable, but as of now the grind to procure resources can be a bit tedious.  As for the gear selection, I’ve found that there are times you create a new item, but it still looks like the same in-game model from the last tier of items. A minor disappointment.  At this point, it really doesn’t seem like the game has that much gear.
Bottom line, the game was worth the purchase.

For a game nearly as old as myself, Quake has held up VERY well. Each level is a medieval maze filled with monsters and creatures straight out of your worst nightmares who all want to kill you. Starting with just a shotgun, you collect your weapons as you progress until you have an arsenal good enough to take on anything you could encounter.
As older games do, Quake doesn't go easy on you. Even on the easy levels, I often found myself in dire need of either health, armor, or ammo. Learning what weapons work best, what traps to avoid, and where to look for secret health packs is vital to your survival in this nightmarish world.
For me, the best part of this game is the movement. Fast movement and the ability to bunnyhop around enemies you just can't fight at the moment really seals the deal on this excellent game.
And let's not forget that a mod of this series led to Team Fortress 2, everyone's favorite game at some point. Also rocket jumping. GOD I love rocket jumping.
Also install the Ultimate Quake Patch. It adds the original soundtrack and a load of other fixes to make this game even more wonderful.

Ibomber Defense Pacific is a Typical TD game and a sequal from the Ibomber franchise (which i have had the pleasure of not playing). I cant realy tell whats so amazing and diffrent from other TD games but it is a Solid TD Game.
The Mechanic in the game is no more than place diffrent tower with diffrent specific skills to prevent enemys from reaching your Base! The towers you get to Place is the Turret a fast shooting but low dmg output, The Cannon with long range and heavy damage but slow, We got the bomb tower which slowly generate bombs that you can drop anywhere on the map, The Flamethrower who burns and slows enemys. The Comm's towers who increases the range of other towers and provides extra income.
the Missile tower who shoots medium hige damage in an area (works best in straight lines). and the last tower the Anti Air tower.
During the Missions or maps you can complete secondary objectives often killing crates or buildings on the map or defend specific objects! After the mission is complete you are awarded with points which you use to uppgrade your tower. you get more points if you complete the secondary objective and/or if you dont leak and all your towers survived.
There is also a Level progression in the game where you earn some xp after each mission, the only important thing about this is that you can unlock some perks to your own benefit. The game alows you to use up to 3 perks, the perks can increase your starting money of each level or boost the defense of your tower etc. it does help sometimes and it gives you a reason to continue play to advance in rank and increase score.
The Whole Game is good for an TD and the difficult level is well balanced through the game, but i dont think it is an amazing game.. the game whould be good on a mobile phone to kill time when your not close to your PC.

I actually don't enjoy racing games all that much, but I do remember loving Burnout and Need For Speed Most Wanted. Those games were pretty good back in my Xbox days.
Test Drive Unlimited 2 is however different from these, as well as different from another racing game I loved which I can't remember the name of.
What I've enjoyed the most in this game, is actually the poker... Yup, I have to admit where I spent 75%+ of my time in the game was in a DLC casino. However, the driving in this game is good. I really do enjoy just cruising around for minutes to hours at a time and look at the landscape. Plus sometimes I♥♥♥♥♥♥off the cops and go for a challenging getaway run!
Now, if I was to say anything negative there would pretty much only be 2 things to say.
1. The driving tests are way too hard for getting a license. I have consistently been in the top 40% of every multiplayer challenge I participated in, so my skills have to be better than average, yet I've only ever passed 1 single test out of 10. I think there were 10 anyway. I just don't get why these are so hard. Why? I don't see a point in not letting people drive just a little bit below max speed of they prefer it. For a driving game/driving simulator this just feels a bit backwards. 3 of the challenges I've simply been unable to beat, just because their timer requires me to be 2 seconds faster than my best. Yes, I've seriously had roughly the same time 5 times in a row on a challenge, and been just 2 seconds from making it. I really see no reason for these tests being so furiously strict. They are the reason why I just said screw it and spent so much time in the casino, because I tried to forget they even existed.
2. Are the tires coated in soap? No really, a lot of the cars just slip for apparently no reason. Yes swinging left to right a few times can/will cause a car to lose control a bit, but this bad? I really don't think so. I'm just glad that my 2 favorite cars have somehow removed this problem, but I still don't get why the majority (all) of the cars I've driven had this problem before I got to these cars. For this my favorite cars are the casino car which I won from a slot machine, and the 1018 horsepower black race car Koenigsegg CCXR Edition. Both handle great, look great and just feel really nice to drive.
So overall I really do like the game. It's sad that it won't get patched or improved because of its age, but I'll still leave in my top suggestion for a feature that could be added to fix my 2nd issue with this game.
ADD A CLUTCH! Seriously, if you slip in real life, you just hold in the clutch to put the car in free and it will have a lot easier of a time gripping the road again. I don't understand why this can't just be a thing in the game when it so obviously needs it.
Either way, I really enjoyed the game and definitely recomend it to anyone curious about it. I give it a 7/10 for its very good gameplay and very very very few issues/bugs in comparison to other games.
EDIT WARNING:
I forgot to mention that you need to keep in mind this is an abandoned game. Atari does no longer provide services against cheaters or hackers, as well as having stopped maintaining the game. I've seen a few players in the casino, barely enough for a table that took 30+ minutes to assemble, and only 2 people out in the open world. There used to be a lot of players and I have no idea where they went. Judging from other reviews I guess it has to do with the servers being shut down in the past. I have no idea if they are up now, or if something weird is connecting random players together, without connecting everyone to one mega server. Buy it at your own risk or save your money for a different game.

Unlike Europa Universalis or other Paradox titles this game is easier to pick up. Not physically of course. (Do I really need to explain everything? Gosh ... )
Anyway; I had played Europa Universalis IV before I first played this game. I wasn't completely new to Paradox. If you're completely new it might take you a few hours to get into to, since there is almost always a learning curve with Paradox Games. Once you're into it, you'll really enjoy this. That is, if you like World War II (considering you can actually say that you "enjoy" World War II. I'm digressing.)
Play as Hitler and take over the world! Yay! Or play as the country you're from and conquer the world (I managed to do it as the Netherlands).
The only downside, however, in my opinion, after about 100 hours there is no real challenge left. You could play as Luxembourgh as a final challenge, but I don't need to explain to you that that would be extremely stupid and not fun at all.
About the GAMEPLAY then. What do you actually DO in this game?
PREPARING FOR WAR:
- Research new weapons.
- Build factories that produce those weapons.
- Train troops.
- Draw battleplans on the map.
FIGHTING A WAR:
The game has something called "World Tension", which is expressed as a percentage. The number increases if someone declares war or in some other cases. If the number is above a certain percentage, democratic nations can guarantee an other nation's indepence, which basically means that after a couple of years you will automatically be at war with the UK, Canada, South Africa and the USA. If you play as Germany, you therefore can only blitzkrieg one nation (for example the Netherlands or Belgium), before you have to prepare for a World War.
During a war you:
- Wait.
- Wait.
- Change battleplans.
- Hope your factories can create enough equipment to supply your troops.
In conclusion. Buy this game if you like games where you can conquer the world and if you slightly enjoy World War II games.

Okay, so this is a Grand Strategy War Game, and if you aren't familiar with that, essiential this game is about taking control of one faction. There is not linear story path, and there are virtually no bounds, especially through Mods. If you are familiar with the Total War Franchise or any other Real Time Stratedy Games, it's fairly easy to transition into this game. This is my first HOI game, and I really enjoy it!
The AI:
It has its limitations, and will both benefit you and destroy you. When I mean destroy, I mean you let the AI hold a front while you are covering a different theatre, and when you go to check on said front, the AI has lost the front and was pushed back. That could be my incompetence, but I'm sure I would have been able to handle said front myself. None the less, the AI is not the best, but what can you expect. It's hard to make good decisions as a robot sometimes, especially in a game that is very far from binary like this.
The Game Play:
The tutorial really sucks, and I had to go on youtube and watch a 2 hour video to give me the basics. Then I went back to the tutorial and properly did it. Although I think the Tutorial is set up perfectly for Italy as you start off in a war, and allows you to join the Axis so you can learn diplomacy. Overall for the gameplay, once you learned the mechanics and the ins and outs, you get fairly well adjusted and get addicted. You want to conquer the world, and do as much as possible. What is nice is that you have a fairly even playing field with the AI when you play as a minor country. But if you play as a major country, most likely, that specific game will last you around 5 hours due to the poor AI, no matter the difficulty. The Diplomacy part of the game can be a little shotty as you find yourself in a situation where you want something but it wont and cannot happen. Like if you influence a country to become communist like Mexico, it's not guaranteed to join the Comitern because Mexico could be like "Nah, the allies are chill".
Overall Personal Opinion:
It's easy to get sucked into the game and I absolutely love it. I like to sometimes play spectator mode without historical AI and watch the world burn. I get very devoted to my country and I really enjoy the game. It has a steep learning curve in the beginning, but it's well worth it in the end when you really understand the game mechanics. The first week when I bought the game, I have 50 hours already, that 2 out of the 7 days I spent on the game. I really do enjoy it, but if you want something with more of a story, or a linear plot, this is not the game for you. This game is really worth it during any sale, because at $40.00 it can be a bit overpriced in my opinion. But I don't regret the $40.00 I spent.
P.S. Don't waste your time on the DLC when you can get free mods that are easily 2X better than the DLC itself.

UPDATED: This review started out as "Not Recommended" because it was unplayable for me for quite awhile due to technical problems; I couldn't play the game for more than a few minutes before it crashed Then I figured out how to get my dual Radeon HD 6950s to work with it; I believe there was a patch also that probably fixed things for me. So after playing the game for awhile, I changed my review to 'Recommend". It was my sort of game. I tend to gravitate toward these type of creepy walking simulator games and sometimes they end up being disappointing or utter trash (like "All Is Dust"). Well, this game was drawing me in, but now that I have finished it, I have to say that the ending was disappointing. I am sick of all these games these days with ambiguous endings.
Here's what I liked about the game:
The atmosphere and the setup and the voice acting, music, and sound effects do a good job of setting the tone.
Here's what I didn't like. The puzzles were either spelled out for you, or so incredibly obtuse. Sometimes the game would give you a big clue for the puzzle, but then when you try to do that, it's not what is necessary to solve the puzzle; the solution is much easier than what the clue tells you. ( I am thinking about the plinith puzzle).
The save system is annoying with checkpoints that don't always remember what things you partially accomplished. Sometimes the items you need are in really dark areas amidst lots of debris and trash (Yes, I did turn on the option to make those items glow red when you mouse over them).
The ending wasn't worth it to me all of the slow-walking around I did with the backtracking and the weird puzzles and odd "rules" like I can only carry 5 items at a time. Even when I got the game to run with my video cards, I still had technical problems that made playing annoying. My mouse cursor kept "going out of the game" to my Windows desktop on my other monitor and that was constantly breaking immersion.
When I had switched my review from "Not Recommend" to "Recommend" I said I was gald that I gave the game a second chance and that I hoped the story's ending wouldn't disappoint. Well, it did disappoint, so here I am back at "Not Recommend". I really wanted to like this game a lot more, but it was a grind to get through it, even though it's such a relatively short game. Buyer beware.

I wasn’t very impressed with this game.
This game wasn't what it is advertised to be. That is for certain. In truth, it reminded me of Dear Esther more than anything. Its atmosphere was good but that was about it. Like Dear Esther, it felt more like a “here take a walk around our pretty island” than a decent game.
My thoughts on the story are as follows:
It claims to be a psychological thriller, but I was never on edge at any point during the game. And the “scary” parts were not at all. The story in general didn’t really lead me down a path to the ending’s conclusion. At no point did I think this man was completely nuts. Only two notes really pointed towards this fact and not much else. I guess what I’m trying to say is that this character’s “decline” was not explored very well or given enough time for it to sink in. We as the player didn’t really have the time or information to start making theories of our own as to what happened on the island and to the protagonist or what he had done. And on top of this, there was an illness on the island, so what? It didn’t seem to play into the story at all, other than making the protagonist the only one on the island. The story is left open ended and felt incomplete to me, especially since there was little build up for the conclusion.
In all truthfulness I found the game to be rather boring on the story side of things.
My thoughts on the technical side are as follows:
After reading some of the other reviews, I noticed that several players had issues with frame rate. I’m pleased to say I had no issues at all, but I’ve got a good amount of RAM and a very good and up to date graphics card meant for gaming and working with 3D software.
I found some of the subtle emersion qualities of this game quite fun, like rain splatters on your screen. However, the game was overall very gray and lacking in color which, while lending itself to the isolated atmosphere, made it difficult to see in darker parts of the game like the inside of sheds and buildings. I didn’t turn my gamma up to help this but I figure that would be the solution.
The puzzles I found to be very easy for the most part, although I did get stuck on a couple, but that was because I didn’t find a clue or the puzzle was not explained very well. Other than that they were all pretty logical, which is an accomplishment in this genre since a lot of similar games lean on taxing and nonsensical puzzles to pad out the amount of time spent playing the game.
There are a few complaints I would like to point out about some of the menus, cut scenes and puzzles. The cut scenes would often linger too long on pictures, or a new area. I actually found myself looking away from the computer while waiting on these scenes to end. I think I actually got onto YouTube on my laptop for a couple minutes while waiting during one. While these scenes may have seemed emotional to the developer, the player only needed to see the images for 30 seconds or less to get the point.
Also, during the compass puzzle, the dial turning animation took FOREVER. I was once again checking my watch while waiting on these dials to turn. A faster animation would be much appreciated. This goes for the checkpoint menu as well. When I loaded up the game after I had put it down for a day, I found myself scrolling, and scrolling and scrolling to get to my last checkpoint (which was the 9th one) and the animation for this also took FOREVER. Speeding up the scrolling here would have been very helpful. Speeding up a lot of the game in general would have been a large improvement. Doing so would not have taken away from the atmosphere. It would have made for a more pleasurable experience.
In the end, I wouldn’t recommend this game to a casual game player, but if you are a hard core point and click, puzzle game player I wouldn’t tell you to not give it a shot. Especially if you got it for $2.00 like I did.

Overall I really enjoyed this game, mostly because the atmosphere was so well done. The "wet lens" and vignette effects used do a fantastic job at making you feel small and under pressure, like the rain is really hounding you rather than just seeing it. Story is a little empty and the animations seem unintentionally slow but as an atmospheric experience I see it as step forward. Even though the ending didn’t have the kick I thought I could have, I’m still keen to know more!
I would recommend this game for those on the lookout for innovation no matter how small.
