So... What happens when an overly ambitious publishing house (Take Two Interactive) is jealous of the marketing potential of one of its development houses' franchises... And wants to milk the franchise more thoroughly/ more quickly than that franchises' home development house (Firaxis) is willing to? It hands the franchise over to one of its other development houses (2K Marin) and tells it to make a derivative product that by-and-large is derivative at-best, and delivers no unqiue value... But manages to grab more money more quickly from unsuspecting fanboys of the franchise.
That's what "The Bureau: XCOM Declassified" is, IMO: A money grab. Fortunately, though... The game is good enough in its own right for me to not completely feel as is I've been screwed over twice. (Once by being hoodwinked, and twice by buying a bad game.)
Make no mistake: this isn't XCOM, in the classical sense. Instead, think of it as a complete mod for Mass Effect. That is... Mass Effect with an XCOM skin.
Combat is *not* turn-based. Rather, it is "real-time + bullet-time-style slow-down"  for sake of using special abilities (a la mass effect - complete with selection wheel and everything...). Time is *not* paused when in the selection wheel; rather, time is greatly reduced. Relative to "pure/true XCOM" games, strategy and item management are *greatly* simplified in favor of tactical gunplay. There's no base-building element at all. Weapon and gear are simplified, relative to traditional XCOM games. Flanking/ hidden/ exposed attack bonuses are similar.
(Story-wise... This game is best considered a prequel to the XCOM series (I'm specifically thinking of XCOM: Enemy Unknown - don't have experience with the previous ones).)
Presuming one's expectations are "reset" with the above... I'd recommend purchasing this *at 50% or greater discount only* (not at full price). It *is* sufficiently immersive, has a decent enough of a story line, and a couple of neat twists... Such that it's worth playing through, IMO. Although it has about the right playthrough timelength (when bought at discount), note that it has zero replay value. (IMO)
Simply put... This game looks like (a "period-correct" variant of) XCOM, and resembles XCOM... But it certainly doesn't *feel* like XCOM... And it sure as hell doesn't *play* like XCOM. Despite all of that, however... It's worth a discount buy, as it's not a bad game in its own right.
I do wish they would have left the name "XCOM" out of the title, though. It would have prevented some player disaapointments due to false expectations, IMO.
Really good game for XCOM fans, however maybe little too short otherwise excelent.

I was actually quite disappointed by the beginning few missions of the game, felt overwhelmed by the enemies, and my computer controlled team mates were getting murdered. The enemy difficulty at the start was way more than the units on my squad could handle, and it was essentially a game of shoot and revive.  Was thinking to abandon the game.  However, I stuck with it.
As you and your unit levels, they attain skills, and its those skills controlled by you as the commander make the game remarkable.  As they leveled, the games challenge started to get reasonable, and I had a solid chance.  If you want to play this game, take your beating at the beginning, as it changes, and it gets incredibly fun as you time the different effects to do maximum damage.
Of course the game continues to get harder, with more unique enemies, and very well positioned locations.  And each those battles are challenging and fun.  When your main character isn't grabbing 90% of the kills, you know team dynamics are working.
Thus if you are looking for a challenging tactical squad based combat, and challenging enemies, a little hard pacing at the begnning (it makes up for it throughout the rest of the game, so stick with it), and an interesting Story, get this game. You will enjoy it.  :)

TL:DR This game is easy fun and the best money I have ever spent on a fighting game.
JaeLee is a one person army who is giving Capcom and SNK and Sega a run for their money.
Long version
This game is extremely customizable both graphically, in terms of difficulty level, and in terms of the game play.  All the basic moves are availabe in an in game help screen and very useful.
GRAPHICS :
There is a basic graphics level screen with a low to high pc scale setting and resolution, and a more advanced settings screen for those who want to poke around and customize. There is also one grahical setting "Battle Damage" in the games settings screen which I recommend turning off if your fights lag.
DIFFICULTY
OPPONENTS:
There are five difficulty levels for all game modes  and a customizable handicap for certain non-arcade modes.
LEARNING CURVE FOR MOVES:
You can watch the ai characters  play on any difficulty level to learn moves that aren't in the help screen. There is a completely customizable training mode where you can try out your character's moves against a customizable ai opponent (either stands still, does a certain move or fights). All the moves that aren't documented in game are easily and intuitively learnable in the training mode. There is also a lot of documentation of moves and combos in the steam thread. This has become my favoirte fighting game of all time because the system is so intuitive and well designed.
GAMEPLAY CUSTOMIZATION (REPLAY VALUE)
The difficulty level ramps up as your skill improves which, combined with the different play modes ensures many hours of fun replay even after new content stops being added (as of this post new content, happily, appears to still be in the works).
COMMUNITY & DEV SUPPORT
Apart from the  stream of new and relevant content, the user community is friendly and the developer is diligent in answering new questions and patient with newbies..

Honestly, an all around fun experience and in it's current state definitely worth the $15 price tag for the amount of content offered, I have yet to experience the late game, so I'm speaking to early-mid game content, keep that in mind. Also, this is a very long winded review that goes fairly in-depth with some of the games features, if you don't want to be educated on what you're buying, don't read this.
-Visually appealing
Honestly the graphics aren't bad at all, I don't really have any complaints with this one, are there games with better visuals out there? Sure, but it's generally what you'd expect from a zombie game
-Immersive zombie experience
The game has a really simple questing system, you can just continue along with the objectives to unlock content, or you can explore a pretty large map and just kill zombies!
-Survival
I really like the survival features. You aren't running around for no reason, you REALLY have to search for food and water. I have had an especially difficult time finding things to replenish my thirst. There have been multiple occasions where I'm running around just trying to survive. You don't die when your thirst gauge runs out, but your aiming speed is seriously reduced, which makes it much harder to kill zombies and makes the game more dangerous for you; I like that you don't die, because it makes sense. There is also a limit to how much you can carry, so no running around with 1000 logs in your backpack
-Unit variety
From what I've seen so far there's a pretty wide array of units which you gradually are introduced to throughout the game, I don't want to delve into this too much because of spoilers, but there are animals as well as humans
-Voice overs
Honestly, really like the voiceovers, but that's just me. They are what you'd expect from any post apocalyptic characters and I feel like it was implemented really well in this game
-Weapon variety
For anyone who likes zombie games, we really like a variety of weapons to slay our dead counterparts with. I think the variety is there, I'd like to see a few more options of weapons, I do feel the portfolio to choose from isn't amazingly diversified, however there are enough weapons to choose from to keep me entertained
-Combat
Honestly the combat is pretty fun and you can really crank up the difficulty for bonus XP and also to make the zombies harder to kill. I personally have really enjoyed the harder difficulties, takes tons of ammo to kill them and really adds to the 'fear' of the experience, I had many close calls but overcame MOST of them
-Skill/levelling system
Really I'd have to say this is the feature of the game that really sets it apart from any other zombie shoot-em-up I've played. It's a very MMO-esque system, you take the experience you earn from both killing zombies and completing missions (The higher the difficulty of the missions the more XP) and you use that to enhance your character, either by increasing your player level with the XP to make him/her more powerful, or enhance their skills, for example, doing more damage with melee weapons, or faster stamina generation by leveling those specific skills, it really helps keep the gameplay moving, it gives you something to strive for, which in many zombie games that kind of feature is lacking (No real objective other than kill the zombies and complete missions, there isn't much of a system in place in other games to enhance your character as much as you'd like)
-Camps
I haven't built much of a camp yet, but I do have a few buildings. I think it's really cool that you can design a base on this really large map (Anywhere you want really) and hordes of zombies will come and try to attack you. The buildings within the camp allow you to store items, or craft better weapons, etc. Completing missions unlocks better materials so that you can enhance and build a better base, so you can slay stronger zombies. Keep in mind, to level your character you must level your camp first. So if you need level 10 to equip that certain piece of armor, you'll need to get your camp to level 10, then your character to level 10, then you can equip it. Also, with Co-Op you can build camps with other players, which is really cool, so a random person might join your game and really help you amp up your bases defenses, which is pretty epic. I'm going to touch more on the Co-Op feature below.
-Crafting
The crafting system is similar to other zombie games I've played, you go around, find parts like nails, screws, aluminum cans, etc. and you make different items, from bandages, to weapons, or extra base defenses. I don't really have much of a complaint here on this, because so far I haven't really run into any walls with the crafting, I still have plenty of items I can craft. It's a feature I've really enjoyed and encourages you to experience all areas of the game, including the exploration aspect as well as the mission aspect. All of the features this game offers really go hand in hand, because if you skip out on one you're missing out on a lot of content.
-Gear
So far I haven't seen a huge variety of armor, there's a good variety of weapons but I've only found a few different helmets, haven't really found much in the way of bracers, knee guards, breastplate. There is some armor given to you in the game, but I won't spoil where you find that
-Challenges
Tired of the grindy feeling of killing zombie after zombie for XP? Turn up that difficulty and do a challenge mission, not only are the challenge missions pretty funny, they are actually pretty challenging, and you'll get some pretty hefty rewards for completing them.
-Co-op
Not only can you do all of this by yourself! You can do it with friends! They actually have a server browser, meaning you don't need to add friends on Steam, you can just find a random game and join it! Build with friends, build with randoms, whatever! The big thing with this though is many multiplayer lobbies/servers including my own are restricted to GUEST meaning that guests cannot access private chests, etc. Server hosts for example can however promote people from GUEST to MEMBER, and members can do a lot more than guests are able to, so if you are playing with a trusted friend, the content isn't limited; however playing as a guest, you are relatively restricted in what you can do. This is actually REALLY important, because it will possibly ruin your experience if you start out as a guest, so try hosting your own server first, then go be a guest.
Really, I don't have many, my big complaint is that after awhile it can begin to feel a tad grindy, because the experience costs go up exponentially, however by doing the wide array of missions available on harder difficulties (For bonus XP) you will find it much easier to get levels faster. In the time I've played, my character and my base are level 10, so the XP gain isn't too awful, and with the variety of units offered it really keeps me engaged, there's truly a lot of stuff to do. Not a deal breaker for me, though.
The other thing is the social aspect. It also isn't a big deal for me, but instead of adding a voice or chat function they decided to go with the 'chat wheel' with a few preset helpful sentences, like "Thank You", "Hello", or "I need help" etc. I'm not opposed to having a feature like this, because it's nice in sticky situations, however in addition to the chat wheel, I'd also like a chat or a voice option.
With all of that said, the game is FIFTEEN BUCKS, like come on dude, that's a ton of content for $15. The game seriously is great, in its current state it's totally worth the price, and I am crossing my fingers that they add even more content, this is a game I could totally see myself playing for awhile. Worth the buy, check it out!

iBomber Defense Pacific, which I assume to be sort of follow up to iBomber Defense, continues the tradition of producing an incredibly bland and uninspired game though unlike the original this one does have some upsides to it.
The first thing you probably notice is that you now have slightly more choices to make than simply where to place your turrets down. Turrets have been given the "Dig-In" ability which gives them increased range and firepower but limits them to a very narrow arc of fire. This is a good idea in principle but in reality all it means is that you will spend most of your time simply rotating the turret so it can fire on all enemies.
Also a new addition is an ability building that allows you to drop bombs on your enemies and while this also is a nice improvement that gives you something to do while waiting for money to build up it has little impact on the gameplay.
Perhaps the biggest improvement is the inclusion of a interest system. By building Radar Stations, this game's equivalent of a boost turret, you earn a little extra income each wave depending on how much money you have. This is a nice addition that encourages minimalistic builds and opens up multiple tactics for you to choose on the harder difficulties.
Where iBomber Defense was the bare bones of a tower defense game Pacific manages to be the bare bones of a tower defense game with the bare bones of every tower defense gimmick out there except for a 3D FPS option tacked on. All the additions are nice and were solely needed but none of them are really added in properly and you still play the game feeling like you might as well be playing it in a browser.
Although iBomber Defense Pacific is great improvement over the original it is still a game you play wondering what it's doing on the PC.

As a loose comparison, a game that They Are Billions resembles is Factorio with the biter strength turned to maximum and without the complicated production aspects. That in mind, the focus is different given that it is an RTS. They Are Billions is faster paced and the strategic aspect of the game is different, more resembling older Command and Conquer game with persistent base expansion [which to my knowledge has never been extrapolated upon except for Warzone 2100].
Specifically, They Are Billions specifically begins to resemble a particularly obscure RTS called Warzone 2100 except one is not faced with an enemy belching out units from a fixed base, one is instead faced with waves that stress defenses. The major difference in this game is that that zombies behave mechanically different from standard RTS games insofar this game punishes unsegmented bases because civilian populations can be turned into zombies quickly, and thereby "snowballing" a disaster. This particular mechanic is about the same as thralls in Dwarf Fortress: civilians are infected and soon portions of the map are unusuable due to said infections. The end result is a general anxiety about defenses, as breaches mean infection.
In summary, the game is excellent even in the current state it is functional, playable, and fun.

PROS:

NEUTRAL:

The differences between the game types are extremely minimal since each game type has barely 1 game mechanic in it.
Mediocre controls and slow gameplay make this one a pass.

NOTE: I understand I haven't played much of the game as of yet, but I've gotten through the first world and have a good idea where the game is going.  Mainly, I feel like a lot of the negative reviews here are being a bit unfair and I want to address that.  I will edit the review as I see fit as I continue playing.
First of all, Concursion isn't a platformer.  I could understand why Mario and Meat fans would find a bitter sense of disappointment when they pick up this game: "a platformer with world bending mechanics?  How cool!"  A player can easily see within the first few levels that Concursion isn't trying to rack up to the afor mentioned heros of the sidescrolling world.  If being a world-bending platformer was Concursion's goal, I would probably fault it.  But it's not.
Concusion is the combination (quite literally) of several different genres within one game.  The statement on the blurb is pretty accurate: "a multi-genre game played on the boundaries between worlds."  These worlds, of course, come in the form of different genres (or maybe better thought of as ideas) of games.  Taken alone, each idea would be fairly bare-bones.  Yes, the platforming isn't very deep.  The pac-man isn't very deep.  The space shooter isn't very deep.  But looking at each individual segment isn't at all the point here.  Being that this game is meant to be a combination of all of these genres, they have to be taken very holistically.
As it is, the combination works pretty well.  I've used the interconnection between these worlds in several cool and unique ways to roll my way through each level (which I might point out are so far pretty well paced).  In my head, I've balanced my ability to run in one world with my ability to wall jump in another world with my ability to take more damage in another world all at once, and it feels fairly satisfying as the game is designed for and rewards that sort of thinking.  I feel like I'm playing an action puzzle game, fitting each piece together to create an eventual masterpiece.
This is where the big flaw with Concusion comes in: putting pieces together to create a puzzle is fun, but it always ends up looking like what the puzzle creator wanted it to look like.  Concursion isn't horribly open-ended.  The largest divergents to simply running through a level at top speed are the collection of the green shards, which don't offer any immediate incentive to get for a player only as far as I outside of just simply collecting them.  Personally, I am a completionist, so I try my best to get all the shards in a level as I go through.  The problem for people that don't much care as much is that a lot of the cool puzzling that I've found so far lie in collecting these shards.  If you just run through without a care, you're going to skip the starch and meat and run into a wall of vegetables, which is probably where a lot of players end up.
Overall, Concursion is going to be either hit or miss.  For me, it was hit.  I like the game, I like the mechanics, I like the interplay, and I feel like the people that made the game are just darned nice people.  It's cute, and a good pick-up when you've been working for hours on end.  7.5/10

With the addition of the new episode released by Machine Games called DOPA (I believe people refer to it as Dimensions of Past? What's the A stand for?) I felt like I needed to rework this review.
This is the tightest, bloodiest, most fluid 3D action game you could ever play.
From this and Quake II is where the FPS genre all sprouted.
Quake is a dark, medieval, Lovecraftian themed FPS based on what was going to be a Dungeons and Dragons game. You start of in a strange Hub world where you can select difficulty, the Hard difficulty decoured with a broken bridge surrounded by lava, and walls with dead bodies stapled to it, indicating that it's not for your average player.
Next thing you know, you're in a large room with four Slipgates leading to four separate dimensions, all different, but all overrun by bloody horrors.
It's up to you, the player, to clear all four dimensions of these bloody thirsty monsters, and the overlords of each dimension.
Gameplay:
This game is where terms like 'Rocket Jump' and 'Bhopping' orginated from. This is the grand-daddy of those. The aiming is so incredibly responsive, the guns all feel so satisfying to shoot, even the basic shotgun. The level design is impossible and sensical at the same time, which gives a huge impression that you are just traversing a Cthulu version of M.C. Escher's Crazy Stairs, and it's so good. Enemies can be tricky and all have their own attack mechanics which requires thought. There's PUZZLES for god's sake.
This is a game for "the" FPS entusiast -- there's no reason anyone would not like this game. It's action packed from the first rotweiler running at you from across a bridge to the death of Shub'Niggurath.
If you have any correlation with the aged graphics engine, there's tons of addons and sourceports you can run from, that will still allow you to play within Steam. I play on Darkplaces with the "normal" graphics settings, which gives you close-to-original graphics without all the blurriness.
Overall:
It's Quake, why wouldn't you buy it?

Quake is a masterpiece, plain and simple.
Quake may be one of my favorite games, but I'll try to make this review as unbiased as possible. Created in 1996, Quake was revolutionary at the time. Following after Doom (Both created by the wonderful ID Software), Quake took all of what Doom did right and pushed it into the third dimension. The levels, music, and enemies all go beyond the call of duty and make this game a timeless classic.
Quake is heavily inspired by the works of H.P. Lovecraft, creating a dark and medieval setting. The dark shades of brown, green and bright reds in later levels really play to this note. This is not just to play homage to Lovecraft, but it doubles up as a way to put the player into an uneasy, unfamiliar, and terrifying world. Playing the game in linear order allows you to slowly creep into these unfamiliar waters. The levels are easy to commute, and allow for minor exploration to find secrets and health/ammo packs. When you run into a group of enemies, you rarely feel unprepared. That's not saying that this game is easy, because it'll tear you a new one if you don't watch out. This game isn't about unfairly pairing you with hard enemies; it’s about a gradual learning curve that teaches you to manage ammo, health and enemies.
The enemies in Quake are also inspired by Lovecraft's novels. Otherworldly beings with a cameo appearance by the “Lord of the Wood” are just a sampler of what you are in store for. Like I touched on in my levels section, the enemies never feel too tough to beat. The first enemies you'll face are dogs and soldiers, gradually building up to Fiends, Shamblers, and Spawns (Seriously, ♥♥♥♥ these guys). You are introduced to new weapons semi-regularly, and are given a good amount of time to find out what to use on the different enemies. An example (and quick tip) are the Zombies. You can mow the Zombies down with your shotgun, but after awhile they will stand back up to fight. Then how do you kill them? When the level first starts you are given a grenade launcher. The first enemies you see? Zombies. With this new weapon already ready to fire, you unload on the group to find that you gib (kill) the zombies for good. From that point on you know how to dispose of them, and that you shouldn't waste your grenades on enemies other than zombies (with an exception for tougher enemies).
With this dark fantasy world coming together with the level design and enemies, there's one last piece missing. Music. The music in Quake was composed by Nine-Inch-Nails. I'm not sure that I can say much else than that. The music fits the game perfectly with eerie, yet appropriate tracks. Take a look at the nail gun ammo boxes for a subtle nod.
Nobody is perfect, and sadly this port isn't an exception to that rule. The Steam version of Quake comes without the classic Nine-Inch-Nails soundtrack, and the mouse is locked horizontally. This is quickly fixed however by downloading this fix from the community page -

All in all, Quake is worth the $10 price tag normally, but is an absolute steal during sales, dropping to around $5. The amazing level design, challenging enemies, and great music all come together to create one of video game histories greatest. Never think that you are finished playing Quake. While the main story may have been finished, the lively modding community is doing its job to keep Quake alive. Brand new stories, fun game modes (Team Fortress 2 has roots set in Quake), and many more changes make this game that keeps on giving. I cannot recommend this game more, you'll have to try it for yourself.

A title like The Bureau: XCOM Declassified comes with an heavy burden: the legacy of its ancestors.
So, if you really like the original XCOM and especially the recent XCOM Enemy Within (a great game), this one is complete departure.
You are Willam Carter and you lead a team of two agents in the field, completing a serie of missions to insure the survival of the human race facing a massive alien invasion. You give orders to your mates while being in Concentration mode (a kind of slowmo a la F.E.A.R.) and take charge of (approximately) 80% of the shooting (I haven't played with the sniper or soldier yet). In spite of this good idea, I felt the constant shifting between the characters disorienting, forcing me to adapt to this particular aspect of the game instead of just playing. Maybe a static bird view of the scene would have been more convenient.
As a player, you have to make difficult choices : your team mates profiles (you can only bring two with you), your weaponery (you can only carry two, and your mates only one), and your bagpack (that can changes your stats).
The interesting yet controversial aspect of the game is that the storyline is rich, with multiple credible characters with their own agenda. At the beginning, you simply navigate from one to another to help them, but at the end you face dilemmas that could potentially impact your chances of winning the war (never seen it yet, just suspecting). So you basically have a wild difference in pace between headquarters and the field.
The level design is strong when action takes place in Cold War America, but kinda dull in the alien facilities. Up to the point of a deja vu feeling.
To wrap it up, The Bureau: XCOM Declassified is a decent squad-based shooter, with an honorable storyline and a mediocre-to-great level design. Luckily, it can be played casually.

Clunky combos that don't really "work" and characters have *way* too many animation frames.  I'm sorry but in a fighting game I don't really see the advantage to a 75 frame wind-up of a move that can not ever actually hit the opponent.

I will buy this again in maybe a year.  Possibly two.  But for now I want my darn money back because strip away the glitzy presentation there really isn't a fun game underneath.

Montague's Mount is a difficult game to review: It has so much potential, but falls short on certain aspects of gameplay, which makes it difficult sometimes to appreciate and has alienated many players. If there's anything to be taken away from this review, its that patience above all else, is the most important skill the player will have to possess.
Like many others, I bought and played this game for two simple reasons: I absolutely enjoyed "Dear Esther", and I got given a 80% off coupon, making the game extremely cheap. To be honest, had it not been for the coupon magically landing in my steam account, I would not have heard of this game at all, which reflects rather poorly this game's advertising campaign.
I find that many other reviewers have been quick to slate the game and brush it under the carpet as a failed project, but I can't shake the feeling that they have been overly harsh with their judgment: The game isn't as complete and polished as it ought to be, and to be honest, some of the points I will highlight later have proven to be extremely frustrating indeed, as they were deliberately implemented. However, you should find the patience to stick with it and try and scratch below the surface, you may find yourself to be pleasantly surprised.
The Story & Setting:
The story of Montague's Mount could be described as a melancholic journey where the player attempts to piece together the events that have transpired to himself, his family and the inhabitants of the small Irish community scattered across a small, wind and rain battered island in the Atlantic sea. The plot development closely follows the same mechanics of Dear Esther, by making the player interact with notes, objects and monologues from the main character.
The pacing of the narrative is quite regular at the start, but feels rather rushed by the end, which slightly derails the flow of the story. Unlike Dear Esther, not much information about the island and its inhabitants is provided to the player. The same can be said in regards to the causes of the events which have unfolded prior to the protagonist’s joinery, which was slightly disappointing. I travelled around this island and was constantly under the impression that something ancient and potentially malevolent transpired there in ancient time (many "sacred stone" and pillars can be seen dotted around the island) and maybe a diary entry or two about these, would provide extra depth into the setting of the story.
The translation of all objects in Gaelic is a very nice touch, and the small cultural references that can be found here and there add to the beautiful atmosphere to the game. Anyone which has lived extensively on the British Isles (particularly in small communities, highlands and moors) such as myself, will be quick to relate to how capricious the weather can get and this is very well depicted, as an unrelenting, atrocious weather system which constantly batters the island and the player. The music score is fantastic (a real credit to Andrea Baroni) and melds perfectly with the environment. The dreariness of the island and constant stress amplified by the incessant rain compounds a feeling of constant desperation. On the other hand, the extreme colour desaturation and "grainy" effect are overkill and more often than not, get in the way of gameplay (luckily, these can be easily disabled). The lighting and visuals are nowhere near as good as Dear Esther’s and many bugs and poor effects in regards to lighting and shadows become quickly apparent. These are also damaging to the player's immersion into the environment. I can only put this down to lack of experience in game design and I am sure it can be easily fixed. My only other complaint is that the story ends rather abruptly, leaving many questions unanswered. Ambiguous endings are acceptable; Dear Esther pulls it off extremely well, but here I felt like I was left hanging. Maybe they plan an expansion? It's unclear...
Finally the horror aspect of the game could have easily been dropped. The atmosphere of the island gives enough of an impact without the "Ghost boy" moments, which I'm sorry to say, where rather appalling and failed completely to fit in to the environment.
The Gameplay:
The gameplay is divided into pacing around the island searching for clues, and puzzle solving activities. Pacing is very slow and the reasoning for this I assume, is that your character is injured/sick and can only hobble around (walking stick). This will most likely exasperate the impatient player, as walking around is pretty much all you do in this game, and I myself often grumbled at the idea of having to go backwards, because of the time and effort to get around... However, I can appreciate the reason why this has been put in place; it adds to the feeling of desperation and allowance for gentle pacing around the environment, giving you time (or possibly forcing you) to take in the sights and in this sense, I don't see it as an issue.
The puzzles add an extra dimension to the game which Dear Esther lacked, but they have been the source of major complaints in many of the reviews - Many citing their difficulty and lack of logic.
I fully disagree, and it once again boils down to a question of patience. I didn't find these puzzles particularly challenging, if one takes the time to think about them. On several occasions I found myself stuck, not because of the puzzle's logic but because of poor level design an visuals (such as the semaphore diagram being impossible to decipher due to VERY poor lighting and resolution). This does kill the gameplay...
The Positives:
- Great Atmosphere
- More interactive than Dear Esther
- Good Voice acting
- Beautiful music
- Constant sense of desperation
The Negatives:
- The aparenaces of "Ghost Boy"
- The MANY bugs (fell into the ocean at one point)
- The abrupt ending
- Lack of background information about the island
- Poor visual effects: Lighting and desaturation
Summary:
For the price I bought this game for, I feel it was definitely worth it. Anyone who enjoyed Dear Eshter will enjoy this, and the story will compel you to get to the end, despite the game's bugs and shortcomings. My recommendation is that developers should correct the bugs, increase the plot, improve upon the ending and sort out the visual.
Then... This game will be a true masterpiece.

tl,dr: I get the feeling this game was a college project that got out of hand. I can't recommend buying this game at full price but if you see it on sale pick it up.
This game has some really well composed environments and the engine has some very nice shading options, but the model and texture artists seem to have been modelling for a bygone era. There is a lot of low detail models and textures that could be so much more detailed. The environments are really well composed. A lot of places look very pretty and screenshottable except for the noticeably low resolution textures andrepetetive models. Maybe you guys only had one artist and he was under the pump the entire time? Usually low detail wouldn't bother me but for a game that so heavily advertises its art, and has a setting for 'superb' on graphics, I was expecting something more... impressive. Considering the game was released in 2013, I saw no baked normal maps and the normal maps I did see were obviously generated in photoshop from images. The environment composition was great but the models and textures themselves left me feeling unfulfilled and alienated.
As for the timing of the release, I'm sure you guys have had some pressure from comparison to Dear Esther. And I gotta say, you invited it. Guess which game I am summarizing: A quiet, piano fuelled romp along a deserted island with some old pom narrating about a sickness that cleaned the island out. Gameplay focus on exploration in pretty, gritty environment. Some scaryish bits. After playing both I'll attest they are quite different, but those who liked one would like the other. Maybe you could have delayed the release for a little while, focussed on some of the problems and then released to an audience with not such a fresh memory of your direct competition? More time to bake those normal maps too.
The gameplay itself showed some bad design decisions. For instance, the massive camera shake at the start. I think I played this how it was supposed to be played - late at night, lights off, headphones in - and I think you guys were trying to force the player to feel like a concussion victim. I know I did and I don't usually have motion issues. When I did finally get the walking stick it was a bit
much of a relief. Also the first part with the kid laughing was badly executed. I didn't know if I was still in a cutscene or not because the screen still letterboxes until the player moves. The laughing track was repeated and not creepy and there was no creepy leadup to that scene so it felt really out of place.
What this game
show though, is the capability of a team to band together and get some♥♥♥♥♥♥done. The game seems programmatically sound and, even though there are some bugs and strange occasions, it all works well enough. If this was the entire work of two or three people then I applaud your efforts for getting this thing out the door and shipped on steam. You can only go up from here. If this was a big team then I'm not very impressed with the net product. I'm going to recommend this game though because I like seeing small game studios like you guys get publicity and go on to greater things. Fills me with hope. Hoy ti, mañana yo.

First thing to know:  the awkward, slow walking only lasts for a short time (you have to find something).  Don't be put off!
Really liked this game-- solid effort from PolyPusher, IMO.  It looks like some of the criticism it got in some of the reviews was addressed by the patch.  I never played pre-patch, so I can't compare.  Overall I found the game enjoyable, introspective, psychological, and, well, fun.  Love the exploration element with just enough story (and an interesting one) to keep you going.  It's not a long game, but it's not ultra-short, either.  I think the duration is about right.  You might find a puzzle that annoys you for one reason or another, but overall the puzzles are good.  And don't be put off by the clutter of items in the opening area-- the whole game isn't like that.
You'll like the game if you like exploration, pretty 3D graphics, immersion, and no timed elements (technically the one mini-game is "timed" but if it really bothers you, you can disable it).  It's a pastoral, not an epic.  It rewards taking your time and enjoying the scenery.  Some will find that boring, others will find it just what they want to relax with over a few evenings.
You won't like the game if you want to be able to run fast from screen to screen, need action or cool cutscenes, bright colors, an amazing, gripping story, or super-easy or super-hard puzzles.
For achievement-hunters, if you pay attention at all, you should have no problem getting 19/20 achievements with a little patience.  The last one (finding the crosses) I only got 19/22 from normal gameplay and had to go back and hunt for the other three, including consulting a guide.  And with one exception, the ones I missed were pretty much in front of my face.
Give it a shot.  8.5/10

I started this game off with a couple friends, one controlling movement with a controller, one managing inventory and looking around with a keyboard. We managed to find a walking stick, pick up a few little red glowy wooden tube things, open a gate (in a world record time of: several minutes!), get confused - not creeped out - by a boy sat on a tree stump, because it looked like my computer was struggling so hard to deal with his motion that we only saw him move towards us in three key frames. Maybe this is because this game has Oculus Rift support, so the devs thought you'd blink at the correct moment, to give a creative Dr. Who vibe to the game. We quickly swooped up a gold medal in the world championships for this game by placing a protractor on a sun dial, then quit before we went mad - to play Shovel Knight.
I returned to this game weeks later, and despite having full keyboard control, I cannot for the life of me find out which key I have to press to put that protractor back on that sundial. I think I need to put a valve wheel on something, but I can't figure that out either. Even the controls in the main menu don't give me the glimmer of enlightenment that I so longingly wish for, pray for.
Don't let my play time fool you, I went AFK whilst watching Game of Thrones to get at least some achievements in this game. I initially laughed when I saw an achievement for walking - just walking - but given the unchangable, excrutiatingly slow pace the protaginist has, I can say that walking a few kilometres in this game truly is an achievement.
Perhaps an interesting game to spend a pound on to see what not to do when trying to create an immersive game, but on the whole I strongly suggest you keep that pound, add it to the jar then pick up a game you actually want later on. You probably have enough games to keep you occupied anyway. I know you do. Don't look down in shame, look back at this review. There's a quip or two coming.
Due to the Oculus Rift support, and door lintels being at eye-height, I dub this game "Headbang simulator 2014".
If you already bought this game, give it a go - and if you don't like it, go afk, get those silly achievements and thankfully, some steam trading cards - perhaps someone's way of saying "I'm... I'm sorry for accepting your money".

If you like tower defense games, this one has some novel features in it. Gameplay is extremely fun. You fend off attack waves from ground, air, and water.. Some of the cool features in this game are that there are more than one route that the enemy travels to get to you, forcing you to focus on choke points first and develop out from there. There are bonuses to blow up on the map, including secrets. All units can be developed into beefier units, but also include a feature called 'Dig In' - this allows you to opt out of 360 degree attack capabilities for a cone of attack, but with greater range. You can build bomb towers to give you bombs that can work on land or water. You can construct support towers that extend the range of units in their area of effect. There are ambush attacks and other special combat scenarios, such as enemy return fire that make the game more than just a straight tower defense game. You earn points to increase maximum capability from your towers at the end of the round, depending on how well you do, PLUS you earn perks as rewards for things like 'number of bullets spent' or 'number of times you repair'.. all of these perk progressions are tracked so you can see how far along you are until the next unlock. All in all, I would have to say this is a great little tower defense game and I picked it up for $2. Awesome!

Well, after 20 hours playing this game I can say this : This game is fun and addicting. Why? Because of the gameplay elements. Building your own ship with the parts of defeated foes. Upgrade your crew with skills and stat points. Giving them a sharp knife and a ranged weapon. Upgrade even your weapons! I would like a hardcore options, for testing my skills so far. Let me give you a few tips along the pirate way :
- Give every crew member one skill, like cooking or fishing but not both. Don't bother give them a third skill that mess everything up
- Plunder the ships of enemy pirates after you defeated everybody on that ship (except animals) That's the way you get rich early on.
- Stock rum and food up. To keep your crew happy and moody. (Soup is the best option)
- Sell stuff you really don't need. Plus don't buy stuff you don't need.
And yes, the game has bugs at some point while playing for a long time. Crew members having difficulty returning to your shop after you killed everybody because you blasted everything apart with cannons before boarding time. And true, this game is difficult, but rewarding at times with loot. I'm played on normal so far, and I'm going to have a shot at Hard next playthrough. But I recommend this game for the player that like rogue-like games, loot and the pirate way of life!

TL;DR: I cannot recommend this game in its current state, but you should follow it or otherwise keep it on your radar, because I think it's only going to get better.
Details:
I really like this game. A lot, but it struggles with both a sense of "what do I do next" and a really wonky difficulty curve. Virutally the entire first part of the game is a sunday stroll down easy street, but as you hit the last...I want to say 40% of the game or so...the difficulty suddenly jumps like Super Mario on PCP. Now, watching your carefully contructed empire crumble IS part of the fun (no really) and you get this very real sense of: Okay, if I do this, this and this differently next time, then maybe I can do better. Through trial and error you get better at the game, it's almost Roguelike.
Post Edit: The game is essentially about building to the end waves or wave, using the time allotted to get your economic engine going while keeping your defenses solid enough to hold off the smaller waves that come before the end. The problem here is the same problem FTL faced, where it's all essentially about the shape you're in at the end, and the moment-to-moment decisions don't matter as much. So you can be doing well overall only to find, after nearly two hours of solid play, that there's a hole you didn't account for, a resource you didn't get enough of, or even just that you failed to predict which of your walls the zombies were going to crash against. And two hours is a lot of time to just let scatter to the wind when one of those errors happen. This adds to the lack of tutorial (yet) and poorly explained (or not explained) elements, like the Infected Harpies that lurk on the map edge, to create a potentially frustrating trial-and-error gameplay where the early game becomes repetitive and boring because aside from your random map seed (another trial-and-error mechanic) the early stages of the game change very little.
All of that CAN be explained simply by: It's early access, Alpha specifically, and those complaints will ideally be addressed with future updates and patches. But that doesn't change the fact that now, IN THIS STATE, I cannot recommend the game. But you should follow it, because I think it's only going to get better.
Pre Edit: But the game is AGGRESSIVELY difficult, no tutorial means that learning the building uses and tech trees can be an exercise in futility until you figure out the precise use for some of the buildings. There's also no upgrade for the tower you need to spread your area of control (that you build buildings in) and there's a punishing lack of different soldier types. Add to that the nearly $30 (CDN) Pricetag and I just cannot currently recommend it.
With all that out of the way: It is an Early Access title, the Developers clearly have both a strong vision for the game and a strong sense of how to make both the mechanics and theme work. If you have an extra $30 you could pick it up, but even if you don't you should ABSOLUTELY keep your eye on it. This one is going to be a real sleeper hit I think,

I like this game, and I find myself really wanting to love it but:
-The AI is still a huge mess on the frontlines, especially in planning and mounting offensives. Unless they absolutely dwarf your army, they will feed manpower into your frontline. I've never exceeded a million casualties in a war while the AI will regularly go into several million like it's no big deal.
-I've had the game delete all my used frontlines and assign my armies to old defunct orders I forgot about way back when with no provocation in critical moments. This has happened several times, including once when it completely refused to redraw ANY frontline at all on critical borders.
-There are a lot of redundancies in AI choosing national foci late game. I've had a defeated and puppeted Nation Francaise decide post-war that it's gonna form it's own faction and steal my faction members out from under me, although this means that they can't join any wars that their faction members find themselves in. I've seen America decide to take a stand against Fascism while already at war with Japan. I've had a fascist, puppeted UK consider intervening in Denmark and Norway, both also my puppets. Nothing really bad ever comes of these...just a bizarre simple thing that could have been taken care of and reinforces the 'dumbness' of the AI
- There is no reason for any sort of tactical offensive using the battle planner, as far as my experience has shown. I've never seen a real practical use that's made me consider to not just set generic offensive plans, get the prep bonus, then micromanaging my units into encircling and brute forcing specific points in the line.
There are likely more obvious issues. It's playable, but I've been playing this within the last month and at launch. It hasn't changed a whole lot. Knowing Paradox, they can over time change the game to a more satisfying state, like with EU and CK2, but will they? They've released two DLCs since launch and the game as it stands now shows that they aren't seriously addressing fundamental issues that have been called out from the start.
I don't think I have seen any reason to think that they will do so. A negative review is maybe harsh, but this is just really not what I expect from Paradox. Their non-commital attitude towards making a strong base product disappoints as well as frustrates me.

It's not a hard not recommended, but it's definitely a more repetative and frustrating game than a fun one.
Chief issue, the game doesn't have enough variety. Every match comes down to the same chase. There are differences based on the character selection and experience levels, but that changes the game maybe only 10% from one game to the next. This is fundamentally a game that NEEDS other game modes.
It can be fun, but it doesn't have longevity.
As for frustrations:
1. The game modes
2! character selection doesn't seem to do anything. I literally got stuck playing tracker for nearly half of 10x XP weekend despite it being my last choice. I like tracker, which is why I played it a lot early on, but now I seem eternally stuck as the tracker when all I f'ing want to do is try some monsters now that I actually have money to spend on their perks.
3. Games rarely make it to the relay destruction, because killing all the hunters ends the match. I think this has lead to a few unfortunate design choices. Hunters are way too hard to kill, so that the match doesn't end prematurely. Because the hunters are super hard to kill, the monster is also beefed up so that it takes forever to kill. If hunter teams always respawned at ship regardless of team wipe, those insane values could be ramped down. This would make hunters bolder, and monsters more effective, which would actually be more fun, rather than this frustrating no one can kill anyone battles that we have now.
4. Baaaalance. Some monsters are impossible to kill. Some hunters are practically useless.
If they fix the character select, I might slip this into a hesitant recommend, but honestly the variety thing is a bit of a killer.
For character select I think they should have a system that tracks when a player doesn't get to play the character they want. If you get your second choice, you get 1 point. If you get 3rd, you get 2, and so on. Players with the highest disappointment points get first choice, then next highest and so on. If there's a tie, the player with the higher rank in a class then gets dibs. When you get new points, add them to your last points, unless you got your choice, in which case reset it. Definitely reward these at the end of a match so as to discourage quiting early.

This is technically a negative review, but it's based on my personal experiences rather than on drawbacks of the game itself, so I don't want to ruin its review rating by things that are not directly related to the project's quality. Thus, things that I say below are not really happening because the game is bad; it's just me being not very efficient in it.
So here's my history with Evolve:
> Installed the game
> Got through the tutorial
> Started a singleplayer game as a hunter to get some more training before going online
> Got rekt by the monster
> Started another singleplayer game as a monster
> Got rekt by the hunters
> Understood that I suck at this game and I'd better not go into multiplayer if I can't even defeat an AI
> Uninstalled
Other random things I noticed in the meantime:
- The concept itself is great, but currently it feels very simplistic. I understand that it probably was a necessary decision to prevent the game from dying, but it still doesn't make me happy. For example, there hardly is any significant difference between the classes: it doesn't feel like they have distinct roles, many things can be done by any member of the group.
- Weapons and abilities are all on the same control scheme, which makes switching between them clumsy and not very efficient. If I want to switch between weapons only, I have to memorize that with weapon 1 selected I should only move mouse wheel up, and with weapon 2 I should only move the wheel down, because otherwise I'll run into a mine or some other crap I don't need at the moment.
- Game starts experiencing random lags after some amount of playing.
- Preferred roles hardly mean anything. You say, "I don't want to be a monster". The game says, "In the next match, you will be a monster! Isn't it awesome!"
Overall, I didn't have much fun. Probably this is not my kind of game.

When the developers describe Concursion as different, they are right! I love that you can flip back and forth between the different worlds and have completely different styles of game play.
I have Part One up for the Let's Play:

Devotees of retro and neoretro are no strangers to the mashup: a type of game collection that offers "lite" versions of various game types (SHMUP, platformer, etc.), selectable from a central hub.
, however, takes the concept of "mashup" to a whole new insane sphere by jamming as many as five disparate genres into the
field!  There is no neat pick-and-choose here; you must actively guide the behorned Questy Guy from one sparkle-bordered genre zone to the next, and while he retains his momentum in the crossing, his appearance and moveset alter completely -- as do the characteristics of any enemy that happens to drift over!  Sometimes these shifts occur with such dizzying speed that it almost seems like madness at first, but a meticulous method always becomes evident before long.  The diamond brilliance of the level design shines through this controlled chaos, which is present in endlessly inventive configurations of genre zones and in the occasional wildcard bit that breaks the rules of all
's fractured worlds.
And what of the graphics?  They are a bit coarse perhaps, a bit raw, a bit mismatched, sometimes even a bit MS Paint. In short, Aubrey Beardsley definitely did not serve as chief art director.  But you know what?  The graphics are imperfectly perfect, heta-uma,  prettily pockmarked.  Not only do they suit the merry madness of the level design, but they radiate this bubbly "can do!" exuberance that infected me from the first!  In fact, I almost love the game's awesome attitude (and therefore its art style) as much as its engaging level composition!
With a fantastic chiptune score and an interesting narrative to sweeten the pot,
is a game that every  indie-lover with twitchy fingers should get.  I'm in disbelief that the reviews are not overwhelmingly positive!

I, uh, I c-can explain! J-just give me a sec; it's not what it looks like! I got the game for t-the, um, story! Just listen, I'm going somewhere with this okay? *sigh* Okay, without further ado, I present to you...
LASTING IMPRESSIONS
Hatoful Boyfriend
GENRE
Dating Simulator/Visual Novel
STORY
In Hatoful Boyfriend you take the role of Hiyoko Tosaka, a human going to a prestigious highschool for birds. The school in question is St. Pigeonation’s, and it's known mostly for being the world's greatest gathering place for birds. You're a sophomore now, but you haven't done much to adjust to the atmosphere of Pigeonation's just yet. You're not entirely lost though, as you also have one of the several woo-able birds with you, your hardworking best friend Ryouta Kawara. Along with him you can also bond with narcoleptic math teacher Nanaki Kazuaki, bashful aristocrat Sakuya Le Bel Shirogane, distant bookworm Fujishiro Nageki, suave ladies' man Sakazaki Yuuya, enigmatic doctor Iwamine Shuu, and hyperactive track star Okosan. With so much romance in the air, it's hard to believe the school holds so many dark secrets...
GAMEPLAY
Ever read a book online? It's like that except every once in a while the books asks which choice you want to make. The choices you make will determine which bird you end up with, along with which ending you get for them. [Provided you don't get indesicive and go the way of the dodo, of course.] Each day you will be asked which class you want to take; this decides which trait will be leveled for that day. As previously mentioned, this will affect which ending you get for your desired bird.
VISUALS
Not much to say. It's pictures of birds with various backgrounds. The backgrounds look very nice, and there's quite a large amount of them. You also get a little end card pictures for your gallery after the end of each route. They're gosh darned cute.
SOUNDTRACK
The soundtrack is a delightful mix of royalty-free, classics, and original [I think?] tracks. All of them fit perfectly with any of the situations at hand. [Except maybe when Dance of the Sugar Plum Fairy plays, that's always just plain silly.] There's many tracks from Kevin MacLoed and SENTIVE; the sexy, suave Dispersion Relation, Simply Blue, Daybreak [Personal favorite.], and tons of ones with gibberish for names. The collector's edition is worth is just for the beautiful OST.
SEQUELS [SPOILERS]
Hatoful Boyfriend is the quintessential example of an idea that I've had for a while now; some games should never get sequels. While it's obvious that a bad game shouldn't deserve a sequel; I'm of the opinion that if a game is GOOD enough it shouldn't HAVE a sequel. If a game does all that it wishes, if a game provides a fulfilling, complete experience; it would be insulting to continue where the game left off. You may be thinking 'How does a game about dating birds provide a fulfilling experience?' I'll tell you; it's because the entire dating sim portion of the game is a mere facade. Once you've completed all possible routes at least once, you have the option to unlock BBL; a grim narrative that reveals the lore behind this game's world, the motivations and sins of characters, and completes all story arcs. The dating sim part of Hatoful Boyfriend is there simply to set up characters so that you know who this story is centered around. You know how they act by then, what their situations are, and this only helps to greatly strengthen the story. It's a fantastic conclusion, and it's one that left me speechless. Which brings us back to sequels. As I've said, a sequel to this game woud be a downright insult; a direct sequel that is. A direct sequel would be insulting, as the game would have nowhere to go with the current story; all arcs are completed. However, an indirect sequel would be a very, very smart idea if done correctly. By merely taking the characters we know and love and putting them in a different kind of story; the game has somewhere to go. Oh, and it did go somwhere, as an indirect sequel exists. [Holiday Star is its name if you were wondering. Not yet on steam though.]
FINAL THOUGHTS
I dove this game. To say that this was a pheasant experience would be the understatement of the century. While at first glance, it may look like quite the bad egg, it's surely a narrative you'll never forget. I'm talon you, it's all here! Great soundtrack, amazing characters, bird puns; it's just a quail of a time! The price ain't nothin to go squawkin' about neither, no need to worry about some ludicrous bill. This is the defenition of the phrase 'more than meets the eye' and you'd have to be some hard boiled individual not to enjoy the humor at the least. I know I'm gushing, but I just can't recommend this enough! While you're at it, make sure to kill two birds with one stone and buy the collector's edition with it. The soundtrack alone makes it worth it. Alright, I've egged you on for far too much now, I'll sparrow you of any more. Hatoful Boyfriend has left a resounding lasting impression; it's not what the source material is, it's what you do with it that makes it a golden goose egg. You've got your ducks in a row MediaTonic, keep it up.
And now, in Japanese tradition, a haiku.
Hatoful Boyfriend,
A dating sim about birds.

I still don't know what to call this game. It's kind of a 2D platformer, but then not really 50% of the time. Mostly because there are certainly entirely levels where you play a shmup, fly around with a jetpack, and play pacman for -reasons-. It certainly is, though, quite an enjoyable experience with a few flaws.
The game's biggest strength is its variety; almost every level tries something new, so if you didn't like the last level, well, you don't have to worry because odds are you won't see another like it for the rest of the game. And the game is a pretty decent length too, with 70 levels/bosses across 7 worlds. There's just so many creative ideas here, enough to fill two or three games, but crammed in to one to keep the game constantly fresh longer than any other game I can think of has. It's not the most difficult game, but it's not the easiest game either, and 100% completion definitely takes a bit of effort.
It's not entirely perfect though; it does, visually, not look great, and I worry that people will judge its overall quality as a result of this. The dance thing at the end of levels, especially, is... ow. Painful. But the graphics don't really matter if the gameplay is enjoyable, in the end. And the game only stumbles there occasionally. Personally, I felt the checkpointing in some levels/bosses was not sufficient (at least for normal mode; hardcore mode is totally fine though since that's the point; but some levels where the checkpointing was identical and normal and hardcore tended to be the issues here for me). The bosses also tend to fall flat half of the time; any bosses not fought with the ship or ninja, especially, as you have 2-3 hits and little to no chance of recovering from a hit. They're all creative in their own way but I personally felt some bosses (especially the final boss and its abysmal third phase) needed a checkpoint; only one single boss in the game actually has checkpoints, out of 7. I also felt there was an overreliance on autoscrolling/forced pace levels. Autoscrolling only works if the player has to struggle to keep up (which is the case in some levels, but not most of them). Otherwise it becomes tedious to replay the same segment at the same pace when you fail.
I wouldn't call it a perfect game by any means but I had a ton of fun with it and am looking forward to the bonus levels the devs have mentioned coming in the near future, and I'd certainly recommend you check it out; more than anything else it's unique in a good way.

This game is absolutely amazing and one of the best I have played in a long time.  The premise of the game is that the universe is being torn apart, and there are rifts all over each level which, as you enter them, lead to a different world, which turns you into a different hero with totally different powers.
The 5 characters you play as are a knight, which is very similar to super mario, a ninja, complete with a sword, double jumps and wall hangs, a space ship which leads way into shmup style levels, a little bull thing that plays like pac-man and an astronaut who has a jetpack but no means of attack.
Individually all 5 styles are handled well, the controls for each character are very tight and I never once blamed a death on the controls.  Each character, on its own, is very fun to play, but where this game shines is the way the characters are integrated into one anothers level.  You may think it is just a gimmick, but the reality is that the way the genres cross each other is brilliant and the further you get into the game, the more wild the cross overs become.
The difficulty curve in this game is handled extremely well, this is not an easy game, and you will die a lot but the difficulty progression is very smooth.  The game starts out easy enough as you play a few introductory levels to learn the characters and as you progress the levels and the cross-overs between them get increasingly more challenging, but you never feel overhwhelmed, nor do you feel that anything is cheap.  The beauty of this game is that some things will seem insurmountable when you firts look at them but before you know it you are completing insane challenges like a pro.
There are also 3-4 gems in each level, very similar to the 3 big coins in the new super mario series.  SOme gems are right in your face but tricky to access and others are cleverly hidden, obtaining all these gems is important to the story, but more importantly you will have a blast trying to collect all of them.  This game is also sprinkled with some humorous moments that pays homage to some old games, be sure to read the titles to every level.  The story here is also well done, it is a platformer so don't expect anything crazy but there is more of a story than your average mario clone and even a funny little twist that I will not spoil for you here.
I cannot recommend this game strongly enough, if you are a gamer you owe it to yourself to give it a try, it is unlike anything you have ever played or probably ever will play.  It is an absolute blast from start to finish and I cannot think of a single thing in this game to complain about.

i'm going to start out by saying i do not like this game even though i love the idea behind it and will tell you why that is.
firstly this game is built around hardcore modes. you have 1 life and when you die (and you will) you loose everything. in this game there are armor and weapons and 1 death can erase all that in a second. a character called dustwing which is a mobile hero with lots of movement abilities has roughly 50hp. a static trap that you can get knocked into on a medium difficulty map had delt me 28 damage with mulitple points in armor. that means if you get knockback/stunlock twice your f*cked. there are no options for a casual mode where you keep your gear. if there was this would be my new favorite game.
if you want to get anywhere towards mid to end game you have to pay. you have a tiny 6 slot "freebie" chest and thats it.  to get more storage or the option to have more than 1 character at a time you have to pay.
the game runs beautifully and uses less resources than watching youtube videos in html5 format. so this game will run on your ancient pc no problem.
the characters all look alike, like exactly the same, and the only way to tell your character apart from the others is a white glowing orb around your character. the problem in this lies with the fact that characters are silver so it blends in with character models, the bullets are white, the hit numbers are white, damn near everything in the game is white so on occasion you walk into stuff that damages you because the character you think is yours isnt. normally i wouldnt care but with the hardcore mode and the fact you loose everything this NEEDS changed to a different color. maybe lime green since that color isnt used in game that much.
one other thing that bothers me about this game is the fact it calles itself an mmo. the main thing about mmo's is that they have an economy built by the player base. that is impossible in this game due to the inability to give/trade your stuff away and there is no way to sell anything so you get stuff you dont have room for you just have to drop it and nobody can pick it up since all the items are instanced to your character.
there is an ingame text chat option but you have to register with their website in order to use it and ingame nobody does because of the "hardcore" nature of the game.
the last and biggest issue i have with this game it the leveling system. you only gain experience if you do better than any other time you've played. that means you throw a grenade into a group of baddies and deal 500 points of damage. to get point every again you must deal greater than 500 damage. if you do less than 500 damage you get NOTHING!. to top it off you only get the points WHEN YOU DIE AND LOOSE EVERYTHING! thats right this game extends the playtime by making you repeat the same levels over and over for 0 gain. if you dont level up you cannot play all the characters. they are unlocked at level 1, 3, 5, and 7.  i have played 5.7 hours and i'm just now lvl3 and i do not see that changing anytime soon.
another problem i have with this game is the controlls. pushing up or down on your control stick does not make you jump or crouch or fall through platforms. i can understand why they did this but at the same time its forcing you to learn a new way to play a game at the same time your platforming and being attacked by mobs (aka its rage inducing). on the same topic i'm using a steam controller which i've used for other games like american truck sim and in this game it doesnt want to registed that i'm point the stick down until its almost pointed straight down. this has actually got me killed numerous times since i couldnt shoot the monster at my feet and i watched my bullets shoot straight over its head. oh yeah you also cant shoot straight up or down which adds another layer of difficulty to certain mobs that hang from the cealing and your forced to take damage just to be able to shoot them.
overall i think if this game added a casual mode, way to sell excess gear to a vendor, trading system, and expanded the options for free players this could easily become the next big mmo since it has a retro feel and retro games are making a comeback (a good thing). they get a 10/10 for creativity but 5/10 for execution.

So, this is the first ever XCOM game I play, unlike 95% of the reviewers out there. I own Enemy Unkown, but didn't play it yet.
This game is great.
for one, it's the first game i play in quite some time that pushes my laptop's gfx card to its limit, and forces me to lower the quality, it's fast pced action, with lots of great scenery, effects and eye candy.
secondly, what this game is unique at, and what it does so well, is make shooting ina game hard, but for good reasons.
In other words, just in the second or third level, while playing like I usually play -walking around and shooting all the enemies-, I actually lost, twice, and the game was still in the beggining. I started implementing the strategic tactics the game told you to follow, and I won without changing the game difficulty.
In other words, it puts some real weight into your relative location to your enemy's. if you (or your teammate) is flanking an enemy, you noticably kill them easier than if you shoot at them when they're behind cover.
enemies try to flank you, enemies have classes like your teammates have, and with that they have abilities like yours have.
the way you spread(or not) into the field of a battle decides how suprisingly easy you defeat your enemies, or easily get defeated by them.
It's the most dynamic and intense chess game i've ever played.
True you get to slow down time to give out the orders in succession, but during that time your enemies are moving and shooting, unlike mass effect where time is totally paused.
that brings us to another thing, this game is a ripoff mass effect 1, if you played it you can easily tell. there are many improvements over mass effects, but still many similiarities.
the story was mostly meh, till the unexpected twist at the end.
if you wanted to understand or experience what it means to get the upper ground or strategic advantage of a battleground, this game will teach you.

Are you a fan of isolation, bleak locales, vague stories and pathways blocked by puzzles to do simple things like open a door, or lower a bridge? If so, Montague's Mount is right for you.
You start the game hobbling on a beach and lo and behold, you don't remember a thing. There's things strewn about and everything is derelicte, your first task is finding a stick to use as a crutch which will thankfully stop you from limping and move at a nice walking pace. You'll find a couple notes in the beginning of the game about how to do things and interact with everything, which is really nice, but for the most part you're kind of on your own. That's pretty par for the course for these games and it's better that way, though I did find myself checking a Steam guide every now and then when I got stuck.
Overall the game is fun, if you like these slow and atmospheric titles, but the game does have a couple issues. First, you're slow, now you're not terribly slow but the way the game works is that you open up more and more of the island in a somewhat linear fashion so if you're a ways into the game and want to go all the way back to check? Enjoy walking all of the way back at the not-so-brisk pace you're stuck at. Secondly, I know the game is supposed to be dreary but it's a bit excessive. The island is in perpetual overcast and every 5 or 10 minutes a storm will kick in causing high winds and rain. Trees and foliage look good as they blow around along with their shadows that mimic their movement, but when the rain starts nearly all of the color in game turns to a cold grey, almost black and white. It gets a little bit harder to see things, but the game hardly has much color in it in the first place and losing that when it rains doesn't make it too visually enjoyable. Not a deal breaker, but just strange design choice.

I really enjoyed my time with the first How to Survive, so I expected to have fun with this one as well. But bah, instead of building up with all the knowledge from the first game, the developer decided to run off with a different game direction here.
The first game feels really immersive. As you start that game, the tutorial/story teaches you how to play perfectly, like how you need lit up campfires, how you need to secure bunkers, etc etc. This one leaves you to the wolves, giving you tons of material and doesn't teach you what to do with it.
In the first game, you're really free to explore the open world, searching the nooks and cranny to get crafting materials for that badass weaponry. And as you progress further into the game, more areas are unlocked, giving you a good sense of progression. I've kind of watched Pixel Piracy for a while, and finally took the plunge... and overall I've enjoyed it.
There is a lot of game here, and with that comes good and bad.
Basic Concept - Build a ship, head out to sea. Raid islands, pillage ships. Hire more pirates.
Your Pirates can level up, and you can choose how to train them thought bumping up stats, and giving them skills through books. Your pirates can also die, including your captain - who can be replaced by a first mate eventually.
With ship battles once you've wiped out the opposing crew you can Plunder their ship, or maybe you want to capture their ship, and make it yours. (Or maybe forget to do anything and sail away). Plundering the ship will give you a few ship pieces, and some gold.
Eventually you will increase your skills, and be able to see, and explore more of the map, and travel faster while doing it.
There are a few bounties you can choose to attempt to collect for a few extra coin in your pocket, and occasionally an interesting weapon or piece of equipment.
My experience so far has been... very different from the videos depict. I have a giant ship, few crew, and have it filled with items to build that crew... and of course the odd cannon for good measure. I suppose that's the beauty, you can choose whatever path suits you best.
Also, one of my pirates knocked an enemy pirate grappling onto my ship off with poop :)
+ Open world, minimal instruction. It might turn some people off, but I've always found something very satisfying about having to learn the game.
+ Build you ship as you like. You can make your boat hover if you like --- assuming that's not a glitch.
+ Your pirates are a blank slate. Other than the odd stat or skill they start with, they are completely at your mercy as to how you want to build them.
+ Groups give added control. - I may be imagining it happening, but putting crew members in the Gunner group has them hanging back, and taking pot shots. Ship Crew will do a mix of melee and ranged. (Haven't experimented with much else)
+ Free range to go where you like.
+ Surprising amount of start up options. You can tweak everything from the appearance, to your start to how difficult you want various aspects of the game.
+ Some weird stuff happens, and when you see it you can't help but laugh.
- Glitches. Ranging from minor inconveniences to half hour time sinks they can be frustrating. I haven't hit any game killers, and they've been good about patches, so hopefully this will fade.
- Limited range on pirates cleaning/repairing can lead to the odd pathing melt down.
- Removing food barrels with food in can cause you to lose that food.
- Cannons can be awkward. Can't place cannon balls while out at sea. Timer stills runs even if you don't have ammo for the cannons on deck. No option to Not fire the cannons if you want to save Ammo.
- Much of the game would benefit from a toggle switch, and/or more control over prioritizing.
Overall it's a game worth playing. Most of my grievances come from glitches they've been actively working to remove, and they've built a big enough platform they can do a lot with it in the long run.
