I really wish Steam had the ability to set a "Neutral" review for a game because I don't like down voting a game with promises. But, as it stands now I can't recommend this game for most players.
Challenging games can be fun and enjoyable, they rack your brain and reflexes to try and find a workable solution, but with the way this game is setup that never really occurs. Periodically, the game goes through massive spikes in difficulty for several minutes, and there's not always enough time to ready your forces or base. If something isn't done, say a wall, or turret, or maybe some of your slower units can't muster fast enough you will lose.
Which takes me to the next point, there's no real opportunity to correct your mistakes and learn frm your mistakes. The current game mode is locked into a permanent Iron Man mode, and there is no way to save. Which makes it very difficult (impossible really) and retest layouts and strategies in the face of failure.
Instead, you are constantly forced into a new map, and new set of obstacles at every loss, and as it stands, I'm not convinced every map has a winnable solution. When your base is dropped within sight of a nest of zombie, a so called “Doom Village”, even on the easiest level of difficulty I don't see anyway to win.
There is a set of options to alter the difficulty, and they can make the game last a bit longer, but then you'll be hit with those same difficulty spikes in the form of massive zombie waves from an unknown direction, with over whelming strength. You need strong defenses, but with limited resources you have pick what areas to fortify and strength, and hope when the wave comes that you were right. But if your not, there's no way to try again, to see if maybe there might have been a way to win.
Losing may not be such an issue in most games, except I this instance it can take hours before you realize that you missed something in your base design. Maybe a wall wasn't fully connected. Maybe you miss clicked and sent your troupes outside the watch tower you built for them. The level of frustration and literal agony at seeing hours of work amount to nothing isn't in any sense of the word fun. Nothing was gained, nothing was learned.
All that being said, the game does have a lot of promises. It's visually appealing, has a nice tech tree and for the most part good structure and unit balance. The seems to have a very well designed and robust engine, which true to their word, can handle thousands of active units on a map without stuttering.
Truthfully, I think the engine is by far the best selling point of this game. If they can find a way to better balance it, or add some kind of save system I think this game would be worth the price. Right now however, it's fun for an hour then you realize the futility of trying to progress and learn. Some people may love it, but I don't think most would.

Overall, a pretty good game. Definitely worth the $25 asking price.
Currently, the only game mode is survival. You set how long you want the survival goal to be, and how many infected you want to fight, then get plopped down in a randomly generated map. There are 4 different map "types", each with their own different way of generating maps. I love the randomness, it ensures you can't just find one part of a fixed map that's easily exploitable and win every time.
While the in-game tutorial is a bit bare-bones, it'll teach you what you need to know to get started. But you're going to need a lot more than basic knowledge to survive.
The game is
hard. I've currently only tried it on "challenging" settings (basically "medium" mode), and I'm struggling to get half-way through.  The community hub is full of talk about how beating the final horde on even easier settings is crazily difficult. But that's a good thing, not a bad thing. It
feel like a desperate struggle, in my opinion.
The base-building is pretty good. You've got various traps and defensive options to employ for protecting your colony. There's also 9 resources, 4 that are just fixed numbers that limit certain things (energy buildings add x amount to your max energy, build subtracts x from that pool to run), and the other 5 are resources you generate and store. Various buildings can be built to perform different functions and boost the efficiency of other buildings. Storehouses help you store more goods and boost production of nearby resource-gathering buildings, for instance. If a building is attacked by infected, it can become infected itself. All the workers inside will turn into infecteds, and the building will remain non-functional until you clear the area and repair it. There are also "doom towns" on the map, clusters of infected builings that spawn swarms of enemies if anyone strays too close.
As of the name? It fits. I can honestly see some dedicated players killing at least a few million enemies overall during their playtime of this game. Even on medium horde size, there's still going to be thousands of infected all over the map, and thousands more will arrive on the later hordes. From what I hear, killing a thousand infected in the final horde will just put a small dent in it. According to the devs, up to 20,000 infected can be safely handled at the same time by the game engine. Will that number ever get bigger? Maybe.
However, because this is early access, there is some rough edges. The spelling and grammar is a bit wonky sometimes ("versatil unit"), and I'm not sure the devs know what a SMG is. The biggest issue, however, is pathing. I can understand the infected having dumb pathing (though getting stuck on rocks and such is a bit too dumb), having complex pathing for thousands of units at the same time would eat up CPU like crazy. However, pathing for units you control needs to be seriously improved. They can get caught on stuff just like the infected, including each other. Speaking of CPU cost, the game runs incredibly well. Even when there's hundreds of units on-screen and rushing my defenses, I see no drop in FPS. I have yet to make it to a final horde when the numbers get in the thousands, but I have a feeling my computer will be able to handle that too. And while the graphics are crazy AAA hyper-realistic, they do look very nice and detailed, so it's not like it's just thousands of untextured blobs running around.
Overall I'd probably give this an 8/10. The only things really holding it back is the language, and the pathing. I also hear of other people encountering a bug with their mouse clicks becoming unresponsive, along with a few other notable ones, but I've yet to run into them.

The old cliché “variety is the spice of life” has been the driving concept behind in a number of noteworthy games. Early coin-ops such as Tron or Gorf were conceived around the notion that an amalgam of four or five different diversions could be a bigger draw than merely offering players a single game. Kid Chameleon for the SEGA Genesis/Megadrive tweaked the idea further by offering a protagonist capable of transforming into a variety of forms- each controlling remarkably differently and having their own distinctive set of abilities. The latest title to be built around this design philosophy is Concursion- the inaugural title from Los Angeles-based indie studio Puuba.
A short introductory cinematic sequence divulges the game’s retro-minded ambitions, as a princess is abducted by a reptilian interloper. Fearing apprehension by a party of pursuers, the scaly antagonist covers his tracks with a shower of emerald-colored crystals which trigger the appearance of the game’s eponymous dimensional-portals. Beyond the obvious reference to Miyamoto-san, Concursion flaunts its appreciation for videogame history across a procession of referential humor, with stage names which parody renowned games. The game’s overworld also draws inspiration from Nintendo- with a succession of stage maps much like Super Mario Bros. 3. But where the plumber-protagonist frequently had access to branching level paths, Concursion stubbornly extends a linear trajectory.

I was looking for a new time-waster and although I normally purchase a cheap SHMUP or side-scroller from the PSN but I saw a couple interesting reviews for Concursion and figured I would give it a try.
I knew from the advertising material that it started as a bit of a Mario-Clone but it pretty quickly becomes a combination of the other games highlighted in the gameplay video.  I was immediately reminded of some older Flash games that I had played years ago but the difference was I actually enjoyed playing Concursion for more than a couple minutes.
I have been replaying the levels after completion to go back for the time achievement and the extra Gem Shards that are hidden or hard to pick up, so I can effectively get two/three times the playtime for my money!  (So far I have completely wasted my Friday night and Saturday, ‘cause that’s cool)
I have found myself replaying some levels incessantly, ala SuperMeat Boy, to try and best the time challenge (and also taken a couple breaks because of extreme frustration).  It also has slight puzzle elements that were integrated just enough to not get annoying or change the game.  Sometimes the Maze (PacMan) levels really got in the way of the gameplay, but those seemed to be kept to a minimum.
I loved that some story elements were included and the story itself, but I would have liked to see more, more voice work and MORE story to tie everything together.  Essentially the worlds get “broken” apart and we are running around in them, but the story itself did not need to seem like it was also a little broken.
I thought the music was awesome, it helps the transition elements of gameplay a lot and is generally fun to listen to even when you are replaying a level over and over, I did not find myself muting the music or replacing it with my own, as I often do playing most games.
Unfortunately, I disliked the artwork as much as I loved the music, but as this is a first attempt from Puuba Studios I figure you have to choose where your money and effort go to.  I did eventually become accustomed to it, and I did like how many of the bosses were animated.
I would love to see this game re-skinned and released for PSN (or Xbox Live) with some extra DLC, I would buy it again.  Oh, and how about a Level Editor? I would love to remake some SMB levels with some of these weird tricks thrown in!

If you are new I wouldn't play this game. There are way to many microtransactions. If you are worried about the grind, don't worry. The game literally doesn't start until you are lvl 65. Everything before that is pretty much a tutorial.
Is the game Pay2Win? Yes.
2 Earring slots have to be paid for with real life money to be unlocked. It used to cost voidstone (One of the myriad of in game currencies) they took that away so they could take cash from their dwindling player base.
Other features. They sell tier 2 gear on the market. People argue that this isn't p2w since T3 has to be earned. The time it takes to earn T2 is a tedious task. As I mentioned there are numerous currencies and notoriety you have to earn with also a bunch of different factions to even buy or use items. The grind for that is tedious, time consuming.
Now that isn't bad, grinding and earning gear. That's what mmo's are about right? Except you spend weeks grinding out currencies because there are caps to upgrade ONE piece of gear. Here is a feel for how many pieces of gear that you can all separately upgrade. Helmet, cape, shoulder, chest, glove, legs, boots, 2 earrings, Neck, Trinket, 2 rings, Synergy Crystal, Seal, Planar Focus and 6 planar essences, two one handed/1 two handed and 1 offhand weapon. All of these require multiple upgrades, cost a VAST amount of in game currencies that is almost impossible to earn unless you have a credit card readily available.
And the ongoing insult if cannot perform is “You’re a casual”. Which in itself is dumb. I understand mmo’s require time to get ahead. Yet in this game playing 20 hours a week isn’t enough. You will be left behind in the dust. 40 hours, you better be grinding the whole time. But I suppose non-casuals have played since launch, have been around long enough they already have all the p2w features that Trion has now implemented in their need for greed. So they don’t get the short hand of the stick.
PVP
… that sums it up honestly. Skill? Non-existent. The maps are neat, the queue times are fast and the idea sounds awesome. Pre-65 pvp doesn’t happen unless you like waiting around for hours for one to pop. The game is heavily, and I mean heavily gear dependent. Forget going into pvp thinking you have a chance. You will just be called a casual because you didn’t swipe your credit card before entering. Since pvp gear caps at about T2 you can buy T2 gear meaning you are good to go for pvp. A fully geared player vs some fresh 65’s could 1 v 5 and not drop below 90% That players skill could be average while the other 5 could be the best players on rift but now are in noob gear. Gear literally makes or breaks everything.
Conquest. Don’t bother max gear people just get in premades and walk all over pugs who attempt it. Open world pvp turns into a one sided match. Credit card vs non-credit card. Other factors are people who spent a lot of money on game get awesome boosts like fast mount time, faster mount speed through patron which plays into pvp when someone can cc you and run away and you will never catch up to them. (Very annoying and boring when you actually are winning a fight against team credit card).
So if I had to list pro’s and cons.
Pros:
-	Pve is fun, boss fights are fun.
-	Wardrobe is really sweet. All armor collected becomes unlocked as skins for free.
-	Traveling around isn’t very expensive using the teleporters.
-	Teaming as you level up isn’t bad. Can queue instant adventures, dungeons, and just join adventures who make their party public to share quest mobs.
Cons:
-	Pay2Win: Buying Earrings.
-	Gear grind defines your skill.
-	Pvp is not fun unless you have gear. Give a toddler a remote detonator for a 50 megaton nuke, and an Adult who is in the Navy Seals a hammer and a one mile gap between that toddler. That defines pvp. The most skilled can get stomped on by those with better gear. Hammer vs Nuke. Who wins? *sigh*
-	Hard to earn currencies, high currency requirements for upgrades, and weekly caps keep you from doing upgrades for weeks on end for one of your 25-26 pieces of gear.
-	Cash Grabs, Cash shops. Taking away from players each update to create a paywall that forces you to buy patron.
-	Getting a piece of gear and realizing you need Planewalker: Water. Apparently this zone was free which you can go there for free but you can’t even equip half the gear. It also drops in pvp and in dungeons and usually has nice stats for fresh 65’s.
-	Game gets buggy, really laggy as well. I had some weird glyphdebugger come up that forced me to reinstall. I have had a few other friends and family also run into this where they couldn’t even play the game for the entire day. Sucks when you actually pay for patron and can’t even use it. Miss out on daily log in rewards and minion quests that you are trying to collect.
Indifferent:
-	I don’t mind that there is a cash shop. Selling new souls. (Another powerset tree for your class) That’s fine. They worked hard to create that, it’s an addition to the classes and as long as they aren’t some god mode autowin tree I am fine with it. Charging for some school girl outfit, or a katana is also fine. That is cosmetic. A mount, who cares? Other various features like that, that do not make one stronger or better is fine with me.
In the end.
I don’t mind a company trying to make money. That’s what businesses are designed to do, if it works, sell it. Yet a business is also supposed to try to support its customers, and Trion doesn’t do that. They seem to want to walk all over their player base and then milk them for more money while making them grind for months on end for gear. So if you want to quit your job, stop going to school, leave your kids at the orphanage and become a recluse then this game is for you. Or you can use your credit card daily if you don’t have the time. Either way it’s a cash sink or a time grab. Game is fun, but with all of this…it isn’t.

I thought this would be like a bird's eye version of something like Dead Island but no, it was pretty disappointing.
Firstly, the combat is easy but actually quite annoying, it doesn't feel like you're controlling your swings as a lot of the time you character will swing in a random direction and then they just do random extra swings all the time which makes it a bit tedious and very unsatisfying (unless you use the OP heavy swing in which case you one hit cleave everything near you).
The developer's idea for the quests are really dreadful in my opinion, it's not an open world game as the screenshots make it feel like but instead it puts you in a random scenario whenever you accept a quest and the quests are just "walk around aimlessly and try to find this NPC then talk to them, they go and gather some random loot off the floor or grind X amount of zombies". This quest system completely ruins my immersion and makes it really unenjoyable to do the quests.
The menu systems was a dreadful idea, rather than putting everything on just one menu screen with different tabs they have several different menus with several different tabs, despite have a huge amount of space on all the menus where they could have just put the camp level up and the normal character level up instead of making 2 different pages for ONE BUTTON.
Another thing concerning the levelling, it wasn't really very clear which levels are which, so as far as I was aware at the time there was only one menu (I later found there were multiple after not being able to accept a quest because I was only level 1) and I ended up putting my XP into your "Camp Level" whereas I needed to put it into my "Character Level", so then I had to run back outside of the little crappy sewer place and grind some more zombies for some XP. Having the 2 different levels is a completely stupid idea IMO, there really isn't any need for having to level the camp and your character seperately. You also have a shared XP pool for everything, so camp level, character level, any other perks and whatnot, they all share the same XP pool.
The building (despite some reviews saying the building was amazing) is really quite frustrating with there being huge invisible barriers around everything that stops you from building there. Also having to go any collect so many materials from different places with this not being open world means you have to run back and forth through quest boards and then have to scamper through fairly big scenario zone places looking for tiny little objects that are difficult to see, also not knowing what they look like so you have to check every tiny piece of loot.
If you've ever played some of the Divinity games you can hold ALT to show nearby loot so that it's easy to find, well, yeah this game doesn't have that and instead you have no idea whether there is loot on corpses or not so you just have to run around them spamming F, and most of the loot that you'll find on shelves is really poorly visible.
There is also no camera rotation and the zooming is really nasty, the camera obstruction when you're inside a building is also really unnecessary and really quite lazy. On top of that, you have 3 set zoom levels which you cycle through but wait, it automatically super zooms you in when inside buildings. What's that, you've zoomed out again? Well, if you walk out onto a balcony or something that doesn't count as inside and it will reset it so that every time you walk back into a building it just zooms you in really far again.
In addition, when below half health you get a REALLY loud thumping noise which not only a) does not have to be so incredibly loud and b) why do you even get that on HALF HEALTH? You're barely even low and considering the fact you can just run around whilst healing it doesn't mean you have to worry at all.
Finally, I would like to note after about an hour I finally decided to refund after in order to do even the next quest I had to go and repeat a couple of quests looking through the scenario zones for some junk and one of the items it didn't tell me anything about how I go about obtaining it so I didn't want to spend the next 3 hours wandering around on the off chance I find it.

It has to be said Montague's Mount is a game panned by both gamers and critics alike, Criticism are made of its 'drab' colour scheme, 'pondorous' pace and obscure puzzles. Indeed, many describe it as plain boring. Now, I'm not saying they're wrong, but I feel many missed the point of this game hugely.
Before I go onto why I adored this game, I'll address the flaws.
1: Yes, it's way too dark and finding things is a nightmare among those incredibly shadowy graphics. There is also a real lack of structure in the way the various objects are scattered around. Sometimes they're in a logical place, others it's just pot luck if you find them.
2: Yes, it's slow. CoD this is not. The lack of any run feature is annoying, but given how the game starts out it becomes clear WHY you can't run.
3: Yes, the slow pace can get a little boring, with the wandering back and forth to do this and that forcing you into long slow journeys.
4: And yes, some of the puzzles are absolutely dreadful. The spinners puzzle was quite simply too much for a video game, requiring the gamer to understand morse code. It's something you don't need when you want to just play a game.
5: And also the saves were a little glitchy. Sometimes a checkpoint would actually erase a previous section you'd just done, meaning you had bits of your pick ups but not all.
However, the flaws are compeltely outweighed by the strengths, or maybe it's my kind of game. And here's why.
Montague's Mount is intense. It is easily the most intense game I've ever played, and draws heavily on psychologically disturbing themes to make its mark. For me they work brilliantly - the island is MEANT to be drab and depressing as we are dealing here with some incredibly heavy themes. They get deeper and more powerful the further the game goes, and as far as video games go in general, there are such emotional and psychological barriers this game goes past that other games simply haven't gone near.
The plot is also as well-crafted as it can be without spoon-feeding you all the answers. This is a story designed to make you think, to make you put pieces of a fragmented world together - to decide for yourself the greater meaning of it. The game gives you the tools to make you arrive at your own conclusions without those plot devices feeling half-baked.
I admit some of the mechanics of the gameplay were messy, but the game wasn't about them. The puzzles and methods were just a way of putting together a story, and I admit also that they didn't blend as seamlessly with the story as they could have. Indeed, in many ways the game could have done better without the puzzle element as it doesn't seem to match the greater story overall.
But if you can live with that, and want a dark, intense, psychological thriller with emotionally powerful overtones and disturbing themes, this is unique and hard-hitting.
I can understand why many would hate this, but I felt totally engaged by it throughout and would recommend it on the terms I have done. If you want quality puzzles and amazing graphics, Portal 2 is your man. But if you want plot which cerebrally engages you, this is a fine way to spend your time.
The current sale also helps hugely.

First and foremost this game is a shame and a loss of real potential. Sadly, and arguably prematurely, my rage got the best of me and I quit the game in the middle of saving the professor at the university.
First off, the terrible cutscenes, despite people arguing in favour of them and saying it only looks so ugly because of the purposeful grain effect; they are actually ugly because they are console port level badly encoded and low res. 720p for a videogame cutscene in this day and age is just mindboggling.
The game itself is rather polished, I Experienced no bugs at all during the gameplay; however it still manages to feel like a beta. Small things, such as system shock-esque recordings found everywhere are a great way to add depth were it not for the fact that they are always in the same room as key characters; as such you can never hear the recordings over the repeated bleeting of "HEY CARTER!" "CARTER OVER HERE" "CARTER WE NEED TO TALK". The voice work itself is decent and gives a real sense that some of these characters have been through some♥♥♥♥♥♥as well as the writing being good enough to make me disappointed in my not wanting to play further. However there are some glaring core gameplay issues that are only highlighted by the game being well-optimised.
Despite being a game where tactics are key the mode that allows you to control your units doesnt actually stop combat to allow you time to give orders but only slows it down, with each character having 5 orders to choose from this is rarely enough time to make a plan of action before your squadmates are being shot to pieces. To add insult to injury the squadmate AI is abysmal, they stand in direct fire way too long and within seconds can lose their entire health bar, they often avoid grenade damage by choosing to run headfirst into groups of 6+ enemies, they repeatedly ignore the regoup command and will often find some creative but painful route through the map (always leading to 6+ enemies) and finally and most upsetting of all there is no order/action to take cover.
I can see looking at the skills how they may become better with ranking up, however at the rate at which they rank up you will spend 2/3 of this game babysitting the AI.
This game reminded me of those awful missions that have always cropped up in FPS's over the years where you have to rescue and escort some sub-seasponge level intelligence character through a field of flying metal and blood and they would spend half the mission standing in direct fire when they shouldnt or repeatedly walking into walls.

Frustrating mechanics and general-lackluster polish abound: bad AI, a system that punishes full failure over partial failure (if your squadmates die, they stay dead going forward through the game, but if YOU die the game loads to last checkpoint; thus, if you lose one of your agents, the best strategy is to wait until you too are killed). Skill progression is unexplained, in that your hero (I forgot his name. . . Carter?) aquires alien tech/skills without any explanation how. There are cool moments, but in comparison to other games of its ilk I found it wanting.
It does have some retro, 50's - early 60's charm, but just not that great. Maybe I need to play it on a console for full effect?

TLDR: Excellent replay value and content already for a game in Early Access.  9/10 with lots of potential.
Pros:
+ Resource system is interesting, and revolves mostly around maintaining upkeep levels rather than direct expenses
+ Graphics look really nice but are optimized enough at this stage to keep the game running fine when (literally) thousands of zombies are on screen
+ Interface and commanding of units and buildings feels really fluid and polished.  (I.E. you can d-click peices of wooden wall and mass upgrade them to stone wall as you can afford it, rather than clicking them individually).
+ Steampunk setting is really cool.  Voice acting of units plays into this well as they'll make light-hearted jokes while still mostly appearing to take colony defense seriously.
+ The ability to pause with spacebar and issue commands, much like the Baldur's Gate-type RPGs of old feels really good for this kind of RTS.
+ Mayor system is really cool.  You get to select a choice of 2 random passives when you hit certain population goals, and they're random, but more or less within a tier (i.e. the 2 passives you can choose from when you hit 1,200 pop are generally a lot stronger than the 2 choices available when you hit 200 etc...).
+ Placement of your buildings matters.  There are certain buildings with a large tile proximity around them, such as the Market, Bank and Warehouse, which each amplify the resource output, or upkeep cost of certain buildings within their range.  This gives an added element to city planning.
+ Every military unit is interesting and has a purpose, allowing for different defensive, and offensive (when you attack zombie cities) strategies.
(Neutral): You can't save your game, except when you quit out.  This makes accomplishments very rewarding, while also making mistakes very punishing.  The game doesn't hold your hand at all, but it's not terribly difficult to figure out how things work after a few runs.  I personally love this approach, though it's possibly not for everyone.
Cons:
- Music is repetitive (though pretty good).  I'd bet they'll put out another song or something to break this up in the future.
This game is awesome.  I've already put 30 hours into it after less than a week of purchase, which is quite a lot for an Early Access title that just recently dropped to Steam.  I'm quite impressed and am excited to see where it goes.

In a games industry, that has started to move away from RTS in recent years, It is nice to see indie developers continuing the genre.
They are Billions is a great addition to the genre, even in its early form. The Survival mode is hard, even on the easier difficulties. In the later days, one simple mistake, one slightly underdefended area, can cause you to lose your entire colony. As I have learnt to my detrement several times. The game can be punishing, but it is simply a case of getting better. With the random generation, each game can be easier or harder. You could have only one town on the other side of the map, you could spawn right next to one. You could start in an area with a large amount of resources, or you could have a small forest and that is it. Don't mistake my paragraph about difficulty for a criticism. It's not a bad thing to not be handheld.
Difficulty due to my own poor play aside. The gameplay is solid. The units are fairly well balanced, and the zombie hordes don't get to tough too quickly. Unless of course you decide the best course of action is to attack the town next door when just starting out. The Graphics are nice and crisp, and even the voice acting is fairly good for an indie game. I have heard worse in some AAA games. I'm not sure if it is the game or not, but the screen very occasionally flashes, but that is probably as I am running it in borderless window, so that could be user error on my part.
The only problems I have encounted so far in the few hours of play are pathing issues, where units just run repeatedly into a very menacing wall, or each other, rather than going around. There is the odd spelling or grammar error here and there. I also feel the selection box for the Oil refinery is a tad too big, as the smoke seemed to stop me selecting anything behind it.
The fact that those are the only issues I had so far is a testament to the developers really as far as I am concerned.
In its current state, and from the first few hours, I feel this game is well worth the asking price. If you are looking for an RTS you can get easy wins with, this might not be the product for you. If you are looking for an RTS that can give you a challenge, look no further. I look forward to reviewing the complete product when it is done.

After tapping both the "Yes" and "No" buttons several times in response to the question "Do you recommend this game?" I realized that I'm kind of indecisive about the whole thing. My view on it is completely torn down the middle. In some ways, Rift is incredible. In other ways, it's downright terrible. In the end, I find that "fifty percent" isn't enough to recommend the game. I have to say, sorry, but you should pass on this one. But don't leave without reading why I think so. There's a lot of ground to cover.
Before you comment on this, I reinstalled the game on the Glyph launcher and stopped playing it through Steam. It might not track my hours correctly, but I have been playing for about 3/4s of a year.
1) RIFT borrows
from WoW, especially early iterations of it. The UI is the same, the cooldown and GCD system is exactly the same, the crafting, the queueing for dungeons and battlegrounds-- I'm sorry, "warfronts"-- the talent trees (again, this is more like early WoW, not the garbage "three choice blocks" WoW has nowadays), the combat, the classes, and even the stats each character needs is strikingly similar to WoW. If you've played WoW, you can pick up RIFT very easily.
2) The talent trees are intuitive and creative, because they can be customized. You can have a build-your-own-spec based on three trees you can pick from and place points in. This makes for a very fun experience in creating your own class. Many of the best specs in the game were found by other players just messing around with the custom talent trees.
3) There is something in the game called "Instant Adventures," a sort of endless barrage of instanced questing zones that you can enter with 20-something people. It's the dungeon instance 2.0, and works great. Well, while you're leveling, anyway. After you're max level, they're obsolete.
4) The graphics are breathtaking and realistic. I definitely prefer it over WoW's cartoonish style.
1) At first I thought to say "This game is well-populated" but then I forgot that only two servers really are. The rest are deadzones, especially the oceanic server. If you play in the UK... you will be forced to play on a North American server, in timezones opposite of you. That... sucks.
1) At 65 (the current max level) the game sort of... halts. You will not be getting into raids very soon, and I can guarantee you that. You know why? Because you need a certain amount of "hit rating." This is RIFT's equivalent of "item level," except to an insanely unfair degree. The grind for gear is literally
, and not at all fun. The methods to obtain gear may also be totally obscure to you when you ding 65, as it was for me. There is no set path to take. You
get gear by either
warfronts (and no, you can not buy gear with the tokens you obtain from warfronts-- you have to get it from the box), or by doing what is called "Nightmare Tide Expert Dungeons" which are exactly that-- a nightmare. Neither of these things are the least bit fun to do, so naturally, it seems even worse when you're doing them just to upgrade gear.
Now, when I say you
get gear, that's because gear isn't guaranteed to drop in the box you get for winning a warfront. You have a
at it. And if you're like me, you will lose so many games that the chance at gear is even lower than average. I have so many unspent favor ("honor") points because none of it goes toward anything special. Apparently, people tell me that I will use them later to "upgrade" my new gear I get from the boxes from winning warfronts. And it takes tens of thousands of these tokens just to do that. And yes... you
to upgrade them, because otherwise you won't have enough hit on your gear to do raids... or anything else. So even after you get the pieces you need, you still have to lose hundreds of warfronts, get tokens, upgrade all the pieces... it's awful. God awful.
So, you don't like to PvP? Okay! Do NTEs instead. And wipe constantly on bosses. When you finally do about twenty painful dungeons and get a piece of gear you need, you have to also upgrade THAT with tokens. But not with the PvP tokens. You need "fragments". These rare, coveted Fragments of Darkness and Fragments of Madness are mostly obtained through daily dungeons queues and months and months of weekly quests. I say you'll be doing them for months, because that's how long it'll take you just to upgrade a few pieces of your gear. It is the most sluggish, hellish, most boring end-game I've ever played in my life. It isn't even an "end game". It's just grinding gear. "End game" should imply being able to do things at the end of the game.
Because of this boring charade, most guilds are casual, because they're forced to be. There do exist raiding guilds, but progression is so slow that you never hear a thing about them.
More than one person in RIFT has explained this to me: "Trion Worlds made the grind so long because they want you to give up and shell out the dough to buy all of the gear for credits". At first I thought "that makes no sense," but now... it kind of does. You can buy gear with real money in RIFT-- for hundreds of dollars. No average-income Joe can just buy the gear and P2W because it's so expensive. But over months of time... an impatient person could very well buy the gear they need one piece at a time, and it all adds up. I already know a few people that dumped real money on gear pieces because the grind is so bad. I think what they're saying is true. It's all because of greed.
And no... being a patron ("subscriber") does not help with this. You have to grind it out just as much as the freebies do. Which brings me to my next gripe:
2) Patron status sucks. I get nothing for being a patron exect a crappy weekly "gift" (usually a trove box with junk in it worth nothing) and something called "affinity"-- yet another type of currency stacked upon the already massive mountain of currencies in the game. Affinity buys you mostly casual, cosmetic crap, and very few things that improve your character. Yes, patrons get bonuses toward mount speed and experience... but the increase isn't by very much, so it's not worth it. You also get "loyalty" for spending real money in the game. Loyalty also gives you mostly-cosmetic junk. No gear, though. Or anything else that might be useful.
3) Notoriety ("reputation") grinds. Because having to grind out a faction's rep on top of grinding for gear and grinding for crafting mats adds to the fun!
4) Dream orbs. You remember enchants in WoW? Okay, think of those, but only imagine they once in a while gave you a useless stat on your gear that means nothing to you, so that you're forced to sink hundreds of gold on them to get the stat you need. Sounds like crap, doesn't it? Well, that's because it is.
5) Lockboxes and troves. Trion will dangle rare prizes in your face in hopes that you're stupid enough to drop a hundred bucks on these "limited editions troves" they release. They do that by showing you this sparkly, awesome mount that can be won inside. The chance at getting these mounts is extremely low. It's been tested a few times by people with even more time on their hands than I. You'd have to buy over a hundred boxes at five bucks a piece. Come to find out, people
stupid enough to buy these, so they keep making them. Keep it up, RIFTers. Keep being part of the problem.
6) Plat is hard and slow to earn unless you spend real money on tradeable credits
"Gear-grinding" is used as "game content" in place of real game content.

Just like the Santa Blanca cartel manufactures some of the world's purest cocaine, Ubisoft has made here a wildly addicting, top-quality open world shooter in the form of Ghost Recon Wildlands.
The huge map is a wonder to explore, with plenty of locations and activities wherever you go. The excellent graphics and lighting give this rendition of Bolivia the beauty to match its scale.
Wildlands takes place in July 2019, where the Santa Blanca drug cartel has effectively turned Bolivia (or at least a portion of it) into a narco-state. They've grown so large that the government has essentially allowed them to operate, given that they don't go wild and kill their people (which they still do). After a bombing at the US embassy in La Paz, as well as the torturing and execution of an American DEA agent, both attributed to Santa Blanca, the US forms a four-man task force to deploy to Bolivia and aid the Kataris 26, a local rebel force led by Pac Katari, in destabilizing Santa Blanca. In addition to the cartel, the player must also contend with a Bolivian special forces group called Unidad, which maintains various military bases throughout the map.
Others have complained about the story, but it isn't half bad. The player-character and the AI team members seem a little stale, but I generally enjoyed the other characters (except for El Comandante. He felt a little shoe-horned, for some reason). El Sueno, the leader of the cartel, is honestly pretty badass.
The map is cut into provinces, most of which are the territory of a cartel buchon. Each province is its own miniature story arc where intel must be gathered to start revealing missions on reaching the local buchon, and as you work through the various provinces, you slowly move your way up the cartel's leadership hierarchy. A nice, steady progression is achieved as the player slowly works through these individual areas, charting the regions, completing its missions, and finding minor intel to reveal the locations of guns, attachments, resources, and "rebel ops" (side missions that level up rebel support abilities).
Wildlands supports a multitude of playstyles, with an abundance of guns and attachments to fit any role. Gunplay is satisifying. Shooting over longer distances takes practice as bullet drop is simulated. Nothing beats the feeling of pulling off sniper shots over hundreds of meters once this is accustomed to, however.
The game features a basic skill tree for a handful of categories such as personal effects, drone upgrades, and items such as mines and C4. Skills must be unlocked and then upgraded using skill points, which are earned through levelling up and as pickups throughout the map, as well as resources (gasoline, medicine, comms tools, food) that can be found scattered throughout the map in the form of small caches or larger convoys and guarded transport aircraft, just begging to be stolen.
My only beef with this game is the seeming lack of endgame content. There isn't much to do in campaign mode after completing all of the story missions, but after reaching a maximum level of 30, players can activate "Tier One" mode. Here, tier points are earned instead of XP, and players start at Tier 50, levelling downwards, in order to unlock periodic rewards such as a few cosmetics and guns. Despite Tier 15 and Tier 5 featuring a badass cosmetic and gun respectively, not only does it start to get a little too grindy around Tier 25-30, but the difficulty is locked to the highest ("Extreme") at Tier 35~. This is a mistake. Extreme difficulty feels almost untested; it's cartoonishly difficult, in which perfect stealth is almost your only option, as enemies will detect you quickly and then dispatch you immediately in less than a few seconds with unrealistic accuracy and damage. Tier One rewards are hit-or-miss anyway; generally, they aren't worth it, in my honest opinion. Players can simply opt out of Tier One mode altogether anyway, including being able to toggle it off and on once it's already started without losing their current tier level.
But don't let any of that dissuade you. I know there are people who have sunk hundreds of hours into this game. I'm simply an impatient person who tends to jump from game to game if endgame content isn't particularly strong, and the Tier One struggle pisses me off. I got this while it was on sale for $30, but I would honestly buy it at $60 as well. An extremely solid game.

This game is a wonderful compilation of some of the greatest homages to martial arts films of old. The music and stages together with many unique fighters combine to create a very unique experience unavailable elsewhere in the genre. It comes with the full barrage of game modes expected in a fighter (Arcade, Survival, Team Battle, Training) and a Tournament mode for extra fun.
The controls for this game are simple (Punch, Kick, Weapon, Dash) and are easy to string together to create combos in the system using directional modifiers (Ex: P,P,P, --> P, K, K, --> K, <-- K). As nearly all 2D fighters it features quarter circle specials, supers, throws, and blocking by holding back. Where it excels is how easy it is to start doing cool things right away. Unlike its predecessor (Kings of Kung Fu) it is very responsive and you will not find yourself battling against the controls. The AI is very forgiving at easier levels and presents a decent challenge at higher levels.
If you have ever enjoyed watching martial arts films with stars like Bruce Lee and Jackie Chan, you definitely owe it to yourself to check this gem out. It is a whole lot of fun, especially if you ever get together with a bunch of friends and play the Tournament mode!

This is a coop game, the actual game itself will remind you that you can play coop with other people by pressing Enter every so often. With that dynamic in the game, whatever you do, will be done with you four AI buddies, that can be pretty derpy at times. I believe you can only get those for non unique guns, which are dropped by bosses or whatnot. There are lots of paintjobs for themr if you want to match your character's camo or not.
The level system is interesting, to be able to attribute your skill points to perks, you got to have helped the rebels in some way or another, you have multiple ressources to tag with a tracker for them to gain points and their support.
Rebels can help you in many ways the same way you can control your squad. I have unlocked the mortar for now and it gets useful once in a while to take out a big group of enemies at the same time. Side missions which are only to help them I think will earn you their support and respect.
Enemies belong to two groups, Santa Blanca and Unidad, you'll have to fight both, mostly separately and sometimes both at the same time. Bots are pretty strong but it escalates pretty quickly when you mess with unidad. They work in the same way the cops woth in GTA, with a kind of scale on 1/4 on how much you've triggered them. Santa-Blanca how ever is the cartel to fight, they have taken the multiple regions spanning the game. Theyr difficulty depends mostly on what region you are in.
The story lins is simple; mess with the cartel leaders and you'll have to deal with the big boss. I am not very far in the story line so far, having killed the under-boss of 3 regions so far.

I just finished 'Montague's Mount' with 2 hours and 10 minutes of in-game time, and I am absolutely blown away. It has been years since I was this disappointed in a video game and/or felt this
by the title's description and the feedback on the Steam store page. I paid less than $2.00 USD for 'Montague's Mount,' and it took me less than 3 hours to defeat it. Honestly, I'm so shocked and appaulled by this game that I want to ban myself from ever pursuing ANY additional PolyPusher Studios projects, and I am loathe to blacklist any developer.
If you want "puzzles" that are difficult only due to horrible frame rate issues and intentionally obtuse clue placement, and the added bonus of spending 50% or more of your time back-tracking at a slow pace, by all means purchase this title. I was initially impressed with the music and the stormy seascape atmosphere, but I need a
more than that from a video game to call it worthwhile. The plot was lackluster, and by the "climactic ending" I was totally disinterested; even the creepy kid failed to impress me after the first few encounters.
I also question the term "psychological thriller," because this video game is barely suspenseful at best, and the completely predictable decline in the main character's mental process doesn't feel psychological, it just feels like lazy storytelling.
When I made the decision to purchase this game, I ignored the awful 'Metascore' (per usual with Steam, especially with Indie games), and focused on the 100% positive reviews in the "Most Helpful" category. I cannot believe that not a single Negative review is visible on the store page, and that seems questionable in my book.

Then there are the puzzles. The good thing is they all make sense within this world, there is no "get the hair from the cat to make a mustache" or other such nonsense... but the puzzles you do get require items that are hardly visible on the terrain. The island is littered with garbage, and there is no indication what is useful and can be picked up and what isn't, so you have to click on each item to see if the mouse cursor changes.
I can only recommend this to people who are a huge fan of both Myst and Dear Esther, and who want the puzzles of the former in the latter game.

I don't like to lose games. Esspecially strategy games. I often spend hours struggling against my enemies and at times a simple careless mistake turns my world upside down and before you know it, I've lost.
They Are Billions makes it fun to lose. The game design focuses around building a colony on an infected world. You are literally surrounded by thousands of infected and the deck is stacked against you from the very start. Everything frome expanding to fighting the infected is a challenge but none of it feels heavy handed. The game naturally progresses the waves of infected that attack your settlement - and with a time limit of 100 days (I've as of yet not made it past Day 59) the impetus is to survive at all costs.
The infected come in several varieties from the chubby tank zombies down to the decrepit slow but dangerous in large packs zombies. The game has a myriad of infected to throw at you and mixes them well as the waves increase to challenge your defenses and tactics.
Overall the building is quite simple and easy to understand but it rewards intelligence and punishes careless builders. Each time a building is killed by infected it spawns more infected based on the type of the infected. Having houses too close to your walls might mean that the few infected who broke through turn into hundreds as they convert your colonists into the mindless undead.
I'd recommend this game to anyone who enjoys a challenge - and this review might be more thorough if I wasnt so anxious to get back at it.

Game is in early access but already there's something I personally don't like about the mechanics. You can wind up building your self into a loss right in the begining. Picture the Mars colony builder where there's only one way to build in order for your colonists to survive and you have this game. Now throw in Zombie attacks. The maps are randomly generated which is fine but most of them have tons of open space where there's not one to three easy to defend avenues of approach in the early game. It takes quite a while to put a barracks up so you're stuck with around five troops in the beginning to patrol massive swaths of land. Sometimes it's so open you find your self dedicatiing entirely too much time running around killing zombies with your begining troops that you don't have time to build for the first on-coming wave. If the designers just took out the requirements for power in order to sustain a certain population of colonists then it might be worth playing. Nothing's more frustrating than trying to get a barracks down and then be told you need an additional worker just to find you can't make an additional worker becuase you don't have enough power. Then go try and build power and find that you still don't have enough of a workforce. It's pretty much the end of the game right there. I wish they had made it more like a starcraft type of building game where there's no real power limit other than supply depots or pylons or such. Take the silly ratio out and it would be a lot of fun.

I will start with the resume of 3 days playing Survival at "Alpha Hive", the first colony... tottaly wiped out at 2nd wave. (Will add some thoughts here: nice game, will build defenses faster)
2nd Alpha Hive... this time not at 100% score (actually at 22%), wiped out... (ok, this is not a nice survival game where i can build a regular colony and survive)
3rd Aplha Hive (decided to keep the name until I won) 10 troopers can hold a lot of zombies... wiped out at 4th or 5th wave
4th Alpha Hive, ok... now i understand this... troopers can hold, but i need multiple defense lines to fall back... wiped out
5th Alpha Hive... nice map, there was a small opening in a forest i did not see... wiped out at 3 mins by a single zombie (just sat there looking at them rampage through my city)
6th Alpha Hive (patience...)... decided to go for science, so started to improve tech and get new things... also, my defense grid got better, lasted until 7th wave i think? the smart zombies got rid of my tesla towers before the defences, so everything went dark
7th Alpha Hive, the map is great, already know the units, best lines of defense, defend the tesla towers and upgrade fast... also, decided i needed to expand fast to have more resources... everything ok, my army of troopers, snipers and lucifers can beat everything... but this is the first time i made it to the last wave.... totally wiped out.
8th and 9th Alpha Hive, lasted until last wave, and then wiped out. again. i realized i was low on resources, and that 2 lucifers and a Titan can hold a breach with support of some expendable troopers and a pair of towers...
10th Alpha Hive, expanded, got the 2 lucifers+titan on every access, got rapid response troops at center, towers (not all executors), snipers, walled zones so i could retreat to an inner wall like 3 times... everything looking great. The final wave comes... (at this time i could also calculate the day they were coming thanks to my bro making a record of the dates on the last two games)... to my entire satisfaction, defences are working, outer walls fall, but the lucifers make their work, the titans fight well... and then, disaster... the citi was extended to the map limits on east and west, but not that much on north and south... north wall, 2 hordes get together, so it's a biiiiiiig wave there.... they break the walls, kill the lucifers... swarm the titan, and i'm recalling all units from other zones already pacified, but they are too far away... a few zombies pass the 2nd wall... and get into the city (i know... should have expanded the defences north and south too)... all the units got back to the main center, i demolished all houses in the path of the horde... died anyway.
11th Alpha Hive, same defense strategy, but no upgrading until the end... so i just expanded and defended, got my Lucifers+titans+snipers combo, and at last moment, upgraded all turrets to exterminators (veeeery expensive, but didn't need those coins anymore) also build a small fortress arround the main base... just in case.... the map was hard... very open at borders, but the defences at west and east were specially effective and defeated the hordes real quick. Redeployed those troops to north wall, which was having a hard time... lost a pair of titans and lucifers there, but held... in the meantime, a small canyon pass, almost entirely built with walls and defences had its first line of defense overrun... didnt notice at first... got message of troops dying and notice... (biggest wave ever... probably got two hordes together again.) so, secured al the other walls with minimal troops and send everyone to that zone, troopers are faster, so, they form a human wall (they are all heroes... dead... but heroes) lucifers fall... titans are the second line of defense and die... we have killed tons of zombies but there are more... and then, worst case scenario, everyone on the interior main hall fortress... got a single lucifer there holding, but all the slow snipers from other walls arrive at the center. after a tense 30 seconds or so... we won... (also unlocking the next map :) )
-----

After 3 days and 11 iterations of a colony... 10/10 for me. (yes, that's a perfect score, but dont know any other game that mixes so many aspects i love about building and defending... it's a very personal score.)

I REALLY REALLY WANT to like this game but no. Just no. This game. This game is RIDICULOUSLY bugged. I've had this game since it was released on steam. The concept is great, the art is gorgeous, but the bugs ruin every aspect that is the least bit enjoyable. This game is FAR from being a real non-early access 1.0 game. It just wasn't and still isn't ready...
As of this comment, this worst bugs are:
1. pirates attack random enemies, not the ones closest to them (even though this was "fixed" in the recent update)
2. moral. wow moral. I have the game set to "easy" (where moral only decreases at 40% of "original" speed) yet every crew member needs to be payed literally every 5 minutes. The average crew member needs to be payed about 100 gold every time he is angry. If you try-hard, you can get about 200-400 gold per 5 minutes. Lets see here... lets say you have 10 crew members. Now you defaulty need about 1000 gold every 5 minutes JUST FOR PAYING THEM TO KEEP THEIR MORALS UP, but there is literally no way to make that much money in that time frame. The game is unbeatable. Your sailors will become too greedy because you are making them rich but not as rich as they want so they will start to try and kill each other and you. good luck with that.
3. i've got a decent if not good computer... and i still lag, especially during ship encounters with difficulty over 5 (the ships are starting to get pretty large) and i have no idea why since, you know, THIS IS A PIXEL ART GAME.
4. Food. Don't even get me started there. I finally progressed far enough so that i have several fisherman and cooks to keep cooking fish to keep everyone fed. Before that, I had to try-hard for gold and then spend literally 80-90% of it just buying food from a town to keep everyone from starving to death. New players beware: if your pirates don't kill each other because they aren't the richest of the sea first, then they will surely starve to death.
5. Not exactly a bug, but for $15 this game needs to last longer. I'm assuming that if there were no bugs and the game mechanics were actually balanced, from the current state, you could beat the game in like under 5 hours, even if it is your first time playing.
tl;dr: this game is PRE-early access material. It is only proof of concept. The bugs could be acceptable for an "out-of-early-access" stage, but c'mon... the game mechanics are not even close to being balanced enough for an average gamer to enjoy the experience.

The Bureau: XCOM Declassified isn't bad, it just isn't very good. It's a bit threadbare, feeling like several incomplete ideas that have been rushed out the gate.
Realistically, I suspect The Bureau was completed on a small-ish budget after lingering around in development hell for a few years. Something about the game makes it feel like it's ten years or more old, if it wasn't for some of the DirectX 11 effects looking so sparkly it'd be easy to think it was from the early 2000's. Many of the locations are bare and empty places, feeling like they've been built in a rush, and often with several such vacant sets stitched together without any combat or events to distract, assumably to give the impression of covering a lot of ground in a mission. Other areas have clearly had some time and attention spent on them, and the locations and missions waver back-and-forth on this attention / quality scale, leaving the experience feeling quite jarring. You'll wander from a well-realised street, strewn with debris, bodies and signs of previous life... into an area that feels like it's been imported from a PS2 game.
The mechanics of the game basically play out like Mass Effect's combat, or Mass Effect 3 more specifically. It's a cover-based shooter where you run around with two squadmates, you have abilities with cooldowns, can issue orders and give movement directions to your squad. Enemies come in multiple varieties, some with shields and some with armour, with a few enemy types creating interesting tactical choices (a unit that supplies shields to all other nearby units, for example, if taken out the shields drop and make the fight easier). Unfortunately, where Mass Effect shines in making you care for your squad, here they are just flat cardboard bodies waiting for you to pull their puppet strings. They also keep respawning in front of you whenever you cross through a 'loading door' (frequent area transitions where the game loads the next section as your character very slowly opens a door and looks left and right before giving you control again), which is a bit distracting.
In fact, I felt the game lacked polish in general. I fell through the level geometry and died twice in eight hours of play, once whilst just running down a straight corridor. Audio logs can be found and played, although walking away from them they fade until inaudible (if I have to stand still to listen to them, they may as well be written text!). The controls aren't terrible, but movement feels clunky and stiff, for example; when you run there is absolutely no strafing, not even in a limited fashion, leaving you to clumsily course-correct with your mouse as you charge forward. You also tend to pop in and out of cover randomly at times, especially if strafing in cover, and controlling your squadmates feels awkward (fortunately the game slows down time during this).
Much of the story is told over radio as you run between fights, although there are some cutscenes that deal with exposition. The game also uses a dialogue wheel, just like the Mass Effect series, allowing you to choose between being vaguely rude or agreeable, it's a nice enough touch, although it felt a bit redundant with such small scope for actual meaningful choice. Levels are basically linear paths that open into combat arenas, the main missions last 30 to 60 minutes each, with side missions from 15 to 30 minutes roughly (I only did a couple, they felt fairly pointless). The game isn't overly long with six main missions, the story is mildly amusing with some interesting characters (although the main player character really started to grate on me). The plot felt like it tried to raise the stakes too high a number of times implying that Earth has basically been wiped out and already lost by the midway point of the game, then later claiming it's not as bad as implied, which breaks the suspension of disbelief somewhat.
Imbetween the missions, the game flirts with the idea of being an XCOM-style strategy game where you pick missions and kit out your squad, but with only six main plot missions and (I believe) seven side-quest 'minor missions', it doesn't feel like there's a lot of variety or choice. The equipment feels limited, with only a handful of weapons to equip and the only other equipment slot being a 'backpack' which acts as a kind of modifier for ammo, health regen, or ability cooldowns.
Overall, not a bad game, just not a particularly good one. It feels like it didn't succeed at being the mixture of genres it wanted to be, and it's not particularly good at being any ONE genre either. The plot is so-so, and the clunky and unpolished feel doesn't help. But if you don't mind all this and want a simple squad and cover-based shooter, this might entertain.

A dying game...
I've been gaming for years. I've spent thousands of hours on more MMOs than I'd care to count.
In all that time, I've learned to recognize various signs a game on it's last leg has.
One of them is the increase of micro-transactions. Rift has recently taken various steps such as removing rested exp for free players, limiting dungeon charge accumulation for free players, etc to make their patron packs seem more attractive. This isn't an added benefit for payers, though; it's taking away what was for months (over a year, if memory serves) given to all just to attempt to extort players.
Another is the ramping up of grind. If you aren't planing on paying, then you're missing out on huge increases to your currency gain. One of the most important things for upgrading gear at the time of writing is Abyssal Accelerators, which are bought with Abyssal Crusader Marks. Patrons get an increase of 40% to their marks gain by default, with additional increases being available from "loyalty" (AKA pay more than a threshold to gain this buff) as well as consumables, going for more than a 200% increase.
A third sign is an increase in premium events. As said before, this is simply an attempt to extort money out of it's remaining playerbase; an event shows up with a mount, pet or other vanity item and demands money out of it's players for it. Usually, it includes a lockbox or some other RNG mechanic to obfuscate just how much money the item actually requires on average.
Next, the addition of previously non-existant "Login each day to win prizes!" mobile-style coercion systems. They provide no true benefit to the player other than forcing him to loyally login each and every day for the possibility that he will buy something, and only give the smallest benefits in return.
The last sign I want to talk about is the increase in NPCs to hide the fact the game world is empty. The carnival of the ascended is runing at the time of runing and I have seen a grand total of three other players taking part in the activities, at prime time.
On the other hand, I saw several dozen "reveler" NPCs; they have nothing to say, don't serve any purpose, and in a healthy game wouldn't exist.
In a healthy MMO, there would be plenty of players to render on screen instead and those NPCs would be considered a waste of valuable resources. Rift, however, is not healthy.
So, all in all, while I very much like the game I cannot recommend it due to it's current business practices, the population of the servers, current progression system, monetization model etc.
In it's golden days, this was a great MMO. I might even go so far as to say that until recently it was very decent and a reasonable choice for players looking for a fun free experience. But those days are clearly over and as it stands, this is just the desicated remains of what was once a good game.
If you choose to disregard this warning, I hope you have either plenty of money or plenty of time, ideally both; because without either, you won't get far.
-Sleepy

The way in which the environment is being portrayed is quite frankly amazing (note though that you need a fast machine to see it in all its glory). The voice acting and music are also spot on. So is it all great?

As the story comes out (told through snippets from a book that are left laying around) a picture is built up of a character that is trouble by many things.

Hocus is a simple puzzle game that was originally built in Adobe flash and was heavily inspired by the illusions from M.C Escher. The objective of the game is to simply move a red cube around a geometric shape until you get to the exit point. While the game was conceived in a couple of months, the development itself took 8 months in total and the brain twisting genius responsible for this was a Turkish developer named Yunus Ayyildiz
who openly declares to be also an avid puzzle lover.
With over 100 levels and a intuitive and friendly level editor where you can make your own levels, you should be challenged and enthralled for a number of hours. Easy to pick up and control at first, it does eventually become very daunting with the later levels as you meet the perplexing shapes head on. Thankfully the Zen ambience will soften that frustration and remind you to take deep breaths.
Below are three levels I made with the level editor.

That was tough. That was really tough! You navigate a cube through 100 levels of 3D opitcal illusions. And it can get really hard. Some levels I blasted through in 10 seconds, others I spent 10 minutes on, so it varies. On quite a few occasions I just had to look up a guide because I was completely lost!  The game only cost me $.50 and I it took me 4 hours to beat, so I would say I got well over my monies worth! Definitely reccomend if you're looking for something challenging!
Game opened my mind as to how one can get so creative with optical illusions.

Early Access Impressions:
They describe the game as hard. I will say it is unfinished and unpolished. Too few options to mitigate the difficult situation that comes as the result of the random map. The final "bosswave" is way to hard compared to rest of the game. The easiest setting is boring, with almost no mobs to train on. But at least the final wave is winnable. 56% is ok to play for a new player, but the final wave is punishing. 100% is just mayhem.
The Good Stuff:
-RTS vs the environment: No stupid AI that needs to cheat. We just increase the numbers of zombies thrown at the player.
-Unusual theme for RTS.
- Random maps.
- Detailed adjustments for difficulty.
The Bad Stuff:
- The final wave is way too difficult compared to the previous wave. You can be really on top of the situation. Cleared the entire map. But to win the game you have to defend on all fronts, which is more than 4 times as difficult as just defending versius one front.
- Some maps are really bad and difficult to defend in the beginning and vs the final wave.
- You can be really unlucky with the resources.
- Impossible to build on top of the resources.
- At this difficulty, many, if not most people that buy this game will never see any of the other maps.
- Lacking a non-ironman mode: I wish it had save and load option, so one could try and fail without having to start all over. Could be with achievements disabled. Just to have the option for training wheels to figure out unit compositions etc.
The "I wish for" stuff:
- Quit/surrender button: Too many clicks to give up on a map that is unwinnable.
- More hotkeys in the build menu.
- An easier first map, so you can actually have a tiny bit of progress.
- Maps with fever fronts which makes it easier to defend.
End thoughts:
This really has potential. But the some elements really ruins the fun of the game. I will continue to play this when new updates arrive.

shaolin vs wutang is not your typical fighting game. visually, it's pretty good to look at; from the characters, to the moves, this will definitely remind you of the old kung fu movies from the 70s or 80s. on top of which, the dev has even put in background music from those movies itself! so in terms of both the audio and visuals, this game will definitely take you back to another era, and in that sense, it's very well done.
if you're looking for a competitive fighter however, the likes of street fighter, or king of fighters, or guilty gear, etc. then just maybe you're looking at the wrong game. the controls here feels a bit more loose, and personally, reminds me a lot of games such as say ... mortal kombat I perhaps. not entirely refined, but sufficient for a casual gamer who wants to jump into a fighter, without worrying too much about over-elaborate combos and all that.
the moves available to each character is unique, and fun to look at, especially if you do manage to pull off a decent combo string. the commands however, are identical across the board for all characters it would seem, but again, this would suit a casual gamer too, as they wont have to memorize a whole ton of different commands, but instead just pick the fighter they like best, and still could execute their moves without problems.
all in all, this is a fairly unique fighter. it's a lot of fun, even for myself who have spent over 20 years playing the likes of street fighter, king of fighters, tekken, etc. i really do like the nostalgic trip down memory lane, and that i dont have to overthink things playing this.
besides, where else are you gonna pit donnie yen against jackie chan or bruce lee? highly recommended for fans of those old kung fu flicks, as well as anyone who wants to pick up a more casual fighter. looking forward to what other polishes and add-ons the dev will throw at it on full release.

While I must say that I found Hocus very interesting and entertaining, it is not as simple as just giving my recommendation or not. There are many factors that can change people’s opinions on this game.
Personally, I felt like the gameplay was a bit two-sided. Pun intended. The main reason being that while the puzzles are at times a bit challenging, if you cannot figure it out, all you really must do is just keep trying. There are only so many directions you can move, and odds are you will find the right path eventually. However, I must say that this game would make for a perfect exercise to get your mind thinking outside the box.
The sound and music design of this game was almost perfect in my opinion. It really goes hand in hand with the simple style of the overall experience. I almost fell into a Zen-like state while listening to the calming ambience of wind chimes in the background. The only suggestion I have to future players of this title is to not have your speakers to loud. While the wind chimes are very calming, if too loud, they are ear-splitting.
In my experience, I was able to beat the game in less than 2 hours without a walk-through. Some players might say that there is always the level editor, so that adds as many hours as you would like. However, players such as myself typically do not fiddle around in level editors.
As decent of a game this is for killing some time and exercising your mind, I cannot say that it is worth your money. At least not at full price. I say this due to it being free on mobile devices. Now if you were to tell me that you would rather play it on PC or MAC, then it would be perfectly fine to buy a copy. At that point I would recommend you to at least wait until it goes on sale.

This is one of those games I wish I could leave a neutral recommendation for. Not an upvote, nor a downvote per se.
It's not a terrible game, but it's not a great game either. I guess because it is early access this is to be expected. I mainly purchased it because I love classic Kung Fu cinema, and easily get the references in characters, soundtrack, etc... Thought it would be fun to have in my collection and play around with.
It's actually pretty decent for a 1 man developed game. But if you are looking for a solid fighting game, I'd look elsewhere for something with more polish. This one is just passable right now. It still needs a lot of tweaking and balance. And since it is just a 1 man team, I'm sure this will be a slow process.
As of the time of writing this you have a decent sized roster of combatants, with single and offline multiplayer, and a decent selection of stages and a few modes of traditional play.
Where the game is having issues though that I hope might be tweaked would be the stiffness of moves, lack of diversity in pulling off secials, and other minor annoyances. Every character I have tried has the same list of required inputs to pull off specials, which all stem from quarter circle moves. No variety. There are also throw moves, and "supers" which are earned when filling up a meter. The "super" moves are all short in animation, and all performed the same way. This really gives the player zero incentive to practice the exeuction of moves for every character. I hope this is something that is fixed later on.
In any case, I do love the homage to classic Kung Fu cinema. You have a good roster of fighters featuring mock ups from various movies including characters like Pai Mei, Beggar Su, The Drunken Master, Bruce Lee, and many others. Each with their own fighting style that I hope is expanded upon.
Bottom line, if you like classic Kung Fu movies in the vein of Shaw Brothers, Golden Harvest and others, give this one a look. However, if you want a competent fighter to stand up to the likes of the Street Fighter, King of Fighters and Guilty Gear types of games, I'd probably avoid this one.

Hatoful Boyfriend is a visual novel about birds. It is actually a parody of visual novels, with the classic character archetypes you'd expect in a school setting in an anime/visual novel: the childhood friend, the snob rich guy, the athletic guy...
What differentiates it from other visual novels is, of course, the fact that these characters are all birds. That makes many normal situations inherently hilarious. However, do not dismiss it as just a comedy game. Beneath all the "haha, birds" is a strangely compelling and engrossing story. There's a surprising attention to detail, from the random bird facts it throws out sometimes to the well-thought-out world full of interesting characters.
I have few complaints about the game, but the main one would be the lack of an "auto-skip only seen text" option. To get all the endings you need to replay the game multiple times, which is immensely helped by the auto-skip button. However, the auto-skip will also happily skip over unseen content if you let it be. That can lead to missing certain scenes.
Still, I really like this game. It was far, far better than what I expected and is probably one of the best visual novels I have ever played. I also hate it. Because now nobody will believe me when I say that a game about birds is so good.

Quake is one of the best FPS videogames I have ever had the honour of playing, initially I felt that the campaign was too short I realise that I first did a run-through of this game of the Easy difficulty, which may alter the playing time. Overall, I feel that this was a good purchase and is a new favourite from id Software.

The thing is, most big budget shooters like Call of Duty have set the example for shooters, but they have set a bad example that has lead to the downfall of the FPS genre. It is actually kind of sad, really, to see that games like this one just aren;t made anymore. Quake ism prime example of a game made in a time when gameplay was put over graphics and story, which is how it should be for most FPS. One of the very first FPS rendered in true 3D graphics unlike games before it like Doom, Quake is filled with run-and-gun action, a variety of weapons and enemies, and John Romero's amazing level design. Sure, the graphics are certainly arcadie, but that is what gives the game it's charm. Unfortunately, the graphics and animations are a bit grainy on the steam version when compared to, say, the Dark Places source port. Another problem is that the music is misiing from the steam version, which isn't neccesary to enjot the game, but it would have been an nice addon. Overall, this game will give you far more action than almost any other shooter out there, and for a low price of 10 dollars, Quake is a game everyone needs to play. You are not a true FPS gamer if you haven't played Quake.
