EDIT : I'm pretty sure most have noticed by now, Scott had posted an apology. Scott, you may never read this, but you're one of the very few devs I actually respect, admitting your faults takes bravery, especially towards a massive community. I look forward to the updates and I wish you luck on your future projects.
Since I've been seeing too much unfair bad reviews going on about how the fandom and games are "cancer", and as well as stupid "good" reviews not giving any reason whatsoever as to how the game's good other than "it's cute!", I'm going to try to make a fair review.
Now, before you leave a nasty comment telling me to kill myself for being "autistic", how about you actually READ before you slam your fingers angrily against the keys on the keyboard (And I know people will do exactly that just to get the enjoyment of attempting to "anger" me). I'm not going to focus on the fandom, the fandom shouldn't affect your view of any game anyway.
I may be no video game expert, I haven't got THAT far into game, but I already noticed a couple of bugs.
1. There are long pauses in-battle from time to time, and sometimes the enemies will get two turns on hitting you before you even get a chance to fight back.
2. I don't know if I'm the only one getting this issue, but in the overworld, you can't move diagonally, and sometimes "Freddy" will get stuck if you try to move.
3. Sometimes it will skip a character and move onto the next one without even choosing a move. Again, I don't know if I'm the only getting this issue or not.
Aaaand... onto the problems, besides the bugs.
1. You run into a battle almost every other minute... not even, more like every 15 steps you take to progress.
2. It may have been an early development, but I was ecstatic to see a 3D overworld, only to see a pixelated version of it. Of course, this may be because of the program he uses, even Clickteam Fusion has its limits. Although, I will admit, he could have tried to make it a bit more... pleasant to look at.
3. The textures and meshes look rather blurry, it feels though as if they have been stretched out and just imported right into the game.
4. This has a little bit to do with the bugs, but I honestly wish this had been bug tested before being thrown into the steam store.
5. The overworld pixel of what is supposed to be the character you play as... is just Freddy. Ok, I get it, there's forty characters to play as in-game, but this is why RPGs take a long time to make... and which is why it would be quicker if Scott had a team.
6. It wouldn't have hurt for there to be SOME dialogue other than just Fredbear telling you of what's happening. I know that animatronics are technically emotionless creatures that can't return a "Hello"... in REAL life. There's nothing wrong with spicing up some personality for the characters, or making them exchange dialogue between each other. This was one of the things I was hoping to see in the game, character development. Maybe Scott purposely left them without personality for us to decide who they are, but honestly... it IS nice seeing their CANON personality coming from the creator himself. (Now, I don't know if there is more dialogue or not, I've only played for four minutes).
7. This also has to do with characters... Spring Bonnie and Mangle's genders are HEAVILY debated, Scott knows this. They're only robots, of course, but the arguments are rather tiring and just cringey to read, and it seemed he had only fueled the fire. Knowing him, he likes to mess around with his fans, but after a while, it just gets old.
8. And this, THIS is the biggy. You are given NO information about the attacks. How many turns does this last? What does this do? Does it buff anything? Does it heal you? Does it debuff anything? And no offense... the names of the attacks could have been better. It would have ALSO been nice to learn new attacks or improve a character's stats as you level up... then again, you don't even KNOW the characters' stats. Let alone you can't even check your enemy's stats, the enemy's health is only shown if it's a mini-boss or a boss battle.
Now, with those issues out of the way... I do believe the game is redeemable.
However, it will only be redeemable if Scott works hard, or hires a TEAM to help him out and do some MAJOR updating and bug fixing.
That's the main issue here, Scott believes he can do everything by himself. However, an RPG isn't THAT easy to make. Please don't take this as an offense, Scott, I'm not hating you personally, but there's nothing wrong with having a team to help you out every now and then.
Although, I'm not going to assume his intentions, he is a person with thoughts and feelings after all, just like the rest of us. Maybe he had his reasons, maybe he didn't, who are we to judge? Although, I'm not giving up hope just yet, almost anything can be redeemable.
However, if Scott needs a break, that's fine, he's been making games left and right for about a year.
But back on topic, as for the game, I wouldn't reccomend it for now. But if you enjoy the game, great, if you don't, that's ok, we all have our opinions after all.

I stopped playing this game when my first mate started running in circles with a turd in his hand and a turtle on his head.  He seemed confused as to whether to join his crew in the tavern or practice swords in the cabin.  Or throw the turd away.  Or set the turtle down.  Yes, this is a problem, and I doubt the excuse of the crew having freewill really addresses this.  But more on this later.
Initally it was a fun experience, though the lack of intuitive tutorials made it a little rockier to start than most games.  The overall look of the game, the sound of the music, and the grunts of the pirates were all quite welcoming as well.  As I conquered each island or pirate ship, things got progressively harder in a maneagable sense.  I hired my first mate and named him "Vance the Lance" in honor of the hulking spear he carried.  I got a kick out of his former job as a fantastic male model.  Qualities I definitely need in my pirate crew.
Whatever the case, Vance and I soon had a larger crew to manage, and that's about when the problems started to happen.  Arnold the Brick (because he is dumb as a bag of bricks apparently), had decided he was no longer going to cook the fish he had become so good at catching.  I decided to teach another crew member how to cook expecting this to solve the problem.  Ironically, this crew member nearly died to starvation because he too refused to cook, despite having both the skill and knife to do so.  Meanwhile, Arnold kept providing me fish which I as the player kept placing in hopes of SOMEONE actually cooking it.
The solution to this odd problem was for me to dock at the nearest town and frantically buy fruit for my famished crew.
Now, some would say the real problem here was that the morale must have been poor.  I wish I could say this was the problem, but I had my crew loaded with Rum and Gold, thus spirits were high.  Nope, this was just an example of poor AI.  Which brings us back to my poor first mate.
Poor Vance.  I wanted to help him, but he was so absorbed in his turd/turtle ritual...it was bad.  And that wasn't the only thing I saw.  Many of my pirates couldn't handle things like "crawl over up that ladder" or "walk over there."   I was excited to get cannons, but soon I realized that the AI was very prone to getting choked on that as well.  My cannoneers would frequently take too long to load cannons.  Some would be more inclined to playing cards than loading the cannon.  Your game of solitaire needs to wait guys!  Cannons PLEASSSE!
Then the fights would happen.  I liked the chaos of it all well enough, but sometimes stupid junk would happen.  Like swimming.  My captain has the swimming skill, but he never seems inclined to using it when he innevitably gets knocked into the water.  The knockback can get kinda crazy in the fights too.  Thank goodness there is a reloading button..but sheesh.
Then there was sailing.  I get the use for it, but I kinda wish there were more random occurences that would just happen to break things up.  Something like, mermaid attacks...or giant white whale attacks...or seagull raiding parties...  I don't know...Just something!  Break up the humdrum of pooping pirates derping back and forth on a fictional ship.
The morale/hunger is the last thing that I think needs a bit more tweaking.  Gold is used to pay your crew, which instantly puts them at full morale.  Gold is also used to feed the crew when your sailing.  You can raise their morale and their hunger (how well fed they are) at taverns.  The hunger stat raises reaaaaally slowly, so unless you want to wait all day, your better off buying food for them at the ship (which costs even more gold), or fishing it (which means dealing with finicky AI). They also have to have gold to spend (apparently) to make use of the tavern...but with no way to track what gold each pirate has, it's kinda difficult to keep track of (i.e. When did I last pay them?).  It also bothers me immensly that my captain never seems to eat when he is at the tavern.  It seems he is damned to eating food on a ship instead of with his crew.
Ah well...I bought the game on sale at least, so I'm not OVERLY disgruntled.
Don't get me wrong.  I've enjoyed my time with this game so far...but I think I will stop and wait for them to address some of these issues (hopefully) before I continue my foray into Pixel Piracy.
I'll gladly update this review in the future if some changes actually occur!  Until then, Vance and his turd problem shall remain.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
EDIT:
Thought I might throw some more positives into what I thought about the game:
-Combat is frantic, but I enjoyed the chaos of it.  It isn't so noticeable with small crews, but with larger crews it can be a chaotic blast.
-Creating your own boat is an interesting concept as you progress through the game.  You always have the option of simply taking the enemy boat, but I enjoy plundering them and slowing adding various parts to my own ship.  I'd love to see more cosmetic damage to the ship as you take bombardment shots eventually!
-Charming: I know I said it once before, but I really do like the look and sound of it all.  I'm not a fan of  all the shanties/tavern songs, but I do think that it is a nice touch.  Visually, I enjoy the pixelated nature of the characters and the locales they inhabit.
-Looting makes me feel good, and there is always the chance you'll find something very nice (like a diamond which sells for quite a bit)  I'd love to see more of this expanded, but it seems good enough for now.  I'd love to see plundering expanded (i.e. attacking TRADE ships vs pirate, or attacking cities, or stealing the food stores off a ship)
And lastly, the management is a positive when the game works as I think was intended.  When the AI actually does what you want, and you get into the groove of managing moral vs gold, it is fairly enjoyable.  I would tweak it in different ways personally, but I think the framework in place works well enough. (i.e. I'd make taverns more effective at curing hunger, I'd make paying the crew worth less morale to place more emphasis on buying/finding rum or visiting taverns)

Game has potential but I can not recommend it in this state. Definitely seems unfinished beyond a simple lack of polish. I'll check back in half a year and adjust the review accordingly.
First of all the controls are really tricky. Left-click controls the captain, right-click moves a selected group of pirates to do stuff according to AI. The captain has some more actions available like he can interact with chests or campfires. Usually the pirates don't do what they should. To get them to fish you have to equip a rod every time from deep within the menu. And still they might rather use the training rack than start fishing.
2- Everything's done with the menu and this is really a bad design choice and very time consuming. If I want to check hunger or morale I need to enter the crew menu... also health bars are difficult to spot in tight battle -> crew menu.
Maybe I've overlooked something but that ties in to number 3: barebone tutorial. Some small pages of text. Also they forgot about the cannons. I can't get them to work... (Update: there's a skill for that)
4: bugs. A lot of them. Sometimes you can't access the last enemy on a ship - then you must reload. Sometimes pirates don't follow although they have enough morale and are in the selected group (which is difficult to check btw -> menu).
The looping pirate sounds are probably intended and I find them somewhat charming.
5: scope of content. There are three types of areas: town, ship encounter and island. Fun at first but might get old soon.
I don't mean to hate the game - it has a lot of potential and it's very funny. The pirates drop their poo everywhere on the ship and the cleaner kicks it overboard or sometimes on a pirate and he loses morale - lol.
But just about everything needs to be redone: world map, lack of random encounters, shopping menu, crew menu. Also it's not really "open world" as "open world" usually means "free roaming seemless game-world". It would have been better that way.
Can't even get the game to launch - wish I had read all the negative user reviews about show-stopping bugs

Pixel piracy is a side scrolling pirate/rpg/simulation with rogue elements. To play the game you actually have to click. There is no actual control to the combat or anything else as it is automated so your units hit when its their turn. You can take advantage of this by kiting your enemy to get some extra hits in. It feels kinda like a dice roll because there are evades and dodges and depending on the skills you learned from books your pirate will improve.
To keep your ship going on adventures you'll have to start off with random stats which can really sometimes by chance be your downfall. If your stats are not great your character will not do great until you improve on the stats by grinding on sailing or destroying enemy. This can sometimes just cause you to want to restart the game entirely creating a new captain. The xp system works by killing enemies, using items, or just sailing. You'll also have to balance out everything by feeding yourself and your crew, paying the salary, and leveling them up with books which uses level up points,  customizing your crew into groups, and  building up on your ship with weapons such as swivels and cannon fire. The design on the ship is really fun since you can make it any way you want. Advance levels will involve cannons and other fun mechanics if you get to it.
Though the game offers such fun and quirky mechanics such as shanties, pirates crapping all over ships, fun travel graphics, Animal mounting,  Crap Kicking,  and music, along with great sound effects and music.. The game is suffering from new things such as slow starts, repetitive sail grinds, and low stats character start off which can completely screw you over. I found that the early access was much more fun than the game but if you give it time and invest into the game you'll will find that the later stages of the game gets more fun.

Started playing this game just before and recent big patch, ran great before the patch and not so good afterwards but still playable and enjoyable. i only play singleplayer so my experiance is totally from that point of view.
the idea of the game is to survive and  build a working base (think the Martian), you start off with basic supplies and have t farm up everything else you need, you get a mining tool and rubbish pistol and a tracking device to help you along, its not a hard game and the options to make it harder or easier are simple and changable after you have started which is a nice feature, you can build a base with various addons and furniture for the inside to help you survive, there are a good selection of vehicles each with there own stats. my personal favorite is the G.A.V while it has less storage space its much faster and easier to handle than the Rover.

there is a spaceship which you have to make which you pilot yourself to leave the surface and go into space where you can spacewalk, there is nothing else to really do up there for now, and there is a 2nd planet which is much harder to survive on but yeilds rarer ore for you to mine adding something extra to your experiance.
you cna play in 3rd or 1st person views depending on your preference
all in all while this game is still in its early stages its an enjoyable game, i find it very relaxing (even with the monsters) and i look forward to seeing what future patches add to the game. well worth a look if your into survival games.

StarBreak .
A game I can truly call its own . Yes it does take inspiration from multiple games
but its does them right !
I tag this game as a metroidvania , rougelike-ish, ARPG , MMO.
Why Metroidvania ?
SImple. Any game like metroid or castlevania involves backtracking and item hunting . This game is just that,
to the point where you are learning the maps like castlevania , yes there is RNG for maps , but its low and its hardly noticeable until later game.
Also loot is very similar to games with progressive items like binding of Isaac and Enter the gungeon.
Both passive and active.
Which brings me to rougelike-ish.
I say "ish" because its not completely rougelike. Its mixed , to explain better ill use The Binding of Isaac.
Permadeath is the big "ding" when its comes to the word rougelike. So saying all that , In StarBreak you perform missions, These can be done at anytime at your will, and does not require you to die or restart after completion . Thus allowing total control over building a character!
That winds in with its overall ARPG tag,
This game is a total ARPG aswell, with leveling and item builds , to fighting in various locations fighting massive bosses. Yeah sounds ARPG to me. Your always in the action and that's what makes it great. Never does it draw you to a boring spot in the game for hours!
The platforming is spot on with popular platformers and it does a great job changing the playstyle with each shell you play as. "Shells being the class system in the game"
And lastly , MMO
It is a true MMO , populated zones maxed with players,
Hub worlds packed with spam and 100s of players. Its great.
The best feeling is when you have a team of 50 burn though a level and maybe like 1-2 of you died.
Makes you feel as you were raiding or something along those lines. Total intense action that will keep you coming back
if you are into that sort of fun!
There is NO Pay to WIn, the only thing that you'll be spending money on is convenience , that fact that they allow you to buy shell storage is very nice of them and that should be taken as a reward for our dedication to this game. In my honest standing , these guys need the money. Because ones things forsure, this game will keep on progressing into the future of content and more!
I give this game a 9.5/10 overall, For this game to be this stable and fun at this stage is exciting and makes me hope for the future of StarBreak and the devs.

A decent F-ZeroX clone for Linux+SteamOS (which is rare). Because I am specifically looking for such-a-game, my review will be a comparison of the two (graphics excluded).
Setting up the controls is a bit janky: I tried a generic controller (Nyko AirFlo Ex) and I it would not recognize my Joystick-Right motion while many other games recognize it just fine (Momodora, To the Moon, Jotun, Psychonauts, etc). All preset controllers would leave me spinning in circles. Trying the keyboard controls: Rebinding the space-bar is 'almost' non-functional as it does register as a keybind but reactivates the keybinding act for whatever action you just bound (but it can be 'tricked' to work quickly clicking to a different action in-time). It is actually tied to whatever key is associated with the "ok" confirmation action. Finally I tried my XBoxOne-S controller (as an XBox Preset) but my joystick outright didn't work. However, rebinding it did correctly recognize the joystick-directions and I was finally able to play this game.
Handling feels twice as slippery as F-ZeroX. In F-ZeroX I used the left/right attack bumper for strafing left/right on the track and that is simply not present in Outracer. Also, hitting a wall results in a substantial bump in the opposite direction that seems much bigger then in F-ZeroX.
While I am not very far into this game, I have no idea how to attack. I don't even think that is implemented in this game. Vehicles bump into things and take damage. That seems to be all there is. I can't begin to explain the fun I've had in F-ZeroX, destroying just about every car on a track (while racing) just because I could. That does not seem to be present here.
As a programmer, I feel as though the developer(s) got this game to a runnable state where everything worked fine for them and released it without further testing or improvement. It's sad because it is very close to being a polished game but it seems like theres one little annoyance in every single corner of this game where I just could not outright recommend it.

While most may see this as just another F-Zero clone, yeah I'll be honest, that is kind of what it is, but that doesn't mean it's not worth playing. This game is simple, stright forward, and to the point. You pick a car, and you race on some pretty crazy tracks. While there are many other games on Steam like this, this is a pretty decent one for the price.
One issue I had with this game is the controller setup. You can use an Xbox, PS4 and even a Wii U Pro controller with this game, but you may have to do some rebinding and you'll also need the mouse to move around some of the menus, but for the most part, the controls are pretty solid, especially in the races. Now I'm not pro at AG racing games, so maybe I'm not the best to say how well it handles, but I was able to get through races with 1st place without any issues.
There's also a track editor, although it seems a bit complicated and there's no intro tutorial on how to use it, but all the tracks in the game were made with the editor, so I can imagine some pretty fun creations in here.
The other thing I really liked was the custom music option. The ingame music is okay, but to me it didn't match the amount of hype and excitement I was hoping for. Once I dropped in some songs from F-Zero GX and turned up the car engine volume a bit (It's turned down because of a little bit of sound crackling issues but it doesn't bother me much.), everything was great.
Overall, this is a fun game and it even has 4 player local options. No, it's not as pretty as a couple of the other games on here, but it doesn't pretend to be more than it is while delivering a fast paced, fun experience and I respect that.

This is a fun and enjoyable game from the creators of terraria. However, while this game may look a bit like terraria I would warn that the gameplay is completely different. The game is certianly fun, with plenty of humor to go around, ranging from comical characters for you to hire, to the poop mechanics. The gameplay itself is also entertaining, fully capable of keeping a player's attention for a couple of hours at a time. Sometimes the situations can be a little harsh and perhaps a more in-depth playable tutorial would have been nice, but it's not too difficult to grasp the basics of this game.
The game recently entered full release, however I must say that the game still feels somewhat unfinished. There are still bugs and issues in the game that shouldn't be found in a full release game and need to be fixed. Saying this, however, the creators have been putting out bugfixes like crazy since release and I'm confident that in short time, the game will feel much more finished.
I feel that the game could be much more balanced as well, as all weapons seem to be very clear-cut in terms of what's the best weapon and what's just useless garbage. The pet mechanics also seems like kind of a gimmick though this may just be because I haven't spent much time or effort on pets and haven't found any rewards yet.
I would definitely recommend this game, however, as the price is more than reasonable for what you get out of the game, and I don't doubt that the game will continue getting better as the studio behind it continue updating and bugfixing.

StarBreak is a fun and challenging platformer/dungeon crawler that plays like a combination of Realm of the Mad God and Metal Slug. Though I recommend this game, it certainly isn't suited to everybody.
After choosing from one of four classes (unlocked through exp gained from playing) the player then has to explore levels, fight enemies and eventually kill the boss. Enemies drop stat increases that are capped based on the difficulty of the level and equipment that increase stats and alter your abilities. Ricocheting bullets, bullet spread, armour piercing bullets, to name a few upgrades. I'd like to see more variation, but it still keeps things interesting. The hit-boxes feel tight and accurate, there seems to be no server lag, and I've experienced no frame rate issues.
There is perma-death, and yes, you will die. You will lose your character, you will lose all your inventory (except your stashed items) and you may feel as though you wasted your time. Some people find that frustrating, and that's perfectly fine. I enjoy that death has a weight to it, and that I am genuinely afraid of being killed. I'm terrified to go into the next room in case it's a boss; I'm scared to jump down that hole because of what might be waiting for me; I'm anxious about fighting an enemy that I don't yet fully understand.
Levels are procedurally generated, so every time you repeat a dungeon it's a little bit different. I enjoy them, but I think they're a little too long, and I'd rather get to the more interesting boss fights quicker. The few boss fights I have encountered have been an absolute joy, and so far they've been fantastic, a true highlight. Punishing, to be sure, but oh so rewarding to kill. I'm really looking forward to encountering more of them.
My favourite part of this game is the comradery I built with complete strangers. When you enter a level, other players may already be there, or they may follow you in. Let's say we enter the 1st level with 20 people. The first few sections are an absolute cluster of mayhem and destruction, with enemies mowed down left and right. A few people teleport home because they're low; a few more randomly die. It's disappointing, but you move on. At the mid-boss, a couple more die, lose their character and miss out on loot. I feel bad for them. Now we're a 10 man group, and some of us are low on health.
Despite being low on health, the 10 remaining are strong players, and they all make it to the final boss. But this one is far harder than the mid-boss. At first he seems quick and easy, but the lowest HP member who wasn't prepared for a boss fight dies the moment he gets too close. Suddenly, the boss changes into it's 2nd phase; 2 members are caught off guard, panic, and die. As you're all sure the boss is nearly dead, a few members get too cocky and die getting greedy for damage. By the time the boss falls, 4 of the original 20 remain. The loot tastes like victory, but there was a cost getting here. The fact that death is so harshly punished gives me a real sense of empathy for those that die along the way.
Now onto my least favourite part of this game - the monetisation. If you feel like playing a different class, you have 2 options - die, and lose all the progress of your character, or pay real money and store your character. If you want to store more than 6 items, you have to pay. This is possibly my least favourite form of monetisation. The developers have a great game, and have created inconvenience that you can remove with cash. It thoroughly annoys me, because I'd pay for this game to unlock cosmetics, but I don't want to encourage these atrocious monetisation schemes that revolve around annoying the player into paying. That being said, it could be worse. At least they aren't offering extra lives for money. If any dev reads this, I'd heavily encourage you to rethink your current monetisation.
As a side note, the game is nigh unplayable with a keyboard. If you do not have a controller, do not bother playing. Even with a controller, the controls can be a little awkward. For example, diagonally aiming downwards is incredibly difficult with an analog stick. It's certainly playable, but it could definitely be improved upon.
Overall, I've really enjoyed this game. It's difficult, but rewarding, with great boss design and fun gameplay. That being said, this does not appeal to everyone. Give it a go, but if you find yourself constantly frustrated, find another game.

You are a detective on an underground subway system meant for the robots of the city who stumbles upon a missing persons case. You meet robots programmed for different tasks with different intelligence levels, and ask them questions to unravel the mystery. It's a short game (my runtime was 2 hours), but well worth it for its compelling story. There are some puzzles along the way (namely a cypher and one of those logic puzzles where you match up various descriptors with their owners in a grid, and both of those have a help feature), but really it's about asking the right questions. The animation is minimal, with robots getting on and off the train, and simple movements in the background, but they help to make the story feel more immersive and less like a visual novel (because you WILL do a lot of reading. Fortunately, there is a text speed option, which is handy).
Overall, short, but with a good story. Highly recommend.

Lots of potential here, unfortunately spread a little thin and made near enough unplayable by bugs.
I dare say Pixel Piracy in its current state is more broken than it was when I first played it a few months ago, before the devs claimed it was "complete."  Members of your crew will frequently decide not to follow your orders - this is
a result of the game's morale mechanic, which makes low morale crew members refuse orders, this happens with happy as can be, 100% morale pirates. Sometimes, they'll stand in one place and not listen to anything you say, or even move of their own accord(in order to say, get food, clean or repair the ship). Other times they'll quite happily go wherever you tell them on the ship, but can't grapple onto other ships or an island. In a game where most of the gameplay revolves around commanding your crew, you can see why this is extremely frustrating.
So the game has bugs, those can be fixed, and I trust the devs not to ignore such a glaring issue. What about gameplay? It's... Okay. When I played the early access, I thought it was pretty fun, but it didn't take long before it started to get boring and samey. Now the finished game is out and I find myself thinking more or less the same things. The combat consists of rounding up all your dudes and sending them in the direction of the enemy who is rounding up all his dudes and sending them at you, you meet in the middle and hopefully win. The outcome of a fight is decided by stats and equipment, which is true of a lot of games, but unfortunately there's not a lot of depth or variety to those aspects either. If you win a fight you get some gold, some experience and some (usually uninteresting) loot.
The biggest curveball the combat has to offer is the knockback mechanic, which is far too
a curveball. Even on "easy" knockback settings(knockback reduced to 40%) my dudes were getting knocked back several feet. You don't get enough control over your pirates to do much to avoid it, it doesn't really add anything to the game aside from occasionally instantly killing someone if they get knocked into the ocean. Most of your game overs will be a result of this happening to your captain, and to top it off, if you kill an enemy this way, you can't get the loot they drop. The game's morale system feels a little underdeveloped as well. It's pretty much what it sounds like: if you don't keep your dudes happy they're less willing to fight and if morale gets too low they'll turn on you. There are two main ways to restore your crew's morale: Pay their salary(costs money, obviously) or let them spend some time at a tavern, which is free but taverns are few and far between and you never know if a town has one until you actually dock there. This discourages exploration and makes it advantageous to stay as close to known taverns as you can.
Most of your gold will pay for food and your crew's salaries, the rest you will save up to hire more crewmemebers until you have a big enough crew to take on tougher battles to get more gold, which you'll need because your crew is eating more food. Lather, rinse, repeat. There's variety in the enemies, but only superficially. Mostly, you'll be fighting pirates. Sometimes, you'll be fighting vikings, skeletons, hobos or chinese. Yeah, there's an entire enemy class just called "Chinese." You get slightly different loot from them, but aside from that the only differences are visual, which is hard to pick out given the low detail of the sprites and the visually chaotic combat. It still boils down to throwing all your dudes at them and hoping you come out on top.
So the combat is alright at best, but that's not even what you'll be spending most of your time doing. Most of the time, you'll be sailing between locations. While sailing, you don't really do anything. You watch your crew eat and poop, and listen to them chatter. Occasionally, they'll sing a sea shanty, which isn't very good but if anything it's a welcome release from repeating the same quips ad nauseam. Nothing happens, your ship just sails along a flat, lifeless ocean for a while until you reach your destination. This gets more annoying later in the game as you start travelling further distances at a time. You can sail faster by gluing bits to your boat or with character skills, but spending valuable cash and skill points to reduce tedium doesn't strike me as good game design. You have to go through this every time you move to a different location, which includes heading back to town to buy food and let your crew rest, so half the time you don't even have anything interesting to look forward to. The excessive waiting is what really kills the fun of this game.
All these flaws are a shame because underneath it all there's a fun game that really wants to show itself. Though it doesn't require a lot of thought, managing your crew and gradually building it up to take on tougher fights is satisfying. The music, voices and graphics are all nice, but lack in quantity and get repetitive. It feels like a beta version: a solid foundation, lacking balance and content and with a bunch of bugs that need cleaning up. If the devs continue working on it I still think something good can come out of Pixel Piracy. Unless that happens, don't bother with this.

And during that, you have all kinds terrain, some easy to move over, some extremely difficult. And theres a lot of enemies. I dont want to spoil TOO much of the game, but i DO recommend getting this game and giving it a try, even if you just pop on for a few hours every month or two, as it moves up through development. Before I begin: Don't go down-voting this review because you hate seeing your favorite game getting criticism. Instead, actually read through this review, and take into consideration the things I have to say, as much of what is here could be considered a legitimate reason for viewing a game so negatively. Many issues I will be pointing out here have also been pointed out by not just myself, but others on both sides of the 'aisle'. All I ask is that you allow a guy a moment to offer his opinion.
Seeing as I apparently earned the ire of a few people for being 'negative about a perfect game', I'm rewriting this review to give more people insight into why I cannot recommend this game. I even TRIED to enjoy it, TRIED to play it and see the good in it, even after writing this the first time. As you can plainly see: Not much has changed, and I've only come away from it with more to focus on.
First of all: I still stand by the feeling that this has the 'potential' to be a great game with some pretty interesting mechanics. However, the mechanics are also what make this such a difficult game for me (and others) to like and enjoy. The gameplay is fun when you're on a roll, when you're blasting through enemy after enemy, finding really good gear to use, and just nailing those difficult jumps and attacks when it really matters. But the progression and combat mechanics can also make all of that work you've put into leveling damn-near useless, no matter how good you get.
When you die, you lose everything, including gear and stats. When you enter a new shell, you start back at square 1: bare bones stats, the most basic of weapons, no body or mobility gear, and not one thing to show for the amount of work you put into playing, except for a little pocket change and a tiny handful of experience points. Even then, it's not worth the trouble, as money is currently useless, and your level only dictates which shells you can use.
When out on the field, you pick up stat boosts to enhance your shell's abilities, which is all fine and dandy, as a couple extra HP can mean the difference between life and death. As you collect these stats, you will sometimes find that you max out an ability. This means that you've just maxed out one ability needed for the increase of your shell's MK level! Awesome! But, like I said: You die, you lose it all, and you have to do it all again. The only way to keep those stats is to stay alive through the entire dungeon. What doesn't help is that you have to collect MK II upgrades from harder dungeons, which means...You guessed it. You're gonna lose all that work, and lose that shiny MK II rating. It's not fun, it's not an enjoyable feature, and the only players who claim to see this as enjoyable are the 'hardcore' players, or those who believe the risk-reward system is 'perfect'. Not everyone is a masochist.
If you want to save those stats, plus the gear you managed to scrape up off the ground in a dungeon, you have the choice to purchase the game's premium currency, which can then be used to unlock a shell storage container, allowing you to switch out to another shell when you want to. Buying the currency is the only way to get these handy dandy containers, as, even if you were given the option, you'll almost never be likely to have the cash on-hand to pay for it, seeing as dungeons pay you in literal pocket change.
Oh yeah, you can even buy cosmetics with that same premium currency! But, like every other item in the game, it can be rendered useless, not to mention non-existent, the moment you die. In other words, you're wasting your time and money on something that doesn't even help you. People say it only costs you a few cents, but the amount really starts to add up, as you grab those same items and try a dungeon again. And again. And again. And again. It starts to add up very quickly.
You may be wondering, though: 'Just how easy would it be to die in this game? It all looks easy!'
Trust me. You'll die easily. SO easily, in fact, that you can likely attribute your death to either sluggish framerate, poor terrain generation, enemy placement, or a ridiculous combo of any and all of those things. Or you can attribute it to the often-insane number of players on-screen, which makes jumping and fighting nearly impossible in some situations, and it limits the amount of points you get when you die. Of course, you COULD run a dungeon solo. Wait wherever you spawned in at, give everyone a few minutes to die off or move on, and then you have all of those respawned monsters and a few treasures waiting for you. Just don't expect it to amount to much.
Not only will you be fighting a ton of alien creatures looking to strip away all of those shiny boosts and pieces of gear you've picked up, you'll be fighting the controls as well. If you're using a controller, aiming is VERY clunky, not to mention very frustrating, as it's tied directly to your movement stick (left stick by default, or d-pad). You can only fire left or right, and then diagonally in between those directions. That's it. No shooting straight up or down. There's no precision shooting, and there's little garuntee you'll hit that enemy coming at you at an odd angle, as you have to find that sweet spot to make your shell fire in an upward direction. Controller users also have to wrestle with the VERY unusual right-stick special. Flick your right analog stick up, down, left or right, and you fire off a special skill. It's a pain trying to use that in the middle of a boss battle, especially when you try to quickly go back to your default primary and secondary fire buttons (B and X on Xbox controllers), and more so when you're trying to out-manuever both the boss AND it's minions (wo spawn in so frequently that you'll likely die in a pit of the blasted things).
If you enjoy platforming games, or maybe just enjoy being put through hell for a handful of XP and credits that will do you very little, sure, this game is fun. But for others, myself included, this game just isn't fun. Fighting controls, fighting framerate issues, fighting BS terrain generation and enemy spawning, fighting the game's mechanics...None of that is fun, nor is it worth spending time trying to adjust to it.
And there you have it. My reasons for not enjoying this game, and for not recommending it.

The keyboard control handling is not designed well at all.  Mouse input is not enabled so all of the input must be handled via the keyboard if you do not have a controller/gamepad.  The primary reason why keyboard input is designed poorly which significantly affects the gameplay is using the special combo (its called RS in this game).  Using RS is awkward because either you can use a meta key (shift) plus the direction to boost up/down/left/right (with the default shell) or bind your own keyboard shortcut for each RS direction (up/down/left/right).  This boost requires the opposite direction press.  For instance, if you want to boost forward, you need to hit meta + back arrow.  Its not intuitive and makes controlling the default shell unnecessarily difficult.  It would be so much easier if they implemented mouse control where the boost would go in the direction of where the mouse is pointing.
Input handling for the default shell in my opinion is broken or at the very least horribly designed.  The default shell has the artificial limitation of not being able to move and shoot at the same time unless the shell is in the air.  This limitation does not make any sense and I never played a 2d side scroller that had this requirement.  Imagine playing Contra or any 2d side scroller with this limitation.  Its simply not fun.  And anyone saying 'git good' simply hasn't been alive long enough to understand that the mechanics for 2d side scrollers are well established and adding this limitation does not make sense.
I have heard some say that the default shell would be over powered if they allowed running and shooting.  I say, the rest of their game design is broken if they needed to add this limitation in order to balance the shells.  Running and shooting in a 2d side scroller should be a given.  The developer IS NOT doing anything innovative by adding this limitation and I really do not think anyone needs to 'git good' using such an impractical mechanic.
My advice to the developer is to balance their game within the context of a 2d side scroller.  Allow running and shooting.  Since this game is on Steam, the majority of steam users USE keyboard and mouse input.  Implement mouse aim.  If you do these things, I will change my review as I think the game has potential.
As for now, I simply cannot recommend this title due to the input handling as I think its overall a frustrating experience.

This is a really polished and well executed dialogue puzzle game. It's quite short (I finished it in 2 hours), with some branching dialogue to give replay value. The price reflects its length, however, and it's worth it.
The story itself is excellent. You're a detective robot with high intelligence looking into disappearing robots (known as 'Teks'). You essentially sit on a train that goes around an underground metro that only the Teks use for work. You talk to the various Teks that board your train, and the story is gradually revealed through conversation.
The sci-fi setting, including the robot and sound design, is a great visual expression of this mostly text-based game. Wonderful art. The graphics are very satisfying, and I love the intro to the game.
Definitely recommend.

Subsurface Circular is a nice, short story-driven experience that presents a neat little window into a society of humans and Asimovian robots, with all of the struggles you might expect from humans and robots trying to coexist.
The structure of the game is similar to a visual novel. You are sitting on a train, and various robots enter and exit the train at each stop. Each robot has their own conversation tree, from which you can glean information, obtain or complete Objectives, and learn new Focus Points that you can use to interrogate other robots.
The general flow of the game is pretty linear. Each set of robots that board the train represent a fixed chapter of the story, and you have to puzzle out the right sequence of conversation choices to advance. There are some hidden "side quests", though, and the conversation puzzles are, with a few exceptions, engaging and interesting. The writing does a good job of painting a world struggling with societal problems that emerge from robots becoming more pervasive in a society. The story has a few surprises in it, and by the end, I was pondering some deep thoughts about the world that was presented to me.
The game can be finished in a couple hours, which feels right for the kind of experience being delivered. If you're looking for a short story-focused experience with quality writing, this is an easy one to recommend.

This game is indeed an experience. You have many choices, you shape your personality, you change the fates of other 'Teks', the robot inhabitants that you are a part of. Even though it is short, it is that because of the experience. I'm actually kind of neutral about this game, but I wouldn't RECOMMEND it, per se. Everything about this game shouts "We want to be Mass Effect" - a game franchise I really, really like and I was looking forward to playing something similar, except the devs didn't want to spend enough time on it to actually make it there.
The gameplay itself gets nearest to Mass Effect: It's a three-player team and you give your squadmates orders and they carry it out and you shoot the baddies and I really liked how they put weaponry from their other X-COM game in there. The graphics are ok, but that isn't really a necessity in a good game. They're not Mass Effect level and there are plenty of small graphical glitches. What really ticked me off though was the way the mouth movements coincided with the voice. As in, there is none. The story is chaotic and makes very little sense. Why set the story in the past and then give them all kinds of future tech people in the 2000s can only dream of? It's not exactly alien and it's a bit too late in the timeline to make it look this steampunky. Moreover, I believe the (modern) Enemy Unknown plot and the Bureau plot are some 50 years apart and they still have the exact same laser weapons. But the biggest crux:
The AI is crap. Most of the enemies have a very predictable pattern and will stop at very little to deviate. Squad mates run around like complete doofuses if they're not given orders, unless they're being shot at in which case they will spread their arms and ask for more. You need to manually tell them to preserve their fleshy lives and sit behind cover, but the moment a squadmate falls (or from time to time YOU - because you were too busy instructing your teammates to stop chasing the guys with the laser guns to the fortified position and time doesn't eactly STOP when you're in tactical mode) your other squad-mate will rush out to the fallen's position to resurrect that person. Of course he'll have to, because you have a couple of seconds to get him on his feet or all effort training him will have been for naught. One thing that I particularly like is that some squadmates will go through any lengths to French-kiss a sectopod or an alien grenade. I do appreciate that they don't discriminate.
It's just a few too many genres packed in too little development time. I like that it's also kind of managerially, but at least freeze time and possibly switch to a tactical overview. At the best, let me also plan out my own path to actually make me feel like I'm one of the squad mates. AND FOR THE LOVE OF EVERYTHING THAT IS HOLY TO ANYONE! GIVE MY SQUADMATES SOME ACTUAL INTELLIGENCE!

First of all, this review does not take the almost traditional issues into account that Ubisoft has with this kind of games and multiplayer ( and in particular coop ) sessions.
This game is a beautiful sandbox game that actually runs pretty smooth even on lower specced systems. It reminded me of the first look i had of Just Cause 2 in terms of wow ( or the first time going outside the dungeon in The Elder Scrolls V: Oblivion ). It is graphically stunning taking into account the sheer size of the map.
Keeping the comparison with the Just cause universe, the game has the exact same premise but this time it feels a lot more serious. My experience is that the Ghost Recon games have a detailed "lore" to carry the story and this time it's no different. In that sense this game does not need the multiplayer aspect, but i'm getting to that.
I want to mention the fact that the weapon modelling and especially the weapon sounds are more then good. I found myself taking of the suppresor of weapons to be absolutely thrilled by the gun sounds and how much they seem to be authentic to the weapon model ( mostly :) )
The RPG element of the game also keeps reminding of Just Cause but less oomphy or even more realistic for as far as games go. This is not a bad thing at all. I found myself playing all Just Cause games with a feeling of it being not serious enough, which is OK for a game like that. This game takes that feeling away and i really liked how that turned out.
The Control and behaviour of vehicles deserve a special mention since realism is not really present there, but somehow that adds to the game instead of breaking down the experience. This game is a shooter in it's core and by not focussing on vehicle control, or the need for the player to become a master at it, keeps the focus on the military tactical element of the game. In my opinion that was a really good choice from the developers although the danger of getting bored in vehicles is now real.
As the game stands now with it's patches and DLC it's a complete single player experience worth going for if this kind of game is your cup of tea. With three AI to help you out when you go it alone this game simulates the team aspect that is a returning theme in ghost recon games and again this works very well. The terrible pathing issues with squad based AI as in Operation Flashpoint 2 are far behind us fortunately, the times when the AI starts going nuts is pretty rare and kind of fun when it happens.
Once you get coop working ( again, not going into the long tradition of NAT issues in multiplayer sessions here ) your AI team of 3 men is replaced by the other player(s) and you can finish the story together. As a big coop fan ( i loathe traditional PvP concepts ) i found this game is one of the few big coop experiences that can last longer then just a weekend and with the possibility to mix game difficulty between coop team members ( you can play on hard and your buddy on easy, but still be in the same game ) the threshold of getting into this game is pretty low even if your skill is just moderate.
Conclusion: This "Serious version of Just Cause" is a great continuation of the Ghost Recon series and should keep any sandbox/shooter fan busy for at least 20 hours. I waited for a good price but would have bought this on release if i has known what the game would be like for me.

DISCLAIMER: This game is Early Access. There is only one game mode atm.
One of the most unique games that I've ever played. The only mode out right now is Survival. You pick your difficulty options from: Zombie Population, Number of days to survive. You start out with a single base and 5 units on a randomized map. You need to survive for the specified amount of time while the map is littered with zombies. If you successfully survive the first map, you unlock the next map until 4 of them are unlocked. Each unique map comes with it's perks and disadvantages and it's up to you to strategize on how you want to survive.
Pros:
- Gameplay is smooth and plays like many RTS's out there.
- Each map is randomized in terms of terrain and resources available to you.
- Each UNIQUE map (forest, winter, flatlands, desert) offers different challenges for you to overcome.
- This game is HARD. When I jump into a game, I don't expect to finish the map in one try, and I've failed more than 20 times in the Normal Mode.
- You can only save upon exit, so if you ♥♥♥♥ up you can't go back to a previous save to restart. I really like this aspect as it forces you to be attentive and really plan out your next move.
Cons:
- Some of the pathing at the moment is wonky, but the publishers patch once every week or two so I expect this to get fixed.
- Map Interface is unclear in terms of which tiles are available for me to build on. They need to color-code the tiles for unavailablility when you select a building type in general instead of when you hover over a tile.
- Balance some units. The current meta seems like you never build soldiers and you just mass archers and snipers. I'd like to see soldiers be more useful. Maybe they're useful in later maps but they're not needed on the first two maps.
This game is on track in becoming a classic RTS game. Challenging, yet rewarding and the game is one of the more unique games that I've played in a while.

Do not look at the permanent death as a hindrance. In most games it's a big bummer and in this one... it's not much different. You lose everything you are carrying with you and all your stats return to base. However this game makes it so you feel compelled to do better next time.
The premise is simple: Improve yourself trial after trial. You do not gain Exp in srtings of data to your character. You gain experience by playing the game and feeling how the environment and the enemies move. (technically there is a level system but to be honest here it doesn't do anything)
In a true 2D platformer, StarBreak manages to give you the feeling of transversing a foreign planet, much like Metroid. You and everybody in the dungeon must go forward, defeat enemies and come out victorious without losing your life. And if you do, well try better next life! There are four classes (shells) to choose from once you unlock them all. Each of them have different playstyles to suit your taste.
As you defeant enemies you will come across boosters to your stats. These are divided by tiers in which you have to do a Tier II dungeon to get boosters after you complete your Tier I. This helps build progression.
The best thing I can think that this game has is giving you a goal to work for. Everytime after you die, you will see a list of different statistics showing how well you did in that class. But you also have your own hich scores to beat!
StarBreak makes it so you can massage your own ego by saying that you can do better everytime you die and not just repeating the same process of wasting lives over and over to get the same result.

StarBreak is an amazing 2D side scrolling game, filled with action and A LOT of players! It amazed me at how many people were actually with me while doing an area! 30 People at once, fighting a boss is absolute MADNESS and thats what rocks about it!  Fight with friends or with randoms in completing certain areas. Its so difficult its fun. Not only that, but this FREE game is actually FREE. The stuff that you can decide to pay for are all simple cosmetics that no one will really notice anyway, so it doesnt matter if you actually get it or not. This game was meant to be played, and played for free. Nothing in this game is any sort of P2W BS that many other free games have these days. I believe thats why this game will explode on steam. We just need to give a few weeks, and by then this game will be one of the best releases on steam.  I really do enjoy this game, I play it every day.
The games art style and playtype isn't somethign that you see now a days. It is a shooter, but a platform shooter. It is a platform shooter, but you can only shoot in certain directions. There is no free aim mode or anything like that. Sounds pretty lame doesnt it? Thats the difficulty of it! One of the key points in this game though, is that once you die, you lose everything that the character had! All those hours spent on this character? Ha! To bad! He is now dead, and so is your spirit. You may now close the game to rethink your gaming life. You will feel that a few times while playing this game, but I can assure you that is never the end.
With 4 different classes, each one can become unlocked after a few levels. So if you dont like the beginning class, you are forced to grind on it untill you gain enough account levels to use the next character. One you die, you gain experience based on how well you played that character. It is VERY grindy, but in the end it doesnt really matter ;)
For starters, this isnt a starter game. It will take time to get into the feel of the game before you can really get into it. You in the beginning you may pick it up from time to time, but once you really start to enjoy the game? You might just pick it up before playing anything else that day. Thats how it was for me atleast.
The play style and the graphics are very well done for this game type. The animations and such are very well done too, so bravo on that one!
If you enjoyed Realm Of The Mad God, then you will most likely enjoy this, except this doesnt have all the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that ROTMD had.
The challenge that this game brings is great. Your not able to just pick it up, you have to learn what the game does, how it acts and you have to remember what monsters do what attacks, and what those attacks do. Theres a lot of multi proccessing that your mind has to do while playing this game, and depending on that along with your reaction time will depend on how well you play the game. WIth time comes skill, and with skill comes grind.
The cosmetics that you can buy with real money go away once you die. So, you have wasted money based on your skill. Thats pretty annoying, so if cosmetics could become a perma thing after purchase, that would be great.
The amount of things happening on the screen at once can sometimes be very hard to know whats going on and where. It does help that there is a circle around your own character, but when there are 20 people in the same area, its hard to keep track of where you are. Maybe if you put in a color system, where the player is allowed to change the color of the circle to whatever pleases and catches there eyes better.
Not a whole lot that I can think of at the moment. But once I do find some more stuff I will be putting it in as it comes up.

Similar to the other games, the music and art are delightful, and the story is very pleasant. Subsurface Circular has different gameplay elements compared to the other games, which offers some new perspective.
I have only two dislikes about the game:
-Apart from the voice announcing at which station the metro is arriving, there is no voice acting, and as it was brilliantly performed in the previous games, I was hoping for more on that.
-The story was quite short, as were the stories in the other two games, but here it felt like it could have been longer.
Apart from these dislikes, the game is quite enjoyable, and definitely worth buying.

If you're looking to get this game simply to buy a shooter, I'd advise against it. If you're intrigued by the setting or you'd like to get a look at XCOM from a different angle, I think this game is a good fit.
The idea behind the story is intriguing and while the execution of said idea is very basic at times, I still think it is quite enjoyable. All of the characters you meet are quite basic as well, but they are well defined and memorable. The choices you are given to impact the story feel quite artificial, but are handled alright.
The story definitely delivers on giving a fresh view on the story behind the XCOM project.
As a cover-based shooter the mechanics are solid, with only minor annoyances. Good aim and fast reactions are important assets, however the focus of the game lies on using the abilities of your squad-mates as well as your own to take out key targets. You don't have to be an excellent shooter player to take on the higher difficulties. The interface provided to use the abilities and command your squad works very well (I played it with a controller). It is an important part of the game to learn how to deal with the different kinds of enemies and later on which targets to take out first. The AI of your squad-mates is a bit dumb at times, however I haven't got the feeling it is quite as annoying as other reviews make it out to be.
The "boss" fights in the first few missions feel a bit drawn out, and you'll spend a lot of time running around the whole battle field just to get enough ammo to deal with the enemies. This however gets much better as soon as you discover stronger weapons, at which point it's just about picking the right weapon for the job. The information you get about weapons and other equipment is not very detailed - I would've liked some more extensive explanations.
The Bureau is an interesting mix of strategy and shooter elements. Don't expect the detailed planning of other XCOM titles and don't expect a shooter that relies only on precise execution either. I for one found this mix to be a very enjoyable use of my time.

Lots of things to love about this game. Gameplay is addictive, it's all the right amounts of pirate sim and strategy. My biggest concern before I bought it was that I'd be clicking my index or middle finger sore. Not at all! Fit for a quick casual game session.
Do I recommend it? Yes.
That being said, I consider this game to still be in beta. I can't believe the developers released this game in it's currently bug-riddled state. I write this review after quitting because my captain grappled (I think) over to a ship that I plundered and sunk. Did this result in his death and the end of my current game? Why, yes it did. Is that the only bug I've come across? Funny you should ask because no it is not. Sometimes crew members won't leave the ship (this is important because they need to offload and get crunk to keep up morale.) Sometimes crew members will grab a pile of♥♥♥♥♥♥and walk back and forth in some sort of OCD "oh no, somebody pooped, what do i do what do i do what do i do...?" I even had a guy who decided that training was more important than eating, so he lost half his health to starvation right before a battle. My mom always made sure I was well fed before battle.
These are clearly bugs. Crew AI is whack. However, balance (specifically morale) also needs a little work. I spend more money on rum keeping my pirates happy than I make pillaging. Sometimes I feel that way IRL, but this is supposed to be an escape. I don't want to spend all my money on booze in real life and then in video games too!
Someone called the art 'unpolished.' Yes. Well. It's pixels. I'm totally cool with it: I get the idea and the game never lags. But wtf is up with the shadows on my ship? They are very bizarre and make the game look even more alpha than it is. Just get rid of the shadows if you can't figure out how lighting works.
Summary:
I bought this game on sale for $7. I think I have probably paid more for an alpha or early access game, but I knew what I was getting into in that case. I sincerely hope the devs fix what seem to be just a few really annoying bugs and minor gameplay issues. If they do, this game is worth $15. I STRONGLY recommend not paying $15 for version 1.0.5 because it is not a finished product. In this age of paying for alphas, it is up to the dev to honestly label a game incomplete. I love the current ecosystem of indie games and small devs, but you guys gotta watch that♥♥♥♥♥♥ or we as consumers are going back to EA. Well, maybe not. But you get what I mean.
Buy it the next time it goes on sale. I assume by then it will be a finished product.

The issue I have with HOI4 are the same as the ones I have with EU4 and Stellaris.
I'm tired of huge price tags attached to minor in-game upgrades which, to be frank, should have and would have been included in the base game in the past. By far and away the biggest problem is when mechanics and features which seem necessary parts of good gameplay (passable management of "dominions" and puppets, production licences and tech trees that aren't vomitously generic in this case) are sold off at a later date.
I do understand that Paradox needs to make money - in fact I hope it does - and that making niche games makes it a small market - but there needs to be an upper limit on the amount that you'll charge people to play a decent game. I'm just not going to pay all that money for HOI4. I bought Death and Dishonour - very disappointing. I can see myself in three years time, having spent £150, only for another DLC to come out and leave me feeling as though I don't have the full experience.
I feel justified in fearing this too, after my experience with EU4. I loved it, played it for ages and then the Common Sense DLC came out and the base game changed. We now could upgrade provinces with Monarch points - but only if we bought the DLC. What actually was a fairly important feature was sold to us again - the choice being, don't enjoy any balancing by playing an earlier patch or buy the DLC to make the game playable again.
Will this happen in HOI4? Am I going to boot it up one day to find out that I can't change my country to a facist government because of the latest patch? Or will the AI be able to use features that I haven't paid to get my hands on?
I rate you as making some of the best strategy games I've played and in the past I begrudgingly payed far over the odds to play them. I'm just not prepared to do that anymore, especially when you're making second rate DLC and can't seem to sort out the AI in any of your games.
I can't honestly recommend this game to anybody who doesn't have literally hundreds of pounds to splash out on it over the coming months and years. If you do, great - HOI4 is a fantastic WWII simulator that you'll continue to enjoy for a long time if you can keep up with the DLC machine, I just can't justify the expense any more.
I'm not going to buy any more of your games or DLC Paradox, you've lost a customer in me. Goodbye.

I think the biggest thing that makes Portal interesting is simply that it's a very well thought out game at every step, there's really no lazy sequences or rooms that had no thought put into them. As a game that really innovated essentially a new style of puzzle game, it was always going to score high for infleunce, but should also score high simply on it's own merits as a fun and entertaining game that can actually make you think. The puzzles are good, the environment is interesting, and the narration/story has a really interesting dark sense of humor.
It's not a lengthy game, I beat it in just over 5 hours myself, but it's an extremely well crafted one. I'm really not sure how one could be into video games and not find something to like about Portal.

On the paper StarBreak sounded quite a interesting concept and i wanted to give it a try.
Unfortunately i remained disappointed.
StarBreak is a action "MMO" platformer with pseudo-random generated levels. You and of other players spawn at a central hub from which you can then join different missions (levels) increasingly difficult. Also and most importantly...there is permadeath.
You can only play one mission as soon as spawned, and you'll have to beat the end level boss before you can pass to other levels.
Still ok till, and here comes the bad part.
Now, what happens is that you and another bounch of players (to a max of 50) join the first mission (instanced), and it's a total wreckfest. As long ad you keep up with the group pace you'll annihilate anything in your path without any effort. Not really fun in my opinion. So i decided to slow my pace and find myself more isolated to enjoy the level. And i did...i found myself trying to explore every area, open every loot box, approach monsters with tactic instead of a "50 people wave of death". Pleasant gameplay....till I get to the boss...and i don't stand a single chance, cause the boss is supposed to be killed in group and as good as you can be, your 80hp will not keep you alive for too long.
You die. You restart with nothing.
You rejoin the first mission and this time you stay in a group, which will rush through all the first mission without even blink once. You will probably also kill the boss and get some decent loot. Then you join the next unlocked mission, and possibly die. Well, prepare to redo everything again from mission 1.
The main problem is not permadeath, many games include permadeath in smart engaging ways. The main problem is that to progress in the game you have team up in a boring level rush just to stand a chance against the mission final boss. Remain on your own and you'll be eventually screwed.
Ultimately 1 day after i played the first time, i didn't feel any need to come back for more.... StarBreak is disappointing
I will come back when the game is properly optimised and teh graphics are stable.

Thomas Was Alone is easily one of my favorite games: it's fun and easy on both the ears and the eyes, but more importantly it had a lot of heart. Unfortunately, I can't say I got the same enjoyment out of Volume: it was witty, but it felt lacking in substance--it was trying too hard to repeat the success of Thomas Was Alone but didn't really succeed for me. I consequently approached Subsurface Circular with a certain amount of warines; happily, that wariness was unnecessary. While not quite achieving the greatness of Thomas Was Alone, Subsurface Circular manages to be far more substantial than Volume: it felt genuine and authentic rather than contrived. The story was very compelling. My one (minor) complaint is that David Housden did not do the music, and I felt like the game's music didn't really do it justice. Both visually and thematically, the game benefits from the narrow scope of the setting. The game is quite short, but two endings make it replayable. I highly recommend it.

A terrible, eye-opening introspective into the heart of the human brain. As you boot up the game, all is aglitter with light pinks and rosy reds; one may chuckle with trepidation as they enter their name into the game.
The primary premise, as most people know, is this game is a bird dating simulator. For many, this "wacky" or "zany" allure will prove powerful enough to purchase and play.
BUT BEWARE! These are but the fickle barbs that the game uses to ensnare and corrupt your sanity and morale!
For the first few minutes, you may laugh or giggle uncontrollably.
"Oh, how silly! How profane!" One might think. But the game quickly darkens as this first euphoria of meeting dims. As you sit in front of your computer screen, flickers of artifical light dancing over your face, you begin to become cognizant of a vague uncomfortable feeling. But still, you paid good money for this game, and you will see it to the end.
But as you meet your fellow bird-mates the yawing void in your soul will begin to grow. Slowly, terribly, a horrible realization will encircle and completely shroud your languid body.
"I'm playing a video game about dating birds."
The statement that rang out from your initial experience as a wholly humorous truth will become twisted and malicious as the truth echoes and reverberates off the fear of lonliness inherent in all humans. Your smile will gradually fade, as you find yourself compelled to gain some kind of value out of your time invested, time - hours, minutes, seconds - of a mortal life that can never be redeemed! Your mind reaches out, grasps as the time flows out of your very reach! That minute there could have been spent picking up your room! That hour sliding past could have been used to improve a hobby, or learn a skill!
In the end, you will silently close the application, and do as most humans do in such situations; attempt to cope. Some will find solace in laughing it up to friends in an attempt to inflict the same pain on another being by convincing them, too, to buy the game; some will silently remove the game from their steam library, never to be discussed again, and others still will attempt to salvage their psyche's by writing overly verbose reviews of the game.

Referencing this “cheat sheet”, I was able to get a good ending fairly easily.  I repeated myself, this time going for a different ending...sometime in this third playthrough, something changed.
By the end of that ending, I was actually enjoying what I was doing.  This “Joke of a game” was actually drawing me in, not because of “bird dating sim”, but because of the actual plot and the compelling characters.  My cheat sheet was pointless, I knew all the names.  Everybirdie had their own personality, and their stories had wildly different outcomes, yet were all tied together to help reveal a plot that actually mattered.
As you play through the game more, and achieve different endings you find little bits and pieces about the world.  You read how birds became the dominant lifeform on the planet, how the human race almost fell to extinction, and how bird politics work.
Each story feel completely different.  They all showcase a huge variety of emotions and social conditions.  One story / ending exists entirely for humor, and no deep thought is put into anything.  You are able to laugh your way through a 20 minute story and have a great time.  You re-roll your game, and suddenly your story is filled with great sorrow between all the funny bird puns.  Sadness then turns into happiness as your story becomes complete.  Re-roll again, now you are exploring yet more bird puns, but this time also the impossible expectations sometimes forced onto oneself from their family.  Re-roll, now genocide is brought into the fold.  Re-roll, we are happy and excited again.
What the hell just happened?  This game somehow managed to put an actual fantastic plot full of emotion and lessons of how the world works into...a bird dating simulator.  Somehow this completely over the top game idea is completely overlooked the more you play it and fall in love with it.
Everybirdie should download this game and try it out because “lol bird dating sim”.  You’ll be amazed as the joke suddenly starts being enjoyable and the fact that everyone is a bird spouting bird puns is able to be completely overlooked.

Aside from the bugs that many other negative reviews have mentioned, the gameplay is not that interesting.
Here's how the game actually plays: You pick a location from the world map and then stare at the screen until the ship arrives there. If it's a town, you get off and sell your loot and maybe buy some food. All stores in all towns of the same rank sell the same items, so you'll stop looking at the store's inventories very quickly.
On Islands, you will watch as your crew automatically fights some enemies, then open one treasure chest which always contains some gold and a few grindstones. You could also trigger one random location that either spawns some more enemies or gives you some useless items.
Against pirate ships, you just wait for the enemy to board your ship (or board theirs if they don't do it), watch as your crew automatically fights them and then click the "plunder" button to get some gold and ship parts.
That's the entire game.
Random issues I have encountered:
- Some UI functions simply do nothing if certain preconditions aren't fulfilled, so you never know if the game glitched out or you did something wrong.
- Crew members simply refuse to leave the ship after a few minutes of playing, making it impossible to board enemy ships or islands until you save and reload the game.
- The minute counter of the play timer doesn't revert at 60 minutes, so it showed my play time as 04:273:18 after four hours and 33 minutes of playing.
- The script is full of typos, grammatical errors and horrible dialogue based on internet memes ("Do you even Arrr?").
- The game does not have permadeath, despite what the store page may tell you. Losses won't make you tear your hair out; they'll simply make you reload your last autosave.
- Even if you turn autosaves off the game will still autosave when you exit.
- To use items, you have to pretend that they're an accesory that you want to equip. The help screen doesn't explain this.
- Also, healing items don't get stronger, so when your crew members each have 500+ HP you'll still be stuck with items that restore 5-30 HP. This will eventually make the game unplayable as nearly every enemy will explode on death and deal massive AoE damage to your characters which you cannot adequately heal.
I admit that I still had some fun with Pixel Piracy and that it has some addictive qualities. However, the price is absolutely ridiculous considering that you can pick up games like Transistor or Trails in the Sky for a similar amount of money.
