I know this is a very controversial game, hence it's mixed reviews. My son was all into XCOM and I picked this up for him during a Steam sale and he seemed to love it, quickly finishing it and it's DLC. It took me a while, but finally through the magic of Steam Family Sharing, I decided to give it a go. And honestly, to my shock and dismay. I liked it. No, it's not XCOM the strategy game. No, it doesn't seem to follow the established "lore", such as it is. But if you can approach the game as a tactical rpg-lite squad shooter with a decent story, I think you'll be impressed. For hardcore XCOM fans, think of this as an alternate universe version of XCOM or treat it as it should be, it's own thing. Now onto the review!
+/- Graphics, being built on the Unreal engine, are pretty good. It has some nice particle effects, models are pretty good, and a decently variety of both enemy models and settings. It very much has the "Bioshock" look to the UI and world, while art direction pulls a good 50's vibe and flavor to most everything. Weaknesses are mostly confined to poor facial animations and sometimes stiff looking movements, but overall the game has a clean and consistent look that works really well for the game.
+/- Story and voice acting is played upon very heavily in this title, far, far more in this title than any previous XCOM game. There are multiple NPC's and your own character that are all developed decently well, if not anything exceptional. You can tell they were heavily inspired by the Mass Effect school of Story but they never quite reach those heights. Most dialog is decently written and spoke well, but while enjoyable, there is no top tier level story telling to be had and much of it feels like it contridicts much of what is presented in the XCOM game. Purists might cry foul and let what is presented distract them, but again, pretend it's an alternate version of the XCOM universe and enjoy the more personal ride.
+/- Combat and powers are obviously the main focus here and this is what drives most people batty. One thing I've learned playing through this entire game is that moving your squad mates is mostly an exercise in futility. Just save yourself some pain and let them move themselves. That doesn't mean you don't coordinate them because this is not a game that you win  by playing it as a shooter. Do that and you WILL cry. Powers are everything in this game and using your teams varied abilities is paramount to winning the game.
Using your abilities will greatly slow down time (but not pause), allowing you to choose both your and your teammates abilities and their targets. In this respect (opposed to moving your teammates) the game works very well. Nothing is more satisfying than being pinned down by a sniper, Lifting him out of cover, and focusing fire to take them out quickly. Or taunting an Outsider, which makes them focus on one character and advance, right into a mine dropped by an Engineer. Realizing you can queue up multiple attacks helps you power attack the most dangerous enemiese quickly. I spent much of combat making sure everyone's powers are constantly being used AND upgrading them in a manner that fit my playstyle greatly improved the flow of combat and made the game more enjoyable. I will warn you, as at the start of the game, when you have few abilities, that the game is much more frustrating as the gunplay is at best, competent. This is not a run and gun game - that will kill you fast. Cover, flanking, short bursts, grenades, and abilities will win fights. Nothing else.
This game isn't for everyone, but if you like more tactical FPS, something that's a little different, and something with an interesting 50's take on XCOM, I'd recommend it. You can get it cheap regularly during steam sales and for those sale prices, it's highly recommended. Final score - 3.5/5

If you haven't tried this game, you've missed out on a truly unique experience in the MMORPG's to date as well as a multi-tier character progression unique to Rift. Tired of healing Cleric(DPS Rogue, Warrior Tank, Mage DPS? Want to Heal, DPS, Support, or Tank? A quick (out of combat) role change (which you can set up ahead of time) and you can...even in between battles in the dungeons or raids. Nothing else new really, but the package will keep you entertained for hours and the customization (at least up to the last 5 levels when it's optimize, or scream in frustration/slow to a crawl) is beautiful. Questing is varied and the addition of rifts (3-7 round bouts with planar invaders), footholds (small scale rifts that can pop up virtually anywhere), carnage quests (killing stuff already? There's a lot in here that just isn't up to snuff in my book.
1. The particle animations are almost non-existant. This is the one thng they could take a few days to improve and get the biggest bang for their buck. Even many spell ranged attacks are invisible. And fire looks like orange blobs. I'm willing to forgive attack animations, but when spells all look the same, it really breaks the immersion of picking my own class.
2. Speaking of classes. Having access to three skill sets is pointless. You really only get a almost-never-useful base skill from your 2nd/3rd trees, and maybe a useful passive? Most of the time, it's for 5 points of a stat. So, if you think you can mix and match trees to make a unique character, shelve that. You're basically just selecting your subclass, and the internet is going to tell you how to play it.
I just all seems so sad. There's so much creativity that goes into the skillsets and classes, only for it to never seemingly make an impact on the actual feel of the gameplay. I mean, the technical differences are there, but if I went for technical differences, I get a lot more out of playing a text-based-rpg MUD.
Like I said, it's something that they can fix with just a little effort, raising the texture resolution for the particle effects and increasing the count.
And I'd even forgive that, if they weren't adding new subclasses all the time, creating the same poor visuals over and over.

While I marked this game as recommended it needs A LOT of work. After 20 hours, on the easiest difficulty, I found it exceedingly too difficult (to be considered "easy") based on the snowball potential of making a single mistake.
In the beginning of the game you're given (4) archers and (1) soldier. With the archers you scout and learn the area you've been placed. However, it's a hit or miss due to the random map generation, you may get a great tree placement to get you a lot of wood resources or you may get completely screwed. Re-start the game early if this happens. You need a healthy amount of wood production throughout the game, but it wanes in value once you reach stone and ultimately iron.
Early on the game is extremely brutal and you will struggle (even on the "easiest" difficulty). Late in the game, once you've established a strong defense perimeter with the top tier units from the Foundry, you'll find the game relaxes *significantly* and become quite easy until the final wave (They Are Billions). The final wave absolutely requires the top tier units from the Foundry to sufficiently defend against the zombies, which also makes any wall units practically useless. If there are ANY weak areas in your defenses at the last wave, it's game over. You lose. Do not pass go. You cannot reload the game. Congratulations, you just wasted several hours of your life!
I've marked this game recommended because it is fun and I would love to play it more, but it is extremely difficult and extremely frustrating... especially for being on the "easiest" mode. The game needs a lot of work in the balance department in terms of game modes, zombie AI, and resource management.
Pros:
* They Are Billions!!! I love the idea of a large horde of zombies attacking your city.
* City defense
* City building -- This one hits home for me because I absolutely love city building games.
* Building Research -- I love the aspect of research to improve your buildings / city. I wish there was more!
Cons:
* Exxxxxxxxxxxxxxtremely long time for a single game & no way to speed it up.
* Walls are virtually useless for the billions phase.
* Tesla Towers -- These things are annoying AF. You have to spend resources and a worker every like 4-5 tiles to expand your city for these things. You need like 500 of them. They are evvvvvvverywhere. They're always in the way.
* Resource generation - Sometimes you see large amounts of stone/iron/gold on the ground and only a single quarry can farm it. In fact, not only are resources locked to a single quarry, but the difference between a small node -vs- a large node is typically 1-2 resources making them completely worthless compared to several small nodes. Gathering wood, power, stone, and iron is all fun and games, but sometimes you have to expand really f'ing far (wasting a lot of resources and building A LOT of those stupid Tesla towers) to reach resources you need because the random map generation f'd you.
* Gameplay - A single mistake can ruin your entire game. There is no recovery without significantly over designing your city which takes a large amount of resources... which the game (on "easiest") is very very stingy with.
* Difficulty - The game is extremely imbalanced in terms of "easiest" so you can learn the game -vs- "brutal" I'm a veteran player and I want to be significantly challenged (or have my score on a leaderboard).
* No tutorial (currently)
* Very little Iron research / use. Would be great to see more metal themed / Steampunk from an Iron tier buildings. (Wishful thinking)

Casting enough of these balls will grant you a dice bonus which will have a powerful effect on the gamefield.
You have workers and they will build a wonder for you if you gather stone blocks for them. Each match will provide you construction resources for the wonder. There are cornerstone and capstone in your puzzlefield as well and you will have to move them all the way to the bottom of the field so it will drop down on the belt for the builders. This is required to make wonders. Any runes that has a stone outlining needs to be destroyed and any corner/capstone needs to be sent all the way to the bottom in order to complete a level. Corner and capstones can't be swapped and will block fire/iceballs.

Of course the chances of those rare drops are still slim but the fact that you can't party with a friend who gets an item that you've been grinding for before you is just such a great idea. On top of that someone who gets a health drop at full health and picks it up, doesn't affect you since it drops for you too. The system also accounts for ninja-ing loot. You can't just pick up an item because it's good but for a different shell, or class, because unless you stash it, it's useless, plus you have what I would describe as personal loot. Meaning that when it drops, everyone can see it but they can't just steal it because you will have it on your client and everyone else will get their own drop of the same item. It's someone difficult to describe appropriately.
I'll end this review now since it's turning more into a ramble than a review. In short this is very much a game to play if you want just endless play time and a great loot system.

A STABBY STAB MC-STABBING good time.
Make no mistake, it's not incredibly deep; the scattered notes you find throughout the levels and the Victorian visual art style really try hard to make Dunwall real, but your imagination does a lot of the not-so heavy lifting (especially with the tired plot line). The game beneath this veneer of a steampunk dystopia is based on the solid mechanics that allow you a variety of approaches to each mission. You can bloody the streets in a wash of bodies or leave no trace at all. It's not even that hard to do a stealth run, so by the end you feel like a super ninja. Beautiful to behold, the action in Dishonored flows much better than Deus Ex, making it more fun to play.

First the Bad:
- Occasional missing sounds during cinematics (the odd explosion / falling debris is completely silent)
- In-game looping-motions are sometimes choppy (the odd guard stading around will jump frames from time to time). This does not happen during combat, only on idle guards / base personnel.
- When speaking with people, Carter has only 1-2 different body motions (both being very neutral). This puts his body language at odds with his speach.
- Due to the above, the game sometimes feels rushed.
- The A.I. has trouble making good decisions from time to time. Expect one of your agents to make a pointless suicide run and get everyone killed every few missions. (Note: played on veteran so this may not be a problem at easier difficulties)
- Face animations need a bit of help, mainly on the outsiders.
- Command "node" sometimes gets caught or cannot go through a doorway. Similar problems occur when an enemy is within range but all paths to said enemy are on different levels or go beyond maximum range.
Second, the Good:
- The voice acting is good. The characters feel cliché, but as the game takes place in the late 50's / early 60's this is somewhat expected and hard to get around. Nailed it with cigarettes everywhere though.
- Storyline progresses at a good pace and ramps up at the right moments.
- Responsive controls help though cover is a bit wonky.
- With the exception of what was stated above, animation quality is quite good overall.
- Alien designs and names remain true to XCOM: Enemy Unknown. No multi-worms or brainsuckers thankfully.
- With the excpetion above, the command screen functions well and activating abilities is largely painless.
Third, some Notes:
- This game is a third-person shooter in the XCOM universe. Do not expect your typical XCOM game. There is no base building, no fund management, no "panic" meter. Instead, you get a fairly solid third person shooter.
- The game mentioned something about knocking out enemies via-melee to capture live specimines. I did this a few times but the result was no different from killing them. Either I did something wrong and completed the game without performing research, or R&D was going to be part of this game but was ultimately stripped.
- The game is optimized for a gamepad. Keyboard and mouse is useable but not recommended.
- Side missions seems to just be a tool for leveling up recruits / Carter. You can unlock some extra packs by doing this but as the game progressed the extra packs didn't really help as different packs were just that, different. No pack is really better than another (so long as you exclude the starting pack which gives no bonuses).
TLDR:
- Choppy animations outside of combat
- Not an "XCOM game" (instead third person shooter in XCOM universe)
- Use gamepad
- A.I.  = Derp
- Would play again
- Praise the Sun.
- Try Jumping.

This game is fast-paced, frantic, loud, nervewracking, and a ton of fun. All of the weapons are fun to use and inventive, ranging from a most manly shotgun to the Fickle Finger of God...I mean, the Lightning Gun. The levels are well-designed deathtraps forcing you to think quick on your feet and rewarding you for exploration and skill. Quake is tough, but never made me want to rage quit during my entire playthrough of the game. All in all, this a game I can recommend on a whim to anyone who likes fast-paced old school shooters, but I should add a note to this review: If you are going to play this game (and you should, it's fantastic), you would do well to get a source port to play it on (I play Quake on a source port, hence the 1.8 hours on record). The version on Steam has no music, which is an integral part of any game's atmosphere and feel, Quake in particular. In addition, if you like eye candy (and if you have a beefy enough rig, why wouldn't you?), source ports are the way to go in that regard. You can get the necessary files right here on Steam, and for $10 USD, I don't see how you can go wrong. Quake is more than just a relic of a past era, it's an enduring classic that still manages to compel a jaded modern gamer like me to play it for hours on end. Give it a spin, if you haven't already.

I see the largest complaints are about DLC and how the A. I. work. I don't defend the practice of nickle and diming customers, but for companies to keep the lights on unfortunately these practices are sometimes necessary. I'm glad to say the DLC adds to the experience. If one person has the DLC in your multiplayer match, then all players may utilize it's benefits, so it does not allow someone to have a distinct advantage. The DLC is also prefered over microtransactions.
That being said the modding community is great and offers things the DLC doesn't. I enjoy playing with many of these mods. That being said the paradox DLC works very streamlined in it's focus trees and almost all things work as they should.
I've also see major improvements in the A.I. Though they have a ways to go before the A.I. competes like a skilled player, they are a lot more ample at fighting now rather than before.
Basically you will see people who expect nothing less than perfection and want no DLC or only major additions and I can sympathise with that. However this game comes with a complete experience and the DLC or mods can further enhance that experience.
The point is the game is great and I thought I'd stop playing in a week. Ha no it's gonna be a while.
Update much later: It's still fantastic. I like the changes they are making to the game. Still perfecting strategies and utilizing weapons and technologies better than before.

hocus is a good, short puzzle game that is based around impossible 3D shapes depicted in 2D, reminiscent of M. C. Escher's style. There are 100 standard puzzles and there is also a Workshop for fan-made content. There is also an editor that is very easy to use for you to make your own puzzles. The art style is minimalistic and the music calm and peaceful. The goal is to direct a small cube from a starting point to a hole on a different place on the shape. You'll need to use the odd nature of the impossible shapes (an "impossible angle" as it were) to get the cube from one side to another. Picked it up for $0.49 and I felt it was worth it for that price. I believe you can play this on a smartphone too, so I guess if you need a short, quick brain-teaser to pass the time, this will be enjoyable. Well-optimized and smart, this game doesn't hold your hand, give you any hints, or give you an easy time.
One drawback is that while the sound they chose for the cube as it travels along a path makes sense and is good in theory, it can get annoying after a while. Thankfully you can turn off sound effects (and music, too). Also, it's a bit inconsistent in terms of difficulty. Once you get to about the level 20s, it bounces around between solutions that are easy to find and others that are quite difficult and require a lot of trial and error. Another reviewer said that his problem with the game is that you can usually brute force your way through the game and, well, that's kind of true up to a point. Another thing is that there aren't many levels that are memorable. However, I did like the concept, art and sound design, the customization options, and the skill increase among the first twenty or so puzzles. I beat the game (100 puzzles) in 3.8 hours, which leads me to say it took me an average of 2.28 minutes per puzzle, if that's any indication of the amount of time you'd like to spend per puzzle.
Ultimately I thought this was a good puzzle game that's very simple to understand and makes you think without bogging you down with text, intros, tutorials or plot. Especially recommended if you enjoy the art style of M. C. Escher.  Worth it if it's on sale in my opinion.

The game is too old at this point. It does work on Windows 10, or at least it does for me, but I needed to lower my general screen resolution to the old 800x600 standard to even make the game open, and then it was entirely too tedious and repetitive to be worth doing so. Essentially, it's a generic match-3 set-up where you match up the colors in order to clear all of the blocks below. In doing so, you collect construction materials (accumulated via your number of matches in each level) to use to "build" the world wonders, until you complete one and can then officially move on to the next main stage. I ultimately decided not to even go back in and finish it, as nothing new or interesting was happening.

7 Wonders II carries over much from its
, with a few notable exceptions. While the basic match-3/tile-destroying formula remains, the end goal has now been changed, and instead of a board you can freely rotate to manoeuvre a block along a track and into its target location, you will now have to clear all tiles then guide a cap stone from the top of the board down to the bottom. I personally found this a little boring and less imaginative than the previous game, but I guess that will largely come down to player preference.
Another change is the actual stage structure and progression system. Last time around, there was always seven stages to clear in order to build each Wonder, but now, every Wonder requires a certain amount of blocks to complete its construction, with blocks being rewarded based on your score. As a result, there is no pre-determined number of stages, but rather, you'll now play as many or as few levels as it takes for you to attain a high enough score to receive enough blocks. Failing to acquire all building materials within the allocated time limit and number of lives will force you to repeat the collection process and restart building the Wonder from scratch. Again, whether this can be considered a positive or negative will fall entirely on a player by player basis.
Power-ups make a comeback, but this time being far more numerous with a much greater variety. These can range from exploding all tiles along a cross of two diagonal lines, or teleporting two blocks of your choice for easy matches, or even changing an entire colour set to another colour of your choosing. These are unlocked as you play, then selected prior to each stage, before needing to be powered up by making matches.
While the game is still perfectly entertaining and easy enough to recommend for anyone into the match-3 genre, I personally preferred the mechanics of the first game over this one. Having a set number of stages, and two distinct phases of play were far more satisfying to me than the slightly more basic approach here. Though the presentation has seen an overall improvement, and does have me interested to see what changes they've made to the next installment.

Alright, so I played this game a lot before the most recent update (I believe they're calling it the Unearthed update?). It was fun and mostly an atmosphereic survival game. The enemies needed working on, sure, and the AI was a little "janky" and most enemies spawned only when you were mining (which kinda got annoying, but made it a little more interesting). But, at the center of it, was a rather fun survival/resource management game. A game I would have suggested.
Well, apparently, the developers didn't like that about the game very much because now I can't help but feel like this new update has the game headed in a very...different direction. Now, instead of a creepy, space-fairing survival game, it's more of a crappy space-horror game. Most of the enemies are now inside "dungeons" and these "dungeons" have a HEAVY "James Cameron's Alien" feel to them...only they fall far short. What's more, the "dungeons" force you into combat in a game that has a HORRIBLE combat system.
The combat system was aweful before this update and the update changed nothing. The monsters are still janky, hard to kill, and hit like semi-trucks. What's more, if you have no gun, combat is all but impossible. Did I mention that you don't spawn with a gun? Yeah...that's no longer a thing apparently. Did I also mention that MOST of the "rare" crafting materials are found exclusively in said "dungeons"? Cause they are. What's more, a MASSIVE downscale in surface-available resources has occured. What used to be fields of abundant mining has turned into hard to climb hills with not a resource in sight.
This next bit is a product of an early access game, so take it with a grain of salt:
In addition to the change in game genera, the developers also saw fit to COMPLETELY alter the surface of the world you start on. MEANING; if you had a previous save with any base structures, vehicles, or other buildings, there is no promise that said structures will be on the same plane as the newly formed planet surface. For instance, I had an entire base FLOATING about 300 FEET above a small valley upon loading up the game. This base USED to be on nearly level terrain. So now, I can't even get to my base to deconstruct it and build another one somewhere else.
Which, again...whatever. That's kinda the nature of an early access game, I guess. A huge update comes along and BOOM...your world is useless now. Best to restart.
What I DO have an issue with is the change of genera. I didn't get this game because of it's "creepy" undertones. I got it because it was a very atmospheric take on space survival. NOW I have a space survival horror game...and I HATE horror games! I want old Osiris: New Dawn back...not this ♥♥♥♥♥♥ take on horror where I'm forced to use a now useless assult rifle (it used to be fully automatic, now it's three-round-burst exclusively). Unless this game turns tail back to being a survival game and turns AWAY from being a horror game, I won't be suggesting this to anyone.

- Gameplay : Gameplay and concept of the game is pretty fun. It's also hack n slash, side-scroller game. If you are fans of any of these genre, you might love it. If you never played anything that has permadeath and rogue-like, I suggest you watch someone's video first before you try. If you don't mind about permadeath, then go ahead, StarBreak is fine and challenging!
- Control : This game... totally lacks in control department. I can give example of Castevania and Metroid, where you can shoot UP, DOWN and DIAGONAL (left and right is obvious). But here, you can't shot UP and DOWN. So if the enemy happens to be above you, you either take hits OR you move away to get you space to shoot. If this game exist during 1990's I can forgive the control mechanics. But this is 2016, it SHOULD'VE improved ALOT. But nope, not with StarBreak.
- Sound : The music is pretty catchy and awesome! I like the boss battle theme, it feels like you've met something terrible, BUT you are given spiritual support in form of upbeat music that will lift your spirits! I like it. Really Really like it!
- Graphics : Graphics is... well... pretty bad actually. Not because it's pixelated but because your character is small on screen, and background/foreground detail is not differentiated, meaning that it WILL confuse you to locate enemy projectile, small enemy, or even yourself. It should be made like in Contra or several Castlevania games, where background colour is dimmed so that the actual pane where the game takes place is actuated and not confusing. But talking about animation, it's smooth. Feels good to me.
- System : StarBreak size is small, less than 500mb of installation files. And spec requirement is not high. Also I didn't encounter any crashes/bugs/glitch yet. I'm sure it's stable program, nothing to worry.
- Services : StarBreak implements cash shop where you can buy costumes to your liking. But beware, due to permadeath, all of your cash item WILL BE GONE. FOREVER. So, if you don't mind spending money for items that will be disappeared when you die, you go ahead. For me, nah I'm sane person. Won't just throw away my money like that :)
- Points that I don't like :
* I didn't like permadeath, so this game is clearly not for me.
* Control mechanic is pretty bad. Another major disappointment for a game that should be challenging because of it's design, not of it's horrible control mechanics.
* Although the concept is ok, but once you play it you will feel "bland". Because ingame, you won't gonna have chit chat with fellow players as chat window is too small, has no feature other than "public chat" and you can't invite friends/group to other. This feels like a singleplayer game, with multiplayer drop-in features. For me, this feels weird.
* Cash items gone once you died. A big nope for me.
- Points that I like :
* Challenging gameplay, you will be haunted with "omg pls dont die" feels whenever your character goes below 50% :)  With that, you MUST try to master your classes (Shell) so that you will survive. This game is HARD, so don't expect lenient enemies or easy boss. Even the smallest enemy could kill you fast if you are not careful. Reminds me of my days playing Gradius, it's hard and once you die you basically goes back to level 1 :)) But over time, if you are serious player, you will get better and better.

Essence of the game: Kill all drug cartel fiefs (everyone cartel related really).
The game overall plays out like this:
1. Enter a region.
2. Receive a radio communication from the task giver, where she tells you about the fief in the region, that she has no idea where that person is. However she knows about a couple of points of interests (typically 4-5) which are then marked in gold on the map.
3. You travel to each POI and as you reach each of them, they transform into another POI on the map, some distance away.
4. You travel to that new POI location.
5. Once you've visited all of POIs in the region, a final POI is marked on the map.
6. You travel to the final POI and is tasked with killing or kidnapping a person.
7. You again travel a fair distance to some specific safehouse where you drop the kidnapped person off, and the story progresses a bit. You are told about the impact of the loss of this fief to the cartel organisation.
8. Repeat 26 times from step 1.
This game is long. The main reason for that is cheap padding.
1. A constant back and forth travelling (backtracking) where travelling between a single POI to another may take 3-4 minutes by helicopter or many times that with a land vehicle.
2. In between each step above, you will face an infinite number of enemies, that respawn "as soon as you turn your back on them". Or more accuratly, as soon as you've moved a short distance away.
3. In order to not be annihilated you need to upgrade your skill tree and that is accomplished by... you guessed it, boring fetch quests, travelling to yet other POIs on the map, where you have to kill hordes of respawning enemies.
4. You can't just acquire new and improved weapons and addons for your weapons stash from killed enemies, no you need to travel far and wide to hundreds of additional POIs, where the same "Crate" will exist with a trophy in it.
5. Each item you seek is typically placed as far away from you as possible, while still fitting in the overall story segment. For example, it's almost certain that if there's a village with an item in it, then the item will be located in the highest building, at the top floor, as far away from the stairs as possible. It seems UBI used an algorithm for travelling salesman problem where they inverted the heuristic to produce the location with the furthest travelling distance from any other point on the map.
Liked:
Even though the game has all the problems mentioned in the separate review, the cheap tricks to pad its length, and the constant repetition, I still found it a blast to play, in small chunks.
* Performance, it ran beautifully at 60 FPS on my Intel Core i7 7700k, with a Geforce GTX 1080ti and 16 GB RAM at 1920x1080 resolution. No crashes.
* Voices. Acting was rather good I found and added quite a bit to the immersion. Your team mates respond to surroundings. In the beginning I was impressed by the variety of comments by the AI mates, but found they ran out of ambient dialogue after about 10% into the game. A potential for improvement in UBIs future titles, but as a proof of concept, I think it turned out rather well and applaud the devs for the idea.
* Graphics. The scenery is absolutely stunning. From snow covered mountains to dense jungles. Nothing beats flying a helicopter over cities, canyons, bridges, the jungle and the alps. It's something very relaxing about it. The character models also looked great. Attention to detail was overall very high imo.
* Gunplay. Bullets have trajectories! Head shots are fatal! Unarmored enemies are not bullet sponges! Weapon handling feels a bit on the realistic side when compared to other titles, with weapon weight and stats playing into how the weapons behave. Overall I found gun fights highly enjoyable, which really is a saving grace as you wade through the hordes cartel and unidad soldiers.
* Rebel assistance. This is a new thing I believe in UBI titles. Along with your skill tree, there is a separate branch which allows various forms of assistance from bolivian rebels. The types include sending grunts to help you in gun fights (can make a HUGE difference, especially for timed challenges), calling in mortar strikes (Awesome, especially for taking out pesky drone jammers), helping with recon etc. I found the former two great, while the rest I never saw a use for.
* The story was OK. It's much better than other UBI titles. It also served a purpose, giving you enough of a justification for exploring areas.

Basically you will see people who expect nothing less than perfection and want no DLC or only major additions and I can sympathise with that. However this game comes with a complete experience and the DLC or mods can further enhance that experience.

Being an amateur World War II historian, I have a love-hate relationship with this game, with far more love than hate I assure you.
Pros:
- Change history: South African fascist world empire? You got it. Communist U.S.A.? Glory to Comrade Browder.
- Re-enact history: want to invade the USSR in the winter? Go ahead.
- Production management is streamlined and reasonably intuitive.
- Definite improvement/simplification of ground forces command from previous HoI games.
- Good visuals.
- Lots of immersive mods from the community add to the replayability 100x (though vanilla is plenty replayable).
-Devs are pretty good with taking suggestions and getting feedback, as well as working to address issues.
Cons:
- DLC adding elements that (IMO) should've been delivered on release.
- Border gore (w/out mods, that is) can be infuriating after peace conferences (especially for history buffs).
- Oftentimes you may find yourself wanting to adhere to history more than you want Lord Halifax to be Prime Minister.
- Nation Focus trees for many nations of significance remain generic.
- Frame rate drops significantly around 1941.
TL;DR
In other words: buy it—worth the money, especially for those interested in World War II, grand strategy games.

Though visually impressive and mechanically sound, the weak narrative told by The Bureau may be enough to sour the experience as a whole.
…
From the outset, The Bureau has a lot of good concepts working in its favor. Set in the early ‘60s, the game offers an interesting “what-if?” scenario of an alternate American history. Extraterrestrials have landed (violently) all across the world, and you are placed in direct control of a grizzled, disgraced CIA agent who’s got his finger on a trigger and nothing to lose. In accordance with many recent alien invasion epics, the United States is caught completely off guard, and many cities across the nation fall.
The setting does a lot in the game’s favor. The XCOM agents go into the field wearing fedoras, ties and vests; you storm through classic Americana towns that look like they were pulled from an old television show, with banners for the local high school football game hanging from soda shops. This visual theme plays very well and makes the environments entertaining to stomp through, as it’s a design that really hasn’t been represented often in games as of late. Plus, it’s a very pretty game from start to finish, with admirable levels of polish from character design to skyboxes.
The Bureau handles well, using single-button cover mechanics that have proven tested and true from many other games in this genre. It doesn’t take much wrestling with the thumbsticks in order to scramble between vantage points or mantle over knee-high boxes, which is advantageous when involved in the middle of a firefight. You are given two squadmates to work with in every level, and they can be given orders on where to move, who to attack, or who to buff by slowing down time and giving manual direction. The fact that the game doesn’t outright pause eliminates analysis paralysis, and requires (and rewards) quick thinking for finding synergies in the team depending upon what enemies are thrown out. As this is an XCOM game, the teammates are an expendable resource, and must be utilized or sacrificed accordingly for the greater good of the mission. It is entirely possible to be left with an empty stable going in to an important story mission, but the game is reasonably difficult, provided the player is frequent with commands – the AI is solid on its own, but keeping up on orders will ensure a smoother victory and prevent frustrations from a squaddie who inexplicably charged head-first into a grenade toss on his own.
With all those positives said, it has to be stated that the story, for all it has to work with as a precursor to the more modern XCOM games, fails to deliver a meaningful experience. As this game is only a single-player adventure, the script itself needs to be solid in order to merit a recommendation or a second playthrough. Unfortunately,  it feels as if “multiple storyline paths” were some check-box that needed to be included during the development process, with no actual payoff for any of the options provided, save for one specific path. Depending on whether the game is played in a “good cop” or “bad cop” manner is irrelevant, as the game’s climax pushes the character down one path, regardless of any previous actions. The only reason to play through twice would be to view multiple endings, but even then the story is so frustrating and confusing that it almost sours the twelve previous hours of gameplay.
Despite having some genuinely good gameplay elements, the experience as a whole is meaningless if the game is finished with a sense of unfulfillment and a “what was the point?” attitude. Sadly, The Bureau could be skipped without much being missed, even for hard-core XCOM fans. Not recommended.

7 Wonders II is the sequel to 7 Wonders of the Ancient World. The game is consisting in building wonders by swapping tiles in order to make a chain of 3 or more and break the background stone. Well, it's usually called a match-3 game if you didn't know like me what was this weird category.
I know that I will sound lazy but as I've already written the description of the game on another website, well, I will copy it here. I wish I was more acquainted with english casual game words... But I'll insert some remarks in it that can be only done when reviewing a game.
The gameplay is consisting of swapping adjacent runes on a grid, making matches of three or more to remove them. By doing so, the remaining pieces are falling down, occupying the vacant space. The player has a limited time to reach his objective of breaking the background stone by doing matches.
My first match-3 game was Amazonia on
, which proposes free games to play online. It's not a demo, it's the full game that you can install without having to spend your money for it. Don't be happy so soon because if you're ads allergic, well, the counter-part for offering it free is ads from the sponsors. So, every two or three levels (or 5 minutes for example), you'll have for 20 seconds (sometimes less) an ads. Be reassured, almost all the time, game is paused.
Well, the problem with ads is that in Amazonia, in the second level, ads were crashing the game. In Diner Dash, the ads can appeared in the middle of a level without pausing the game, making me raging when you have Business Woman and Cellphone Addicts, the most precious customers in the game but also the less patients.
Amazonia didn't have a time limit and the matches were only replenishing a tube on which an artifact was placed. Once it has reached the top, you've beaten the level. So, as I couldn't play Amazonia, I turned to Jewel Quest and 7 Wonders II. And I was disoriented because of the time limit and the fact that I needed to turn the background gold by doing matches without bonuses. That's why 7 Wonders II appeared to me as a better game than Jewel Quest... by forgetting that the latter was released earlier than the former.
But what annoys me the most in 7 Wonders II is the time limit. How many times I was really close to beat the level and see... TIME'S UP? If you see suddenly that you don't have time to beat it, you're going into the mode "panic" and you can't see clearly your game. Fortunately, there is a bonus that can freeze time... if you find it for a more difficult level. Me, with my luck, I've always found it before playing an easy one...
In 7 Wonders II, the bricks resulting of this breaking are used for replenishing the bonus bar in order to use it. The bonus can be chosen on the bonuses menu by the player. These ones are appearing on the Wonder and can be reached with construction sets.
The bricks don't replenish immediately your bar, you have to wait that your little builders take them and bring them in the house. That can be anxious when you need the bonus for beating the level when your time's almost up...
Bonuses can be found on the Wonders: reach it and wait for the secret challenge for the map for collecting it. They can be useful: some destroy squares, even one is equipped for destroying the map square, some are used for making more points, etc.. My favorite one is the one that can destroy a entire column of tiles, very useful when you have to collect the big construction set that is one of the conditions for finishing the level.
The construction sets come from the matches: the more you do matches the more you're replenishing the construction set bar. With what you've collected, you can build the Wonder and find bonuses.
When you're doing a match of four runes, you have an iceball appearing, by swapping it, you'll destroy all the runes and background stone of the same line. The fire ball appears after a five-runes match, and destroys both a column and a row. The dice piece appears after using several ice and fire balls, and removes random tiles from the grid. It can very useful to use these balls or dice. You're making combos, meaning more points but also meaning that you can deblock a situation.
You have also a secret Wonder which is unlocked by collecting the 7 "big" map pieces. In each level, a special square can be seen. By matching runes of the same color on it, you can obtain a "little" map piece. When you obtain a certain number of it during the construction of your Wonder, you'll unlock secret challenges and obtain a "big" map piece. Once you have collect the big map piece, every time you'll destroy a colored square, you'll unlock a secret challenge that is only there for points. Some are very difficult, because your number of moves is limited and well, you have also a time limit. It's up to you to find the key for using wisely your moves and beat the challenge.
Also, you have a shuffle bar that is replenishing slowly. It can be useful when no moves are left or if you feel that you're going nowhere.
After this long explanation about the gameplay, well, I need to speak about the graphics and the soundtrack. It will be quick because it's not really the most important in the game.
Graphics and animations are really good. They're simple, colored and well, in a sort of false 3D. The background (behind the board) is the Wonder you're currently building and well, with the time passing, you can see it even at night. It's nice to see that the day/night cycle is included in it.
The little characters, despite being all the same (except for the old man, the architect probably, the woman that is walking from time to time or the muscular builders, only collecting the big construction set), are very amusing. Some of them aren't collecting bricks: they eat, they do some tricks, some are even sick, meaning that the "ambulance" will be out, etc..
The soundtrack is nice. Nothing really to say... except the music when you need to hurry up. That's very darker and stressing. Anyway, 7 Wonders II is not the game with sophisticated soundtrack like in Painkiller, Half-Life 2 or Will Rock.
The replay value can be high if you're addicted to the game. Lifetime can be long if you're loosing too often. But 7 Wonders isn't Jewel Quest, it doesn't bring you something new when you have finished the game a first time. The gameplay is repetitive for every level. Always doing the same: swapping, swapping and swapping.
In the end, 7 Wonders II is a very good game. Building Wonders like Stonehenge, the Taj Mahal, the Moai statues or the Great Wall is a good idea, an other way to propose a match-3 time. The bonuses are also very helpful and without it, I wouldn't have finished the game. The characters are cute, well, for me, it's cute. Perhaps that some of you will find them ridiculous... But the repetitive gameplay and the time which is running too fast can be frustrating for players. Despite its flaws, I'm recommending it for people wanting to try a good match-3 game.
NB: I've written this review in 2008 - my opinion didn't really change about the game, it's still very enjoyable.

As a fan of text adventures, this was a refreshing new take on a genre I enjoy. Simplicity is used to great effect - the setting, characters and visuals focus in on the text itself, which is entirely the point. A novel approach to dialogue options and conversation modifiers, too.
The story is interesting, well written, and easily digestible in a short sitting. It doesn't drag, but it feels substantial regardless of its length.
My only sticking point was that the story seems - aside from a big finish - to be a little more linear than I was hoping for, compared to the nostalgic experiences I'm reminded of while playing. Choices typically appear come full circle, but this doesn't really matter. There are elements to the story progression that are optional, so it's certainly not a dressed-up visual novel, and it definitely feels like engaging gameplay.
The interactive developer commentary unlocked after completing the game is interesting, humorous, and presented quite uniquely within the game in a way that adds useful context. The soundtrack is also a wonderful listen, and I've picked it up multiple times.
A great short story about AI and choices. If you're a fan of sci-fi, this needs to be on your radar.

StarBreak is a roguelike co-operative platformer that's centered around player progression.
When I say "centered around player progression" I say it as opposed to classic in-game character progression, which is what MMO's and most games do these days.
StarBreak has permadeath. If you die with your character (your shell, as the game calls it), all his stuff is lost, he's gone forever (god bless his soul) and you win experience points that level up your Soul based on how far he got. Having a higher soul level lets you unlock the other characters that have completely different playstyles from the original one you get.
What a lot of people don't seem to understand is that the level progression is entirely artificial. They make you wait to play the other characters because they want to player to get more experienced with the game and enemies to be able to know how to react to different situations according to the unlocked character and it's difficulty.
This game has basically no progression other than the stash, because as mentioned before it's a game about player progression.
Getting further and further into the game can only be done through first-hand experience with the enemies, which feel consistent and fair given how they're placed strategically on the terrain.
This is basically how it goes, in order:
1.You'll get hit by stuff you see coming.
2.You'll get hit by stuff you saw coming, but couldnt manage to avoid it.
3.You'll get hit a lot by stuff you didn't know could do X in X way.
4.You'll die to situations you couldn't predict other than experiencing them.
Now, all of the above will gradually go away, until you can control your character consistenyl and be constantly aware of the environment, which feels extremely rewarding for the player, complemented by it's MMO aspect:
There is a cash currency in the game, known as UC. With it, you can buy additional stashes and player slots, coupled with a few vanity hats on rotation.Additional stashes are useful if you're keeping the equipment for the next character, and the hats are lost on death too. What I would argue goes against the main point of the game, are the additional player slots.
Having additional player slots means you get more loot efficiency than other players that don't, should you choose to play more characters at once. In a game about not dying and getting as far as possible, being able to change shells sort of kills the feeling of only having one life as, since there's no trading, you're essentially saving the equipment you can't use with the current shell, to yourself. Not your "future" self, but your "now" self. A possibility free players don't have.
It is however, not a game for everyone. It seems extremely unforgiving in certain aspects and I feel like having to explain the fun of the game to someone else defeats the purpose if the person itself didn't find it fun. Many don't like it for it's permadeath aspect, yet I feel like they're just missing the point entirely.
While it is quite sad to lose all the progress in a simple mistake, a lot of the times, to me, felt justified. Be it a bit of bad luck, bad positioning or a tough enemy: whenever I was about to die, I could feel it in my veins that those were my last moments, and that was exactly how it was meant to be.
The game is what it is. There's no point in trying to make it something that it is not. Removing permadeath would remove a lot of the tension which IMO is a huge part of StarBreak.
If you liked the early days megaman and metroid, you'll probably have a blast with this game. The multiplayer aspect works really well with it, more than i'd initially thought it would. Coupled with the permadeath, it's a game where while in lower levels you just shrug off character deaths, later on you really feel for them, and i've sacrificed myself more than once in hopeless boss fights to let the other players teleport back to base (takes like 10 seconds of standing still) by providing them with cover fire. As another review said: "It felt like ♥♥♥♥ing Starship Troopers."
Some more technical points:
The gamepad feel is great. I used and Xbox controller for it and it's already binded, with some emotes custom-bound to the D-pad. What bothers me is the second character's (Duskwing) dash control, since for some reason the special dash is canceled if you let your movement stick go back to neutral position. It can be really ♥♥♥♥ing confusing to see her just stall after doing the dash because you moved your stick to the same direction she's going, but that's minor once you get used to it. (THIS ISSUE WAS FIXED A FEW DAYS AFTER THIS REVIEW, CHEERS DEVS)
Needless to say, it runs well. The graphics aren't intensive, keeping it in a stable 60 fps, and the design aesthetics never feel off from the visual pacing aswell.
Sound wise, the effects have a pleasant hit-noise and the music's good. It's not that memorable, but it definitely sets the scene for each environment and scenario presented, enough to make cold-blooded people have a decent surge of adrenaline.
All in all, it's a great free to play time-killer and tons of fun for those that like the jump'n'shoot genre and/or want to fool around with friends. It may feel rewarding to beat enemies you previously died to whilst growing as a player yourself, but it's always more satisfying when you do it with other people.

Then outta nowhere the atmosphere gets uneasy. All the characters speak as if they've got something to hide. Small things, at first, but the more routes you go down and the more you play the more you're starting to piece things together and you don't even know if you want to see what the final outcome of this unsettling puzzle may be.
Once you complete all 14 'normal' endings, you unlock the secret, ridiculously unsettling "BBL" route that explains everything and ties all the individual routes together, and THAT'S where it REALLY gets good.♥♥♥♥♥♥gets crazy. Suddenly you find yourself in a mystery murder novel, then some disturbing horror survival♥♥♥♥♥♥ then comes the angsty backstories that rips your heart out so bad you gotta slap yourself to remember this is a dating sim about ♥♥♥♥ing BIRDS.
Hatoful Boyfriend has just the right amount of balance between shock factor, humour, feels and downright horrifying. It's a game that goes beautifully from light humour, to dark humour, then just plain dark with no hesitation and so well written and paced that it will always leaves you at a loss for words. This was much more than I bargained for when I signed up for a silly dating game about pigeons in highschool.

Doom's Big Brother.
This is the heavy hitter of id Software's library. Quake is an evolution not just for FPS games, but games as a medium.
In Quake, you fight through 4 episodes of Adrenaline pumping action, much like Doom, albeit with a much much MUCH darker atmosphere. The game is quite a lot faster than Doom, with Speedrunning being quite popular with the game. Gameplay remains unchanged from Doom. You move through the levels, killing everything in your path, then leaving via exit.
The game doesn't have many bosses, only really 2 (End of Episode 1 and the Final Boss), but the encounters are memorable. The enemies are all interesting, and frightening, with such enemies as the giant Shambler, Ogres that hurl grenades at you, and Fiends that claw you into bits.
The maps are inspired by several dark fantasy influences, notably that of H. P. Lovecraft; most notably, the end boss of the first episode is named Chthon, and the final boss is named Shub-N iggurath, although there is little resemblance to the original literary descriptions. Some levels have Lovecraftian names as well, such as the Vaults of Zin or the Ebon Fortress.
The original Quake runs on DOSBox, but you have the option to run GLQuake. Regardless of which version you want to play, make sure you look for source-ports, such as Quake Epsilon, or FTEQW to name a few to play the game at its max potential. The games soundtrack ran off of red book cd, so look for the Ultimate Quake patch as well if you want the great soundtrack as well (100% must install.) Also look for multiplayer source ports as well because the Quake community, like the Doom community, is still alive and kicking.
Quake is as great as Doom is, with darker tones, and faster gameplay. If you enjoyed Doom, or just wanna play an arcadey fps, Quake is the game for you.

Quake, along with Doom and Doom 2, is one of the best FPS games in existence. If you liked Doom and/or have grown tired of modern military FPS games, and haven't played Quake before, then I think you really should give Quake a shot. It's a great game. (You can skip Quake 2 and not really miss much).
The game is fast and fluid, it has the best grenade "tinkle sound" in any game, the best jump/hump sound in existence, and the guns, like Doom, are in 'the middle', so the avatar feels like some kind of supernatural tank. Unlike a lot of contemporary 'Early 3D' games that look like complete♥♥♥♥♥due to the low level of polygons, I think Quake still manages to pull it off it's look. (Though only if you play it in non-GL mode. Bilinear filtering on tiny textures looks terrible, and is one of the main reasons early 3D games (e.g. Sin) look so bad). I really like the light/shadow of the levels and the particle effects, though the levels are a bit on the brown side, admittedly.
All of the levels are weird and abstract, and don't just look like the crate storage rooms used in Quake 2 and every game since then. The low poly, highly angular level geometry helps this as well. Some of them (e.g. episode 2?) are even weird checker-board castles and such. There's also a lot of up/down movement in those levels, with the famous concept of speed running being possible by a few well placed explosions giving the player the ability to bypass huge amounts of level if they're skilled or completely lucky. There's definitely still an 'explorable' mental-map-forming aspect to a lot of the maps, much like Doom, (though it lacks an automap) and this allows the maps to contain secrets and easter eggs, something I really miss in later games. Most of all there's no attempt at cutscenes or 'story' or anything. It's like Doom in that it's pretty much pure-play. (Actually, there might be a few camera changes in the game that kind of look a bit like cutscenes?). Quake is a very non-modal game, as everything is done in that first person view. Even the choice of difficulty and a episode is performed in-game by running through portals.
I'd like to think that the reason I like Quake 1 isn't rose-tinted nostalgia, as I actually never played Quake at the time of release, but only long after I'd played Quake 2 and Half-Life. I've not played Quake as much as Doom1/2, so the initial Quake levels don't fill me with as much dread/boredom as the early Doom levels. (I've played Doom/2 practically from their time of release). Quake also isn't just a boring tech-demo, like Unreal or Quake 2 (which I also played at the contemporary time), but is fun from the first second of being in-game.
If someone liked Doom and has grown tired of modern military FPS games, and hasn't played Quake before, then I think they they really should give Quake a shot. It's a great game. (You can skip Quake 2 and not really miss much).
Overall: Quake is great!

Ah, the Classic Quake. The first true 3D FPS game. 13 years on, how well has it aged?
Surprisingly well actually. I suppose the first thing to note is that the game played a lot like DooM, I personally like to consider it one of the 3 DooM 3's also consisting of DooM64 and the actual DooM 3. But I Digress.
Quake, as the first FPS to use actual Ploygons manages to hold up quite well, you have the basic DooM style controls, using the arrow keys to turn, Ctrl to shoot and WASD to move (That is unless you're using the Ultimate Quake Patch, but I'll get to that later). and it does feel like a well-rounded experience that manages to hold up today. Of course it has graphically aged poorly with Jerky animation (this can be fixed with the UQP) but to fully enjoy the game you have to put your mindset back in 1996 where the best looking 3D was Virtua Fighter, This game puts you in a realisting looking (for the time) environments and gives frigtening enemies that have never been seen before.
Story Wise the game doesn't offer much, but the game doesn't really need to, you're just a guy (Who I like to call Quakeguy) who must stop evil creatures from an Alternate Dimension. It is sweet and simple.
All weapons handle well, from the Shotgun, Nailgun, Their 'Super' Counterparts, Rocket Launcher, Grenade Launcher, all are simplistic in their design and manage to hit their target with a bit of help from auto aim (Again, UQP). The game features a fun Fast paced game that is perfect for speedrunners and delivers on the retro feeling and boasts great level design.
The Enemies themselves are actually made creepier with an effect that would not exist if the game had more polygons, The Gothic scenery makes the mood and feel of the game and gives the game It's own unique identity.
Unfortunatly the game has some problems cause by some sort of steam optimisation. The Music is Non-Existant, even though there exists OST tracks on YouTube, none are featured in this game. This is Where the Ultimate Quake Patch comes into effect. The UQP fixes a lot of the Steam problems as well as some more of the poorly aged parts: Enemies have now got fluent animation, Mouse Control is Enabled, Improved Lighting and Particle effects as well as the OST added. Personally though I thought the 1996 graphics and improved lighting and effects were too distracting and I had no idea how to get the game to look like the Original game with just the Soundtrack so I removed it.
The game still has a great Charm to it and is memorable for it's environments and enemies. The game is still fun without the UQP but may turn people off with the lack of soundtrack.
I suppose the bottom line is that Quake is a Good, if not Great game the has fun retro gameplay but naturally has not aged well in many areas. This leads to 3 possiblities for interest in the consumers purchase:
1) Buy the game on GOG where it (apparently) plays Just like the Steam release but with working OST
2) Buy on Steam with UQP, if you aren't bothered by the clashing graphics and enjoy updated versions of old games then this should be fine for you
3) Just buy the Steam release as it is and Play some 'Through the Fire and Flames' to the game and enjoy it for what it is.
Quake is a Landmark in the FPS genre that doesn't hold up as well as it's older brothers DooM and Wolfenstein but leaves it's mark in it's creative level design and fun fast gameplay.
FINAL VERDICT: RECCOMEND

Before I purchase a game on steam I ALWAYS go through the reviews to see what the players think, and this is the first time I've felt compelled to write a review for a video game.
At first I was skeptical, the whole "Stranded on a planet trying to survive" gimick has been attempted numerous amounts of times and no game can REALLY grasp it. Osiris: New Dawn is the only game I've found that really grasps the idea of being stranded.
-Graphics are very smooth, the planet and moon are very nicely created. Scenery makes you feel something.
-Aliens are well balanced. You can't just walk into a horde of crabs with a pistol and expect your pure marksmanship to win you the fight. You have to prepare for encounters.
-Vehicles are fun to use. Super over-powered and you can really mow down any alien horde with the GAV.
-Realistic. You have to account for food, water, air, etc. Everything you do takes resources.
-You get a droid. Imagine having your own little BB-8, or BT-7274, or R2D2, or Morty. Whatever you want to name it.
-Out of all the different development teams I've seen on steam, I can safely say that this one cares. They're grinding to improve the game and fix bugs. They keep the community updated and don't give us BS, which is what we want.
-Game starts out really slow. Your first night you're 100% dead unless you use all of your assault rifle ammo (Which I reccomend do not doing). Progression is very tedious until you make vehicles and then you begin to snowball and tasks that were difficult before are now pointless and too easy to do.
-Resources are scarce. Well, let me rephrase myself: Resources that you NEED are scarce. I find myself hording a lot of minerals that are supposed to be difficult to find by the hundreds while base minerals I scavenge for hours.
-Once you get past the part in the game where you think the farther out you venture and deeper you go the cooler and more valuable things that you can find goes away, you realize there's nothing special about getting resources that are 100M away in comparison to finding the same in a cave 1000M away. There's no reward for players to stack up on vital resources to brave the wilderness to find something cool when all they will find are whole lot of HOOPLAH.
-Basic item crafting is useless, same with the buffs that you can craft.
-Skill tree is 100% unbalanaced. You can get hundreds of points in engineering and get zero in science.
-Space travel is pointless because there's nothing unique about the other planet in comparison to the one you're on (That I have seen).
-Droid is 100% useless unless it's for defense. It can't repair anything because it'll get stuck, and mining is pointless due to the radius not being large enough
I know it may seem like there are more cons than pros, but most of the cons are due to it still being in Early Access. All of the above cons can be fixed with updates and patches. Don't let the cons get in the way of the fact that it is still a great game, and once it's out of Beta it will be the best planet survival game on the market.

I did own this game for a short time on PS3 before picking it up again on PC. The UpLauncher is completely redundant and annoying. Takes far too long to do whatever it does just to get the game loaded. This can be replaced with a more streamlined community made launcher that is much faster. The controls and/or physics are comical. The cars feel like bricks on wheels. When it comes to driving, use a controller. Whether it be for a console or PC directly, use it. I did attempt to use a steering wheel and that went nowhere. The cars’ handling becomes twitchy and recalcitrant. There are bits of glitches as expected. Most are ones I experienced on the console version. Gameplay visual performance is well optimized. On an older machine I was able to have a few the settings on High or Very High while most remained on Medium. Behind the scenes performance is lacking. You can easily tell this a port from most likely the XBOX version to PC rather than a full PC build from the start. The basic storyline can be finished in a matter of days. So don’t expect it to last long.
Not all is bad! All of the content on the PC is identical to the console versions. There is almost 2,000 miles of open road to explore spread among two islands. There are 176 cars to drive about in ranging from classics to suvs to supercars. Lesser known small time automakers like Ascari and Ginetta are present. There is enough side content to keep you busy in solo or offline mode. (I think the servers a dead now? I can’t seem to get online at all.) The environment is well made and adequate for an arcade racer. If you simply want to cruise an open world and look at scenery, this game fits that well. If you are an avid car fan, there is just something pleasing about saving up to buy that one car you have had your eye on. There is plethora of dream cars to fill your garages with. Engine sounds are decent. Some are less than accurate.
Overall, I would suggest this game simply for the open world and car selection. Not for the racing or the story. There is an avid community still present for this game. Improvements and more content can be found via an unofficial patch.

So, I thought I would love this game after reading some of the reviews for it. Not at all. The reviews I saw all talk about this game's freedom, and your ability to explore worlds that are different every time, but... well, it all feels very same-y. Sail to an island, defeat the enemies on that island, and grab the treasure. Or, sail to an enemy ship, defeat the ship, grab the treasure. Or, sail to a town, stock up, and leave. Repeat. Everything else just improves your chance of doing these things without dying; there's not much room for roleplaying, serious gameplay choices, or discovery.
This basic formula is fun, granted, but it's not what comes to mind when the game describes itself as a "real time strategy/sandbox/simulation game." On top of that the experience is marred by a lot of unprofessional design flaws. Why can't I run away from ship-to-ship combat when it's obvious the enemy is not interested in fighting me? Why are all the sound effects panned all the way to one side  unless I have the camera in an arbitrary position away from the action? Why can't I grab the items I want from my old ship when capturing a new one, instead of being forced to leave everything behind? There's typos galore, the zoom in function doesn't seem to work, pirates only have about one thing to say per voice and spam it like crazy, etc, etc. Little gripes like that add up and take you out of the game like nothing else.
I can't recommend buying this in it's current state. It has a certain level of arcade-like addictivity to it but so far I haven't seen anything to merit the 10/10 reviews it's getting.

I am not going to dispute the quality of Quake, as I personally believe that it is one of the finest First Person Shooters ever made.  I would also argue that the game still holds up today.
What I am going to draw attention to is the simple fact that the version on sale on Steam does not have its soundtrack.  This is quite unnacceptable.  While you can get it back through mods the fact that this is necessary is an horrendous oversight that plainly should not be tolerated.
Arguably the soundtrack is a major draw if not the major draw to this game.  Great ambient work by Trent Reznor that sets the mood  as a perfect compliment for the level design and art design.  Without it, much of the atmosphere is lost, and much of what made it a special complete experience is lost.  There simply is no excuse for leaving this out.
However, as I said, it is a fine game.  Even with that in mind, simply put we should demand better treatment for our classics than what we have on display here.

StarBreak provides a fun experience for several hours, until you've really boosted a character and then got killed in some cheap way by a fireball and lost all that progress –– forever. It's absurdly hard to progress with the current permadeath system. The only small, glimmering hope you receive from dying is a marginal amount of XP so that you can eventually buy other 'shells' to die with. Ultimately, the fun of platforming with a dozen other people and seeing your screen light up in a cacophony of neon lasers is outweighed by the fact that whatever effort you're putting into it will amount to nothing when your shell is killed.
The visuals are great, but the microtransactions seem pretty meaningless. The items you buy with in-game currency and even microtransaction money are *still* lost when you die, along with all your boosts, stats, and sense of purpose as to why you're playing this game.
Lastly, I didn't enjoy how the grouping of players would be so variable. If you spawned into a dungeon, you'd spawn with a few other people, no matter how far they were through the dungeon. More often than not, I'd somehow find myself alone on the map within a matter of minutes. Being that even the first dungeon's boss is nigh-impossible to kill by yourself as a MKI or MKII, and that the boss's area seems to lock itself when you enter, you pretty much shoot yourself in the foot if you're not with a group of 5-10 people at all times.
For the player looking to try this:
– It's free, so you've got nothing to lose.
– Stay with the group at all times.
– Get a weapon with more range than the starting shotgun.
Ultimately, StarBreak provides several hours of mindless entertainment, but the excitement quickly drops into cataclysmic nothingness. The visuals are fantastic and the game could run with max settings on a broken toaster. I recommend this game solely because it's free, but I would not recommend pouring any real money into the game, because you will lose whatever you buy.

Like Kings of Kung Fu before it, this is another love letter from Jae Lee to Hong Kong cinema. Where the first film was a playful nod at the Hollywood interpretation of the genre, this goes traditional, with a focus on some of the iconic characters and styles that populated Shaw Brothers and Golden Harvest films since the 60s (saw one reviewer said the 70s, um, you're off a decade - "Come Drink With Me" for example [the spiritual successor to Crouching Tiger and part of the Golden Swallow series]  1966 but some of the first of these films go back to 1949, with movies like "The True Story of Wong Fei-hung".)
Enough history lesson, now about the game. Shaolin vs. WuTang shows several improvements over Kings of Kung Fu. The controls feel tighter and more responsive, each combatant has an "authentic" weapon associated with the combatant's style of fighting (or in the case of the Silver beared  master [think Pai Mei]) true to the nature of the character protrayed in films. The graphics show a huge improvement over Kings of Kung Fu, which, honestly released only a year ago, shows Jae Lee and his team are getting better. Like KOKF, all the moves are authentic, well animated and with the added bonus of slow motion special effects and a righteous ripped from Hong Kong cinema soundtrack.
Someone complained about the lack of tutorial, and that's a rubbish complaint. Some of the best fighting games didn't have no stinking tutorials. You got a move list card and had to discover and figure it out yourself. Maybe I am showing my age, but have IQs dropped sharply while I was away? You don't need no stinking tutorial, there is a practice mode to hone your chops with and like Street Fighter 2 or Tekken 2, you are thrust into match after match with some character appropriate pre-match banter from the combatants. IMHO, the new frills, clean and focus on fighting is welcome, and if you need a hand holding tutorial, maybe you should go play a Pokemon game or something. FFS.

Like Kings of Kung Fu before it, this is another love letter from Jae Lee to Hong Kong cinema. Where the first film was a playful nod at the Hollywood interpretation of the genre, this goes traditional, with a focus on some of the iconic characters and styles that populated Shaw Brothers and Golden Harvest films since the 60s (saw one reviewer said the 70s, um, you're off a decade - "Come Drink With Me" for example [the spiritual successor to Crouching Tiger and part of the Golden Swallow series]  1966 but some of the first of these films go back to 1949, with movies like "The True Story of Wong Fei-hung".)
Enough history lesson, now about the game. Shaolin vs. WuTang shows several improvements over Kings of Kung Fu. The controls feel tighter and more responsive, each combatant has an "authentic" weapon associated with the combatant's style of fighting (or in the case of the Silver beared  master [think Pai Mei]) true to the nature of the character protrayed in films. The graphics show a huge improvement over Kings of Kung Fu, which, honestly released only a year ago, shows Jae Lee and his team are getting better. Like KOKF, all the moves are authentic, well animated and with the added bonus of slow motion special effects and a righteous ripped from Hong Kong cinema soundtrack.
Someone complained about the lack of tutorial, and that's a rubbish complaint. Some of the best fighting games didn't have no stinking tutorials. You got a move list card and had to discover and figure it out yourself. Maybe I am showing my age, but have IQs dropped sharply while I was away? The town was quiet. Activity had died down in the new quarter as the rumour spread. They were coming. They were more numerous than ever before. Doom had came for us.
As the horde started pounding at the north and west defenses it soon became obvious that the hastily erected palissade wouldn't be enough to protect the new quarter and that the executor towers wouldn't stem the flow of reaching, screaming undead.
I ordered the Titans to fall back and decided to sacrifice our last rangers in a delaying action so the snipers could retreat to the old quarter.
Then a runner came to my office and breathlessly told me the news: the southern wall had fallen and all that stood between the undead and the old quarter was now an old wooden palissade, a balista and a single sniper.
As the walls between the old and new quarter started to break down under the pounding of the infected citizens I ordered another delaying action, sacrificing a titan as to allow more snipers and everyone else to regroup around our command center.
The end was nigh, they were unstopable. I walked toward the window of my office and addressed what was left of our once great military might.
Men! Today we will know whether we have earned the right to inherit the Earth. Today we will fight, today we might die but know that we will be the last heroes one way or another for never will there be a greater and more pressing danger to fight!
As the cheers died down I heard them. They had breached the palissade and started ransacking the old quarter's houses. More and more of my fellow citizens turned against us as we prepared for our last stand. The titans took a step, the snipers started firing and all hell broke lose.
...
What seemed like hours of mindless killing had taken but a few minutes. Now the flow started to slacken. The last of them had been dealt with. We had won, but at what price. Only I, a few titans, a lone farmer and 6 executor tower operators had survived the onslaught.
11/10 Pyrrhic victory is best victory!

Kill the Bad Guy has been on my wishlist for a while. I like games where there is an overhead view of everything and seemingly anything can be manipulated. Kill the Bad guy is a puzzle type game where the player can use one or more objects (by combining them) to eliminate the target. The game doesn't change in any sense beyond that, you are buying a puzzle game where you will have about 60 levels of killing the target in certain scenarios given certain objects. Adding a steam workshop or some sort of community involvement probably would have added another layer of re playability to this game.
Objects are selected and have to be moved by clicking the move icon (obviously). It's not quite drag and drop, but more of click, click, and try clicking over here to see if they combine. The indicating icons above objects help diversify what can be connected with what. What is neat though is that multi-player was given in the game. Once the game is done, there isn't really much else, but from time to time multi-player is worth coming back to. Just sucks if your friends don't have it because there is a shortage of players.
The game is good by premise, but I feel it could have been better. Adding a community mod behind it, allowing for customizable levels (or a level builder), maybe even custom items would have been interesting. Mini-games even could have made another impact. Multiplayer definitely does give it a backing now and makes it worth a second look. Re playability isn't critically high, but it's somewhat there. As a standalone game the rating is 6.25/10, as an Indie
