After watching NorthernLion's 'Let's Look At' for Subsurface Circular, I was immediately intrigued by its concept and aesthetic. I didn't even finish the whole video before I stopped it to add the game to my wishlist. I love narrative-based games, so I was waiting for a chance to pick this up and experience it for myself. I finally got to during the Autumn Sale.
Now that I've played through the whole thing, I have to say that the game was well worth the price I paid! I loved the writing in Thomas Was Alone, despite not having finished it, and the dialogue in Subsurface Circular is just as witty and sharp as it was in TWA. The clean UI and minimal art style sell the idea of a future world, and I really liked the intuitive way of communicating with other characters to solve puzzles (and I don't even like puzzles usually).
I think the story is quite thought provoking as well, and speaks to current anxieties about automation and the future of AI. For such a short game, I'd definitely recommend playing it all in one sitting to get the full experience. It's a linear narrative, for sure, but I think it's a good one. (I also love how the developer commentary is integrated so deeply into the game; I really want to go through the whole thing one more time just to see what Mike Bithell thinks about different aspects of development.)
I only wish there was more voice acting or at least more music playing to break up the quiet humming of the train. The music I
hear was so good, I wish I could have listened to it more, because at times my eyes started to glaze over when there was too much text on screen and nothing was there to break it up. However, those irks are not enough of a negative to change how I feel about the experience.
If you have a couple of hours to spare and like text adventures reimagined in a modern context, try it out!

For full transparency, I didn't like either of the other two games from this team, so if you did - take my opinion with a grain of salt. The only thing
that I'm right about is that the core gameplay mechanic is beat. The mechanic of 'dialogue tree choice exhaustion' is not fun. It hinges on needing a super interesting story which is dangerous because not everyone will be moved equally.
Please note I've played ~50% of this game. I tried to perservere to the end but had to throw the towel in. I found my mind wandering and then
dialogue quickly slid into
which quickly lead to me mashing straight through the conversations.
You simply engage in dialogue with other robots and choose pre-defined dialogue options. Okay, let's strip away the stylish exterior (which is meaningless, really) and just look at the gameplay first. The core gameplay loop is all too familiar for fans of point-n-clicks:
1. Talk to a person
2. Exhause all possible dialogue options (generic responses consist of the first choice being 'positive' and the second 'negative' - yeah, you've been here before many times)
3. Find new information
4. Go to next person
5. Rinse and repeat
The cycle was fine decades ago, but we've come a long way baby.
+I guess the stylish graphics/cinematography is nice enough - it does feel paper thin, though.
+Even though I wasn't moved by the universe/setting/story, I have to give credit that at least it was unique.
-Even after changing the option, the dialogue was horribly slow.
-Why did it look like they were typing? I'm not sure what it's like to 'link' to a robot, but I would assume we could just 'talk' with no typing delay.
-I hate it when I am roleplaying a character and I actually have to create backstory on-the-fly instead of just 'being born' into the story in this moment, and seeing things from this point forward. Hope that makes sense. Another way to put this is that I don't like to have to choose dialogue options about details of past cases (for example), that I (IRL) have no information about. I did not experience that, so I feel awkward 'making it up'.
-The core mechanic of simply exhausting choices with every NPC is... Well... Exhausting. It's tedious and ho-hum. It's been done so many times before. And it's always a mechanic that's part of a much bigger game. Here, the whole game is this little mechanic.
-The story did not interest me enough. Again, I give credit for something original, but I could care less how it all pans out.
-It's completely linear - no matter what you say (in the first hour, at least) will funnel you to the exact same conclusion you are meant to arrive at.
-Finally, because of the short game length, the devs clearly are concerned with people either just watching a LetsPlay or playing and then refunding, and I get that BUT why not just make it a bigger experience?

I have my verdict on Osiris: New Dawn
Its f*****g brilliant. For the first time in ages, I actually felt on the edge of my seat. I wake up, broken helmet visor, breached suit, losing oxygen to the hostile planet I now reside upon. The temperature outside is a warm 92 Degree's Celsius (197.6 Fahrenheit) and I have so many flashing warning signs across my shattered glass visor, I am barely able to breath myself. It's a little overwhelming. Big letters and numbers at the bottom of my visor tell me I have 0 oxygen left and I can hear that I am now suffocating. Winds are blowing like a hurricane, and I am basically crawling upon the sand surface of this planet I am yet to understand in the slightest.
I begin by salvaging what's right in front of me, an inflatable dome habitat, and I proceed to fumble about till I find the magic button that inflates the damn thing. I must have been without air for only a minute, but it sure did feel like more, as I finally found some duct tape in a survival kit and smacked it on my helmet to pressurise my suit.
Holy s***. I am liking It so far. And I dont want to spoil anything more, but there is something scary as all hell, as you watch a massive centipede creature burst out of the sand and rocks, fly over head and make an epic landing as it spins around to face you. All the while you stare in amazement of how cool it is before having it lunge at you and pull your legs out from beneath you. You then quickly realise how you should stop fumbling for your gun, just grab it, and shoot the damn thing!
Enjoying this game so far...
Story aside -
Pros -
Beautiful environment.
Breath taking visuals.
Realistic fogging and build up of dirt on helmet visor.
Responsive Developers (considering its such a small team.. very good community commincation imo)
Animations are remarkable.
Player movement.
Creature Movement.
Level of difficuluty is very nice. Difficult to get resources, but not life draining. (Might help to be in a team?)
Cons - (In my opinon, these let the game down a bit)
Building system, whilst very nice, doesnt have a smooth placement system. Everything snaps around, instead of a smooth rotation option, the building will snap at 45 degree increments, and when placing a building, it seems to snap along the ground. (Just adds a little bit of grindiness where it isnt needed. Not gaming breaking of course)
Lack of fulfilling tutorial. When I was playing it took me a while to figure out how to place walls on the habitat frame. A lot of other things to get you started were mentioned and walked through, but it was a bit confusing for me to realise to use the multitool. (Could have just been me though).
Not all classes are complete yet. It doesnt break the game in any way, but I think I would like to see a bit of prioritzation over that. I know that when I play with friends, we want the option to be different and have different advantages over each class. (They are adding a new class in the next update. 27/4 I believe).
Ores are a bit weird. Whilst titanium can be gathered from a rock (which is confusing considering it is an alloy) the fact that I will be mining Iron one moment, copper the next, back to Iron, then finishing with Aluminium... all in the matter of mining one rock on the ground... I would prefer easily distinguishable rocks and maybe less variation in the random ores. It isn't a problem, but it is confusing imo.
Other than those cons, I havent had any problems with the game. It is early access, and it is going very well. I hope this game gets some more suppot as it has got a good future ahead of it, if it continues on its current path.
Definetely worth the buy, even at full price. 9/10

This review was written and published before the inclusion of the game's multiplayer feature and thus it is not mentioned throughout.
Watching over a man in a garish yellow jacket and a bullseye mask while rigging various death traps conveniently placed into his path, one might feel like a god. Granted, a god that will ultimately be faced with ending the life of a being lesser than itself in order to proceed, but a god all the same.
That's the basic premise of Kill The Bad Guy. It's a game where you'll be doing little else than what it says on the tin.
Certainly there's some degree of enjoyment in the act of killing what the game builds up to be one of many comically exaggerated abominations toward humanity. Whether it be smashing them with an oncoming vehicle to see their body flying off into the distance or diverting their path so that they just happen to pass beneath a sign sharp enough to decapitate them. The array of options afforded to accomplishing the core goal varies from level to level, with some feeling almost depressingly empty at times.
What the game lacks in an abundance of diversity, it attempts to compensate for by offering a stylized presentation and a (sometimes dark) sense of humor.
The spare use of color in the world opens up the possibility to have memorable death tableaus, with the previously white surroundings often becoming awash with the blood of a given bad guy. Think of it as a literal take on the opening credit sequence from the film adaptation of
. Much of the game's intended humor comes in the form of flavor text provided for each of the game's 60 or so bad guys. Many are parodies of real world figures (Hitler, Saddam Hussein, Justin Bieber, etc.) with equally fictionalized takes on their criminal acts or atrocities, as the case may warrant.
For all its style, humor and simple yet deceptively complex premise, Kill The Bad Guy suffers from a number of flaws. Chief among them being a woefully inadequate and frustrating camera system, an interface that often hinders more than it helps and AI that seems prone to random outbursts.
Overall, Kill The Bad Guy is interesting, violent to an absurd degree and often challenging (though at times for the wrong reasons) but becomes repetitive far too quickly. Some questionable design choices and lingering bugs aside - you have a game that, once finished entirely, won't leave you with a strong desire to replay it.

A fresh take on the RTS genre that adds an element of tower defense. The objective is to start with very little and build your colony up until it can last 100 days at which point you unlock the next map. It has classic RTS elements such as resource gathering and city building but the randomly generated map is covered in roaming zombies and hordes making expansion and gathering resources difficult especially in the early game. Also, every X days you will be attacked by a wave of zombies. The closer the game gets to 100 days, the more zombies the horde brings. The game is definitely no joke in terms of difficulty, and you will most likely lose over and over at first. For me this is a postive, but I can see how people would not enjoy this. While you can make it easier, you wont be able to unlock the next levels if you do so. Whilst the game is still early access and subject to change, once you have learnt which units and technologies are the most powerful you lose alot of the variety in the game as you start building the same things every playthrough. There is no save feature that allows to you to undo your mistakes as every time you close or leave the game it will auto save over your latest save. This makes the game extremely punishing and not for the feint heart.You may find yourself playing for hours and hours only to lose it all in seconds. You cant really play this game casually, every second counts and any mistake can cause the fall of your colony. So if you enjoy a challenge, and you like RTS games and a zombie theme sounds interesting, you will probably enjoy this game.
Final Verdict = 9/10

This might sound odd, but the game needs a fast forward button.
Let me explain. This game is a very interesting combination of wave survival, RTS, and production chain management. The core of the game is to balance the expense of your resources on various buildings and units to defend against increasingly difficult zombie assaults. Thankfully, during the time sensitive portions (like at the start of a new game) you can click the pause button, and spend as much time needed to plan and strategize. A single mistake can easily cause a game over, so it feels like the game should move fast, let you pause when you need to, and move at a speed that lets you practice getting your building orders right so you can grow as quickly as possible. Yet no matter how well I was doing, and infact more so when I was doing well, I felt like a great deal of time was spent waiting for resources to stock up, buildings to finish, units to train, or the next big wave to arrive so I  had something to do. As it stands my best run went for about four or five hours before I got a game over because I did something stupid out of boredom and curiosity.
I love base building, and I love this kind of perma death survival, but for them work together the game needs to be able to move fast enough that when I get a game over I feel eager to hop right back in, rather than groan at how long it will take to reach the same point.

Unfortunately, I found this game to be boring.  It felt like one of those mazes that came on your placemat in restaurants as a kid.  You have the choice of tracing from the ending back towards your cube to figure out the route, or just randomly moving around the level hoping to stumble onto the end.  The graphics are great and the mechanics are solid, but it just doesn't provide enough "puzzle" for people like myself.  I thought it would be a mental challenge going into it, but it was not that.
While I hate to click the thumbs down on this one due to its overall quality, delivery, and uniqueness, I have to thumb it down for myself as it is not a real puzzle as I was expecting.  For those just wanting to kill some time and like the concept of Escher's art in a game, you could do a lot worse than Hocus.

My review, honestly, may be slightly biased, simply because I am a heavy admirer of Escher's works, and pretty much any other illustration that challenges the eyes' and mind's perception of reality, perspective, and 3D space. However, I'll do my best to make sure my review is balanced.
Initially, from a glance at pictures and trailers, this game might look, to some, to be intellectually intimidating. Don't let it intimidate you. I won't lie; as the puzzles progress, each puzzle does get harder and harder. However, admirably, the first few act as easy-peazy tutorials to ease you gently into the evolving entanglement of harder and harder puzzles that come later. The relaxing chime music helps to keep you calm and relaxed, too (trust me; you'll need it with the harder puzzles).
The objective of each puzzle is simple in concept: Guide the red cube along the structure until you manage to get it to arrive at the matching red recess elsewhere on the structure. However, as puzzles progress to increasing difficulty and complexity, you will find this harder and harder to accomplish.
The "structures" are based on the perspective-illusion illustrations by Dutch artist Maurits Cornelis Escher. The objects portrayed in his perspective-illusion illustrations were objects that essentially could not exist in reality ("impossible objects"), but could still be illustrated in perspective based drawings. The general idea of these perspetive illusions have been replicated as puzzles of increasing complexity in this puzzle game.
As the puzzles gain in challenge level, you'll find your perception of perspective and 3D space being challenged harder and harder. What you think you see, or thought you saw, is not in fact what is. One plane of travel might at one point be accessible by one means of travel, but then by another from another point. There could be any number of ways to get that little red cube into the little red recess. And it's rare that it will ever be the way you initially think it is.
Pros:
- Eases you in gently with a few VERY simple tutorial puzzles first.
- Very simple graphics and interface; will likely run on most modern machines without trouble.
- Very relaxing chime music (although comes through somewhat loud at first, but can always be turned down).
- Intellectually engaging (if that's what you like).
- Lots and lots of puzzles to occupy you.
- A recent feature added: Editor. I haven't tried it yet, but apparently it lets you make your own puzzles (I think). Either way, it sounds like a cool feature to try.
- Puzzles are "unlocked" as they're completed, allowing you to turn off the game and return to your last spot at any point, as well as play from any previously unlocked puzzle as a starting point the next time you play.
- Cheap price tag: I got it on sale 50% off for CDN$1.09, but even with that, the base price comes in at at a comfy CDN$2.18 (PS: not sure what that comes to in USD, but it's probably less, as USD$ is worth more than CDN$, last I checked).
Cons:
- As mentioned, music comes through a little loud, at first, but can always be turned down.
- The mouse control for the game is a little sticky/sluggish feeling at times, but is manageable, if you're patient (the game does say it recommends analog stick on a controller. But I don't have one. But mouse control IS available; just a little sticky/sluggish feeling).
Conclusion:
If cheap but intellectually engaging puzzle games are something you enjoy - especially if you enjoy geometry, and/or the works of Escher - then this is a game for you. Highly recommended, and totally worth the few cheap bucks. Give it a shot. :)

This is the closest thing to Forza Horizon on PC... for better or worse. And trust me, the worse is pretty bad. But first, the better.
The game is spread across multiple hawaiian islands, in an open world campaign, which is pretty awesome. It also has a great selection of cars, missions, races and other things to participate in, such as painting your cars and altering your avatars appearance, clothing and hairstyle. So far, so good, the game really can be quite fun. I'd rate the physics as either one of the most realistic arcade games I've played, or one of the least realistic simcades I've played. But on to the negatives.
The game rarely works without modification, I had to use a standalone launcher (which takes away my ability to gain Steam achievements) to make the game work consistantly. Even still, I can only play a couple hours before the game crashes. But really... I'm ok with that. I'll tell you now what really, truly infuriates me.
There are certain timed missions in the game, that are absolutely, positively impossible to complete without driving like a balls to the wall, completely suicidal  lunatic. Take Mad Max style driving, and turn it up my 5. Then, add to that the fact that the most unpredictable traffic in the world is included, and the customer who's car you're delivering doesn't want it scratched, or driven off road, and welcome to the most utterly infuriating racing game ever known to man. I literally can't tell you the number of times that all I've needed to complete a mission is one more damn second, and everything would have been fine. But the game creators set time limits that apparently only God would be able to achieve, because not only must you be a driving god, you must also be the luckiest son of a ♥♥♥♥♥ in the world for traffic not to cut you of and screw up your entire damn race.
Now, I know the above paragraph is utterly critical, and even hateful of the game, but I still recommend it... especially on sale. I bought the game for $5, and I've gotten my moneys worth out of it already. I just really wish these particular missions were not made so freaking impossible. The other 95% of the game is fantastic, but that 5% of the games missions completely, and utterly infuriates me. Other than that (and the instability, and utter lack of reliable online support, and need to launch the game through a third party launcher) the game is pretty fun. Just be sure to pick up the universal launcher so you can play offline.

I've played this game a few more hours than steam shows, because I had a lot of fun with it for a week until I lost one of my great characters. Just like with RotMG, losing a character hurts a lot. Be prepared to die ALL THE TIME -- this game doesn't joke around.
The game is exremely skill based with lots of room for you to "git gud." Combat is fun and very unforgiving, just like Dark Souls. The loot system works with a set amount of base items that can have anywhere from 1-5 "modifiers" on it, like extra crit damage, double shot, explosive bullets, and more. Each character has a nice arrangment of weapons to choose from.
The greatest part of this game are the boss battles -- they're insanely awesome! Remember back when arcade games had giant bosses that fill a ton of your screen? Starbreak has no shortage of those. This game has a neat concept, and fun gameplay, but that's overshadowed by silly business practices.
This game is a bit of a rogue-lite, where your character dies, and their "shell" (body) is gone forever, along with whatever equipment you've carried with you, where you respawn in your home as a soul and activate a new "shell" to continue playing.
The concept seems pretty fun right? except when combined with stupid business practices like cosmetics...yes you heard me right...cosmetics in this game ALSO are destroyed along with your shell once it dies, and cosmetics cost UC, which is a form of currency only obtainable as far as I know through IRL money purchases.
So you're literally just wasting money on this game if you care about cosmetics, because upon death your cosmetics are gone, unless you CONVENIENTLY give them more money for a stupid shell storage space which sounds stupid in it's concept, because it sounds like keeping a "shell" with your favorite weapons/armor/cosmetics in a safe to NEVER use again since, once it dies, so does everything that comes with it.
The worst part about this corrupt business practice? is that currently you HAVE TO DIE in order to level up! so you're forced to throw away your cosmetics if you care about progression at all! I've heard talk that the devs are considering a way to remedy this, but I assume their silly business practices will still be in.
This game is NOT P2W by any means, but it IS P2C (pay 2 convenience), and to me that's just as bad as pay to win, considering their storage spaces are less than your own inventory, and of course, you have to pay UC to buy additional storage spaces.
I liked playing the game for a bit, but currently? I'm going to stay away from it and play better 2D side scrollers out there.
EDIT: as an added note I find it funny when people try to debate how with the rogue-lite elements it's justifiable that you lose everything upon death, but they conveniently want to ignore how you still keep your EC with you, which is ingame currency, which by their logic, should also be destroyed upon death since you don't have a bank in your home to keep that ingame currency

I think Dishonored is one of the finest stealth games made in years, with it's fleshed out world, interesting characters and unique art style. It's a game I think both action and stealth fans will find fun in, and with that said, onto the pros and cons
Pros:
Pretty gwaphics, oh man those polygons. (The graphics are still quite nice due to how stylised they are, plus if you use SweetFX, the lighting is amazing.)
A simple story told many a time but told in a very enjoyable way.
The movement system involving Blink (A short distance teleport ability.) is very fluid, allowing easy and fun travel across the levels.
The fun and unique non-lethal options, most of them being an ironic and poetic end for each of the targets.
The combat system is just as fluid as the movement system, allowing for fun and creative kills with a wide variety gadgets and weapons.
The large levels that offer many routes to the objective.
The chaos system, which changes the game on based on how you play. (Kill lots of people, characters become paranoid,   more guards and an overall darker outcome. On the other end of the spectrum, kill few people and the world just seems a little brighter.)
How alive and real the world feels, thanks in part to the lore books and letters scattered throughout.
Fair priced and worthwhile DLC. (Though the Void Walker's Arsenal is pretty throw away, just being a compilation of pre-order bonuses.)
Cons:
The length. (The game is very short, but it at least warrants multiple playthroughs. Sadly, this doesn't make up for it entirely.)
The lack of variety of gadgets for stealth and non-lethal.
Once you get to know the game, it gets pretty easy.
This one's very specific, but there's a glitch that stops you completing the game with a ghost rating on all levels while doing high chaos, which really buggers my perfectionist biscuit. Maybe it won't bother you, though.
In summary;
Despite being a short game (If you're good, you can beat it in a few hours. Thirty minutes if you use glitches.), each minute of it is extremely enjoyable, and at the current price of ten euros (or your regional equivalent), I'd say it's totally worth it.

The Bureau: XCOM Declassified is not the best third-person shooter around, but it's decent enough for the price.
You play as Agent William Carter as he battles against an unexpected threat not of this world as part of the newly formed XCOM organization. To do this, you must utilize the skills of your small team of elite agents, your own abilities (including the nifty ability to slow down time), and the many conveniently chest-high (and some full-size) walls, cars and other cover objects scattered about.
The third person shooter aspect is basic but solid. Taking cover and flanking those in cover is very important for both sides, so you'll need to move around to avoid getting flanked and to flank enemies. To encourage the usage of both, those in cover are resistant to damage unless flanked. This gives it a somewhat different dynamic to most cover shooters, which simply make it difficult to hit a target behind cover.
This is a very tactical game on any difficulty, and you won't be able to do everything yourself. Your small team of accompanying agents will come in handy, though you will need to micro them a lot even on the easiest difficulty as they're not the brightest and the aliens will keep changing positions to get an advantage on you. However, if deployed and used right, they're the most effective weapon against the alien threat you have. Their abilities in particular can make them indispensible in any firefight. These abilities also encourage you to keep a large, regularly rotating squad, as no one agent can have all of them and some are more useful than others depending on the situation.
The story is mostly linear and not all that special (though there's a brilliant twist near the end). Basically, aliens suddenly invade Cold War America and do all sort of nasty things, and you have to stop them by shooting them repeatedly and stealing their stuff so you can do it better on the next mission. The atmosphere throughout the game is pretty good though, and does make you feel like you're in the 1960s. Also, there aren't any reused maps, each mission has a unique one.
I would recommend this, though I would advise getting it when it's discounted. Also, Hangar 6 R&D is worth buying even if you normally avoid DLC like the plague.

Osiris: New Dawn...so much to say.
Let's begin by talking about the game: Flying in your spaceship, drinking a hot cup of tea, watching your daily dose of "Man vs. Wild" tv series when suddently your spacepod decides to malfunction, exiting near-lightspeed in order to test your "crash-dummy" skills. No big deal, this happens once in a blue moon (pun intended) to everyone, but nonetheless, here we are, PROTEUS II. But where is here? Well, an identical looking planet to URANUS happens to be near the moon you crashed on, and the fun thing is that that planet (which your moon is orbiting) is a GAS planet, which makes the irony outstanding. This planet has four moons, two of them available to explore at the moment of typing (13.04.2017): PROTEUS II & AZIEL.
First thing you do in the game? Use some good old-fashioned duct-tape to patch out your broken glass helmet and decide to look for shelter. Realising no one is present on the planet (except your alien friends), you decide to take out your 12-high-school-class-years knowledge about physics, chemistry and biology and build your own city (with blackjack and...well, you get the idea).
This game offers lots of things to do if you know how to play and are charmed by the vast space. So, my advice, instead of google-searching where every mineral and resource and metal that you require is, you better start exploring. Also try to keep it realistic, don't hover everywhere like a retard, but instead walk or run, keep your robot friend OMPA close (I call it "bob" cause he is a buzz-kill-bob sometimes) and your enemies, well, not closer. While the night is still young, get out your gun and walk slowly, watch left&right sometimes, try to find minerals and then run for the hills.
The story is up to you. At the moment we know this much: You are here, listening to Michael Jackson's "You are not alone" song, and the truth is that you are or were not alone. It seems that someone was here before you, as you can find old relics and former bases. You have everything in your mind, literally. You can create anything from chemistry, combine it with physics, split the atom, find Higgs boson, and voila: You're ready for the party. The party means mining, fighting the aliens, confronting the bad weather, dodging the meteor shower, screaming like a little girl when you first encounter Indlewrath, creating and repairing your base on a constant basis, and exploring caves and the moon itself.
The resources are nicely scattered, making this game a really good product of exploring. While you explore the game, the game explores you: What type of person are you?
Calm and curious? Then you will search far and wide, will embrace the wipes and will help the community evolve with both found bugs and suggestions.
Angry and frustrated? Then you will say "I don't need those 152 steel for the laboratory, time to stock on Assault Rifle Magazine and kill those who stood in my way and killed me 151 times".
This really is all about nature vs. nurture.
A good thing I like about this game is the vast options you have at your disposal (emphasis on the word disposal) when creating your own universe. You can set an insane amount of aliens with full strenght and life, while your character will rip off a page of the "Jacknife" hand-book and secretly curse you for giving him low minerals and xp.
OR, you can go full ballistics and make'em aliens cheap and young, while giving yourself the upper hand. Or anywhere between those two options presented above.
Now, when you're big and strong and ready to leave for AZIEL, you're going to be in for a surprise. You're not going to find an expedition team there waiting for you with "Dance Party, U.S.A". No. You are alone, once again. You're going to have to make trips back to mommy's dearest moon and get some resources that are not available on AZIEL, suffocate on the amount of cursing let out when trying to find PROTEUS II at night, worry about the fuel and that you have to find resources again, in order to grow your new base. I personally love this challenge.
The combat is sweet, you have two weapons at your disposal, one with unlimited ammo and one with nice power but limited ammo. Every alien has a weakness that can be exploited, and one of them can be looted and its loot can be used to create a vehicle, which is really nice thought of the devs. That's the thing in this game, everything on this planet has a meaning (can't wait to find out what took out Indlewrath's ancestors) and a usefulness, it's up to you to find out why.
And the best part, ladies and gentleman? It's Early Access. Yep, you read it here fir...nvm. This game has so much to offer and it's just Early Access. Just imagine how much more there is to do, keeping in mind that it can only grow from here on! The "Loading Screen" shows us lots of planets and moons, the moons (mostly PROTEUS II atm) are vast and can be explored, never getting tired of them, learning them and using them at your peril, the species are kind of vast for an Early Access, you can build buildings and connect them to one another, making a really big base.
The graphics are great, exquisite, astounding, astonishing, eye-popping and breathtaking. The shadows COULD use a little bit of work, but everything connects with everything, be it first-person-view or third-person-view.
The game can be played in: Single-Player, PUBLIC Multi-player (18 players) and PRIVATE Multi-player (5 players). I like playing private multiplayer, screaming and also silently judging other's behaviour, but nonetheless working together to achieve the maximum we can and also have fun while doing this.
Conclusion: This game is fun, it has a huge potential, get it and have fun with it. This is the longest review I ever wrote and this is the game I played most from my list of games. I honestly meant every single word I wrote and hope it helped you in taking a decision. If not,♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ell m8, sorry for wasting your time.

Okay, so I'm a huge fan of Kings of Kung Fu (the first game Jae Lee made). It had a small roster, but fighters with very unique flow, range, and tempo. The fighting styles all played completely differently, the combos were based off of a LK RK, LP RP system. Most of the moves made sense as far as advancing and retreating attacks, it punished you harshly for spamming, and you could flow most of the moves together into free form combos.
Shaolin V Wutang however is a huge step back from Kings of Kung Fu. The flow is akward, there is no quick step, all of the moves don't flow into eachother. The left/right system is swapped out for a kick, punch, weapon, roll system(the telegraphed roll, being the only way to change up range quickly). All of this combined makes for a low tempo, stand and combo kind of fighting system. Gone is the constant range manipulation, and fast tempo organic combos from Kings of Kung Fu.
Verdict: Buy Kings of Kung Fu, also buy this so Jae makes KOK2.

First off, I do not pretend to be any sort of expert on this game, as my highest character is only in the mid-20s as far as level.
I can legitimately say that this is one of the best MMOs I have ever played. I'm sure a lot of people get their first look and say 'only 4 classes? WTF is this?!' sometimes without giving the game a chance.
If I had to pick 1 thing (and that IS difficult) that was my favorite aspect of this game, it would have to be the class system. It's like a well-done house-ruling version of D&D or Pathfinder, if you were allowed a range of options with a particular class, essentially multi-classing; just on a more specialized level. For example: I mainly play a Mage. Starting out, this sounds a little boring. Get a fireball, or some lightning, learn spells as you go along. To my surprise, the Mage can fill essentially any role (other than a tank, of course), with relative ease, and a pretty easy learning curve.
One of the best examples of RIFT's flexibility was one raid I was in several days ago. Being a raid of at least 8 people (from what I remember) we obviously had representatives of each class. I played my general DPS Mage, but that was where the stereotypes ended. The Warrior of the party was a buffing, threat-management type of build, while our main tank was the Cleric, with healing being held up by another Mage and the Rogue! Now, as I said, I may not be an expert, but a Rogue acting as a raid's Healer? I'm pretty sure that's not something you see every day.
The only thing I could say that I don't like (and it's pretty minor) is the teleport system, where in the first zone you have 2, maybe 3 places that you can teleport to, and you can only teleport from very specific places. However, this is coming from the person who also plays LoTRO and Archeage, so I'm definitely jaded. And also, the graphics being pretty intensive isn't the best for low-end machines.
In conclusion, I would heartily recommend this game, at a solid 9/10.

Positives: Wonderful setting, competent shooting mechanics, cool concept, beautiful art, functional music.
Negatives: Frustrating AI, inconsistent characterisation, apparently baffling story (although I personally didn't get that far), an unlikable protagonist, other tiny problems with combat (described below).
If you go into this expecting a game like Mass Effect rather than X-COM, you won't feel particularly cheated, but the gameplay just isn't as solid as a Mass Effect game.
I wanted so badly to love this game - I loved the setting, I loved the concept, and I thought it was really wonderful that the developers were trying a bunch of new things. However, while this game isn't broken and it isn't terrible, there are just so many flaws that drag it into mediocre territory. After about 3 hours, I lost interest, and I simply wasn't having fun.
The biggest thing that frustrated me was the inconsistent characterisation on display, especially from the protagonist. He's painted as a noir-like loose cannon that gets the job done, but this is just frustrating - he  bafflingly switches from treating characters with respect to ignoring orders just because, and seems seriously shaken up by the loss of a character he's just met despite being grumbly and disaffected about everything. It's as if the writers couldn't decide who they wanted him to be.
I also have a few issues with the combat which were individually not deal-breakers but were frustrating when added together:
- Control is often taken away from the player for unplayable cut-scenes which add absolutely nothing to the game
- Weapons lack impact, many enemies take a frustrating amount of damage to put down
- Combat scenes feel like they drag on too long consistently, additional spawning enemies feel frustrating
- Because there is no crosshair outside of aiming, bringing up the sniper scope doesn't necessarily point it at the enemy you were looking at. Add this to the insane amounts of time between shots and for reloading the sniper rifle, and one of the most satisfying weapons becomes one of the most frustrating
- Cover mechanics more complicated than they need to be when it comes to rounding corners or leaving cover
- Team mate AI is often bad. Engineers stand in front of their own turrets taking damage without moving. Your squadmates mindlessly hang around detonating mines. And they never seem to do any damage - they seem to fulfill more of a babysitting role. I understand that this is to make the player feel empowered but I'd at least like my team of crack professionals to be competent!
The tone of the game switches frequently - an audio log found in a university plays a professor reproaching his assistant for 'not following his intuition and relying on evidence'. Because that's what being a scientist is like....? And I seriously have to question why an institution that's meant to be the best of the best is so full of 'loose cannons who don't play by the rules'. If this is meant to tie in to any sort of X-Com canon, I've never considered my squaddies in other games to be dismissed alcoholics or police with a criminal history. It's a pity that this little thought was put into the setting and characterisation because the artwork is convincing and consistently impressive.
I would have loved for this game to be so much more. I'd pick it up on sale if the above issues don't bother you much.

I'm going to say this. It is not a terrible game, HOWEVER it is not worth $30, maybe $10 - $15. I luckily got it in a Xcom bundle for a good price.
The game has it's ups and downs with a nice leveling system (however limited it may be) and the choice of what two allies you bring with you is cool (Engi, medic, sniper, ect). The game is a nice 1960's Mass Effect third person strategy game. You give commands to your team members while also taking to the field and shooting aliens.
The story is good, you're escorting an item when things go wrong and an alien invasion starts. You join up with a secret military group and fight back in an interesting dispatch soldiers to some missions while fighting in other missions. Without giving away too much I will just say that the game has a fantastic mind blowing twist towards the end that I did not see coming.
One negative I found with the game is the friendly AI that you bring with you. I started on the highest difficulty and at first had no issues as I was able to give basic orders to my allies, ie take cover and support me, but you need to be very specific with where you want your allies to go and what path you want them to take. If you are not you will end up seeing your ally run right through the crossfire being mowed down in seconds. Also sometimes though it seemed random, your allies would run back to you after completing a task, very infuriating when you're taking on a spider machine with 5+ aliens and you're waiting for your ally to complete their flanking order you gave them only to find them standing next to you. I ended up toning down the difficulty so I could complete the game while still enjoying it.
I also ended up just bringing two engi allies with me because i found being able to deploy two turrets and two land mines very useful and effective. Moreso than the other classes with my playstyle.
I do believe you should buy this game, just at a lower price.

They are billions strongly reminds me of Stronghold, the first game, not the lackluster tirade of followup nonsense. This game is really quite brilliant. Build as well as you can, as greedily as you can. Then get punished for a slight mistake with a cascade of failures that ultimately costs you the game. Learn to be paranoid, to build double and triple airlocks. If you're not writing down stats and details to optimize your build and your overall strategy, you're doing it wrong.
That said, They are billions not perfect:
- The mayors are gimmicky, some bonuses are amazing to the point of breaking the game, many others are basically worthless
- Controls bug out when commanding larger groups. Clicking will send your units running off into the horizon (or into a horde of zombies) instead of the place you're clicking
- The basic build order is simple enough, but the advanced stuff is fairly opaque. Oil and engineering units are good examples: how much do you need? What is the exact value? Lucifer vs Thanatos vs Titan which one should you build? The game does little to explain it for you and mistakes tend to cost you dearly.
Spoilers, I'll insert a short build order/priority list so you don't have to waste a game figuring things out:
1 Build houses
2 Build basic military units
3 Once you run out of food/energy/space, build more farms/mills/walls so you can keep building more houses
4 Build resource buildings
5 Everything else
Lucifer vs Thanatos vs Titan = only titans will really save you in the end because of spitters. But titans also attract MASSIVe hordes when they fire, so be prepared for that.

(This may contain spoilers)
This is an early access game so I understand there needs to be improvement and is still being developed.
So with this review I just hope to lend any feedback to the developers in hopes that the game becomes even better than it is right now.
Some things I witnissed / wish where included in the game.
- Unit balancing issues.
Some units are just more useful for almost every situation of the game. Currently I only use 3 different units total.
Kind of disapointed that the Titan wasn't one of them. Since it feels very satisfying getting to that stage.
- Traps
They suck... Though It would be fun to incorperate them but just doesnt feel useful. Possibly I havent played enough to be able to uncover a better use case. So just as a first impression.
- Unit Identification
Hard to figure out where stray units are. End up having to just either clump them all together or selecting in random areas to check.
- Multiplayer Mode.
I absolutly love the ability to pause in the game and know that this wouldn't work in a multiplayer setting. Though a few of my friends have expressed the interest in being able to do cooperative play. I agree that this is something that would be incredibly fun and possibly even more challenging.
- Speed up time
With the addition of pause / being able to speed up time might be pretty cool.
- Multiple Unit creation
Sort of difficult to figure out how many units are being created when you have multiple buildings on a control group.
- Bugs
Totally understandable. As a developer myself I will just list what I witnessed rather than criticizing,
- Blade trap upgrade wasn't awarded when upgraded.
- Units attack move gets buggy and they start to path in diffirent directions.
- Sometimes when building gates they ended up interconnecting each other and blocking off the entrance
- Pretty sure units can clump together and phase through walls or terrain sometimes. It happened to my unit and also of a zombie unit when there was a separation.
- I'm not sure if this is just myself but sometimes clicking on certain buildings doesn't feel responsive and i end up accidently destroying something totally unknown. (I'm also happy there is a confirmation on destroying multiple).

Things I loved.
- Unit aggro.
The ability to micro manage units because of unit aggro is incredibly fun and satisfying.
- Multiple resources
Kind of gives the game an understandable hierarchy. Also macro management of everything really starts to require some thought on what types of buildings to produce in later stages.
- Pause
It can get frustrating but this ability makes it so much more liesure and i love the mechanic for it. Strategizing is also a very large part of the game and it enables you to do so without being rushed.
- THEY ARE BILLIONS!
This REALLY came as a surpise the first time and was overly confident before the fact. Totally got killed. Loved it.
I don't really like to buy too many early access games but I was pretty excited about this one and really hope it continues to improve and succeed. This is an excellent, albeit short, text-based game about the uses of AI in society and whether or not they can actually be considered a part of society. Although this subject matter has been explored before, Subsurface Circular shies away from spending too much time waxing philosophical, and rather focuses on a singular sequence of events. The whole game takes place on the titular subway train. You, as an AI detective, have conversations with other AI to investigate the disappearance of a number of AI linked to a certain antagonist. Your job is to uncover the link. You have various key words to use in conversations in order to progress the story and uncover the information you need. It's incredibly engrossing and kept me thinking about the ramifications of my words throughout the game. There is, of course, a decision to be made in the end, and that one had me staring at my options for a few minutes before I made my choice. I wholeheartedly recommend this game, as the only complaint I could muster is that at one point I felt like I got stuck in a conversation loop until I figured out the mechanic that I needed to take advantage of to progress. This is another excellent game by Mike Bithell and is worth the asking price.

Subsurface? Maybe. Sub-par? Not at all.
Just as I was settling in for a night of Japanese takeout and Overwatch, Thomas Was Alone designer Mike Bithell dropped a surprise release on Steam. So I abandoned my post faster than a Royal Mail employee on a Friday night and grabbed a copy of this robot detective game. Apart from a few sly tweets and whispers in the industry, no one had any idea this game was coming.
Subsurface Circular is a spins a casual, yet brittle tale of class, religion and power, with undertones of revolution and an ever-present nod towards the old ‘Robots will prevail’ tech dystopia. It tells a story and builds mystery in a single setting by consistently changing its direction, tone and characters, providing a different interaction in every scene.
Your journey begins, and you, a robot detective, are your help is requested from a worried
Tek with a missing friend. ‘Tek’, is the term for robots in this game, and there’s lots of different ones, which you’ll meet throughout your train ride. Robots get on and off the train, and it’s your job to talk to each of them, and solve the mystery of the missing Tek.
The plot juggles themes like AI, conspiracy and human rights, but keeps it light and mostly on surface level as your investigation progresses. Each Tek you talk to requires something from you, be it a phrase, piece of information or the answer to a riddle. Some Teks even work as a pair, and your interaction with one will affect another’s responses. That was clever, Bithell. You smart little thing.
The fact that your character does not move throughout the entire game, is a testament to the astuteness of the narrative; an entire plot revolves around you, and you don’t even need to leave your seat. The interactions are so well calculated, that I didn’t have a clue what was going on until the carefully placed reveals. Every robot has it’s own thing going on, its dialogue laced with a special wit generally found in the works of team Bithell, and I thoroughly adored the 4th wall-shattering fedora tip towards Thomas Was Alone.
Subsurface Circular was a glorious little spin of a classic sci-fi concept, that didn’t require a lot of time or commitment to enjoy. It’s design and scripting were spot on, and I was particularly impressed by it’s smooth, sleek UI. That, and I’m still buzzing over the part where I had to emotionally manipulate a pair of robots to retrieve the information I needed. Subsurface Circular is a canny, resourceful little release, and I hope team Bithell have similar ideas in the bank, because this one was lovely.

Osiris: New Dawn is a great space themed survival game. I am a big fan of survival games so I jumped at the chance to play one that was set in a space themed environment that appeared to be so well polished visually.
Note: I have read a lot about people having issues with hackers and griefers on multiplayer servers. I simply did not bother with multiplayer and played the single player game. I am just as happy playing by myself. So this review is from a single player standpoint.
The game is well done, but still needs quite a bit of content and balancing. I found it rather difficult at first, as you get mauled by alien monsters relentlessly, and when you first start, your stats are so low that it makes it almost impossible to survive. I spent a lot of time hiding up in trees, or on top of tall rocks, shooting down at the monsters, which got to be a bit annoying. There is also what I feel to be a bit of a flaw, in that when you try to aim directly below you, your aiming angle stops too soon and you can not actually aim down, so the monsters get under whatever you are standing on, and you can't shoot them. you have to wait for them to eventually move out into your firing range, and then you get a couple shots at them before they are back under you and you are unable to hit them.
So after spending a lot of time doing this, and then running like mad to gather resources before having to hide again, I finally got enough resources to build a habitat, which you can then hide under, and the monsters can't fit under it, so you can then shoot at them freely. And this is the true turning point. after you have a habitat setup, you start to gain stat points and your fire arms abilities level up. soon after, you can handle most of the monsters easy. hiding under the habitat felt very much like cheating and I would rather have had a better balance between weapon damage and enemy damage to player. Maybe make it so a single monster is easy to kill but have them attack in more numbers to make it dangerous?
I then gathered resources and built out the Lab to build vehicles and in no time I was able to build the starship, the mech, a rover, etc... There is only one other "planet" you can travel to, which is another moon that has yet to be fleshed out, so it is just there for easy resources. Now there is nothing to do and I am waiting on more content and polish. I feel that the balance needs a lot of work because it really was a night and day turning point, once I was able to gather resources and build, everything came way too easy.
Issues the developers need to fix:
1) The assault rifle will let you reload it when it is full, and it will eat a full clip. so you can literally sit and reload the weapon repeatedly until you have no ammo left. It needs to be fixed so it only adds the amount of rounds that are missing and doesnt allow you to reload if it is full. I am a game dev and this is a very easy fix. No idea how it is still an issue.
2) The skill tree has many skills you must put points into to unlock, but I found that I was able to build all of the vehicles without ever spending points to unlock those skills in the skill tree. Maybe this is to make things easier for people while it's under development? not sure, but it needs to be fixed. This is part of the reason it was so easy for me to just build everything. I didn't have to build up skill points to unlock them, I simply needed to have the resources and it allowed me to build whatever I wanted.
3) I unlocked the ability to build heavy weapons in the skill tree but never saw the weapons in any of the "workbenches"  to build them.
Two things I dislike about the game are:
1) The developers have added silly primitive weapons you can craft that just seem way out of place in a space themed game. It would be easy enough to make these blade weapons appear futuristic, or even scientific, but someone chose to make them look primitive and it does not fit.
2) The aiming issue I previously mentioned. It's most annoying and causes you to focus on a limitation of the game's design, not a limitation of your player. it simply comes across as a flaw.
My system is an i5-6600K @ 3.5GHz, 32GB memory, Nvidia GeForce GTX 960, and I ran the game on max settings, max draw distance, etc. with no frame rate issues, no video glitches, no technical issues at all. Not sure why a lot of people talk about glitches. I saw none. To be honest, my computer transcodes video streaming via Plex to my PS4 all day, everyday, while I play games and such and I still have no issues.
TL;DR:
Osiris: New Dawn is an excellent survival game that is still in heavy development with serveral flaws. It has great visuals, great sounds, and excellent use of music. I essentially finished all available content, and I enjoyed my 26 hours spent playing the game. I look forward to the final product.
If you like to support good game development via early access, then this is one worth supporting, but be aware that there are a few frustrations, and a lot of work and balancing still needed.
If, on the other hand, you expect a complete game when you purchase an Early Access game (why you would, I have no idea), you should wait until the game reaches full release.
Recommended

Re-writing the review, since this game has changed from my first play.
Carrying over from my first review; the product is underwhelming in almost any department; the graphic is the only part where you can tell that some time has been spent upon; although it is not an eye candy tech demo, so it is not enough to hold the whole castle of sand that this game is.
Let's start from the beginning: the game promised to be an exploration survival game;  which was interesting, since I already played a ton of plain survival games; and was hoping for Osiris to cover the gap between the bland No Man Sky, the FPS-less space adventure called Elite Dangerous, and the neverending project called Star Citizen, but sadly at least at the current state, the game is not even close to where it could be.
The ideas were great in the beginning, you crash landed; have to survive; enough to build a settlement to build a spaceship; then you can leave behind this trashy planet full of horrific creatures...eventually go in space, build a space station; then explore other planets in the system, and from what I understood at the time, you could either plan your return back home (basically imagine Subnautica and the Martian having a child), or explore.
The game started well with a small area on the planet; you mine, build stuff; eventually make a base and the spaceship, so you can fly out of the planet. In space you could find a space station but it was just a placeholder; hopes where high; especially when the first expansion included the icy moon to visit.
Then, the developers decided to scrap everything and re-do most of what they did; pushing the game to become basically Rust in space (or any other survival grindfest game you can imagine; they are all the same in the end); multiplayer suffered from cheating and griefing; so you go for solo player; which offer basically a more refined grind mechanic to accumulate skill points; increasing difficulty to a real survival game (which may be a good thing, not judging that aspect, since you can remove enemies completely, if you like so), adn adding "dungeons", which are underground tunnels with enemies.
Now that you have the picture about the game; let's check the various areas, starting with graphic.
It is not bad; very good at immerse you for the first couple of hours; then you realize that there is not much to see. Animations are fine; nothing special, in line with other games based on Unity engine.
The audio is also average; good effects and nice background music; which change when you get attacked or an enemy is chasing you. Effects are in the norm, with the sounds you may expect in a game these days.
Gameplay is really basic. You start with few tools, need to grind your materials, build stone stuff (make sense, you can salvage the debris of your spaceship, which is represented as a tiny capsule, but nothing is sufficient to do anything) and try to survive basically as much as you can; because your objective at this point, is to survive. You grind resources; with your hammer; break the hammer, and you need to craft another one or use rocks. No Man Sky grinding in comparison will look fun... and not because of the grind per se, which is part of many games; but for the inhuman amount of resources you need, to get to a reasonable point. Just as example, you need to complete hundreds of points just to get the inflatable habitat.
The whole thing has to be revised; that's a given, but the concern is that there is nothing really to do in this post-stamp size planet; where everything is a desert, beside your starting area. Either you harvest resources, or you survive attacks (if you decide to enable aliens). The only variation is the dungeons; and once you run them, the only incentive to run them again is to get more resources for more grind galore.
The game is Early Access; but fundamentally it seems plagued by a mix of "not sure where to go next, so let's just shuffle what we have and change it place", spiced with "we want to make a great product but we have little knowledge so we make a lot of mistakes". Often the patches introduce more serious bugs than the ones it fixes; there is a total lack of quality control in the devs process, and this affect a lot of users. You can see the major complains about the game all over the various reviews, so no reason for me to say the same things over and over.
In general, the game could be awesome; but at this point I am not sure what will be of this game. The latest patch are changing this game from something oriented to exploration, to another survival clone but in space; so if this is your thing, and you don't mind playing the same stuff over and over, you may like this game. I can't really recommend this game, in its current state.
The developers seems to realize recently that they need to listen to their customer base; so I still have hope for the game, but for the price they ask; what is offered is really minimal; and matter not if you go to the movie for a 2H movie for the same price; we can't make such childish conparisons, especially when talking about early access games.
For now, wait and see what the developers will come up with; if it is on sale; buy it but only if it is in the 10 dollars range.

Hearts of Iron IV is an amazing World War II strategy game. If that's all that you need to hear and don't want to read the details, that's perfectly fine. But be warned, this game is very difficult at first. The learning curve is huge in this one!
What do I mean when I say this game is hard? Well, there's a lot of mechanics and features that you will need to learn. It's actually very overwhelming at first. There are so many tabs and buttons that I don't even know STILL what 20% of them DO. Keep in mind as well that I have had the game for quite some time. Something as basic as deploying and training a division will take time! Playing the Tutorial and even watching a couple of Let's Play Videos/ Tutorial Videos is a MUST. However, this game gives you A LOT of fun stuff to do and a load of content! I would also recommend playing as a major power first, as they give you some great advantages and options that are unique to them. This game is also great if you love history, as there are LOADS of events that are referenced from the 1930's and 40's (Specifically Disasters in the World and very Important Worldy Events). Some are even interactable, like the Spanish Civil War. But is this game fun? Well, if you are a fan of strategy and war, 100% Not everything has to stick by history exactly either. You can puppet Greece as England or start a fascist uprising in the United States of America. Right now, I'm playing as the WWII version of the Paris Commune in France allied with Republican Spain under the faction "International Workers Commune". This game has also pretty detailed accuracies on the weapons, tanks, artillery etc. that was used in the war by the year that you are researching them in. Meaning a heavy tank reseached in 1940 is going to be signifigantly better than a Great War tank from 1918. This game also allows you to do a fascist, democratic or communist route. Even though there not super different from each other, they each give you unique options for how you want to play. Democratic Routes have restrictions on certain laws but fascist or communist ones don't, which can be a lot of ♥♥♥♥ing fun. :D
SO GET THIS GAME! IT'S WORTH THE 40 BUCKS!

Once you fix that -you can really enjoy a well made game, made with alot, and i do mean alot of effort art wise character desing wise and most of all multiclass creation wise. The Player vs Player expirience in the game is one of the best pvp in MMORPG games. Thou the free account leveling xp gain is significantly slower it can be managed to maxing out one character. I chose a mage for this game since it offered the most variety of combinations in all directions from the classic Firemage, to an all lighting mage -which i especially like- to a Necromanser Summoner- and a melle mage- a healer mage druid alike and both priest alike - considering common architypes in most MMOS this game offers you all that with one character- your main. The story itself has a alot of minievents and short animations and the quests are very well written if you ever read them- cause most common questing method that most players use is going straight for quest objectives and never reading a single quest when they have completed like over 500 quests in their playtime. And yeah my mage is max level ;-} .The profesions are not that easy to max out but not that hard at the same time-it takes exacly that -time.  The numeruous spells and a ablities at your disposal are very well manageble by key binding shortcuts that the game inspires by giving you a few pointed out at the start. The best way is to bind 1-6 numbers to LShift, LCtrl and LAlt and the others on closest keys like T, G, Z,X,C. And soon enough youll have like 1-2 interupt buttons, sevral stun buttons, root button mana shield button, earth shield button ect, and Many single target and Area Of Effect with diferent visual efects options as spells, youll get a feeling od driving not a jet but a interstelar command ship as a mage from all the buttons youll have as options -not to mention the offencive and defencive macros you can make yourself which burst a combionation of spells in bulk -and are quite easy to make. From there on its only musclememory of the fingers and fasts reflexes on autopilot. Its that why  the PvP in the game is so interesting - cause not only you have to know your own main's class but you have to know the others players spells to be able to counter,block, deflect, and stragezie by predicting cooldown holes in defence of you opponent in in matter of seconds- but theres ralrly any team coordination in pvp -its basicly havoc combat last man standing action- thou there is a gang up ganking tendency  that can be very persistant which most players find anyoning and solve with a an purpose disconect a.k.a "ragequit". The game offers so much more than other mmorpgs even Guildwars 2 copyed the dinamic events feature from RIft which turned up to be a keypoint for the success of that game. Every mmo copyes the next or the previous one and that is like very normal but you can backtracked who and when came up with certain mmo inovations-which Rift has many while offering the basic and expanded lore features in its own RPG fantasy universe.The dungeons and raids are especially interesting and fun and they do function normaly and the basic bag restrictions are there but are unoticeble. I recomend this game becouse of mixture of science fiction and epic fantasy in the story foremost and becouse all of the above.

A really neat little puzzle/strategy game, with multiple ways to complete the objective of, unsurprisingly, killing the bad guy. To give you an idea of its quality as a time-waster, I've only given it two play sessions and am somewhere around level 60.
Most of the 'bad guys' are based on real people or famous fictional characters, including Saddam Hussein, Freddie Kreuger and even Oscar Pistorius. It's kept fresh by the addition of obstacles to getting your target such as roving witnesses, security cameras and bodyguards who also need to be taken out.
The only frustration I've encountered has been in the emphasis on making a lucky shot with a spear shot from a makeshift ballista or with a box falling from the roof of a building. You can spend a good long while planning your moves, only to have them scuppered by the fixed perspective making it incredibly difficult to tell where you shot will go. These occurrences are few and far between, however, and you can speed up time and restart instantly to quell the anger they conjure.
Very addicting puzzle game. The mini games are also fun with zombie defense, angry dogs and lemmings.

The concept is neat, but each scenario is samey, and difficulty is derived from trial and error that comes from floaty and kinaesthetically displeasing physics. Menus are fine, and the visual style is neat, but audio is best muted. Kill The Bad Guy is about figuring out exactly what the developer wants you to do, and no deviation from this course is permitted. Don't let me completely dissuade you, though - if you're genuinely interested, download the demo before you buy. I'm sure there's some audience out there for this, but I am clearly not it.

So let me just say that I LOVE THIS GAME. Here is why I love it. It requires thinking, has a very good sense of humor that is dark and quirky. Basically there are 66 levels, (possibly more for all I know) which has a sort of angry birds type of system, where every level you try to complete the object (kill the bad guy) and earn all the stars, (five to six for each level.) You must kill the bad guy in each level by making it look like an accident and trying not to get caught by civilians, police, cameras, or the target himself. It's very much a puzzle game, where you must think of a way to kill your target with what the level presents you. I feel like this game is sort of speaking out with how our government treats criminals, by treating them better than they deserve, when really they just be killed rather than try to weasel out of their consequences and live peacefully under government protection. Lastly the music, the music is also pretty good, surprisingly. It's alot of fun and definetely worth the 15 dollars.

I was playing local coop, and we played for like 3 hours.
There is no food in the game. The best you can do is replay the first mission and hoard berries. There is a "kitchen" building, but not one of the ingredients necessary to make anything was available after 3 hours playing.
There is no way to grow food, the forests and swamps are empty, the few animals that appear bolt out of the screen in 2 seconds and then despawn. You are 100% of the time with hunger and thirst, making your char useless because your health gets reduced to 10%, your stamina doesn't recover, and your damage is reduced.
Besides all that, everything is a huge grind, inventory management makes me want to poke my eyes out, and the base facilities are useless as no ingredients are available to do anything after all that time playing. The game is very repetitive. After 3 hours we both decided not to play this game ever again.

Ah, Osiris. How much fun you bestowed upon me.
But seriously, it actually is very fun. I got into the game super easily, and was ensnared in its fun-trap. Until I got up to 16 hours or so. About that time, if you've played earnestly and your goal is to get a spaceship, you will have gathered enough resources and materials to build a ship and fly off the planet. Yay! But then the novelty of space wears off within 5 minutes of flight, and you soon realize that there is only 1 other planet you can travel to. Not only is there just one other planet, but that planet makes your deserted, little, sand planet feel like paradise! There is ABSOLUTELY nothing to do on the planet, except admire the icy scenery.
When I reached the icy hunk of rock, I was so dissapointed. But I thought,  "Hey, I'll just fly back and build up my base on Proteus 2 (main planet)!" Yeah right. I spent another 30 minutes trying to find my planet, but it had vanished entirely from the map. I was on the brink of tears, when I realized I couldn't go home. Seriously. I felt like crying. Luckily, I hadn't saved, so I force quit my game, and hoped it would put me back on Proteus 2. I haven't built up enough courage to launch the game again to see if it put me back home.
This all sounds pretty negative, so why did I give it a positive review? Because it is one of the best space survival games I have ever played. I felt like I was legitimately stranded on a planet. If you have watched "The Martian", this game replicates that feeling of loneliness, and desperation for survival. It was fantastic. I loved the first 14 hours of it all. And the last 2 hours weren't miserable, just dissapointing. I wouldn't buy this game at full price, but on sale it is worth it. If you intend to buy it, just be warned that it is still in early access, and needs a lot of stuff added to make it totally worth the $25 USD price tag. But I am glad to help support the devs of this game, and I hope they keep up the good work.

Hearts of Iron IV is an amazing World War II strategy game. If that's all that you need to hear and don't want to read the details, that's perfectly fine. But be warned, this game is very difficult at first. The learning curve is huge in this one!
What do I mean when I say this game is hard? Well, there's a lot of mechanics and features that you will need to learn. It's actually very overwhelming at first. There are so many tabs and buttons that I don't even know STILL what 20% of them DO. Keep in mind as well that I have had the game for quite some time. Something as basic as deploying and training a division will take time! Playing the Tutorial and even watching a couple of Let's Play Videos/ Tutorial Videos is a MUST. However, this game gives you A LOT of fun stuff to do and a load of content! I would also recommend playing as a major power first, as they give you some great advantages and options that are unique to them. This game is also great if you love history, as there are LOADS of events that are referenced from the 1930's and 40's (Specifically Disasters in the World and very Important Worldy Events). Some are even interactable, like the Spanish Civil War. But is this game fun? Well, if you are a fan of strategy and war, 100% Not everything has to stick by history exactly either. You can puppet Greece as England or start a fascist uprising in the United States of America. Right now, I'm playing as the WWII version of the Paris Commune in France allied with Republican Spain under the faction "International Workers Commune". This game has also pretty detailed accuracies on the weapons, tanks, artillery etc. that was used in the war by the year that you are researching them in. Meaning a heavy tank reseached in 1940 is going to be signifigantly better than a Great War tank from 1918. This game also allows you to do a fascist, democratic or communist route. Even though there not super different from each other, they each give you unique options for how you want to play. Democratic Routes have restrictions on certain laws but fascist or communist ones don't, which can be a lot of ♥♥♥♥ing fun. :D
SO GET THIS GAME! IT'S WORTH THE 40 BUCKS!

Alright, so I got this as it published, and when I looked then all I saw were amazing positive reviews from people who played it and loved it. two days later the top three reviews are all against it, so I figured i'd post my own with my thoughts on the game.
Pixel Piracy is an amazing concept and style of game that i myself have looked for for a while. the developers are extremely dedicated and even though there are a few bugs they are working very hard to fix them as soon as they find them, as I have already witnessed.
Pros:
Its a very fun rpg style rouge-like with allot of customization and reasonable difficulty. it has a cute but well done style and is very addicting.
you can do pretty much whatever you want with the game
the dev's are amazing and determined to make the game as good as it can be as fast as they can, and though there are still bugs past full release, within three days they posted 4 patches fixing a very large number of them and adding lots of content as well. most of the problems ive seen people having so far are due to not being used to the style of rougelike, because i think that the idea of your crew members having a mind of their own and picking their own target, or deciding what to do based on morale or hunger is allot of fun and an interesting challenge.
Cons:
Though it has been fully released, there are some AI problems which I hope will be fixed soon, since everyone is already complaining about them I wont bother to add to it.
The Pricing of items is a little off when it comes to selling weapons, because i've never heard of an oyster shell being worth a crap ton of swords.
What makes up for the cons is that it still is pretty easily ignorable and the dev's are determined to fix them as we speak. if you don't mind waiting a few weeks or playing with a bug or two I absolutely recommend playing this game, its addicting interesting and has an insane amount of potential. I'll also edit this as I can think of more, but I love the feel of the game and the potential it has and I don't mind letting the dev's do their magic behind the game so I can enjoy a pirate filled gem of awesome just ready to be complete.

Permadeath platformer mmo. Basically the weirdest combinations of 3 words to describe a game. Starbreak is really different from the games you’re used to playing.
-Tight controls, although they take some getting used to at first.
-Great soundtrack.
-Large scale boss battles. Think Terraria large.
-Not pay2win
My thoughts as an ex-player of Realm of the Mad God:
I think this game expands on the fundamental ideals of rotmg very well.
There isn't too much grinding to find equipment, while in realm you need to get lucky to find potions/equipment. In Starbreak, the equivalent of stat potions are dropped frequently.
Because of this, the game rewards skill by progressing you quickly, but an unskilled player will be met with permadeath. This challenges players to master the different zones and learn enemy attack patterns, and it challenges new players to reach a higher mark/defeat a higher zone every life.
High end characters are a lot stronger than new ones, but not as much as they were in realm.
Verdict?
I think this game is great, and it can only get better as more content is added. You should try it, but keep in mind that this type of gameplay isn't for everyone.
Also, one tip, never, EVER go into the strands.

Being a big fan of 2d sidescrollers with an old school feel, I honestly expected to like this game more.  That said, it's still pretty enjoyable, and it's free to play, so overall no complaints and still a thumbs up....just not as enthusiastic of a thumbs up as I expected to give this game before I actually played it.
On the plus side:
- Fun sidescrolling, platforming action; if you like Contra, Metroid, CastleVania, etc you'll probably like this
- Pretty cool art style; some different pallets in use here, a lot of nice contrast
- Free
- Big mobs of people all mowing through someplace...everyone fights, nobody quits
On the not-so-great side:
- The cash cost of the currency you use to buy "extras" is out of whack; stuff is just too expensive
- While I've seen some say that the cash stuff is a convenience, and can appreciate that perspective, some of it seems pretty useful (e.g. the ability to store a character with all their equipment for later use)
- Fun, but staying power remains to be seen....I thought I would play this most of the evening on (Steam) release day, but find myself done after about 2 hours
It's free, so if you ever thought it would be cool to play a game like Contra, with some light RPG elements and a whole slew of random people, why not try it?
