Quake is a game that is difficult to describe accurately. It is an experience that takes everything you think you know about first person shooters gets thrown out the window and replaced by a new standard.
Quake is the first truly 3D first person game, no longer are the enemies and objects in the world represented by mere 2D sprites but are instead rendered in full glorious 3D letting you view them from every angle. This also opens up the maps and up, down, left and right are now all equal and most all be checked to find that one pesky monster shooting at you.
The weapons are plentiful and varied from the grenade launcher which, thanks to the 3D engine, can be used to bounce grenades off walls and ceilings to hit enemies that are hiding to the iconic lightning gun and extremely entertaining nail gun. All the weapons have excellent sound effects and animations and use them efficiently leaves you feeling powerful.
Using the weapons efficiently however requires more skill than ever before, aiming in the general direction of your enemies will not suffice and only a steady mouse hand will prevail against the alien hordes.
Map design is of an equally high quality with a great emphasis on atmospheric lightning and a decent about of nooks and crannies to find hidden goodies in. The multi-player maps are equally well balanced and will reward only the most skilled among you.
Throughout the maps, both single- and multi-player, you will encounter power-ups that grant you various short lived bonuses such as increased damage, more health, invisibility and other good stuff. Knowledge of their locations can quickly turn defeat into victory for the observant player.
Graphically there is not much to say. Quake simply sets the bar and it is up to the rest of the world to follow.
An excellent soundtrack sets the mood throughout the game and creates a dark and tense atmosphere that only increases as you progress through the levels.
All in all Quake is perhaps the greatest first person shooter every released simply because of how many firsts it can boast. Without it nothing would be the same and for that reason alone this is a game that no self respecting gamer can go without.
One of the greatest games ever.

Oh Quake, how I love thee.  Quake II was my introduction into First-Person Shooter, and after I had absorbed as much of it as I could I went to its predecessor and played that.  And boy are they different games.
The funny thing about Quake is how different the games have been.  First there is Quake with a gothic feel that isn’t far from the Doom mold. Then you have Quake 2, which wasn’t intended on being a Quake game until they were unable to gain the rights they were looking for, and decided to just use the name Quake II.  It has a very technological theme with aliens.  After which there was Quake III Arena, which took all the great things created and learned from Quake and Quake II’s multiplayer, making almost a third setting/storyline, with characters from previous ID titles.  And finally there is Quake 4, which is a direct sequel to Quake II, back the the technological aliens.  And there is rumor of the next Quake game going back to the gothic style.
While the story isn’t entirely there, Quake is ultimately an excellent game.  And maybe it’s simply because I just played all the great games in the right order.  Where each game fed into the next, and really displayed how they were truly remarkable.

Good mobile game, but not a good PC port.
The concept is simple: you roll a cube into a hole over the faces of an impossible-looking structure. It's a kind of maze which you solve by backtracking in your head. It takes a while before you can do it without making mistakes. (Or you can solve the level with trial-and-error, but that's no fun.) None of the levels is hard.

hocus is a small logic game where you control a cube and roll to a target place. The twist in the gameplay is that the whole level design is based on the
.
You might get afraid of complex controls in those levels but don't worry, you can use a mouse (click to a place to move to), or a gamepad with analog stick, which I'd recommend. If you ever get lost or you won't know which directions you can move to, there's a circle with arrows on top of the screen that shows you. This can be really helpful at times when you'll be just wandering around the level, unable to find the right path.
The game has totally 65 levels, and all those have low difficulty. You can track the right way before any movement, or just move randomly until you find the right way in few minutes; it's up to you. This game can be a nice relaxing experience if you don't mind the ubiquitous optical illusion. It took me 98 minutes to beat all levels.
Graphic style is minimalistic, which fits the game perfectly. The aural experience of hocus is made of a tranquil song and a sound for the cube's movement. While the game is ported from mobile platform, it's still a polished experience, I haven't found a single gameplay or visual bug through my playthrough.
hocus isn't a game that would make people excited, but it's a sleeper in many people's backlogs that deserves a play. It may be short but it offers you enough to enjoy levels designed with M. C. Escher's optical illusion in mind; you'll be done in about hour and half, and I think it's ok for a unique 2€ game.

After I was murdered during my first playthrough because I hadn't romanced anybirdie (oops spoilers?) I was hooked
You have several birds that you can "romance" (nothing squicky happens DON'T WORRY GEEZ) and at first you think that's what the whole game is gonna be like, right? Just romancing bird after bird?
Nope.
Those romance paths serve as an introduction to those characters. The real story starts once you've finished most (all?) endings. A new route opens after that, and then things get much crazier, and yet much more coherent, way darker and more serious. You completely forget about the silliness of the premise, and everything about it that you would make fun of or that you would find too ridiciulous to take seriously is at some point adressed. Like the fact that humans and birds have different lifespans, that birds don't have the same dexterity, the cause of birds becoming so much more advanced, and every consequence that it has on the world and the relationship between species. The game is incredibly self-aware, and manages to play straight some very silly concepts with an unexpected, skilled and serious delivery. It's wonderful.
If the game was just about the romance paths, I don't think it would be enough for me to recommend. Though those stories DEFINITELY have their moments, a couple of them are sad, some are creepy or epic as all hell, but some are underwhelming, and most of them end a bit too abruptly. You only get a glimpse of who each character really is. The Hurtful Boyfriend route is where they really shine, and it's glorious, creepy, tense and twisted.
If you're going to play this game, definitely play it to the end.

You play a character who either in melee or ranged kills litteraly thousands of Zombies in order to accomplish the various missions given by NPCs, these tasks give you XP to improve your camp and skills. The armory f.ex. gives you the option to manufacture weapons and can be upgraded as you level your camp. I havn´t had to grind much outside of the missions until lvl 10 which to me is a plus, however the missions themselves tend to be a bit tedious and overly repetitive, maybe its actually what is to be expected ... this is a survival game where killing zombies is your thing. I guess grinding and overly repetitive chores belong to most survival games now a days.
Perhaps due to lack of skill on my part the game favors ranged combat a lot, it´s simply too easy to get hit in melee while ranged combat is for the most part the safest and actually easiest bet. There are things that can kill you very fast and I like to stay alive for as long as possible, some sort of shield would have been nice to help with melee.
Again, given the price its a thumbs up, I already recorded 16 hours of gameplay and in no way do I feel let down, my best advice for you is to watch some game play on youtube and get a feeling for wether you will enjoy the game.

Well hello kiddies! Are you looking for a fun game that marches to the beat of a different drum? One that allows you to use that big ‘ole brain sack of yours to punish the evil doers of the world? Are you willing to operate above the law to get these guys? Well that is exactly what Exkee’s Kill The Bad Guy game will let you do. It’s already out now on Steam for PC, Mac and Linux. What is even better is that it does not even require really big balls on your machine to run either. Which is great for those who may not get into much PC gaming but would like to have a few fun little titles on their machines to give their controllers a rest and work out their underworked lonely mice that some of us seem to forget about. It crosses genres a bit in being a rag-doll physics based puzzler/strategy game…..Oh and I was dead serious I did kill the bad guy while he was watching porn…
I really liked this game a lot and it brings some really good things to the table. Ok now upon first booting up the game I was treated to a really catchy hip-hop title track for the menu screen which made me crank up my volume a little higher, and the background music for levels continues the enjoyably catchy trend with a down tempo number that’s a bit reminiscent of some of the tunes you would hear in a 60s era spy flick which sets the mood very nice.
The game is really pleasing on the eyes too with its really nice monochromatic silhouettes of the buildings, yellow shirted villains, innocents bystanders, surveillance cameras, as well interactive objects are all rendered completely black, and last but not least the oh so satisfying red blood stain left after you do your job proper. The graphics are simple but in my opinion its a good way. When you put them all together you are upon first glance are viewing what appears to be a harmonious utopia that is of course until you leave the town painted with the blood of the guilty.
Ok. So let’s start to get a bit deeper into the game. There are 60 main missions and 6 bonus missions to unlock. Each mission has 5 objectives: of course there is the primary objective of killing the bad guy, a secondary mission you have to figure out by a clue given in the pre-mission dossier/or for those who aren’t good with riddles, through random experimentation with a levels interactive elements, kill the villain in the first day of the operation, finding the villain’s hidden passport in each level, and final objective is to quickly catch his tooth which goes airborne usually really far and very fast when you kill the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
The game can be controlled by the mouse exclusively but you can also control via keyboard with a default secondary layout or configure your own control preferences. The first few missions are relatively simple with very obvious ways to take out your target and usually very quickly. Before each mission you’re a presented with a dossier file on the bad guy in which you are targeting. This may seem a bit odd but this was my favorite part of the game to be honest. Each mission file was written very cleverly most times parodying vile people pulled right from news articles and tabloid both current and past with very effective and humorous tongue in cheek humor (and since I am a bit of a news junkie this really made me happy). Then after a completing a slew of missions you a treated with a cut scene advancing the story and reminding you of your purpose. Once you begin finally start the game you will quickly notice the bad guy strolling through town and will be travelling a pretty repetitive path (though a few times he changed it up randomly which caught me of guard) through that particular part of whichever city he or she may be hiding out in, and if he leaves before your masterful plans of assassination are able to be put in motion and you can’t taking his life a day passes…and you have to try again which means this objective is now lost. Fear not though because you can easily repeat every mission with your unlocked achievements already still unlocked for you in your menu screen. The first few missions also occasionally give you some hints on how get stuff done, interact with objects or on how to control the game, as well as what the icons in the gameplay screen do. Like clicking on the eye shows you the bad guys field of vision, which is important because if he you constructing something he thinks is even remotely dangerous or of suspect he will quickly flee and you will be rewarded with a mission failed screen. Other interactive icons allow you to pause the game and take a look at that particular map to try and make your gameplan, there is also a speed up time icon which is set at 1x by default and can also be toggled to 2x and 4x speeds. The display up top features an icon of the bad guy which when clicked immediately centers the screen on the missions target, there are also icons that indicate if you have achieved you alternate objectives.
As is with most games the further in the more complicated it becomes to take the bad guy out, as well as more and more interactive items become usable to kill your target. Remember in each mission you are trying to make it look like an accident so keep that in mind. Eventually after you complete a good amount of mission innocent people begin to show up wandering through your target sites, police are on patrol, surveillance cameras watching, and the Bad Guy’s bodyguards must never suspect you…If any of these see you take the bad guy out it’s an instant fail the mission.
For those gamers who are into being an exhibitionist there is the ability to upload and share your favorite kills with your friends and the whole damn interwebz if you so desire. In fact right in the settings there is a direct sign in option to Twitch for those who use it. Other community features are that the game has are Steam Achievements, Steam Leaderboards, as well as Steam Trading Cards
It is the perfect game when you only have a very small window of time to get some gaming in. Most levels can be finished in a few short minutes. You get to have some fun, kills some time and quickly run off to do what you must. You not left having to run off and be on some huge plot cliffhanger wishing you could have watched that 10 minute cinematic cut scene and having had venture through that dungeon which seemed like it took half the day to get the super laser sword of doom.
Ok….now for what really irked me in this game. There is really nothing in the game that tells you what the interactive objects do minus a few sparse exceptions…or what objects needed to be/or could be combined with other ones…and there were a few times I got very annoyed and spent way to long trying to figure out how to activate a trap or what I needed to combine to what to get the job done efficiently. And this happened every few levels pretty regularly. This really held back wanting to play for long periods of time as I was becoming somewhat frequent for me. There some missions I would end up wasting multiple days on me trying to get items to do things they were not even capable of doing. Also there were some traps I couldn’t really identify…so I had no idea what I was supposed to do with it. And it is not because of it appearing too small on my screen. I am playing on a monitor that is very large in 1920 x 1080 on the highest possible graphics settings here.
So the game isn’t perfect but it is still a lot of fun. It’s a great little time killer that will make laugh and some perhaps if you are the faint of heart wince a bit. It’s also pretty entertaining to watch as well. A few of my pals sat here and laughed over my shoulder for some of the kills for quite a while. I do hope that some of my gripes might be addressed in an update patch perhaps in the future if the team is able.

I bought the Collector's Edition so I will do a small review of the game and a look over the extras you get.
I love visual novels and when I first got this game I thought it was going to be a very sweet but quite gimmicky. I played the demo on the original site and boy was I wrong. Yes the game can indeed be very sweet but it can also be very dark. The game had a depth and was so well written that I had never expected. Now I will say I have played LOADS of visual novel games and am very finicky about which ones I buy. The moment this game came to Steam I bought it the first moment I noticed it was there.
Its well written, the characters are well developed and believeable (with the exception of Okasan and Aghel but that's how they are supposed to be), the music is lovely and well fitted to the areas they are used, it had multiple endings which depended on your stats in some cases, you actually LEARN the birds names which were chosen to represent the men you can be with in this game and its just engrossing. The game itself is a definite recommend.
Now I will look at the extra you get with Hatoful Boyfriend Collectors Edition:
It comes with the soundtrack which as I said its a lovely soundtrack and it seems to include all of the songs.
The wallpapers was disappointing. It just came with two wallpapers featuring the purple heart background and fantail pigeons.
The comic is short but sweet. Each character has two mini comics (4 frames) after them. It doesn't add to the story in any way its just quite sweet. Though there was only one that made me laugh.
The yearbook. I will say this now its not a yearbook. Its actually just a virtual artbook made to look like a yearbook which disappointed me greatly. I hoped it would be Tosaka's year book with pictures of her class inside and signed with a message from each of the main characters but no such luck. The art work is quite nice but not what I was expecting.
The actual game is definitely worth a buy but the collector's edition I'd advise you only get if it was on offer for a £1 or two (three if you really want it) Its not worth its £5 price tag.

I feel the trailer is completely misleading as to what the game is actually like. It shows what seems like open ended, tile-by-tile modular ship building, and then artillery gameplay similar to Worms between these ships, with a hint of Dwarf Fortress thrown in for good measure. I was instantly won over. The reality is, while there is tile-by-tile ship building, it's in practice purely cosmetical. It doesn't affect gameplay in any way. In fact, there is no strategy or tactics to speak of regarding much of anything you do in Pixel Pirates. It goes like this:
1 - You select an "encounter" on the map - whose "level" is conveniently visible to you.
2 - Your pirates sail to it and then go over and whack the hopelessly outmatched occupants of the ship/island/whatever. And if they aren't hopelessly outmatched, there isn't anything you can do to turn the tides either, the only orders you can give are to either fight or retreat; go select lower encounters instead.
3 - If your pirates leveled up, decide which attribute to raise. Doesn't make much of a difference, just accept that they now can whack tougher stuff
4 - If food is low, restock
5 - If there's excess cash, buy more pirates so you can whack tougher stuff
5 - Rinse and repeat.
There's no depth whatsoever to anything. Promises of procedural generation? Well, it's procedurally generated in the same sense that Minefield for Windows is procedurally generated. Nothing interesting ever happens. Nothing actually requiring your input ever happens.

So normally I would write a more concise review analyzing a game, and looking at all the good parts of it but also all of it's faults. Pixel Piracy is this special case where I absolutely adore the concept it delivers and the gameplay, but the execution is so god damn awful I can't bring myself to play it anymore, I wanted to play it to the end and explore everything, have a massive powerful crew that would dominate the seven seas. Instead we're left with a game that, to put it simply, is badly made. It doesn't work, and yet it 'released' mere days ago. Anyway, here's a list of about everything wrong with this game that will ruin your experience. Some issues may not seem important but do realize that all of them create unfair situations where the player is not at fault and yet the game will end up punishing them anyway or worse, just straight up giving them a situation they cannot get out of because of the god awful AI. So, here's the list.
-Crew members acknowledge orders for maybe 1 second before ignoring it and going back to doing something that will probably get them killed or worse
-Categorizing Crew members doesn't help much because giving them orders is a waste of time when they continue to do whatever the hell they want anyway. This can lead to crew members with no combat experience or health running out against high level pirates for no good reason. The above point also means that no matter how many times you try to move the low level crew member away from combat, they'll still just run back in and get themselves killed.
-Your designated cook refuses to cook because you gave him a secondary job role and he's decided that's more important than cooking food for the captain or any of your crew which leads to the unfair death of you or your crew for no good reason other than the fact your cook decided that patching up the tiny bit of damage the ship took is more important than keeping the crew alive. The same goes for the cook having other jobs like Fishing. The same also happens if they're using interactable furniture like a Card set or Set of Swords. Apparently getting that straight flush is more important than helping your captain not starve to death. The same issue can also occur just from having your ship docked at an island, I don't know why it just bloody does.
-Crew members who refuse to eat even when he's starving to death and you do actually have supplies of food. This relates to the above problem, if they have any kind of job or they're interacting with something menial, they will refuse to eat even when they're low on health because of starvation. This leads to numerous deaths.
-Having multiple people who use cannons and multiple cannons and yet all of the crew members will use the same single cannon which makes it completely redundant, also half of the time a person who can use cannons simply won't for no reason
-Crewmembers in combat refusing to target the enemy you picked for more than a second before choosing their own choice, which most of the time is the enemy with the most health instead of focusing down the person you just spent the last 30 seconds wittling down.
-Ultimate skills are trash, it's impossible to tell when they're actually being used and that's because most of the time they're never being used, they're pointless and in 30 hours of playing I have only seen a crew member use one once, and it was useless
-Selling cargo is useless and yields such a pathetic amount of gold. This is a game based around piracy, where people stole cargo from others to explot for themselves or sell for riches. In this however, you can steal hundreds of weapons, food and all sorts of other stuff and your reward for doing so is 1 gold per weapon no matter how powerful it is.
Pixel Piracy is one of the most annoying games I have ever played. It doesn't listen. I don't think I've ever had to complain about a game not listening to me, where the AI is so brain dead that the simplest of concepts is beyond them, and it always ends up punishing you, for the developers misgivings. I can't recommend this game, please don't buy it in it's current state. This review was written as of version 1.0.4
Also it took them all the way til 1.0.0 to add quest markers.

For Metroidvania (fans of Metroid/Castlevania-style games which includes stuff like Strider, Dust an Elysian Tail, Rogue Legacy, etc.), this is a must-try.   It's essentially a Metroidvania game but with MMO systems and permadeath in place, challenging you to build up characters and play smart to see how far you can get.   Death has its rewards though, as you gain experience which can go towards unlocking new classes (called Shells) that offer different playstyles.
While you can just rush along with the other players running to the right towards the next area, I personally find it more fun to take my time and explore each area before moving on, as you get more powerups and most of the places that are off the main pathway lead to enemies that drop chests full of loot.   Loot of course being potential weapon/equipment upgrades and currency used towards buying more upgrades.
The F2P model seems very fair and so far doesn't feel restrictive or pay to win in any regards.   Stash and Shell Storage seem to be the primary things you can buy with cash shop currency, and are largely conveniences that can lessen the impact of death (as you can store more items for your next Shell or keep Shells that you already geared up on standby).   Only other thing I've noticed with a price tag are stat-less cosmetic head items, with likely more cosmetics to come in the future.
Overall this game shows a lot of promise and doesn't have any of the red flags of normal F2P games.   Definitely a must-try for fans of the Metroidvania genre who like a bit of Roguelike thrown in.

At first the game felt buggy, vehicules feel werid and helis is even worse, pretty arcady. Since the game is all about long distance traveling to shutdown leaders of areas, driving or flying is pretty crucial. Once you get over it, you can enjoy the game.
The girl that coordinates (barely) everything, "Bowman" at first makes passive-agressive comments and whatnot but once you progress in the game, she gets pretty funny. Instead of laughing about you and your squad, she calls enemy leaders by funny names and is pretty funny all around. (cannot quote, it's too offensive for steam :) )
This is a coop game, the actual game itself will remind you that you can play coop with other people by pressing Enter every so often. With that dynamic in the game, whatever you do, will be done with you four AI buddies, that can be pretty derpy at times. Do not worry, they have no feelings and can teleport in your car or to you if there is not enough space. Like I said, they are always with you. They have personnalities tho, every once in a while you can hear them talk and complain about the fictionnal state of Bolivia and other things. With that said, when there are enemies around they are pretty useful. Whether its a firefight or you died, they will revive you and kill everything.
The gun system is pretty normal i'd say, not particularly blown away nor unimpressed. You have to get parts for your gun by looting. I believe you can only get those for non unique guns, which are dropped by bosses or whatnot. There are lots of paintjobs for themr if you want to match your character's camo or not.
The level system is interesting, to be able to attribute your skill points to perks, you got to have helped the rebels in some way or another, you have multiple ressources to tag with a tracker for them to gain points and their support.
Rebels can help you in many ways the same way you can control your squad. I have unlocked the mortar for now and it gets useful once in a while to take out a big group of enemies at the same time. Side missions which are only to help them I think will earn you their support and respect.
Enemies belong to two groups, Santa Blanca and Unidad, you'll have to fight both, mostly separately and sometimes both at the same time. Bots are pretty strong but it escalates pretty quickly when you mess with unidad. They work in the same way the cops woth in GTA, with a kind of scale on 1/4 on how much you've triggered them. Santa-Blanca how ever is the cartel to fight, they have taken the multiple regions spanning the game. Therefore there are many checkpoints alongside the road every so often, in the bigger cities, ofthen there wil be intel on their operations as well as multiple groups of them ready to take you out on sight. Theyr difficulty depends mostly on what region you are in.
The story lins is simple; mess with the cartel leaders and you'll have to deal with the big boss. I am not very far in the story line so far, having killed the under-boss of 3 regions so far.
This game is similar to GTA in terms of some mechanics but very far as well. You get screamed at by your squad members anytime you kill a civilian, as it should be since the game's meaning if often lost when you can almost play as god, letting people live and kill others without retribution. I have not gone there but it's explained that you "gameover" if you do this too much.
TL;DR: Fun, long, driving and shooting at bad guys, completing mission with buddies untill the big boss gets very angry.

I bought this game for only $4.99, so my judgement of this game would be quite different from someone who purchased it for $59.99. That being said, the game is good as it is bad. The story starts out pretty good, but by the end, becomes little more than incomprehensible gibberish. The combat is solid enough, and forces you to use cover, but enemies love grenade spam tactics.
To make it worse, the snap-lock cover can become really finicky and stick you to places you rather not be ending your life with a quick dose of lasers and grenades. I like the reliance on abilites, including your squadmates, however, the pitiful AI makes more than half encounters end in fustruation as you are forced to babysit them and manually extract any real use out of them.
DirectX11 API is broken with framerates dipping into the low 20's, and this is on a very powerful rig. The graphics are pretty, nothing exceptional but the variance of American landscapes powered by Unreal 3 is a nice treat to the eyes. The Alien locales, on the other hand, are of the generic "shiny grey metallic tile" SCI-FI variety.
The best way to summarize this game is to call it a inferior Mass Effect clone set in 1962. It is by no means a bad game, and surely worth $4.99 in entertainment money, but to expect more from such a quality developer of the Bioshock games, you'll only end up dissapointed.

If I had to describe this game in one word: patchwork. Not unfinished, but very obviously underwent a lot of huge changes at the last minute.
A bit of backstory first:
As any XCOM fan knows, when this game was first unveiled under the name of just "XCOM", a first person shooter than had absolutely nothing to do with the beloved alien invasion franchise, there was a massive outcry that rivaled the controversy surrounding Mass Effect 3's terrible ending. Of course, our Lord and Savior Firaxis descended from the heavens about a year later and gave us a really good remake, but the question still remained whether or not they'd still try and release the much-hated FPS anyway. Some time passed, and it eventually resurfaced as a quasi-RTS third person shooter. Beyond some really cool trailers, its release went along rather quietly as 2K just shuffled it out the door.
Now, onto the game itself. I described it as patchwork, and here's a few of the quirks I noticed:
- The combat is...surprisingly decent. The weapons available are kind of unbalanced though, and once you get your hands on a heavy plasma pistol, you'll never use anything else. The quasi-RTS system I mentioned earlier actually works pretty well, although I'm not particlarly fond that the game merely slows down when you open the menu, and doesn't stop time like in any of the ME games.
- Dialouge with literally everyone in the game is awkward and stilted. Characters cut each other off constantly and a lot of the lines feel like they were meant for something else.
- The game itself isn't terribly stable. I'd often hit huge drops in framefrate randomly.
Basically, the game was overhauled very late in development, and it shows. It'll occupy you for a weekend, but don't buy it for full price.

As you can see the review area is changing, because people like myself who had passion for this game for whatever reasons, are now leaving and moving on. What once was mostly positive reviews, now "mixed" are now changing to negative.
Lots of bugs, Developers losing focus, Updates also losing focus and making changes that were perfect already, Developers re-working items that were fine, instead of working on important areas so that users could just play the game (even simple elements of the game), They are now redesigning a few things which initially caught my eye, and brought me here to this game in the first place, ..these new update changes now make me want to leave.
One thing I can't stand is when people start messing with things that are perfect, especially when they have "core" elements they should be working on, not visuals and designs which again were simply perfect.
I really enjoyed this game at first, as many did that are also leaving this game for various reasons and also changing their reviews to negative. But the more I see from the new update the more I already dislike it. I was loving the Buck Rogers, nostalgic sort of look it did have with the ship. This will be disapearing quickly, and it's slowly changing and starting to look like every space game/sci-fi costume movie/tv/game theme out there right now. Some other video I've seen, show some costume changes that really are "not my cup of tea". I'm not sure if they are getting rid of the original Spacesuit yet, but the one I saw recently was not cool to me. The original ship will be history though which is a disappointment.
Many will like the way it's changing far as visuals and design, but it's not for me. I'm very picky about what games I test, or play. If I like how something looks, feels, and controls, I'm probably going to test it if I'm interested in the content. But once you start changing those elements that got my attention in the first place, I'm out of here.
The game really does have promise, when that will be? God knows. With the exception of bugs, bugs and more bugs, (they don't care to want to deal with much of them either), very little content, hackers, more hackers, server resets because of hackers, limited playability, crashes for some, and Network drops,....you get the idea,.. it's a decent game, ..even fun at times but don't expect too much from it right now, (you can get everything in just a couple days if you play wise). Don't expect too much to be coming out far as content, ..because when they say they are working hard, they probably are working hard, ..but it's just in the wrong direction!
Not much feedback either from Developers, very limited. I have great communication with many Developers when I'm testing or playing games. Communication to the users testing the game is key to progressing in the right direction for not only an enjoyable game, but a completed one. It also keeps the community more interested in the game, to which they will keep testing and want to play, to see a completion.

"It's all about the poop."
*edit*
Okay, all humour aside, I feel I should say something more constructive about this game.
PROS:
* Sandbox world, you get to pick the direction you go. Want to be a solo captain with no crew? Sure. Want a huge mess of expendables? Sure, that's possible too.
* Updated weekly at the least. Friday of every week the developer has released a patch faithfully for as long as I've had the game (since 0.5 alpha). He has hired a full time developer to continue working on updates for the game, and has promised to continue doing so well after release.
* Very fun RPG system for leveling your pirates in different ways. Melee combat, ranged combat, cannoneering, assassin, etc. There's many different ways you can go by choosing how you assign your stats and which skills you learn.
* The graphics are awesome, if you are into the retro-"pixel" style that's the fad these days. This game is well crafted with fluid movement (for 2D sprites lol) and some nice effects for cannons and such. A lot of care was put into making the game look great.
* Scaling difficulty. It's very well balanced for multiple playthroughs. Playing on the hardest difficulty for hunger, morale, and knockback is very difficult! (Alpha/Beta testers will laugh at this. The hardest mode used to be the standard.)
CONS:
* BUGS. Oof. It's quite obvious that this is their first game, and it shows. There are a lot of quirks with this game, from the odd graphical glitch to truly game-breaking bugs, they have always seemed to stay with the game thus far. Given that the development has been very active though, I must amend a caveat to say that any really bad bugs have never lasted past the next week's patch. See above.
* Very clunky interface. The dialogs in this game are very Engrish (developer is European), and could be streamlined a LOT more, and there is a distinct lack of keyboard shortcuts for those of you who are into that (I am). There is a LOT of polishing that could be done here. This is, IMHO, the weakest part of this game.
* Learning curve is a little steep. Very few items have an adequate explanation of what they do, and it can be quite hard to manage combat when you are first beginning, but after a few tries, it can be mastered. The developers have added a help guide (F1), but it needs more polish as well.
* Well... polish! This game still feels unfinished. The menus and interface feel disjointed from the rest of the experience, and there's still a lot of bugs. I strongly commend them for releasing the game and giving it the visibility it deserves, but IMHO it probably should have waited another month after adding any major changes/systems to debug them.
FINAL THOUGHTS:
* Is this game worth getting? If you love sandbox games, and love the idea of being a marauding pirate, then YES! This game is endearing and will grow on you quickly, despite the bugs. I've played it through 8 times since I first got it in alpha, and every time it's been a super fun experience.
* If you are averse to a buggy experience, or are not SUPER DUPER EXCITED about being a pirate, then I would recommend you wait a while for some of the bugs to get squashed out.

This game was simply pretty fun. A lot of the negative reviews come talk about the bad AI, but I never had huge problems with that. Sure, occasionally they'd leave cover for no reason or do other stupid positioning things, but it was never anything game-breaking, just an occasional minor annoyance. My one main problem with the game was that when you go into tactical mode where you're giving orders to your team, it doesn't paus the action, just puts it in slow-motion. This can lead to issues with trying to set up combos or time certain things correctly, because by the time you're done giving orders, the enemy might have moved or your first operative will have already started doing their action. But once you get used to the timing, it stops being really noticable. The story was pretty good, and I enjoyed getting to choose which classes to take into the field, therefore completely changing up how you fight in battles. This isn't anything like the other XCOM games, but if you go into it knowing that, then it's a fine game on its own.
So my conclusion is, this was a decent game that doesn't deserve all the negativity it got. I don't know if I would have paid full price for it (and I didn't, because of reading the negative reviews), but if you can catch it on sale, it's definitely worth it if you enjoy third-person, squad-based shooters.

A stylish short text adventure, like a Twine with a well crafted visual environment and UI. It touches on some interesting and thought provoking themes. In that respect, it's kind of like My Dinner With Andre only on a subway car instead of a restaurant. With robots.
OK, maybe not at all like that, but this game does give you some serious food for thought, as well as being an interesting and well written mystery with some unexpected turns.
There is a bit of replayability, too, mostly because the Game+ mode adds some interesting developer commentary, in the form of an additional robot you can question during gameplay (which is a pretty clever way of doing it). You can ask the robot lots of questions about the design process, art direction, themes, dialogue, etc. and it's almost feels like doing an AMA with Mike Bithell. If you're interested at all in game design, and about the themes written into this and why it was created, that's kind of a great bonus.
You can also replay to see the differences in how you approach each encounter, and the result of your choices, but that's relatively minor, as there aren't a billion different endings or achievements (thank god).
Well worth checking out at the paltry price they're asking for it.

A fresh take on a combination of genres, Subsurface Circular tells a rich, intriguing noir detective story within a dystopian cyberpunk setting. In the backdrop of one singular train carraige, this Bithell 'short' pulls players into a mystery which heavily explores concepts such as intelligence, free will, and human cultures. The game offers very little in terms of action; players are restricted to conversational choices, and some interesting puzzles, but it is more narrative than game.
If you are interested in a good cyberpunk/noir story with interesting characters and premise, I would highly recommend Subsurface Circular.

Design by subtraction, Subsurface CIrcular builds on the basic structure of a text adventure with a host visual delights to keep you immersed. A universe constructed throught the interaction of your stranded main character and a host of curious figures that paint a caleidoscopic vision of society. Both a exercise in speculative fiction and a commentary on our current world and the impeding role of automatization in labor force, Subsurface Circular succeds in making the player think and delights us with intrigue.

I was wondering why so many people were giving this bad reviews and I came to my answer when attempting to play the game for several hours. The issues can be broken down in these several parts:
Controls - Movement is wonky because interacting with the environment to get behind cover, hop over barriers, climbing up to areas, or plain running are all linked to the Shift key. So imagine hiding behind cover and a grenade is thrown to the left of you, so obviously you would want to step away from cover and run to the right. However, it has happened more than once where I attempted to run, but went back into cover and then took the grenade hit.
AI - Your AI controlled squad is not particularly helpful. While they can shoot enemies that stay in one spot long enough, they really can't deal with more than one enemy out and about. These guys seem to get shot up from cover very easily and they let you know because they will scream when just getting their knees scrapped.
Difficulty - Enemies are quite bullet resistant in the head area outside of sniper rifle fire. This becomes quite frustrating when very early on some of them get shields put on them repeatedly.
Pacing - Whoever designed the missions didn't quite consider what would happen if players used certain weapons. This makes various parts rather irritating. This is especially true when the Muton is first introduced. Nothing short of repeated shotguns to the face would somewhat quickly take that thing down, but when you have a sniper rifle and regular rifle, it's a lot harder than it needs to be. There's also the fact that a lot gets thrown at you. In the first mission, you fight commanders, a Muton, a sectopod, and a fricking assault ship. It's very much a pain with regular guns.
The game itself is probably about a 6/10, but I can't recommend it given how it annoyed rather than intrigued me to play more.

I really liked this game in concept and design. However, 2 major flaws prohibit it's enjoyment (and 1 minor gripe).
1) The difficulty curve is ridiculous. The game is difficult at any level but the degree of difficulty between levels feels completely nonlinear. On several playthroughs on anything higher than "Easy" I started directly next to a zombie town (their base). On others I was rushed before I even had time to build a barracks (or whatever it's called in the game). All of the screeshots above with more than a dozen zombies in them is of a game in which the player is right about to lose. That should give you an idea of what you are in for most of the time.
2) The amount of time invested on a single playthrough is too much. Resource gathering happens on a time interval and IMO the interval between when resources are gathered should be shortened.
A typical "easy" or "accessible" level of difficulty  (120-150 in-game days respectively) takes about 6 hours to play.
Here's the order of a playthrough:
Beginning phase: In the first 30 mins-hour you establish a base and you'll occasionally receive a few piddly rushes against your walls.
Middle phase: After you're well-established, you move out and sweep the map of zombies while you expand or build up your base's defense.
End phase: The final phase of a game is the "They Are Billions" cluster♥♥♥♥ zombie rush from every angle of the map. That takes ~5 minutes in which you either beat them back and win or watch your town crumble in failure.
That middle section spans several hours before the final fight in which you will most likely lose because the amount of zombies you've faced up to this point is nowhere in line with the amount of zombies in the final rush  (see point 1). The mid-phase is as boring as watching paint dry; a complete time sink. You could play on higher difficulties (fewer days) but that only means that you have way fewer resources to build your base, shortening your inevitable demise but not making the mid-game any more fun.
The exciting parts of the game are the beginning and end (whether or not you are a masochist or just want to watch the world burn). If you lose you get to watch hours of your effort steadily crumble and if you win you get a boring splash screen. Congrats.
<Minor gripe> The screenshots above show things which are not implemented yet. I get it that it's an Early Access game, but I don't think they should show the things like big steel walls and huge radar dishes if they aren't implemented. Just add them later once they're in the public release.
Conclusion)
If they shortened the play-time investment and made the survival mode not such a 6-hour buzzkill I would likely change my reccommendation because the concept is still unique and fun.

I usually get grumpy about mobile games getting ported to Steam, but I also have a soft spot for optical illusions and games based on them.
Hocus has a simple premise and is easy to start playing. Player input consists only of choosing which direction to move the red cube in an effort to guide it to the exit (or is it the entrance?). Once a direction is chosen, the cube moves until it reaches a junction, where it waits for your next instruction. There is no camera movement, because the fixed perspective is essential to the puzzle.
The early levels are simplified to get you accustomed to the rules. Later levels are more complex, but not necessarily more
. The only real downside with this kind of game is that since movement is necessarily limited to six possible directions, it becomes more of a 3D maze than a puzzle as many would think of it (I am totally fine with this, though). There are a few sections (especially in late levels) wherein many joints have only 2 available directions, and you spend more time moving/waiting than thinking/deciding. Most levels have more than one path to the exit, though the last few steps are usually fairly specific.
The splash screen states that the use of an analog gamepad is recommended, but I had a much easier time controlling the game by clicking with my mouse.
I've seen a few people get bent out of shape over the price difference between this version and the mobile version. Here are some solutions:
I've also seen a few complaints about how the actual game takes place in portrait mode (common practice for games that start out as mobile) with wide border sections on the left and right. This is evident to anybody who either watched the video or looked at the screenshots. In the actual game, the "empty" space is taken up by a slightly blurred version of the preceding and subsequent puzzles. This fact has no impact on the gameplay, and I think that using raw screenshots would have confused shoppers, as there would appear to be three puzzles on screen at once. Personally, I would have preferred solid white space on the sides, both for added focus on the puzzle at hand, and to fit in with the minimalist/tranquil aesthetic.
Additional levels will be added (at least 10 have been announced so far), and I assume they'll be around the same difficulty as the existing late-game levels.
It's a short, inexpensive puzzle, and I enjoyed it.

Well, with a little over 100 hours in this game, I figured now would be a good time to write a review on it. Anyone who enjoys other Paradox games like CKII or EUIV or even Victoria II is fairly likely to enjoy this game too. I'd say it's easier to do a world conquest in this game than in just about any other Paradox game, so if that's your thing, this game is probably for you, if you can get past the learning curve. Speaking of the learning curve, let's go over pros and cons of the game.
Pros:
- Replayability: HoI IV has quite a bit of replayability, as there are various different nations to play as, each with their own historical challenges and benefits.
- Complex front line system: War is waged differently in HoI IV than in other Paradox franchises. Troops are arranged in front lines, and typically spread-out divisions take the place of massive congregations of soldiers marching from province to province like in CKII or EUIV.
- World War II: As a major nation in WWII, one oftentimes has to take into account different fronts, naval invasions, conscription, unrest, terrain, etc. Once WWII breaks out, the game gets a lot more interesting, especially when playing as a major power.
- Mods: HoI IV has some excellent mods on the Workshop, most notably The Great War, Kaiserreich, and Road to '56. Whil the base game can get boring quickly, mods such as these can help to keep it interesting.
Cons:
- Oftentimes boring minor nations: Due to an apparent lack of effort put into many of the minor nations in HoI IV, playing as them can sometimes be quite boring, at least until WWII breaks out (even then it can be stressful fighting with ~15 divisions while the Soviets have hundreds). The United States guaranteeing all of Latin America, while technically historically accurate to a degree, also makes simply attacking Chile as Argentina difficult.
- Pricey DLC: Especially since many DLC features should either be free or can be unlocked in a slightly different fashion in a mod, people like me aren't really tempted to buy DLC for this game.
- Dumb A.I.: The A.I. in HoI IV is oftentimes just plain stupid. I've conquered the Soviets before with around 120 divisions (while they had around 300) simply by drawing an offensive line in the Urals and attacking during the summer, while defending in the winter. Since the A.I. isn't too bright, they never really caught on to my obvious plan until it was too late, that is if they caught on at all. Sometimes I find myself relying on stupid A.I. in order to overcome a more powerful enemy, such as a major nation. While there have been attempts to fix the A.I. in the past, it's still fairly stupid. Things like constant naval invasions on a singular coastline and leaving open gaps in their lines makes the A.I. disappointing in this game much of the time. One can almost always rely on Hitler attacking the Soviets in 1941 all the time. Sometimes he even does it too early before France is even finished off, making Hitler perhaps the dumbest A.I. in this game.
- Seeming lack of effort: Now yes, there has been plenty of effort put into certain areas of HoI IV, such as the battle system, technology, front lines, air support, etc., but it feels like Paradox didn't really embrace WWII as much as they could have. Things like a national focus tree for nations such as Romania, Hungary, Yugoslavia, Spain, and China should easily have been in the base game, but they were excluded, and are likely to be added later as DLC (not that that matters too much, because of mods).
- It's boring when not at war: HoI IV is made to represent the complex strategy of WWII, but what happens when that war is over? What happens when Nazi Germany is defeated in 1939 after a 2-year war or something? Well, not much. Nations will continue to build up their armies after WWII, and starting WWIII becomes an enticing option. In a game all about war, there is obviously not much to do during peacetime.
Overall, I'd give HoI IV an 8/10. If I hadn't been able to sink over 100 hours into the game, I may have called it a 7/10, and without mods it's probably closer to a 6/10, but it's probably going to be worth the money. Just be wary of the DLC especially.

So... This edition of the East Tower saga features a boy named Kuon who wants to escape reality... So for some reason, he is trapped in an endless loop... and so are you. How... nice. You again play Sakuya (you can rename her), a young woman who... does not want to act girly. As such, when offered the chance to be a test subject for her cousin's new attraction for women, she manages to convince him to let her try the other attraction... the one geared towards men. In the first few moments, she finds herself trapped with one of the four other participants. Oh, and since she can choose her avatar, she chose to partake as a male. Oh, and the real Kuon... may not be that old...
There are three endings. The bad ending is unlocked if you make a wrong choice (one of which unlocks a CG). The neutral/friendship ending depends on you choosing the lesser of two choices at the end of a stage. And the good/love ending is the better of those two choices. Oh, and choosing that better one also unlocks a small additional scene for the story (and accompanying CGs). There is a split in the route for the Love Act/Scene/Chapter, as you can choose to have Kuon in his real form or adult form.
The game is beautiful, at least for the time. I begin to think these were made back-to-back, as the small issues seem to get only slightly better each volume.
Also, my suggestion would be to buy the East Tower Complete Edition. Especially as the last volume is almost three quarters of the price of the bundle...
Hilarious game with time loops and split personalties galore; can't recommend it enough!

Having recently purchased East Tower-Kuon in a game bundle, I was finally able to continue the series. Those familiar with the East Tower series will know that East Tower-Kuon is the third game. As it's been a few months since I played East Tower-Takashi (the second game in the series), my memory has gotten a little rusty. But let's see how I do. ;)
Basically, like the first two games in the series, you take on the role of Sakuya. East Tower is an attraction where the participants enter the Dream World through their consciousness, and Sakuya is one of those participants. So this time around, Sakuya is paired up with Kuon, and there are the usual obstacles to pass and all. However, Kuon's route is different from Akio's and Takashi's in that Sakuya finds out that the game keeps repeating itself. I won't spoil as to why this happens although I did find this twist to be interesting and made Kuon's route different from the previous ones. If you especially go on Kuon's love route, there is a teaser at the end and let's just say that it made me quite curious to play East Tower-Kurenai soon. ;)
I suppose my opinion of the game is the same as for the previous two games. I liked the story, as those who know me know that I think story is the most important element in a visual novel. The art was pretty good as well. In regards to the writing, there were grammar errors here and there and perhaps some polishing of them would have been a good idea although I am nitpicking here. These errors can be overlooked, as I thought the story was intriguing.
Overall, I'd say that if you liked the first two games in the East Tower series, then you'll end up liking East Tower-Kuon as well. I'll soon be playing East Tower-Takashi and I'll be posting a review of it as soon as I'm done. XD

This review covers all 4 of the East Tower games in one. Simply put, the game isn't very good. The art has occasional good moments but most of it is pretty bad. The story is set up in such a way that it could lend itself to an interesting discussion of gender identity and digital sexuality but it instead chooses to do cliché "oops, I tripped and grabbed your boob" moments. There are dialog options but the game is still very linear; you either die instantly, find a solution, or pick a solution that gives you a bit of extra dialog.
I would not recommend any of these games except for Kurenai (which was admittedly pretty good). However, there are parts of the Kurenai story that won't make any sense without playing at least a bit of the other ones.
The game is also way too expensive. I bought them all as a set with 40% off ($18 total) and I feel ripped-off. There are much better VNs available for much less. Takashi, Kuon, and Akio were each only about 1.5 hours of play time, which is not a great value.
Finally, every time you finish a section (and there are at least 7 sections per game) the game tries to get you to post to social media. That really pisses me off. It takes me out of the moment to try to get me to advertise for a game that I paid for. Dear game devs, please don't do that!

Given the fact that East Tower: Akio, East Tower: Takashi and East Tower: Kuon share the same universe, even if East Tower: Kuon is more complex than the two previous, nearly whole of the review is a copy/paste of these.
Sakuya is a woman wishing to be a man since an incident in her childhood. She makes everything in her power to look like one. Her cousin Daiki works for Dreamworld and needs her help to try a new virtual attraction called West Tower, reserved for women. However, Sakuya managed to convince him to let her try the East Tower, reserved for men. She ends with four other testers, trapped in the virtual world, though she's happy to see that she's a man in it...
This is the same beginning in each Each Tower game. Once in the virtual world, Sakuya will team up with one of the guys. In the first of the series, she's Akio's partner, whose virtual form is a child, in the second, she's Takashi's, a boy admiring so much his sister that he took her appearance. East Tower is an attraction that will confront everyone to their own insecurities and fears.
I will go straight the point: this is a visual novel, where you have choices to make. Each stage must be cleared to advance in the story, you don't have any skills or relationships to improve/destroy. However, choices are mattering: you can get a bad ending immediately where you have to begin the stage again (not the entire story), a best friend ending (by scoring A on each stage) and a romance ending (by clearing each stage with a S). If you follow the romance route, you'll end up with an extra chapter. However, some stages don't have a A rank, only a S one - in that case, for the best friend route, it's considered as if it was a A.
Choices are generally made during the challenges proposed for the team. It's much rare to see them outside of them, before or after them. True, without skills or anything to worry, the game is easier than any other visuel novel I've already played (apart Shan Gui, which is more an interactive book), even the first Heileen was more complex and even Blue Rose was more complicated. I don't mind at all this lack of difficulty. However, in Kuon, the game propose a little more choice than Akio and Takashi, as you will have to save and load your progress for achievements.
I find very interesting the fact that the guy will be your best friend at the end, as the bad ending isn't a "you're alone", "you're killed", etc.. However, should you choose to pursue him, it means that your character is also evolving and accepting herself more.
Let's speak about Kuon. He's appearing as a cool man, however, he's very cold towards Sakuya at first because of an unexpected event in the game - she doesn't remember it but she will experience the same thing as him. Kuon uses his adult form to be more forward, as he's shy in the reality. Kuon is also showing some dual personality, making him the shy guy that has a bold and "pervert" side (though Sakuya is calling every guy pervert). You still have the A and S ending, however, you can choose which form you prefer: the current one or the adult form. It's not influencing the ending in itself but well, there is an achievement about it and it's changing his appearance for the last stage. I understand why Kuon is acting like that, however, I largerly prefer Akio or Takashi for that matter. Kuon has a nice voice as an adult and as a child, it's also perfect.
Indeed, the visual novel has voice acting... in Japanese. I don't understand a thing but as the subtitles are in English, I could follow the story. The only character not voiced is you. However, I find it really good. It's always fun to hear something in a foreign language, it's reminding me some good memories with some anime.
As for the style, it's really in a manga style, reminding me of The Rose of Versailles or anything directed to girls - because it's clearly stated in the official website that it's a visual novel for them (but everyone is welcome to play it). I loved it. I also loved the HUD, kinda hi-tech and with a good shade of green.
The music is very good too, very adapted to each scene. I really liked it.
East Tower: Kuon is a little good moment I've spent, though it wasn't really the same fun because of Kuon's personality, without having to think too much. The twist in the story is interesting, making Kuon last longer than Akio or Takashi. It's not the best visual novel out there, I admit that, however, it's still worthy of a purchase and you'll learn more about East Tower in itself and wondering what's happening really.

This is a game that you should play only after playing either Akio or Takashi, the other two games in this series. Is this worth the nine bucks price tag? Only if it came with Akio and/or the Takashi version. By itself, not really. This particular game of the series had an interesting twist, which was surprising. In conclusion, I'd recommend it, sure, but not by itself.

Simple labyrinth.
Looks cool, plays meh. The game presents a simple labyrinth that you have to navigate; as should be obvious from the screenshots, there aren't that many branches, so the labyrinths are rather simply structured, if nicely presented. I spent ~2 hours to solve all 65 of these. The problem with this is that this would've taken even less time if the game wasn't so very slow. And I'm not even talking about the 5-second wait as you select a level that is spent watching some simple 2D animation, I'm talking about watching the red cube trundle along with an annoying electronic sound. You see, the cube moves automatically along any leg of the labyrinth once you set it in motion with a swipe of the mouse or a flick of the joystick, because unless it is at a branch it can't go anywhere else anyway, but while you can think 3 turns ahead easily, you have to watch the cube actually complete the journey. Slowly. Which bores me a lot, in fact so much so that I can only take this game in small doses or I'd get the urge to smash things.
I suspect this slowness was introduced to hide the fact that there isn't really a lot to the labyrinths - if you could just swipe the cube along the legs quickly, you'd just as quickly blast through the game, which wouldn't be a problem if it had 200 levels or only cost less than a dollar (which it did in the sale).
So why would you want to play this? Besides looking cool, the labyrinths are really rather simple (so far, anyway, like I said I've completed 40 of 65), which means there isn't really any feeling of accomplishment that would offset persisting through the annoying slowness of the game which thus becomes its fatal flaw.
Unless you want to show off by playing something that looks more like modern art than a game, there's no reason to buy this -- and if you do, you really ought to get it for your smartphone, shouldn't you?

When they announced this game couple years ago I had really high expectations. I started to play this franchise years ago with Hearts Of Iron 2. Then the other games Darkest Hour,Arsenal Of Democracy, Hearts Of Iron 3 etc.
When they released Hearts Of Iron 3 it had problems that some HoI veterans can remember. But during the time, Paradox fixed this problems with patches,dlcs etc. Yes HoI 3 was a complicated game and the order of army-war system was complicated since you had to attach every single division with hand to HQ's and HQ's to other HQ's. But it had a depth, it was not an arcade game, when you were commanding your armies and making operations you actually felt like a Field Marshal commanding his army. Again HoI 3 veterans know what im saying especially if they made operations in the Eastern Front as Germany or Soviet Union.
However for some or most of the players, HoI 3 was a really complex game because of this order of war system.
So Paradox decided to make next game (HoI 4) a bit more easy and a arcade game which is completely understandble since majority of the players wanted a arcade strategy game.
When HoI 4 was available at pre-order I immediately purchased from Steam with high hopes. But when I started to play after its release, something was terribly wrong with the game. There were no sign of 'depth' from the previous HoI games. Everything was totally random. When Germany started the World War 2 it wasnt called World War 2. It was called 'German-Polish War'. I dont even want to mention maniac AI who likes to do naval invasion everyday! This naval invasions can drive you crazy since there is no end of them.
But the biggest insult is the weird acting AI. Its been 1 year since the game is released but German AI still cant make a naval or air invasion to the Britain. They send their every available unit to the random and stupid places like 'Norway or Yugoslavian border' while leaving Soviet border completely exposed and empty. With this oppurtunity Soviet Union easily marches to the Berlin without any serious defence.
There is another issue which effects the game completely. When you capitulate a country (if they are in any faction, like Allies or Comintern or etc.) they continue fighting like nothing happened to their country. They still have full armies running around and fighting against you. They have plenty of weapons, equipments and even naval forces which is absurd  and totally unlogical.
Also when USA joins to war on the Allied side. Even if you capitulate every other Allied nation except America. Allies continue to fight like nothing happens. In one of my games I literally dominated Europe and Asia (with the help of Japan) and forced every Allied nation to capitulate except USA and Canada. But they continued to fight. Now you are probably saying that USA is the bastion of Democracy and cannot capitulate. Sure, it makes sense but after getting nuked literally like thousand times and constant air bombardments they still continued fighting like nothing happened to their country!
There must be an option which you can trigger a 'peace' between Axis powers and America (something similar to Cold War but between Third Reich and USA). Even HoI 2 (or Darkest Hour not sure) had an event which gets triggered when only fighting Allied nation remains USA and there must be a stalemate between USA and Third Reich. It triggers a peace and starts a cold war between this two nation. Which leads to alternate scenarios.
If you managed come to this far in my review thank you so much for reading. As an Hearts Of Iron veteran. Im sad to say that after 1 year this game still has some issuses related with the AI and other things. And lack of 'strategic depth' is a huge issue for the old veterans like me. If you can accept weird World War 2 scenarios and a somewhat broken AI. Buy this game. But dont consider this game as a deep strategic game where you can do detailed operations and deep planning.

Subsurface Circular is a text adventure game developed and published by Mike Bithell or his company known as Bithell Games, the same company behind the amazing Thomas Was Alone and Volume. While some people may be turned off by a text adventure game where you don't really do anything but select a few choice here and there and see the outcome, I think that with Subsurface Circular, it allowed Mike Bithell to write engaging stories, beautiful and heartfelt stories
Everything from the writing, to the concept behind robotics and the human race in the possible near future, the UI and the sound design are all spot-on. If you like the concept of a future where robots and humans work hand in hand to provide a sustainable future and what happens when power is left in the wrong hands, then this is the game for you!
Subsurface Circular is a short sci-fi story about the role of robots in a near future society where robots coexist with humans, how they take the jobs of humans, how humans cope with robots around them. It's about people, and robots-who-are-people, and where society's going with the idea
It is presented in a very pleasant style. The choices are interesting, the focus system is interesting, and you can manipulate your fellow robots as you try to get to the bottom of a simple missing person case
Although short and only took me roughly an hour and a half, within that hour and a half I was more drawn into the story and what was trying to be conveyed then playing a 15 hour campaign where the story is not even as well written and explained as Subsurface Circular

The East Tower series is a set of otome visual novels that are different than your standard Japanese otome game. If this review peaks your interest, I would recommend buying the whole bundle as it is cheaper than buying each one individually. The 4 games together give 15+ hours of game play.
Note: If you read my reviews on any of the other games (Akio,Takashi, Kuon, Kurenai) aren't terribly different
I was surprised at how much I ended up liking game. I think a lot of that has to do as a Otome game addict I was getting a little burnt out on the mobile games. (When I say burnt out, I think I have played the main story line of more than 80 characters on mobile otome games.) East Tower Kuon is the third installment the series and starts to reveal more of the overarching plot of the ET series. The order which the game is recommended is Akio, Takashi, Kuon then Kurenai. I would recommend this game even to just VN fans (not necessarily otome fans) because it explores interesting themes and has a great overarching plot.
The story is what got me hooked on this game, I love a different story than your more standard otome game that ET has. The Kuon route is cute for your standard shouta stereotype but has a bit of a twist too. I especially like how this game explores gender related sexuality in a very interesting way. Gender fluidity is something much different to be explored in a VN/Otome game, especially for a Japanese market. Sakuya (the MC, name changeable) bends the standard female protagonist role, rebelling against the female stereotype, actually starts the virtual game as a male character.
The voice acting is very nice for an indie game. I liked some of the unique voices in the game (Daiki specifically). I wouldn't say that there is any blaring miscasts in the voice acting. Of course this being an indie game, there aren't the big shot seiyuus (voice actors) to really make the voice acting really shine.
I was not big on the art style that ET has, but I grew attached to the characters anyway, which is a good sign as the likeability of the character is not just based on the art. I would say the thing that bothers me the most is the roundness of the faces, especially the young versions of the characters. I think of all the VN/Otome games ET has to take the cake on roundness of faces. There are more CGs than I was expecting for an indie game. The backgrounds in ET are interesting, I really like how the game world is portrayed. I would really say that the only (slight) drawback to this game is the art style, but it is still nice in its own way.
Seems like the East Tower games grow longer and longer when you keep on playing those in order. Lovely series for otome&visual novel fans. I've been giggling and having fun while playing.

It's been awhile since I've played Gears of War...
For those that have played Enemy Unknown, this is NOT the same thing. There are the obvious surface similarities - squad based, aliens, and obviously, the brand name. Beyond that, this is a different ballpark entirely. Instead of a table top strategy game, pushing units around, and dealing in percentages with a combat system reminiscent of old school Fallout, now the game runs in real time, with a third person over the shoulder view for what is really another shooter. The movement and cover system is akin to the Gears combat movement system. In fact, I'd call it a Gears clone if it didn't have the obviously superior ability to issue orders to your squad - something that franchise sorely lacked. Playing this, parallels to the Uncharted franchise also come to mind, especially regarding things like ammo management and having to scout around the battlefield for reloads. Other parallels can be drawn to Mass Effect, as many others have here.
This is NOT Enemy Unknown. It certainly isn't up to the level of difficult brutality that Enemy Unknown is.
Will I keep playing it and finish the campaign? Sure.
Is it fun? Yeah.
Would I drop 20 bucks on it? No.
Coming from Enemy Unknown to this, I can understand how people would be a bit disappointed.
Pick it up on sale, or get it bundled in with some other XCOM games.
6.5/10

Battles can get hectic, so staying in cover and ordering your teammates do the work for you is vital. But that's what XCOM is all about: hiding in bushes and commanding people to their death. And every death hurts you deep inside, even if not as much as in Enemy Unknown, but still. You just get fond to your teammates.
Only thing missing are the redshirds you send to suicide runs to flush out stinky aliens from their holes, but two squad mates are enough, as witnessed by many other 3rd Person Shooters. Any more teammates just would make the battles even more cluttered.
Was it worth it? To me: yes!  With a mindblowing scifi plot, where gameplay mechanics were well integrated, and 60's themed environments I can recommend it. Last level especially is something beautiful.

Dishonored is a 2012 stealth action-adventure video game developed by Arkane Studios and published by Bethesda Softworks. Set in the fictional, plague-ridden industrial city of Dunwall, Dishonored follows the story of Corvo Attano, bodyguard to the Empress of the Isles. He is framed for her murder and forced to become an assassin, seeking revenge on those who conspired against him. Corvo is aided in his quest by the Loyalists—a resistance group fighting to reclaim Dunwall, and the Outsider—a powerful being who imbues Corvo with magical abilities. Several noted actors including Susan Sarandon, Brad Dourif, Carrie Fisher, Michael Madsen, Lena Headey and Chloë Grace Moretz provided voice work for the game.
The game is played from a first-person perspective and allows the player to undertake a series of assassination missions in a variety of ways, with an emphasis on player choice. Missions can be completed through stealth, combat, or a combination of both. Exploring each level opens new paths and alternatives for accomplishing mission goals, and it is possible to complete all missions, eliminating all of Corvo's targets, in a non-lethal manner. The story and missions are changed in response to the player's violent actions or lack thereof. Magical abilities and equipment are designed to be combined to create new and varied effects.
During its three years in production, several versions of Dishonored were developed. Before the creation of Dunwall—inspired by late nineteenth-century London and Edinburgh—the game was set to take place in medieval Japan and seventeenth-century London. During development, test players discovered methods of exploiting the available powers and abilities to achieve unexpected outcomes; instead of restricting these techniques, the designers attempted to redesign levels to accommodate them. Dishonored's music score was produced by composer Daniel Licht to represent London in the nineteenth century.
Dishonored received positive reviews, focusing on the missions' individual narratives and the freedom available in completing them. Criticism fell on the overarching narrative, which was considered predictable, and problems in controlling the player's character. The game won several awards, including the 2012 Spike Video Game award for Best Action-Adventure Game and the 2013 BAFTA award for Best Game, and was repeatedly recognized as the best action-adventure game of 2012 and one of that year's best games. Dishonored was initially released on 9 October 2012, for Microsoft Windows, PlayStation 3, and Xbox 360, and was later supplemented with additional content focusing on the assassin Daud and his quest for redemption.
