Firstly, we can all agree that Ubisoft is a **** company that prioritises revenue over good gameplay experience but for this game I think the folks over Ubisoft Paris, Ubisoft Bucharest, Ubisoft Milan and others did a good job at making this game. This is one of the better single player experiences in the current industry today. Now I’m not saying that this is the best game but from the usual Ubisoft suspects, this game does stands out. Though it does have some flaws but ill cover that in a bit more detail later.
Now the best thing about Ghost Recon Wildlands is the setting, the story of Wildlands is the focal point and main point of the game and all others stuff are add-ons to the base game. The story revolves around hunting down El Sueno who is an all mighty drug lord that rules over all of Bolivia as if it’s his own country. This story echoes the real-life story of Pablo Escobar and his reign of terror and the effort it took to take him down (though Pablo Escobar was in Columbia not Bolivia which is why the Bolivian Government was cheesed off because of where they choose to set this story. I don’t want to get into politics so read the articles about this elsewhere).
The game does a great job of modelling the entirety of Bolivia and they also place many informational collectables for you to learn the beliefs and stories of the Bolivian people. They also model the power struggle of the cartel very well that if feels like this cartel is held together by strings and the fear of El Sueno. The operators that you play as also have very unique personalities that make the world feel more real (though the amount of dialogue between the 4 operators are very limited and will repeat if you pass by old areas so it can become annoying after a while)
Now for the game play aspect I won’t praise so highly like I did the previous segments, because though the base gameplay of stealth co-op play is great fun, it becomes repetitive really fast. The game is only a lot more fun is you have friends while playing the game to mess around with or else the game becomes a boring collect-a-thon. This is also not helped by the games second ending that only happens if you defeat 100% of the bosses in the game (I don’t know it you also have to collect 100% of all items because I collected them long before I defeated the bosses). However, the game doesn’t end after defeating El Sueno, because the game is still being updated with special events and the recent Predator event (Which was amazing BTW).
The gameplay aspect is also hammered by the bad multiplayer connection issues. The multiplayer of this game suffers pretty much like all other Ubisoft titles (It’s like they don’t know how to make a proper multiplayer game). The game will lag a lot when you open up a multiplayer session that the game becomes unplayable for the most part. The only way I was able to make this become less of an issue was to make sure that the friend that host the game must have the steady’s internet connection (that host must also become the driver because the lag will make driving impossible with this game).
Also, the multiplayer versus mode feels tacked on just because Ubisoft Corporate wanted to turn the game into a multiplayer game because that’s what they do to all games. If Ubisoft Corporate had the chance to change the core game they would have definitely tried to put loot boxes in it, so we are lucky that they didn’t get the chance to do that. The only micro transactions in this game is purely cosmetic and don’t affect the game play at all. The DLC however I can’t say much off because I only played “Fallen Ghost” and that DLC was just a glorified hard mode with extra feature (Fallen Ghost is still good but just way too short and only fun if played with multiplayer since the single player just feels like the same old repetition from the base game). I didn’t buy Narco Road because driving in this game is S*** so good luck trying to race.
So, in short this is a great single player game with great story and add-on content with mediocre DLC and broken servers for the Multiplayer. Personally, I think the base game is the only worth wild item in the whole series with the rest just options that I wouldn’t really improve much from it unless you want some more missions.

How could this game have been considered ready to publish?
This product is a borderline scam. There are so many things wrong with it I don't even know where to start.
Was it ever even tested? I've played for maybe 4-5 hours and have already found two gamebreaking bugs, and countless minor ones.
The game in general is just completely devoid of polish. Why are there social media links on the main menu? Is this a flash game? The timer would have me believe that I have sunk 2 hours and 159 minutes into my current playthrough. Why did the developers feel obliged to invent a new system of time measurement? Why is there text floating in the air on islands?
The AI is completely nonexistent. Crewmembers will run right through enemies instead of attacking them and will never attack neutral characters unless I do so with my captain. Pathing is horrible. Being given a shorter path and a longer one, crewmembers inevitably take the latter. They also sometimes get stuck on single blocks, which they should be able to climb.
Sometimes they refuse to eat and simply die of hunger. Their salary is random and the game lies as to how much pay the crew wants.
There are numerous design problems that should have been fixed before the game was released. Blocks destroyed by cannons turn into unwalkable floor, which means characters may end up stuck. I really wanted to like this game, the art style is kind of captivating, i find the pirates squeaky voices kind of cute, it has a neat little rpg system for your pirates! it basically checks all the boxes i need!  I 'beat the game' or at least, i killed the 4 legendary pirates, i believe there is an end game screen if you clear the entire map as well, but i don't think i really enjoyed it.
Even though it is officially out of early access now, it should not be.  The UI is confusing, there are a series of buttons at the bottom of the screen that control everything, only several of them don't actually do anything (most notably, the attack button seems to be completely non-functional, you attack just by moving your units to a hostile), and the ones that do let you accomplish things are explained very badly or not at all (even in the games help system, it kind of just assumes you already know what you're doing).  It took me hours before i realized how to select my hired crew of pirates (you click on a set of bars with pirate group names on them at the top, when clicked the bar will change from black to a very dark maroon), i still am not sure how to change the groups my pirates are in to make them more easily selectable.
These problems continue in every part of the ui, the shipbuilding screen is hard to use, and obscured by unnecessary parts of the ui (if your captain is nearby a shopkeeper, you cannot build your ship without also viewing the shopkeepers inventory), on top of that, there is a grey overlay that persists while trying to build your ship, also, if you remove a part, it does not go back to your inventory until you leave the screen and come back.  The crew screen is bad at presenting information, some of my crew have what appears to be medals on their portraits, i cannot find out what these mean, there is no further info on them, some pirates have them, some don't, no mouseover/extra info as to why.  When on an individual crewman's page, skills are learned through books, which after much trial and error, it was found that to use them, you have to put the book in the crewmans equipment slot? somewhat confusing, improving stats of a crewman is done by using TP (gained from leveling) and then clicking on what appears to be a golden poop, i assume this was meant to be an arrow up, but it looks nothing like one.  Its not apparent how skills work, there is a skill called cannon mastery, my ship has several piles of ammo and plenty of cannons, but despite the fact that all 10 of my crewman have the skill, they almost never decide to use it, and almost never more than once, also i've never seen anyone even try to use the swivel gun.  That brings to my next point about the crew! despite their morale being maxed out, along with full bellies, ample supplies of rum and food, sometimes they'll just go crazy and shoot someone, just for kicks, no warning! one second you'll have a crew of 10, the next, they've all shot each other! and despite the captain still being alive, its game over anyways.  Also, the entire game is covered in a weird blur effect, i guess it was an artistic choice, but it honestly makes the game look drastically worse than the screenshots you see above, you can turn the effect down in your settings, but not completely off.  The rest of the ui is at least mediocre, the world map is kind of boring, but functional, the animals screen, i have not been able to figure out as of yet, sometimes the buttons just don't do anything at all, sometimes they start working if you click on them several times.  The game makes this absolutely horrible high volume noise at the intro whenever you load it (at the Quadro-Delta developer logo), i actually almost quit right there.
In conclusion, this could be at least a good game if they completely throw out every last aspect (seriously, every single bit, the ui is horrible, redo every single screen) of the ui and start from scratch.  The actual game is lacking in variety in some areas, there are not very many different ships you will be fighting along with every island being nearly the same, and there are a few things that i don't think add to the experience, like pirates pooping everywhere which was cute for about a minute (with the constant influx of new pirates after they randomly shoot each other, i get tired of teaching each one to poop).  But, still the game behind that miserable ui seems like it might be at least a little fun after completely starting over on the ui (100% redo of the ui, every part is bad).
08/01/14: I've heard that the UI was recently updated? I never played when the game was in early access under the old ui, but whatever was changed, change it back, it cannot be worse.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

In general, HOI IV is lots of fun; it allows you to change the course of history by playing as great nations and taking over the world, while you can also just screw around as some random insignificant country. Realism (when it comes to production and research) has increased significantly in comparison to HOI III (although making it a lot more difficult in certain aspects) and the game definitely looks a whole lot better.
A big uprade in comparison to HOI III is the availability of mods. The modding community has increased the game's playability quite a bit, adding some interesting scenarios in the progress (like WWI, what would've happened if Germany had lost the Franco-Prussian war, etc.).
Downside is, however, Paradox still uses the same game engine as in previous HOI games, the same engine as in HOI II to be exact. Result: after about 5 in-game years, time progression starts slowing down more and more (with large events even causing time freezes), thus reducing playability.
Furthermore, the DLC policy of the game is ridiculous; asking loads of money for DLC's that contain AI fixes and focus tree expansions that should've been available in patches within a year after the initial game release.
Finally, the AI seems to be mentally ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ at times, making single player pretty boring as you can simply blitzkrieg the living hell out of entire Europe while playing as Germany. Multiplayer gets a bit more interesting, since you have players who can actually make strategic decisions, unlike the AI.
To conclude; if you're interested in playing a WWII Grand Strategy game with a terrible game engine and DLC policy, go ahead and buy HOI IV. If you do, just make sure to wait until the next steam sale and download a couple of mods to make it more interesting.
Update: I have recently bought the two main DLC's available for the game, Death or Dishonour and Together for Victory. Reason: single player got pretty boring, just being able to play as the major countries as they are the only ones with interesting national focus trees. These two DLC's do enhance a lot of national focus trees for countries that would otherwise be downright boring to play, however, you're required to spend an insane amount of money on these DLC's.
Bottomline; you only need these DLC's to enhance the single player experience for the game, playing multiplayer with a friend who does own them still gives you all the benefits as long as you're playing with this friend. Thing is, Paradox charges way too much for it, even while on sale I find the DLC's too expensive considering the amount of extras they supply.

Interesting premise, seems like some great tech behind it. Been following the development of Racecraft since it started, and got in on the closed beta early on.
Pros:
-Great track generation system, they may all look similar but the procedural nature keeps things fresh.
-Graphics seem pretty clean and slick.
-Download size is nice and small, which is a nice change for modern racing games.
Cons:
-Performance is pretty poor. My system can handle most games on medium-high with 60fps. With Racecraft I get 25fps in the menus, 10-15fps when on track
-Menu is absolute garbage. Reminds me of a console game ported to PC, circa 2005. Mouse is completely unusable and controls for navigating around are weird.
-Lack of vehicle choice. Yes I get it's early access alpha, but despite the screenshots showing multiple cars, you can only drive one red one.
-Painful car setup options. It's done whilst you're on track by pressing left alt, then tapping right alt to select the option, then holding right alt until your tweaks are just right. I've never seen such poorly implemented UI decisions.
-AI cars are very floaty, they tend to drift over the track and never really have any feeling of being out there with
TL;DR If you can buy it cheap, then get it, otherwise hold off on this one. It has a good concept but the execution at this stage of the early access is not enough to warrant a $19.99 price tag.

One of the best driving games you will ever play.
This game is a mixed bag. As far as single player goes; it's a great driving game if you like time trials or just relaxing cross country driving. Singleplayer races aren't very difficult because the ai is pretty easy but a lot of the time trials and other solo challenges are fairly fun and some will require some practice. Singleplayer isn't too special, though. It's not bad but the game was clearly designed with multiplayer as the main focus.
Because as for the multiplayer.. You're given the choice to either play online or offline when creating and in-game profile. If you choose to play online then you'll seemlessly see other players driving around the island that you can use voice or text chat with. Challenging other players is encouraged since you get rank points for doing things such as adding people to your friend list or doing challenges with others. There's also ai police that drive around which will get upset if you act malicious towards other drivers. Being too much of a bully will put you into a police chase and if any other players are nearby, they'll be given the choice of getting a police car and being sent after you. The fun of this feature is partially off-set by how most players drive Bugatti's and other supercars making them hard to catch but it's still a nice tough. You can also bet money against others in these challenges which adds a little more purpose.
One of the best parts of the game that shines is the world compared to other driving/racing games. You're given two detailed recreations of both Ibiza and Oahu. In a lot of cases you can actually use a real map to help navigate both of the islands. There's all sorts of roads and highways and rural trails that you can drive on, and if you really want to you can just drive off the road completely. There's no invisible walls keeping you from driving off the road and nearly every mountain has a way to the top if your car can handle the slopes (and there are cars specifically meant for offroading.)
To top of the world's detail.. You can go into various shops and buy clothes or haircuts or cosmetic surgery. You can walk into dealer ships to look at cars in detail and buy them and you can even buy houses and apartments. If you're playing online, you'll also see other players walking around in the public areas, otherwise you can invite them into your home for shenanigans. Here in 2015, it's no GTA Online but it's still wonderful if you're looking for a more relaxed environment where someone won't try to blow you up every few minutes. Also the soundtrack is pretty chill and varied.
With that said, it's pretty much a recreational driving MMO with no monthly subscription and a cash shop that only consists of a few completely optional cars that only cost around a dollar each to unlock (the DLC only unlocks them; you still have to pay for them with ingame money so it still retains a degree of balance.) The only DLC that's mandatory for certain features is the Casino DLC which lets you gamble and win a Casino-exlusive car, and the motorcycle DLC. But seeing as DLC is very cheap, it's not too big of a deal.
Tl;dr buy it if you wanna kill time with cars and endless roads. You get a ton of that pricetag of $20..
Though, keep in mind that some people have a hard time setting up the mandatory account with Atari.
Once you get past that, you're in for a good time.

Worth the money at half price (or better), but has several drawbacks that do not warrant a purchase at full price in my opinion. If you invest money into the game, be sure to reach the "BBL ending"; achieved through obtaining endings for all other routes. It makes the game a worthwhile investment, whilst the regular routes are poor at best.

The majority of the game grinding endings to get to the proper storyline ("BBL ending") is arduous, filled with ridiculous and often out-of-place dialogue that feels like it's pandering to the common internet idiot of today. Text is filled with "memes" and comical-at-best attempts at humour, with lavish and over-the-top hyperbole. Whether or not you "get" the references, you will be appalled at how hard the translators (and/or original story-writers, if the translations were properly adapted) try to fit them into as many situations as possible.

• The inclusion of a 'fast-text' skip for the same scenes that will inevitably be repeated is a god-send; makes walking back through the game to achieve the alternate endings bearable.
• The final ending, and the story leading up to it (along with the glimmers of actual storyline in the shallow individual endings), is engrossing, and well worth the time to complete. The tone is different to that of the rest of the game, and justifies this as a purchase, if nothing else.

In Hatoful Boyfriend you play as the only human student in a high school for pigeons. The reasons why you have enrolled are not thoroughly explained, palming off any questions with skill that rivals destiny (none at all).
The game features heavily on puns; "Good morning, everyBIRDY!" and "His feathers would make anyBIRDY proud". These puns seem to be inspired by friendship is magic, which is the only form of media to come close to repeating the same "every(pony/birdy)" pun as often as possible in the shortest amount of time.
The gameplay mainly consists of computer created still images with blocks of flowing text underneath. This gets boring fast, especially with the repetitive music the plays in the background. Despite the poor writing, however, there were several Pokémon references: I was hit by a super effective wing attack while I considered joining the athletics club.
Occasionally you get to make a decision between multiple boring options. I chose to join the student council and attend math class, this allowed me to increase my wisdom by 5! As it turns out some choices have no bearing on the game, with subsequent text blocks forcing you into another choice. Other stats include vitality and charisma which you increase by taking gym and music respectively.
I was forced to play a female character, but once I got over being called Miss Qark I accepted the idea of having to find the perfect feathered boyfriend. One of the character's love for pudding rivaled my own for cheesecake, and I was instantly attracted. I reached the 1 hour mark before I had a chance to sleep with anybirdy and decided to stop playing before my sexual preferences were irreversibly altered.
I would rate this game a 5/5 for the puns, Pokémon references, and the, rather handsome, pudding loving pigeon however the game failed to cater to the needs of all sexual orientations. Due to this blatant discrimination the final score is 1.5/5.

I'm surprised this game got mixed reviews, to be honest.  I think it's because it has the "XCOM" name on it, and XCOM games are typically turn-based strategy (which made some people angry).  I actually played XCOM Enemy Unknown right before Bureau, and they are very different genres, but I liked them both for what they were.  Bureau is a cover based shooter with lite RPG and agent-building elements, pseudo turn-based strategy in the form of slow-motion pausing to issue orders to your squad mates and use your own abilities, and a story emphasis.  It's kind of like the Mass Effect games.
It has an interesting story, detailed graphics and plenty of times I found myself taking screenshots because it looked so cool. The Bureau: XCOM Declassified is a squad-based 3rd-person cover shooter, where you are part of an elite US-agency, fighting an alien invasion in the 1960ies. There is not a lot good about that game, and a few bad things.
Gameplay and controls
You have your base, where you can walk around and talk to a few people. Sometimes you have to look for someone or something, and it can get tedious. But the main part of the game of course is fighting aliens. As said, it is a cover shooter, so cover is king. There is a twist in the mechanics, as you do more damage if an alien is flanked (and you receive more damage, if you are flanked). This leads to the frustrating effect, that even if you shoot at some aliens head, it might take you up to a whole magazine to kill it that way, if it is not flanked. To flank aliens, you are supposed to use your squad mates. Problem is, they are not very smart: If you try to flank the aliens yourself, in most circumstances, your squad mates follow you automatically, so everybody again ends on the same side of the aliens and no flanking. By pressing space you can enter command mode, where time is considerably slowed. In this mode you can order your squad mates and use abilities. So you can tell your squad mates where to go eg to flank the enemy. Again, problem is, then they do not watch out, if they are flanked, so you end up micromanaging their every move. This was what ruined the whole flank/cover thing for me. As mentioned, there are abilities, like Heal, Mine, Shield etc. All those abilities have to be activated manually. I felt they were not well curved, meaning abilities which were very useful when you get them become ineffective later on, but there are often no new abilities to replace it. If health reaches zero, the characters do not die, they start to bleed out. You have a short time to revive them, otherwise its permadeath for your squadmates or game over if its you. Reviving team mates is one of the few things, your squad mates do even if not commanded (sometimes). By killing enemies you gain experience and level up, which means more health and new powers. Controls are okay, there are a few little things, which I found annoying, like if you want to plant a mine, you have to move the cursor there as if you were walking, that means around covers and barricades, although mines are thrown within a indicated circle; you can assign buttons to functions, but some are fixed. There are quite a few different enemies, but besides that some are a little stronger or have shields, there are only 4 different types. The covers might be on different places on the battlefield, but again, they are always similar - so most fights feel the some as the one before or after.
Presentation
I found the music forgettable and underwhelming. The voice acting was as good as can be expected, although I found the characters and their execution somehow generic. Also your squad mates always have the same voice actors, no matter who you pick - it feels lazy, when you hire a Russian agent, who does not speak English, but as soon as the mission starts he speaks with the same American voice as everybody else. Graphics are technically up to par, as far as I can judge. The surroundings are generic - there are basically three different kinds of surroundings in the levels, and although they obviously tried, they seem the same. The faces of the characters, including some of the aliens, are well done, but as there are only very few alien types - partly with generic variations like "elite" or with shields - they again lack variety. I found the resolution of the pre-rendered cutscenes surprisingly low - but there are only very few.
Story, game length, replayability
As said, you defend the earth against an alien invasion by being part of some semi-clandestine organisation and characters are somehow generic. The story has its moments, but on other instances has plotholes and dei ex machina and is not improved by being told very elliptic. The first 2/3 of the game the story is as can be expected by the setting. But then there is a plot twist and the story becomes something very different. Not bad, but the two parts don't fit well together. Also there are multiple endings - at some point you have to choose, but you have no idea, what and why, and no indication, which decision brings which ending. As the game saves automatically, you can not go back. It took me a little over 10h to beat the game including all side missions on Veteran (2nd hardest) difficulty. I already mentioned, that the game feels rather repetitive, therefore I do not feel any inclination to every replay it.
Difficulty and DLC
You can pick between 4 difficulties. Two extra missions DLC are available, with both of which I did not bother. But there is an extra weapon DLC. Is the game intentionally unbalanced, so you need this weapon? I personally found the game unbalanced, but mostly in the end: As said, several of the abilities lose their usefulness later in the game, but there are not enough to replace them, while the enemies become stronger and more numerous. So the final battles are frustrating, but the extra weapon is only useful in the first half of the game, before you get better weapons "conventionally".
Overall 5/10
The basis of the game is mediocre, with a few good ideas sprinkled in here and there, but more flaws - some very minor (controls), some a matter of taste (story) and some unexpected (unbalanced and extra weapon DLC). I played it with very low expectations, even those where not fulfilled: 5 of 10.

The writing is excellent, as is to be expected from Blithell. It doesn't outstay its welcome and is the right price for what you get.
The game takes place entirely in a single carriage on a circular metro line. You are a robot detective, interviewing your fellow passengers to figure out why other robots are disappearing. This is a great concept, and I love short stories that take place entirely in one setting.
However, the game does seem to think that interviewing randomers who happen to use your carriage is a good substitute for, like, methodical investigation. A robot on my train would pass on a third-hand rumour and it would say, "Ooh, you found out something useful there!"
Additionally, the callback to "Thomas Was Alone" was really awkwardly wedged in there.
But these criticisms are minor compared to this single point in the game's favour: at one point, the game actually made me get up and find some scrap paper, write out a logic table, and solve it. Brilliant. Worth it for that alone.

An interesting concept that doesn't overstay its welcome, and a mystery with a satisfying conclusion and clever twist. There are a few puzzles that feel like they were included because someone thought there needed to be a "game" there, and I think they're to the detriment of the narrative - the real reason to play this game is for the writing. If you enjoyed the SNES Shadowrun or TES3:Morrowind's "keyword" dialogue systems, you'll feel right at home here. The game is a bit short at about 90 minutes to 2 hours in length (depending on your reading speed) but feels satisfyingly tight and compact as a result.
Personal rating 9.5/10, well worth your time and money.

Dishonored is one of the few games that takes a mechanic and builds an entire world around it successfully. Most stealth games I've played take on the task of creating the "greatest stealth game ever," yet the aspects always feel rushed and uninteresting, only an addition to ship their stealth mechanic sim as a presentable product. Take Thief for example. It has so many great mechanics; lock picking, using arrows to scale buildings or extinguish torches, even sneaking past birds. Yet it falls short with a copy-paste story and a world that feels dead without the main character. Dishonored, however, manages to have all the essentials of a stealth game; multiple approaches, interesting abilities, and satisfying kills, but it also manages to include all the other (very unique) aspects of a good game. Engaging story, multiple endings based on your actions, and an ambient environment that feels open world, even though its not. Not to mention that the game is topped off with some fantastic visuals and atmosphere that have aged
well. For anyone who is looking to get into the stealth genre, this is the
introduction, a definite recommend.

I seldom write extravagant reviews, primarily because very few games, I feel, are worthy of outstanding praise. And yet, when I come across a game such as this, I can't help but notice it is completely worthy of excessive embellishment. In any case, I'm here to write a review, and a review this game shall have. Pixel Piracy boasts a very unique and captivating game experience, in which the player commandeers a crew of motley pirates, and endeavors to train them to be the best in the seven seas. To this effect, the player sails throughout a vast majority of isles and remote locales, all the while looting, plundering, and slamming down rum. The game is portrayed in a cheerful and endearing pixelized style, the likes of which are seldom seen in modern gaming. Initially, I was somewhat put off by these graphical limitations, but the game subsequently won my gaming heart with it's original gameplay, cheerful soundtrack, and many different ways to customize your swash-buckling experience. I wish to thank the developers for bringing this adventure to our PCs, and chastise them for getting me horribly addicted. I speak in jest of course; I am truly glad that I got the chance to obtain this one-of a kind adventure.

Free to Play: No Trials. No Tricks. No Traps.
That sentence is a complete lie nowadays, playing as f2p became basically a trial, once you get to level cap, surprise, you need to buy Earring Slots and Planewalker to be strong enough for raids. Want to PVP instead? Prepare to get one-shot by wallet warriors with BIS gear that you can't even damage below 10%.
If you want to be competitive in either PVP or PVE you simply wont be even close without paying, I bought the planewalker cheapest (20$) package just so I can raid and pvp on “even” ground (earrings and gear which makes huge diffrence, earrings by itself is like 10-15%% of your stats), but even with that purchase it’s impossible to keep up with the people buying monthly sub, as they earn more currency, have higher caps etc. You might think it’s not really pay2win since you can get same stuff for free with time, well technically yes, BUT it takes so long by the time lets say you get tier one set for your class, the game is already in t3, once you are halfway in t2 gear its already t4 out, etc etc. Basically paying players have huge advantage all the time, both pve/pvp they will simply have more stats than someone playing for free. I used to recommend this game as best f2p mmo out, but since last expansion it went completely pay2win, buying rex isnt really viable anymore to keep up, due to rex prices inflating so much it’s close to impossible to farm plat for it to sustain montly sub like that (price tripled on EU during few months i was playing, I assume now it’s way more especially latest move by trion, making earring and planewarlker cash only)
Tl;dr Newest Endgame Raids are not possible without spending money, being competitive in pvp either. As f2p you will only be able to do older content tier’s (most likely 2 tier’s behind the current newest), and pvp is not even worth trying without mid-end gear. F2p is only viable if you play super casually, since its basically trial, but then you might as well go play GW2 which does it better for casual play, or Blade and Soul for pvp, Tera etc.

To some extent, this isn't a kind of game you can recommend to friends you play games with. It's not a game meant to be shared in the modern sense like MMORPGs, Mobas, mmoFPS, arena shooters and alike. It's more like a book you enjoy for yourself more than for some sort of auxiliary entertainment that comes from satisfying mechanics or epic visuals.
In its base, Subsurface Circular is a very small window into a very complex and almost organic society that feels familiar but is distant enough to enjoy without much background. To the visual novel reader, the sort of engaging text options will feel familiar, but as opposed to directing a story and wooing other characters, it's more of a service to fill you in this potrayal of a life when stripped down to its core, but then jammed into the struggling everyman. If anything, the main protagonist is our gate to a world that I desparately wish could be traversed and explored.
The only downside is its length, which varies by reading speeding, yet it's its own experience. Half the price of a movie, but double the level of immersion and story-telling than the majority of them.

Everything from the writing, to the ideas, to the UI, to the sound design is spot-on. One of the most polished IF titles I've ever played. If the concept seems appealing to you, please, please buy it. It's very good.
But just in case you're not willing to buy a sci-fi interactive fiction game without some more words: it's essentially a short sci-fi story about the role of robots in a near-future society. It's about how robots coexist with humans, how they take the jobs of humans, how humans cope with robots around them. It's about people, and robots-who-are-people, and where society's going.
It's a lot to think about, presented in a very pleasant style. The choices are interesting, the focus system is interesting, and you can manipulate your fellow robots as you try to get to the bottom of a missing persons case.
It took me roughly two hours of reading to get all of the achievements and both endings, and I'm very happy to experience it.
Long story short: enjoy this! Support the dev so they make more like this! Enjoy how charming the robots are!
not a completely original story, ultimately, but told from a refreshing perspective and exceedingly well-produced.

Like a fair number of other games today XCOM Declassified is a case of the mistaken identity.  Bureau is a great game solid 3D person action with surprisingly deep tactical elements, great visuals, and nice (for the pulp genre) story.
The problem is the game has a lot more in common with Mass Effect than with XCom.
Combat, squad management, agent powers, level design... everything is patterned after Mass Effect.  Even story really - loose team-building part, replace Reapers with Outsiders, replace indoctrination with infection... few more similar changes... put the whole thing on 1960s Earth = Mass Effect Deja Vu.
The bottom line, if you are looking for an XCom game - you might as well pass.  If Mass Effect streamlined for combat missions and set in 60s sounds interesting - the game is more than worth the price tag.
Note: Keep in mind the game really is tactical, on anything but the easiest difficulty expect to spend more of your time commanding the squad than pulling a trigger.

The soundtrack in the game isn't memorable but is decent. During the cutscenes it feels like some sound is missing such as footsteps.
In the end X-COM: Declassified is an enjoyable game. It could be lacking in some parts but it can bring you in on other parts. Pick up this title when it's on sale. Don't buy the game for more than the twenty dollar price tag.

It also incorporates a dialogue system (at which point you'll likely feel like the game is trying really hard to be a Mass Effect clone, and not a very good one at that), chock-full of extremely bland and abrasive dialogue. I tried to listen to conversations, but quickly began skipping through because of just how remarkably uninteresting everything was.
The game feels underdeveloped, awkward, messy, buggy, and uninspired. It has a worse combat system than the first Mass Effect, the production value of an indie title, and the humanity and passion of the worst COD titles.
I generally have a knack for enjoying things in spite (often, in light) of how much negative press it's gotten, but this game is far beyond any amount of patience I have. Maybe it gets better, I don't know, and I don't feel like spending the time to find out. If you want a number, eh, I'll say 4/10 from what I played.
Oh, and PhysX is buggy and defaults to the CPU in spite of what Nvidia Control Panel settings you have. There's probably some config file swap fix or whatnot, but I honestly felt entirely uncompelled to explore that.

To make it short and painless, the game does nothing really well.
Story: Bad
Action: not really exciting
Tactical elements: fake
Basically a cover shooter with some tactical elements, neither the shooter part nor the tactical part work satisfyingly. 3rd Person shooter controls feel cumbersome, getting into cover and especially getting out of it (due to the huge amounts of grenades thrown at you in higher difficulty), aiming, running, jumping over obstacles, and even picking up ammo often gets a challenge of its own. Your squad, even though equipped with nice abilities, constantly dies of AI stupidity, beating the game only becomes possible because enemy AI is not any better. Speaking of the enemy, combat is dull and gets repetitive soon, instead of playing out the strengths of the tactical command UI, the game constantly throws you into small arena-like areas where you fight waves after waves of increasingly armored and shielded enemies (gimmicks like the rocket turret soon become entirely useless against enemies they dont even scratch. Like Mutons. And there are a lot of Mutons). Little example for the badness of game design: There are enemies you better attack from behind. So the obvious idea would be to tell your squad to get into cover to divert the enemy to sneak behind it to get a good shot. Often though, there simply is no "behind the enemy", and even if there is, your stupid squad will follow you automatically if you get more than a few meters away from them (of course they not rarely die in this attempt to follow you).
Regarding the story, a lot more potential was wasted here. Alien Invasion meeting 1960s Cold War Paranoia is a great idea but they dont really made anything interesting about it. Instead of facing the claustrophobia of living in a subterranean bunker base while hell breaks loose on the world, you have to persecute the obligatory Shodan-Skynet core villain who you just need to kill to stop the entire invasion. Biggest joke: in the end, it just gets covered up, but if you actually get so far to see the end you have already stopped following the idiotic plot anyway. Steam says I put 25 hs into this crap. Needless to say it was wasted time....

Rating: 9/10
Overview: First Person Stealth/Action
The Good:
+Steampunk with a Victoria era aesthetic provides an unique look not seen in any game
+ The level design is phenomenal, rivaling the level design in the Deus Ex series. Every level provides multiple ways of completing objectives. Every level is fun to explore and encourages multiple playthroughs to see how events unfold.
+ By playing more action oriented, killing lots of enemies, later levels will be different than those who took a stealthier approach. Later levels will have more enemies, characters will speak to you differently and major objectives will also be different. This is something that really sets itself apart from other games in the genre.
+ The main story and characters are interesting and every level has books, notes, and letters scattered around that flesh out the world, locations and lore.
+ By finding runes you can upgrade certain powers. The main power is ‘blink’; the ability to move very fast covering a short distance. By using this power, you can move to hard to reach areas and discover new pathways to complete objectives.
+ Lots of graphical/gameplay options
+ voice acting
+ The 3 pieces of DLC are also excellent. The fist is the Dunwall Trials. 10 levels that feature combat, stealth, and speed
challenges with a lot of interesting ideas thrown in the mix. These trials are difficult and getting the achievements even harder. The other 2 pieces of DLC tell the story of another character where you play through 6 more levels which are just as equally good if not better than the main game.
The Average:
+/- Despite the great art style, textures seem blurry and low resolution.
The Bad:
-  If you decide to play stealthy and want a no alert, no kill playthrough, you may accidently alert or kill someone without knowing it and the only way of discovering this is at the end of mission, in which case you would have to replay the entire mission over again.
Conclusion:
I love this game and the genre itself. The art style, level design and gameplay all come together in one complete package. Like all stealth games, it can be very slow paced which is why you also have the option of killing your way through with sword and pistol.

Final Score: 95/100

A very important game in gaming history. It added and extra dimension when it came to FPS's and it was a landmark achievement at the time. Today, however, the third dimension is used in pretty much every game now, but Quake still holds up as a whole. It plays like a silky-smooth old-school FPS with deep/nonlinear level exploration, fast-paced projectile dodging, and a variety of differentweapons and powerups used to kill a variety of  monsters. If you like old-school FPS games, you'll love this.
There is one major flaw however, one massive issue that brings the whole game down, and it's not Quake's fault, it's Steam's. There is none of the original music. When Quake was orignally released, there were two discs: one with the game, and one with the music. When they released it onto Steam, they didn't bother putting the music in with it. Why? It takes so much away from the game's atmosphere. Oh well, the gameplay is still fantastic and that's all that matters really.
As great game if you want some creepy, old-school action. Just make sure you have your own music playlist ready before playing though.

Somewhat lacking in features still (like the ability to rebind any keyboard hotkeys, this is important devs!), but the gameplay is crazy addictive and extremely fun. Feels like I'm playing Red Alert for the first time all over again. Extensive, but intuitive tech trees that reward strong early game macro. By investing in infrastructure early on and trying to minimize spending on defenses and army I was able to build a nice size base by my third attempt (the first two games I was overrun within the first 10 days while I was getting used to the zombie aggro and figuring out how greedy I could be with my base defenses in the early game).
If you're remotely a fan of RTS pick this game up!! I'm having fun with the genre for the first time since ~2010 when SC2 first released. More than fun, actually. I started my first round just to try the game and see if it was worth the purchase I made, and suddenly three hours have disappeared! It's pretty rare that I get sucked into a new game like that these days, so it was cool to experience that "holy crap where did the last few hours go?!" feeling again.
The gameplay is definitely way more about macro than micro, but if you're one of those people who loved to play Command and Conquer by stacking defenses and building the most insane base possible before annihilating your helpless CPU opponent, you will LOVE this game.

As with all Early Access games, this review is only valid until the problems are resolved, which I think they would be seeing as they are only detreimental to the game, and not as a form of difficulty (I think).
The simple problem is, in its current state, the game is much to hard. I have played four games to the final wave, where the infected come from all sides, and every time I lost for the same reason. Towers and solders have two targeting modes, one where they target the closet enemy, and one where they target the "highest level". How the game determines what is highest level I could not tell you, but what I could tell you is that it is objectively wrong. Other then the base line infected, I have noticed three other kinds so far, a harpy that can climb your walls, a fatty tank that does more damage and takes more as well, and a spitter type that does damage from a distance, with the last one being the most dangerous. Towers however seem to prefer to target the tank units, even if they are takeing damage from spitters. Towers will stop working after being damaged to about 60% hp, where as walls stay standing and block infected right up to zero hitpoints. The spitter infected also priority target towers over anything else, leading to my towers being dissabled before the infected are through my walls. Setting the towers to target highest level enemies causes them to shoot at the big tank units, which are actualy a very low threat seeing as they can be blocked by smaller infected from reaching your walls, and telling them to manualy target the spitters is neigh on impossable, seeing as the infected pack so densely that half the time you can't even physicly click on them.
This leads to a scenario where your walls take damage and fall at a linear rate, but once one tower goes down from the spitters, not only is your only real viable souce of damage gone, but now the spitters who toke it down will join others to hit the next tower, leading not only to an exponential drop in defensive power, but a cascadeing effect as the buildings behind your towers get infected, spawning more damn zombies only for it to repeat at your next layer of walls. And all of this was on a 22% difficulty rating, according to the game, with the defualt settings being 180%!
Other then that, a few minor gripes would be unit pathfinding can be quite awkward, alerts when walls and solders are takeing damage sometimes dont apear untill after said unit is dead/almost dead, and clicking buttons on the ui sometimes wont register. The map generation can also be quite unfair, with infected villages placed right on your doorstep, poor resource spread, and some unsavory terrian force restarts untill you generate a good starting point, so possibly tweaking the land generation to be a bit more helpfull, at least right around your colony center, would go a long way.
Like I said in the beginning, if these problems are solved, or if you think you are up to the challange of a very difficult game, this would be worth your time and money, but at its current state I do believe it to be a little unfair.

At first glance, this game could appear to be just another VN. But after going through all of it, I've realized it's a work of art.
Absolutely beautiful, and there's nothing I can say that would do it justice.

Facts:
- There are two halves to the game
- The first half of the game is primarily dating and getting to know each NPC
- You play as a 15 year old Japanese girl who is trying to establish some form of a relationship with each character in the game
- The second half of the game adds a lot of context to the game
- There is a save state function (which is really helpful for completionists)
- There are some spelling and grammatical errors with some subtle character scripts (as of writing this review and finishing this game) - Grammar Nazis stay away from this game
- This game is mainly text based with scripted RPG elements, lots of reading is involved - non-bookworms and COD kiddies beware
- Graphics are static images which little to no animation
- Character models are two dimensional images
Opinions:
- Replayability is high as every playthrough seems to add more depth to the whole game
- Some character endings are a little tricky to obtain (in relation to achievements)
- Very well written story, I reckon anyways
- The first part of the story is long and can quite easily lose you, but is rewarding when you arrive at the second half of the game
- Music is interesting, built the atmosphere up quite well
- Game is made well and hence rarely crashes. However, in the eleven hours that I have played, issues I experienced were: script lines overflowing, saves not loading properly, overlapping texts, multiple option textboxes overriding the default layout, subtle music track changeover issue and the dreaded blank screens. However most of these issues were resolved by reloading the game and/or rebooting the game
- At the time of this review, the trading cards go for approximately 20 cents per piece
TLDR: Overall, I started this game with very unrealistic negative bias towards the game as I thought it would be a dating sim and just like every other dating sim that I HAVE READ ABOUT, its about a protagonist who ends up with ALL the NPCs. However six hours in, I was proven right...AND wrong as there is much more to THIS avian/human dating sim that meets the eye.
I would say if you love to immerse yourself in story and like reading a lot then this is a game for you. Or if you really enjoy anime/manga or gimmicky games, this is also for you.

Mike Bithell has always been a fascinating developer for me. Thomas Was Alone was a great example of how putting a bit of context to an simple platforming game could make it feel like so much more.
Subsurface Circular is very similar in that aspect. It's a basic text adventure where you play as a detective tasked with solving a disappearance case that is not what it seems. I don't want to spoil anything here, but the writing here is on par with his previous games. There's a captivating story here, with little twists and turns that keep it from feeling like your typical sci-fi story.
If you're interested in seeing an Asmov-inspired sci-fi narrative unfold with your choices adding an interesting depth to the mix, you won't want to miss this. Absolutely worth the time and money I spent on it.
Surprising chat-puzzler. Don't expect tons of story branching, but good SF questions asked, in a convincing world. Short and good.

This game is... different. It is basically a "choose your own adventure" novel. There is no gameplay apart from clicking and reading and making choices. No quicktime-events like in The Walking Dead or The Wolf Among Us. If that does not suit you, do not buy this game. If, however, you are a fan of stories and twisted narrative, you should definitely get it. The protagonist is a human, attending a bird-school and the main goal is to flirt and date the various characters that can be met. This sounds crazy and boring, but it is not. This game is just f*cked up. The graphics are not worth mentioning, the soundtrack however suits the game pretty nicely. The writing can get you hooked, if you are ready to ignore the typos that occur from time to time. The first playthrough should take about 2 hours, but there is replay-value, as there are several different endings. It is not for everybody, but if you want something new and crazy, this is probably a game for you.

Subsurface Circular is a strange little thing. It's not really a game, though it has a few middling puzzles. It's billed as an interactive adventure with a branching story, but the story branches about as much as a wallet chain.
And that story makes about zero sense. That's disappointing, because I quite liked Thomas Was Alone, one of the previous efforts by this developer.
I don't think Subsurface Circular deserves the high praise it has received, because it does not adequately sell the Big Moral Choice it poses at the end of the story. I also think the choice of ending comes off more as a cop out than the ambiguity tease it apparently intended.
On the plus side, this is a good game to play with a 4yo in the house. No disturbing imagery, and it's easy to pick up and put down. Probably better to experience on a tablet than a desktop computer if they ever release it in mobileland.

This one's storyline is quite melancholy, but it's easy to see what will unfold and I didn't feel taken by surprise by the story's events. I really wanted to like this game. The visuals are gorgeous, the story *should* be compelling, and I was hoping for a Firewatch-esque kind of emotional reaction, based on what I knew of the game going in.
Unfortunately, the actor doing the narration is very flat and dull, and despite such a tragic storyline, the way it's delivered fails to bring out any sort of emotional response. I'm the kind of person who cries at the drop of a hat during movies/games, and this didn't elicit a single tear (and the subject matter should have queued the waterworks, without going too much into spoiler territory.)
The levels also tend to go on a bit long, there were a few times when I was actively confused as to what I was supposed to be doing, and at times the pauses between narration were so long I found myself getting bored. For a game that only took ~2 hours to complete in a sitting, the downtime was excessive. At no point was I excited or involved in the storyline, and I only kept playing to see if it would get better. When I reached the final scene, my thoughts were 'So... That was it?'

Relaxing
Bottle : Pilgrim is an interesting game about a man trying to discover himself about his flaws and learn to move on. Game is a nice walking sim with a relaxing design to it, but that's about it.
Gameplay
There isn't much here more than taking a nice walk, collecting items in each chapter, and listening to a story of a man trying to express his tale.
Sound
Voice acting is ok, but not inspired much. The dialogue is actually really well writen, and enjoyable to hear; however, the voice actor doesn't seem to be deeply invested in the role, in what seems like lacking emotion.
Controls
They work, but sometimes can be jerky. Found my mouse acting up for time to time, but it was fine enough. I really wish I could walk faster too.
Graphics
This is one of the better parts of the game.  Unreal Engine delivers a beautiful image and the environments are a joy to look at. Play it on the highest settings if you can and enjoy the view.
Overall
Bottle : Pilgrim has its flaws, but delivers a fine enough experience for the price. It's very short, but good enough to sit down and relax too. There's no complications to it. It's just a nice game to go along with on a ride.
Recommended.

is Tonguç Bodur's most recent game, and a sequel to his 2016 title,
. After playing both games, I can safely declare that the developer had come a long way in just a year. This one is a breathtaking visual display, and a heart wrecking one in means of narrative - also a slightly longer game, considering the journey itself is a real-time experience for the protagonist.
If you have played developer's earlier games and are familiar with the name, you'd know that he is a proud master of the walking simulation genre, combining marvelous visual experiences and a simple, yet beautiful storyline, dotted with metaphorical anecdotes. I am yet to play his many other earlier games, but I can tell that this one is an elaborate art work which would successfully invoke feelings of loss and reconciliation in you.
, being a sequel, mostly reveals mysteries of the previous game by attaching an identity and a definitive storyline to our previously nameless protagonist. In this game, "the man who endured a loss" has a voice, and as you explore the environment - a pilgrimage that he takes every year, as he names it - narrates his own story of loss, addiction and grief. Yet, contrary to the previous game, this one ends on a brighter note, embracing the notion of dealing with loss and overcoming addiction, proving one's own wisdom and temperance. "The man who endured a loss" is an ordinary man, with ordinary life choices and tragedies. The simplicity of his story harbors the beauty of life itself, and a single man's capability to overcome his own misfortune and carry on, even at the face of most tragic events.
The environment design is a visual feast, arranged in Unreal 4 Engine. The light shimmering through the clouds on an afternoon sky, rain droplets dotting on a wild landscape and the freezing tundra of a mountain highland are just a handful of stunning sceneries that you will encounter. The environment, alongside carefully arranged sound effects to imitate "being there", - the crush of snow under your shoes, the rustling of bushes in the wind etc. - portrays the pilgrimage of a man who has lost all. Now, he takes this journey, accompanied only by his own memory lane, to prove that he is more than his own mistakes today.
Can I recommend this game? Sure, as a beautiful experience and a simple, yet effective story, I can. As a gaming experience? Well, one really shouldn't expect what would be beyond the genre from this one. As a walking simulator, it is a masterfully crafted one. So, if you enjoy the genre itself, this is one you wouldn't like to miss at all. Enjoy!

Bottle: Pilgrim is the latest creation from solo developer Tonguc Bodur. Anyone familiar with his previous work knows that they wear the "walking simulator" tag proudly. They are generally brief, averaging a few hours to complete, usually narrated, and with a background soundtrack. I think most gamers are clearly divided on walking sims, either you enjoy them or you don't. I find them to be a welcome diversion from the mainstream releases, an occasional oasis of contemplation, reflection and tranquility amidst all the shooting and blowing things up.
Sure, I love blowing things up as much as anyone. But once in a while a little break is nice, and what better way to take a breather and regain one's bearings than a walk in the woods? Or a stroll along the beach at sunset? Or a brisk outing in a wintery snowscape? Or a reflective amble through a gentle drizzle with the distant sounds of thunder? Why not all of the above? In Bottle: Pilgrim you can.
And that's the beauty of Tonguc Bodur's work, the creation of a world space, an atmosphere, in which to simply be. Sure, "simply being" is not for everyone, there is something more than a little Zen about it. But for those who enjoy games sometimes just for the atmosphere and being immersed in another world, you can't go wrong with his this game.
This latest in his oeuvre show definite signs of maturing. From the scripted sequences to the brilliant finale scene, and the welcome addition of hidden objects to find, the honing of his skills with UE4 is easily apparent. These worlds are crafted with loving care and attention to detail, from the light effects to the sounds of footfalls, all the tiny minutae comprise an atmosphere that is easy to get figuratively lost in.
I also found the story and narration in Pilgrim to be better, more mature, than in his previous games. The narrator is also the writer and this is his first outing as a voice actor, so I can excuse what I thought was an inappropriately calm delivery in the recollection of a powerfully tragic event.
All in all, I consider Pilgrim to be Tonguc Bodur's best work to date. These small worlds he has created are gorgeous and, combined with the soundtrack, create an atmosphere of sublime beauty. When the soul of a poet puts all his heart and mind into the expression of a video game, it transcends into art. Here he has made a space where it is a true pleasure to simply be.

Sets the right mood for a 60's alien invasion type scenario. As a third person shooter with tactical aspects, the game is competent at what it does (think Mass Effect style gameplay). Compared to other games within the XCOM franchise, however, this game lacks some depth to customization and tactical decisions you can make.

All in all it was well worth the bundled price with the predecessors of the series. I love enemy unknown and grew up on terror from the deep. This is nothing like these, expect a cover tactical shooter that is driven by a narrative akin to the series. Life forms from somewhere else have arrived, and they are terribly aggressive and we apes (sorry creationists), being the busy little warriors we are are now tasked with overcoming a dominant invasion force by doing what we love--killing stuff with noisy things.
This is a story-driven XCOM shooter. It was refreshing to play as the agents themselves and the story was good enough to keep the player going. Fighting enemies in real and slowed time makes mutons much more menacing. You also can't count on a team of snipers as your squad will always be three people. Fights are exciting as maps are well arranged to encourage scattering your team to flank, support, or divert enemies. I would recommend keeping the difficulty up high as lower levels allow for easily exploitable AI. At one point I was dropping teams of five monsters in a couple seconds mainly through well placed powers and team members.
Unfortunately, there isn't much in the way of variation in outcomes so don't expect anything quite so dynamic.
Worth a single run through but I do not feel compelled to replay it.
I'd give it a 6.5 out of 10, fun but borrows too much to stand out.

There's a lot to like and dislike about The Bureau. The connection with it and Enemy Unknown are tenous at best; other than name, and a visual callback in the form of EXALT in Enemy Within, the two games are completely seperate.
The visual style is good, and distinctive. The 60's era, Cold Era setting is unique and distinctive, and the game looks fantastic. Curiously, the game decides to give each of your individual classes a completely different look. While this helps you to identify them instantly, it also doesn't really lend a sense of being in an organized unit, more like a guerilla organization. Perhaps they meant to get the sense of desperation across, though it came across as more like a dysfunction junction.
The story is passable. The twist is surprising, but not earth shattering. If you're perceptive in fact, perhaps you would've seen it coming.
Audio work is steller. Weapons, they sound good. Other than the Scatter Laser, which for some reason is like an animal squealingl everytime you pull the trigger, the rest of the weapons sound solid and dependable, and you can really feel the hurt that you put out. The audio cues that your squadmates give are loud and clear, and the spoken dialogue is pretty good.
Gameplay is okay. This is a cover based shooter, and it shows. In fact, it shows too much; you can tell an ambush is coming by the suspicious amount of cover. Though it generally blends well with the environment, it's a telling sign when you come across a series of low walls between you and your objective, and some conspicious explosive objects, but no enemies in sight. You always have two squadmates with you, but they might as well not be around. We'll get to that in a bit. With your squaddies you can outflank the enemy, but with the plethora of cover busting abilies at your disposal, you really just need to wait for your cooldowns. Oddly enough, the game doesn't let you free-throw your grenades, instead making them a targetted AoE ability with no cool down.
Now on to the AI. The enemy AI is good. Stunning, even. It will pin you down with suppressing fire while flanking your position. It will flush you out with grenades. It will take advantage of an advancing muton to rush your position, flanking you while you deal with the muton, which by the way can take a literal storm of bullets and still keep coming. But surely, you must be thinking, with your two squadmates, it'll be difficult but manageable.
No. It's fustrating, that's what it is.
Because your own team AI is astoundingly bad. Your squadmates won't use their own abilities on their own initiative. They will often expose themselves to enemy fire to empty their clip, and get downed in the process. They won't relocate when getting flanked. They'll spend almost all of the time in combat asking you for orders or asking for healing. They get downed very easily, because I saw with my own two eyes my squadmates roll away from an enemy grenade, only to run back to it because it was the closest cover. It's not a squad based shooter. It's a solo shooter, with two of the enemy on your side. Its a shame, because as  the enemy AI shows, 2K CAN develop intelligent AI, they just decided to hand the player possibly one of the most ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ friendly AIs in video game history. Perhaps they didn't want it to be too easy for the player, but as the AI stands, it's the most fustrating thing to experience in the game.
In conclusion, if you can weather the terrible friendly AI (which I did, just barely), the game isn't that bad. Taken on its own, as a seperate part of the XCOM family, it's a good inclusion in its own right. This game could have been so much more; all they had to do was increase the competence of your teammates. But as it stands, it's extremely fustrating.

If you own a Logitech G25, G27, or any other steering wheel made for PC then you know how fun they can be and how much they can enhance your in-game experience. The biggest challenge of such a steering wheel is finding a good game in which you can use it. Test Drive Unlimited 2 is both amazing and awful in this regard.
For starters, I love the fact that it automatically recognizes my G27 wheel since a lot of games don't. I also really like that I can use my six speed shifter, my paddle shifters, or simply put the transmission as automatic. In manual transmission mode you can even choose whether you want to use a clutch pedal, or if you want the clutch to be automated.
As I stated before, there are also several bad aspects of the game. I'm just going to be blunt about it and say the handling is atrocious, even nauseating. Not everyone may encounter this issue, but for me the force feedback system ruins the handling. Force feedback itself is a great feature and greatly enhances driving experience, however, I had to turn the system off altogether in TU2. When left on it randomly jerks the wheel left and right in an extremely annoying fashion. It's almost as if it wants to simulate driving under the influence (I'm not kidding it's that absurd). After I turn force feedback off, the problem is miraculously fixed and the car is sober again! But now, the handling becomes similar to that of a canal boat. It's like power steering no longer exists. Even the mighty Ferrari 458 handles like a Prius without force feedback, and that just pisses me off.

Nothing has changed since my original review. The game is still extremely laggy, there is still no mouse control in the menus, all menus are still locked behind the procedural track generator... none of these have improved whatsoever. In fact, playing the game from a fresh install on my new computer corrupted Steam and forced me to reinstall it and restart my computer to get everything working again.
Racecraft is still nowhere near being a playable game worth anyone's time or money.
---------
We need to start this off with a warning. The developers of Racecraft, Vae Victus, have only done one other Steam game, Victory: The Age of Racing. They abandoned the game for two years, then made it free-to-play and have still yet to update it in any way. This studio's track record is small but horrible, so please bear that in mind.
Racecraft is designed to be a procedurally-generated driving game, its gameplay being based in simulation with some arcade modifications to it. It was a formula that worked fairly well in Victory, and it's been refined here in Racecraft. Driving feels tight yet fluid enough so that it doesn't feel stiff, and the sense of speed is there. When it comes down to the core gameplay, Racecraft has got many of the checkboxes marked. My biggest concern with one of the previous versions in the closed Alpha was that there were a lot of symbols and signs on the track that I couldn't identify. My racing history is mostly in Need for Speed - I'm not a racing sim gamer - so it would have been helpful to have some explanation on what the track signs meant.
Outside of gameplay design, Racecraft falls short of being a stable game to play in. Again, keep in mind that this is still Early Access, so things are bound to be, well, Early Access. But there's a myriad of issues present in the current version. 1) The game
crashed on me while I was preparing to write this review. 2) The menus are extremely slow to respond, slow to animate, and
(as a game releasing on Steam in 2016, that last part shouldn't even be there). 3) The game's menus are locked behind the procedural track generator, so you'll be waiting a while before you can even change the game from fullscreen or turning off its effects or what have you. 4) Gameplay itself is incredibly sluggish, even when I turn off all effects, get out of fullscreen, and lower the resolution.
There also seems to be some sort of issue with controller support. Sometimes it recognizes my Logitech Wireless Gamepad F710, sometimes it doesn't. For the record, Racecraft will fully support wheels (if it doesn't already), so if you have one of those peripherals you're in luck here. It should also be stated that Racecraft requires DirectX 11 or newer, so if you're running DirectX 10 or older (which millions of Steam accounts still are), you won't be able to play Racecraft.
Because of the many issues with the game, I cannot recommend Racecraft in its current state. I look forward to future updates, and as I stated in my disclaimer I will update this review as such, but for now I advise staying away.

The ratings show that the community (with thousands of reviews) judged this game more-or-less positive, and more recently, 'mixed'. How come Paradox, probably the most wonderful strategy game developer extant, managed to more or less botch the delivery of a highly expected game like this, frustrating so many experient gamers? There is a reason for that.
Nowadays we are living times of 'dumbing-down' games. HoI4 suffered from that somewhat. There are new features here that are definitivelly an improvement from HoI2 and 3, but in overall the game seems less.. what's the word I'm looking for? Well, just 'less'.
An excellent improvement was the interface that easilly lets you group several units in one big command (even an armygroup-level command), assign it just one leader, and plan an attack  simply dragging the expected end-front for the whole operation and setting an stance for the army. THere is even a pause button, to halt and resume an entire operation. That was an excellent improvement, over the system found in Ho3 (which is good, mind you, but very labor-intensive).
Another excellent improvement is towards building equipment, designing templates to your divisions from a batch of said equipment, deploying and training those divisions. I love the system.
And also, lets all admit, the game just looks wonderful.
But ....
This is a case where the sum of the parts equals less than the whole. In all the game feels lacking. In fast tempo, you can end the game in a few hours. There is little to do, since the new policies system reduces your game to unlocking a few lackluster modifiers in slightlly different orders. Managing air units is a bore. Naval units less so, but still. The AI is pretty square, both the enemy as well as your own, when let to manage your operations. Managing land units yourself is, converselly, a little polluted. There is no more of Ho3's brilliant depiction of army organization (everything is either within one big command, or avulse in the world). In a nutshell, the game is kinda pale and bleek. It looks amazing, but it feels empty.
How come a game with such an ambitious scope (the world, no less!), with thousands of things to do, managed to feel so empty and devoid of colour?
IMO this comes from the perceived feel that a game must appeal to everyone, which is not necessarilly so. People looking for a simple strategic game may get overwhelmed, as people drooling for the good old paradox standard may get disapointed (as was I).
And I also take issue with the damn tendency to deliver games tailored to be slowly improved via DLCs, in little ten-dollars increments. DLCs are a welcome thing if they are constantly re-inventing a game (as it happens with CK2 and EU4), but in this case the vanilla game was delivered in a kinda week state and the DLC released so far tend to be more of the 'content pack' type ("but this 10 dollar DLC and play as New Zealand, with half a dozen new cosmetic options for that tiny country! Yeeeaaaayyy").
To sum things up, this game had a lot of potential to be great from the start, but it seems it will take a long road of DLCs to get there, if it gets there at all. A pity: so fat, it is merely 'ok'. It saddens me to see this become the norm for paradox games, once a sacred cow in the already-thin strategy games market.
Still... I recomend it, though. Paradox deserves support. I confess I bougth it already antecipating it would be less than great, and that it would take a few years for me to get to like it, after it got more polished. One can only hope.
