If you're looking for a comparison to How to Survive 1, look elsewhere.  Now that that's out of the way, How to Survive 2 is very much a "one step forward, one step back" kind of game.  There are some things it does very well, punctuated by regular bouts of puzzling laziness in terms of development.
Environments are pretty detailed, but they are also repetitive.  Technically, rotating existing buildings to keep things visually interesting was a good tactic to save development time, but it's overused.
Sound design - what sound design?  As far as I could tell there are two songs in the game - the intro screen, and whenever you pull too many zombies.  I'm pretty sure I even detect the same public-domain zombie noise that Minecraft uses.
The game's content is doled out at a shuffling zombie's pace.  It consists of building your camp up on a large "camp map", and instanced quests with their own maps.  It isn't the sprawling free-roam map I was hoping for.  At ten, then five-level intervals you're required to survive a zombie siege (which you trigger) in order to raise the camp and its buildings higher, thus getting new gear and new quests.
There is technically no over-arching plot, just "do stuff, build up the camp."  Most quests are just there to get materials.  Others double-back in the sense that you do a quest for Character A, then one for Character B to sabotage A, then another quest for Character A to fix the results of your own sabotage.  This kind of backpedaling destroys any sense of progress, assuming you were meant to feel any such thing to begin with.   At least some of the characters are obviously from the first game (which I never played), with only brief glimpses to illustrate their relationships to each other.  In particular, one character is made out to be the antagonist (?), but you never hear about him doing anything nefarious.  If he's supposed to be the bad guy, the game utterly fails at demonstrating this, even moreso if it's based off his reputation or actions in the previous game.  So, half the game's quests are directed at subverting this not-really-a-bad guy, and then sometimes fixing those subversions.
The UI, well.. Functions.  Being able to sort equipment by level would have been nice, because looking for menu items that shifted place depending on whether or not you can craft them will eat up most of your time.
Sometimes the crafting system is a little borked.  Some recipes need basic components that you can't make until quite a bit later than the recipes that need them.  Some things are baffingly gated - you can make a homemade assault rifle in the first ten levels, but need to wait until your late 40's to make a throwing spear.  Apart from this, the game typically gives you new recipes within a level or two, but sometimes the crafting chain unexpectedly ends.   The level cap for the character/camp/buildings is 51, through ALL of which the Armory unlocks new recipes, but the Chemistry lab's recipe list ends around level 20.  Because new recipes aren't guaranteed EVERY building level, you wind up♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥away resources on at least a few levels of a building that's been tapped out.
Models look good - what few there are.  Character customization options are limited, and each weapon type has ONE model.  Every assault rifle will look like every other assault rifle.  Don't get me wrong, these are really nice models, and it's not as though you spend an inordinate amount of time zoomed in, but --- really?
Other things are just absent altogether.  2016 is my 20th anniversary playing horror games, and this is the first zombie game I've played WITH NO SHOTGUN.  Not even a blunderbuss you could cram bits of lead into.  What the hell?
The camp has its own buildings and traps you can place, but several of the game's quirks prevent this from being a truly engaging experience.  For one thing, there exist zero ways to completely block off all paths of entry into your camp while still being able to get in yourself.  Gates, for some weird ♥♥♥♥ing reason, don't exist in the post-apocalypse.  The only thing you can do is stick a low-fence in the perimeter somewhere, which the zombies can still climb over, and traps in front of it to hopefully kill them before they do.
There are only three damaging traps in the game.  For whatever reason, the game has serious problems with inclines.  Got a narrow ramp up to a plateau with plenty of horizontal clearance that you wanna stick Rotating Arms on?  Too ♥♥♥♥in' bad.  Want to place a ground-spike trap in the same area?  Maybe.  Or maybe just a low fence.  Or maybe nothing at all, even though there is plenty of room for such things. Being unable to clear away trees for more space makes it worse.  That's even assuming the zombies' pathing makes sense, which it usually doesn't.  Sometimes they try to go through the fences, taking the most difficult way towards you as possible, and sometimes they take the path of least resistance - which if you've ever intelligently designed a base in other defense games, probably has most of the traps.  Zombies occasionally spawn inside the fence-line if it's far enough away from actual buildings, and sometimes they proceed along the expected geographical routes into the base.  Normally I'd applaud this mild unpredictability, but add to the fact that the game is essentially a cakewalk, it also means that avid base-builders are going to find the siege mechanic severely lacking.
Camp level slowly unlocks new zombie types, but the only challenge to be had is if you purposely increase the level of a mission above that of your character.  It's largely the same zombies, only they eat more ammo to put down, and maybe there are a few more on the map.  Zombie types are particularly uninspired and are purely ripped from other games/instances of zombie lore.  At no time did I ever feel like I was in danger, unless I purposely "went loud" with my weaponry.
Ammo isn't scarce, either.  I played up until level 25 with a bow/crossbow (which thankfully has recoverable ammo) and an assault rifle for crowd control.  By the time level 25 rolled around, I took stock of materials and discovered I could make a whopping 9600 lead rounds.  The game REALLY wants you to go loud, because frankly that's where the fun is.
For multiplayer, your camp and character are saved separately.  Your camp is also persistent, meaning other people can access it even when you're not online, and there's a private box for items.  You set permissions on an individual basis, and people can join any mission in progress from anywhere else.  I've only played with a couple friends, but the system seems solid.
The grinding in the game isn't too bad.  The game will remember where you got the most of any item in case you need more later.  This is ingenious and the devs deserve praise for such a system.  Outside of that, there are very few items in the game I had to grind for, so even though the actual progression through the game is fairly slow, you won't spend countless hours grinding for most things.  However, if you like to bash your way through the objectives and leave the rest of the loot,  you're going to be repeating missions a lot more, and possibly be missing some items entirely.  This will lead you to the online wiki, which is complete garbage, or the Steam forums, half of which seems to be in other languages.
So, why do I recommend this game after ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ all over it?  It's unlike any zombie game I've ever played, and even if the game is purposely padded, slow, and could have been so much more, I estimate I got at least 80 hours out of it, which is astronomical for the price tag.

Omni Link is a promising early access visual novel with some top-down shooter elements mixed in. I'm about an hour into the story and I'm enjoying it greatly.
-Pros:
--Great art and music.
--Strong story.
--Plenty of choices (I'm currently unsure just how much these affect the game as I'm not that far in but there are a lot of them so far).
--Easy and hard difficulty modes for each persons playstyle.
--Usable ships seem to have abilities depending on the ship type. One I've encountered has a shield for example and another can warp.
--Short but sweet tutorial that shows you the ropes then drops you right into some gameplay.
--You can have a computer-controlled fleet following you doing the hard work if you're bad at video games like me.
-Cons (These are likely due to it being early access and may not apply to the final product):
--Menus leave a lot to be desired, little to no options at all (There is however, a windowed mode accessable by hitting alt+enter)
--Only one save allowed that I know of which is a bit daft in a game with choices, saving is just hitting "save" and "load".
--No chat controls (i.e. dialogue history if you miss a bit or skip if you die and need to get back from a save point.)
All things considered, I would recommend keeping an eye on this early access game as the only gripes I have found within the game are easily fixable with a future update.
I'll be following this game closely and I look forward to playing it when its finished!
This review will be occasionally modified when the game updates and when I get further in.

The Bureau is a third person shooter game that includes strategic gameplay and an interesting plot. It doesn't fail to challange you in different situations and strategies for shooting up aliens in this old-styled sci-fi game. You find yourself in a world where extra-terrestrial aliens are taking over the world and you, being apart of the bureau, an elite team of hunters, plan to stop them once and for all. Its controls are a little clunky but you can always bind new keys to your liking. Overall, its an addictive shooter with a different gameplay system than any other shooter you've seen before.

Indulge yourself in the revival of the X-Com series, now with even less soldiers, missions, strategy and one less hyphen than the original series name. The trademark perma-death of your agents in the X-Com series is still retained. However, never worry about that one sucker agent you left behind in the battlefield to die (die forever), because you can still commit suicide to save his pitiful life from perma-death.

With great graphics and astounding recreation of the Cold War era-1950s atmosphere, The Bureau: XCOM Declassified stands out unique as a fusion game of third-person shooter and strategy. Many X-Com fans think that the less-strategic gameplay undermines the great graphics of the game, but frankly this overlooked piece of creation is nice to play. Choose the Commander difficulty and you will have to think twice before shooting the interstellar mafias up. Although it is the highest difficulty, it offers what I would call as Normal in regards to the strategy-making. Through Commander difficulty, the game bears more resemblance to its predecessors than it would when lesser difficulties are chosen.
The Bureau sure has many things to be questioned, from the equippable alien weapons which are found so freely lying on the battlefield to the inconsistent nature of the genre, but it also has features worth taking note of, such as the high-level language in the conversations and the interesting take on the alien invasion plot. The gameplay of The Bureau: XCOM Declassified might not be as strategic as the X-Com series, but it adds another unique facet of the strategy genre to the name XCOM.

This is certianly the absolute best multiplayer co-op "PVE" style of video game I've played this decade, even topping my previous #1 on the list "Torchlight II".  I play all sorts of games in all sorts of themes and genres, but I'm super picky when it comes to certain aspects, with my #1 priority being the gameplay itself, especially focusing on multiplayer playability.  If the game isn't fun to play as a group, I usually don't care to spend much time on it.  Wildlands does not have this problem.
More good things about the game:
Wildlands is a 10 / 10 on gameplay, environment design, progression systems, multiplayer systems and networking, storyline, and port optimization is pretty good.  The game is BEAUTIFUL.  The game is HARD but scales really nicely with more squad-mates.  Rewards are better for playing on harder difficulties.  The loot grind (for guns, attachments, upgrades, etc) is entirely "optional" and does not significantly interfere with gameplay.  No recurring cost encountered yet and i'm 70 hours in already... I think I've completed about 60-65% of the story missions and still plenty of things to do... expecting to get about 100 hours out of the game first playthrough which I say is pretty good.  Also you don't really have to worry about out-progressing your friends.  All the missions work no matter who is where in the story.  You might not get "storyline" credit for something you haven't unlocked yet, so just watch out for that, but I think about 80% of the missions are available RIGHT AWAY due to the completely open world design.   It's amazing.  Difficulty levels also merge together in co-op mode (I believe your difficulty applies to you personally) though I'm not 100% sure how this works.  I believe the difficulty impacts how enemies can detect you and how much damage they do to you individually (basically, your teammates may have a "handicap" if they play on easier difficulty level).  This system is incredible and way ahead of its time.
What's bad about it:
Uplay is some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.  Had some issues getting the game to run due to Uplay issues and outdated graphics drivers.  I've seen a few glitches here and there.  Price point is a little steep for some people but you're really getting what you pay for here.  (also it goes on sale for $30 semi-frequently)  Single player is really not as much fun.... probably comparable to Farcry series but a little less immersive (less crafting, survival aspects, etc)... but I don't play the SP much at all.  Replayability is also questionable, I haven't beat the game yet but I imagine it will be somewhat like replaying Borderlands 2 or something like that... you can scale up the difficulty to make it more interesting but I dunno if that makes it any more fun.
It's a bit long winded but I had to get it out of me.  This game is way ahead of its time and a 10/10 in my book.  Well freaking done.

Occasionally a game provides me with such an incredible personal experience that I want to share it and recommend it. Subsurface Circular just did exactly that. I bought it and played it through - which took about 90 minutes, including a couple of quick interruptions - and I could not put it down until I completed the story. This is an interactive novel of the highest calibre. The puzzles the game presents are excellent and well thought-through, the writing is tonally spot-on and characterful, and the visuals that accompany it all give you enough of an atmosphere that the story can focus on being a story, and not on exposition. Add to this an excellent soundscape, and everything in this game does exactly no more than it needs to in order to service the story and the discovery, and in today's AAA culture that is a very undervalued trait. I cannot recommend this game enough, and I look forward to experiencing the differences the next time I play.

Subsurface Circular is a cross between a choose-your-own-adventure book, a text adventure and a mystery novel.    You take the part of a 'detective' on the underground, where you are presented with a mystery to solve.   You can chat to other commuters on the subway to ask them about the investigation.  Some you can also do little favours for.
The wonderful thing about the game is that it explores (tangentially) the ultimate goal of robotics and AI:  Once we can make bots which are as good as us, what role will /they/ want in the partnership?   Will we end up being surpassed?
The dialog tree is a set of constrained choices, not free-form.  Other than the tannoy announcements, everything is purely text-based.   This meshes nicely with the idea that the 'bots are communicating over a private chat channel, like IM.   It also means that you can imprint your own voices and feelings onto the 'bots themselves.
The game is minimalistic, insofar as there's one location (a train carriage), and one type of person to talk to (bots).  The bots have some morphological variation, but are all built along the same lines.  They all sit, move, and talk differently. They all have different 'buttons' you can push to elicit different responses.   For the most part what you choose doesn't affect things too much, but in some (restricted) cases, you can earn an achievement or two by being persistent or following a humorous avenue of dialog.
It lasts about 2 to 3 hours.  The pace can be changed, but it's a relaxing "sit back and enjoy the story" kind of game, so the default speed feels about right.   The graphics are lovely, with great use of motion, lighting, texturing and depth blurring.    The 'bots all move in a convincing 'bottish' way, and they all feel solid'.
Overall, I really enjoyed Subsurface Circular.  It was highly relaxing, thought-provoking, and gave just enough humour to give a wry smile from time to time.   There are a few times when the setup seems a tad obvious (e.g. in one part a bot needs another type of bot, and lo and behold that exact bot type happens to also sit down at the same time).  Doing this gave a little mini-game, but broke the flow a little by the coincidence.   Of course, perhaps it was a forced coincidence? I dunno. That's too many levels of indirect thinking for me at this time of night.
I paid about £4 for it, and that feels about right for something of this length.  If it's on sale any cheaper it'd be a steal, grab it! :)

TRS made the decisions that killed the original version by splitting the community with DLC.  When there were less than 200 players they went free to play - good move! Day breaks on the dusty Mars-like planet that you have been stranded on. The threat of the terrifying, gigantic gnats that lurk in the night has faded, and your search for some more plutonium has begun.
You see a faint greenish rock glistening in the morning sun across a seemingly barren crater. You begin your trek, only to find a quickly rising shadow darken the ground beneath your feet.
It’s the worm.
Anyone who has played Osiris: New Dawn is all too familiar with the worm. It’s the most intimidating of the aliens inhabiting the planet Proteus 2, and without a nimble evasion, it’s the end of your journey there.
Worms aside, there’s a lot to like about Osiris. Aesthetically, it taps into sci-fi tropes of Martian exploration. While Proteus 2 isn’t our little red neighbor, it certainly is inspired by the planet and fiction set there.
Like most survival games, much of the gameplay revolves around resource gathering and crafting. There are about 30 different raw resources spread across the planet that can be gathered to craft new equipment, utilities and structures.
There are standard utilities that need to be made — things like a forge for crafting tools and weapons and a excrement collector for creating fertile soil. Yes, you’ll have to go full-Matt Damon and farm to stay properly fed on the red planet.
You can build fully fledged bases that house barracks, biodomes and tech labs. There’s also a bunch of furniture to outfit your habitat with that will further expand your production abilities.
Building vehicles is probably the most fun to be had in the lab, although they come a little late into the playthrough. You likely won’t be building the transportation devices until well past the halfway mark of the content, meaning navigating the early stages of the game are a bit of a grind.
Unlocking the spaceship will allow you to venture into the outer atmosphere of the planet, where you can mine new resources on orbiting asteroids and fight an ever-growing fear of falling to your death in the process.
Crafting weapons will help keep you safe as you venture out for more diverse resources on the surface of Proteus 2. The planet features 8 hostile aliens and a handful of non-aggressive creatures. Generic sniper and assault rifles will aid you in the ongoing fight against the planet’s wildlife, as will the more rugged-looking melee weapons, such as the crab scythe.
Just don’t test any of them out against the worm.
Osiris: New Dawn is still in Early Access and currently offers about 20 hours worth of content. While there are both public and private servers to play on, increasing complaints of hacking on the public servers is an inclination to play them at your own risk.

I purchased the game around early April and clocked about 15 hrs on single-player and a private server before the latest patch. I did play a few hours after the patch in single-player, but with the aliens turned off :P
First, Osiris: New Dawn is written by a TINY team. Fenix Fire was literally a couple, at least for the duration of the development of their previous game, and I don't know if they managed to bring new people on board. That said, they're doing a great job. The game is more than worth the $25.
Off the bat, one of my favorite things about the game is that you can play this single-player, or on a private server with friends, or on a public server, and thanks to the alien encounter toggle, you can have your experience be full of alien ambushes or a (relatively) relaxed one focused on safe exploration.
Some of the mechanics changed with the patch, the big one being resources. The great part is that several new kinds of resources were added - there's now way more than one berry tree in the entire map, there's more plants you can eat (and they are easier to find), and gaseous nitrogen is now obtainable on the starter map. The second big change, which I think is great but some have disliked, is that ore deposits are now classified into and only appear as two groups (maybe three or four, I haven't explored the caves yet): base metals and precious metals. Each group yields a few possible different kinds of ores by varying chance, though you can also look at the color of the ore to get an idea of whether an ore is, say, predominantly aluminum. On the one hand, it can be a bit inconvenient to get a few types of ore (namely plutonium), but on the other hand, I've actually had an easier time acquiring large amounts of metals and the deposits are now bigger on average, from what I remember.
There are currently two classes, with two more coming, though the main difference is just which skills they start out with, and with enough effort both classes can achieve a fully unlocked skill tree. It still makes the game a little easier to play in groups. There are also some other fun features, like a cave system to explore, meteors that occasionally fall (and may land VERY close to you), sandstorms, cookable alien meat, and eventually players will be able to tame and ride certain aliens. The new patch added much more interesting and mountainous terrain, along with abandoned equipment and bases (and what appear to be giant alien skeletons?) to find. Osiris tries hard, and succeeds, in offering a space colonization/survival experience that's realistic enough to be immersive but still entertaining and easy to pick up.
Still, I don't know how hard Osiris is meant to be. The devs have said that they want the game to be more on the "fun" side but have also sort of hinted that whatever dangers are currently present in-game are going to be nothing compared to what they have planned. Currently, it's not *terribly* hard (maybe a 4 or 5 out of 10 in difficulty, with 10 being the hardest), even for someone like me who doesn't play a whole lot of games, and once you figure everything out things become much easier. I've seen some people describe the game as a joke, but honestly the game difficulty varies depending on the settings you decide to play on, how many people you're playing with, etc. Osiris has all kinds of ominous (but sometimes happy) music and some freaky monsters, and nighttime as a new player is basically a 20-minute anxiety attack, but after an hour or two you kind of get used to everything and it stops being scary. Maybe this is ok - space colonization is less intimidating once you're a veteran, right? But I guess if you're looking for a constantly fear and anxiety-inducing game, Osiris isn't it, and I don't know if it wants to be.
Lastly, from hearsay, the public-server multiplayer is apparently populated by a non-insignificant number of trolls, and a security update to the game was only added a few weeks ago. I have faith that the devs will get multiplayer security and anti-troll functions to a better point sometime in the future, but at the moment, it looks like they're mostly focused on new content and fixing major issues pointed out by the player base on the forums (Use the wiki and go on the Steam forums, you will have a much better time, especially if you run into bugs, etc.) I do recommend at least starting out in single player or on a private server (both of which are still pretty fun) before jumping into public servers.
A few bugs I've noticed from the latest patch, but nothing really serious other than the airlock, which got fixed:
-some of the visuals are a bit buggy; nothing so far that impedes gameplay, just things like towers in the distance sometimes disappearing if you face them directly, or some "seams" appearing on the ground as you approach them.
-lake water is not really liquid, it's just a visual layer at this point, but the lakes are new.
-Airlock structures were disappearing, but apparently this is fixed.
-Do keep in mind that you will probably have to disable your touch screen to play.
All in all, I do recommend the game if you've ever wanted to build your own space base and enjoy exploration (and maybe feeling badass from eating aliens for dinner). It is still in alpha, and there are probably very few people working on the game, so while it's still in early access, don't have your expectations too high - do expect bugs, and do expect slow-ish updates. But, this is a cool game you can easily pick up yourself or with friends: $25 for what I'm quite sure will be hours of gameplay, and much more content to come.

There's not much I can say about Quake you haven't heard elsewhere. It's fun, it's dark, it's immersive, and it firmly established many of the conventions of FPS gaming we now take for granted. There would be no Team Fortress 2 without Quake, and that is why I wield the Original with pride. Id Software may have moved on to bigger things with Rage, but plans for Doom 4 make me believe that a new Quake may lurk somewhere beyond the horizon. It's important to know your roots in gaming, and while I got my online start in Starsiege: Tribes, my favorite singleplayer FPS of yore was probably Quake, if not Half-Life. Quake gave me my love of shotguns and grenade launchers and if an FPS cannot deliver me satisfying examples of such, then it does not measure up to my expectations for what constitutes adequate firepower. You can keep your assault rifles, throwing knives and tactical nukes. Give me a little buckshot and a little boom, and I will give you delicious interdimensional demon gibs.

Quake is like Doom except the physics feel much nicer and you can jump, aim up and down and there's an increased emphasis on movement in general. The trade off is that there's smaller groups of enemies (rarely more than two at a time) and they're all a bit more bullet-spongey. The weapons can also be a tad unimaginative (no BFG here, just a gun that shoots lightning and chews through it's max amount of ammo in seconds).
A lot of people dislike this game's visuals for relying a lot on the color brown. Personally, I don't mind this, as I feel that the more complex lighting and architecture of the maps (compared to Doom) compensates for this. That and the crappy low-poly monster models (that are still surprisingly well animated) combine with the rusted look of the game to create a wonderful aesthetic of low-tech creepiness. (I'd compare it to Silent Hill, but no part of Quake is ever set in a foggy town in the countryside - though there is at least one user-made map set in Innsmouth.)
This game also has excellent sound design by NIN's Trent Reznor. Don't bother with that EpiQuake junk, the game's audio is perfect enough as it is ... and on that note, I have to explain exactly why I'm giving this a thumbs down, even though I've just been gushing about the game.
It's because the Steam version doesn't include Trent Reznor's ambient soundtrack that Quake played off it's CD as in-game music. Unlike Hexen, there aren't any MIDI tracks or anything for the game to fall back on if the CD is missing - just nothing. The in-game sounds of wind and flickering torches are slightly more audible, and that's as good a compromise as you get.
Now, I can understand the absence if it was a rights issue with Reznor, but that supposedly wasn't the case. Apparently, it was because when id put the Steam version of the game together (which runs in DOSBox) they couldn't figure out how to simply rip the tracks off the CD in OGG format and configure DOSBox to load those files in lieu of redbook audio. Maybe John Carmack was too busy working on his new engine for whatever that game no one cared about was called.
Regardless, get Quake if you can find the original CD release on the cheap - which you probably will, as it's not a particularly rare game, nor one as valued by collectors as Doom (though be careful not to buy a  shareware version by accident). Alternatively, wait and see if this ever shows up on
- as those guys will probably put more effort into a basic digital release of this game than it's own developers.
------------------
TL;DR, Quake is a very good game, but don't buy it here or you will get a version without music.

TDU2 is a very unique game. It's a driving game with heavy emphasis on social elements, such as real estate, clubs, clothing, and even (wait for it) hairstyles. That being said, I wouldn't see why anyone would want to play this offline, as most of the fun is found online. It was very buggy and otherwise a forgettable game at launch, but after numerous patches, both official and unofficial, I can certainly say that this game has had most of the kinks ironed out, and it's now a playable and fun game. TDU2 features more than 80 vehicles, miles and miles of drivable area, and several game modes for you to enjoy.
This game features a little over 80 cars (more if you count mods, DLC, and prize cars), ranging from humble little cars like the Volkswagen Golf, to explosive hypercars such as the Bugatti Veyron. However, I will say something about the selection of cars in this game, and that is that I am very disappointed in the bias of cars. There are literally FIVE Pagani Zondas for you to choose from, 10 Ferraris, 4 Bugatti Veyrons, but not a single Honda, Mazda, or Toyota? Now that's just biased as hell. I would honestly rather be able to drive a preppy car like a Mazda RX7, Honda Civic, or Toyota Supra than I would some insane hypercar like the Ferrari 599XX, which almost guarantees that I'm going to crash it while going 250MPH, thanks to this game's ridiculous driving physics. The game does allow for you to explore more than 100 miles of in game area, spanning two islands, Hawaii and Ibiza, as well as several in game shops and points of interest. Still, I feel like the game would be a bit more enjoyable if the physics didn't make me so prone to crashing. Speaking of the physics, let's talk about them real quick.
Initially, I found the physics to be extremely jarring. The start of the game requires you to drive Tess, the game's main antagonist, to her photoshoot in her daddy's Ferrari. Every teenage boy's wet dream, right? Well, yeah, if I could actually drive the car without smashing it into every single corner. The cars in this game are able to accelerate very quickly, but holy hell, the braking and handling is just AWFUL. It literally felt like I was playing a 2011 version of Outrun, except I was in a much faster Ferrari, and the b!tch was yelling at me to slow the F down every 5 seconds. After finally making it to the photoshoot, my "avatar" (who is literally the most metrosexual person I've ever seen, holy hell) descended from the vehicle, along with the damsel in distress, and were quickly escorted into the building. After that, I was given a quick walkaround of my now smashed to hell and back Ferrari, and then the screen faded into the "cutscene".
You can get into police chases and races and all that good stuff, so I guess the actual gameplay is very redeeming.
Let me give a quick piece of advice about the player models/storyline in this game:
. Pretend it doesn't exist. Pretend you're playing Forza Horizon on the PC, I don't really care. Just do whatever it takes to get past this game's godawful acting.
Oh my god. Ohhhhh my god. The voice acting in this game. Oh my f*ck. Eden Games would've done a better job having Microsoft Sam voice all the characters in this game, because at least that woulda been rather funny. But this? Jesus H. Christ. Why must all the characters in this game talk like *gasp* THIS? (Pretend that I'm flicking my wrist in the most gay way possible as I'm saying that). Like seriously, you think Dragon Age Inquisition catered too much to the gay crowd? Not even close, sweetheart, this game is a whole new level of metrosexual. I'm talking this game will pimpslap you if it sees you trying to play without wearing Michael Kors pants and a Gucci suit.
As if the voice acting weren't bad enough, the ingame music is just plain garbage, as if the guy who was hired to pick the music had to meet some sort of racial quota, so he went on World Star Hiphop and picked out the most Liberal sounding music he could find. Other than mediocre hip hop, you can choose from dad rock, or the occasional electro/house song. And that REALLY pisses me off, because the song used in the game's trailer is one of my favorite songs of all time, Ghosts 'n' Stuff by Deadmau5. And that's literally the only song in the game that won't make your ears bleed. Disappointing, isn't it? Thankfully, you can mod in your own music with a bit of effort, but the fact that that feature was included in TDU1 but NOT in TDU2, that makes me extremely mad. Honestly, I would recommend TDU over TDU2, if it weren't for the fact that Atari killed the TDU multiplayer.
The graphics are probably the most redeeming part of the game. For a 2011 game, I have to admit that these graphics are top notch, and I'm pretty sure even FM3 or GT5 didn't look THIS good. However, you will need a very good computer to run it at max graphics, and I'd honestly recommend a 144hz monitor to go along with it, since you don't want to have all that motion blur when driving your car around Ibiza at 250 MPH. One of the super unique features of this game is that you can actually get into a car dealer and look around your car, get inside, start the engine, open the doors, and even roll down the windows. How many games allow you to roll down the windows? Almost none. The surrounding environment is very lush and vivid, certainly FAR better than the grayish brown filter that seems to be employed in almost all modern racing games. However, about the graphics, the game doesn't go into very much detail with car damage. You can scrape up your car, get it muddy, and crack a window or two, but that's about it. I understand that the licensers (i.e. Ferrari, Bugatti, Koenigsegg) don't want to see their precious 2 million dollar hypercars getting thrashed about, but it still breaks the immersion a bit. Speaking of immersiveness, you can visually upgrade your car to a certain extent by adding vinyls, paint, and rims, but that's about it. I understand that the licensers don't want their cars being adorned with pink neon and 30" spinners, but again, it kinda breaks the immersion.
I gotta admit, the multiplayer is one of the coolest parts about this game. One of the best features from my favorite game, NFS Underground 2, is that you can challenge another racer at any time simply by pulling up behind them and flashing your hi beams. This is also implemented in TDU2, and you can even set your own wager, giving a new meaning to "big dog on the block". Other than that, you can spiff up your "avatar" (I really, really hate that word. Why can't we say "player" or "racer"?) by buying him new hats, glasses, suits, pants, gloves, and hairstyles, to really wow your friends/opponents. You can also buy your own pad to REALLY wow them, ranging from the basic trailer park, to the all inclusive 300' yacht. All in all, I must say that the MP is really a great example of how a racing MMO is PROPERLY done, and I'd definitely recommend this game over NFS World or HEAT Online.
All in all, TDU2 is a very unique concept for the racing genre, and defnitely a step in the right direction for MMOs as a whole. The in game music and player models are absolute @$$, but if you can look past them, then I'm certain you'll have plenty of fun with TDU2

A wonderful experience for an early access, I have seen a lot of small updates (clearly bug fixes) since it went to Alpha on Steam, which is good to see as it means the developers are paying attention.
Nothing is perfect and that applies just as much for this game as it does for AAA games being released, what counts is forward movement.
Having only survival mode available at this time does leave a little to be desired. But the designers do allow you to change the difficulty to allow more casual gamers to have some fun or for those of you who like a real challenge you can 'up the ante' and go full hardcore. Word of warning, just the 100% difficulty mode is not easy to beat and whilst I have come close, still no win yet. Also at this time the only option is 'Ironman mode' which means you cannot load past saves just because you did something silly early game, you have to adapt and overcome... Or die. You can save but only when you choose to exit and the game has auto-saves (just in case of a unfortunate crash - which I am yet to have).
The building are lovely and has a nice tech tree that I hope to see expanded later on as they develop the game further. Some of the building upgrades don't make much sense, as when you upgrade the mill (basic power plant) the maintenance cost is not worth the additional power you gain. Maybe this is on purpose to force you to decide to either upgrade or expand, but right now it seems like something that was simply overlooked.
Graphics are acceptable and slightly comic in appearance, which in most games I would not enjoy, but here they seemed to have pulled it off.
Unit path finding can be a little annoying at times, as if you want to send a single unit somewhere and they have to pass through a group of your stationary units often they will get stuck and simply give up and next you know you find them standing by themselves. This is not a huge deal and will hopefully be corrected in later updates.
Map generation is random, so just because you play the same map, does not mean you will get the same layout. This is good and bad, as it offers a challenge and you don't get bored of the same of maps over and over. In saying that, I have loaded a map on more than one occasion and found myself cursing the screen as I found my 'Command centre' smack bang in the middle of mountains that made early expanding and building un-enjoyable.
Normally I would warn off people from buying early access, as I have both read and experienced WHY too many disappointments, but looking at this game and having those ongoing updates. I'm confident this is money well spent.

It's basically Stronghold with Zombies in a cyberpunk setting.

The economy of the game is well done, you've got to think about what you're doing and how you use the limited space to your advantage. And you always need more, there's no point in which you just settle down and keep the game running to get an easier life. The clock is ticking, the zombies are comming.
The gameplay not only looks and feels great, but it is a rolemodel for how to make an RTS. The controls are perfect. The pathfinding behaviour of groups is extremely good. The game keeps running smooth. If you want to see RTS done exactly right, this is it. I hope once the game is finished, they'll release the engine.

A spectacular fighting game like no other: in this game two slim "dolls" have to defeat eachother either by doing the most damage to the opponent via physical attacks or by grounding them, what makes this game so unique compared to other fighting games is that for doing anything you have to control the doll's single joints to "shape" its movements. After you set every joint's behavior the game executes the movements for a fraction of a second and then freezes again, allowing you to make different actions every time and shape the character's action in any way you like trough the entire battle.
This makes the fights extremely "physical" and it allows you to execute almost all kind of attacks, proof of this are the many servers with specific combat styles to use. Grabs, breaks and limb detachement allow for extra damage and realism (even if the game's objective is not simulating real-life combat, as the gravity is extremely low and that makes the characters pretty "floaty"...); while it's realy hard to get used to it, learning how to play and archieving wins is extremely satisfying and you'll rarely win by luck.
Game modifiers (big heads, fat characters etc.), weapons (swords, knives, bats...) and crazy stages allow for more variety; it's a must-have if you love original fighting games.

If you're looking for a game that plays like a movie or book with compelling characters and an interesting journey, this is absolutely not it, even though it claims to be based on literally a book franchise. The entire game is dependent upon your self-motivation and the story happens in a random order.
I enjoy games like Hitman, Splinter Cell Blacklist and past Ghost Recon games like Future Soldier. This game is absolutely nothing like any of those. It plays like Fallout without the will to live.
I've put 6 hours in the game, I don't care about anybody in it and the story is so complex I can't follow it. Maybe that's because I haven't had any interaction with the story in hours and hours because I keep trying to take down an entire prison with three people, lesser sync shot and drone capabilities than in prior franchise games and without a proper tutorial teaching me the controls. I didn't know there was an order wheel until literally hour 6.
This game seems to take the open world concept so literally that it includes, like, all of Bolivia as the game's world so you can't keep track of anything. It's not clear how to evade enemies, and as soon as any alarm anywhere is sounded the entire country is after you and attack helicopters start shooting you down and you're basically toast-- I can't even figure out how to restart the mission at that point-- I just have to get killed on purpose, revived, then killed again. Plus, I routinely encounter massive confusion about what's saved and what isn't when I die.
I have to spend the entire game in a car for two reasons: because everything is miles and miles away, and so that my team isn't immediately mowed down in four seconds by two guys in a Dodge Durango because I walk us into the wrong place by accident. Unfortunately, the driving mechanic is so bad that I can't even stay on the road (and I play Dirt and Forza very well.)
And all of this would be basically ok if the world wasn't totally un-compelling, unrelatable, and so ridiculously open that it's drowning in its own incoherence and meaninglessness.
This must have been based on a two-page Tom Clancy novel I've never heard of where there's just a description of Bolivia having drug cartels in it. I don't know about you, but I have absolutely no desire to spend tens/hundreds of hours of my life hanging out in a war-torn cartel-run nation where I'm outmatched in firepower, manpower and equipment without any sense of narrative or purpose. Like seriously-- what's our point here, anyway? Helping out some rebels in some other country solve some conflict that has no relationship with me or my life? Hitman, Blacklist and other games in this series had a compelling enough narrative that I knew what was happening at any given time and why I was where I was.
This game is DOA for me, as much as I absolutely didn't want that to be the case. Somehow, even purchasing a game literally based on a book isn't enough to get a narrative. Instead, it's just "here's a country and no resources. have at it. you four are elite, so you shouldn't need anything of any kind to liberate a nation and prop up a peace-loving rebel regime." I don't want to escape from my life into the Peace Corps. Who does? I could be angry about something else and taking it out on this game, but it sure seems to me like a massive disappointment.

This game can be both incredibly engaging, and incredibly infuriating. I have been playing at the highest difficulty, with no HUD, and that has required me to play very tactically, forcing me to engage with systems I would have otherwise left untouched. The semi-realistic ballistics (It doesn't appear to take wind into account), adds a subtle level of difficulty as it requires you to understand how your weapon will work in any given situation. I took the time to document the individual characteristics of my favored weapons, things such as bullet drop and travel time, which is something I couldn't say for any other game I've played. My playstyle has been centered around using sniper rifles, and making shots at long range (400+ meters) has proven to be very satisfying. The game is exceptional when playing with friends. Playing spotter for my friend as he infiltrates a base was some of the best gameplay I've experienced this year. The version of Bolivia in the game is beautiful and expansive, with a wide variety of environments, from salt flats to mountain jungles. This combined with the dynamic weather leads to picturesque, almost breathtaking views. There were moments in my playthrough where these vistas lined up with the games soundtrack in a rather sublime way.
However, the game is not without it's flaws. The story is completely forgettable, serving as little more than an excuse to get to the next mission. The variety among the side missions leaves something to be desired. You will find yourself stealing the same planes and stopping the same convoys over and over again. The AI leaves something to be desired, and I have found myself yelling in frustration at multiple times playing the game. The 3 teammate NPC's are next to worthless outside of there use for sync shot. All to often I find myself being flanked and killed by enemies while my teammates did nothing to help. More often than not they will prioritize reviving you over killing enemies. This has led to situations where they are reviving me in front of the enemy who just took me down, who then proceeds to immediately open fire again, usually resulting in being knocked right back down again. They are constantly repeating the same boring dialog, and telling the same unfunny jokes over and over again. The rebel NPC's that are meant to act as your reinforcements have proven to be more of a hindrance than anything. I have had them show up and engage the enemy while I am trying to infiltrate a base, blowing my cover and getting me killed (cause as soon as the enemy are fighting the rebels, they know exactly where I am as well). The environments have a tendency to be finicky, with many surfaces seeming like they should  be climbable when they were not. There were multiple times where I found myself stuck in some mountain cliff, forcing me to abandon whatever I was doing and fast travel away.
Also, the cars don't have horns. Come on Ubi, it's 2017, put a horn on that car.
Overall, I've really enjoyed my time with Wildlands. I would recommend picking it up either if you have a friend you plan to play it with, or if you happen to see it on sale.

'The Bureau' is yet another prequel, this time for 'XCOM: Enemy Unknown', the hard as nails turn-based strategy game. Xcom is mainstreaming and it works rather well: decisions are now made in real time (with a Max Payne like slow mo break when you are commanding your other troops), and you can control 'Carter', the hero, like in any third person shooter. The beginning of the adventure is impressive, going around in the 60s USA under an alien invasion brings back some proper 2K Nostalgia with touches of steampunk (telekinesis, and tesla rifles) but eventually gameplay becomes repetitive as there is no progression like in the first game. Your soldiers only have 5 ranks (but the new turret throwing engineer category is cool) and the levels are totally linear. You just push through with your 3 man team (you can't make it bigger later in the game - even if some NPC do join on certain missions) and there is very little strategy involved. It's probably worth playing on veteran at least for more of a challenge. All in all there are about 20 missions (around a dozen 1-2h major ones and a few 15min minor ones), so it's basically half the gameplay time of the original. The story and dialogue are rather good and the new outsiders with vertical mouths are fun to chat with. You don't have the same sense of Doom and crisis management you felt in the original but it's still pretty fun.

Hmm, I could've sworn I've reviewed this game before. Oh, wait, I did. I reviewed the original Evolve when it first got released, so I'll just repeat the intro to that one. Evolve: Stage Two is a 4v1 monster hunting game in which a team of 4 hunters attempts to track and then kill a large monster. That being said, Evolve Stage One was an absolute catastrophe. The price tag was too high, the egregious marketing of their DLC was ridiculous, and their attempts at balancing the game post-release were laughable at best due to being tied to the console update schedule, which is bloated in itself. That being said, into the actual review.
Well, the first problem, the price tag, has very clearly gone down a considerable margin into the Free-to-Play zone. Instead of buying hunters and monsters through the use of real money, you now can use Silver Keys that are granted to you throughout matches, and frankly, they're easy to get. You can get nearly everything in the game using these keys now, cosmetics included, which has greatly increased the value of picking up the game, and in all honesty, for a Free-to-Play game, the experience isn't bad, but by no means is it good. At the very least, Turtle Rock Studios seems to have repented for its prior money-whoring sins by making most of the items in-game achievable for free, which is commendable for any developer.
However, it's not all sunshine and roses in the world of Evolve, as there are several glaring problems with the game, still. The balance state of the game is absolutely chaotic. Every week, a new monster is overpowered and a new hunter is nerfed to the bare minimum of utility, and it's impossible to effectively get good at any monster or hunter at the moment because of the constant harsh rebalances. Evolve: Stage Two is trying to balance for the highest of top-tier gameplay, but that is unfortunately ruining the game for everyone below the top 5% of their playerbase in terms of skill due to the unfounded rebalances of most of the game's cast. In all honesty, most of the rebalances don't even make sense in the first place. It just seems like the Turtle Rock developers spin a wheel around with all of the monsters names on it and use that to determine which monster gets to be boring to fight against every patch.
Finally, there is very little variance in any of the maps at the moment. "But Zombie Chicken, you devilishly handsome fraud, you! That was a problem in stage one as well!" Yes, it was, but it was less of a problem, because in stage two, only four maps are available, and the rest have been shoved off for "repurposing." This creates an incredible amount of repitition, and as of the last update, the developers have heard our cries, and felt the need to shove an absolutely pointless "map variant," or map that's exactly like another map but with gimmicks, down our throats. Cataclysm is the newest map, and it's literally just a re-hash of one of the 4 maps already in Stage Two, but with meteors falling from above. That's it.
All that being said, I do appreciate Turtle Rock Studios for attempting to bring back a franchise that they could've simply left for dead, and then slapping a Free-to-Play price tag on it, but at the moment, I simply can't recommend this game at this moment. Every match is won and lost the minute the players pick their characters and whichever hunter or monster you're supposed to pick changes almost weekly. Every match feels the same, and it's more of a "Oh, boy, I hope the monster doesn't pick ________ this time," situation than an actual game.
I do not recommend this game,

Unlike some of the existing reviewers, I never played the original game so from that standpoint I don't have the benefit of a baseline to form a comparison. However, the sequel as a novelty to any gamer does not place you in the lurch simply because you didn't have the benefit of experiencing the first game and you can jump right into the action without feeling you are lost in the mix.  What is How to Survive 2? Well, for any of you that have never tried this franchise the game lives up to its name, because everything that you do in this game is exactly as the title suggests, "how to survive".  For any of you that have played survival horror type games, this game lives up to its name and makes a nice addition to the genre.
As the protagonist the game drops you onto a main map called the "Camp".  The Camp (map) is not massive relatively to other open world games, but large enough to keep things interesting if you decide to traverse the map, and definitely in abundance when you need to run around looking for resources to upgrade your personal camp within the Camp to build structures that make various weapons, armor, accessories, break down resources and provide defenses, food, and a trunk to store your items and resources.  That brings me to my next point, the game's entire and unilateral purpose is to find resources to increase your chances of survival and upgrade your camp structures.  You gain experience through completing quests and dispatching the undead, and you use the experience points to level up your personal camp, which then based on your camp level you can increase your avatar's level to match the camp's level.  As you increase your camp and avatar level during the first ten levels you begin to unlock various camp structures that you can build and items you can create using resources to benefit your character's combat prowess. You use resources found around the Camp and through engaging in quests offered by the various "Quest Givers" that you unlock as you progress in the game and mostly through performing quests offered by the main "Quest Giver", Kovac.  Kovac introduces you into his world and guides you through an organic tutorial of quests that teaches you how to play, what to collect to start building your camp, and beyond that more or less what you need to do in this game to maintain efficiency and better your proficiency.  Each quest takes you somewhere off the Camp map into another open world type map for you to complete the quest requirements, find resources sometimes very specific to that map, and then upon completion, receive a reward of resources from the Quest Giver.  Some quest maps are huge relatively to others, and most quests take place either within a decrepit city or within a swamp like area.
As you progress through the levels, you can upgrade your various camp structures you build to create better weapons, armor, food, metal resources to build better items, or potions - not in the magical sense, but that buff your health, recovery, speed, etc akin to drinking soda in real life giving you a boost of quick energy from the sugar.  At various camp level thresholds, which are generally incremental ten levels, you have to pass a test before you can reach the next level where you switch on a Pylon you built in the first ten levels through completing a quest offered by Kovac that sends a signal to reach out to fictional survivors that never manifest in the game but you have to battle off the hordes of undead that attack your camp as they are attracted to the signals emanating from the Pylon.
New quests unlock linearly as you complete each quest offered by the various Quest Giver, and each Quest Giver has a different motif of quests that follow his particular story line diverse from the others to afford some amout of subjective personality to each archetype of the Quest Givers.  This game is all about repeating quests offered by those same Quest Givers to propound sufficient resources to survive, progress, and build more effective structures, weapons, armor, bullets, arrows, etc. The higher you level your camp the more advanced resources become available to you, the better items you can build, and the undead become more difficult.  The game also throws out new more menacing undead, of which some of them are simply nightmarish, or necrotic animals that vary in the damage they do to your character.  Everything you need to survive, thrive and be effective in combat is craftable, and each time you level your camp the monsters in the Camp (region) become stronger and more resilient to your attacks requiring you to upgrade your weapons and armor to rise to the occasion and not become obsolete.
The game has a storyline through the quests you undertake from the Quest Givers, and you will find yourself redundantly and frequently completing the offered quests to locate and collect the resources you may be short of in your Trunk, which is where you store all of your items, to continue upgrading your camp, equipment and resources necessary to survive.  You have to find water and food to survive, and the hungrier you get or if you find yourself thirsty, you will also find yourself more ineffective in combat as it effects your stamina and strength as you would expect from depriving yourself of food and fluids.  The undead attack your camp in the Camp map, and you build defenses to keep them at bay long enough to dispatch them so they do not attack your camp structures that you use resources to build items.
Finally, you can have up to five avatars (characters), and you can play in your local camp along with any online camp that you create or any other player may have created for which you have joined.  While your Local camp is exclusive to you and intended for solo play, by joining or creating an Online camp, you can either set your camp to Private requiring other players to be invited to your camp Online, or Public, allowing players to join your camp at their discretion.  Clearly, you will need to be careful if you make your Online Camp Public by setting default authorizations to the players that join to avoid them stealing all of your resources and destroying your buildings within your camp. You can set various levels of authority that you as the Online Camp host can grant each player and or set by default for those invited to their Online Camp if Public.  The benefit of the player's ability to jump from camp to camp, private, public or local is that whatever experience you gain in the process of completing quests or killing the undead, and or resources amassed you take along with you.
The game is played isometrically and the environment is used more to direct the player rather than something that the player can interact with other than doors and drawers you can open and or unlock with the proper picklocking skill.  Sometimes quest maps are designed like puzzles requiring you to enter homes, line up trash bins to jump over barriers, or the top floor of stores to leap over the railing and get passed a wall or set of fences that otherwise block access to the other side of the environment from the ground.
If you enjoy resource collecting, button mashing real time combat, level based gameplay, item/food/weapon/armor crafting, survival genre games, and simple structure building you will enjoy this game.  It is best played with a friend or two, and if played Online you can play with up to four total players active at any one time in the Camp or in a quest.  The developers promise additional content as the game progresses, and if that includes new quest givers, maps, and items you can build then the game will only get better with each DLC introduced and offered.

Well I am very sad to say this Paradox phase of mine has gone now.  Too much DLC with a consistent lacking in AI performance that keeps the player hoping the next DLC may fix it.  Nice one Paradox you had me good time.

The ratings show that the community (with thousands of reviews) judged this game more-or-less positive, and more recently, 'mixed'. How come Paradox, probably the most wonderful strategy game developer extant, managed to more or less botch the delivery of a highly expected game like this, frustrating so many experient gamers? There is a reason for that.
Nowadays we are living times of 'dumbing-down' games. HoI4 suffered from that somewhat. There are new features here that are definitivelly an improvement from HoI2 and 3, but in overall the game seems less.. what's the word I'm looking for? Well, just 'less'.
An excellent improvement was the interface that easilly lets you group several units in one big command (even an armygroup-level command), assign it just one leader, and plan an attack  simply dragging the expected end-front for the whole operation and setting an stance for the army. THere is even a pause button, to halt and resume an entire operation. That was an excellent improvement, over the system found in Ho3 (which is good, mind you, but very labor-intensive).
Another excellent improvement is towards building equipment, designing templates to your divisions from a batch of said equipment, deploying and training those divisions. I love the system.
And also, lets all admit, the game just looks wonderful.
But ....
This is a case where the sum of the parts equals less than the whole. In all the game feels lacking. In fast tempo, you can end the game in a few hours. There is little to do, since the new policies system reduces your game to unlocking a few lackluster modifiers in slightlly different orders. Managing air units is a bore. Naval units less so, but still. The AI is pretty square, both the enemy as well as your own, when let to manage your operations. Managing land units yourself is, converselly, a little polluted. There is no more of Ho3's brilliant depiction of army organization (everything is either within one big command, or avulse in the world). In a nutshell, the game is kinda pale and bleek. It looks amazing, but it feels empty.
How come a game with such an ambitious scope (the world, no less!), with thousands of things to do, managed to feel so empty and devoid of colour?
IMO this comes from the perceived feel that a game must appeal to everyone, which is not necessarilly so. People looking for a simple strategic game may get overwhelmed, as people drooling for the good old paradox standard may get disapointed (as was I).
And I also take issue with the damn tendency to deliver games tailored to be slowly improved via DLCs, in little ten-dollars increments. DLCs are a welcome thing if they are constantly re-inventing a game (as it happens with CK2 and EU4), but in this case the vanilla game was delivered in a kinda week state and the DLC released so far tend to be more of the 'content pack' type ("but this 10 dollar DLC and play as New Zealand, with half a dozen new cosmetic options for that tiny country! Yeeeaaaayyy").
To sum things up, this game had a lot of potential to be great from the start, but it seems it will take a long road of DLCs to get there, if it gets there at all. A pity: so fat, it is merely 'ok'. It saddens me to see this become the norm for paradox games, once a sacred cow in the already-thin strategy games market.
Still... I recomend it, though. Paradox deserves support. I confess I bougth it already antecipating it would be less than great, and that it would take a few years for me to get to like it, after it got more polished. One can only hope.

So, as I'm playing this again, I think remembering what I loved about this game should help on why someone should pick this up.
-Easy to learn, hard to master combat controls
To make your character move their limbs, you need to move their joints. To move their joints, you can use the mouse wheel (my preference), z, x, or c, or mouse clicks. With a combination of joints flexing, you can pretty much do anything, and knowing what it is should be best learned by themselves.
-Simplistic Fights
There are a lot of game modes, or "mods" in this game. Most often than not, to make the enemy lose is by making his limbs fall to the floor by any means necessarry. To do so, you need huge foresight, skills, and fast clicks, since you could only move so many joints in your body before it is done. My preferred fights are Aikido, Greykido, Wushu and Mushu (I'm♥♥♥♥♥♥at the last two).
-No "Pay to win" stuff
Most of the things you can buy using the in-game currency is cosmetics and hats. Actually, for some VERY skilled players, hats give them an advantage, for headbutts and stuff like that.

I think after nearly 100 hours of playing, I can safely review the game. First and foremost, if you prefer playing with other people, either make sure you have a group of friends who play or are fine with randomly hooking up with others online, Solo mode is fun enough, but it get's really boring sometimes.
Over all, this is well worth the price tag. Plenty of things to do in game, plenty of regions and weapons. Enough side missions to keep you busy for the most part. Now this isn't Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim, which is massive and you can get hundreds of hours of play without ever touching the main quest line in the game, but Wildlands is definitely fun. HOWEVER!!!!!!!!!!! THERE IS NO ♥♥♥♥ING JUMP BUTTON!!!!! Really the only major complaint I have about the game. It's an open world, over the shoulder shooter with RPG elements, whose game is similar in map set up as LoZ Breath of the Wilds, Horizon Zero Dawn, Skyrim and Borderlands. Except without a jump button. I've had to exit the game to the main menu and re-enter just to unstick myself where a JUMP BUTTON would've gotten me out, a lot too. I seriously will take 5 hours explaining why a 3-d openworld, NEXT GEN, RPG-esque game SHOULD HAVE A MOTHER LOVING JUMP BUTTON.
But anyways, gameplay, world, visuals, content, weaponry, they are all great, very well done. Another small issue, minus the usual complaints about enemies in either direction, and the vehicles being difficult to drive, is that the weapon selection, while large and nice, never really see's new weapons added into the game, except with set versions or some wepons which you don't get the pain skin they use and cannot customize them except maybe putting on a silencer. This and the lack of uniquely different weapons limits the types of players. You're either Long Range, Mid-Range (the all around player), or CQB with SMG's and shotty's, or "Heavy" gunner with a very small number of weapons that would be considered "Heavy" class. I believe you have 4 different shotguns and 5 or 6 different LMG's? while you have over 10 snipers, at least 20 Assault Rifles, and close to, if not more than, 20 SMG's. Only 2 or 3 full auto pistols, and maybe 10 pistols, minus special versions of weapons and DLC's which add some old fashioned weapons (Musket Rifle and Pistol being the most notable). So with all of this in mind, I'd say it is still worth the price tag, but it still lacks a lot of potential greatness.
The DLC's, I cannot really say much about since I haven't really gotten into them yet, but the Fallen Ghosts DLC adds the Fallen Ghosts campaign, and adds a couple new weapons (while removing a couple too) Like the PSG Sniper and a crossbow. Don't know why they just could add it into the base game, but o-well.

is an underrated though admittedly unpolished gem that shouldn't be overlooked by XCOM fans. Yes, it has an interface only a mother could love. There are some strange glitches at points, like Agent Carter not delivering his dialogue at all in one conversation thus requiring the player to skip forward. And the frame rate gets pretty iffy at times, particularly if you choose to use the DirectX 11 (DX11) version.
But under the rough edges is a genuinely entertaining game. The story definitely evokes the XCOM vibe in all its facets, depicting humanity itself under assault from a creepy bunch of mysterious "outsiders". The graphics are quite good, particularly with DX11 (though I don't think it's worth the frame-rate hit most of the time), the audio is solid, and the game mechanics are fun. It
got old finding synergies in the interplay between the various skills of the agents under my command.
It feels like a game that changed directions multiple times and was stitched together at the last minute, leaving a few holes here and there and some rough seams. But it's the first non-traditional XCOM game I've played that I've quite enjoyed once I got past its faults. It's definitely worth it if you can pick it up cheap.

Rating 7.5/10
Overview: Cover Based- Third Person Shooter
The Good:
+I really loved the 1960's American setting. Both artistically and technically the developers did a good job making this game feel alive.
+The game takes place across a series of locations each one unique in its own way. The game has a lot of good set pieces
+Side quests are fleshed out and fun to play
+ The game allows you to take 2 squad members with you into battle. You can customize your squad any way you like. There are four classes to choose from:  support, sniper, engineer, and commando. Each class has its own set of abilities and weapons to choose from. You pick whatever you want to suit your playstyle.
+ The game has a wide variety of abilities not only for the main character but your squad as well. The abilities are varied for each class and serve a very practical purpose in battle
The Average:
The story starts off strong and is constantly building up to something...problem is, the story starts getting too convoluted for its own good. Eventually it gets so ridiculous it becomes hard to care about the story. By the end of the game I was playing it just to see the next setting.
The characters are also one dimensional and a bit stereotypical.
The game doesn't do a whole lot to change up the game play formula. Every side quest/main mission plays out the same way, kill lots of enemies, move on to the next area...repeat.
The Bad:
- Your teammates are completely useless. First they don't manually use there abilities, you have to manually select them for them to use it. Some people may like this, I did not.  The second major problem is that they make very stupid decisions resulting in death. The pop out of cover at the wrong time and get shot at, move to locations where the enemies are, etc.   The third major problem is that they do very little damage, 99% of the kills will come from you.
For a game that is supposed to be a "tactical" shooter , there is nothing tactical about it. Because of the stupidity of your teammates the game plays out like a solo third person shooter. You only have teammates to choose their abilities.
Conclusion
For all the fun I had with this game, it does have some serious faults. I would have liked to see more variety in the gameplay and stronger A.I. I still think its worth playing especially if you like cover based shooters.

TL,DR: This had potential, but it remained unrealized. Not terrible, but can't really recommend spending money on it, much less 20$.
Storyline: Aliens invade, only the secret XCOM unit stands in their way. Could have been an interesting look at how XCOM got started, was instead a confused mix of side missions that had no influence on anything (trust me, you need neither the equipment nor the people you get) and a main storyline that lost me half way through because of plot holes and lack of immersion. Without spoilers, only so much: I finished it, and I still don't understand either the human's OR alien's motivations for anything.
Gameplay: Mass Effect style shooter with squad and cover mechanics. It's just that your squad is useless and the cover is badly realized It does not seem to matter whether you hit someone, it matter whether they are "flanked" - the game just doesn't tell you about the damage bonus this gets you. Add in the fact that it's a typical console port - savepoints, doors that close level parts behind you, etc. - and the very bad AI and it's just not that good. There's many small details here that just bug me, things like enemies with infinite grenades or jogging slowly through your base again and again just to see whether they might be some new conversation, that add up over the play time and eventually pretty much ruin the experience.
Graphics: Are fine, but not really all that important.
Sound: Similarly fine, but nothing to write home about.
Overall: Not terribly bad and at least made me want to finish it (if only out of principle), but the final verdict is much more "meh" than "yay".

Gameplay - Mass Effect 2 clone. However, I felt it was more crucial to employ squadmember skills during battle than what i was used to in Mass Effect 2 on similar difficult. This is a good thing. (Saying Mass Effect 2 since i haven't yet completed 3)
Difficulty - I played it on the second hardest difficulty and although the learning curve was alright, it started out alot tougher than expected. Expect a hard time against your first Muton unless you're above average in tactics and how you pick your squads.
Graphics - The graphics are alright. I'm not really that good on judging them though since i put gameplay first. Everything reminded me again of Mass Effect 2, though the the backdrop is the early 60s in the US. The main character animation during story dialogues was repetive though.
Story - I expected a lot more shallow story from the get go. It really suprised me how it twists and turns later on. The side missions were quite a bit lacking though, and again something picked up from the Mass Effect franchise. I didn't really feel there were any rewards to them either.
Sound - Music and sound effects were solid. Voice acting above average and in style with what i feel is true for the 60s. There are also quite a few references to early 60s rock music.
The Bad - Although i encountered no gamebreaking bugs, there are a few annoying ones. Like dialogue looping after the sequence is finished, items that have been checked will glow again after a side mission if you have tips on in options and a few glitchy things now and then.
Bottom line - Anyone with interest in 3rd person action, bioshock rpgs or the Xcom franchise should find value here. I really enjoyed it while not expecting it to be anything more than a twitchy, corridor, action game.

A delightful visual novel taking place on the underground train service of a future city. As a detective robot you decide to go against your programming and take on a case given to you by a stranger in a panic, and not one given to you by the government. So starts your circular adventure as you try and unravel the mysteries that lurk below the surface in this city rife with robots. Will you solve the mystery?
PROS:
+ Hot robots! - Oh boy do I like some attractive robots and this game has more attracive robots than you could shake a stick of RAM at. The designs of the robots are delightful and varied.
+ Would you look at that writing! - There's lots of reading afoot and the words are good! Subsurface Circular has great writing and dances with ideas that will, hopefully, leave you thinking and constantly wondering about the robots to come.
+ Are the robots real? - The characters you come across are great and I really enjoyed talking to them, well, not talking.... forming a wireless connection with them. Robot stuff.
CONS:
- Is it a puzzle? - There's not much actual puzzling afoot as you sit down and ride the train. For the most part you do just read through the conversations and give them varying prompts of information that you have learned about previously. To be fair I wouldn't really call this a negative because there's still a sense of achievement to be gained from prompting robots with questions to get what little bit of information they may have and then running off (in a metaphorical sense, you're very much sat down) and talk to the next attractive robot. So, this really doesn't count as a negative, but I guess some people may be expecting a bit more than a visual novel with a greater level of interaction than your average VN.
- Help I can't stop thinking about it! - It's been months and I'm still sometimes finding myself thinking about this game. Did I make the right choice? What does it mean for our society in real life? Do I have an odd attraction to actual robots? I can't sleep at night as these haunt me, which probably is a bit of a con because it's ruined my life, but in a good way.
Overall Subsurface Circular is a delightfully small game that you can knock out in an afternoon and it's definitely worth it. An enrapturing tale that'll hopefully leaving you chomping at the ... CPU (that's a robot thing?) to continue to the bottom of this case.

Making it FTP has brought thousands of players to it and the devs are actively adding characters, maps, and working to keep this game supported. I find myself enjoying this game hours on end everyday with all the new characters as well as grinding for more silver keys, or whatever you call them, too unlock more goodies to play with. Bit of a history with this title. Preordered for 360 back in the day, didn't really get into it, returned it. Bought it again a couple years later, got further than before, but still wasn't quite feeling it. Finally try it on PC when it was cheap, I can finally enjoy myself with mouse precision, fast load times, and hotkeys for glorious save scumming.
+Multiple pathways to traverse, multiple tools and techniques for tackling a mission
+Play as a ghost, parkouring and teleporting around the place, or dive into the fray with your sword and pistol ready
+Your actions, who you kill, save, or neutralize, they all have effects on later missions.
+City has a unique art style. Mix of colonial and sci-fi to make a world that isn't quite steampunk, but something all its own. Half Life 2's City 17 comes to mind, especially since the same guy did art direction for both games
+Lore is intriguing, the city has some history and mystique to it
+/-You have some tools to make it through a fight, but unless you invest your coin in combat-related perks you'll pay for going loud
+/-Short, but this encourages multiple playthroughs with different skills and equipment
-Voice acting is subpar, many repeated lines, particularly that dialogue about getting together for whiskey and cigars
-Textures aren't very pretty
