There are 9 birds who are dateable, each has one unique story and each story concludes in an ending. 3 endings can be extended to 'true endings' by visiting certain classes and gaining points (you are a student). These endings are somewhat surprising and often either expectedly funny or exceptionally emotional.
After you romanced each bird once, you gain the ability to play the 'Bad Boys Love'-Story. This story is heartwrecking! It concludes every other storyline by answering any leftover questions. It plays maybe 5 times as long as a normal storyline and it can be quite difficult to follow at times, but in the end (and inbetween), at least i found myself near tears ;_;

And bird-dating.

It is bloody Quake!
Best game ever. EVER.
Grandfather of FPS genre and Golden Source for so many other titles. I've spent countless hours in LAN games and QuakeWorld. Made of WIN and Rocket jump.

This game is legendary in the FPS genre for good reason. At the time, it was a technical milestone for its superbly impressive 3D engine (which is quite dated, of course), which would later go on to power games like Dark Forces 2: Jedi Knight and Half-Life. It pioneered online multiplayer. It spawned a series of FPS's responsible for defining the genre throughout the 90's and beyond, though Quake 3 is probably the most widely-known of the lot these days. Ultimately, Quake 1 is an insanely fun, action-packed FPS that I can do nothing but recommend to everyone who enjoys the FPS genre. It's both great to see the history of the genre as well as still being an absolute blast to play.

Quake is probably one of the best video games of all time. It changed gaming forever and gaming wouldn't be what it is today without it. A lot of games came about because of what Quake was/is. Half-life series? Yep. Playing this is going back to the roots of FPS gaming, not to mention it revolutionized multiplayer gaming and game modding.
The graphics are dated, but nearly 15 years later and this game is still one of my favorites. I go back and play it all the time. Hard to forget late night deathmatch sessions and Quakespy. Best war game ever, even better than Distant Worlds: Universe (but barely). Most war games are simple over-glorified resource management simulators. They require lots of micromanaging, and victory is usually measured in clicks-per-minute. The strategies hardly resemble anything in the real world.
HoI4 is the best done war game that includes realistic aspects of actual warfare, such as a supply chain, limited manpower, and dealing with resistance in occupied territories. You also learn a lot about WWII, why it happened the way it did, and how it could have ended differently. And, it gives you a better perspective on real world conflicts today.
They made HoI4 more gamey than their HoI3, and not everything is accurate unfortunately. I hope they move towards more accuracy in future games. However, the Battle Planning feature is indispensable. I would rather play HoI4 over HoI3 just because it practically eliminates micromanaging altogether.

I tried to give it a chance
I honestly did. I went into it expecting a decent game that just used X-com names, and after all, it can't be worse than X-com Enforcer, now could it?
Well, it can. Enforcer had its over the top, fast paced shooting with loads of weapons to amuse you. The Bureau has chest high walls to protect their chest high walls that you can sit behind.
I only got about 3 hours in until I just plain could not play any more. With poor controls(Very obviously a console port that they didn't care enough about to make it work for PC), and absolutely awful AI. Several times have I seen the AI just run right into the open without any cover without any prompting whatsoever, and several more times did I wonder if the AI actually follows your commands or knows what end of their gun to point at the enemy. After some experimenting I found the answers to these questions.
No, they do not know what end of their gun goes to the enemy, and they do not understand 'go sit in cover here so I can flank them' either. And speaking of flanking, you will need to do it. For the first few minutes I wondered why the aliens had titanium skulls, but then I realised a headshot and a torso shot are about the same. You get a flat damage bonus if you flank your opponent though. Good concept - but it just doesn't work with the braindead AI and clumsy controls. It isn't actually explained anywhere either, so unless you're quick to figure things out you'll blow all your ammo on an alien who is 'in cover' but still sticking most of his head and torso out for you to shoot(And deal nearly no damage because of this 'cover'), get frustrated, and quit.
The story seemed interesting enough and I did want to see what was next, but I just can't justify spending more time on it than I already have. The story just can't carry the rest of the game and I can't really care enough to play further.
Oh, and the glass physics were pretty good. It was nice to see parts of the glass shatter under fire without the whole window immediately collapsing. If only that attention to detail could have been spend on the rest of the game as well it may have been good

Subsurface Circular is a small game that can only really be given a short review. But luckily, the game still makes a fresh change of pace from most games on the market. As a visual novel or rather, text based adventure, it certainly delivers.
You play as a Tek Dectective, a smart robot on the underground train on the Subsurface Circular line of a city. You are soon brought into an investigation to try and discover a truth.
I won't spoil you on the details, but it is a facinating and thoughtful story which makes you stop and think about what is actually happening in the world this game portrays, with little mentions of the other works the devolopers made, leading to a decision which you will be struggling to make a decision on.
As you play through the game, you will find yourself solving puzzles which may prove tricky at first, but there is normally a logical and clever way of sorting them out, making them very rewarding to do.
Now, the game is short, and is meant to be played in a single sitting. But I do believe that you will get your moneys worth. Now, if you don't like text based adventures or visual novels, then don't get this game. But for those who want something a little bit different or like such games, you will certainly enjoy this one.

The story itself explores some pretty conventional "robot future" possibilities, but it's the way you uncover the world by talking to the passengers, without ever leaving the train, which gives it its charm. There's some interesting, tought-provoking decisions to take towards the ends, with a good ending that wrap itself up nicely.

This is the exact kind of game I'm down with playing these days: Cheap, thoughtful, and relatively short in a way that suggests they didn't feel the need to pad out the length with reiterations of the same gameplay concepts.
In some ways, it's the opposite of Bithell's earlier work, Thomas Was Alone, since this game has almost no voicework, but also uses conversation as a mechanic, something the player had no control over in the TWA.
Games like this live or die on the strength of the writing, and Subsurface Circular succeeds remarkably well on this front. There wasn't a single conversation I found tedious, every character revealed some new aspect of this future robot culture. It seems to follow the basic concept that if a mechanic or a concept doesn't advance the story or provide something interesting, just cut it out.
I would love it if people like Bithell kept putting out these sort of games, it's a satisfying use of my time.

Imagine Far Cry with a Rainbow Six-esque story mode in third person. Unlike previous Ghost Recon games, this game is not linear at all. It is set in an open world game, and has missions much like Far Cry.
The only complaints I have is for a game who tries to be realistic, all the reloading animations are wrong, the bullet drop is ridiculously exagerrated to the point where you have to use the 600m mark on the ACOG's ACSS reticle for a 250m shot. If you pay attention to your AI teammates shots, you will notice that most of them impact the ground, but still do damage to the enemy. Not only that, but instead of suppressors increasing muzzle velocity like in real life, an in-game suppressor will significantly decrease your weapon's damage output. You have to get a "perk" in order to nullify that. The damage system is hit-points based, unless you score a headshot, or the enemy is unaware.
Additionally, flying and driving is terrible. With an Xbox 360 controller, the camera control is awful. I found it impossible to land airplanes, flying helicopters was too easy, and driving would be find if it were not for the camera.
The storyline is good, however. I got about 72 hours to finish it with the "good" ending. If you are expecting a good storyline with call of duty realism, this is the game for you. If you expect more from Tom Clancy games, this isn't your game.

Despite a few bugs that haven't been resolved, I felt that Wildlands was a solid game all things considered. The stealth system is janky (ex. enemies shooting moarters at your location when you're just hunted) and Unidad has been a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ But man, the game at the end of the day was really fun. I played it all entirely in co-op and got over 50 hours of gameplay. You're getting a good mix of missions and a lot of weapons. I also found the tier system later in the game and the graphics to be nice.

All in all, it's fun enough.  I don't regret buying the game.
There are bugs.  Enough bugs that f I had paid full price I would feel like I overpaid for a game that behaves like it's in beta.
No jumping, so if you want to climb over a fence or a rock, it has to be "climbable."  It's very frustrating to be in the middle of a mission and then stuck between a garbage can and a fence with no way out.  Exit game, restart mission from scratch.
You quickly learn that if you're about to pull the lever to "start the first antenna" you'd better have a helicopter parked nearby because you have a very short timer to start the second one, and it's not very close.  Those missions aren't very fun.  There are maybe a dozen mission types.
Driving vehicles, planes, helicopters is painful, terrible.  It makes it easier to land the plane when you realize zero finesse is required, throttle down, keep the nose up, slam it into the ground.
The A.I. is predictable and simple.  "Let's rush them, there's bound to be more of us than them!" will be shouted even when there is only one bad guy left, but sure enough, he'll probably advance.
It's very comparable to Farcry series.  I enjoyed that game too, but it becomes a grind.  Unlock skills and weapons, maybe a dozen total different mission types with different layouts but the same scenario.
7/10.  I got it on sale, I am satisfied.

Is it worth it? Yes it is! Why? Because it's free.
Other than that, it has its fun times. Playing with other people who communicate well with you make it worth the while.
ON THE OTHER HAND.... if you decide that you want to play hunt be prepared for a long wait time. Why you may ask??? Well because while playing hunt the monster isn't AI, someone has to play them. Everyone knows in the game that being the monster means that you are going to take an "L" because there are 4 hunters against one (not so powerful) monster. Unless you are playing with people that don't really understand what they are doing in this game. I thought I was going to spend hundereds of hours playing this game, I thought wrong. Once you become the monster the drive to keep playing this game goes down 100 fold.
Some of you may think that I'm being a sore loser, but let me explain the other reasons why that may not be true.
On average you may get like 100-200 (in some very rare cases up to 800) "tokens" if you will, at the end of the round.
The average unlockable character is 5500.... That's a long time to be stuck playing the same few characters. On top of that, you can also buy perks and skins with said tokens, at the same price that you would pay for a character (in some cases, sometimes more sometimes less.)
The round times can last anywhere from 5 mins all the way to 40 mins! That's a pretty long time to play especially if you are just going to get 100 tokens.
The variety of classes in my opinion is a plus! To be able to unlock them though is a joke. Although, you may find yourself playing with one class for an extended period of time if you like the class. All of a sudden the next game, you get thrown into a class you may have not even played before and then 12 year old kids are yelling at you because you have no idea what you are doing.
If you like a game to casually play for maybe a day or so, I recommend this game. If not, there are PLENTY of games out there that are better suited for you.
Again, this is my opinion of the game, take it as you will.

You'll have to excuse me here, but I cannot avoid comparing this game with Deus Ex. And I mean this in a positive point of view. While Deus Ex sits in a Cyberpunk universe, Dishonored depicts the life of a master assassin in a Steampunk world. I cannot emphasize how much I appreciate the opportunity to play the game without killing anyone (many games out there should consider this as well), while still providing multiple ways to complete certain missions.
The storyline is interesting and sufficiently deep. Like in many recent games, there are multiple side quests in each level. Moreover, your actions in previous levels bring consequences later on, and may result in a different ending. Many books and notes are scattered around the levels, leaving enough lore to those genuinely interested in them, without forcing the player to read everything. Cut scenes can be skipped as well.
Although the game provides you a reasonable assortment of weapons, tools and special powers, you might easily end up not using most of them. For instance, you would not use the pistol very much in a pacifist stealth run. There aren't many items for facilitating this particular strategy other than sleep darts and a charm that makes non-lethal knockouts faster. On the other hand, such an approach is meant to be challenging anyway.
The controls are fair for an FPS. The graphics are also decent for its age, although the mouth animations look a bit awkward, as if they were yawning on each word. Deus Ex HR did it a bit better on that end, but this is just a minor nitpick.
Overall, it's a nice experience. If you liked Deus Ex, this one is worth trying out.

Zotrix is like a top down arcade shooter bullet hell where you play as a spaceship shooting everything. That being said, the game has pros and cons to it, although from what I found, the cons outweighed the pros.
The good parts of this game is that the gameplay is actually pretty fun. When you are shooting stuff, it is smooth, sometimes refreshing, and is challenging to dodge and shoot enemies. Also, the game features some pretty good music, which I enjoyed.
The bad parts of this game is that the interface is too needlessly complex early on. They overload you with so much stuff just to start, and then throw you in. The beginning is actually not that bad, and I was able to figure out quite a bit of stuff, but it was kind of annoying. Additionally, everything is too cheap. You can literally buy a tier 3 item after finishing your second level. Also each level is the same with no real differences, causing the game to be pretty repetitive and not super stimulating.
Overall, if the devs improved the game a bit, made the interface better, and made more unique missions, the game would be better and I would give it a positive review. I wish there was a neutral option, but since there isn't, I will be leaving a not recommend.

Zotrix is an oldschool topdown scrolling shooter with trading elements. It has had some love put into it and is a modernish take on pattern based shooters. The quests and trading system give it some legs but the problem is that this style of shooter, with waves of enemies moving in pre set patterns; is boring, and when it isn't boring it is overwhelming. It's an interesting design choice but I feel they should have gone full bullet hell mode with a larger variety of permanent powerups and that would have probably been more fun to play.
-the game world is nicely fleshed out
-controls well, interface mostly makes sense
-the storyline seems interesting
-resource trading is a bit confusing at first
-the shooting is below average, just didn't find it that engaging
-the enemy ships are sometimes just shapes and mostly look shabby
-lots of powerups but only a few permanent ones
At the end of the day zotrix is a decent game but not a very exciting shooter. I wanted to like it and I think it does what it does quite well. Worth a look for space merchants but most  players will probably find it a bit dull

*scroll down for the TLDR pros and cons*
I've only played one full round on the easiest difficulty but I think this game is great fun. It has no tutorial but that's why I started on the easiest settings. After about day 60 in game (about 2 hours?) I started to figure out how everything works.
This game has amazing potential and as it is right this second I would say YES to buying it. It does have some glitches every now and then and the game can get frame issues with massive hordes on the screen. But I imagine they will be fixed in time (as I have not seen anything game braking yet)
I can tell that on higher difficulties that this game could be a little rage inducing. Even on 3% difficulty multiplier (out of a max 340% on first map) I had quite a few close calls. One thing to note is that as it stands now there are 4 maps. But to unlock each map you need to beat the one before it with a specific multiplier. This isn't a horrible idea and it does force people to really test themselves, I don't think it's a bad decision to add this feature but the game as is, is already kinda difficult, I'm not that good at these games so it's possible I may never get to experience latter levels which kind of sucks. Would be nice if there was a customs scenario option that has all maps open to you but no scores are recorded or uploaded to leaderboards. But it will allow those not good enough to unlock all levels to still play the full game.
The graphics are very appealing and smooth. I love the art style and the randomly generated maps and hordes force you to play with strategy and clever base planning (since it's possible and easy to accidentally block off your army from running through your base and they need to go the long way around. EASY TO LOSE WHEN YOU BLOCK OFF YOUR ARMY) rather than basing your victories off memory and layouts of the map and resource locations. Every map offers its own challenges and not 1 play through will feel the same.
All that being said it still needs more work and balancing. I personally feel like buildings could use more health before becoming infected. I think the zombies should be weaker but contrast that change by adding more infected. That way there is still a real risk of losing the whole game, but it's more satisfying to kill thousands at once rather than hundreds (on easier difficulties, higher ones get insane hordes)
For all I know the creators of this game want it to be hard even at a basic level. But it's so rewarding when you complete a wave.
-----------TLDR-----------
Pros:
-good graphics
-appealing art style
-randomly generated maps
-massive hordes of zombies
-not too difficult to learn how to play
-Immersive
-strategic base building
-has replay ability as is
Cons:
-can get laggy
-has some bugs (early access, can't mark it down too much)
-not a huge variety of buildings
-market building could be better
-must complete levels at specific multiplier to unlock new area
-pretty difficult by default
All in all it's a good game and I'm excited to see it when it's fully released with all the content of campaign and whatever else may be added!
--------change suggestions--------
As a final note if any developer were to read this, I think more building variety and a future custom game option (where you can fine tune things like horde size and strength, resource abundance and worth, map style and horde frequency) could really add a lot of playability to the game. Survival already offers loads of replay ability. And I'm sure the campaign will offer a lot as well, but customs scenarios could add just that little bit extra.
I think zombies should be just a tad weaker in strength and health but more in numbers.

I played just under ten hours of it on the night of February 28th into March 1st on the year 2015, straight through. The first hour and a half wasn't with out any difficulty as I had to fix a small issue with the launcher. It still doesn't work right, but I can open the game which is good enough for me. That ate up my first 15 minutes. Unfortunately I did not take that as a sign of things to come.
The next hour and fifteen minutes was spent trying to get the G27 to cooperate with my preferred settings. It wasn't until the end of that hour and fifteen that I realized that it was my fault that it wouldn't cooperate. Just one small issue, I wasn't clicking the right button to save my settings.
Once I got the controls sorted, the next 8 and a half hours was spent mostly cruising in my classic Mustang. The world is huge and open for you to explore, and there are two maps to explore. The driving could have been better polished, but it is still quite enjoyable. Additionally I find it nice to have the option to have Automatic, Sequential (Paddle shifting), H-Shifter or H-Shifter + Clutch options for driving. I drive the Mustang in Automatic mode as it has a 3 speed Auto. I prefer to keep things traditional in the game. If I drove a manual car, then I would be grabbing my own gears with the stick.
Finally towards the last two hours of it, I got a buddy of mine in this game and he and I cruised around. The multiplayer has to be the biggest flaw as it only works when it wants to. Other players can also be annoying as they constantly follow you and challenge you to unwanted races, but with the average population of 10 at the most, you can imagine why. If for some reason you're disconnected from the online play, how ever, you can still play and save your progress just fine. You would just be alone as all.
The game is nearly perfect if you want to go cruising around. It challenges your driving in multiple different ways with different style of driving with different types of cars. If you can get the multiplayer to work, you can go cruising with your friends. Or you can stick to single player and rack up Championships and Licenses to make more in-game money that can be used to cloth your avatar or trick out your ride, or even buy a house!
One last thing to mention is that the strongest of cars, the best lookers, you have to pay real-money for. Suggesting it has a pay to win model, but anyone can spend money on a nice car and not know how to drive it. In this scenario, it's all about perspectives.

This game has so many negative reviews and a bad rap. I I liked the game enough to finish it.
First, this is NOT a turn-based strategy game the XCOM franchise is known for. Much of the negative reviews are from those who were misinformed about the genre. This game is a somewhat unremarkable squad shooter from a third person perspective.
Get this game if you are fascinated with the storyline of the XCOM universe. I enjoyed the progression enough to finish the game. Exploring and listening to the audio diaries is amusing and adds to the story. Much of the missions are unfortunately generic i.e. kill all enemies on the map. Main character is also deliberately unlikeable (cannot say more without story spoilers). Units you recruit are generic and easy to level up with automated side missions. You'll very quickly have a roster of forgettable squadmates you can choose from. The gameplay is rather easy overall, with occasional difficulty spikes when you aren’t doing exactly what the game expects you to.
Buy the game if you enjoy playing generic squad shooters and like the XCOM setting and more backstory. But don’t expect much. It's worth buying as a bundle with XCOM:EU since you are getting this pennies. I’d give it a 6/10.

Best war game ever, even better than Distant Worlds: Universe (but barely). Most war games are simple over-glorified resource management simulators. They require lots of micromanaging, and victory is usually measured in clicks-per-minute. The strategies hardly resemble anything in the real world.
HoI4 is the best done war game that includes realistic aspects of actual warfare, such as a supply chain, limited manpower, and dealing with resistance in occupied territories. You also learn a lot about WWII, why it happened the way it did, and how it could have ended differently. And, it gives you a better perspective on real world conflicts today.
They made HoI4 more gamey than their HoI3, and not everything is accurate unfortunately. I hope they move towards more accuracy in future games. However, the Battle Planning feature is indispensable. I would rather play HoI4 over HoI3 just because it practically eliminates micromanaging altogether.

Ghost Recon wildlands to me was an enjoyable experience, but I will not say that will be for everyone. Now keep in mind I will adress single player only.
Story:
I mean you know how it will end from the start and indeed both endings are both plausible and realistic, world aint a happy ever after place after all. What is in between though I found quite enjoyable while never to shocking or creative it all worked out quite nicely and showed a decently grim world. I do wish your targets where a bit more resistant to talking requiring some less nice means from our end to get the info as well that would have added to the realism feel no question.
Gameplay:
I enjoy it a lot, but there are few games that allow me to scout out an location from distance and then start sniping the outlying patrols from 400-500m away in a modern setting so that alone would sell me. That said it is far from realistic and the disappearing bodies makes things extremely easy when you play it stealthy. The only times I would go loud is when I wanted to, otherwise I could snipe out most bases or even just go in there and clear them out with a single magazine of my beloved Five-seveN. Either way the gunplay feels nice, the only thing that was missing for me was bullets being affected by wind to make the sniping a bit harder. (Also can we finally accept that supressors are not siliencers? But I guess that would make stealth a lot harder requiring a easy mele takedown option)
The weapons:
Large selection of current day weapons, though they are not exactly true to real life I guess for balance reasons like most asault rifles starting out with 20 round mags that clearly are the models of 30 round mags. Minor details like that can be annoying, but overall weapon choice is wide and most can be modified to further suit your needs.
The Rides:
Cars and the likes are a bit more limited which means that after a few hours you likely seen all the game has to offer on that front. I will say they control quite decently and overal do their jobs quite fine though the APCs can be a ♥♥♥♥♥ to control requiring quite some getting used to and if you get those on a wet road it feels like you are in control of a hovercraft :P The helos are nice in general, though a bit samy and in my opinion to common meaning you tend to fly just about everywhere, cause sneak in clear out the base, get what you need and steal their helo cause why not? The planes on the other hand are outright terrible, no rudder control at all whomever designed that should be forced to spend some hours in a flight sim.
Conclusion:
Got it on sale for 30 bucks, got nearly 60 hours in it by now so it is save to say I had fun despite some of the issues and well the to be fair quite large number of bugs and smaller glitches. Still if any of those had been to bad I sure as hell would not have put in this many hours so I would recommend the game if you enjoy the main gameplay loop of clearing out locations of badguys in your favourite manner.

You'll have to excuse me here, but I cannot avoid comparing this game with Deus Ex. And I mean this in a positive point of view. While Deus Ex sits in a Cyberpunk universe, Dishonored depicts the life of a master assassin in a Steampunk world. I cannot emphasize how much I appreciate the opportunity to play the game without killing anyone (many games out there should consider this as well), while still providing multiple ways to complete certain missions.
The storyline is interesting and sufficiently deep. Like in many recent games, there are multiple side quests in each level. Moreover, your actions in previous levels bring consequences later on, and may result in a different ending. Many books and notes are scattered around the levels, leaving enough lore to those genuinely interested in them, without forcing the player to read everything. Cut scenes can be skipped as well.
Although the game provides you a reasonable assortment of weapons, tools and special powers, you might easily end up not using most of them. For instance, you would not use the pistol very much in a pacifist stealth run. There aren't many items for facilitating this particular strategy other than sleep darts and a charm that makes non-lethal knockouts faster. On the other hand, such an approach is meant to be challenging anyway.
The controls are fair for an FPS. The graphics are also decent for its age, although the mouth animations look a bit awkward, as if they were yawning on each word. Deus Ex HR did it a bit better on that end, but this is just a minor nitpick.
Overall, it's a nice experience. If you liked Deus Ex, this one is worth trying out.

Subsurface Circular plays for me like the videogame equivalent of the best 'bottle episodes', or narratives given the theatrical restriction of one setting to really focus on and amplify smaller details of the writing. A self-proclaimed 'Bithell Short', SC's formal restrictions (dialogue tree-driven, mouse click short form narrative) and writerly restraint (it takes place entirely on the eponymous underground train system transporting robots to various locations on the surface that we only hear about in conversation) free it of the wide burden and bloat that can afflict even the best open world games of larger scale. It hits a goldilocks zone for me of not too committal, not too complexly-interfaced, and not overwhelming (exploration is possible, but within the comforting corridors of conversation, not vast vistas or sprawling streets). You don't often see the short form in video games, and I appreciated being able to play this one through in one sitting if I wanted, or pick it up in bits and pieces when not afforded an abundance of play time.
I also enjoy the story, and would love to keep seeing what has already been a trend this year of sci fi video games tackling genre tread territory with the fresh perspective of contemporary angles and issues. SC is set in a world in which labor has been automated, and that hasn't ushered in a post-scarcity utopia so much as created a new underclass of sentient machines targeted by neo-Luddite hate groups. You are one of these robots, a model relegated to the task of detective and investigating a series of robot disappearances. I shouldn't say any more for fear of spoilers, but I found the narrative engaging, at points surprising, and always with a range of tonality that is absolutely charming.
If you're into narrative driven games and futurist sci-fi, definitely check this out.

Dishonored is a great game. Maybe even an amazing game. However, this is due to the sum of its pieces, rather than specifics, as this game is littered with issues ranging from mildly annoying to downright hysterical.
+ Unrivaled stealth/action gameplay
+ Terrific level design
+ Interesting and unique setting
+ Power system really adds to overall gameplay
+ Strong replay value
+ Practically glitch free
+ Good PC port with solid performance, mouse support on all menus and an FOV slider going up to 110. My only issue is that the amount of different settings left a bit to be desired, especially in the graphics section.
+ Choice between combinations of going stealthy, loud, lethal and nonlethal
-Story is alright, I guess. I didn’t feel too invested in it, and some characters were entirely forgettable, but it did have its good parts here and there, as I found myself taking quite a liking to certain characters.
- Chaos system really missed the mark, with one death making the difference between high or low, rather than different characters and killing methods having different weights (e.g. killing a civilian is more punishing than killing some random gangbanger, or burning a man to death is more punishing than killing him in his sleep)
- Going nonlethal can be very boring, repetitive and tedious. Even worse, the game constantly dangles cool weapons in front of your face all game but...
- Going lethal/having fun is strongly punished, with it leading to the bad ending, as well everyone around you generally acting like a bit more of a prick
- Even though there is a wide variety of gadgets and powers, most of them are close to useless, with your trusty sword being far more effective in most situations.
- Voice acting is laughably bad, with the laughable part being completely non-hyperbolic. Even though it can provide a bit of unintentional comic relief every once in awhile, it quickly grows stale.
- The game is way too easy. Even on the hardest difficulty, the game offers no challenge so long as you avoid conflict.
If you value gameplay over narrative, Dishonored is your calling. I loved the hell out of this game and have played it multiple times over, and still open it up every once in a while just to experience the streets of Dunwall once more. However, that being said, if mindlessly assassinating guard after guard doesn’t sound like your cup of tea, I suggest you look elsewhere.

This is not the type of game I would normally purchase. I enjoy mechanically intensive games almost exclusively. I purchased this game on a whim and am very happy I did so. The game took me about an hour and forty minutes to complete but it felt like no time at all. The game is engaging, the story is deep, and it touches on so many aspects of culture and society.
It's a game that entirely features robots, and you never leave where you are. Despite this, the game manages to discuss immigration, racism, slavery, human (and non-human) rights, and so much more. The game does not tell you what to think of these issues, rather it presents you with a society that contains these issues and lets you make of it what you will.
I wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone and everyone. It will surprise you and leave you satisfied in so many ways.

All in all, it feels too repetitive and bland.
The music is great, although each level consists of aiming at ships that appear from the edges of the screen. The story is progressed mainly by following different routes from starbase to starbase.
As far as I could tell, there was no feedback as to exactly how long was in each route. As such, it made each map--especially the earlier routes--drone on, and on, and on. The backgrounds are all black with stars as the cargo ship you're 'protecting' moves from the bottom of the screen to somewhere in the middle of the screen.
For upgrades, you buy resources and collect money through the various routes and space stations, which all offer their own slightly-unique selection of goods. They're nothing special: shields, added blasters, missiles/bombs, but adds just a little bit of customizability to an otherwise uninspired game.
All in all, the game would benefit from a form of timer or distance bar, as well as having more variety during routes/missions.
But, as I see it, the game is too bland to recommend for sh'mup fans.

There are also still a few bugs in the game. Often when the last wave of a level is finished it takes one or two minutes of flying through empty space until the level finally ends. The basic idea of the game is very cool. It makes me sad to see so much wasted potential. This could easily be a really fun game if the developers fix the balancing, add some variety and give the player a reason to use trading. In the current state it's just a textbook example of game design gone wrong.

In it's current form, I would not recommend this game but it definitely looks promising. The issues below are what pushed me away. If they address these, I'd be more than happy to give this game another chance. If the majority of these things won't be a problem for you, then it may be worth checking out.
After having played the game for about two hours and doing two games (which will be explained later), I ultimately felt lost with no direction to go. Outside of general metals, I had no clue where to even get basic materials to build the vast variety of items that you can build. I don't mind large exploration, but as I explored, I didn't encounter new things, just the same stuff I've already harvested.
It also wasn't a good feeling dying immediately before I realized that the tape in my inventory patches up my suit. The UI is a bit overwhelming at first so if there was a message on how to fix the suit, I didn't see it. You're also required to stay hydrated, but on a Mars-like planet where there's no indication of liquid, I'm not sure where to get water. Survival mode is fine, but I think you should be given a direction for basic survival. Show me how to get water, then make the resource difficult to get.
There was also a bug I encountered (I hope its a bug): Mining for resources was very - VERY - picky. Resources appear to be multiple nodes clumped together, but the hitbox to get them to break apart seems ridiculously small. I have to move my cursor along the node, waiting to hit the sweet spot. Otherwise, I'm just aimlessly swinging at it.
Enemy fights were frustrating. If they get up close to you, it's difficult. And if they hit you with a melee attack, it forces your camera to move as your character reacts to the attack. I actually had to start a new game because there were two of them that were at my spawn/camp, so I couldn't easily get my corpse, had no ammo for my assault rifle, and the pistol does nearly no damage to them, especially because it's very difficult to aim at them as they go all over the place. They literally spawn camped me. Let's just say I dreaded fights, wasn't excited for them, even at a low spawn rate.
Finally, the the game didn't run nearly as smoothly as the promo videos show, which made the enemy fights that much more frustrating. This could be my machine's age ... but considering I'm just moving around, mining resources and doing some random fights, that shouldn't very demanding on my system.
---
On the positive side, this game is very pretty and the environment does make you feel like you're on a different planet. The weather effects and how it impacts your visibility with your visor is amazing. When it's dark, it's friggin' dark. The storm effects were pretty as well.
There's a lot of upgrade aspects - everything you do provides some form of experience, so everything improves as you continue to do it. There's personal stat upgrades, and then science/battle/engineering upgrades through a skill tree. So no matter what you do, you're improving your character.
The number of items to build is massive - even overwhelming at first. It's pretty clear they want you to be able to build a massive base with a lot of unique visuals.
It's unfortunate that all this stuff seems difficult to get, as well as the vehicles that will help you navigate more quickly/easily. I would have loved to learn how to get more of this stuff. But the fact that I felt so lost after having spent about two hours on the game, I ultimately just lost interest.
I'll keep an eye out on this game and see if things improved. But if you were to ask me if I should buy the game, I'd suggest waiting. But again, if the items above won't be an issue for you, it may be worth checking out.

Quests are the main form of progression in this game, so you'd think they'd be fun right? Wrong. Go here and pickup this, go there and kill that. That's all the quests ever consist of. Want to get into basebuilding instead? Guess what, the materials only spawn in quest areas.
There are also these "survival" mechanics the devs just threw in to make the game seem more hardcore or something. These are basically just hunger and thirst which don't seem to do anything unless they hit zero. They go down annoyingly quickly unless you upgrade them which is just a waste of xp.
Did I mention that to keep playing the missions, you have to level up? Sounds logical right? Nope. You've got two levels, one is your camp level, another is you character level. To level up you spend your xp on progressing an xp bar to the next level. Bafflingly, the camp and character level are tied together for some reason, so you character level cannot be any greater than your camp level. I'm pretty sure leveling your camp and character don't actually provide any benefits other than giving you access to more quests (if you can call that a benefit). Outside of the quests there isn't really much to do so leveling your character is a top priority if you want some reason to play the game. But xp has actual important uses too. You can upgrade your characters abilities which include doing more damage with certain weapons and using less stamina, or even making the hunger bar go down slower. These are all fun and good, but have fun trying to upgrade them when you've spent all your xp on leveling up your character/camp
There's character customization in this game but I don't even know why they bothered. I think there are maybe 2-3 male models and 1 female. They have maybe 3 hairstyles to choose from and the clothes are basically just variations of the same thing.
Finally there are basically no graphics options to choose from at all. You can choose resolution and shadow quality and that's literally it. No basic AA or even texture quality.

Hopefully this will give some of you hope that have seen some of the reviews of "40 hours and still haven't beaten it" or "Brutal difficulty" a second thought and give this review and more importantly the game a chance. I'd like to start off this review by saying I'm probably classifiied as a casual gamer, but that doesn't make me very good at them. I enjoy playing a large variety of games, but i'm not particularly exceptional at figuring them out and I don't spend a lot of time searching for optimal build paths, best practices etc.
First of all, in my opinion the game is wonderful. It's fun to play, their survival mode makes each round a little bit of a different challenge and with the scaling difficulty you can make it as brutal or forgiving as you like. It has your classic RTS elements of micro and macro management, made more nuanced by a pause function. No 2 rounds are exactly the same terrain or challenge, although many share similiarites (RNG will do that for ya). The design is well fleshed out, with multiple technology tiers available and a relatively easy economic system to figure out and scaling difficulty in monsters on the map and in waves and Mayor bonuses (bonus economic multipliers or free to build buildings at certain population levels) feel neither too important or game breaking in medium and below difficulties. This is by far the best "Early access" game I have played in a very long time.
I'd like to specifically address the difficulty in this section before I finish up my brief review. It is not the easiest thing in the world to figure out, but every single time you lose, to me, was a FUN learning experience and helped you understand what you needed to focus on and do better next time. There was no hand holding tutorial, all of the information is right there in your game information panels. You develop your own little tricks and build paths, and start to understand how everything works the more you play making it more and more rewarding, until you've finally beaten the maps on a difficulty that will allow you to unlock the next "map" type which unlocks a more nuanced and unique challenge. It's an asthetically pleasing game, the art and sound design is satisfying and I really can't wait to see where they take this game next. Definitely worth your money.

God... That was painful...
I did one playthrough, it took me about an hour and twenty minutes, but I'm glad it's over. The writing is terrible, the average fanfic is better written. The characters are introduced with just a few lines of text leaving no time to get to know them (or even just keep their names apart). I toughed it out because everyone says there's these dark themes and all coming later, well, they didn't. I got threatened by a couple of pigeons (why on earth the protagonist didn't just kick them I don't know, who's scared of three pigeons??) and some other bird kicked the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of them, a couple of birds were screaming at eachother and then proposed/accepted mariage... and the bird I had been in most contact with, well, the 'twist' was visible from a mile away.
All the choices you have to make seem completely arbitrary as well. Obviously they will decide which story path you choose, but the choices are do I go to gym or music? Do I get a job or not? There's no deep dialogue where your answers actually matter...
So, it's a gag game right? Well all the reviews say that's what it portrays itself as but there were supposed to be way deeper issues. As I said I didn't find any, but honestly it's not funny either. Jokes don't go deeper than the fact that 'everybody' becomes 'everybirdy' (shoot me now). The story can't be taken seriously either because immersion is constantly broken by things that don't make sense (silly things like a bird having a book under their arm? what arm?)
To clarify, I'm not very experienced with visual novels, but I did play katawa shoujo before this and I should just say, if you're curious about the genre... go download that (it's free, google it). That game has awesome writing and deep emotional storytelling. This reads like a not particularly talented 14 year old girl came up with it. For the life of me I can't imagine why this game gets so many positive reviews.
edit: Just as an addendum... Apparently, this dark sinister plot doesn't actually show itself until you have completed certain story arcs, at which point you get a choice right at the start of the game and you get this 'real' story. The problem I have with that is, if you know exactly what to do, I believe you still have to play the game at least 5 times before you get this story. Considering the fact that I didn't even find the first playthrough enjoyable, are we really expected to subject us to this torture 5 times before it supposedly gets good? No, I'm pretty sure I can say that this game is crap without putting myself through that.
Also, if you do choose to go through it multiple times, keep in mind that the interface is actually kind of crap as well. There is no way to go back to skipped conversation and there is no way to autoskip what you've already read before. From other reviews I see that a scene may start out the same and then veer off halfway through, making it all but impossible to quickly skip through known content without missing anything.

I mainly picked up this game simply because Re-Logic, the makers of Terraria, said they were behind that game. Now come the 1.0 release, I'm able to give my honest opinion after a couple hours in with a lv. 13 captain:
The game is very relaxing. It's got some humor in it and a couple of references in it as well (The ones I noticed are from Pirates of the Carribean), what's worth mentioning here however is that there is an emphasis on pirates taking dumps, more than you might expect at a glance, which to some is funny, others maybe not so much. That said, you might want to spend some of your first gold pieces on a Cleaner skill book.
Another thing to take note of is that the game still does not have much in the way of content: So far I've only seen pirate ships (Without cannons, we'll see how that works out once I get there) and islands. There is little variety in the types of encounters you might see while playing, which does make the gameplay a bit repetitive. Of course, every one of these encounters will be different, with different ship layouts and assortment of enemies, which makes it feel less of a chore. Also there'll be future content patches for this game, which may further add to the experience.
The game also has a fair amount of equipment for customizing your troops, as well as different combat mechanics such as critical hits, bleeding and of course, the drowning of your deckhands should you get swarmed by enemies that attack one character and there is no wall behind you. This causes slight issues because as I was playing through this game I did not manage to have complete control over what enemy my deckmates were attacking, which makes the tactical element of the game a bit harder to execute.
There's plenty of charm in the game as well. Many of your new recruits have "special" abilities that makes them interesting. I had one that made my pirate attack its teammates every once in a while, resulting in him eventually getting killed when vikings boarded my ship. There's plenty more out there and that is something I definitely approve of.
That said, it is an indie game, and for it being an indie game it's definitely not bad. I quite liked spending some hours seeing my Dubstarr & Co. slicing up enemies with his Falcon Blade, and come another day when I fancy some pixellated pirate caretaking, I'll probably look back at my save file and play some more.
Plus for what you pay for it, this game's worth it. Especially now with its launch deal of -50%.

If you want the old fasioned idea of a shooter, where you could run at around 60 mp/h, carry like 10 guns and need first aid kits to heal damage, then look no further than the original Quake. Fast paced, and skillful, Quake really scratches an itch that other shooters might not be hitting. If games like Doom interest you, then this will. However it's not very similar to games like Painkiller, though it may look it at face value. Painkiller and Hard Reset for example have you fighting huge hordes at a time, whereas Quake tend to throw smaller groups are you and concentrates more on navigating a maze. Sometimes the way out of the maze isn't obvious, and you'll be sprinting around trying to find it for a while. If that sounds like your thing then you should pick it up.

-------TL;DR-------     in comments.
My view is that The Bureau: XCOM Declassified was the developers’ way of further expanding the potential player base for the franchise; as such, it is NOT NECESSARILY loyal to what long-time fans of the series might expect – it is an action game meant to intrigue those ignorant of XCOM (such as myself) into trying other installments of the Turn-Based-Strategy series. I grabbed XCOM: Enemy Unknown and DLC in a sale; The Bureau was part of that deal. I played EU/Within first, since I figured The Bureau was a prequel (…does that make sense?). I had downloaded the demo of EU and (kind of) knew what I was getting into; having only recently made the jump from console to PC, I’ve rarely ever really invested time in a strategy game (excepting Civilization V). Enemy Unknown seemed (and definitely is) a game worthy of forsaking others for, albeit being quite infuriating (considering my limited scope in gaming, i.e. shooters, (modern) RPG’s, sandboxes, shooters – I’ve even less exposure to “Random Number Generation”). Enemy Unknown is the first XCOM game I’ve played. I appreciate the over-the-shoulder Action Cam implemented in EU, which appeals to players who might not have played many strategy games before; a way to satisfy those of us who strain to garner pleasure from setting the attacks in motion, without being able to actually control the aggressor during.
The Bureau is the reverse of Enemy Unknown; it is a third-person-shooter that retains (as best as possible) the strategy inherent in the franchise. You control every action of your team: boots on the ground, you engage in firefights with the Outsiders, able to slow the action to a crawwwwl for the purpose of designating commands to your mates, queueing their actions.
The possibility for monotony is relative: I didn’t find the gameplay to be repetitive or dull; on the contrary, strategy must always evolve, as enemies are prone to flank and decimate you. Whether to move is always a calculated risk; to play cautiously is also a risk – it’s not wise to try and hole up in a corner. The action is reminiscent of Mass Effect, but (considering how I remember playing M.E.) maintaining (baby-sitting) your allies in The Bureau is absolutely necessary, as opposed to being able to have some confidence in M.E. that the AI of Jack and Garrus could be commensurate enough. I’m almost certain that the considerable amount of managing your allies that's required in combat is intentional; that is to say, it’s not simply “derpy” AI. In all other XCOM games, Panic is THE factor. Your Squad in The Bureau is not susceptible to Panic, per se, but leaving your Squad to their own devices will amount to leaving them idle; as you are the Leader, they look to you for guidance. Without it, they’ve no plan of action, no source of inspiration from which to divine the will to fight. You must be aware of everything to ensure y’all are an effective team, meaning Order Them Around Constantly. Without exaggeration, I can often find that I’ve spent a third of the total battle time in the slow-motion Tactical Radial, just ensuring my Squad is being utilized as effective as possible.
There are Side Missions that you can pick from the map (of North America, strictly); these are unique, in that I’ve seen no other game utilize them in such a way.
Scenario: Team of scientists was working on a breakthrough in weapon technologies before the Invasion; these assets are under siege; rescue them.
How you go about this: You must send a team of “X” Skill, that is, the combined total of all members’ levels for this Away Team must reach or exceed “X.” Pick your team, send them off, do a mission of your own; upon returning to HQ, your Away Team will have returned, having both leveled and acquired new gear, i.e. Backpack Modifier (dictates Buffs).
This is an ingenious method of utilizing Side Missions. From what I’ve seen, your team can’t fail the mission (a nice break from the harshness that is traditional XCOM). Send your lowest level Squaddies [you can have 2 of each class; From the start, you are given at least one soldier from two of the four classes. As for the other Squad slots, you can customize everything about the soldiers you enlist, from their Background to their Method of Operation (determines Buffs given them)] on these missions so that they won’t drag you down on your own missions; level them in this manner; have some soldiers in reserve for if/when some of your team dies.
There are also Side Missions you can do yourself; they play as regular Story Missions do, though I enjoyed the locales of the Side Missions more and the objectives are more varied (technically) than “Fight to the end.”
For the first half, the story seems standard and bland; without spoiling too much, once you get to the dam, things start picking up rapidly. I exclaimed “Woah” quite a few times after this point, and also a couple times in the first mission.
The main issue I found with The Bureau is the tantalizing but too-inaccessible base. You regroup at XCOM HQ when not skirmishing towards an objective in the field; you have free reign over most major areas of the base; you see more sealed doors than there are rooms through which you can explore. (Regardless of how much more minimal the management system is in EU when compared to previous installments) I was expecting at least as much control over the goings-on of the base in The Bureau as you have in EU. Granted, you are not the Commander/Director, but you ARE the Agent to whom the Director defers, that he uses for all significant operations – I would have figured that you’d have more power to oversee and specify research and whatnot beyond “Push this button to watch the new prototype weapon fire from this rig.”
Despite this qualm, immersion and depth is not nonexistent. Set in the 1960’s, The Bureau is built on the premise of legitimate first (combative) contact, entailing total ignorance of the Outsiders. While making your rounds through HQ, you’ll hear conversations, speculations, proposals and so forth from the base personnel regarding the war and conditions within the base, of Humanity as a whole. You’ll uncover notes and recordings while in the field, detailing the civilian/martial victims’ ultimately fatal encounters with the (")monsters.(") Yes, some of these are tedious to sit through and are uninspired… they exist though.
I’m usually one of the first people to come to the defense of developers, in the sense: “I’m sure they did the best they could; it was no doubt due to whatever constraints befell them that better mechanics or what-have-you were not implemented – I doubt they omitted what could have significantly improved the quality of their game due to sheer evil, ignorance, or laziness.” Granted, I never know anything regarding the actuality in such a case, just as I don’t in this instance;
I would assume that, having plastered the namesake of such a massive and iconic franchise, the first shooter spin-off (that I’m aware of, again, Enemy Unknown was my first foray into XCOM) could have rivaled the scope of Mass Effect itself. Instead, it’s a better-than-decent, less-than-stellar tactical shooter. Perhaps they opted to not actually compete with Mass Effect, as it were; don't build up what you might falter in delivering?

Story: 9/10
Great start, Great twist, Great choice in endings. Not going to go too much into this because it would require spoilers. Let's just say the beginning is REALLY important to remember throughout the entire game. It's where the great twist towards the end started planting itself.
Gameplay: 8/10
A better experience than mass effect. Uses the same sort of control ( keyboard mouse/gamepad ) set up as Mass Effect franchise but it's more responsive and more action packed. Running is actually useful and you can do tight turns while running without the clunky stop and move turning mass effect had/s. Cover is useful here and needed. If you're not in cover you're dead, this isn't a run and gun. You NEED to tell your squad what to do. Management of your squad is your duty. This isn't made easy for you by having overpowered teammates.
Flanking enemy entrenchments and positions is key to winning. Falling back and moving is the only way to survive being pinned down. If you've played XCOM: Enemy Unknown you'll be familiar with the systems in play here. I will say it is dumbed down at the beginning but the Infiltrator boss fight is when the game shows it's real design. Enemies do NOT run at you like idiots they take cover and try to get you to reveal yourself by dropping grenades and setting up flanking maneuvers. As you progress enemies get more aggressive, the shielded enemies have a tendancy of flanking your team and trying to strike from vantage points. Enemies with higher health are more likely to push and attack aggressively, while enemies with lower health pools tend to hang back in cover while pressuring flanks.
Glitches: Not really a problem.
I've seen a bunch of posts about this game being glitchy and in truth, I saw almost no glitches. I had 3 things happen that didn't really break the game. To fix them I just simply picked the "reload checkpoint" option in the pause menu.
1. There was a sound glitch where sounds were sort of cut off as they were fading out. making it sound like there was a stutter in dialog or just simply dialog, music, or battle sounds being cut prematurely. reload checkpoint fixed this.
2. Squad member got stuck inside of something while reviving. During a mission a squad member was stuck in a bookcase when he went to try to revive a squaddie and even though I was down a team member it didn't make a difference I still finished the fight and he immediately became "unstuck" and teleported out of the glitch on his own.
3. This one didn't cause me trouble but I did have to "load a save" that was a couple of minutes behind my progress. I just lost about 3 minutes of progress and it wasn't even in a firefight but right before a boss fight. These gates are supposed to close and the way into the fight arena is supposed to be closed off. Well I spawned in a checkpointed save INSIDE the rubble. There's AMPLE checkpoints in the game and I never found myself "redo'ing" an entire fight.
Sound(track): 8/10
There's not really much to say about it, everything fits, from the 1960's music in the quiet streets of an overrun town to the creepy alien noises and loud bangs everything fits. The guns later in the game sound really good. Crisp reloading sounds let you know what gun you're using. Every gun's reload sound is different, some pop, some crackle, some wind up. You'll know when a squad mate is pinned down and can't attack, they're constantly telling you about their situation ( I'm pinned down! Need healing! I'm about to go down commander! We're being flanked! ) or asking for orders. They'll also yell out what they're using so you always know what's on cooldown ( Turret out! Cloaking! )
Length: 5/10
Unfortunately, this is where I am a bit disappointed. The game isn't that long to be honest. My first playthrough trying to do everything possible without outside help of any sort ( walkthrough, videos, wiki ) clocked in at 17 hours of gameplay. I didn't get ALL the base investigations but I'm pretty sure I got most of them, if anything I probably missed out on 1 or 2 at most adding something in the 15 to 20 minute range. This is the only thing that's disappointing about this game. Although all missions felt handcrafted and well made some weren't longer than 10 minutes ( side missions ) some more would have been nice.
Closing this out, Yes I recommend it. The campaign was a blast with really awesome moments. Everything felt handcrafted not just another generic "this is where you fight, this is where you walk" sort of campaign. It was refreshing to play a game with such a different look at the genre. This game felt... Special. It's the only way I can describe it. The addition of the squad management was really a nice touch. Giving out the commands on what to attack and what skills to use made me feel useful in the game and didn't make me feel like I was along for the ride.
All engagements were engaging and I had to participate in the positioning of my squad which made me think more about my next step instead of mindlessly shooting at enemies that were running at me.

Part 1: Monster flees, eating everything it can whilst avoiding detection from hunters because it is far too weak.
Part 2: Monster eats enough to grow into a big boy, powerful enough to pulverize anything in its path.
Part 3: Humans put up a meager fight that lasts mere seconds, dying one-by-one to the monster.
This is how all of your games will go in Evolve, I guarantee it. You either catch the monster in the first minute of the game, killing him instantly, or you fail to catch the monster (most likely because he/she is playing as the Gorgon or Wraith) and die to it instantly when it obtains stage 2 or stage 3.
There are a few things very wrong with this game, the first being that it is very linear, forcing you into one "track" so to speak, playing the same way as hunter/monster everytime in order to achieve victory. If you play for a few hours, you eventually will get tired of doing what is essentially the same thing again and again.
The second big problem is balancing. The monster can only be killed at stage 1, and, with effort, stage 2. At stage 3, it is possible to kill the monster, but, with the monsters enhanced powers, it is nearly impossible. One would think that the hunters are at least capable of capturing and killing the monster at stage 1. That is not true. Of course, I should note that new/unexperienced players will be captured and killed easily at stage 1, as they are unknowing about how to play. However, a player with at least a grasp with what he or she is doing will never be caught by the humans at stage 1/2, as the traversal skills for each monster have far too quick of a cooldown to even be able to keep up with. The monsters can run circles around you without you being able to catch them, for they are just too mobile.
The third issue I have is the problem with disconnecting. It has happened far too often that people do not get their preferred role in the matchmaking. To alleviate this, they simply disconnect and just search for another match. This leaves the players who were beginning the game either without a player, or having to search for more players in order to play the game. I feel that there should be punishment for leaving games, as it is not fair to anyone that people leave without punishment to get their way, when you've been waiting patiently to get yours. I should not be punished because I was randomly selected to get the class I want, and someone else didn't.
The least I can say is that it is free-to-play. That is a very honorable thing that Turtle Rock Studios did. You don't see games tagged as "free-to-play" ever being completely free. This, however, is. I have a deep respect for this game and its developers for that reason.

The Bureau: XCOM Declassified is a 3rd person squad based tactical RPG running on a linear storyline. Although it is squad-based, your companions are random generated AI with customisable faces, class, voices etc.
The storyline was extremely dull, dialogue very poor and gameplay elements weren't anything you haven't seen before in other games.
The game also suffers from a few very annoying bugs such as falling out of the world, several crash issues and poor FPS.

If you have money to splash then by all means, go for it but don't be surprised if it wasn't as good as you thought it would be because it really was a boring game.

Subsurface Circular is fundamentally a text-based story game where you play as a robot detective, and the graphics, dialog, and premise itself build an awesome environment for those text conversations to take place in. It is not a long game (~2 hours plus a bit more cleaning up achievements), but it is a good one. I had massive expectations for the game as it is from the same team as the gem Thomas Was Alone, perhaps unrealistically high, so while I was a little let down by the fact that I wasn't sucked into the game, I did really enjoy it in the end. There are 2 (I don't think there's any other than 2) puzzles in the game which are suprising difficult for being seemingly a very small part of the game, but there is a built-in aid to solve them which does help, and they should be solvable by pretty much any player.
Gameplay takes place as text-based conversations with other robots on a train where your dialoge is choosen from a set of options you're given each time it is your turn to speak. You talk to a variety of robots from a variety of occupations, and the game does a great job painting a world and making each conversation seem unique. The game takes place as a 3D render of the robots as they sit on, enter, and exit the train which makes the game feel much more full than if it were simply the text. The rendering is nice and the intro scene is really neat. The music that plays is choosen well, but is mostly background. The story is interesting (as you would hope from a story-driven detective game), but not overwhelmingly so, and up until the end I would have had few qualms about getting up and taking a break if I had needed too, contrary to a game like OneShot that keeps you wanting to play more and more in the same sitting.
In terms of achievements, most are tied to progression and will be awarded in a single playthrough, and the others can be gotten in a few minutes by going back and replaying specific parts of specific scenes (you can choose to replay specific portions of the game once you've beaten it). A few may not be immidiately obvious as to how they are earned, but there are discussions on the game's Steam forum to help you figure it out.
I guess the purpose of reviews is to help you answer the question: Should I buy this game? And I think the answer in this case is, yes, you should play through this game. However if you aren't super intrigued by the game's style, perhaps you should wait for a sale as it is on the short side, so the price may be a tad steep in some people's eyes.
A Note (Mild Spoiler): After playing through this game I played back through Thomas Was Alone, and I really like how this game made subtle references to it. A twin-stick vertical shooter-- what a novel idea! Unfortunately it is wasted on the most boring, repetitive arcade game ever made.
While I like the intuitive concept of non-linear mission selection, equipment stores and resource trading, any pilot worth his salt will have enough to purchase the best ship, and the best equipment, after just a few missions, rendering the entire in-game economy completely worthless. Once you buy the best shield, you never lose it-- even if it is fried during battle it will be back again for your next flight.
The game's array of drones, bombs and missiles are totally superfluous, except to hasten the destruction of enemy waves, since nearly everything is destructible in seconds with the standard blaster. If you destroy enemies too quickly, you effectively throw off the game's scripting and have to twiddle your thumbs for upwards of a MINUTE until the mission catches up and starts throwing enemies at you again. GOD.
Speaking of missions, there are 40 story-based "levels" in all, but they are all the same. You just battle the same dozen enemies in the same dozen attack patterns against the same boring starscape backdrop over, and over, and over, and over again, with the occasional invincible boss encounter, until you "beat" the game. The story is boring and involves nothing more than political espionage; the true motives of the titular Zotrix that you mass-murder throughout is never extrapolated upon. it never rises above title-card after title-card of he did this, she said that, go here, now go there. Nothing INTERESTING happens.
This game took me 30 hours to beat over three months because I could only handle one or two missions at a time before succumbing to sheer bordom. Half of that time was spent completing more tedious "side" missions to access story-oriented routes. The game justifies these detours through your accrument of resources, which, as I already mentioned, are useless after the first half hour. There is little challenge to combat once you learn to master "diving" to avoid collisions. Every level trickle-feeds you the same two weapon-upgrades, and nothing else.
I hate to rag on Zotrix because it is technically sound and feels like the outline of a much better game... unfortunately, it is not that game nor will it ever be.

The Are Billions has some good qualities, and its biggest problem isn't its flaws so much as that it is highly repeditive which each game being predicatable and pretty much the exact same thing.
One of the major flaws is that the most important thing in the game is the random world created.  If it is a good random world with a good start location, you will do well.  If it isn't, you will do poorly.
Basically, the entire "strategy" for the game comes down to restarting until you get a good start location.  A location with wood, stone, iron, and farmland next to the base and in such a way that there is also a large area of additional open space for living quarters.  To win, you need to build a market and a bank surrounded by housing.  Then have a few clusters of stone, iron, oil, wood and open farmland together so you can build several in range of a warehouse.  The warehouse, the bank, and the market all cost a set amount and make the right buildings close to them work better.  If you are able to get enough of them in a small area you can get the bonuses and thus have a good economy.  This is necessary because every building has an ongoing cost and benefit and they are carefully balanced so that everything depends on being lucky to have a good location where everything is right -- PURE LUCK.  Then, you build your defenses.
Then comes the next huge downside.  The game is completly about stay alive for a short time.  Even at the longest setting, that is 150 days of game time.  Then, it ends.
The game also works to require basically that you follow an almost exact build order every game.  You build the same basic buildings.  Then rearch upgrades, and build those, then research, then build.  As such, every game is almost exactly the same.  Build up.  Win or lose.  Start again.  You can't play after you win.
There are is no real variability.  First, you build a couple tents, a hunting or fishing building for food, a building to gather wood, and then a quary to mine stone and a reasearch building.  You research, and then upgrade everything you already built and buy another reasearch building. Basically, then you reapeat the process.  Meanwhile you build walls around your town with towers, and upgrade.   That's it.  Expand, build the same few buildings or their upgraded form, defend. Wait.
A few small attacks will kill you if you didn't build walls.  Then there is a big attack and you win or lose and the game ends.
I cannot stress enough how little strategy is involved.  The game completely depends on what world is randomly generated.  If you start win a world with nice, big open spaces and the resources you need close, you will do well.  If you start and there are not big open spaces, you can't cluster the buildings together enough to benefit from the bonuses of the Warehouses, Banks, and Markets, and will lose.
Every building has an ongoing cost.  So if you don't have the right geography, the math is against you.  Every productive building requires workers and energy.  Workers require food, and energy requires a building that costs resources every turn.  Homes for workers require energy.  The buildings that make energy require workers (and some require food and stone also every day).  Buildings to make wood, and other resources require energy and workers.  Everything requires defense which requires workers and resources and costs money each turn.  If you can't group buidings together and take advantage of bonuses, you can't afford decent defense.  If you do get a nice open area, you can build your defenses in a circle or square and fill it with stuff in the center that produces what you need.  If you are stuck with a lot of mountain or forrest or water in the area you have to defend, it wastes space and so you have to defend area that proivdes you wih nothing, something you can't afford.
There is no variety.  Basically there are a few resources and the buildings for them upgrade and you need to get them all.  This isn't a game where you can pick a strategy, and there is no varrability at all in what you need to survive.
There is no chance to build a civilization as the game ends so qukickly.  The maps are small.  The AI isn't to smart.  It really comes down to every game being playing for a set number of days and then getting  big attack and there isn't really any difference if you win or lose.  Just one little screen saying you won or lost.  It is boring and you never get a feeling of it mattering.  I mean, so what if you survive 80 or 150 days or whatever?  You still have the game end.
Big dissapointment.  I strongly suggest not buying the game unless they give it away free or maybe if you are personally friends with someone involved in creating it or something.

As of writing this review paradox hasn't butchered this game to death with Dlc. So for right now this is a definite buy. The combat system in this game is phenomenal and excels past that at times. While lacking the subtleties of diplomacy that paradox games have done so well with in the past diplomatic actions are certainly present. What this game lacks in diplomacy it more then makes up for in the combat and warfare mechanics. Customizable unit templates offer constant new angles for experienced players to consider. In addition there are just enough different unit types to make the combat between individual units satisfying and fun. In addition the only flaw with the combat are some occasional glitches with the frontline mechanics. This however is not nearly enough to make the combat poor just enough to be a nuisance at times. The factions system is another good feature in theory. However this leads to my one major problem with the warfare. The lack of an effective separate peace mechanics make peace after war is over a drag. In addition if you are a minor power you can feel cheated when the major countries in your faction surrender and you are suck on the tail end of a peace deal without even fighting for yourself. Also it's very annoying for the attacker who may have focused on army production in order to take their home continent to find themselves stuck at war for years while they build up a navy. Altogether the combat itself is great but there's almost not enough of it at times. All together an extremely solid game with a phenomenal combat system and solid base mechanics 7/10

If you like taking out strongholds in Far cry games then you will love this game, because thats basically all you will do in this game over and over again.

The dialog between the team can be quiet humerous and interesting for such generic characters with little to no backstory at all which i liked.
Playing Solo can be fun but playing coop is were it is at, planning out how to take down a base in combat or by stealth is very enjoyable and its when this plans fail and you have the fight your way out is where this game really shines.

And that is another thing i like about this game , you can do almost every boss in any order when ever you want , its open ended. Killing a boss will give you a unique weapon which can be interesting but i never really found myself changing guns in this game at all.
The gun mechanics in this game are amazing and the hud is so so good, you have the option to change rate of fire, swap to a sholder view while shooting, adjust your scope and even a grenade launcher which is ridiculously op for taking down cars and choppers.   My favorite loadout was the starting machine gun with a silencer and a double optic scope that allowed me to adjust for medium to short range mid combat easily.
Overal this game also looks amazing , in the right side of the map especially in the jungles and swamp areas, this game has such a realism to it that makes even just driving around fun, and basically 90% of this game is you driving to missions which can be very annoying given you can clear most outposts in under a minute with a full squad.
