Whoo-wee, Osiris: New Dawn, a huge ball of good potential. Out of all of the ten hours i've spent playing this game, i've enjoyed nine of them. Keep in mind this game is still in early access, so this is mainly a critique as compared to a full on review.
The Stuff.
1: A fairly well thought out crafting and survival system. The only fluke in the survival is fixing your suit....with duct tape. Just, what? I mean, duct tape can fix everything but pregnancy, sure, but a space suit should be the exception of what it can't fix.
2: The mobs are way to damn aggressive, and can see a hell of a lot better than i can, as well as farther. I mean sure, you could call it realism 'n' such. Alien world with different species, sure they can see better. But, they literally pop out of the ground or out of thin air to attack. Popping out of the ground with the skeliopod monsters makes sense in a way, but the crab monsters? The shouldn't just be able to do that, they should have spawn points where they crawl out of the ground, and that you can plug to prevent them from spawning next to you (30 meter radius) when you're in your base. The skeliopods should have some kind of a hive system in the caves, kill a hive in a certain area, it's safe from them spawning.
3: The damned weather is annoying as hell, changes to often, and sorta makes sense because of that. The one thing that really bugs me yet again is how well i can't see as compared to the mobs. They are affcted in no way at all sight wise by the sand/dust storms, simply because the storms are PNG files with you centered, if you fall faster than the storm, you can see it trying to catch up with you. I mean, if you're just gonna kinda lazily do the weather like that, just don't do it until you have a better, and less annoying system.
4: There is no tutorial in this game. At all. It tells you to go and collect some stuff, and basically just says "Good luck bucko, that's all ya know!". I spent a good part of my first hour wondering what in the hell im supposed to be doing, before getting hit my a meteor and dying.
5: As an almost final point for the stuff list here, the respawning system is an utter pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ With the high aggressiveness of the mobs around you, the fact you respawn with no weapons what so ever, makes it so much more annoying to die. If you dont have a base of operations set up, or are trying to play with your freind whos about five clicks north of you, if you die, you have no weapons anymore. Kaput sir. And good luck spawning anywhere close to your corpse to get your weapons. If you respawned with even just the little pistol they give you, would be amazing.
6: And as a last thought kind of thing, resources. Your initial spawn point in the world seems to be utterly random, which can be good, and horrid at the same time. Resources are sometimes impossible to find, even when scouring the entire map for a single resource. Carbon in particular took about 8 hours to find just a few small deposits. But i load into a multiplayer later with a friend, carbon abundant, but no magnesium. There really needs to be more of a balance with how things spawn, and a minimum limit in specific "zones" on the entire small map.
So i would honestly reccommend buying this game to support the devs, as they seem to be taking great lengths to make this game look and feel great. I also understand that this game is in early access and i beleive in alpha if i remember correctly. I'm just hoping that this game doesn't turn out to be like The Forest, which is prepetually in alpha, or Rust, which was abandoned by the devs.
And to the devs if you ever read this: Please, keep up the good work.

On paper, this would be one of my favorite games. I love top-down arcade shooters, and resource trading/management, and upgrade loops. Zotrix has all of these things, and it does them all in a very mediocre way.
The shooting, where you'll spend most of your time, is incredibly boring and easy. Enemies will slowly march onto the screen, single file, where you will immediately wipe them all out by firing in a straight line - even without any upgrades. As the game grows in difficulty (at a glacier pace), occasionally two lines of enemies will come out simultaneously, which means you might miss a few, so you'll get fewer credits at the end of the level.
You're never really in danger, and you easily become disinterested. This is not how you should feel when you're alone in space against thousands of aliens.
Resource trading is also devoid of complexity or meaningful choices. Different stations sell different resources at different prices - but you can preview the price of any resource of every station before making the trip, meaning that there is no decision making, no research, and no risk at all. You can expect a small (5-10%) profit every single time you make a jump. This adds absolutely nothing to the game.
Upgrades are weird and usually trivial. It's hard to know what things do or why you'd need them. Nothing that I found changes the game at all; it's simply bigger numbers (more damage to a primary blaster cannon, etc).
On top of all this, you'll find numerous quality-of-life annoyances throughout the entire game. There's no Sell All button in the resource trading, so you have to type in all the numbers by hand (also, no numpad support). Sound effects for shooting are obnoxiously loud, completely obscuring the music. English is likely not the developer's first language - you'll see numerous grammatical oddities. Et cetera.
Zotrix is an unpolished, uninteresting game that does not even come close to its potential. Avoid.

The Mole, the Mob, & the Meatball, the third episode of Sam & Max Season 1 starts up with the duo creating an activity with a deck of cards in their not as always calm neighborhood. Sybil is now a professional trial witness and regards it to be her ideal job, while Bosco has switched from a British disguise to a Frenchman disguise believeing that he is targeted by the mafia. Sam & Max receive a phone call from the commissioner on a new case. Their mission is to locate a mole who hasn't reported back to the police after he infiltrated the Toy Mafia's turf. The only lead Sam & Max have is the base of operations for the Toy Mafia which is "Ted E. Bear's Mafia Free Playland & Casino" the place that the mole may be held against his will, incognito with the mafia, or is dead. Upon their arrival to the swanky establishment, they realize that all of the employees wear striped suits, fedoras, and all pack their own guns despite the place is advertised as "mafia free". What's more the employees are all wearing a meant-to-be-cute-yet-just-a-little-silly bear head masks. The masks are the same design as the bear toy that hypnotised Myra Stump. Which implies that the Toy Mafia is behind the hypnotism business that Sam & Max have been encountering lately. From this point the duo must try to figure out where the mole by snooping around the casino and try to gain an audience from Don Ted E. Bear himself. This episode was fun to play like the previous two episodes. The casino was filled with great moments, the high light would be the password sequence and Max remarking the card player Leonard Steakcharmer resembling Boris Krinkle from Telltale's Poker game. Another good nod to Telltale's earlier works. Overrall, I'd rank this in my top 10 favorite episodes of the three seasons of Sam & Max.

The third episode of the season feels helplessly short, but the interesting tasks and the sheer absurdity of trying to find a mole within an Italian mafia family wearing oversized bear masks easily entertains us throughout those 90 or so minutes.
The Freelance Police finally do something other than pestering former television stars in this episode; our duo has to do actual police work when their new job pits them against the insidious Toy Mafia.
As expected form an episodic TellTale series, we get plenty of returning elements, like Sybil’s new job, Bosco’s fresh “invention” for a ridiculous price, and three mandatory independent jobs to reach our final goal, the mole put inside the Toy Mafia. Although we can see the TellTale formula peeking around the corner, the puzzles are clever enough to hide it; whether we need to win at cards, stage a death (or two) or bypass the latest Bosco-Tech security, we can bet that the solution will involve some really crazy and funny task.
The only problem is that despite the abundance of humour, the episode feels criminally short; unless you get stuck on some of the more exotic solutions, you can complete the whole thing under two hours.

I remember seeing ads for Test Drive Unlimited 2 back before it was released and being absolutely floored with the freedom and graphical fidelity promised. Several years later I had all but forgotten it’s existence when suddenly it popped up in the steam winter sale. What perfect timing! I was itching for a good open world driving game and along comes one that I had wanted so badly on sale for just a few bucks.
Well 10 hours later my itch is gone, but TDU2 makes a terrible scratcher. I’m not sure if I would have been as disappointed had I picked up the game in its prime, but with the multiplayer non-existent and the game itself being an absolute nightmare to install and get running due to the servers being neglected for the past 3 or 4 years, there is little left to be loved about this game. It’s really cool to see all the car brands licensed and buying houses to decorate definitely appeals to the Sims lover in me, but finding the dealers is a pain and the game world is unfathomably massive. It’s fun to drive and the cars handle well, but the amount of mundane driving about you end up doing causes your eyes to glaze over. By the 8th or 9th hour of play I found myself watching Netflix while I systematically scour a city for a particular dealer or make my way across the world to a different race. At that point I realized it just wasn't that fun and I uninstalled it.

I can't recommend this game for most people.

It's not entriely acracde, nor simulation. This game really dumbs down, well, everything. The acting, animations and premises are stiff, emotionless and basically only serve to illustrate why this game failed so miserablely on release. It's the age-old, tried to do so many things, that it can't do anything well. It's pretty, as long as you don't look to hard, and it's fun if you're not expecting much. There's a lot that is just frustrating. Somehow, I've managed to log a couple hundred hours on this game despite all it's faults. Probably for lack of a suitable alternative.

Somewhat pretty, if dated.
The Bad:
Online play sucks, when it works, populated by tools.
Console-audience focused development is obvious.
Single-player racing, while passable, is pretty uninspired.
Some of the vehicle dynamics, like the consideration of torque curve vs horsepower curve or lack of adjustability in cars that have it from the factory, much less would get it as soon as you started swapping parts.
The Ugly:
All the non driving-related fluff.
Poor tuning and performance options.
Overall lack of diversity in traffic, there will be the same density of cars on dead-ends as freeways, day or night, rain or shine.
Nagging NPCs, GPS and feature commentary.
Some notable marquees are absent, while you can't help notice others.

Played this game for months, and the game is pretty fun for a standard fantasy MMO. The graphics are beautiful on a good machine. The classes are vary multi purpose like a cleric can be a healer or switch to a damage dealer build when needed. Or a rouge can be a ranged damage dealer or a dagger swinging tanker the next. It does have a story being something like a religious war, but one can just go close down rifts, fight off invasion events, or participate in raid dungeons to level up. The game is pretty much designed to be a serious PvP game. There's a server or shard dedicated to open world PvP, and all shards have toggleable PvP status. PvP can happen anywhere in the game being open world. But this is only if you ether enter the PvP shard or flag yourself for it. PvP doesn't feel like the main focus here. The races to play as are interesting. Sure the Dwarf women don't have beards, but oh well head cannon Vs creativity I guess. The community is fantastic enough with only the occasional troll.
It does have some minor drawbacks. The ingame store can get a bit expensive and even sell things that one can get for ingame currency eventually. It has a nice leveling down system called mentoring where one can down level there character for low level areas. But some won't or forget to do this when they are in these areas, and can end an invasion event too soon and other typical ingame trolling behavior. Sometimes a stealth rouge from an opposite faction would sneak to the capital city and kill the auctioneer for the auction house preventing other players to their business there. Not much to do there but go to another shard or log for a time and hope he/she's not around then. But trolling and spamming is vary light for a ftp game.
It gets basic for an MMO, but its hardly a boring MMO too. Its pretty balanced, and that can be good enough for casual entertainment.

Mission objective, free the rebel prisoners. Landed helicopter close enough to recon the mission objective area to find out that it has a surprisingly solid setup. A massive bowl shaped canyon surrounded on all sides by huge cliff walls. Only one narrow, well-guarded way in. Deploy drone. Crap. Drone jammer. Judging by the red blobs everywhere on the mini map, this was going to be tough without any intel on enemy positions. I dig my binoculars out of my pack and peer down into the canyon the old-fashioned way. I spot combatants everywhere. The canyon walls have multi floored walkways build on to them with prison cells hollowed out in the walls. Four floors high. Must be hundreds of cells. Guards everywhere. Snipers. Alarms. Panel and spot lights. Going to make it difficult even if I wait till night. I spot the generator... with no lights near it. There’s my in. I'll wait till night, parachute in near the generator and shut it down to kill the lights. Without the lights I can just sneak around, silently drop a guard or two and take my time opening cell doors and let the rebels out to occupy the guards.
I run around and knock out a few supply missions while I wait till night, jump in my chopper and pass directly over the canyon… bail out and carefully aim my chute near the dark spot close to the generator. I’m off a little and quickly go prone, holding my breath and hoping no one saw me. Seconds eek by but feel like an eternity. No alarms. Just as I exhale.. my chopper crashes somewhere nearby and explodes. Crap. I didn’t think about that. Red dots flash everywhere as guards go into high alert. I shoot out some lights and take out three guards that have drawn a bead on me with my MP5. My only hope is to make it to the generator to shut off all the lights and alarms. I shoot out a light panel illuminating the path between me and the generator  and make a run for it. The ground erupts around me in gunfire. I shoot out the lock and dive to the switch to kill the power and go prone behind a concrete barrier surrounding the generator. All the lights die. Also… all the cell doors open. They were rigged to the power system, apparently. Didn’t expect that.
Green dots appear on the mini map EVERYWHERE. Sweet. The rebels are free. Gunfire erupts all over. All hell breaks loose. As many guards as there are, there are a lot more rebels now. I watch as the red dots wink out. I pop up and take out a few myself.
A few minutes later, my mission is accomplished and I’m feeling awesome. Not my usual silent, in-and-out without ever being spotted method and it hurt my stealth profile score a bit, but it worked. And it was epic.

It is games like this that make me wish STEAM had a "Neutral" button instead of a strict "Recommend/Don't Recommend" button. I have mixed feelings about this game, allow me to break it down like this:
The Good:
> Interesting story with an intriquing plot twist.
> Enjoyable 1950's era environment.
> Nice variety of weapons and equipment ("backpacks") to enable most any playstyle.
> Graphics are decent, the game is built on the Unreal engine, its not current big budget graphics but I don't mind them.
The Not-So-Good:
> They tried too hard to make a tactical squad based third person shooter with cover mechanics that feels very clunky. The cover mechanic requires you to sprint at a wall and basically super-glue yourself to it. This system doesn't seem to want to let you "leave" said wall if say, a grenade is thrown at you, which happens A LOT.
> The story itself is rather short, you can power through it without any trouble in a couple hours.
If you are looking for a tie-in game for XCOM: Enemy Unkown, this is NOT it. This game has little-to-no relation to Enemy Unkown and contains none of the base management mechanics that Enemy Unkown has.
So, in short, this game is worth a look if you get it on sale or as part of a Humble Bundle, but I just cannot recommend buying it at full price. I would put it in the $15 game bracket. Its better than bargain bin game quality but should not command a higher price than around $15.

You play this game as "Agent Carter", whom is tasked with the responsibility of trying to save the human race from a new global threat. The game takes place in the 1960's making the aesthetics and technology seen in this game very engaging and interesting.

I don't want to spoil anything about the story, basically you play as "Agent Carter", you're a member of a top secret organization that was originally intended to fight against the Soviet Union in the 1960's but a new threat reveals itself and you've been called to save the whole human race.
while the story sounds pretty sterio-typical "save the humans, because you're a freaking super hero!" there were some very interesting twists and turns in the story, I highly recommend at least one play through on the easiest difficulty to at least see how the story unwinds.
As has been the theme, I started playing this game the wrong way. This game is more like a "turn based FPS", because you go into "strategy mode" which puts everyone in slow motion, and you give orders to your agents to do various attacks.
This is the first Xcom game I've played, but I've been told the games tend to be very strategy oriented, ergo this is actually a black sheep of the Xcom family. As far as black sheep go... I found myself enjoying the story. I've been trying to finish the hardest difficulty which has opened a whole new world of hurt, but that's not important right now.
The game is put in a 3rd person shooter perspective, but you will need to rely on your NPC allies, by giving them orders... flanking, upgrading technology, and various other things to take into consideration. The game is far more challenging than one might initially let on.

Basic achievement categories: Beat the game, Do this new thing ___ amount of times, Beat the game on the hardest difficulty, do this thing differently, buy our DLC to get 100% on your achievements.
Yes, this game requires you to buy the DLC, which as always, is very disappointing to see. but maybe someday I'll return to this game to get the DLC. But at this point I intend to try the hardest difficulty, if I can't beat it I'll call it good and pack it away and move on to another game, but I digress.
The Bureau: XCOM Declassified is $19.99 I've spent 19 hours playing this game (10/11/14), I will probably put in about 5-6 more hours to beat the game again on the hardest difficulty (if I can make it), this game is worth its value, in my opinion. I got the game in a humble bundle, which I would recommend to anyone wanting to buy it, or at least wait for a steam sale of 50% or better.

This game seems to be best played by someone who likes a mix of shooter and strategy. I found the game interesting and fun to play, but as I've said, to many who have played other Xcom games this is a black sheep.
I recommend this game to someone who is looking to play a different styled shooter game. You could play through the game using your own shooting ability on the easiest difficulty if you wanted, the story itself will take only about 7-12 hours.

I started off playing survivor type games with No Man's Sky, a game I actually sunk dozens of hours into playing, and thoroughly enjoy. I love space games and I believed that No Man's Sky would be the one I would lose all of my free time on. I had some complaints yes, but it was a relaxing playthrough and I just had a lot of fun mining, building, exploring and killing pirates. With that being said Osiris: New Dawn...is NOT relaxing. You start the game off creating your character, such as it is, setting up your world with minor play style options like, "how many death monsters do you want? Infested? OKAY you want death!" and then you are flung onto a barren wasteland of a planet...did I mention you have a suit breach? As you scramble to find the patch tape to repair your suit (after figuring out what can help you)  watching your o2 levels drop alarmingly, and making sure you aren't going to die immediately  you notice pieces of your escape pod are scattered throughout your "landing" area. You use your chisel and bop those pieces into resources you can use. Then you take a look around and notice how absolutely beautiful of a place this planet looks. And then you hear music...heart-pounding, epic adrenaline inducing music that gets you fired up! You look around but you see nothing...Again you see nothing but you hear it. A soul shattering shriek and then your HUD turns red as you see a carapace leg shoot out from behind you to the left..And your suit is breached again. As you scramble to equip your weapon, all the while running in frantic directions trying to get away from the horror. You then bring up your assault rifle...or depending on how freaked out you are, your pistol, and turn around and blind-fire at the "thing" chasing you...Except it is not just ONE thing it's three. One spider-like bug called a young crab monster, and two centipede face hugger looking snake dealios called Skeliopods...So you then fire at them all at once and hit nothing as they all charge you and dodge you. After a long battle of hit and run you end up 1.5km away from where you were with no ammo and three dead bugs sinking into the ground...You then see the words "Ezekiel  Crater" fade on and off the screen. You have a minute to catch your breath until you hear a sound from your worst nightmares. A roar and then a crack and you see dust fly into the air from across the crater. Maybe the sun is in your eyes because a creature cannot possibly be that large, and it can't possibly be out to get little ol' you right? As the sky darkens around you you come to your senses and snap out of your dazed amazement and try to run out of the shadow. But then a video plays as a giant freaking sandworm with a huge mouth surrounds you and plummets back into the ground it's long body seemingly taking an eternity to disappear. Taking your life with you. Then the words "you have died, would you like to try again?" come up as if laughing at you. "I don't know do I?"
Yes. Yes I do.
♥♥♥♥ that was amazing. And that was MY experience in the first five or so minutes. I spent the rest of the 3-4 hours learning how to play the game, carefully mining stuff to build things...finding my bodies scattered throughout the map to revover my inventory, and cowering in my flimsy inflatable pod at night...Night time is for the birds y'all.
All in all I had an amazing time playing this game, and as I watched a few youtubers have different experiences and remembered going through some similar hardships, I felt liek I have never felt in a game liek this before.
Genuine excitement.
This game is something I didn't know that I wanted. It is fun, scary, relaxing (when you aren't being attacked) intricate, mezmerizing, and frustrating all at the same time. I also would suggest that they add the ability to change weapons when jumping. As well as make strafing faster.
One other thing is to make resources more abundant. Yes it is a barren world but going 900meters to find carbon fighting aliens and getting stuck in storms ALL WHILE ON FOOT kind of sucks haha. But I guess that's part of the charm. It is really well polished. I hope they get more crafting options in there too, and maybe add the ability to move your colony elsewhere when you get the bigger vehicles. I won't spoil much more of it but basically for an unfinished game, it is more finished than most games of it's like. I do hear they plan on adding a tn of more things, more planets, alien races and a story! So Be on the lookout for Fenix Fire and Osiris: New Dawn in the future! Episode 3 of Sam & Max Season 1 is a brilliant point and click adventure from Telltale Games.
It is 3 times as good as the previous two episodes in my opinion. It is a familiar concept to fans of the series, you follow the detective dog and his sociopathic rabbit buddy on their absurd cases. This time they are to infiltrate the 'Toy Mafia', a group of mobsters that produce hypnotic toy bears. It dosen't often feel like you are just wondering and wasting time (unless you are searching for clues), you always have a goal to get to by using different items. Due to the constant objectives, the game feels very fluid in its pacing. The graphics are certainly dated, but in a 10 year old point and click the graphical fidelity should not be one of your highest concerns. It does however have some offputting resolution selections, the highest setting being 1600x800 (this can easily be fixed by dowloading and using the 'Tell Tale Games Custom Resolution Tool', just look it up on Google).
The humour is on point, the back and forth between Sam and Max in different situations is sure to make the game more enjoyable. The puzzles are satisfying when finished and are completable without a walkthrough (the same can't be said for Episode 1+2, in my situation at least). The episode was short and sweet (I completed it in 1hour 40mins) making it a suitable game to play one afternoon. The ending felt a little rushed and ended on an odd note but seeing as there is another episode it is hardly an issue.
I would highly reccomend this to anybody who wants to try out point and clicks and is a fan of quality humour.

This game puts you in charge of a Pirate Captain with Irritable Bowel Syndrome and allows you to recruit a crew of incontinent sailors.  Your pirates will drop large, steaming piles of human dung all over your ship wherever they are standing, whenever they feel the need to go -- which is often. Seagulls will land on your ship and when one of your pirates scares them away, the birds will also drop a deuce on your deck.  Inevitably, the pirate involved in the confrontation will pinch off a loaf in celebration. The piles of poo will make your crew sick, but they WILL. NOT. STOP. The only way to mitigate this fecal onslaught is by equipping your crew with Diapers, and levelling up one of several poop-related skills from a modest skill tree.  There is a "perk" that makes a crew member into a Poop Machine.  You can train them in Toilet Mastery.
The game also features some light exploration and simplistic point-and-click combat.
PROS: There are very few Pirate-themed games out there. This is one of them.
CONS: This is a game about pooping.
UPDATE: The game has made it out of Early Access. Congratulations are due!
These are several "improvements" added in version 1.0, as per the changelog:
* BETTER POOP SPLASH EFFECT
* Pirates will no longer poop if they are hungry (less than 50% hunger)
* Pirates will now clean the nearest poop instead of any old poop
* Flying poop now deals 5% max HP damage (as opposed to a small fixed value)
In a way, it's refreshing that they are sticking to their guns with this.

I bought this game the day it came out on steam and have enjoyed it since. Don't let my low hours fool you, I play in offline mode quite a bit so go ahead and throw maybe 60+ hours onto my time.
Do you like the idea of having a ridiculously named pirate captain? In charge of a swarthy band of crazed misfits as you loot and plunder the seas until your cargo bay bulges and your decks are stained with the blood of your enemies? Or how about discovering new lands and killing the inhabitants.....maybe you find treasure...maybe you barely escape by the tip of your Falcon blade. This game is all about the experience, and my god what an experience.
Okay so yes the game isn't very easy to begin with for some people. I could see how you could get frustrated with the low amount of gold, tiny ship, and little to no help as far as a tutorial goes. Stick with it is all I have to say. This game has a huge amount of character and an infinate replayability that is rare by todays standards. How good is this game? I will be the first to say that this game single handedly cleansed me of my Minecraft addiction.
From the cling and clang of blades to the strange and lovable pirate songs, this game has tons going for it. The music hands down is my favorite aspect of the game. It has incredible atmosphere and is just so well done, so polished that you will be humming the tunes for months. Grog filled tavern ballads, seagulls, waves crashing, weird pirate accents, there won't be a time in the game where you aren't immersed.
The awesome rpg like elements of raising your band of pirates can be staggering at times. You will invest in your crew and you will slowly by your hand shape and mold them into what they are. The skills you can train your pirates work on a level system, the higher the level the more efficent they become at said duties. Cleaning the decks, fishing, cooking, learning to be more hygenic, battle prowess skills.....there are even ultimate skills that cost a small fortune to obtain. So yes when a member of your crew dies in battle you will feel a sense of loss in certain ways.
Building your own ship is one of the greatest things this game has going for it. Want a floating pile of poo? Done. Want a huge skull and crossbones? Easy. How about an intricate blimp? Difficult to manage but doable. Basically if you can think it up you can build it as your pirate ship to a certain degree. Remember this is Pixel Piracy not a 3d game, you are working on a 2d landscape with blocks and other objects. As you progress in the game you can make some truly magnificent ships that you will be proud of.
Edit 1: I am inserting this edit for the sole purpose of talking about the issues with bugs and other problems. Currently this game has a ton of bugs and glitches, so many in fact that it is difficult to even begin to create a list for you. Now this edit comes after final release and several subsequent updates. You will experience bugs and glitches, no game will be free of them and I must warn and also encourage you at the same time. The developers are highly motivated to make this game the best it can be and you can help as well by becoming active on the forums by pointing out issues. These issues don't change my recommendation for purchase, the game is still highly addictive and a blast to play.
I could go on and on but I won't ruin the rest of the game for you. Just ask yourself a few simple questions if you are on the fence about this purchase. Do you like Pirates? Do you like rpg like elements? Do you enjoy 2d masterpieces like terraria etc? This game is insanely fun and can easily suck hours and hours out of your life. Subsurface Circular puts you into the mind of a detective robot in a world you can only glean about by investigating robot passengers on a train.
What sounds like an excellent concept for a game could turn out being very hard. For example, the game could be too linear, being more of a book because the developers didn't have the skill/time to implement a world but are so proud of it then over inform you or force you to do the old "rub every noun against every source of information until the game is beat" type gameplay. SC ignores both options and forges ahead, writing a tale worthy of Asimov but giving you characters you care about and a narrative filled with choices.
While sound is minimal, it's well implemented. From the train calling out your stations to the ambient noise, there's plenty of sound going on. Graphically the game isn't anything you'll call home about. The simple meshes work well for the visuals provided, but the texture resolution and lighting won't have you pulling the game out as a benchmark. Nor should it, given the relatively low price point for entertainment value. The game runs about 2 hours per playthrough and as far as I can tell has three endings to get you to that amount of playtime.
This game is
in terms of narrative and one that I highly recommend for anyone even slightly interested. The mood and tone are set early on and survives the entire game. The story is so good, I'm going to be completing those as well, just to see the other endings. I recommend the game if you're even a little interested in story based games or if you're looking for something really good and really different.

TLDR Version --
-If GTA V and Just Cause 2 and 3 had a beautiful baby, this would be it.
-It has a great, massive open world, tons of content, tons of guns, and fun stealth mechanics (and I normally hate stealth games)
-The base game alone is worth it
-Negative reviews are overly picky, this game isn't Arma and isn't meant to be hyper-realistic vs. a great balance of fun vs. realism.
-Probably one of my top 3 purchases in the past 2 years.
-Has a touch of the 1990s "Covert Action" in it, and great informational cut-scenes (but the cut scenes do not interrupt the action, nor are you forced to play them).
- High replayablity factor
-Great game for gun-fans, if you have ever taken apart your own gun or understand the parts, this has a lot of appeal for you.
-Very forgiving game-play with relatively low frustration factor, and the ability to do missions your way, either going in guns blazing or doing it stealth and meticulously taking out sentries and enemies.
Longer review --  the options for this are myriad and they are great.  Customize your character (both male and female),  The guns are highly customizable and brilliantly depicted, with incentive to earn more parts on stand-alone missions.  I had a lot of fun just swapping different guns depending on the mood and needs of the mission.  Bullet trajectory is modeled somewhat, and is enough to keep things interesting yet fun.
Controls are very intuitive, and I found myself using a Xbox-style controller instead of a mouse, and I'm usually a mosue person for FPS's, to the point that I would always use the mouse for combat in GTA V.  In this game, I haven't used the mouse once, so that shows how well things are balanced.  While running around is in 3rd person mode, aimed shots are in first person, and the attention to detail on iron sights and scope options is very much appreciated.
Sound is an important component to the game, both for the ambience (much like GTA, including radio shows, music on the radio, eetc.) and for the actual special effects for weapons.  Firefights without suppression (and most guns do come with suppressors) are a feast for the ears.
The map itself is huge (someone online said it was 4-5 times the size of the GTA V map) and varied enough to make a difference location to location in terms of the different provinces.
Vehicle simulation is just ok, which makes sense, since this is more of a combat and gun simulator vs. a vehicle simulator.  Thus, GTA V has better driving, but that's because GTA V is about driving.  This game is about combat, so the guns and combat are more exquisitely modeled.
So far the AI seems fine to me.  It is somewhat predictable, but doesn't do anything stupid, and is a challenge enough.  Enemies do show up fast, but given the leeway you have in other dimensions to stay stealthy, it is balanced enough to keep things fair and fun.

I am going to compare this to another game that not many others make the connection but I am sure others wonder about.
Just Cause 3. I was skeptical about jumping into a jungle terrorist shooter because I have already put a solid amount of time into Just Cause and completed each mission base etc. But something I always wanted from the Just cause series is stealth and tactical gameplay. The most tacticle that JC3 can be is sniping from very afar, even melee alerts every soldier.
Now Ghost Recon Wildlands is not the most advanced military simulation but regarding your squad they can be told to open fire on a group, hold back, follow, and of course sync shotting enemies.
To point out the big listed takeaways I'll cut to the chase.
+Wildlands Pros+
+++Giant world. Seriously most games I do not believe in fast traveling because the game is open world and filled with roads and enemies for a reason, but this is a giant country made of 15 or nations. 3-4 nations probably would have been plenty
+++Wide selection of weapons. After 20ish hours I was finally done hunting for favorite personalized parts. This was very enjoyable creating a weapon by finding the pieces I wanted.
+++Useful land mass. In this I mean that in a game like JC3 the jungles and oceans do not contain much of reason to go through, besides seperate the world and make the world big obviously. With Wildlands there are many sites, cocaine farms, hideouts etc to run into. As well as using the treeline and mountains as a sniping position.
+++Variety of landscapes. Snow, mounatin, jungle, swamp, desert, badlands, salt flats, urban warfare, village, mines, worksites, factories.
*Specialty*
***Ultra Realisim. This is an odd pro because it is one that no other game makes me think of. Many many games happen in modern times and have increased bullet damage etc. But Wildlands packages all of its assets into something that feels so realistic that often times I forget that I am playing a video game and am completely pulled into the game world. Obviously JC3 has a arcadey speed action feel. Wildlands is easily one of my favorite games I own, and though it has sold well due to reviews I can see this becoming number 1 on future "hidden gems" lists.
-Common Cons-
---People have called it repetive. But honestly it is in the sense of repeated mission types. The game is all about assassinating leaders, sneaking out of bases with intel, sabataging equipment, through caves, jungle bases, villages, hospitals, chemical labs. HONESTLY these types of mission is all the game is but they do not get old, no one becomes bored of that type of mission!
---Bad driving Controls. I will agree with this the cars are very slidy which after some time just becomes more drifty than it is a hinderance
---Bad team AI. This can be broken down as that as a tac-shooter there really is not many options for utilizing your team.
---Weapon parts are useless. This I will tether back to the realisim factor. Yes there are a ton of parts and you can beat the game without the extra parts, but then again in real life adding a laser pointer, or folded stock is not going to dramatically change the gunplay expierence.
---Respawning Bases and enemies. This complaint confuses me because never would I complain that I can go back to big or my favorite bases to re take down. Instantly makes the game replayable forever if you enjoy the combat.
---Story. The story actually is a con because it is generally devoid of moral, value, and character. You are a very abiding soldier who will do exactly what you are told, the ends justfys the means!

I was pretty disappointed in this game.  There was 1 gem, the rest was very underwhelming.
Gameplay: highly repetative.  Every level is a corridor.  You skill up quickly and you're using max level agents all with the same abilities for more than half the game.  Gun play and cover system feels like it was ripped directly from Mass Effect.
Story: *Spolier warning* highly problematic.  While it reuses the familiar aliens, some of them are jumbled up in terms of ability and concept.  We can tell this game is intended as a prequel to Enemy Unkown (which I played first), based on general story elements and the music (ending music for The Bureau is the theme for Enemy Unknown).  In EU the aliens are all controlled by the Etherials, in TB the Outsiders control all the aliens.  EU: Outsider is a "being of pure energy" while the Etherial is physicalish.  TB: Etherial is pure energy, Outsiders are very tangible.
Also, if you get any of the "good" endings in TB, you have to wonder why you don't start out EU with plasma weapons and cool backpacks that give you shields and other goodies.  The only logical conclusion is that you chose the Weaver ending...which is an annoying ending as you watch all the tech vanish for no good reason.
*Major Spoiler* Continuity aside, there is one well written section where gameplay and story meld together to form a cool experience.  It's the point where Carter tries to break away from the Etherial that you realize, you haven't been playing Carter, you've playing as Asaru controlling Carter, and all of the Player based abilities to slow time and issue orders while gaining a 3rd person view of the field is merely a part of Asaru's abilities when riding a host.  That was well written.  Whoever did that ought to write more games.

Portal 1 is a good game for logic reasoning. There is a good many puzzles in the Portal 1. I like to be challenged in logic reasoning only to find better reasoning system in my mind. I want to expand all of my notions about logic reasoning. That is why I play Portal and read philosophy.

You enjoy light, charming puzzle platformers
The game that launched a thousand memes. If, by now, you haven't come across them, I want the address of the rock you have brilliantly been able to hide under all this time (and yet still have Steam access).
Jokes aside, Portal was (and still is) a very refreshing and intuitive platform puzzler, though a little short. It's very approachable and suits a nice range of skill levels, with the main game solvable without being frustrating (frustration is for the advanced chambers!)
Your Portal Gun (not a real thing, regrettably) simply lets you open one end of a portal - ultimately giving you a 2-way path from one spot to another. The aim is to solve a range of puzzles with this neat mechanic: Sometimes its moving objects about, others it's using physics to launch yourself to previously-inaccessible locations. Simple, distinct, but very clever.
To ground expectations though (as can be a little overhyped), you only get around 2-4 hours out of it if you're a dab hand at puzzles. The 19 levels aren't the tutorial... they're actually the bulk of the game. There are also a few annoying physics-based elements where you need to hit a specific spot whilst flying at high speed, not helped as your orientation can spiral all over the place when launched through portals... so can sometimes be a bit fast-paced for what would otherwise be a gentle thinking game.
That said - It has a nice 'clean' feel to it, balanced with the dry wit of the autonomous voice leading you through, giving the game a delightful charm.
It's a simple title, but a very likeable one.

Firstly I want to talk about the game, then I'll talk about why I recommend the game.
GAME OVERVIEW:
You have the option of making the game take more days before the end game horde spawns (easiest is 150 days, hardest is 80 days, normal is 100 days) and you have the option of increasing/decreasing the amount of already exhisting zombies on the map in order to make base expansion easier. I left all my settings on the default of 100. After choosing your settings you spawn in a randomly generated map and must begin building your colony. The early game is pretty easy since it gives you 4 archers and a soldier to explore with. You have to juggle a ton of micro-managment resources such as energy, food, workers, stone, wood, iron, oil, research, unit training, etc as well as explore the map and build defenses, but this is mitigated by the fact that you can pause and resume the game whenever you like. When the game is paused you can build buildings, destroy buildings, research, train units, order units, etc. It is a very nice feature but it gets boring doing it all the time, however, the game is very difficult and basically forces you to pause all the time and micro-manage or you will not survive very long.
GAMEPLAY:
The early game is easy once you get the hang of it. You will find that the best strategy is double layer walls and a ballista turret or two which paired with your initial fighters will get you until at least day 30 or so on normal. After a set amount of days you will get attacked by a horde of zombies. The game will alert you that you are about to be attacked, it will tell the general direction of the zombie horde (North, South, East, or West) which indicates what side of the map the horde will come at you from. The hordes will take the shortest path from the side of the map they spawn in on to your command center. You only have 8 hours to move troops and prepare defenses once the horde spanws. Soldiers and snipers are basically worthless and you don't want to stray very far from your walls if you are using them or you will lose them because they are very slow and can't run away if overwhelmed. I really would only train rangers and build ballistas until you get the engineering center, then you can crank out thanatos and titans. The mid game is easy if you set up your early game well, you need insane gold generation by overlapping market and bank on as many stone houses as possible. This needs to replicated so you have at least two areas where a market and bank have as many stone houses on them as possible or you will NOT have the gold generation for late game. Late game is the only fun part. At around day 70 you start getting hit by huge waves of zombies and at that point you need lots of titans and thanatos. You could build executioner towers but they have massive upkeep cost and you can't move them like you can with your military units. The furthest I made it was day 80 because I got attacked from the "north" but actually the zombies hit me from the west and the soldiers are so slow that they couldn't make it there in time.
This game is extremely fun for the first couple of play throughs as you learn the ropes and start trying out different strategies, but it is extremly repetative once you nail the early and mid game. Every game is an "iron man" mode, meaning that you can not save or load. If you mess up one fight (like me not guessing the right attack direction) then you will lose everything and will be forced to replay from day one. Now, this isn't a problem when you are learning the ropes since you won't last long, but if you survive for 60,70,80,90 days or more and make one mistake, you lose 5 or more hours of your day which is not something that is very fun for most people. Also, I don't think that the size of the zombie hordes change on "easy" mode, you just have more days to prepare for each horde attack.
Now, there are multiple maps but you need to beat the initial map on normal difficulty before you unlock them. I have not unlocked them but they are similar to the original being randomly generated every time. The game doesn't have many buildings and it only has 6 units, but it gets very annoying micro-managing all the resources. You need energy to build every building. In order to generate energy you need to build a mill (early game) or power plant (mid-late game) which requires workers. If you don't have enough workers then you need to build more houses. In order to build more houses you need food. You need energy to build more farms to get food. The cycle is vicous sometimes, I think you get the idea and it only gets worse once you start taking into account the upkeep of late game buildings and units. I think it takes away from the zombie fighting when 95% of the game is just a city builder but thats just my opinion.
SUMMARY:
So after all those complaints, why am I still recommending this game? Because I have hopes that the devs will add more features to the game such as weekly challenge mode maps, a campain, etc. not simply because "I died, 10/10 would become zombie and die again". If they added multiplayer and save/load then the game would be awesome, but right now I can't really say if the game is worth 22$ since most of your time will be boring filler between the horde attacks and one mistake will ruin many many hours of playtime.

This is the most complete Early Access game I've ever played, and I've tried several. There is definitely a difficulty spike to overcome and since each map requires the prior one to be beaten, you can get a little sick of seeing the same canyons on the first level.
But once you do you'll notice there's a clear pattern for working through each map. I've beat each map at standard settings such that the score factors work out to 100%, 120% and 140%. Haven't finished the last map yet. The third map took only a single try, though it was still quite fun.
The key to beating the levels (until the devs do a little rebalancing) is the following:
Start clearing map immediately. The starting soldier should be veteran before you even have a second soldier.
Mid game, ~14 soldiers + ~10 snipers should be moving through the map at all times clearing zombies. Don't leave this to the AI on the Search and Destroy (Chase) mode.
Late game, have way more than double walls. Wall your walls with walls, set up some autoturrets (I seriously hope you didn't actually pay for the great ballista or shock tower...) More walls gives your soldiers on the walls and autoturrets plenty of time to clear out mobs. At least two thanatos should exist at every possible attack point. A couple (2-3) lucifers at potential weak points is a good idea - they are excellent at holding the gap but suck if the big guys get them. Towers should be at least 50/50 soldiers/snipers.

+ Quality of music selection was decent, and complemented the game's atmosphere
+ You can play around with your vehicles' accessories, such as deployable roofs, turn signals, and windows; not at all functional, but it is the little attention to detail that I appreciate
+ Fast travel is available for discovered points of interest, stripping away some of the monotony of driving from waypoint to waypoint
+ Healthy variation in biomes and terrain types
+ Absolutely massive traversible maps (Even better when you unlock Hawaii)
+ Reasonable variety of cars available in-game, and your choice of starter vehicles can actually remain viable alternatives for much of the early-mid game
+ Off-road tracks are some of the most fun in the game, and could be very creative in design and technical challenge
+ Funds are not too hard to come-by, reducing chances you will get bogged down and find yourself in a rut
+ Cars, character, and homes are shockingly customizable
+ Social aspects are both well-implemented and go a long way to improving potential replay value; being able to drive up to other players in real-time and challenge them to a race by flashing my headlights is a lot of fun, and I felt that it really added to the experience
+ Licenses are required to unlock different types of races and challenges; this expanded a feeling of progression
- Some of the requirements for leveling up are not adequately explained
- Despite the quality of many (not all) of the songs, the overall soundtrack is severely limited; there are only two available radio stations, and they cycle between, perhaps, 14 total tracks
- NPC drivers boast fairly awful AI, and prove far too easy to overcome
- Occasional, disappointing framerate stutters and other visual bugs that I had expected to be ironed out
- Invasive, time-consuming, unnecessary DRM; requires additional downloads and the creation of a third-party account (hosted on a poorly designed and barely function Web site, no less)
- Character animations, models, and voice-acting are rock-bottom abysmal
- Some game progress (such as requirements found under the 'social' category) requires getting large numbers of human-controlled players on your friends list and in-game, playing with you; simply put, however, this game doesn't appear to boast the player population to warrant this, and it will make these hurdles difficult to overcome

While modern iterations of the Quake franchise continue to attract new players, there has recently been a clear recognition of the true importance of the very first Quake in shaping the multiplayer FPS games we play today. Clients such as ezQuake, nQuake, and FuhQuake all continue to prolong the multiplayer life of this true classic as well as adding the various options, toolsets, and graphical improvements that most are familiar with today. From Dennis 'Thresh' Fong winning John Carmack's Ferrari 328 at the 1997 Red Annihilation Tournament to the current Quake Live MLG, CPL, Intel Masters, Tek9, and QuakeCon events (to mention just a few), there has rarely been a lapse in the competitive interest this game continues to generate.
It is now 20 years since the game's release and there are simply too many happy memories to recount. Without a doubt one of the greatest games ever made and an essential title in any game collection.

This game will twist the very fabric of your reality. Every bird you encounter after this game will seem to hold an intriguing mystery, a sinister backstory, and a beguiling air. If you like adventure, romance, conspiracy, murder, and birds, this is the game for you. The first half of the game is as promised - a fun, wacky dating sim involving birds and school life. Some strange things may pique your interest, but it all seems part of the fun. Then you get to the second half of the story (only unlocked once you have played through dating all the birds, except San) and everything, EVERYTHING gets turned on its head.
I have no words to describe the mind-bending experience that is the second half. Not so much a game as an extremely gripping visual novel that's a wild ride from start to finish. Everything is explained, all loose ends tied, a game that must be played twice - nay, three times to fully comprehend the utter brilliance of its story. At times touching and melancholic, at times hilarious and baffling, but always with a keen sense of incredulity ("I can't believe these are BIRDS"), this is a game that will haunt you, I promise. If you ever get an avian-related game, forget Flappy Bird, GET THIS GAME.

Unfortunately, it really has no poetic language, no charm, and no depth to the writing style. It is simply indicative in all instances, stating what happens and who does something. The main character is a typical girl and writes typically. There's no philosophical dialogue, and barely even character insight.
It gets the job done, but I don't like the job it is doing. The task of quickly showing 2 minute scenes, switching between random choices and introducing a too-large amount of birds so quickly innundates any reader which is attempting to read at a normal or fast pace.
I really want to iterate this. Each scene lasts a matter of minutes.

This game is a bit of a black sheep amongst the XCOM family. It bears the name, deals with alien invasions and you;re part of a top secret government agency tasked with fighting them... but that's about as far as the similarities go.
The Bureau is a 3rd person squad-based cover shooter, and that's what turns a lot of people off to it. XCOM traditionally is a turn-based isometric game. Does it not being like the previous XCOMs make it a bad game? No, not really. That's not to say it's great, but it's not bad either.
The Bureau has its faults; The squad controls are clunky on both KB/m and controller, the UI looks like it was designed only for consoles in a lot of places, your squad mates will sometimes switch cover when they shouldn't... the list goes on, and much of it is just minor things.
As I said, the game isn't the greatest, but it's good enough at what it does to get a passing mark.

What to say here.  The idea is ok, but they really seem to have gone out of their way to make it as generic as possible.  It is sort of based on the good (modern) XCOM--you lead a group of 2 other guys into combat, give them orders, etc--but it just doesn't work all that well.  It's perfectly servicable, but its not groundbreaking, or even memorable.  At all.
To me, the issue is the setting.  Why set this in the 50s?  What was the story goal they were working for?  If they just wanted to "show the beginning of XCOM", they did a terrible job.  These people couldn't bust a speakeasy, much less an alien invasion.  Compare this, for instance, with Bletchley Park.  There, you had people (in roughly the same time) doing amazing things.  Here, in this game, you have...guys sleeping on the sofa in their office.  They miss the feeling of people who are well ahead of their time.
So why have I recommended it?  Because there are a lot worse ways you could spend some time.  If you want to buy it, do so during a sale.  If you can get it for single digits and are interested, it's worth it.  Otherwise, save your time and money.

I had my eye on this game for a while, as I was making a similar game to Zotrix a while ago. The idea of a simple shoot 'em up with a more modular ship appealed to me, and I finally grabbed it.
In a way, I had a lot of fun with it, as I was just looking for a mindless game. Shooting stuff is fun!
Unfortunately, the pacing, progression and difficulty curve are all completely off. I don't know how the game was in Early Access for 4 months and these glaring issues haven't been dealt with...
It's a basic modular shoot 'em up, with levels being composed of several preset waves. The waves are fairly well done, it was fun to play, for a while.
The first problem happened right at the beginning. So, the game has several different space stations that you need to go to to complete quests and buy equipment. The paths have different levels of difficulty, which is good. However, the beginning of the game is really bad!
Instead of introducing the shop and resource mechanics, you go for a 2-3 missions without being able to buy anything
. On the third mission, it's also incredibly hard to get to the end without buying anything. I restarted the game 3 or 4 times before I managed to buy the
right item to beat the level. Where was the problem?
In part, it was in how the game explains its upgrades. Items are divided into "permanent" and "expendable" upgrades. It seemed clear that expendable would be consumables, while permanent would be... well, permanent. That's not quite the case... Shields and Drones, for examples, are listed as expendable, but they actually carry over from mission to mission! The only "expendable" feature is that, for a given level, they can be destroyed and do not replenish until you finish that level.
From their description, I assumed shields were just a consumable that would be activated for 20 seconds, or so. Turns out, they were actually all I needed to beat the mission.
That's not all, though. The first, cheaper shields, are useless. They get destroyed by bullets too easily, rendering them useless. The higher level shields, on the other hand, are basically indestructible by bullets. The only way of destroying them, is by having ships ramming into you. Several in a row.
Well, ok... just a minor misunderstanding.
The bigger problem is: the higher level shields are really cheap! I bought the second highest on the third mission, and a couple of missions later I had the best. I was almost invincible. The only tough mission was the third. And that's because the game didn't communicate as it should have...
Anyway, fast forward a bit, after a few mindless levels, I started looking at the resource trading and more expensive upgrades. In each level you gain some resources and credits. The resources you get are almost laughable, not really of any use. The credits are fine.
The thing is, the economy is extremely basic. Assuming you're following the missions, you see what the next station is, and the game tells you which resources are higher. Then, you buy all the resources available to you, and sell on the next station. After a few levels, you have all the money you want.
The game has 40 missions (each consisting of more than 2 levels, generally). Before the 15th mission, my ship was fully upgraded. I had virtually infinite money as resources. Only I had 25 missions left. At this point... what's the point?
The story isn't particularly good, as the actual missions are simply "Go from here, to here, to there" because of a random excuse. There is no consequence or choice at all. It reminds me of a Clicker game, in some ways. Or an MMO, with the power creep thing. You just go around the places getting more powerful. The level don't keep up at all.
I was steam rolling the game... With no purpose at all.
The game has secondary weapons, like missiles or bombs. But you buy these individually. And if you use a missile, it's gone. Moreover, they're far, far weaker than your main weapon! It's useless. The drones are also a nice idea, but pointless is execution. They shoot automatically, but, again, they're very weak, and they also miss a lot.
The levels are very basic too, as you leave exactly as you got in. There are "upgrades" in each level, as you start with a single shot, but can collect double and triple shot for that level. It's very linear, though, and you'll also get both upgrades at the same points.
...
Oh well. There are other minor annoyances (and the music is simply there, tracks playing without a point) and some of the sound-effects overpowering everything else and being annoying.
I was very negative in this review... Which doesn't really reflect my experience!
I enjoyed the game a lot, as it was exactly what I was looking to play at the time. Something mindless and simple. It was cool!
But the game itself, objectively speaking, has some very critical problems that make me not recommend it.
I enjoyed my time, but I stopped playing after mission 18 because the game didn't keep up with the player. That's a huge  problem.
If you think you'll enjoy it anyway, give it a go, the shooting can be fun! :)

I love this game. It could be because I have an extreme bias for this genre, or any game that reminds me of a misspent (debatable) youth in Arcade/Pizza joints when the quarter was king. I don't think it's just that, though. Zotrix is an excellent retro top-down shooter in it's own right, but it is boosted to even greater heights by the more modern RPG elements woven in. The action is pretty fast-paced, but never seems to skew too far out of reach in it's difficult moments, even as you level up. It stays challenging, but never frustrating to the point of rage-quit. It has a pretty great soundtrack as well, and all the great pew-pew laser sounds you would expect from a title of this sort. If you're looking for a good time, a trip down memory lane, a compelling little twist an a familiar genre, or all of the above, then this is definitely the game for you. Just play it already, but remember....I got next.

A truly excellent game, much better than I had expected. It feels like a rogue-like RTS, an unforgiving one.
Even in early access, it still feels very polished and will no doubt keep you on your toes for hours.
Obligatory pro/con list follows below:
Pros:
- Very cool concept, very different take on RTS.
- Already very polished gameplay with many hours of fun.
- Runs smoothly for the most part, even with a lot of units on the screen (I've only encountered noticable performance hits once)
- Delightfully challenging, with multiple interesting ways to tweak the difficulty level.
Cons:
- Variety in buildings is a bit lacking. Many buildings are just upgrades of the previous.
- Very small amount of different units (both base and advanced).
- Advanced units seem underwhelming considering their research and upkeep requirements.
- Pathfinding needs an overhaul, units often get stuck in each other or get stuck trying to cross water or mountains.

Let's get this out of the way: this is a terrible racing game. The driving physics are broken, the cars aren't balanced relative to the classes the game puts them in, vehicle upgrades are extremely generic and there is no tuning whatsoever.
Race events range from laughably easy (most races with actual AI racers due to the laughably bad AI) to frustratingly difficult (the time trials where the AI posts amazing times that don't match up at all to their actual racing skill in the races). The game also forces you to go through various licensing challenges to even enter the race events which are a series of frustrating time trials, often in spin-happy RWD cars.
If you're looking for a racing sim, stop reading this now and go look elsewhere.
As for specifically what wrong with this game:
The physics engine heavily favors AWD cars, RWD cars spin out way too easily and its near impossible to recover once that happens. Even the AWD cars will randomly spin out at times, but at least they're more resistant to it and much easier to recover.
In most vehicle classes, there is one "I WIN" car that is so much better than all other cars in the class that the others aren't even worth considering for racing.
Vehicle upgrades are limited to speed, acceleration, and braking with 4 levels for each. There is no option to tune or put better tires on to try to fix the crazy tailspin on most of the cars.
So why did I recommend this game? Simply put, it's an excellent driving game. You have two real world islands to explore, (Ibizia and Oahu) and both are 1:1 scale that completely dwarfs the world in the likes of Forza Horizon. There are plenty of hidden secrets to find and scenic vistas, and a completely free multiplayer free roam where you can randomly encounter other players crusing around and potentially challenge them to a race.
There's a few other quirks worth mentioning as well. You have the option to customize your avatar, but no matter what you do they look weird. You also have a limited number of garage spots for new cars and you have to buy new houses to get more which gets very expensive very quickly and is the main financial limiting factor early in the game. The monetary cost of cosmetic things is way high ($300 for a haircut!?!). 5 machine activation limit is unecessary additional drm to be aware of, at least it gives you an activation back if you uninstall it.
The game is moddable and there are a few community patches to add new cars and fix some of the issues, but I haven't seen any patches that manage to fully fix all the issues with the game.
Overall, I still recommend this game if you enjoy just driving around and exploring more than racing.

The game that launched a thousand memes. If, by now, you haven't come across them, I want the address of the rock you have brilliantly been able to hide under all this time (and yet still have Steam access).
Jokes aside, Portal was (and still is) a very refreshing and intuitive platform puzzler, though a little short. It's very approachable and suits a nice range of skill levels, with the main game solvable without being frustrating (frustration is for the advanced chambers!)
Your Portal Gun (not a real thing, regrettably) simply lets you open one end of a portal - ultimately giving you a 2-way path from one spot to another. The aim is to solve a range of puzzles with this neat mechanic: Sometimes its moving objects about, others it's using physics to launch yourself to previously-inaccessible locations. Simple, distinct, but very clever.
To ground expectations though (as can be a little overhyped), you only get around 2-4 hours out of it if you're a dab hand at puzzles. The 19 levels aren't the tutorial... they're actually the bulk of the game. There are also a few annoying physics-based elements where you need to hit a specific spot whilst flying at high speed, not helped as your orientation can spiral all over the place when launched through portals... so can sometimes be a bit fast-paced for what would otherwise be a gentle thinking game.
That said - It has a nice 'clean' feel to it, balanced with the dry wit of the autonomous voice leading you through, giving the game a delightful charm.
It's a simple title, but a very likeable one.

tl;dr
Feels like a F2P game where the devs realized halfway through that noone really likes those games, then removed the P and released what was there.
Longer explanation
While definately set in the same universe as H2S1, this is an entirely different game. It has basebuilding, missions, skill leveling (as opposed to skill unlocking) and a worldmap to discover.
Unfortunately, that is also what makes it feel F2Py.
You get missions at certain places in the world, mostly from Kovac and two other places in his bunker. There's also NPCs in the world (who happily watch you get mauled in front of them) that can give you missions. Once you accept a mission, you get teleported onto a separate map to complete the relatively simple tasks (fetch a number of object x, find person y) and then teleport back to receive rewards in the form of material and XP. As far as I am now, there is no way to receive most materials outside of repeatedly grinding missions. Were this a F2P game, this would be where you would be asked to pay to receive materials, and what makes me feel like this game started out as F2P.
Edit: You can craft after all, it was a mistake on my part.
All these design decisions would make sense on a F2P (I say F2P a lot in this review...) game on a phone, but not for a PC game.

Fair warning; all you really do in this game is read unvoiced dialog, make dialog choices, and solve the occasional word/logic puzzle. However, the compulsion involved is one of mystery. Beating around the bush, nipping at clues, catching the odd 'Red' herring (inside joke), and still not getting the full scope until the very end.
Ultimately I enjoyed the totality of my experience with the game. I will make one complaint that the "ending" is two binary extremes. However, you can still infer your own contextual conclusion to your A or B choice.
Narratively the game explores the beaten path that is automation taking over our general work-force. Something that's been tackled many times since the first major automation boom in the 80's. It also mixes in the implications of true AI of various complexities having taken over such general labor, and even specialized work. You are a Detective AI Tek(robot), and you find yourself investigating not only the main plot, but also the subset context of the world itself. Bound to a subway train for the entirety of the experience.
I hate movies that are confined to singular spaces or relatively small locations, and yet I didn't dislike this game confining me to a single seat on a subway train car. Because the frequent delivery of world-building kept my mind's eye imagining the world outside. This made a 'world' of difference.
The only kind of person I can see not enjoying the experience this has to offer is a self-absorbed, conceited, narcissist.
The game costs less than a typical meal for one person, and lasts longer. No cost/hour excuses allowed.

I got a good couple hours of gameplay out of it and I feel like it's worth the price despite its length. Both the plot and the game aesthetic kept me hooked during the entirety of the experience. It's not very sophisticated in terms of puzzles or real detective work (at least not to the degree that some other detective-oriented games like Darkness Within are) but in this case it serves to give you a good sense of accomplishment without having any moments that drag on. It's very streamlined in how the story unfolds and though it is rather linear, you have the option of pursuing different lines of inquiry as you please. Your choices feel weighty and do carry consequences.
Overally, definitely fun and intriguing. I would like to see more games of this kind.

To start this off, I DID NOT buy this game, a friend gifted it to me and I'm very glad he helped me discover this gem.
So, Dishonored is kind of a hardcore stealth game where you have 2 paths in each mission except the first one, stealth or loud. These paths change the ending of the game and make it happy/chaotic depending on your overall level of "chaos". You kill people, your chaos level rises and adds up, this is for the loud option. There is also stealth which requires patience and game knowledge in my opinion, to achieve the best non chaotic ending possible, believe it or not, you should NOT kill anyone nor get detected until the end of the game. So yes, it is possible to completely finish the game without causing any harm to others. Your level of chaos also gives shape to your relationships with other NPC's for example, if your level of chaos is low, they will respect you, if it's high, you will make them hate you.
So this was the gameplay part, now the graphics part, to be honest, this game doesn't require a beast at all you can run it with some decent or kind of a low end pc normally which surprises me because it has GORGEOUS visuals for a 2012 game.
Well overall, I think this game is a must-play for everyone who likes story based stealth games.

EDIT 2: ok so i have now played through this game seven times now with it taking up 70 hours of my life so i think it's about time i give the game the review it deserves. You play as Corvo Attano(don't know if i spelled that last name right) a man framed for the death of the empress and is given mystical powers from a man known as the outsider. And from their the game is pretty much yours.
The game utalizes linear but open maps so it gives you many many ways to tackel your objectives. You can decide to go in guns blazing or you can choose to sneak your way through your ememies. And while the game is more challengeing to play stealthfully it does reward you with the good ending.
The karma system is also handled very well. Your choices not only effect the ending, but the entire game as well. Certain events will only happen if your chaos level (karma) is high and some events will only take place if your chaos level is low. A low chaos ending will take place if you kill nobody or if you kill a small amount of people.
Also the game never forces you to kill any of your targets, you can preform non-leathal take downs of the targets. But in order to pull these off you have to do some dectective work and explore the map, find out what it is that you have to do in order to take them down in a non-leathal monor. And once you figure out what you have to do the game feels extremly rewarding.
Also each level is so perfectly designed and so memorable. The only problems I have with this game is the fact that it's just too short. I feel like a game this good should be a twenty hour game, not a ten hour game. Also there's no way to tell how high or low your chaos level is during a level, for that you have to wait till the end of the level.
BUT other than that this game is nearly PERFECT

Portal is an absolute classic. It’s one of those games that define video games as a whole, on a tier similar to Super Mario Bros. I wouldn’t be surprised if a lot of people picked it up just to see what all the fuss was about. Though, even if that’s not enough for you to get this game, I can assure you that it’s definitely worth picking up on its own merits besides its popularity.
As the name suggests, Portal is a game about portals. You walk through one and come out the other. The concept, while somewhat hard to explain, is easy to pick up (pretty sure the store page has a neat little video showing it). However, most of the game has you creating your own two portals on most surfaces to solve puzzles. The game is actually rather direct about where to place portals (you’ll see isolated portal-able surfaces very clearly a lot of times), but finding out the sequence of events of when to place the portals there and what goes through it is where the puzzle-solving aspect comes in. The difficulty of puzzles goes up rather nicely as the game progresses, and any moment I got stuck wasn’t frustrating or too out there…I just had to plan ahead. And this game is literally about puzzles; you’re in a test chamber designed entirely around using the portal gun, which means there are no convoluted puzzles involving a changing environment or the like.
Portal’s cool portal concept to solve puzzles could’ve carried the game alone, but on top of it all is a story. While the story about you being a lab rat and the robot putting you through all the tests (named GLaDOS) is a thing, the game got a lot of its fame from its great writing. A lot of the game’s writing is her coming up on the intercom and teasing you. I assure you, it’s hilarious.
The only real downside of this game is its length. It can be beaten in only a few hours even if you struggle through puzzles. While it’s short, it definitely doesn’t just feel like a tech demo for the portal gun concept; it’s a full game. Just a short one. Some might argue it’s just the right length, but I found myself at the climax and thinking, “Aw, it’s already almost over?”
Even if the game is short, though, that doesn’t mean it’s a bad thing. No part of it feels like it’s dragged out. I’d definitely pick this up, not only just to see what all the hubbub is about, but also because the game itself is a solid package.

Wow, how this game has changed in the last few months. What a wonderful little pirate sim this game has become. Most of the rough edges have been removed and the game is being polished to a mirror sheen. The game still has some annoying proclivities (like the inability to unequip items) but loads of improvements have been made in the gameplay and the level of polish that goes into the game.
It's a wonderful mix of rogue-like map-crawling and minecraft-like creativity. The game's loop is immensely satisfying: Go out to sea, raid some islands/merchant ships/pirates, kill stuff, take their loot and then pull into town and upgrade ship/crew. Repeat. Bonus points for the how the game lets you BUILD YOUR OWN SHIP, tile by tile, into the hulking monstrosity that would become the terror of the high seas. Even more bonus points for in-depth crew customization and new options for grouping and controlling your crew.
If anything, the game is still a bit short on content. There isn't quite enough variety yet in the types of challenges that the game presents. Sure, there are bigger ships to take on, tougher mobs, but unlike games like Diablo III or Minecraft, the approach these challenges never really changes. It's always a game of who has the bigger numbers -- more pirates, more cannons, gear with higher stats... The game never really forces you to adapt to different types of challenges using means other than higher numbers.
Don't let these minor quibbles discourage you! The developers of this game are wicked smart and they seem to know exactly what their game needs. Regardless of the game's early access status, I feel confident in stating that you'll likely get your share of laughs and fun out of the game.
