- Beautiful environment with a delightfully unique Victorian London/steampunk-but-not-really theme.
- Seamless fusion of conventional weaponry with magical abilities.
- Daunting, dynamic soundtrack and sound effects.
- Engaging, well thought-out plot with multiple twists that reacts to the player's actions.
- Exhilerating stealth and espionage experiences
- Dynamic world which changes and responds to the player's playstyle and reputation.
- Multiple ways to reach every objective.
- Many secrets, easter eggs and side quests mean completionists can put in four or five playthroughs.
- Many different playstyles - you can slaughter everyone in your path,or you can finish the game without taking a single life, you can run through the streets with guns blazing or skirt along rooftops unseen by anyone, etc. etc.
Why I hate Dishonored:
- Autosaves are somewhat infrequent.

There are numerous factors to this game, some are positive, some are negative but overall I believe the balance is tipped towards the negative side. I will cover each factor to keep the review clean.
Story
The game has an interesting and overall fresh setting which I have to admit I liked a lot. Coldwar era, everyone scared of Reds, and overall one can't help but wonder that in such an era, where not just disbelief and distrust hinder the human side but even technically, they are way behind than the "modern" human resistance of Xcom: Enemy unknown, a game from the same developers, that is connected to this one.
On the other hand the story develops towards open confrontation with the aliens which makes the whole thing unbelievable - especially after the developers going out of their way of providing hints about the connection with the other Xcom game, where we know nothing about previous alien encounters... while an open war with aliens ought to be something hard to forget for humanity.
Even not considering the connection to the other game's storyline, it feels strange that while we are practically in open war with the aliens yet it just doesn't feel like it.  Aand this is where gameplay kicks in.
Gameplay
You control the protagonist, commanding a small team of men, issuing tactical orders in the heat of battle. Sounds nice. Problem is the way this plays out.
Control can be truly clunky at times, certain abilities do things that just doesn't seem logical (an ability that forces an enemy out of cover looks the same as any other shot etc.) or just plain skip explanation how they do it but what truly kills it is the ai. Dishing out orders can be a pain while under fire and while time slows to a near complete halt you find yourself panicing. Not because of enemies outnumbering you or anything but simply because even seemingly solid orders can get yourself killed since your teammates tend to perform actions in a suicidal manner. That becomes apparent first when you are hit by a grenade attack and they either run away in fear (mostly right towards the enemy, exposing themselves even with tons of cover around, etc.) or just stay and get fried. Another problem is the effect of cover which tends to be erratic. You are in cover yet the enemy seems to have no problem whatsoever hitting you - and your teammates die fast.
Enemies tend to be foolish too and while they do expose a lot of themselves it is still hard to take them down - even the weakest sectoids. Sure, later you can get upgraded equipment but honestly, when I see an enemy that is supposeldy physically weak (sectoids) soak up 10+ shots to the head from a carbine without flinching... I feel somewhat annoyed.
Graphics
The game has what it takes to provide proper visuals while it's engine would be capable of far more realistic looks - this art style is alright. Certainly not the best looking one around (even considering age) but no problem.
On the other hand the design of certain things can be... strange, even forced.
Some aliens look like the generally known versions, greys etc., modelled practically the same way as the ones in Xcom Enemy Unkown, thus providing a certain amount of consistency which is always nice while the other group of enemies consist of metallic... machines?... mainly following a geometric theme. Both groups are fine on their own but making them appear together, they just don't fit. Not because alien enemies cannot be diverse and varied or sorts - simply because the technological level of the metallic enemies seem to vastly outclass the "flesh and blood" enemies, resulting in a difference that makes one think that they are not even from the same game.
Overall the game can be good, with enough patience you can ignore the problems I have mentioned... but honestly, not worth it. Ai and controls are core mechanics, if they are messed up, your whole experience will be plagued by fails that you can hardly do anything about. I as a player don't like it when the game just decides that I win or lose and honestly, that's how this felt.

I feel like this is a great game with a strong story. it is short but sweet and there are so many ways you can play it. Here are a list of pros and cons from my personal experience:
Pros:
- Great story that really captures your attention. It's strong and the characters are believable.
- Great graphics (besides  the arms sticking into the body)
- So many ways to play. If you die, you will have to think of a better strategy. Different agents offer different tactical adantages and disadvantages. It actually makes you think about what you are doing.

- Short but sweet. It doesn't last for over 20 hours but I feel this was a good decision. Dragging it out would ruin the story and get a bit repetitive.
Cons:
- Game constantly crashed randomly. Just fully closed, no warning or windows error. The first time it happened, I thought I quit the game by accident (was in menu)
- Pausing during the game. I have a beast of a computer but I would find that it would freeze sometimes and audio would mute. It return to a playable state afterwards though. This only happened 2-3 times.
- Repetitive. I know that there are allot of ways to play and allot of enemies but once you get the hang of it, it really comes down to the same strategy. Hide, use your agents and play their role. Kill the enemy and proceed. It honestly isn't that bad but I was feeling it towards the end.

Toribash. Easily one of my favourite games. I'll list some of the pros and cons below, but first, remember that this is pretty biased, because this game was also one of my first games i was really dedicated to as a small child. That aside, lets gets started.
----------------------------------------------------------PROS-----------------------------------------------------------------
+Great fun with friends.
+Community can be very helpful (and hilarious) at times.
+A feeling of accomplishment every time you win.
+++Ability to create or buy custom textures for every single part of your body.
+++Ability to make custom flames, sound effects, and trails.
+You can make REAL LIFE MONEY if you're an artist making textures.
+TONS of game modes , or "Mods", to choose from.
--------------------------------------------------------CONS----------------------------------------------------------------
-Hard to learn, much harder to master.
-HUGE Learning curve.
-Sometimes the community can be a bit rude.
-Some market items are WAY over priced.
-Gaining in game cash, or "Toricredits" Can be very slow at first.
-There are no low level tourneys. That means a white belt could fight a god belt over a measley 500 tc.
-The high level belts, (10th dan+) Are just a crawl to get through.
-A new player can win a tourney by "shoveling" everyone out of the ring.
----------------------------------------------------OVERALL-----------------------------------------------------------------
Over all, I think this game is REALLY worth getting if you're ready to really dedicate some time to learning balance, openers, and recoveries. And even if you're not willing to dedicate time, it's still a hilarious game to sit down and play with your friends. So, in my opinion, Toribash is a game everyone should try at least once. Happy bashing, everyone!
(Oh, and P.S., don't be discouraged by my playtime, I played a good 200 hours on the non steam version.)

This game is a love letter to classic RTS games with a little bit of roguelike thrown in. The mechanics are very straight forward in the RTS department. Build, expand, mine, kill, die (more on dying later). Each play through, you're asked to live till some target date (e.g. Day 100) without succumbing to the zombie hordes. In each of these play throughs, you effectively work towards the same goals each time, but how you accomplish it will vary between matches because the maps are proceedurally generated.
This game is hard. I'm 36 hours in and I haven't lived through a single play through on difficulties varrying from 55-100%. The mechanics are simple enough that even people not farmiliar with RTS can pick it up, but I think it will be a rewarding challenge even for veterans of the genre.
Back to the dying bit, you are probably going to lose a lot at this game. All it takes is a single zombie to make it into your base unnoticed to spread the infection like wildfire across your colony. What was once a bustling steam punk city can become plague infested breeding pit for zombies in a mater of seconds.
I find this fun. Others may not. If you loved classic RTS games like Warcraft, Starcraft, CnC (especially any of the mods in those games), you will probably love this. If you're totally new to the RTS genre, this is a fun introduction that (at least initially) won't overwhelm you.

[[[Pre-review notes: They Are Billions is my first EVER RTS-style game, so any mention of difficulty I make should be taken with a grain of salt.]]]
Well this was certainly an unexpected joy to behold!
"They Are Billions" is an RTS (Real-Time-Strategy) game in which you are responsible for helping a colony survive the zombie apocalypse .
It has quite a lot of managing, but it's never overwhelming thanks to an easily-readable UI and, for those newer or less-experienced with the RTS genre, allows you to modify two parameters of the game's difficulty;
1. Length - the more days there are, the more time you have until a colossal horde comes to ruin your day.
2. Zombie population. This is pretty self-explanatory; this affects how many wild zombies exist on the map. This also affects how many appear during the scripted swarms.
"They Are Billions" is delightfully difficult, even on the easier settings - however I don't feel this is a bad thing! Difficult games breed strategies and fresh thinking - and I have certainly become more adept at managing large areas at a time better than I used to be.
My ONLY real issues, albeit more of a nitpick, is that when you're trying to place buildings behind other buildings, the one that's already placed doesn't become transparent, making it more difficult to place accurately - this is especially prevalent when trying to apply a wall around the main keep.
I also wish we were able to at LEAST clear away any ore spots we don't want, as those can get in the way of a nice, clean build. (Unless I'm just missing a method to do so)
With that all said and done, They Are Billions is easily a 9/10 game - and I make no jokes when I say I will be editing this review in the future to give it a 10/10 once the game becomes more polished and complete.

Let me start by saying much of the playtime I've had so far is outstanding. I haven't sampled multi-player much, deciding instead to get my feet wet in single-player before diving into a far more cutthroat world. The game is fast enough to remain engaging, but slow enough that you get some time out of it (unlike an A-B-C game). I've built myself a small first base, and have gotten as far as exploring the local asteroid belt and a quick jaunt to a nearby moon.
The good:
The game is pretty straight forward, engaging, and just straight up fun. It strikes a good balance as a survival game, neither being too easy or too difficult. Resources are fairly well balanced, so you can get up and running quickly to survive, but you wont thrive as easily.
The bad:
A few criticisms. Firstly, and most glaringly, after you reach the point where I am now at, there is not an apparent PURPOSE to the game. I've secured my position, have a functional base, and can get off the planet. Unfortunately, going anywhere seems to simply be an exercise in restarting the same process, except I can bring materials with me. The lack of a storyline or motivating factor past this is really a killer.
Second, as one can expect with games in test phase, there are glitches. The most serious, and apparently one thats been discussed at length is the fact that insect enemies ignore your base walls and can attack you inside. This really violates the very spirit of the word "Shelter". Second, I had a suit breach from an interior attack, and still lost pressure, nevermind being inside an oxygen safe zone, which seems a little silly. Thirdly, attacks on the base noticeably increased after the construction of a Laboratory. Not sure if there's a reason for it, but I definitely am getting hit more often, and it's pushing me towards abandoning the base for a new location that might be safer.
Finally, theres a fundamental lack of information I found on starting. Simple things like what the portable scanner is useful for aren't really explained, and then there's the complex "Dear god what the hell is that 50 story tall worm thats heading right for me but I cant shoot?!" is it an enemy or is it simply a decorative animation?
I do recommend the game, but I hope to see improvements on the single-player experience. I'll plan to add/update this review after getting more multi-player under my belt.

As my car hurtles over the tallest cliff in Hawaii, I take one last look in the rear-view mirror. How did it come to this? For the longest time I was just another loser, content with a mundane life and those brief moments of escapism. Somehow over the course of nearly 30 hours in Test Drive Unlimited 2, I became a monster.
Sometimes when people play videogames, it's to get away, like a virtual vacation. But there are those times, where I don't want to be a plumber, a rodent with an attitude, a criminal, or Laura Bailey. I just want to drive around in expensive automobiles. In the real world I own two cars, one of them has a busted alternator. The other? No brakes. Despite being unable to start or stop, I've maintained the same driving job for the past decade. I'm always driving through the same neighborhoods meeting the same people every moment of every day. On top of all that, if Florida is considered America's♥♥♥♥♥♥ then I live in one of its hemorrhoids. But hey, all I need is an hour or two a day of wonderfully escapist adventures and I'm golden.
I was a fan of Test Drive Unlimited 1 on the Xbox 360. The handling wasn't particularly good, but the atmosphere and sense of exploration was excellent. With a few fixes, better graphics, and more content, it could be my ideal driving game. I'm not sure what I was expecting with the sequel. I read all of the reviews, noted that there are major problems such as Securom, dysfunctional servers, and so on. I considered the possibility that this game might not even work. But I gave it a shot anyway...
...I'm at a party...alright..cool I guess. Apparently I'm a woman now. It's just like Skyrim except I'm wearing clothes and I don't think I have a six-foot-long p-.
"PepsimanVsJoe! Enjoying your birthday party?"
Oh It's my birthday? I had no idea. Apparently I'm a silent-protagonist so all I can do is smile.
"Come check out your gift! It's a brand new car!"
No way! This is one of those end-game vehicles. I must be dreaming. This is so totally meta.
Sure enough the real game begins, I lose my job, only to get an offer to join a racing group for some show called Solar Crown. This is so ridiculous. I head to the used car dealer for my first actual virtual vehicle.
"HOLY♥♥♥♥♥♥" I say to myself.
The dealer? He has small hands. The driving school instructor? A regular Alex Smith. It's no wonder none of them have gone for a handshake, it would be like if I held up my finger so a baby could grab it. After sleep-driving through my first test I say "Thank you very much." to the instructor. Apparently I'm a very-thankful-and-not-quite-silent protagonist. The only words I ever say are to express gratitude.
On the road, the handling is...well it's about as bad as TDU1. In my mind that's good enough, because I'm finally living the dream again, cruising through hundreds of miles of beautiful Ibiza, and eventually Hawaii. As with the previous game, everyone needs help getting around the islands. There's the drunk guy who wants me to speed, the sick girls that throw up if I slam on the brakes, the random woman who always calls me adorable, and...wait a minute. It's happening again isn't it? The same people, requesting me to do the same favors for them over and over. Don't they have anything to say? While I'm driving we could discuss those bonus features on DVDs, or what tiny-handed men are good for aside from making origami birds out of starburst wrappers. Instead it's always "I'm going to be late!" or "I just broke a nail" or "Whoa ho! Look at that speed!"
The people I compete with are slightly more developed, but it's also a facade. Miami Harris is little more than an untimely Paris Hilton joke. Then there's the Wilder brothers. Oh look at us! We're so extreme...ly shallow! Tess Wintory never figures out her daddy issues. Her dad Stuart is just a useless old prick. If I'm expected to race against these jerks all the time, at least a little effort could have been expended to develop them. But who am I to talk? I have the least character development of all. Oh sure, I've bought several houses, over a dozen cars, and a couple wardrobes. I've also gotten plastic surgery so many times I've forgotten what I originally looked like. In fact I just got some work done earlier today. The nose wasn't right.
Aside from a few minor changes and additions, TDU2 isn't really much of a sequel. In some ways it's even a step back. Motorcycles are locked behind a DLC wall. The races are organized in a Grand Prix setup, with the winner being the person who attains the most points. However that model is dumped for the major championships races because....???? It doesn't make any sense. A casino would have been nice to hang out at, but that's also DLC. All of the other additions seem to be multiplayer-centric, which is pointless when half the people that buy this game can't even get it to work.
But does any of that truly matter to me? I got what I wanted right? My virtual fantasy of owning expensive cars, several houses (that I can't interact with), and free reign over a beautiful...but lifeless island. Lifeless except for the same 12-15 idiots who sit around impotently while I drive them around or beat them to the ground in the championships. Nearly 30 hours of this dream has become a nightmare, and I suspect that it won't end anytime soon.
So where we did leave off? Oh right...I was hurtling over the tallest cliff in Hawaii. Yes, I'm throwing it all away. Soon it will all be-
I hit the rocks, then the water...suddenly I'm back on the road again...my car is a little scratched but it isn't even wet. I knew it wouldn't work anyway, but can you blame me for trying?
It's that time again. I remove the bandages from my last trip under the knife and check the rear-view mirror.
The nose still isn't right.

This game is pretty good. Frustrating? Yes. Difficult. YES. In space? YES!
The only thing I don't understand is the optimization of the particle effects. My CPU and GPU (i5 and the highest radeon series) are equipped to handle that stuff, yet I get severe lag when too many particles are on the screen, with a density of 20 parts/cm^2 or greater. I know, one can turn the particles down, or even off, but I don't need to. My computer can handle what the game is doing, but for some reason the game is way, way too taxing in terms of particle effects.
One UI thing that bothered me was the fact that you can go to the resource trade menu from the equipment store menu, but not the other way around. It's nit-picky, but that's what critiques are about.
The graphics are amazing, so I have no issues there.
The music is one of my favorite parts of this game. I would list the artists here, but there is a metric ton of people behind the music design, relative to how small the game is. There are also sound bars that are present in the main menu and the starting screen. Each level begins with a (usually) different-than-the-last-one-heard soundtrack, with the title of said soundtrack appearing on the screen. Obviously this game had a big focus on sound quality.
The gameplay is pretty much what this genre is all about; you fly a colorful collection of pixels around a black and white background, shooting squares at other collections of squares as they shoot squares back at you. The game features newtonian mechanics. For example, there is a pushback effect from shooting, which is actually pretty unique in 2D space shooters. The ship, however, just kind of stops. This is counter-intuitive, unless the ship has some kind of RCS that the player can't see, which is what I'm guessing.
The innovation here is that it's a 2D space shooter with resource trading and upgrading. It's not a roguelike, like FTL. It isn't as huge and encouraging of exploration as in EVE online. It also isn't just some boring Galaga clone. It's some hybrid of those games.
If you want to play a casual space shooter and feel an actual feeling of accomplishment after beating a level without ejecting out of your ship, play this.

The game is definitely better then the original in my opinion, it's an interesting take on the survival horror genre, quasi hub based gameplay using a mission system that gives you the ability to set the difficulty of each instance based mission.
Progression is mostly linear, weapon choices are limited and on a vertical progression curve.  It's a fairly simple game but so is Killing Floor 2 so what do you expect.  The price point is excellent though, if you like zombie killing and would like to try out an isometric view one this is definitely a good pick.
End game is mostly non-existant though, which is a shame.  The game will become quite a grind after the first 20-30 hours but the good thing is that by then you'll have gotten your moneies worth.
The community is actually fairly good, the only issue is interacting with them will always be an issue since the game doesn't support text chat, you only have the ability to talk to other players using a group of scripted lines like Yes, No, I'm hungry, Follow me, etc.
As stated though the game is definitely worth the price, the developers listen to the community and implement new updates at a decent pace as well so this game is worth the money imo.

While playing the game I checked around the first area and discovered a call for help from another survivor.
"Help me!  Oh god.  It chased me into the house and is trying to get in!" he said over the crackling static of a radio before his inevitable horror movie-esque demise occurred as they broke through the door.

A skinny zombie?  Those freaky zombies that shriek and act like Hunters from Left 4 dead?  Or perhaps some deadly new enemy?

Moment's later the wave of voracious undead poultry swept over the horizon and ran my character down before slowly devouring my character whole.  My character's demise was as excruciating as it was delicious.

Why I love Dishonored:
- Beautiful environment with a delightfully unique Victorian London/steampunk-but-not-really theme.
- Seamless fusion of conventional weaponry with magical abilities.
- Daunting, dynamic soundtrack and sound effects.
- Engaging, well thought-out plot with multiple twists that reacts to the player's actions.
- Exhilerating stealth and espionage experiences
- Dynamic world which changes and responds to the player's playstyle and reputation.
- Multiple ways to reach every objective.
- Many secrets, easter eggs and side quests mean completionists can put in four or five playthroughs.
- Many different playstyles - you can slaughter everyone in your path,or you can finish the game without taking a single life, you can run through the streets with guns blazing or skirt along rooftops unseen by anyone, etc. etc.
Why I hate Dishonored:
- Autosaves are somewhat infrequent.
- ... that's all I can think of.
Overall: it's not perfect, but Dishonored is well worth your money in my opinion. A beautiful world mixed with interesting mechanics with an engaging story and many different playstyles means that this game is a recommended purchase for basically anybody.

Hearts of Iron IV is simply said awesome. im going to talk about 3 perspectives because these are the biggest ones i feel.
Political System:  Amazing. You can make your country Fascist, Communist, Democratic, some random things as well, and it is really good. You gain politcal power per day, and with that you have to 'buy' a policy or advisor. With advisors you can aim to change your regime from for example democratic ***hires Fascist Demagogue*** to Fascist. I love it.
War: Fighting a war is always fun when you are on the winning side. This game does that okayish. Inevitable Attrition (god i HATE this mechanic) meaning your divisions run out of supplies on the frontline and cant fight and proceed is annoying. I somehow never find to counter even though i maximize Infrastructure and emphasize on the production of the supplies needed. Also bad AI (AI not capturing all of the provinces wanted or missing some parts which creates bordergore, or the loosing of a war while your army is extremely superior) gets frustrating. BUT in the end it is always satisfying when the land you captured capitulates and you can take it all.
Community: The modding is the gamechanger in this game. Some things that Paradox does poorly gets addressed by at least 3 mods in the workshop. It makes the game better. Alot. Active community with things like the Millennium Mod (modern day setting) and improved AI (still bad but better) makes me enjoy this game far more than without.

My first video game, and definetly my favorite. Portal combines a fresh new approach to the puzzle genre, which is what makes this game a classic. The witty dialouge from the main antagonist, GLaDOS, keeps the player in stiches as you navigate through the chambers of Aperture Science. As the game progresses, each test gradually becomes more difficult and can be very frustrating at times. Nevertheless, these tests provide a unique mental challenge, and can be very fun once you get the hang of it. At first glance, this game may seem to have no story or background, but once the player realizes that GLaDOS was their enemy all along, that opinion quickly changes. Once the character defeats the narcisistic supercomputer, they are given a very satisfying ending, accompanied by the cake and their companion cube. Although this game was great, the brilliance of this franchise is truly shown in the sequel, Portal 2. Complete with a whole new plethora of characters, a co-op and perpetual mode, and the return of GLaDOS, this game gives you a whole new perspective on the franchise, while still maintaining the charm of the original. Characters such as the dim-witted Wheatley and the ambitious Cave Johnson kept players on the edge of their seats. Also, new mechanics were introduced, such as the excursion funnel, the discouragement redirection cube, mobility gels, and lasers (which replaced the high-energy pellet from the original). I believe the most striking part of this game is that the player gets to see GLaDOS' human side, Caroline. She soon changes her role as a character, from an antagonist to an ally in chapters 7-9. After defeating the corrupt Wheatley in an epic boss battle, GLADoS no longer has the will to kill Chell anymore, and she lets her free along with the original companion cube that was euthanized in the first game. Overall, these two games are a must-play and would definetly recommend them to anyone, regardless of their age or skill.

So the world has gone to hell, and your left fending for yourself and your colonists! Good luck! This city builder is a fun - but at times frustrating experience. Is it worth the money in beta? I would say so. It is playable as is, but there are a few kinks that needs to be sorted out.
Simple and easy to understand strategic element. You got to build smart and  managing the precious space you got is maybe the most tactical thing about this game.
A few notes worth noting for the devs:
- Pathing: So whoever wrote the code to move a billion zombies across the map is brilliant. Can you please put that guy/girl in charge of the pathfinding for your soldiers? Because they are shodding horrible at current. You can send out 2-3 people in a group and they will not be able to move because they bump into EACHOTHER.
- Pathing: Getting in and out of towers is silly now. Soldiers get stuck in between buildings and if they exit vs a wall - they are trapped. Microing them to exit the right side needs to be fixed. Especially in a game where time is of the essence
- Diagonal walls 2 tiles deep needs to be.... diagonal. Right now you end up with weird flukes where you try to reinforce a section but instead just create strange weakspots because it cant be 3 tiles across anywhere.
- AI handeling "hunt and search" needs to keep the group tight. One man vs a zombie horde = bad. A group - can clean up pretty good. But you got to babysit them as they will wedge out and (bad 1) Attract zombies all around at once getting smothered. and (bad 2) sometimes 1-2 guys will trail off and engage the horde in an oposite direction. Good function. Not well implemented. Lets be able to "send them off" and have them keep tight
- Needs a button to show healthbars for people. Now you got to hover and hope what soldier status is up front before rotating.
- So i know the gameplay is about surviving waves of attack. But having a huge wave hit your base from a direction and then - sneaily - sort of have smaller waves try to backdoor you makes NO SENSE. Zombies are not coordinated. Sometimes you can have bad luck but away with the code that makes "your attacked from every direction at once" happen. That is just lazy♥♥♥♥♥♥and does not make a game FUN. it is more like "ha ha we stepped on your sandcastle because we gave the zombies extra powers" kind of♥♥♥♥♥♥
- One constantly gets locked in a misbalance of "not enough power to build a new house" and "cant build a powerplant because you dont have enough houses". That makes for some grueling microing where you got to turn something off, or sort of "manage around" a two phase lock. Needs to be fixed or recalculated. Happens way to easy.
- sometimes a small zombie goes into a house to attack it, and suddenly - the infected appears as LARGE bloating zombies. What the heck? Stop that. Again - that would be weird cheating. That tiny peasent did not just become a hulking colossus. No fun. fix.
But: I do recomend the game. It is beta and fun already. Limited build options so far but once sorted it can be a good fun adventure for a few nights. Score (for what it is now) 6/10 - but with sorted issues and more featuers: 7.5/10

Early Access Review as of 4/13/2015
Name: Zotrix
Dev: Zerobit Game [Friendly Chaps]
Genre: Arcade Shooter, Economic Management, Bullet Hell
Along comes a game, a game that bravely claims that it follows the olden ways of playstyle  that of the arcade shooter genre. Now we question this little game, we belittle and ask it, "Are you really what you claim to be?" And that little game rear its Early Access head and said. "Yes"
And that my good man and woman of steam and of the internet is what Zotrix claim and manages to land for. An arcade shooter game with elements of modern day gaming mechanic instead of sticking to retro style graphics alone to earn free nostalgia point. It's uhh... fun. In a rather brutal and uncompromising way.
I wish I was joking but in this game of arcade shooter it actually has elements of trading and resource management. To give a little insights we human have basically conquer the world and made colonies on mars when suddenly *poof* aliens came and destroy us. So you, another faceless grunt who ate the propaganda the world leader told you must now defend the colonies and cargo ships from further incursion. For mankind!
You start with a peashooter and a weak ship then you must choose a mission, look longingly at the upgrades and then shoot all the enemies that come in your screen and not die! Basically thats it but the added gameplay elements made for a more different experience than the rest, for example powerups are limited only to upgrade your main gun but you can add other side weapons, drones and shields to your ships so it can take on the bigger foes that plague the later missions. Speaking of which missions have difficulty number with higher being more difficult and adding more varied enemy type.
Your peashooter cant last long without upgrades and Zotrix allow you to do just that with the money and materials you have earned! The inventory of each station is randomized when you arrived so some important upgrades like shields might not be available. Speaking of which you also get material needed to actually make those upgrade. I suppose you're not really buying them but rather employing the people on the station to make those upgrades. Make sense.
Eventually you start getting harder and harder missions but i manage to finish a level 10 threat mission with nothing more than my peashooter craft and a pair of very powerful side arm so that counts.
You can also nullify shots by shooting at it as it comes or if you're about to crash, pressing space ducks you into 3d space for a few moment so you can avoid all those 2d shots from the other spaceships.
Good, good. Lots of custom track in the game and most of them are techno beat which i like, hopefully the dev release the soundtrack. A minor complain is while the sound effects and music are awesome the difference a level 2 shot makes and a level 3 shot make is rather jarring at the moment.
Nice retro graphics there, background is a clear contrast color along with the shots thus making it easy to see which is a common issue in a shoot em up game.
Graphics for the rest of the game is is functional and does not detract from the overall experience. All in all good.
The little game was beaten with its face on the ground so i reach up and said. "Fine, you're good." And that is what i say to Zotrix. A fun little game that does what it claims to do with good execution.
Scoring Methology [Courtesy of Meat King]:
-	S-Rank: excellent
-	A-Rank: very good
-	B-Rank: solid
-	C-Rank: satisfactory
-	D-Rank: inferior
Verdict for early access review of Zotrix: A-Rank

I voted for this game on Greenlight and I bought a copy as soon as it became available for Linux and it doesn't disappoint.  Overall, it's a very fun game.  It's a retro style bullet hell arcade twin stick shooter with really catchy music.  The game play is fun and addicting.  The levels aren't long, but there appear to be plenty of them.  You can choose which route you take, which alters which levels you do and adds to the replay value.  At present, there are plenty of levels to choose from and there will be even more once the game gets a full release.  The game has beautifully colorful 2D classic arcade top-down graphics.  It also has really low system requirements.  The game even runs at full speed on my 1 GHz dual core laptop with 3GB RAM and AMD HD6290 graphics. So, it can probably run on most anything.
There are only a couple minor issues right now, but its Eary Access and you have to expect these things.  One issue is that the Upgrades feature doesn't work in Linux.  Pushing that on either my laptop or my gaming desktop causes the game to crash.  This makes the game considerably more difficult as the levels progress and the enemies become tougher.  The second issue is that the controller support is a bit lacking.  The left (movement) stick is fine, but the right (aiming) stick has limited range and stays on the left side of the screen, making it about impossible to switch directions of fire.  But, that's not a deal breaker as the keyboard and mouse controls work fine.  Plus, the dev team on this game seems really friendly and they're active on the discussions boards.  They're actively seeking feedback and looking for problems, so I expect they'll have these problems ironed out before too long.  Once they do, the game will be perfect.

The Bureau is a professionally-developed ‘prequel’ to arguably the best series of PC games ever developed. It attempts bring the infamous tactical combat series to the console with Mass Effect inspired squad-based real-time battles. It utterly fails as a PC game and shames the XCOM title.
Writers attempted to push the envelope in a few areas: two major characters include a gay Australian medical doctor and a senior female agent who struggles with the patriarchy of the era. Unfortunately, there is still the trope German scientists and the uncreatively written, guilt-driven by typical lost-love protagonist. The main quest develops much too fast, introducing new characters and pivots before the lead agent has sufficiently investigated the story or the player can understand justification for the last plot twist. The non-combat ‘investigation’ missions teased early on in development were never realized.
Checkpoint saves, specifically before [skip-able] cutscenes break the games flow. For large battles, this is very demoralizing as failure to defeat a large end-boss means playing through waves of weak enemies ramping up to the climax that you've already seen several times. Combat is at its best when it clones gameplay that we've already seen in BioWare games. Special abilities distributed amongst your always-leveling squad are over-powered compared to level design which teases tactical flanking but is never effective at harder difficulties.
Several weapons and items are under-powered and the player has no motivation to explore strategies with them, others (e.g. the blaster launcher) are all-but-required for taking down large enemies. The 'equipment pack' modifier to soldier abilities doesn’t hold a candle to mother XCOM’s soldier customization options. A total conversion of the XCOM:EU for the 60s era would suffice better than this poorly executed attempt at a prequel. Not only would I recommend not buying this, I'd avoid playing it too.

is a third-person, action/adventure with a new and improved crafting system, randomized environments and more quests than ever before. It is set in the aftermath of a zombie apocalypse and several years after the events of the first game.
The crafting system, in particular, is extremely deep and focused as well as being relatively easy to use. Within the base, workstations can be created such as an Armoury to create weapons and bullets or a Foundry which allows the creation of different armour sets, that are then used to protect and customize the main protagonist.
There is a lot of possibilities when it comes to crafting and players will spend hours gathering resources needed to make whatever they want. It doesn't feel like a grind, it feels like a necessary step to further along the survival of the character. More importantly, is that it is fun and doesn't get boring.
As players taken on quests and kill enemies, they are rewarded with experience points which can be used to upgrade the character, obtain new skills or craft new items. Experience points are used for everything,  and will need to be acquired in huge numbers to be able to upgrade everything.
During any mission, a tactical mindset needs to be employed. This title, is packed full of zombies, and they are sensitive to sound, that means firing a weapon should be a last resort. This really ramps up the tension and overall playstyles will need to be changed on the fly to suit the situation. One minute the protagonist is slowly picking off zombies one by one, then all of a sudden too much noise was made and a horde comes running towards the character. Suddenly, players are fighting for their lives, running away and desperately trying not to be overrun by the different types of infected that are on offer.

This is an extremely well-made and entertaining game. It is somewhat short but it is easily overlooked with the sheer quality of this game. It is easily my favorite game of all time.
When I think of stealth games then I immediately think of Dishonored.

- A great stealth game. If you liked Thief, you'll like Dishonored.
- The game description is a little misleading, in that the premise is more about seeking justice than exacting cold hard revenge. Nor do you have to play as an assassin. You have the option of finishing every mission with non-lethal means, and you are rewarded in the long run for doing so (achievements, etc). But you can also play as a brazen assassin, if that's your thing.
- Gameplay mechanics are really good. In particular, the jumping and climbing mechanisms are great (for anyone whose biggest gripe for HL2 was killing yourself by falling off ladders). The levels include lots of options for climbing over things and under things, and for getting around difficult situations creatively.
- Good worldbuilding and atmosphere that also mimicks the steampunk aspects of Thief. Solid characterization. The main story won't knock your socks off, but it's logical and consistent. The city levels were well designed, not too big, not too small.
- I also liked the fact that there weren't *too* many options for abilities and optimizing your character. It's not an overwhelming choice.
- The graphics hold up well -- stunning, even -- though the game is 4 years old at this point. Runs very well on my very middling computer. Not a single crash or stutter.
- Took me just over 30 hours, including side quests (but not DLC).
- 11/10 will definitely play again.

Quite simply an icon of PC gaming among all genres and times. If you consider yourself a first person shooter enthusiast and haven't played this title, then your views are without context. Fourteen years after its release, Quake is very much among my top three FPS experiences. Do yourself a favour, get with the times and pick up a copy today.

Aside from DooM, this is really the game that started it all. The nostalgia factor is extremely heavy for those gamers who were around for the birth of the FPS, hardware accelerated 3D engines, online gaming, mods, clans, and the birth of a then underground movement known as the "gaming community". Quake took everything DooM did and flushed it out to really kick start the PC FPS community we know and love today. GldSource came from this engine/game (and really, in some respects, Valve). TF came from the Quake community. Do you know how many dozens of current game engines are based on original Quake code? If you started your FPS fandom with Half-Life, you were actually a generation late. DooM may be the grandaddy of the FPS, but Quake is still YOUR daddy whether you know it or not.
Absolute classic.

Quake Pioneered the following innovation in First Person Shooters:
-Recharging personal shields (every FPS today copies it)
-Dual wielding
-Dedicated grenade button
-Dedicated melee button (melee is actually useful in Quake)
-Complex characters (Ranger, Shub-Niggurath)
-Involving and deep storyline
-Saved PC gaming
-Made LAN parties cool
-Saving and sharing replays
-First ever FPS to include a map editor
-Perfectly streamlined online play
-Vehicles
-It is so good that games nowadays are referred to as "Quake clones," and some, like Unreal, try to be a "Quake killer"
-Orchestral music (before it everything was just bleepbloop synthesized music)
-AI that becomes more intelligent on higher difficulties instead of just having more health.
John Carmack's greatest achievment

I bought 'They are Billions' Beta Access about 1 months ago, it was a Thursday and it was 8pm. When I launched my first survival match against a billions of Zombies, I was amazed. Not only does it feel like an old school strategy game like Age of Empires or Command & Conquer (Red Alert: Yuri's Revenge ftw), it is refreshing, enjoyable and thoroughly developed.
BUT...
A BIG BUTT: I cannot recommend you this game if you don't have much time, because THEY ARE BILLIONS IS ADDICTING AF.
I played at 8pm till midnight, and I had to force myself to stop it, because I had work the next day and I had to go to sleep. Elsewhere I would've probably played till 3am or even more.
The controls are really good. Since my childhood I'm a gamer addict, I can still remember my Sega Mega Drive till this day and how much fun I had back then. Since then my passion hasn't gone, and I've played a lot, and I mean A LOT of games. I played many strategy games, especially the 'big and very promising' hyped games everyone was talking, and I was left disappointed. Some important functions were left out at most strategy games like grouping up units with CTRL + 1, 2, 3, 4 and so on. But not in They Are Billions!
And I really love that you have a patrol function for your units, this is such an underrated implementation in most strategy games. Especially the 'Walk to this position and attack everything in your way'. You might be thinking I'm overreacting, but I had strategy games where they implemented such 'walk to this position and attack everything in your way', but your units then CHASED THE ENEMY ACROSS THE DAMN MAP. This was so frustrating!
But not here. They only attack on their path, and then go to their designated location.
They are Billions really deserves the title of "Strategy". And if you are a fan of your units chasing enemies across the map: Don't worry. The devs of They are Billions even included a function "Chase" so you can chase your enemies across the map.

For starters, the game has two unique halves (roughly equivalent to each other in playtime), so I have decided to review each part seperately since they provide completely different motivations for someone to buy the game.
First half of Hatoful Boyfriend (the comedy):
If you're even slightly familiar with anime/visual novel tropes, you'll appreciate the sheer absurdity and satire that unfolds as you become acquainted with HB's diverse avian cast. Yes, you really do get to date pigeons (as a human being), and there's enough variety in the storylines that it stays amusing well past the first fifteen minutes. Meta-awareness and references keep things from getting too redundant even on the tenth attempt. It's sort of the "Stanley Parable" of dating simulations in this genre, in spirit at least. Laugh-out-loud funny in many parts. Great let's-play material either solo or in a group of friends.
Second half of Hatoful Boyfriend (the tragedy):
This is the part where the story truly begins--AFTER you've achieved the 13 possible dating ends from the first half. Notice that I said "story" and not the game itself. From this point onward, interactivity is very limited and sporadic such that choices become meaningless (technically, this is because this section is considered the game's 14th ending). But in return, you're rewarded with a surprisingly dark and emotionally meaningful story. The game changes from "lol u can d8 birds" to taking itself seriously and running ALL the way with it to fill you in on the 90% context you didn't even know was missing from the first half. This is the most I can say without giving away spoilers. You COULD look at this half as spending almost two hours reading... well, a visual novel, which is what it still is. But if you already enjoyed playing through the first half for its own sake, then I think you'll find it well worth the effort to finish the rest of it in what turns out to be a genuinely intriguing story for its own sake, not just for the initial parody element.

This is no ordinary pigeon dating simulator. Yes, you can flirt with and persue a bird of your choice, but it's so much more than that. Not only must you choose between Yuuya, the man-about-town and his smooth words, his half-brother Sakuya, the haughty aristocrat with a secret past, or any of the other mysterious and unusual birds at St. Pigeonation's... You must ford the confusing waters of an international conspiracy. Will you join the track team or the student council? Will you encounter the darkness beneath you all? Will you go to the fair with Ryouta, your friend and ally? Or will you take the arm of Shuu, the dastardly and intimidating physician? 10/10 GOTY

At first glance, "Hatoful Boyfriend" appears to be nothing more than a wacky idea.  "What if we replaced all the stock characters in an anime dating sim with birds?  Wouldn't that be wacky!"  Such a concept would last about 10 minutes, then it would get old and everyone would move on to the latest "wacky" simulator on Steam.  Surprisingly, "Hatoful Boyfriend" is more than that.  It functions not only as a satire on the overused and eye-roll-inducing anime character tropes, but it quickly takes those caricatures in unexpected directions and develops them into nuanced and, at times, shockingly original characters.  Some of these story arcs had me laughing out loud while some had me somewhat emotionally invested in the silly birds.
"Hatoful Boyfriend" starts off as a novel premise, but builds into a sharp satire and a surprisingly deep and dark story.  It does take a few playthroughs before the latter portion shows itself, but for those willing to venture into "Hatoful Boyfriend" (and have it appear on your Steam profile), it's a worthwhile trip.  :coocoo:

Subsurface Circular is a good game in what it desires to be. This is the phrase that I wish to start this review. It's very hard to present the plot without spoiling everything, mainly because it's simple, short and sweet like the game itself. Basically you are a Tek, a robot, more specifically humans finally realized that they are too busy or too lazy to do their own jobs and decided to create the Teks. Robots. Built to take over normal jobs like psychiatrics, athletes, librarians, nannies etc. leaving the scientists, presidents and other "big fish in the sea" to control the rest. What is indeed interesting about is that they have a consciousness, making them more emotional and thoughtful of what is happening around them. That's where you come in. You are a detective Tek, and after an encounter with another robot that approached you in the subway metro regarding the disappearance of his friend, you accept the case and start asking the passengers of the train about information. While you will progress in the game you realize that this whole case is much more deep and happening at a bigger scale.
While I was playing the game I felt like I was watching a theatrical play and I was making all the choices, possibly because everything happened in this train and no where else. The story unravels itself based on the dialogue which makes it more unique then the other choice games I am used to. Basically in some stations Teks come and go and you have to ask them questions regarding their life, profession and lastly the case. Basted on your encounters you will meet different personalities and gather more information. The story takes a dark turn when you, as a robot, start to question yourself if the humans have a hidden hatred for Teks and they are the ones guilty for the disappearances or the robots.
The dialogue is very realistic. The robots make the whole conversations have taste by simply talking about their chores, problems and life. The subject involving life, to me, was indeed interesting and I think it will be for whoever decides to play this game. I say this mainly because the developers did a fantastic job describing life through the "eyes" of a robot.
BUT not everything is perfect and I have to say that the plot becomes boring dragging down along with it the gameplay itself. It feels like the choices you make have no impact and the entire idea of  Teks "come and go" in a subway metro become quickly repetitive. This is the main flaw of the game, the fact that nothing interesting is happening and the end makes everything feel like it was for nothing, very unsatisfying and predictable. Hell, I half expected the game to turn up like that 1994 movie Speed with Sandra Bullock and the characters to realize there is a bomb in the train and there is no way of stopping but no, everything remained the same.
Not much to say. Beautiful visuals, no frame drops and I am firmly positive that it will work smoothly on any decent graphic card. The music was calming and had a happy-go-lucky feeling along with it.
The hidden meaning of this game it's what should motivate you to buy it, not to say that it has a perfect price. With all the questions and details about the disappearances I started to look at the bigger picture and see what this game wants me to understand. After finishing the game I went with my friends to McDonald's and while I was waiting for my friend to come with our orders I started looking around me and spotted an employee that was mopping the floor,the father who was laughing with his daughter while eating, the taxi guy who came to have a launch break and the angry man in the suit who was talking on the phone. Nothing wrong with that after all it is a busy place and a bunch of people come and go, but I saw them for the first time at a bigger scale. The idea of this game was to bring attention to the way society works at a more emotional level. How the mediocre class works almost like robots everyday to live their life, sustain their families and how the high society treats them like robots and their whole existence revolves around work, not seeing that they are talking and working with humans. As a human being, we have feelings, needs, problems and family. Everyday we pass each other on the street not knowing what happens around us, too filled up with stress, jobs and technology to see that we are not equal by money or importance but by respect and honor. Two things that this game wanted express through simple conversations by Teks and how humans feel like their only existence on this planet is to serve them, and they are wrong. Just because they are invisible to them that doesn't mean that they do not think about the actions that they make, actions that led to this amazing story. The game is truly touching once you observe and understand the true meaning of it.

Started as a brilliant Idea for a game, had it's issues but they were slowly being worked out by the developers. Stage 2 started of as a great improvement to the game, revitilizing a dwindling playerbase. The game was fun, very fun, but after a while you start to notice the cracks in the foundations of it.
The most important one being game balance. It's a bloody rollercoaster tilting the game something fierce in either Hunters or Monster way. Last week I was winning 80% of the matches as monsters, after latest patch I've lost all 5 games I've played. Usually when you lose as monster the enemy team has a few specific really good combos of Hunters, but now it doesn't matter what heroes they picked, they would cut through your armor like butter while you're trying to break down a brick wall using your forehead.
Take this example, you end up reaching Stage 3, your super form. Before patch I had never lost a game at this point, the entire purpose of the game is to kill the monster before they reach stage 3, or at least have them badly battered and wounded, otherewise you won't stand a chance. Yet I didn't manage to down (let alone kill) a single hunter. Because some hunter combos are beyond impossible to beat.
Add that into a terrible ranking system, where 1 win after placement matches took me into the next tier (Silver 3), but because of a hacker that instakilled me at spawn in the next game I didn't just deranked, but after another 9 game winstreak I had still not ranked back up to Silver 3.
The game is good fun as long as you don't care for balance, or if you win or lose. But it's not competetive right now, and the balancing rollercoaster is a joke.

I really didn’t expect to enjoy Dishonored when I first played it but, quite frankly, it’s one of the best stealth games I’ve ever played, not that I’ve played that many, and would probably be top of the list if not for Batman Arkham Asylum. The key behind Dishonored is that it presents you with a linier path approachable in any number of different ways. Go high, go low, sneak through buildings, stay outside or just endeavour to kill everything in sight. Of course the later isn’t nearly as easy as it may sound and will most likely end in you getting torn into 17 equally sized pieces. It only helps the game that the story is pretty damn compelling and a lot of the characters are genuinely interesting, if a little creepy to look at for any extended period of time. And, sure, the mid game twist (spoilers) is kinda played out but actually well executed and introduces a part of the game that feels fresh and new again. Then we come to the Outsider and the magical mechanics and, for sure, these are the elements that truly make the game. The Outsider really adds mystery and true intrigue to the game and the magic powers offers a level  of uniqueness that other stealth games just don’t offer. Dishonored really is the game that non stealth fans, like me, can enjoy even after a somewhat poor history with them and I thoroughly look forward to what Dishonored 2 has to offer. Hopefully more Outsider and less uncanny valley.
What an amazing story! Bethesda does one thing right repeatedly, and that is world-building. It was a very enjoyable short play.

Graphics - 8/10 - Dishonored has really aesthetic graphics, which arent high quality, but are still appealing. Its still worth picking up in 2017 is you care about graphics a lot.
Story - 9/10 - The story of Dishonored is pretty great. Its an assassination based game, and you obviously have targets to take out. However you really feel the weight of the story. The ending has a lot of weight from how you played the game, and there are many alternate ways to play everything in the game, arguably the greatest part of the game.
Gameplay - 9.5/10 - Dishonored is so goddamn fun to play with. It feels like putting together a blueprint of how you want to tackle each level, which are all different and creative. You can play Dishonored in many different ways, and they all feel amazing.
Difficulty - 6/10 - Dishonored is often blamed for its lack of difficulty and poor AI. Even on its hardest difficulty, it still feels pretty cut and dry how you can avoid enemies. Its a real shame because a harder game would really push you to finding creative ways to take down levels.
Content - 9/10 - A pretty short game gets a whole lot longer when you really spend time in the levels, reading the books, exploring the sidelines of the levels, and using the Heart to hear about even more about the incredibly entertaining lore.
Music - 7.5/10 - Not a whole lot to say. The music is fine, and usually pretty unnoticable. However the sound design is very atmospheric, and you always feel immeresed in the world.
Replayability - 9/10 - Theres a reason people have played through Dishonored a dozen times. It never gets boring. You always find a new way to play a level, a new combination with your powers, a new person to kill, or a new person to help.
Overall - 9/10 - Dishonored is my favorite stealth/action game of all time, and I would never stop enjoying its content. Especially at its already low price, its worth a buy even if you only play it once.

Volume remains my favorite of the three though, and I am very much looking forward to Bithell#4 in a few years.

EDIT THIS REVIEW CHANGED FROM POSITIVE TO NEGATIVE:
After playing at max level for a multitude of hours the grinding has become rather overwhelming. Token farming is so bad it pretty much defaults you to the in-game store. This is especially bad when upgrading items, an absolute necessity. There have also been a lot of bugs in higher raid tiers, which seem rushed. Cash shop now sells high level gear, making the game effectively P2W. Now there's an expansion coming and it's hard to say if this is not just a new ploy to make a quick buck off the game.
Other than its peers (LOTRO, Neverwinter, etc.), Trion is very shady about the ways it makes you pay up. While LOTRO requires about €150 worth of expansion packs and quest packs, it's up-front about it, while Rift lures you in with the free-to-play only to throw things like locked items (Planeswalker: Water) and locked item slots (Earrings) in your face.
The way this game is managed is truly sad. Whether that's the fault of Trion, or that there's simply not enough room for a decent smaller MMO to sustain itself, is hard to say. As I have seen similar things happen with other games. Going back on promises (GW2), lackluster content (SWOTR), or bugs and poor support (Neverwinter). Though each of these games is still healthy and doesn't have a declining playerbase. It seems Rift is just the victim of poor management.
The stuff below still applies generally, but it too covered under shenanigans I've come to expect from 'F2P' that it makes it hard to enjoy the game for what it is.
-------------------------------------------------------

What started out as a fun venture with a few(3) friends (upon the release of f2p Evolve), soon devolved into utter confusion and rage at what is defined as "balance" in the game.
For starters, we're not complete amateurs in the fps/teamwork compartments (CS/TF2/Overwatch). We watched videos and took to heart tips from veteran players. So we're average, or probably a bit better than that.
We INITIALLY enjoyed the game for the wow-factor of working together against a giant monster. But beyond that, we wanted to give the game a fair run - to see if it ended up being enjoyable for the long term (note that we clocked 25+ hours together).
That being said. The game is NOT enjoyable in its current state.
First of all, YES. I understand that it is a 4v1 game where teamwork is crucial to win. And to be fair, we lost more often than not during the early levels of the game. But when we lost, it felt like we knew where we slipped up, the game was balanced, and the monster player jumped on our misplay as it should be (whether that was a simple out-of-position, 2 players clumped, failing to cc properly, etc). But it FELT like we could win (multiple successful dome fights and health damage before stage 2/3).
Eventually, we got better and we did start winning (even against some god-tier monsters that are notorious for one-shotting/out-damaging healers). Even now I have a positive win rate on my account (I mained Medic and maxed my juking skills).
But then the nerf hammer smashed the hunters and the highly skilled monsters came out of their dens.
It felt like we were playing against the house, blindfolded, and tied to the chair.
You see, when a game is set up to be 4v1, the challenge comes from the 4 to perform their "roles" optimally. The four are constantly being challenged to work together seamlessly and any victory is grasped through the blood, sweat, and tears of our intrepid beast-hunters. The monster simply has to outrun the hunters (base move is high already), down a hunter (surprisingly easy for skilled monster players), then leisurely decide which cupcake he would like to have next.
Now, you might say, "the nerfs are marginal" and "you guys are just bad". Perhaps. But when you nerf the amount of heal/shield and increase their CDs then also buff monsters (albeit slightly), the tilt factor for a monster cleaning house just got higher (also the increase in respawn timers). Volatile games became the norm vs the exception. And that is VERY bad for a team that needs perfection to accomplish a gargantuan task. (Side note: lowering damage for hunters across the board also made it much harder for hunters to do lasting damage on a monster - the fact that they can just speed off and regenerate most of their shield in one go is like an adult bullying a kid for their lunch money)
Long story short, a game that originally provided some measure of satisfaction and enjoyment (assuming a communicative team/friends), ended up being frustrating and more of a chore than a game. Any game where mistakes are overly punished is catering towards an elitist demographic.
(TL;DR)
Game is inherently unbalanced - initial "fun/novelty" factor wears off when games become one-sided monster stomps
Note to developers: I don't think this game should be balanced from the perspective of "oh we need monster and hunter wins to be the same, 50/50". There are 4 players on one side, 1 on the other. It's hard enough on the 4 already (average gamer perspective). Plus I would want to see what the breakdown is on monster wins vs hunter wins by player level. But more than that, in my spiel above I commented on how punishing the game can be to the average gamer. Rather than monsters just curb stomping most players, the back and forth between being hunter and being hunted - that primal base is what made the game "fun". By focusing on higher level/elitist play, the game becomes increasingly daunting for newcomers/average players.

Fans of XCOM will probably think this is some squad-shooter that someone just slapped the "xcom" tag on to try and boost sales after the success of XCOM: Enemy Unknown.  With the exception of the setting and mobs you fight, this game has virtually nothing in common with XCOM.
First off there is no research or crafting of any kind.  This was one of the staples of XCOM, that you had to collect alien tech and research it quickly to keep up with the alien escalation.  In this game, the aliens conveniently leave weapons lying around for you to find.  Once found they can be equipped on every squadmate capable of using the specific type of gun.  No manufacturing required either.  Thus, two of the main features of an XCOM game (R&D) are eliminated.
Second, your squadmates are utterly braindead.  Seriously, they will stand there getting shot it the face while yelling "commander what do I do?"  Often after you tell them to move to full cover, they will inexplicably run out of said cover right into enemy fire.  This requires constant babysitting by you, breaking up the flow of the real time combat.  Their special abilities are somewhat useful, but you'll find that most of the mobs you'll have to kill yourself, as they apparently cannot shoot the side of the proverbial barn.
Talking to people at HQ is someone annoying.  You cannot run inside the base, forcing you to walk to everywhere you want to go.  Frequently you'll have to move from one side of the base to another in order to proceed.  Then when you do get there the animations are a bit "robotic".  The voice acting is fine, but everyone you speak to looks like they just got the body 10 mins ago and are still trying to figure out how to work it.
The game map allows you to pick missions, but unlike previous XCOM games there is no pressure to pick the most pressing.  Before, you'd only be able to deal with one threat and have to decide which one is more pressing.  In this game, no problem the aliens take their time and you can beat the missions one at a time at your convenience.
Finally, the main protagonist, Carter, is possibly the most unlikeable character in gaming.  He has the stereotyped "angry guy who lost his family but blames himself" backstory.  Yet, he never tries to redeem himself.  Pretty much he starts the game an a-hole and just continues being an a-hole.   At one point, he does something so stupid you want to reach into the game and strangle him.
Overall, this is a half-baked attempt to cash in on the resurgence of XCOM popularity.  Even if you're not a fan of XCOM games, there are far better squad-based shooter games out there.  If you do love XCOM I'd strongly suggest skipping this game.  Even though I got it on sale it was not worth the sale price,

It's easy to see how this game got savaged not for being what it is, but for not being a different game entirely. But on its own merits I really enjoyed it. If it has a primary failing I'd say it's not enough.
Almost everything begged to be expanded on just a little more, from the aliens to the tech to the main characters. It felt like there should have been at least one or two more main missions, a few more side missions, maybe some more viable weapons, maybe another enemy type... you see what I'm getting at. The game left me seriously wanting more - not just "replay it" more (though I'll probably be getting around to that soon enough) but just more content. The feel of this game would have benefited greatly from 2K Marin having just a little more time and money.
But I still had a fantastic time with it. The weapons felt good, and upgrading to the alien weapons felt even better. The powers also felt great, and I never ended up regretting my choices. (Sure, they're kind of limited overall, but they're still fun.) Carter is well-built for holding and pushing at the enemy line, but can easily be played to sow confusion among the enemy's numbers. Your squadmates all had solid power choices as well, with each class fairly well balanced to its role and begging to fit different playstyles. I stuck mostly with the same squadmates throughout the game, as well as the same equipment, but am already considering how to change stuff up for next time. Nearly all the kills will still fall on your shoulders, but judicious use of your squadmates' powers will make it a lot easier - the Support agent's shield bubble is a lifesaver, and everyone else is full of ways to keep the enemies off your flanks or help crack a defensive point.
I'm not much of a third-person/cover shooter player, but really, if this is a POOR representative of the genre, then I definitely need to play more. I'm not totally certain I'd buy this full price, but that's mostly because of financial considerations. I got it on sale and it was well worth what I paid.

Zotrix is a space shooter coming from an experienced Indie game development team - ZeroBit Games. Zotrix is also their first game published on steam platform.
Whilst, as any early access game there is a lot of room for improvement the game runs rather smooth and promises quite a lot. I've had the privilege of discussing the game with its developers and the impression gained is quite positive. Aside the fact of ZeroBit's constant feedback collection and the friendly nature of its developers there is also no lack of ideas and possible twists the game could take.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------
The game runs smoothly, which is really important for the type of games that is Zotrix. It is pleasing to the eye and with the adjustable amount of particles you may choose whatever you are most comfortable with.
Suitable music throughout the stages. I feel as if the music volume is a bit too low and SFX a bit too high by default, but you can adjust them to how you feel works the best and from there to enjoy the experience that it builds up.
At the current stage, players can select from an alright variety of upgrades for the ship which are not permanent. Every upgrade bought can be lost with the destruction of your ship and will have to be re-purchased. The story itself is currently not too big, but I can positively say that the possibilities of further development are endless and the game might become much bigger than it currently is depending from the path developers continue guiding the game to.
There is currently a very interesting mechanic in the game that allows you to go "in the background" by pressing space and thus avoid enemy bullets easily. Whilst I try to play without using this function, it is very good in case you cannot beat a level and in that way it provides an easy way out of a sticky situation in case you decide you need it. There are also small instructions currently implemented in the game that you may access by pressing f1 during the mission.
Recommended!

Sadly the common complaint that Wildlands becomes repetitive does bear some truth.  Most of the missions are of the "kidnap the VIP" sort, or the basic “Search and Destroy”.  A few of the missions involving the bigger cartel heads are more creative, but it still doesn't make up for that feeling of sameness.  Hell, even the final mission suffers from this problem – once you reach the rendezvous point, it’s basically a speedrun from the ambush point to the Mausoleum, only without Rebel support.
I think I've narrowed it down to a matter of convenience - particularly, the helicopters.  Having helos available to quickly whisk you from one area to the next make it far too easy to exploit the AI's weaknesses, as well as quickly bypass the enemy's defenses.  One too many a mission (especially the extraction/kidnap missions) could be made trivial by merely getting an armed light chopper, buzzing the few enemies near the target, identifying any major threats, and then swooping in to grab them.  And while the game will try to pursue you with their own choppers at times, they're pretty easy to dodge and out-maneuver.  And yes, even the final mission can be made trivial if you find yourself an armed chopper.
It’s big enough of a problem that I’ve wondered just how much of a positive impact it would’ve had on the game if Ubisoft either made the choppers extremely rare and expensive to use, or limited them to special scenarios or support calls with no direct player control (basically, the same way Metal Gear Solid V handled Pequod, the extraction chopper).  Certainly would’ve made the extraction missions a lot trickier.
Ok, now that my biggest gripe is out of the way, let’s get to the good part, and why I’ve bothered to spend roughly 85 hours playing it.  For one, the core gameplay loop of finding a target, scouting out the area, silently infiltrating the base, and gradually eliminating the guards is fun, and stays fun even hours into the game.  Collecting the gun mods becomes quickly addictive too, since you’ll begin to try and figure out just where to grab what you need to create the ideal loadout.  The game gives you a clue where to search by telling you which province each weapon mod is located in, but beyond that you’ll have to grab intel to figure out the rest.  Admittedly, there are indeed a few firearms that outshine the rest by a wide margin.  Case in point, the sniper rifles.  The moment you find a high-powered sniper with good range and penetration, there’s little reason to use that weapon slot for anything else.  Doubly so since the game strongly encourages players to snipe targets from long distances, and with little difficulty aside from bullet drop and delay.  And shotguns?  Forget it, aside from El Sueno’s SILENCIO! (a heavily modified Russian Saiga auto-shotgun with a drum barrel), none of them are practical, even when breaching interiors.
But if you manage to find a buddy to play with, oh man, are you in for a treat: this game is a BLAST to play with friends in co-op.  Yeah, you’ll probably constantly screw up the total stealth missions thanks to your bumbling real-life teammates, only to start accusing one another as to whom alerted the guards first, but that’s part of the fun, isn’t it?!
But for the one thing Wildlands does better than almost every other game out there, it's the absolutely GORGEOUS vistas.  It really speaks volumes for how beautiful Ubisoft's virtual rendition of Bolivia is when you constantly feel like stopping for selfies and overview pictures of valleys, mountaintops, canyons and sunsets. Or even just pictures of rebels huddled around a campfire and searchlights in the middle of a midnight rainstorm.  Steam’s built-in image-capturing utility is serviceable, but… personally, I prefer the quality of the pictures that Nvidia’s Ancel option affords, especially since it allows you to shift the angle of the camera, zoom in and out of a scene, change the graphics resolution and overall quality before taking a shot… lots of neat stuff.
Now, for the Ghost War 4vs4 PvP multiplayer.  I don’t really have much to say… got a feeling the other reviewers on Reddit or other forums will help make or break this aspect of the game, but certainly not me.  It reminds me of what the Sniper Elite games were trying to accomplish with their multiplayer, only they somewhat managed to surpass that in the sense that it is genuinely difficult to pick out enemies in this mode from the shrubbery.  If the bullet physics were improved, the sniping in this game would be something beautiful.  Oh, and for the most part, these matchups are truly about the stealth, not run-and-gun 360-no-scope kills.  The loudest, most-trigger happy team will be the first to be spotted and blasted away, whilst the most cautious and patient teams will bring home the bacon, every time.
In conclusion, Ghost Recon: Wildlands is one solid purchase if you’re into tactical shooters or stealth games like the Metal Gear series, especially with friends to play with. However it will become dull after a point, which is where the addition of the Ghost War mode will make or break the package for you.
