The Bureau is a decent game, but not what you might expect from an XCOM game.
It plays like an action game rather than a strategy game.
The action is fine and at times quite challenging.
Where the game shines is the plot and the characters. They make you feel like part of the events, rather then some distant controller.
The main advantages of the game are the the design, which looks very sixties, the character who you care about and the plot which keeps you involved.
The disadvantages are the reduced role of strategy (not a problem for me, but it is for many XCOM fans), the fact that your units have little character (it's a shame they weren't as well plotted as the main NPCs) and the relatively short length of the game.
All in all, i'd recommend getting this game as it is a good one in its own way.

While not as good as XCOM: Enemy Unknown, The Bureau still holds up as a solid game. While the plot is a prequel to Enemy Unknown, the gameplay is actually more reminiscent of Mass Effect: Combat is a third-person shooter with two squadmates and the ability to slow down time to use special abilities. Conversations are handled with an interface very similar to Mass Effect's.

Wasn't that thrilling of an experience. I purchased it during the super sale for $4 so for me it seemed like a fair deal. The story line was incredibly forced and full of plot holes. I don't understand how this is a "precursor" game to the Xcom series, anything on this scale would easily be left in history. But as flimsy as a setup as it is, the logic with the rest of the series is sound with a significant suspension of belief on the part of the player.
There are dialog branches with base NPCs between missions but they only turn out a few seemingly pointless developments to the story as a whole. At first it seemed like they wanted me to discuss and build relationships with the other NPCs, as in an RPG like Dragon Age, but it didn't really add anything to the game and the dialog was basic and boring.
The squad combat is much like Mass Effect, so much to the point that they give the in game characters arm bands that give them force powers like "push" and "pick up" However at the Squaddie difficulty level that I played it was integrated well enough into the game and at this difficulty level I'd say it was just one notch below challenging. It is not new, it is not unique, and it is also a little more flat than in other similar games. There are some underlying issues with the combat, the squadmates are for lack of a better word aimless. They won't initiate skills or anything without direct commands. If I had to micromanage my squad I'm much more into the turn based strategy of other Xcom games.
As for the atmosphere of the game, it doesn't really get anything quite right. The research / RPG elements of Xcom are completely watered down. You find guns in a level and bam. immediate access. The only technical tweaking you get to do is with the backpack item. You find schematics littered throughout the game and the backpack give you modest but unnoticeable powerups. I kept the same backpack on through 80% of the game on most of my squad.
The gameplay is short, but not absurdly short. There are a few attempts at giving the characters and story roots other than the games overall atmosphere of "oh snap aliens abound!" but they aren't worth the time to listen to the dialog. It's much more linear than other games of this nature (which I don't really hold against it), there are numerous attempts to jazz it up throughout but it just doesn't really come together. You get the reveal that human testing is going on. Then in the next room one of your squad mates "notices" all the testing for the first time as if it was the first mention of it in the game. So the game writers definitely didn't fine tune the pacing and reveals of the story through plot.  If the game was any longer, it would have been too long, and that is not a good thing.
All in all I don't recommend this game, there are too many other better games if you want squad/tactical shooter action, better strategy games, better implementations of the Xcom monicker in other games. This is the kind of game you pick up at a steep discount.

What a surprise. I read many nay-saying reviews about this one but picked it out of the sale with all DLC for under a fiver on a whim. It was well worth it!
General tactical game mechanic is almost exactly the same as Mass Effect 2/3, slightly better actually. 2 team members to order about, picked from a roster of crew that you can customise to suit your play style, the typical classes like engineer, sniper, support etc - its by no means perfect, you can't strip out its console friendly interface roots but its generally okay.
As with any tactical shooter as soon as your AI team mates think for themselves your like WTF are you doing? and when they are not thinking for themselves your like WTF are you doing? Dammed if they do or don't pretty much all the time, baby sit them, go here-stay there. I didn't have any huge problems with the AI other than them running into enemy fire and randomly jumping out of cover to smash a window or something. Mass Effect 2/3 covery-style system and err... 'powers' like lift, push are almost plagiaristic but acceptible given the way they are presented. Certian commands appear to be missing, such as if you would like a squad member to fall in but leave another one on a position, the command simply doesn't exist. There is no 'hold fire' and there isn't any automatic use of 'powers' option for AI, you have to think for everyone, all the time in battle.
There is a big problem with the issuing of orders, when in tactical mode you become sort of like a ghost and everything is in bullet time. You are able to issue orders to your squad but in this mode however you are still restrained by walls and barriers. So to place a mine or call a fire mission in to that critical location you have to 'move' there as a human would, like down some stairs and around the wall... you can't just move the cursor there and click go. Its definitely to do with this title being a console port and you can work around it but its very, very annoying.
Voice acting, plot, atmosphere - authentic and brilliant, its XCom but probably not as you know it. You don't really need to be a fan of the series to play this, its a bit off piste - The Xcom theme is there with some alien name drops, tech name drops and a bit of background but its heavily diluted. The plot at the end it gets a bit... erm, out of hand probably the best way to say it - still hugely enjoyable but not quite what I thought.
As I got it under a fiver in the sale with all DLC I suspect it'll be there again, next time its there I'd get it if you're looking for a pretty decent story to sink into for a bit with a few tactical elements thrown in.
[EDIT] Hanger 6 DLC
You get to play DeSilva which is a character in the main story that unfortunately isn't built in enough, but this DLC changes that. Worth it if its 'included' probably adds about 2-2.5 hours if your embracing  all the dialogue and reading all the documents as well as the missions. Some good firefights here.

TPS with cover, small-scale squad and rudimentary leveling and gear management mechanics.
+ High levels of detail, quality and polish (it looks, sounds and feels good)
+ Special setting (American 50ths/60ths, with some related music, places designed accordingly and historical remarks and story-related influences)
+ Some interesting characters with a pretty great voice acting and very nice animations/motion capturing
+ Good immersion. Story is nice. Nothing too special, but it has some interesting points. Apparently there are multiple endings, since you can make some critical choices towards the end of the game.
+ Good action. Squad mechanics are nice. You fight in a squad of three. Not overly complex. You can slow down/almost pause the game ("battle focus") to examine the field and give orders without sweating: Go into cover, attack that enemy, use special powers to buff/debuff units, place mines or turrets, push enemies around or draw them out of cover and such things. I played on second least difficulty. Combat can get tense at times. Keeping great distance to enemies worked the best. They try to flank you and if you don't pay attention they can harm you badly that way, but with battle focus you can avoid these situations fairly well (most enemies are highlighted through walls when using that feature, so unless they cloak or teleport around or use other means of faster movement they cannot really sneak up on you too easily).
? I've seen another review criticize the saving system. It's autosave and checkpoints only. I think that's better than having to save yourself. Quicksave and all may encourage some people to attempt mending every mistake they make in combat right away rather than to live through with the consequences (in case of "The Bureau" it means the death of agents - which I did avoid by loading checkpoints). At least that's what I always tend to do in games that give me direct means of saving (which can destroy immersion and challenge). So I think I'm glad how the saving works in this game.
? I wish there was a "stay in cover" order. I sometimes wouldn't want my squad members to expose themselves to the enemy at all. They act somewhat autonomous, if they do their health may get shot down badly. If you choose good cover spots and keep enemies distracted a bit with "minions" or by attracting fire yourself this usually isn't happening too quickly, and when they are very low on health they seem to stay behind cover completely, but I would have prefered taking less chances there in a few situations.
- Controls are irritating a bit. You sprint with SHIFT and go into cover with that as well. Because of that when sprinting close to objects you sometimes go into cover without wanting it. I couldn't find or remember a specific button to pull out of the "Move there" order either (I did improvise with another order). Sprinting itself feels a bit odd or "strict" too. You can only sprint forward, not into diagonal directions, so you might feel slighty less "mobile" than you'd expect from most other action titles. Moving around the HQ can feel tedious at times because you cannot sprint there.
- Allied A.I. is sometimes making strange moves. In particular when their position is getting overrun or pressed by hostile grenades they would sometimes leap/flee into the direction of the enemies rather than fall back. If you don't call them back a bit as they step into the open exposing themselves they may get hurt badly. But that's about all of "strangeness" I've noticed there.
- Using some abilities/powers can feel a bit tedious. Like if you want to spawn a minion you need to move a cursor from your character to the target location. But that cursor gets blocked by cover objects. Even if you are technically in range of the place you want to spawn your minion at you may not be able to do so (or not as easily). It makes no logical sense because your characters "throw" glowing balls to make stuff spawn, meaning that hip-high cover elements shouldn't be hindering you as much as they sometimes do.
- When things get messy it's sometimes hard to keep track of the skill/power queue. Every squad member has five possible actions (attack, move, special power 1-3). Sometimes you may issue around all across the members and get mildly lost. You can chain them, but you just don't see the chain. But it's not too dramatic, after all you can practically pause the action and look around and regain your bearings.
- A few strange bugs. Like sometimes I couldn't zoom in with my guns anymore, or the eyebrows of one character wouldn't load (funny, actually). Nothing dealbreaking though. Falling through the floor or something as mentioned by another reviewer I had never happen to myself. One time the game crashed, but I may blame myself for that because I've been switching out of the game to my desktop for several hours. That aside the game usually worked very stable.

Pixel Piracy is a wonderful rouge-like pirate simulator that has great potential and a lot of character!
Although the game is currently in early stages of development, it is clear that the developers are focused and on track to providing players with a quirky, creative and immersive game that will no doubt continue to satisfy.
The Pros:
* Simple yet effective point and click system for controlling your pirate crew, split them in to groups and give pirates special skills like fishing, cannon mastery, combat focus and sailing
* Improving loot system that gradually lets you obtain more powerful loot as your level increases and enemies become more deadly
* Explore far away islands all with their own features, some may have pirates inhabiting them, some may have tribesmen and others may just be populated by monkeys gaurding a treasure chest and hitting you with bananas.
* Build your own ship using a variety of parts that come in different styles such as oriental and barbarian. Ships can be as creative as you wish and vary from small one level sloops to multi level war frigates of cannonball carnage!
* Manage and protect your crew and equip them with pistols and swords as well as special equipment that can help improve base stats or... well... stop them from using the poop deck to literally. As the pirates level you obtain TP which allows you to increase stats that affect your strength, dodge ability, crit ability, armour, health regeneration and much more!
Current Cons
* Morale currently decreases far too fast while sailing between destinations even when particular effort has been made to make the pirates feel more comfortable in their surroundings (plants and rum)
* Dynasty ships tend to be rather... explosive and tend to be nothing more than piles of burning wood the minute they try to fire one of their cannons
* Lamps on the ships currently cause major performance lag
* Limited range of pistols or ranged weaponary
Updates i would like to see in the future
* Establish pirate colonies on uninhabited islands, start of with small port buildings, create training grounds for your pirates, blacksmithes, treasure stashes, war rooms etc, and eventually build more permanent forts out of rock with high walls and mounted cannons for other pirates to try and plunder.
* Obtain treasure maps from plundered ships which give clues to buried loot
* More ways to improve morale on a ship, maybe by keeping the ship clean of poop or boosted morale after victory in battle.
* Rum (Food Category) should contain more than 2 servings per floor slot on the ship - maybe give the option to buy larger barrels at a higher price with incremental discounts?
* Random monster encounters while at sea (white whale or kraken?) with the chance to obtain more unique and strange loot (such as a hat made from a tentacle sucker?!)
*The ability to seek out undiscovered islands (not on the map) by placing a pirate in the crows nest of a ship and increasing a particular skill? (Land Ho!!)
* Undead Pirates and spooky ship parts!!
All in All a thoroughly enjoyable game which i hope will continue to suprise me with new features and fun things to do!

Hearts of Iron though i will admit is more fun and is perchance the most fun ive had in a WW2 simulation when modded. . Vanilla i personally think it is horrible. But the game engine and basic mechanics of the game have made it a modders dream. If you want realism without modding, you might want to go to a different game, because this game in vanilla is very inaccurate and boring. Unless you want to play one of the giants of the war (ie: United States, France, Germany , Japan, China, Soviet Union,or the United Kingdom) Vanilla has nothing for you. If you want to play brazil, you need mods. If you want to play Siam , you need mods. If you want to have more specialized units for different terrain types other than the generic (marines, mountaineers, and paratroopers) you need mods.

Nearly 300 hours in, and this game is still great.  Far from perfect.  It's got some of standard Paradox DS issues, such as AI issues, but they really only stand out because the majority of the game is so good.. and most of those bugs are simply ones that you have to accept because you're playing a videogame (AI isn't as good as a human, for example).
The DLC-hating reviews on here are the main reason I chose to post this review.  Hate the DLC and/or the prices?  Well... you may very well be an idiot, but if you have a well-reasoned basis for your opinion, then that's fine.  But holy cow, go to the DLC page.  Don't give a negative review to the BASE GAME because you hate the fact that they continue to support the game w/ DLC years after its released (CK2, for example, is going on seven years).  I'm sorry that you hate the fact that game developers want to get paid, but there's a REASON most devs don't continue to support their games year-in-and-year-out... because of diminishing revenue.
PDS supports their games w/ free patches and they release EXTRA content for those of us who want it and who want to pay slightly higher prices in order to continue to support the company.  Those who want the DLC but want to pay lower prices simply need wait a few months, their DLC is ALWAYS on sale... usually at the time of release of new DLC.
The game is great enough to warrant a review anyway, but the idiots giving negative marks to a game they admit they like just infuriate me to no end, so they inspired me to post this.
Anywayz... the depth is amazing.  It's technically turned-based (each turn is 1 hour) but it basically plays as a pausable realtime grand-strategy wargame.  You can appoint ministers (up to 18 I believe) to assist with things and you can design your divisions down to the batallion level.  That's what I mean by amazing depth.  It's also got plenty of flavor events, such as Earhart and the '36 Olympics.  And, of course, the game is incredibly mod-friendly.  If you find shortcomings in the base game and/or the DLC, then head to the workshop.  There's PLENTY of amazing stuff there.
*IF* you find the videos and reviews interesting, you'll most likely absolutely love the game.  If you read the reviews and watch the videos and think "people are entertained by this?  YAWN!!!!!" then you'll probably hate this game.
If you're reading this you're probably at least moderately curious... so you'd likely really enjoy it!

I bought into this game based solely on it's concept. I want to love this game so much, it has, at least in theory, everything I want in a space game. Spaceships that you can walk around in, planets you can visit, multiple factions you can join, a free roaming (but sometimes limited for story reasons) sandbox universe... It even has in-ship fighting where you can get boarded by enemies or board enemy spacecraft to comandeer it yourself.
The game is a few years old, and the mileage doesn't give it any compliments. It has aged, and it hasn't aged well. It most likely wasn't even very visual-heavy back when it was first released back in 2007 either. But that can be forgiven. The real problem with this game is how the awesome concept is being executed. It's executed poorly. I walk around, doing stuff, going, "Ah, wow, this would have been cool if they had made it like that," or "this is kind of amazing, I wish they had expanded on that" etc. Also, the planets and stations feel copy pasted and empty, defeating the purpose of being able to visit them anyway.
In short, though it has many features, none of them feel fleshed out, and some are flat out stupid in their lack of polish. The story isn't anything to write home about either, possibly due to poor translation and sub par voice acting. Want to spend 5-8 hours tops fooling around in a semi open sandbox space sim thingy? It's 5 Euros or your regional equivalent. Is it worth it? Your call. I bought it, played it for a bit, kinda liked it, it was average. But I left it feeling unsatisfied. I would recommend waiting for another game that does this but better.

As others have already said, Zombasite combines, refines, and evolves all of the best gameplay mechanics and features introduced seperately in prior Soldak games. If you do not like Action RPGs or you value graphics heavily, this may not be the game for you. However, if you enjoy Action RPGs and place a premium value on both good gameplay mechanics and customization, there is a chance you will like it as much as I do. A demo is available for you to try it and find out if its particular style appeals to you. The quest generation system can keep you busy enough that you have to prioritize your objectives and go back to the other quests later as their severity escalates. There is always something to do, up to a desperately frantic pace depending on how you picked your settings for your current game. While it is still in early access at the time of my review, it is already a lot of fun. The only real negative I have experienced so far is that the management of npc morale for your settlement is a bit opaque without much explanation, but this aspect of the game is being worked on.
Update 1`/2017: An expansion is on the way with a new class and multiple new features, including improved town management. The developer has also been patching into Zombasite for free various improvements that he has developed for his next full game, which remains untitled at this time.

I was a great fan of Depths of Peril. It aged horrendously but in terms of game mechanics it was pretty nice and uncommon.
Zombasite is by the same guys, Soldak, and it reuses *a lot* of assets from that game, some have been improved but are still generally the same assets.
Unfortunately it feels like the game is still using that seriously dated engine this dev team used years and years ago and it's starting to show with *extremely* oversized UI and at times simplistic gameplay.
The performance is kind of strange as well. I never once dip under 60FPS regardless of the settings I use at 1080p (I avoided going 1440 / 2160p), however a GTX 980Ti (Boosted Gigabyte edition) has to actually get rid of more heat on this game than on graphically-intricate games like Anno 2205. I'd put it down to early-access but I actually think it's just their severely dated engine.
I'd love to give this a good review, but I think Soldak has shot themselves in the foot by using some really dated mechanics and then just pulling old content across the board.
Maybe a 5.5/10?

I want to tell you to buy Zombasite. I really do. Sure, the graphics look like PSX era stuff, and it takes a moment to get used to the maze-like map as opposed to other, more open overowrlds to ARPG games. That didn't matter. The game took hold of me initially.
The good:
This is an ARPG set in a fantasy world with a zombie parasite running rampant. You're the leader of (one) clan of survivors trying to make your way. This means recruiting new people to your cause, maintaining a town, and keeping up supplies. You have relations with other towns, all of them being other races of sentient beings, never human. You can adventure with them, trade items, declare war, have defensive pacts. It's amazingly deep.
The controls are solid, sometimes movement is a LITTLE wonky, I have found a building I should clearly have been able to walk through, that I just...couldn't. This only happened once though. Sometimes you run around a pillar the longer way instead of diving right in to the enemy you clicked to attack. Of well. The character classes are fun, varried, and seem somewhat balanced.
The Bad:
Map generation is...bleh. I've acutally had it where I started in my town, and the only connecting area had no exits other than another clan's town. This wouldn't be so bad, I (eventually) discovered there was an exit from the 2nd town to another zone. BUT! That clan was warlike, and hated me. Had to start a new map, incurring an EXP penalty.
You have a nemesis. Cool right? A guy to fight against! One to STRIVE to beat! Eh...it's parked way out in some super high level area, so you have to work to get to it. Not a big deal, seems reasonable. However, there is a thing your nemesis can do...invade your town. I thought this would be cool, have to suddenly pop back to town to fight off some event. After all, your town has an inventory, for stronger gates, and to hire guards. I thought it would be like a whole 2nd character I was buildng up.
I've yet to find a single guard I could equip, all of them have some HIGH level requirements, and the gates break REALLY easy. This means I'm coming home a lot to fight off the invasions. Not BAD yet, right? Well, those invasions start to happen pretty frequently. They can destroy houses in town, and you need your houses for the...bluh...happyness mechanic. See below, in the worst.
So, with constant, damaging invasions happening, the devs decided that, screw town portals. You know those things that every ARPG ever has? Yeah. You get ONE per MAP. Sure, evey area of the map has waypoints you can teleport back to town form. The maps are build like a maze though, and when you're miles of winding paths from the nearest waypoint, your town is DONE FOR by the time you can get back.
The Worst:
You know those survivors I talked about recruiting? Well, they have a stat. Happyness. This is where the game breaks down completely. In every playthrough, (As of writing this, I've played 7 hours, and started MANY maps to try to figure this out.) all of my survivors happyness levels just plummet. They start rebellions and are generally just agressive little ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. The thing is, there is no (revealed) reason for this. You can hover your mouse over their happyness level, and it will give you a breakdown of what is causing them to be more or less happy. This becomes broken because, all listed effects are green, and thus should be gaining happy levels.
Again, for emphasis. ALL shown information leads you to think NOTHING is wrong, but they are becoming more and more unhappy. THAT is a BROKEN mechanic.
All of your characters have traits, and those traits determine what they do and do not like. They don't all start revealed though. This wouldn't be TERRIBLE, but the hidden ones STILL MATTER! The onlyreason I can find from an extensive forum post, is those unrevealed traits are making them unhappy.
Summary/ TL;DR:
Potentially fantastic game is broken by a few poor choices. It is in early access though, so maybe it will get better. I will be keeping an eye on this, and updating this review if things settle down.

This is a really amazing game, it is a great mashup of genres. It combines the complex character customization of games like Diablo 2 / Titan Quest with many Roguelike elements such as completely random world generation and harsh debuffs that can kill you, and that's not even mentioning the 4x aspect of managing relations with other clans that can both help and hurt you.  I won't go into too many other details because other reviewers have done a better job explaining how awesome the game is.
One of the negative reviews says they couldn't feel their characters power but had only played for 6 hours. That's kind of ridiculous, it takes probably a few hours to complete a world and you usually get between 8-12 levels per world (set to tiny at fast with 20% exp buff), so it's pretty unlikely they were past level 20. The max level of the characters is 100, and each 25 levels you enter a new challenge level. In any case, yes it takes more than 6 hours to become powerful, and it should.
The only con to this game is it's done by a tiny shop and the graphics/sounds aren't great yet. Get over it, it's completely worth it. It's still in early access so maybe if this game can get the hype that it deserves they can spend some more tiny polishing and bringing in talent.

I have recently been on a survival/building game binge and finally gave in and bought Osiris. At a glance it appears to be one of the prettier survival games but it's light on content. After putting in 20 hours and completing most of what is currently in the game I'd have to say it shows a lot of promise and potential but I cannot recommend it to most people. Bellow i'll try to narrow down who I think can leave this game enjoying it and who will likely end up hating its current state.
WHO SHOULD AVOID THIS GAME UNTIL FURTHER DEVELOPMENT
+People looking for a combat focused survival game. Osiris has combat in it, but it is not where the game shines. For the majority of the game your only ranged weapons will be an energy pistol and a assault rifle. There are a few upgrades to these that can be found in rare drops but weapon variety is very low. On top of that the enemy AI of the game has an early access feel and after awhile you'll learn how to use jetpack tricks to dodge most enemy attacks. I died a lot in my first few days and then went on a 15+ day stretch without dying once i learned the enemy mechanics. Combat quickly becomes a minor obstacle and is very likely going to leave anyone looking for a challenging combat focused survival game disappointed.
+People Looking for a multiplayer game to play with all their friends. Multiplayer is supported in Osiris but given the fact I got through most the content in 20 hours there really isn't enough there for multiple people to do. Two players might be fine but anymore than that and you're likely going to run out of stuff to do in a couple hours. You could join a PVP server and fight against other players setting up bases, though games like Empyrion and Rust will give you a lot more mileage.
+People looking for an in depth base building system. Osiris has several buildings, vehicles, weapons, and items that the player can craft. But base design is highly limited as far as uniqueness and creativity. Buildings only snap together in a few ways and only a couple items can be placed in each one meaning most player's bases will end up being similar. Seen one greenhouse or laboratory and you've seen them all.
WHO WOULD LIKELY ENJOY THIS GAME IN ITS CURRENT STATE
+People who enjoy atmospheric games and exploration. Despite all the negativity above I enjoyed my time in Osiris and felt it was an amazingly beautiful game when approached as an exploration game, similar to Subnautica. The planet feels like a real alien planet and is clearly has the touch of design about it, rather than procedural generation. Sand storms,  dangerous meteor showers, giant skeletons of ancient beasts spread across the landscape, deep caves, and the aliens you encounter make for a fun adventure. If you look at the base building as a way to help you survive, the vehicles as ways to help you farm, then you can have a lot of fun mapping out the planet and getting enough resources to finally hit the big goalpost of making a spaceship to travel off planet. Currently you can mine asteroids, and visit one other planet that is a frozen wasteland with differently lifeforms but much less developed than the main planet. The way you travel from planet to planet feels a lot like no man's sky and is extremely immersive.
+People wanting to help the devs of a promising game with feedback and funds. Osiris is a beautiful game with amazing potential. However its hard to tell if it will be the next Subnautica or another abandoned game that never lived up to its developers vision. If you have the money to spare to help out an impressive start of a game and enjoy seeing games grow over time than Id have to say this is one of the more promising early access games Ive seen in a long time given how little time its had in early access. Its always a gamble but Im willing to give the devs a chance and try and help them some along the way. But if you're tight on money and looking for a game to give you a lot of hours of gameplay you'd be better off going with Subnautica, Empyrion, Rust, or other survival games that have had more years in early access to flesh out their content, and check out Osiris again after its had more development.

Like many others, I started playing this game based on its reputation. "Hah, a bird dating simulator! How wacky!" And on that front, it doesn't disappoint. It's a fun sendup of a lot of dating sim tropes, but there are little hints dropped in the game (and a few big ones) that something is VERY, VERY WRONG with the world and your character's situation. I was interested by all this and kept digging until I could find more.
And then I found have Bad Boys Love (BBL), a spoiler-tastic scenario that explores all those wrong things and so much more. The game abruptly shifts gears from comedy to mystery to tragedy, and it all feels 100% natural. I was near tears from the tragic life circumstances and trials of birds. BIRDS, FOR ODIN'S SAKE. While the game would be worth a recommendation just on its comedic merits, the quality of writing in BBL goes above and beyond all expectations; I haven't felt so moved by a dating sim/visual novel since Katawa Shoujo or A Drug that Makes You Dream. I cannot stress this enough: A BIRD DATING SIM DELIVERS A SERIOUS, MOVING PLOTLINE THAT STANDS TALL AGAINST THE BEST IN THE BIZ. THIS IS NOT A DRILL. THERE IS NO PUNCHLINE.
Everyone should play this game. Just suspend your disbelief a little more than usual, and you'll find a mindblowing game awaiting you. It is not without its faults (dodgy grammar in a few spots, replay-unfriendly dialogue skip button that will blow right past lines you haven't read before, lack of more... bird pictures for emotion [???]), but this is a gaming experience unlike anything out there. Give it a chance. Its uniqueness alone makes it worth a glance.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Its hard for me to decide whether I'm enjoying this game or not, for these specific reasons, and I'll start off with talking about the first game..
I played the first game ALOT when it was free monthly game on Xbox One. I beat the entire game, and the DLC, and leveled up multiple characters, and even replayed the game with my brother when he visited local offline. The first game I thought was amazing, and deserved more attention than it got. I loved the first game because of MANY MANY reasons. The game allowed you to choose a character, that was different than the others. So one character was good at melee, another ranged shooting, etc...They all had their own perk tree, with special abilities, and that already was a great start. Then the game was completely open world (except for when you couldn't progress due to needing specific weapons like explosives to blow barries up), but for the most part it was completely open world, traveling back and forth between all the islands. During that traveling, you came to new areas, new enemies, new difficulties, new NPC's who gave you missions/side missions etc. The game felt like a survival game, and the entire time had a storyline you were trying accomplish. The entire first game was amazing, and had TONS of other things like each character had their own execution moves on zombies, so there was varitey as well. The main part that also made it feel like a survival game, was finding recipes and/or learning to make things on your own. Finding those specific parts were difficult too. Im sure I'm leaving stuff out, but you get the point about the first game, it was very very good. Now onto the this game....
The game just doesn't have that same feel. The open world is not technically an open world. You talk to Kovac and NPC's and you accept quests. When you accept the quests, it loads you up into that world/area, so its not part of the main island you're on and you cant travel there by foot or any means, so its not really open world. Its the same exact thing like playing Forza 6, or Forza Horizon 2. Forza 6, you pick car, mission and or track etc and it loads you to start line, where as Horizon 2 is completely open world and you drive around to missions, side missions, collectibles, car meets etc. You stay on a main island to build a camp, and the upgrading system is complete crap to the first game. No perk tree, no special abilities, you just get XP from killing and doing missions, then use that XP to buy your character to the next level, buy camp to next level, and buy your skills (which is not a skill tree really). You cant even learn recipes because they automatically are given to you just from using XP to level character and camp up. So no exploration or discovery to make you feel like you found awesome new weapons etc. Also, whats annoying is you find materials sooooo easy. I can find like 100 cloth in 10 minutes, just run around the island and grab 100 medicinal plants, wood, etc because materials are EVERYWHERE, so the survival aspect is gone too. Basically this entire game is killing and doing missions, getting XP, and using that XP to buy your characters level, camp level and skills. Each mission LOADS you to a new area, like Forza 6 etc, and when you complete those tasks, you come back to the island. No multiple characters with their own perk trees, special abilities, melee combat is dull unlike first game, no special finishing moves etc. The game is the same, but different in the worst way.
With all that being said, its hard to recommend the game, even though it still has it core value, which is awesome graphics with cool gameplay, awesome zombie types etc. Its an amazing game in a way, if you played the first game you would understand what I mean, but they changed it up so much (even though alot is the same) that its different in a bad way. I'm disappointed and just wish they kept the same concept like different characters with their own perk trees, special abilities, melee combat finishing moves, completely open world, allowing you to go anywhere you want and not like Forza 6, leveling up normally and not so quick, not using XP to upgrade character and camp and skills (would rather level up from killing alot and finishing quests, getting 1 skill point here and there to level perks up, etc). The game comes out Sept 8th I believe So i dont see any of this happening, but either way, its still enjoyable because of the core gameplay. So its up to you to try it out, its cheap anyways right now

The bones of a great game are here and you'll definitely have some fun playing it. I've just reached level 12 and think I can make some solid points now.
1. Graphical issues
There are a number of graphical issues. I don't mean driver issues, or card issues, but rather just things with the models and meshes that haven't been done right.
a) The bow scope when attached to the bow is on the wrong riser (below the hand instead of above it. This goes for when the bow is stowed, viewed in upgrading, and wielded.
b) Tool tips can get stuck open when working with your inventory
c) When wearing the upgraded backpack, the bow sticks out straight back. Not sure if this is intentional but it looks silly.
d) Very limited selection of character meshes and textures. There is only one female model (there are 4 male models). Don't be expecting to really customise your character.
2. Questing, Leveling, and Exploring, Camp
The way quests work is that you can rank a quest up (increases the number, level, and range of enemy types) and increase your experience reward but this does not seem to affect the quest rewards or the salvage you find.
It is cumbersome to check what quests you have available from who and what level the quest is. There is no quest tracker as you might expect, to find what quests you have you must visit each npc and get to their list of quests.
The crafting interface will tell you what quest you can best find an item on, but it doesn't tell you which NPC the quest belongs to.
When building your camp, placing buildings is a big mess of trial and error. There is no way to see the bounding boxes of existing buildings and walls and no way to know where you have free space and how much since what seems like open land may actually be inside the bounding box of another structure. You can only deploy within a short range of yourself, however there is no way to quickly select components to build or deploy. You have to go through the camp menu, open the camp inventory, and select the item to deploy - only to find out you're not in the right spot and can't reach where you wanted to put it, meaning you have to move, then open the camp menu again, etc etc.
You level up your camp and your character by spending XP, and then spend more XP on skills for your character (which are gated by level thresholds). When your camp levels up, so does the level of the enemies in the overworld/camp map. You'll often find yourself trying to keep up with enemy difficulty since weapons are gated about 1 level out of balance. You'll need level 11 to build and wield weapons you need for level 10 combat. Sometimes this is a result of quest that reward items required to craft those weapons being gated to a level, even when the weapon itself is not.
3. Combat
The combat feels pretty good, but needs polish. There is no indicator on melee weapons for which ones hit multiple enemies with a swing, and which ones are single target only. Range weapon lock-on works well 90% of the time, and the other 10% frustrates the hell out of you as it insists on holding target on the mob at the back, while you're being charged by three others, or ignores the big exploding guy to target a slow moving walker.
4. Gear
Gear is pretty limited and everyone is going to be wearing the same stuff. There are a number of unexplained stats and the lack of a character sheet makes it impossible to know what they do mechanically.

8/10

The Russians can be weird cats when it comes to open-world gaming.  Their strategy seems to be "throw everything in".  Sometimes, this works, as in the case of "Space Rangers" and "The Precursors".  In the case of Parkan 2, it doesn't.  What you get here is an open-world sci-fi thing that combines both a poor, repetitive space shooter/trader, and a really poor FPS.   Combine that with low-budget, constant asset reuse, and remarkably bad translation and voice overs (the same guy literally voices over multiple characters, and it's beyond terrible) and you have a real dog.  If you really want something like Parkan, head over to Gamer's Gate and pick up "The Precursors" -- while it has a similar lack of polish typical to Russian games, it is far better at doing what Parkan 2 tries to do, plus there's a community patch that fixes most of its problems.

A mix of a captivating storyline, unique gameplay, and amazing graphics makes Subsurface Circular an amazing game.

You are a robot detective riding a train. Your goal? To discover the cause behind the many disappearances of robots that have been happening recently. You will begin to question subjects on the train as you move from stop to stop, learning more along the way. It turns out that there is a lot more going on than originally thought.

The gameplay is smooth and not as boring as text based games usually are. The game tries its hardest to streamline the user along and uncover the whole truth behind the mysterious events with additions such as focus points or objectives, and the story is explained multiple times (sidenote: the train won't move to the next important stop until you uncover all the information possible). However, gameplay can be a bit boring at times. You may need to bounce between conversations with several robots before getting your answer and that gets repetitive after a while.

Subsurface Circular is a great game and I recommend it. The fact is evident that Mike Bithell Games did an amazing job with the design of this title, however, I'm afraid most gamers really don't care for it, especially those that crave games with more energetic gameplay. Many people won't buy a game for just 2-4 hours of standalone gameplay. Uh-yeah its good. 8/10.

I'm a fan of Mike Bithell's other games, and saw him tweet about this one with very little promotion. Decided to buy it on the strength of his previous work, and enjoyed it a lot.

But the store is interesting enough and short enough to complete in a single session, and the conceit and writing is entertaining and sometimes thought provoking. Think all of the on the nose, dialogue-driven moral movements of modern Deux Ex without the combat.
Enjoyed a lot, would recommend if you like games that are mostly dialogue choices.

I'm a new comer to portal. I've seen friends play it and understood it was puzzle based but never got around to playing it in its entirety... until last weekend. I have to say the hype for this game was huge when it came out but I never really understood why it got as much love as it did. After playing through it I could finally see why so many have come to love the franchise and is still a topic of discussion to this day.
As far as gameplay goes were looking at a first person puzzle game. We use a portal gun to create two portals (which allow us to enter through one and come out the other in a different place in the room) to progress through the level. It’s a simple premise, get from point A to point B but there is so much depth to the game. You can reach the end of a level in multiple ways, it’s not a one solution type of puzzle game. I've found that the levels have a good learning curve to them. The tutorial levels work well at getting you acquainted with the games mechanics and the levels get progressively more difficult as you complete each stage.
The stand out sections for me where at levels with robots aiming to kill you, requiring you to take risks and think differently to avoid death and also the infamous final stage which is easy to find out about on the internet as I did know how it played out before but it was a fun stage none the less.
The story revolves around character you’re playing as going through a facility "testing" the portal gun. You are assisted by character called GLaDOS who is an AI unit that directs you by voice. A few laughs were had listening to GLaDOSs “advice” and seeing where the story goes with her. Portal starts and ends on a great note. You are dropped into the world without any clues as to what’s going on, making your way from level to level, slowly discovering the truth of what the facility is. Portal tells a great story without overwhelming with exposition and staged moments.
The graphics look good enough. Portal came out in 2007 and it’s easy to see the age of the game. All in all I was surprised at how well the game worked with newer hardware. I managed to run Portal on an ultra wide screen with 3440 x 1440 resolution. It ran smoothly, I didn't encounter any issues playing through it all.
Portal holds up as a great first entry into the franchise. As someone who hadn't played it for a decade I can safely say that it’s a great game for all types of players who enjoy puzzles mixed in with an interesting narrative. The mechanics and physics in the game are very entertaining to mess with and it’s a game that encourages creativity in getting through the levels. It took me roughly three hours for a complete play through. Some may find this short but Portal definitely has a lasting impact and will have you thinking about the moments well after the credits roll.

The name sucks, and the graphics are not great.  I don't care.  Zombasite is one of my favorite games of 2015/2016, just like Drox Operative (Soldak's previous game) was one of my favorite games of 2012.  I like how there are so many factions that can be fighting or allying with each other.  I like how party members have personality traits that affect their interaction with other party members or clan members.  I like how elite monsters start sending out scouts and raiding as they get stronger (they level up, too).  Basically, Zombasite has the kind of dynamic environment I enjoy experiencing.
One example: I got six NPCs to join one of my clans.  Two of them started flirting and married each other, and then one of them got killed during a hunting trip (you can send out NPCs on independent missions to collect food or other resources, but you can escort them if you wish) by an elite monster.  The spouse went insane and went berserk, and the surviving party members had to put her down.  Her husband became a ghost and attacked the party, and we ended up running away.  The survivors became unhappy, one started secretly poisoning the others, and he eventually let in a raid party of monsters that killed the remaining clan members.   That was pretty sad... but also pretty cool!
Character creation can be fun to experiment with.  You can select from one of several classes, or you can create a hybrid character with fewer (but more specialized) skills.
I do wish the 'intelligent zombie virus' was more of a threat.  I'd like to see coordinated attacks by infected monsters and NPCs.  I'd like to see zombies overrun a weak clan so they can zombify the population and eventually overwhelm stronger clans.  I'd also like to see zombie squads surround and flank clan parties so they become outnumbered, rather than just trickle individually into their weapons and spells.
(reviewed version: 0.913)

PROs:
+innovative game mechanics:
+you lead a clan and can recruit NPCs and make them part of your clan (tip: followers have unique abilities so make sure the ones you invite will be extremely useful like 700% buff to foraging, create food randomly, increase happiness for the clan etc).
+you also need to manage your clan's food, insanity and happiness
+Dynamic world: every quest can be failed if you don't complete it in time, this includes stuff like your followers becoming insane or enemies mounting a siege on your village
+Class creation is surprising in depth, you can choose between 9 classes (which have 3 skill trees each) or become a hybrid and choose between any 2 skill trees (protip: Necromancer tree is one of the best starting skill trees with AOE and ability to summon minions)
CONS:
-Horrible name. Yeah I know zombie+parasite but it's still a horrible name for a game, also I fail to see the difference of zombasite from your typical zombie virus
-Horrible graphics, effects, sound and music. This is still in early access but they haven't changed their engine from Din's Curse everything looks like an early 90's game. Compare this to torchlight 2 or Titan Quest or Diablo 2 those games look way better even if they're really old now.
-Map is confusing, since the setting is "Jungle" you have lot of fauna however this makes it hard to see where the places you can go since everything has leaves in the background
-Inadequate tutorial: Probably the biggest con for me, yes there is a tutorial page and some context sensitive pop ups but someone playing this for the first time will likely be confused. If you haven't played any previous SOLDAK games sugges you watch some videos on youtube so you won't get lost.
-Skills need tweaking, the game needs to overhaul their skills because a lot of skills suck and don't scale well whereas others are OP OP.
Despite all the cons though the gameplay is addicting, I have 18 hours played but all this is just in 3 days, I play it and lose all track of time. Highly recommended from a long time ARPG fan.

TL;DR: I really wanted to like this game. Tons of good ideas, borrowed from various game genres. But skill trees and fighting are plagued by huge negative points (imho), and since we're talking about a hack'n'slash, that's a deal breaker.
Positive:
Like in many other games of this developper, there are a lot of good ideas:
- Living map/quest system
- Customizable difficulty
- The zombie parameter is actually quite interesting
- Tons of loot of various rarity levels.
- 4 victory conditions / map is another good idea.
- Being able to opt for a hybrid class (at a cost) is cool.
BUT the negative points are a deal breaker IMHO.
Negative:
- Skill trees and whole classes need a lot of refining. Some skills are clearly useless. Others are incredibly strong, like, only interesting skill in the tree. Some scale terribly, and are useless quite rapidly, no matter how many points you invest in them. A few actually get worse with the scaling. Attack and cast speed are also weird. A lot of potential builds are non-viable because of all of this.
- Action itself isn't really dynamic. Compared to other hack'n'slashes like Path of Exile or Grim Dawn, this is shocking. You cannot "feel" your power. You are auto-attacking A LOT, and many skills feel exactly like an auto-attack. AoE skills are scarce, meaning it takes a lot of time to clean trash mobs.
- Vocabulary is not really accurate. Again, compared to PoE, where a specific word means a very specific thing, here, you regularly wonder how do things stack together.
- Oh, and visuals are dated. Not really a deal breaker, but one could expect a bit better.

In case you're not a zombie fan (I'm definitely sick of zombie games) I barely even notice that they are included. They can infect you but it's just a matter of drinking a potion and it goes away. The fact modding will be heavily supported means I'm sure people could even strip out the whole zombie aspect and just make it a standard fantasy setting!

Lots of loot
Strategy aspects with your villagers, managing food etc.
Infinite replayability!
Cons:
Graphics could be a little less 2000ish
Sound and music could use an overhaul
Who do I reccomend this to?
Action RPG fans, roguelike fans and people who enjoy dynaic and procedurally generated worlds.
Who do I not reccomend this to?
People who only care about graphics and people who need a strict story/guidance in the game.

Did you like Mass Effect? Did you enjoy the tactical aspects of it? Were you♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off beyond belief when they started easing out the tactical features for straight up combat in the sequels? Were you also intimidated by the WALLS OF TEXT within Mass Effect lore? Do you desire something a little more... generic? Familiar? Bland? If you said yes to these then welcome to The Bureau: XCOM Declassified. It's a good game but it pales in comparison to a large number of cover based shooters, espcially the Mass Effect series that a LOT of this game is influenced from.
And like I said, it's a good game. It's slow to start and if you don't spend time emphasizing tactical commands you ARE going to die. A lot. Your teammates will make sure to tell you this, constantly. Whether it's jumping to other pieces of cover INTO enemy fire, whining after taking a few shots to damage and asking you if you're alright when you take similar damage, or freaking out when enemies start slowly approaching right into your line of fire. The AI is actually somewhat sharp, though pathfinding is pathetic so you may never actually notice. The story's alright as well, but characters are pretty damn dull and uninteresting. Plus while some games relish in giving you choice and letting you watch the consequences this game goes "here's an important choice, WHOOPS, WE'RE GOING TO DO THIS INSTEAD" while still vaguely referencing the choice you made in the background. There's a bit of a reason for this later in the plot (which was okay but used in a REALLY hamfisted way) but it still feels lazy.
So ultimately that's what I can say about this game: from the Mass Effect styled menus, and faithful work to the source material, it's built to be an alright game, but it never goes further than that. It tries some interesting things, but you can feel that not a lot of love went into making sure the game stood on its own two feet.

Played it with a friend, and we thought it was super cute and refreshing compared to other choose-your-own-adventure game. Few things to note: The story's based in England (obvious from the intro map), and the "instant oatmeal" is more likely porridge (hence the achievement name). Also, there are many who take issue with Sam's "lack of growth"; however, we understood her to be on the far end of the social anxiety spectrum--that she's not just afraid of dealing with people but of the POTENTIAL of dealing with people (think of it like being afraid of snakes, which typically encompases being afraid of even being NEAR snakes, i.e. I don't have to handle a snake to be terrified of it or being close to it)--so, the fact that she even braved the kitchen seemed like a pretty big step. The simplicity of the art was delightful, and the sound design was on point! Definitely looking forward to more from the creators!

A cute game with an interesting premise that unfortunately doesn't subvert the genre enough to make it not feel like an actual dating-sim.
Dating sims are one of those really untouchable games for me, I think they are dumb, weird and creepy. Yet, Hatoful Boyfriend seemed like it was going to really appeal to the masses through a bit of satire, parody and commentary. I guess it does do that in a way, if not much, which is probably why it's had a radiating but mild success in other demographics. But I expected more, like some more gameplay, or branching interactions to really throw the competitors of the genre in the mud since they rely only on horrible anime pseudo porn. If it were to be a great parody AND to also include some legit gameplay, animations or more story depth and length, to really show others how to really make an interesting 'dating' sim at the same time would have elevated it to a great GAME, not some cheap feeling visual novella with around 10 input screens.
Hatoful Boyfriend on the surface seems to only jest at the dialog of the genre in a very absurd  'lol dating games amirite?!' sort of way. Sure, some of the writing is silly, a bit fun, sometimes humorous and sometimes dark. But that's all you get, it still feels like i'm just playing an odd dating simulator after a few playthroughs.  Call me crazy but if there was a hint of a descent into madness, I would have liked to have seen a glimpse of it within the first hour of playing so I would be enticed to keep on digging deeper.
Maybe I was expecting something along the lines of The Stanley Parable or (more hoping) Frog Fractions from what I heard from other people. But alas it doesn't. If it does, however, devolve into an exciting madness, I did not get that impression during my time playing.
As a side note: It would have been nice to remember your username each time you played through but this is just nitpicking.
Anyway, maybe I'm wrong about the whole thing and everything I said actually exists and things get crazy and engaging or even quite long. But it never seems to, and it never did.
It's a shame really, I hope someone does revisit this type of game again and really make it into something odd, slick and compelling.

So I recieved this game as a gift from my brother yesterday. It was recommended to him from a mutual friend and decided to purchase two copies for the both of us, cos apparently I'm a decent critic and he wanted my "professional" opinion.
After an hour of simultaneous play, we both came to the consensus that our friend played a tasteless prank on us. It's also worth pointing out that this game is published by 505 Games, the same lot responsible for Payday 2, a thinly veiled piece of shovelware that somehow has a fanbase not detracted by its developers recent display of hypocrisy.
The following is a retelling of my one and a half hours of gameplay. If you're not in for the long haul, then scroll to the bottom Mr. ADD.
Starting up the game, I made immediate note of the lack of ANY sort of graphics options. The options screen consisted of audio sliders (which lacked a master volume option), two gameplay toggles, and little else. To give the developers some credit, you can apparently play the game with three of your friends on the same pc provided you happen to own three gamepads, which not even Halo does anymore.
Pressing local game, I was greeted with a terrible animation/broadcast which doubles as flimsy worldbuilding and flimsy character motivation. To explain both, a mysterious virus turns people into zombies and society has broken down. Never heard that one before. Second, your avatar is a survivor (big shock) and the broadcast gives you some wierdly specific coordinates under the thinly veiled promise that some Russain guy has "supplies". So, obviously, you character being a PhD of Social Science Math, decides that trusting some random schmuck with radio equipment during the zombie apocolapse is just a fantastic idea.
So I spawned into the overworld and I'm told by the delayed turorial popup that I should turn on the map and speak to the person nearby. It was an intercom. It was at this point that my contacts' Russain accent started to bug me. This game takes place in Louisiana, by the way. I didn't even need to research US state demographics to know something was up then, and sure enough the Russain population in Louisiana is negligable compared to New York and California. It was like in Sharknado 2 when the main characters just so happened to recuit the one White taxi driver in Manhattan.
As for the gameplay, it's your standard Diablo clone plus zombies. I can't speak for the first game, but let me list to you my set of universal combos: Click once, Click twice, Click Three times, Click twice and hold the third, hold left mouse button, and sprint then click. Also, of the many elements EKO Software could've lifted from Diablo, they used the stamina bar. The one thing from Diablo everyone can agree was extremely annoying. The first mission our gas masked "friend" sends us on was uneventful, so let me tell you about the second one.
"Loot the city for food, water, and oil". Sounds simple enough. What I wasn't expecting was for the phsyics engine to show its' age and start phasing zombies heads into the walls and floors. A cluster of telephone wires also appeared to be floating above a lamp post with no support. Interestingly, I can't even blame dodgy level generation because this mission wasn't procedurally generated. This was the fault of a level designer who selected the wrong map prop to connect to the power lines and either didn't notice or didn't care enough to fix it. Whatever the case, It gave me a good laugh and turned the level into an unintentional comedy piece.
So then we enter the bunker where our mystery man is holed up and the first thing I saw was several zombies in hamster wheels. Right behind them was our lovable contact. I deduced on the spot that Mr. Gas mask was most likely a self insert fantasy from one of the developers.
The following mission was equally as uneventful as the first, so I'm just gonna skip to the fourth which I'm titling: "My breaking point". So the objective of My breaking point was fairly straightforward: break into the house and find a gun. Here is where I would elaborate on the gunplay of this game, but unfortunately, I was unable to pick the lock and enter said house. This could probably be blamed on the games' poorly handled tutorials, in that most of them don't exist and the ones that do appear ten seconds after you've abandoned all hope. At the time, I had discovered that this game had a non-linear skill system and that one of the skills was for lockpicking! Placing three points into the skill did nothing. Yup. I went so far as to try finding a walkthough for this one mission, but all I found were fourm posts talking about how terrible this game is. The next logical step was to quit the game, obviously. Continued exposure did not offer pleasant images to my psyche.
To sum up my opinion, this game did a terrible job giving me, the player, motivation to even continue. My character has no backstory or personality (even visually), so I have no investment in them. Mr. Self Insert is just perfect at everything apparently and is employing me as his gilded indentured servant, so I hated him. The combat couldn't hold me, it was a clunkier version of every other top-down dungeon crawler I had played before. Just about everything else in this game was poorly explained, if there even was an explaination. It was a strange mix of bewilderment, frustration, and apathy that I would not recommend in a million years to even my worst enemy.
I'm going to end this review with some quotes I found on the game's official Steam page. It was translated directly from French, so I hardly blame them.
-Be careful when you got out by night,-
-You can now kill zombies in a cooler way thanks to the finish moves and gory effects !-
[EDIT]
It also recently came to my attention that EKO Software, being the mature adults they are, have been abusing Steams' lax review policing to downvote negative criticism and upvote naive praise of their subpar product. They've also been creating obvious alt accounts and are using them to create even more false praise for a game that doesn't deserve it. Standard practice for desperate "indie" developers on Steam nowadays, but I'm surprised these developers managed to evade widespread criticism unlike The Slaughtering Grounds. Expect this review to be buried under a heap of poorly worded objections from accounts with three games and one review.
TL:DR
This game is poorly made from a game design standpoint. I don't recommend it, especially if you have high blood pressure.
A very good game! A very unique approach and it's really worth it.

Who said you couldn't have yet another zombie game?
Anyhow, How To Survive 2 is a sequel to the first.
The time of this review was in Early Access, which means most of the negatives are gone when it is out of Early Access.
Negative first.
-It isn't the best port to PC from consoles, as you can see in the corners the "Press = to join".
-It lacks Exhaustion which the previous had, and Water Holes too, making it much more harder to survive, not to mention that its a confusing control scheme of looking at stats (Ex. Thirst 5, Hunger 0.30 or somewhere along that line(This also counts for most percentages or numbers like armor).
-It has clipping issues where zombies can go through walls.
-Instead of just a few island like the last one it has quests, and a massive world map (Which I do not like as the smaller islands were easier to navigate(However this issue is resolved by a mechanic).
-Some voice lines are mute(But as an Early Access this is excusable).
-The leveling is made strange by how it works(To explain to raise your level you need exp, but you also need exp to raise your camp level, in which then you need a higher level camp to raise your level higher(Ex. To get to level 3. your camp must be level 3 first.)
-The backpack system is weird as shizzah with decimals and such, unlike the first game where it was simple slots.
-There is a lack of classes, unlike the first one, but has a fair bit of customization.
Now for the positives.
-It has plenty of content for a Early Access(Many games on steam are half-arsed garbage(Ex. Romero's Aftermath(<-- Don't get that game)
-It is fun(For me).
-It brought new mechanics to the table while keeping the same premise.
-High level cap (Level 50).
-It has a "Fast Travel" feature to go to bunkers you have discovered on the free roam map.
Sorry for the text book of text, but its a review.

Summary: A game that is as rewarding as it is difficult. The learning curve is about as sky-high as is possible for a game, since the tutorial is not nearly strong enough to teach beginners the most basic principles of joints, momentum control, etc. If you stick with it and get good enough to play competently, it is a very fun and competitively fair game with a very moderate community (some nice people, some ragers, mostly quiet).
At first, you will be terrible at this game, and you'll have no idea what's going on. Chances are, you'll feel like this for a long, long time. But eventually you'll just start to get better and better at understanding the mechanics and how your joints work together. I highly recommend just doing a free-play (solo with a non-moving bot) and moving one joint at a time, to see how it affects your Tori. Understanding movement is ultimately just piecing these single movements together in increasingly complex ways (pretty impossible to learn quickly, it just comes with experience).
After you figure out how to move, then you can start learning the intermediate techniques like building and manipulating momentum or reading into your opponent's moves. There are a surprising number of Youtube tutorials for all skill levels of Toribash players, so look into those if you really want to get better.
Competitively, this game is very well balanced. No amount of play time or money spent will make one fighter intrinsically stronger than the other. It all come down to each player's individual skill. Unless the more skilled fighter makes a mistake, they will usually win. However, once you get decent enough to understand different openers and offensive/reactive play styles, you may be able to set yourself up to counter a more skilled opponent's move (especially if they usually open with the exact same move).
If you really stick with this game and put the time in to get better, you'll find a competitively deep experience with almost limitless combat options and an incredibly high skill cap. If you just want to play casually, you'll find a whole lot of flailing and a few cheap laughs. Either way, it's free, so why not give it a shot?

9/10 (EA Placeholder, will review properly later.)
In all honesty, if you don't like Soldak brand of action RPGs then you probably won't change your mind for this.  The textures and graphics are slightly improved (at the cost of poor optimization in beta, but I'm sure that'll get ironed out as things progress).
On the other hand, if you do like the very unique concepts that Soldak brings to the action RPG genre, this is the next best iteration in their succession of games.  You have clans, one of which is headed by the player character, and you complete quests for your own clan as well as others (if you want to stay on their good side).  In 4x strategy fashion you'll want to choose your friends carefully, and let the troublesome clans suffer through their problems.  Then again, that might lead to an early raid on your own settlement, or one of your friends, at which point you'll be forced into a bad situation  that will probably result in many deaths, or just one in the case of hardcore characters.
You have a great and inspired class skill tree, which offers as many combinations as are listed on the tin.  Powerful traits are added to mix things up even more, adding a layer of progression that is common to all classes, and can make your character's skillset,  in tandem with their equipment, very unique.
In short, so far it's looking so good for Soldak's new RPG, and it is as true an RPG as is being made these days, with meaningful choices that impact gameplay.  RPGs are games of choice, afterall.

First impression: this game will be a good title in Soldak's lineup. It draws on the lessons learned from previous games, adds a healthy dose of zombie apocalypse, and mixes it into a nice cocktail. It mixes Din's Curse's Action-RPG combat and dungeon crawling, Depths of Peril's clans and outside world, with Drox Operative's diplomacy and mission system.
That said, it's definitely a beta title that still needs some polishing and bug hunting. (Note: I wrote this on 15 October 2015, a day after early access was released.) The developer is very responsive and accessible, so do join the Soldak forums and leave your feedback to help make the game better.
Edit on 10 November 2015. There have been 5 patches to the game since it was released as early access; roughly one per week. They have addressed the bugs reported by players, as well as a lot of gameplay and balance issues. The developer is following his own tradition (see previous 4 titles) of incremental patching to polish the game to make it more stable and fun with every patch. So far, Early Access is progressing exemplary.

Soldak is one of the only innovators in the ARPG genre. With there previous titles "Din's Curse", "Depths of Peril", and "Drox Operative", I was blown away at how unique they were. Zombasite mixes a lot of the great features from all the games and creates yet another amazing experience.
It is developers like Soldak; I wish someone walked up to them and said "Hey, here's 100 million dollars, make the greatest ARPG game ever." Because I know they would.
***For all the newcomers to Soldak games I will give you a rundown on what to expect:
-Every "playthrough" you spawn in a town that grants you random quests, both main quests and optional quests. While you are hunting and doing quests, AI controlled clans are also doing the same quests in the same zones. The entire world is DYNAMIC. If an enemy clan kills a boss before you, quest failed.
-Factor in bosses and enemies being dynamic as well. Bosses get promoted to become stronger and certain enemies can take over zones and become stronger.
-Factor in "followers" which are random adventurers you find while exploring to join your party and/or your clan to protect your city from invasion.
-Factor in these "followers" gaining levels and having random skills to use like you. As well as being fully equipped with items. You can also send your followers on scavenger hunts for food and potions.
-Factor in endless replayability in many forms. When you create a character, you can activate many different difficult challenges that make the game different. Maybe a mode where you can ONLY equip artifact or above items.
-Factor in full customization via simple mods. If you think experience gain is too slow or too fast, you can reduce it via a text file. If you want the base run speed to be faster, you can edit the text file. Or if you think the base game is just right, don't touch anything.
-Factor in online multiplayer.
One of the greatest ARPG's ever.
