STOP! Don't spend full price on this game. Its not worth it. Here's why:
The Bureau: XCOM Declassified is a game that went through tremendous development hell. In its early stages, as the game was being made, there was a tremendous backlash from fans of the original X-Com series. The problem was the use of the name X-Com for a game that had none of the look or relation to the original X-Com series outside of alien invasion. If 2K simply called it The Bureau UFO Invasion Declassified, they could've made the game as intended... But no, they stubbornly decided to keep the X-Com name attached to the project which only served to severely interfere with and cripple its development process.
Playing this game, its clear it was far along in development before the s*** hit the fan, and the project stalled as 2K struggled with methods to make the game more familiar to fans of the original X-com (by finding ways to make references to 2K's X-com reboot. A game I don't think would have been made if The Bureau X-com Declassified didn't♥♥♥♥♥♥off those fans of the original X-com)
The result is a 3rd person shooter whose quality swings between mediocre and ok. Periodically you'll come across areas and level designs that seem overly generic and somewhat rushed or unfinished. The Bureau also has a sort of identity crisis by featuring Enemy Unknown fodder enemies fighting along side the aliens unique to this game.
The story itself is a trainwreck. The end game story isn't just insulting and confusing, its practically nonsensical. Without spoiling anything, its hard not to feel bad for agent Carter.
Personally, I find the game ok at best. I've already played it to completion on PS3 and I wouldn't recommend it. Especially not to an X-com fan. The only reason I have it is Steam keeps running a sale where you can buy X-Com Enemy Unknown and get this game with it for spare change.

There are some things to like about this game, but as a whole, it feels unfinished. Not incomplete, but simply that at some stage in its development, the team realized it wasn't going to do well, and they cobbled together the parts they were working on to form a whole, joining up bits and pieces willy-nilly.
I believe it was meant to have a branching storyline. Instead, only one set of events is allowed to happen, and because of this, you appear to make choices that are immediately undone.
There appears to have been an upgrade, or finding technology mechanic, involving a tool to discover new items.  Instead, you simply start to find new alien weapons after certain levels.
Customization is very cut down, and unappealing.
The combat system, which is really the only real gameplay mechanic (there are halfhearted attempts at sidequests in the base, but they are obviously vestigial) is lackluster. It might have been interesting, but is plagued by bad AI by your companions, who are powerful enough that you can't ignore them, and weak enough that you feel more like a nanny, wasting time telling them how to not kill themselves rather than feeling like you are making use of them.
Strategy is lumpy. It might have been good, but would have needed some smoothing out. Obviously, mobility was meant to be a priority, so combat arenas - and there is no freeform combat, only heavily engineered arenas with clear signifiers to inform you you are about to have a fight - often have reinforcements arriving from unexpected avenues. But they usually do this incredibly close to the actual field of battle.  You can see enemies miles away across the field if they have officially entered it, but when they do enter, they could actually be within melee range right away. This means that rather than forcing the player to adapt to a changing battlefield, what usually happens is you get stomped on by unfairly appearing enemies the first time you play an arena, then you can strategize based on where you know they will appear in on subsequent playthroughs. This is not ideal.
The toughest enemies jump around the battlefield, negating a feeling that you are ever in control of a position. Armour and shields are an interesting mechanic, but they don't really gel properly. Ideally, one would expect you use a heavy weapon or special ability to remove armour from a narrow area on a target's body, for example, then snipe them precisely in that area to kill them. In actuality, armoured enemies have high hitpoints as well, and even the alien sniper rifle requires more than a full clip to finish them, so you do find yourself just randomly blasting them with a heavy weapon both before and after armour has been broken.
Some interesting ideas for companion abilities fail rather spectacularly. You can have a sniper NPC, for example, whose abilities allow him to cloak, and then assume a position other characters wouldn't be able to reach because of it. NPCs gain bonuses for attacking enemies who are not properly in cover from their angle, and are flanked, so this should work out well. Furthermore, most arenas are designed with this in mind, so they have spots specifically for the sniper. This is hamfisted, but appreciated. However, the NPCs AI appears to force them to return to your side if they leave your specifically designate field of command, and since these sniper spots are usually on the far edge of your command area, it means that if you decide to move just a little bit too far from where you initially gave the command, these shining examples of tactical know-how will suddenly decide to charge headfirst through the most dangerous field of combat, unstealthed, to be close to you again. When you couple this with the mechanic where the player and NPCs have to be revived if injured, but they have a time limit which does not reset if injured again (so subsequent KOs give you less and less time to revive them) this is catastrophic: the further away an NPC goes down, you see, the worse the calamity is, and this NPC appears to be specifically designed to collapse on the other end of the battlefield. This is, frankly, ridiculous, because it seems to me it could have been fixed any number of ways, but the issue, along with several others involving NPCs, likely wasn't given enough time once the game's death clock was activated.
I like the 1950's/early 1960s aesthetic. Some of the characters have a real sense of personality and fit within the time period well. Even the clichés aren't bad. But the story clatters along, clearly going too fast to have anything sink in. Your first real mission expect you to feel bad for the death of a character you literally haven't had time to learn the name of.  Twice the game tries to pull the rug out from under you with plot twists, which I think I would have appreciated a lot, but it simply did not have enough time to back any of it up to give it the proper impact.
The alien aesthetic is, frankly, terrible. Not only does it fail to live up to the 50s/60s aesthetic, it is incredibly bland and generic. We have seen the 'pointy humanoids living in Tron world' look far, far too often for this to be interesting to look at. The alien guns feel almost like placeholders, being merely upgrades for the human weaponry for the most part. None of them feel like they have any impact either, with most gunfights feeling like bland watergun fights, spiced up only by the fact that grenades and melee attacks from the enemy can offer instant KOs from nearly full health.
All in all, a failure of a game, even ignoring the fact that it was a bad idea to remake this property in this form.  It feels like they were trying to make something that incorporated the earlier XCOM's mentalities, but either couldn't make it work, or gave up halfway through trying.  Cannot recommend.

Just want to echo Zanyscum's lengthy review below. I'm typically an FPS/TPS kinda guy. Even ME I didn't play very strategically but just ran around taking cover and blasting (and reviving). I was afraid the action in The Bureau would be off-putting, too "removed" (too tactical) for my tastes. (WHERE'S THE ACTION?)
And I must admit during the first encounters,  it seems counterintuitive when, as soon as you enter a battlefield and things heat up, instead of jumping in and lining up shots and chucking grenades at aliens, you actually STOP the action and begin giving orders to your AI companions instead. This sort of play is old news for strategy fans. But since this is (at least in part) a straight-up over-the-shoulder TPS, freezing the action isn't necessarily what you'd be looking for or expecting.
But giving it time and coming to some modicum of understanding regarding the mechanics of it all, it works quite well. The game is actually surprisingly tense as a tactical affair, but also requires some twitch moves too when it comes to the over-the-shoulder shooting involved. In a manner of speaking, unlike a typical FPS or TPS which requires you only pay attention to yourself and that's it (most of the time), here you have to spread your brain out, allocate it into several different areas--keeping your guys alive, making sure you are using their abilities to maximum effect, constantly readjusting their positions, while also getting well-placed shots in yourself in real-time. In essence you are playing multiple third-person characters all at once. Neat and actually challenging.
Of course, this kind of gameplay lives and dies on how well-behaved your AI companions are--and this facet of the game is a little hit and miss. When the action resumes after you give orders, they don't always go precisely where they are told (I've had guys hop a fence and stand directly in enemy fire instead of hiding behind the fence as I ordered them to), they ignore some orders outright, they charge in of their own accord (in essence mucking up your plans, which is, of course, on purpose--the game's way of just complicating things). But I'd say, 85% of the time, they do pretty well. I've seen worse AI companions...much worse.
It's worth noting that the game is buggy too--it has crashed on me twice, but luckily not in the middle of anything important. And in another instance, I wandered around an empty battlefield after a fight was over in slow-mo as Carter held the walkie-talkie to his head....and no one was saying anything. After 3 minutes, finally the dialogue started up and the game continued. Uhhhh. Also, there are some sound issues with sound effects disappearing (some of which can be fixed by playing in simple stereo and not in any kind of surround sound). The animations can be a little stiff at times--this is especially evident when characters are talking. Lip movement is definitely challenged here, unfortunately. But you get over it. The characters approach being caricatures for the most part (although some attempt at depth is made)--but the game is using 1950's-60's sci-fi as its source material, so you can't ask for heavy melodrama a la The Last of Us. That said, I DO LIKE the fact that this game is NOT a goofy send-up or parody of the old-school sci-fi trope. No, the game takes itself dead seriously (narratively speaking), which always is a winner in my book. After all, this is potentially the end of the world for God's sake.
On the up side, the visuals are sharp-as-tacks (I'm playing in 2560x1600 at ultra settings), beautiful use of color, though some of the far-distance backgrounds are poorly painted/pixelated, which wrecks the immersion a little. Seeing massive alien structures plopped down amidst a sea of wheat in rural America in the late 50's, basically tearing a farmer's field in half, is my kinda thing. Seeing the classic small-town corner soda-pop store decimated by alien blasts and black goo and surrounded by bloody teen corpses wearing poodle skirts and argyle sweaters--yeah, it's all there, and very cool.
If you are an FPS/TPS single-player type of person, and if you started getting a tad bored toward the end of Wolfenstein: The New Order, then give The Bureau a go if you are looking to expand your repertoire--and your gaming brain--a bit.

A mostly lighthearted take on social anxiety - very charmingly written and drawn. If you have 20 minutes, just give it a try, and maybe come back later?
I only have a couple reservations: it's essentially navigating a conversation tree without running out of a finite, depleting resource; which would be fine if all paths led some place fun or meaningful. Instead, some just seem to result in a death state, in a similar fashion as adventure games used to do decades ago. Choice-consequence chains are what you could expect for someone suffering from social anxiety, and well sign-posted, thus having only failed once, I cannot rule out having seen one of the less well-realized endings. With choose-your-own-adventure games, it's not uncommon.
It may as well be intended, to underline how social anxiety can be a serious, crippling condition for the sufferer, to those who may otherwise tempted to dismiss it, because of the game's light tone. OTOH from a mechanical standpoint it wasn't a big deal, the game simply rewinds to just before your bad decision.
I take it you're supposed to go back and make different choices, see how things play out but, unlike something like Emily Is Away, where the game is just humorous shades of not-going-to-happen, I was happier just finishing it once than risking inflicting more failure on a young, anxiety-ridden lady, albeit a virtual one. I also felt the ending was a little abrupt, and was expecting a minimum of closure that simply wasn't there - back to the safety of her room, her hunger sated.

I don't often go to the trouble of reviewing games, especially not in written format; moreso I share my views amongst my friends, but I felt compelled to leave my 2c on this game.
Having had been burnt on pre-purchase / early access games in the past, I am pleasantly surprised to admit that I had decided to give this game a go.  The merit here being that the developer already has a successful indie title behind their name (Terraria) and the fact that price point seemed right (steam flash sale).
This game is awesome!  I love RPG games, I love pixel art (though we've seen a little too much of that of late), and I love the commitment that the developers have genuinely promised to deliver
The game requires somewhat of a learning curve, don't expect it to be simple out the gate, though I believe that this might largely be due to the fact that a proper tutorial hasn't been implemented in the game yet.  It took me around about an hour to work out the core fundamentals.  It reminds me of Final Fantasy in a way, but I can't really directly compare this game to any specific title, it borrows a lot from a lot of different RPGs, but delivers it in a unique way
I haven't had the greatest amount of time spent with this game, so whilst this is an "early access" title, I consider this to be my early preview of the game.
I am very excited about the future of this game, including multiplayer, and I am very much looking forward to the weekend where I can sacrifice sleep time in order to progress further in the game.
The difficulty curve seems about right, sort of like Fallout in a way, quite punishing until you can get on your feet, but still challenging that it isn't a push over (yet), like what the struggles involve in the Wasteland until you get power armor and you are just wrecking everything.  It is hard for me to comment on what the end game is like since I haven't been that far, but I am definitely interested in what other tales this story might tell.
It would be hard not to recommend this game to somebody who likes RPGs, who finds the aspect of pirate pillaging exciting, and can appreciate the charm of pixel graphics, and cheerful humor.
8/10 from me thus far!

Osiris: New Dawn is an open-world first person survival game currently in Steam Early Access. The game was launched in Early Access on Sep 28, 2016 and as of the time of this report is in Update version 1.096.
- $24.99; will increase as more content is added.

In order to survive on a hostile alien planet, you'll need to maintain your hunger, thirst, oxygen levels, and integrity of your space suit. You're given the tools necessary to do this at the start, but you'll need to develop a reliable food and water source eventually. Oxygen is restored any time you enter a structure, and you have a handy roll of tape to repair your suit when it's damaged.
Weather is a factor here, but one that is more aggravating than hazardous. Rain and sandstorms cloud up the screen to the point of obscurity.  There's also the occasional meteor shower, but they're mostly harmless.
There's also a night and day cycle; during the nightime hours, monsters appear in greater frequency.
Setting up a private server doesn’t require port forwarding and only those who are invited can access it -- even when you’re not online.
When creating a server, you can choose PvE or PvP and the region. There are also several advanced options you can use to tailor your survival experience:
--For enemies, you can control hostile alien encounter frequency, their health, and their attack power. You can also control the resource yield, the resource recharge, and chances at special loot.
--For the characters on your private server, you can control the rate at which your characters levels up, how much XP they received, their proficiency and how many points they’ll get per level. You also get to control the rate at which your structures degrade.
Alternatively, you can hop online and play with (or against) the Osiris community. We haven’t had the chance to try the PvP as that is not an area we have experience.
When you start the game, you’re spawned on one of two planets--either desert or ice--and are given a quick tutorial for the basics including: patching your suit, using the tools you receive by, default, setting up structures (in this case an impermanent housing unit), and decryption.
After that, what you make of yourself is entirely up to you. You can set up a base as long as the terrain is flat enough. There isn't the ability to terraform, so you may have to travel some distance to find a place that offers some natural defenses as well as nearby resources.
As of right now, combat in Osiris is a little underwhelming. The standard pistol that you’re given barely scratches the hard outer shells of the planets alien life. You’re also given an assault rifle, but unlike the pistol it, requires ammo. The small supply you’re given dwindles down to nothing in no time and if you want to craft more, you’ll need to venture far underground -- which is quite dangerous.
Melee is another option, but if an enemy is in range of you, chances are it’s breaching your suit, so you’ll suffocate faster the harder you fight.
Osiris does some interesting things with building.
Rather than set down a complete building, you first place the framework and then craft each individual panel of, say, a biodome for cultivating plants, using additional resources. In that example, glass would be the primary ingredient.
There are different stations that you can build to open up more complex recipes, including furniture, and vehicles. You can play chemist and synthesise Hydrogen and Oxygen together to make clean drinking water, Lithium to make batteries, and other realistic synergies.
So long as you have the required materials in your inventory or the inventory of the station you’re using, you can craft to your hearts content.
Materials include gases collected from vents, organic matter from plants and the aliens you slay, minerals mined from the earth, and fancier things like rubber, wiring, and plastic that you craft yourself.
The selection isn’t huge, but what is available now is pretty awesome.
.Bottom line.
The planet is huge, but the building and crafting options are limited. This is a great survival game in the making, but you could do to wait for further updates before investing in this one.
It's not completely my style, but it is a fun game nonetheless.

This game is in the early stages and it's already so very playable. In it's current state you probably have about 20-30 hours of playtime unless you have more players involved and INFINITE time if played as a PVP game.
The best parts of the game are that it's so immersive, difficult and very rewarding for taking risks. The bad is that the content is not all there, though what is definately makes you wonder what craziness they will add in later. There are a few bugs you may run into though the developers are working hard to fix them. You may also find that the controls are a bit goofy at times but you do get used to them.
The reason I recommend this game is due to options. This is what no mans sky should have been and aside from the fact that it's not procedural or infinite, still makes this game so much more. It's so rare to find a game with such depth, this is the ARK of space.
Graphics: 9/10 - Amazing effects and shaders, great atmosphere and overall graphics. I don't think I've ever actually felt like I was in a game until I played this.
Combat: 7/10 - I'm pretty strict on combat and while it's fairly a straight forward shooter, different ships/vehicles give you a lot of options when exploring. I LOVE how difficult the AI is and the fact they strafe you, run around and try to dodge your bullets. It's so lifelike.
Sound: 8/10 - The clunking of mining is satisfying, the shooting of monsters is satisfying, the atmospheric music is satisfying. The only thing they could do to make it better is to clean up some of the audio that breaks up (Probably just a bug)
Overall: 9/10 - Definately one of the best games I've played in awhile. It's like a combination of Ark Survival and Astroneer. The only thing needed now is content and maybe a few extra "things to do" in the world. If you want a PVE space game, you may want to wait on content but if you want a great experience with updates in the future... check it out.

Even taking things slow and stepping away while the game idles, it clocked in just under 2 hours and I'm only missing 3 achievements.  YMMV on how you measure value vs. length, but that won't be covered below.
That being said, Subsurface Circular is an interesting title whose simple play undersells the work that went into it.  First and foremost, it is not going to be a game for everyone.  When you strip away all the glam of the game, it is little more than a conversation simulator.  You do not move, you do not shoot, you don't do anything except select questions and responses.  However, it's the content of what is being said and asked that makes Subsurface Circular a fascinating journey that doesn't demand a lot of your time.  Shorter than any Peter Jackson movie and more entertaining than at least three of them, those looking for a more cerebral experience might want to take a ride on this subway for robots.
Without spoiling anything, you are a robot detective riding a train underground and as you meet and speak with passengers that come and go, a mystery unfolds and, true to your designation, you try to start figuring it out.  That's it.  There's some gamey convenience here like the fact that despite the train car clearly having at least 18 seats, no more than 4 will ever ride it at the same time and they will always take a seat next to you.  This could very well be a clever nod to the fact that you, the player, never get out of your seat to solve this mystery, either, it's more likely the result of a singular focus - to have the player pull at a thread and unravel a ball of yarn.
Even though this game could entirely be accomplished in text, some TLC went into the aesthetics of the game, from the train and its riders to the floaty dialogue boxes.  Everything seems purposefully laid out in the Subsurface Circular and I personally appreciate the artistic
that permeates the whole thing.  Even from the very get-go, you can wiggle your mouse during the intro slideshow and for some reason, I thought that was a pretty neat touch.
At the end of the day, however, I don't think the game will blow anyone's mind.  It's incredibly deliberate in its design goals and I think the fact that it nails what it's trying to do is what makes this something that will be endearing to several gamers.  On the other hand, a subset of the gaming populace will quite simply not care.  It's not so much that they wouldn't 'get' it, but rather it just won't speak to everyone, especially the crowd that revels in twitchier, competitive play.
Subsurface Circular is like sitting down to play through a chess problem.  You have a goal, and you pay attention, observe, and act in accordance with reaching that goal.  It's a reflective process and I think by the time you reach the game's conclusion, you will understand that feeling of lone pursuit.  It's definitely something I think people should try out, even if it's not particularly your cuppa.  The most it demands of you is an afternoon.

When I first saw the trailers of this game I expected it to be more like a sort of L.A. Noir, solving mysteries and a bit more...discreet...
It deserved more credit than that, as it is true to the first XCOM game and nicely converted to an FPS with some interesting choices to be made, and then again, the illusion of other interesting choices...
There are several plot twists, deep and sudden, and the storyline itself kept me interested through the entire game. You don't actually get to build bases, but you are a commander taking 2 fellow XCOM agents into the field...and bases...and spaceships...and other complexes.
With this most excellent addition to the series I expect to see the next game with all previous features incorporated, maybe even some multiplayer coop; We already had the GeoScape and Battlescape tactical pieces, add to that the flight simulator we saw in XCOM Interceptor (maybe extend on that to be a real flight sim), the base design, research, development and maintenance, and now the FPS. I was playing X-Com UFO Defence (1994) and Enemy Unknown (2012) so comparison of The Bureau to previous games was natural.
First of all this one is not a turn-based strategy but real time FPP/TPP. You may slow time to observe battlefield and issue orders to squad mates but for your movement and targetting you need to exit the slo-mo mode and you play (almost) typical shooter. What is still different from a typical shooter is a concept of partial/full cover, being flanked, exposed etc. introduced in latest UFO Enemy Unknown. You're rewarded for flanking enemy by greater damage inflicted. Many times I was putting headshots in an alien asking myself why this sonofa6|+ch doesn't die until I understood that he is in full cover and my excellent :) targeting still results in relatively less damage than more "strategic" approach.
This is very interesting game that introduces concepts from turn based strategy game into a TPP/FPP shooter but in very natural and smooth way. If you're not alergic to shooters you may find it very interesting as I did.
And one more thing, you take much less squad members on mission (two) and I think this is exact number that is still manageable in slo-mo mode, yet makes this not a simple shooter with more slo-mo than in Max Payne :) but an interesting strategy-shooter combination, a must-try to UFO series fans.

The Bureau is a mish-mash of half ideas and borrowed concepts that never comes together. The gameplay and structure is reminiscent of the Mass Effect games: You start in a base, pick a mission from a map, grab two followers and go on a third person cover-shoot with light tactical squad elemets. Damage on the field is like XCOM: done based on the kind of cover the enemy is in, meaning unless you can get a head shot it is necessary to flank enemies in order to effectively dispatch them.
This all sounds fine in theory, the problem is execution. The game does not have the interactive story elements of Mass Effect, nor the interesting characters. Squad-mates taken on missions are randoms with no personality, meaning they are little more than a set of skills accumulated throughout the game. If they die, they're dead forever and trying to level a new squadie late game is tantamount to suicide since they can't take more than a couple of hits. Their AI is questionable at the best of times: Orders to do a flanking manoeuvre typically result in them making a B-line across an open killzone and if you move too far from them, they break cover and jog directly back to you, regardless of circumstance. This forces you to micro-manage them constantly as you can't trust them with even the most basic of orders.
Admittedly Mass Effect doesn't handle these combat elements much better but it gives your character more personal power to handle combat situations whereas The Bureau strips you of them. Mass Effect makes using your allies and their questionable AI an option while The Bureau makes it a necessity without compensating the decision, punishing you with perma-death if you attempt to get creative or if the AI spazes out.
The story is OK on it's own but as an XCOM prequel it makes no sense and ends with an unsatisfying meta-element which I won't spoil. The initially charming 50's low-tech setting becomes bland as tile sets are frequently reused and gives way to generic alien ship backdrops.
Mass Effect distracts you from it's inadequacies with a more complete package of interesting characters, interactions and locations. If it didn't have these things it would only be a semi-competent cover shooter, which is what The Bureau is.

Finally beat the first level but was under a 22% victory condition (easy population and 120 minute time).  The game is addictively challenging yet simple:  Build a base and survive an onslaught of zombies for a set period of time.
The progression is easy to grasp since there are not a wide variety of units...yet, which I hope changes cuz there is definite room for expansion in this department such as maybe Artillery Towers, transport like vehicles, etc etc.  But what makes this game so fundamentally great is 2 primary things:   RNG maps and the fear of losing.  You cannot save the game to then go back at that certain point and fix a mistake.  Though this has been asked for by some, I entirely disagree with it being implemented.  The fact that you can pause the game indefinitely is plenty fine.  Why is this important?  Like I said, it creates a fear of losing.  And the further you progress in a game, the more this fear builds because then you wonder:  am I prepared?  There is no trial and error.  You have to pause the game on the go (which is hands down your greatest weapon in your arsenal) to then best strategize your future development.  There are times I probably spend 5 to 10 minutes with the game paused just to analyze my next plan of action for expanding my colony.  And with procedurally developed maps, this strategy can alter from game to game.
But like anything, you eventually figure out the tricks.  You learn how to not bite off more than you can chew when expanding to new territory.  You learn how to best place resource buildings for optimization.  You create contingency plans to fall back to other walls/towers in case one side of the colony is overran--and yes, if a group of zombies does destroy some buildings, its very much possilbe to recover from as long as you PLAN AHEAD.
The game punishes you for not being prepared or not being fully aware.  Its plain and simple.
The game has tremendous amounts of potential.  There is plenty of room for expansion and I cannot wait to see what is brought to the table.  Right now there are 4 different types of maps that offer varying play styles due to layout.  But I would like to see a little more variety in types of zombies in the mid to late game along with greater variety in buildings and units.  Also, a greater balance between units.  I have found no reason to use traps.  Just stacking layers of walls seems best.  Maybe a fast "suicidal" zombie that can explode on impact and deal large dmg to structures but traps can stop them quickly? Idk.  Could be multiple ways to improve this.

I can understand why Dishonored got positive reviews. I can’t understand why it received universal acclaim. To start, it’s hideous. People call the graphics “stylized,” but Life Is Strange aimed for a similar aesthetic and its characters didn’t have the faces of deformed ape men. Just looking at the textures shows they’re polygonal, drab, and made of what appears to be wet river clay. It’s not a stylistic choice; it’s Bethesda not knowing how to make something run well and look good at the same time. But graphics aren’t nearly as important as gameplay and story, so I’ll let ugly texture mapping slide. In terms of story, Dishonored brings little interesting to the table. You’re Corvo (a name that should belong to a cartoon cat) and an evil tyrant frames you for murder. You have to kill him. But first, you have to kill other people, because you’re part of an underground resistance. That’s basically it. As with most Bethesda games, lore abounds in the Dishonored universe (primarily involving plague and the hunting of whales). The problem is that you don’t interact with that lore in any meaningful way. The plague is just something that happens in the background. No one imporant contracts it and there's no fear of becoming sick, no matter how many rats you cross or corpses you handle. Characters are shallow and the story doesn’t last long enough to give them room to grow. Even Lady Emily (who becomes the hero in the sequel) only occupies about five minutes of screen time. Corvo himself is a silent protagonist to allow players to “better immerse themselves” in the role. But the developers fail to understand that good character writing is exactly what makes a story immersive. A universe full of lore needs a strong protagonist to explore it and make it resonate. But Dishonored feels disconnected. The world comes across as empty and dead – not just because of the plague, but because it’s devoid of emotion. Characters don’t do much but wander silently around a base. There’s very little interaction, no dialogue choices, and no way to influence the grand scheme of events.  You can choose to be good or evil, but there’s no advantage to being evil, other than causing mayhem for the fun of it. The game rewards good behavior and punishes killing sprees by adding more enemies and swarms of rats to pester you. Dishonored claims to be open-ended, but ultimately forces players to follow its rules: and the name of the game is stealth. In that regard, I can see the appeal. Anyone looking for a cloak-and-dagger experience will find plenty of hiding in the shadows here. The game allows for varied approaches in taking out enemies, whether it be with traps, darts, or an old fashioned knife in the back. Corvo also possesses a limited bag of magical powers (for some reason) that allow him to teleport, see through walls, and bend time. The key word is “limited”. Don’t expect Bioshock layers of variety. Ultimately, that lack of variety is Dishonored’s greatest detriment. There are only a handful of levels to explore and their design is surprisingly linear. You start at point A and end at point B. This is not an open-world, Skyrim experience – and it doesn’t have to be. But when every level has maybe three buildings to explore and your main base is a lone building surrounded by deserted streets, the game feels cramped. It’s too short, too frustrating, and too lifeless to earn the praise it received. For anyone who hasn’t played the game, don’t buy it with the preconceived notion that you’ll love it. Too many games get a passing grade because of loyalty to the developers. This is one of those cases.

Nearly 300 hours in, and this game is still great.  Far from perfect.  It's got some of standard Paradox DS issues, such as AI issues, but they really only stand out because the majority of the game is so good.. and most of those bugs are simply ones that you have to accept because you're playing a videogame (AI isn't as good as a human, for example).
The DLC-hating reviews on here are the main reason I chose to post this review.  Hate the DLC and/or the prices?  Well... you may very well be an idiot, but if you have a well-reasoned basis for your opinion, then that's fine.  But holy cow, go to the DLC page.  Don't give a negative review to the BASE GAME because you hate the fact that they continue to support the game w/ DLC years after its released (CK2, for example, is going on seven years).  I'm sorry that you hate the fact that game developers want to get paid, but there's a REASON most devs don't continue to support their games year-in-and-year-out... because of diminishing revenue.
PDS supports their games w/ free patches and they release EXTRA content for those of us who want it and who want to pay slightly higher prices in order to continue to support the company.  Those who want the DLC but want to pay lower prices simply need wait a few months, their DLC is ALWAYS on sale... usually at the time of release of new DLC.
The game is great enough to warrant a review anyway, but the idiots giving negative marks to a game they admit they like just infuriate me to no end, so they inspired me to post this.
Anywayz... the depth is amazing.  It's technically turned-based (each turn is 1 hour) but it basically plays as a pausable realtime grand-strategy wargame.  You can appoint ministers (up to 18 I believe) to assist with things and you can design your divisions down to the batallion level.  That's what I mean by amazing depth.  It's also got plenty of flavor events, such as Earhart and the '36 Olympics.  And, of course, the game is incredibly mod-friendly.  If you find shortcomings in the base game and/or the DLC, then head to the workshop.  There's PLENTY of amazing stuff there.
*IF* you find the videos and reviews interesting, you'll most likely absolutely love the game.  If you read the reviews and watch the videos and think "people are entertained by this?  YAWN!!!!!" then you'll probably hate this game.
If you're reading this you're probably at least moderately curious... so you'd likely really enjoy it!

7/10: Excellent
After a brief first playthrough of this game, I would say that it achieves a setting that is finite in its intitial design, yet broad enough for the players imagination to expand it, and a mystery narrative structured well enough so that you feel compelled to witness what events are further down the line.
I appreciate that dialogue is used again in a game to pose a puzzle rather than complete exposition. Well written dialogue achieves setting, exposition, provocation and story with apropriate balance to each so that one does not outweigh the other, and to have this dialogue utilise much of its provocation within its puzzle, yet remain so unnassuming as to suspend belief, speaks of a talented writer.
My only qualm would be how the story was concluded. Without spoilers, I would propose that it lacked a small amount of gravity in places. Not a huge defecit, but enought to where it is noticeable in the aftertaste.
Anyway, great project, I really enjoyed my time with it, and it gives me the hope that storytelling for videogames can crawl out of the current rut.

I love the game, but I'm leaving a thumbs down until certain game breaking features are fixed.  These are things that can absolutely ruin your playthrough and leave you staring in disbelief because of poorly implemented features.
1 - Double click mechanics are broken.  I'm not sure what is involved in how the game measures double clicks to select all, but I actually just had a playthrough where I went to delete a single tent and ended up deleting my entire civilization of tents.  Not recoverable.
2 - Click lag.  This is probably related to the first one, but having grown up playing Warcraft and Starcraft (not that well, to be fair) I've come to expect a certain amount of fluidity when it comes to maneuvering units and switching between different control groups.  I can't tell you how many times I have had instances where in flipping back and forth between soldiers and rangers to kite the enemy and block with soldiers, the orders get mixed up and all of the sudden I have my soldiers running away and my rangers standing stoic as they get slaughtered.
3 - City of Doom spawns.  If you spawn next to one without a major chokepoint between you, you're probably going to have a bad time.
4 - Ironman Mode.  Come on guys.  Put the achievements behind Ironman criteria if you want to, but let us mess around with the game.
EXTRA - I'd love to see some TD aspects like using walls to funnel enemies if they have a way through, but maybe that opens it up to being a little too exploit-y.  Just a thought.
EXTRAEXTRA - Let us get full refunds until a building is completed.  It just slows down the pacing of the game that you can only get a full refund on construction if it's paused.
There's some more issues, but honestly I was so frustrated with what happened (deleting all my tents) to what started as a choice spawn that I quit and wrote this review.  I'm going to keep playing, but this game will be even better when they tighten up some of these mechanics.

This installment of the XCOM franchise is different than the rest of the series, but has a lot of similar gameplay.
Set in the late 50's you play as CIA agent William Carter. Agent Carter is recruited by the newly formed XCOM project when an unknown alien threat surprises earth by attacking. The set up is very similar to XCOM tradition, choose a location and attack the enemy. The combat system is not the same though, there is no better way to describe it's missions than "Just like mass effect" A third person view and you enable a system called "Battle Mode" which is like the system used in other XCOMs except it slows time almost to a halt and you issue commands to your fellow soldiers. Each soldier has there class and specialties and you upgrade them with experience, and yes, they die.
This game stays true to the XCOM lore, same enemies, same terms, and it's pretty much XCOM except the different battle system and you play as a character who actually moves throughout the base you create.
THere are some flaws to this game too. Some places that look like valuable cover cannot be used as cover at all.
AI allies are not that smart. They'll stay in cover even if the cover is blown and wait for you to order them to move.
The story is good. It's basically the backstory of how the original XCOM was formed. It was cool to see the first Skyranger and first use of Elerium.
I've only played 3 hours, and I hope that XCOM's reach goes world wide because so far all the missions are just in the US. This seems to stray from traditional XCOM saving the whole world thing.
Overall I give it 7 out of 10 KHAAAAAAAAAN!'s.

I've been playing evolve nonstop recently, and I've been doing my best to get everyone I know involved in the game, which hasn't happened for any title I've played in a long while.
I'm a huge fan of the character diversity and team strategy involved with playing Evolve.  Each match plays out differently based on the reactionary movements of both the hunters and the monster, and the maps are expansive and well designed for this sort of play.
A common complaint I see from founders (besides the rewards, which were adressed after the initial launch) is that the trapper rework giving the hunters a compass to the monsters position removes the stealth aspect of the game.  While this may be valid in high levels of play, the reality is that the change overall lowers the entry barrier for new players coming into the game, as without the planet scanner many newer teams would be relying on either blindky following footprints or getting lost altogether.  At higher levels of play, I can assure you that it's still definitely possible to be sneaky, it's just now more about knowing the maps and looking for opportunities.
The main gripe I'd have with the game is the current progression system, and how keys are currently earned.  Finishing a round itself usually gives you less then 100 keys for around 10 minutes of play, but leveling the characters (cosmetically, you just get a ribbon) as well as doing hidden objectives (simple ones like "play 200 games") end up giving you the majority of your income to buy new characters and perks, which can be frustrating when you get out of a 15 minute game and only get 60 keys, then lose the next in five minutes and get 800 for an arbitrary milestone.
This certainly isn't a dealbreaker however, getting a character you like and the perks you want probably won't take more than 10k-15k keys, and since the game is currently blind pick with no character bans you won't need to own more than one character for each role you play, in theory.  There's also a free rotation of characters that changes weekly, and everything is unlocked from the start in bot matches for testing purposes.
In the end however, the game is free to play.  Download it, try it, and come to your own conclusions.  Just don't skip the tutorials when you do.

I have tried so many Early Access survival games and hated almost all of them, often not because of the games themselves but because their developers either do not know what they are doing or simply do not care. When I stumbled upon this little game called
I was initially very hesitant to drop £20 up front but the science fiction nerd in me just wouldn't shut up.
To start with this game is beautiful and the screenshots don't even entirely do it justice. Sometimes I'll find myself being distracted by the scenery and the condensation running down the inside of my helmet, sometimes I'll find myself literally squinting at my screen during a dust storm. It's exceptionally immersive and it can be difficult not to waste time seeing what strange things are over the next ridge.
In terms of gameplay all of the elements are there, in terms of functionality this game shows more from half a year of Early Access than most titles do in two or even three or more years. The alien wildlife is terrifying, the environment is hostile, the building system is functional and working fine, the crafting system is reasonably deep and straightforward.
Technically speaking I encounter the occasional crash when loading into a universe but typically the game is very stable. The interface is very well designed and scales very well to high resolutions. I do wish the game ran a little better, especially on multiplayer servers, but when I compare how it looks to other Early Access titles that look and run like crap I am a little more forgiving. Hopefully the developers will continue to expand the graphics options so that we can tweak performance to suit our individual systems.
I am expecting great things as the developers continue to add more to the game. Having read their vision for adding new worlds and expanding the range of alien life forms in the game I can't wait to see what comes next, now I just need to convince some friends to try it out.

This game has a good point it's trying to make but unfortunetly it falls flat and comes off to me as an unrealistic portrayal. The only reason for this is because we aren't given enough time to get to know the main character.
My point is, everyone experiences anxiety in their life and whether it's crippling or just something that you get from time to time is the important part. Here it's impossible to tell if this is just a socially challenged adolescent too baby to get out of their comfort zone or a person actually too worried about the worst case scenario to function. Anxiety is too easily described by other developmental challanges everyone goes through. This is why I am so hung up on this very important distinction and I don't believe the game does a good enough job of showing that difference.
As for the game itself. Based on the theme and it's length there are few things to say. Not being able to skip the timer sections was annoying. Because having to reset when you fail and go through it all again was annoying. The way it plays out is pretty much worst case scenario in every possible way except the decided right way. It would have been nice to explore the anxiety and watch it play out in more ways than just total meltdown or hurray I made oatmeal. Aside from that because you already know your character is going to completely break down if you don't choose the correct option it's not even fun to explore the other options at all. In fact it kind of took any sympathy I might have had for the character away. The game reinforces the idea that if a perfect scenario doesn't play out for these types of people or if they ever feel uncomfortable then they won't be able to function or have a mental break. This is just not true and again for a heavy topic just exploring the way it makes you feel and not how you live through it or deal with the difficulties when life doesn't go your way again takes away any sympathy I was feeling because it's not a good representation if you leave out those aspects.
I enjoyed the first 3 minutes. It had less substance than I thought it would and I just can't recommend it for the reasons above.

Really not engaging and repetitive. It may be unfair to compare to Nethack or ADOM but they're free, and Terraria is just so much more interesting, and Sid Meier's Pirates handles the pirate domain a lot better. The official launch needs to improve on a LOT of things in order to make this game worthwhile. Some examples on frustrations below.
Even though pirates that run off to a tavern for a beer sound like a great idea the joke runs out fast and gets frustrating as they sometimes refuse to leave in what appears to be an UI glitch. The UI makes targeting an individual enemy from a group possible but tedious, so fighting effectively is also tedious. And the inventory UI is horrible.
Morale of pirates wanes quickly and healing seems to take forever despite training appropriate skills. Another frustration is you might have thousands of gold coins worth of loot but only the skill trainer will purchase them, and there are about 6 different kinds of traders with 1-4 traders on a town island, so it is quite possible you run out of rum, out of gold, eventually having your crew mutiny despite being in civilization and completely loaded with treasure nobody wants to buy.
Challenges of combat seem to be limited to how many instant health items you brought with you, and as long as you train your pirates swimming, beach attacks are a case of either knocking enemies into the sea in case of multiple enemies, or bringing enough people to swarm the enemy while spamming HP items. I don't think the scaling of enemies is well thought out either.
Cannons aren't worth much when you get them, since either you're pummeling semi-harmless merchantmen which you could beat anyway, or if opposing pirates they board your ship too fast and you're only blasting them after they run away in terror to their own boat, which means you're only shooting at the enemy after you have practically won.
I wanted to like this game, but it is just not even close to enjoyable yet. In the end you appear to spend most of your time staring at a ship where some guys are catching fish, some are pooping on the deck, some guys are kicking poop off the deck, and the rest are eating, drinking rum, or cooking fish. After the novelty wears off the fun is lost quickly and you're just traveling around the map having a repetitive encounter after another. If pooping pirates (or pirates in diapers, for real) sounds like hours of fun, go for it though.

Let me preface this by saying that I got this game in a Humble Bundle, and it was in the lowest tier of that Humble Bundle. Ostensibly I paid less than a dollar for this game. So it's hard for me to make a judgement call on value with this, since even the worst game that you play for two hours and only cost you 33 cents, well... you've got your money's worth.
Let me continue by saying that this game is a steaming pile of dog♥♥♥♥♥♥ The controls are rubbish, the graphics options are nearly non-existant, constant fps problems, the animations are laughably bad (the lip syncing is actually pretty hilarious, It's like watching a poorly dubbed movie), and to cap it all off... The most egregious problem.... It's boring.
It had such a promising premise. 1950's alien attack conspiracy government shizzwa, capped with an rpg system over shooter controls. But it's clunky. Everything works but it feels incomplete. Floaty movement, bad AI, shooting that doesn't care where your crosshairs are situated, and the constant stream of dialogue that makes you stop in your tracks while you listen to them talk about stuff that you already know (because you were there when it happened).
I can forgive a game that doesn't have a great story but plays well. I can even love a game with a wonderful story and sub-par gameplay. The fact that this game feels like they weren't even trying? It's sad really, because it has the bones of a successful story and decent gameplay. Pure execution failure.

My absolute favourite visual novel available on Steam. I highly recommend this one to everyone, not only by artstyle or music, which is sublime, but also by story. It's such a emotional/fragile story in how it develops and at times you could be a bit frustrated how the main character holds herself back but you learn why. I very much like how they put the choices in character, you can be strong-willed or more passive.
The VN isn't in-your-face yuri but the tension is very well done. It makes your heart flutter and rooting for their love multiple times. At the same time it holds on to the reality of feelings and vulnerability very well.
Each "side-character" gets their time to shine in this VN, you learn bits from their character. And if you haven't got enough of them don't be sad, this is only the first season. With saying that this certainly has a story of its own, which (in my case) hungers for the next VNs in the series.
It's certainly worth the money; I finished one main route and a redo to get the ending I wanted with skip function, 30 hours in. Solid choices all around, it gives you a little feedback once you make the decision (which can be handy for 'save-scumming' into the path you want. No grudges here to those who do). It's rather hard not getting 'bad'-endings, but it doesn't take away from the story. Skip function for those who want to replay into different choices. It gives you an indicator (in the icon of a butterfly) for the choices you made on your past reading). Enough save slots, could do with a bit more but not a major thing. Nice lay-out, very fitting to the story and characters. I don't know what else to name here. It's a solid VN game.
If you like yuri then this might be the pinnacle VN for you, I'm not mainly into yuri but this still is my favourite VN. It just hits the spot in the perfect way and I truly appreciate that. Certainly pick this one up. Enjoy the journey!

'Coming out of Deus Ex: Human Revolution, Dishonoured just looks like a clunky mess of a game that is trying so hard to be Deus Ex but fails. I cannot for the love of my life figure out when I am in cover or not, something that DX resolves with the press of a button. The idiot who decided that the choke and block commands should be binded together needs to be shot too. But I'll give him a chance, I'll let him hold the Left Control button to choke me before I do shoot him - just that it will most likely fail and he ends up flailing his sword like an idiot behind me, and I will spin around and see him and shoot him in the face. I guess I'd save up for Mankind Divided instead.
Edit: Note to the fanbase. I know you guys love this game, but as I play it the stealth mechanics feel completely unpolished and the gameplay loop is way too boring with just 9 abilities to go by. If you love the game, good for you, I don't and feel free to convince me with proper arguments if you are able to come up with any. And no, I don't need to 'git gud', the game needs to.'
Edit 2: Well, now that I've finally forced myself through a whole sitting of the campaign, I think it is fair for an re-evaluation. I love Dunwall. The world they created here may just be my favourite game world ever, and I've played literally hundreds of games that have tried to give me that feeling, but the dynamic, asymmetrical nature of Dunwall makes it feel organic and realistic and really a great place to explore and find loot in. My complains in the initial review still holds true, however. 1, there is not enough abilities to play around, but thankfully the game doesn't last long enough for them to feel weary, although I'm gonna say if that remains so on a second High Chaos playthrough where both stealth and killing abilities are utilised. Dark Sight, Windblast, Vitality did nothing for me because there were more effective ways of despatching enemies, and extra health is not useful in a ghost playthrough. 2, I still hate the stealth without a stealth button, the choking prompt that does not appear until you are standing at a precise spot behind your opponent, which can be fixed by making the choking range wider hopefully fixed in the sequel, still annoyed me until the end game. 3, the game starts off way too slow, thankfully it doesn't remain so that way and once blink is in your possession it gets much better. 4, man this game is buggy with AIs doing stupid♥♥♥♥♥♥all the time, but I get it, it's not easy doing a complex interactive sim.
Dishonoured is that kind of Video game. If the mechanics worked the way it is supposed to, and if it didn't have all those little problems with bugs and the choking it would be so easy to recommend it. Let's put it this way - if you are someone that easily succumbs to minor frustrations like me, maybe this is not for you. I literally had to sit myself down for 10 hours before I started enjoying it, and even so I was from time to time muttering about how much fun I was not having repeating sections because a guard was at a place they weren't supposed to be, or choking fails, or you are in cover but then you are discovered for no reason. I was screaming profanities at the screen more than I do while playing Plants vs Zombies Heroes, my number 1 rage inducing game that would be dethroned if I played Dishonoured anymore (which I'm going to). That being said, I have to turn this into a thumbs up. What an amazing game.

[Note that this is a review of Osiris: New Dawn as a single-player experience. I have not played co-op or PvP]
With ten hours in Osiris: New Dawn, I'm ready to recommend the game to those looking for an interplanetary sci-fi survival game. In those ten hours, I've built a small but stable base on Proteus 2, the starting moon, charted the area around me, and built a space ship that can take me to the other (currently available) planet, Aziel. I still plan on expanding and beautifying my Proteus 2 base, establishing a permanent base on Aziel, and exploring the new planet. I expect that going through all the content solo will take ~15-20 hours.
So why should you spend those hours in the Gliese 581 system?
> Top notch visuals
Well, just look at the screenshots. The game looks fantastic, and runs very smoothly on my system.
> Immersive ambience
Dust storms block out the sun, meteors scream as they smash into the moon, the rings of Proteus quietly hover over it all. O:ND uses its graphics and sound to suck you into the world.
> Solid combat
Proteus 2 is crawling with aliens who want to kill you. Fortunately, killing them right back is a lot of fun. Your gun works well, the aliens move unpredictably, and fights are short but fun. I play on "dangerous" alien settings, which I recommend for solo play, or even "casual".
> Reasonable survival
So many survival games make your health and hydration meters empty at lightspeed, so you have to eat five three-course meals and drink a lake worth of water in each game day. It's absurd and distracting. O:ND is much more reasonable, and you won't have to worry about eating or drinking for multiple in game days. Nutrition and hydration are crucial needs you need to satisfy, not constant nags that distract you and slow your progress.
> Outstanding theme
O:ND takes place in a real star system, Gliese 581, and while most of the game is handwaving nonsense (space monsters! mining with a hammer!), it at least draws inspiration from a real place, real science. It wants to make you feel like an astronaut surviving in the face of an unforgiving alien world, (The Martian is a repeated inspiration), and it succeeds.
The biggest flaw (other than the usual raft of early access bugs and missing/still-in-development content) is that at heart the game is about node smacking. You'll smack various metal nodes for metal resources, you'll trap gas in barrels, you'll see meters crash into the ground and run over to pick up the resources that pop out of them. Even playing solo with all resource options set to high, the meat of the game is smacking nodes with your chisel. And frankly, that's tired gameplay.  I've had a lot of fun with the time I've spent with O:ND, but if each new planet they add is simply a new setting to punch trees, it'll be hard to hang in there for the long haul. There is some hope: you start with a robot who can do some basic mining for you, and if the developers expand on tools like this so the mid to late game becomes more about automating the tree punching through various machines, O:ND will really shine as something special.

Imagine being on a alient planet, it's storming, dark, can see maybe 30 feet in front of you with  your light. You come walking over a ridge and down into a crater, you have your AR ready and you are looking around as you walk slowly down the slope. You hear a rumbling in the distance, your eyes darting around trying to find the source, you do a complete 360 view and when you come back around. Even in the dim light you can see the a monsterous shadow form against the sheets of rain and dust that fills the horizon. It grows bigger and bigger, towering a couple of hundred feet into the air above you. It's siz is massive, as your gaze follows it up, you realize it is heading towards you, then suddenly it appears to open it's maw, you can see a giant tongue thrasing in the air, it's jaw wide open as it starts to bare down on you. You stand frozen, the size of it's massive jaws could cover an entire football field, end to end. You realize you have to run and start doing so, with everything you have. gasping for air, the Life support systems in your space suite barely keeping up, you are draining your oxygen quicker then it can replenish. Then you realize you are screaming, in your helmet. You make a quick dash to the ridge of the crater, scrambling up, using every ounce of strength you have, using your pack boosters to try to climbe faster, using more of your oxygen. The giant creature suddenly slams into the ground, burrowing deep in the martian soil, missing you by inches. You reach the top and fall over the ridge, rolling down the other side of the crater, you lay there for a few moments as you finally stop. Staring up at the light peering through the clouds. The Red Dwarf that calls this system home makes you feel safe for the moment. Your wife is looking at you as she sits next to you, with this very very confused and amused look on her face. The ultimate pay to win game of all pay to win games. You can buy EVERYTHING for real money. Buying it for anything else takes a long♥♥♥♥♥time. You can buy boosts for everything: experience, money, currency collecting, artifact collecting, crafting experience, mounting speed, mount summoning speed...
Getting from 1-60 takes about a few weeks, and getting from 60-65 takes just as long (if not longer).  Unless you buy and use those experience boosts (max time of 2 hrs).
Once you finally hit level 65, you find there's NOTHING you can do. You can't do raids, cuz you don't have enough gear. You can't do expert dungeons, cuz you don't have enough gear. The only things you can do are nightmare rifts and events, which net you a certain type of currency.
Currency in this game is a way of saying "♥♥♥♥ YOU, give us money" by the designers. Basically, you get so god damned little currency from anything and gear costs so god damned much currency, it takes *literally* 3+ weeks to get a single peice of gear. I know what you're thinking: "Oh, he's just exaggerating when he says 3+ weeks. I can grind that out in a week." No. I mean literally 3 weeks. Take for example the chest peice for a cleric at level 65. It costs 21500 of a currency. When you're in the shop page looking at the chest peice, it displays how much of that currency you have in the bottom left of the window. When you mouse over that little currency, it says "You can gain x of y maximum this week." That y is 7000 for the chest peice currency. 21500 / 7000 = 3 with a remainder of 500. That's where I get 3+ weeks from. And trust me, it'll take you the ENTIRE damn week of grinding the same thing over and over again to gather the 7000 of that currency because you get so little from anything (~100 at a time). This is without mentioning that there's 40+ different currencies in this game, each currency gets you something different, from vanity items to gear to mounts to minions and so on.
However, you can always buy this stuff for real money. That little button to buy things with real money is always directly to the right of the button to buy it for in-game currency. For the level 65 gear, it's ~30-40 dollars PER peice of gear.
Yes, MMO's are all about the grind. I don't mind grinding, as long as it's well balanced and takes a reasonable amount of time. For this game, it takes much longer than what I'd call reasonable.
Inventory size becomes a problem within 10 minutes of playing the game. There are about a dozen different crafting ingredients per teir of each crafting profession. You start off with 4 bag slots, but you can buy up to, I think, 9 bag slots (for real money, of course). So, your inventory fills to the brim with just crafting ingredients almost instantly. If you ever plan on doing any profession, as you're leveling up, you want to keep those ingredients, but you don't know which ones to keep for which professions, so you end up keeping them all, and trust me, you'll need them. Unless you want to over-pay for them on the auction house later, or end up having to grind lower level mobs and areas for those ingredients.
So, all-in-all, if you plan on doing much without extreme annoyance, you'll end up spending $10+ for extra bag slots. For the bags themselves, you can craft most of them, buy them on the Auction House for an inordinate amount of money, or, of course, buy them for real money in the shop.
The bank has the exact same problem as the player's inventory, small amount of bag slots but you can buy more for real money.
Skills in this game are actually a positive. I like them. They're a litte bit complicated and are pretty unique for each class and each soul. Different combos are required to max dps, tanking capability, and healing capacity.
The basic rules are: use cheap skills and small cooldowns to power up your more expensive and powerful skills.
Each class has a set of different souls. Each soul has a different role: tanking, damaging, healing, or supporting. After buying all the "soul packs" for the game, you can perform every role on every class. This is pretty awesome for me, because I like to pour all my time and effort into one character and eff the alts. I also like the freedom to choose any of the roles on my one class. This form of purchasing, I don't have a real problem with (as long as it's a reasonable price). You're buying base game functionality that they worked long and hard on, and it's permenantly unlocked for your account forever, not some peice of gear for 20 bucks that you'll have to replace in a week or a bag slot for a character to hold more useless junk.
The prices for the soul packs are reasonable, $20. However, in the most recent update, Into the Wilds, they added a whole new class, the Primalist. To buy JUST the primalist and his six souls, you'll have to shell out ~$45. And they've promised more souls for that class in the future, which I'm sure they'll market for another $20. It never ends with these people.
It was this last update that finally pushed me over the edge. Previously, I was defending this game to my friends, but now, I just can't. It's too much. Just damn ridiculous.
Dungeons in this game are pretty fun. They require some know-how and can be pretty challenging. The bosses don't just lie down and die, giving you free loot. Sometimes you have to CC the add, or silience the add, or kite the main boss. It requires actual strategy, not just tank 'n spank.
The only real con I can find with this game is the micro-transactions. However, they mess up EVERYTHING. Like every "Free to Play" game ever, they scew the balancing to favor those throwing money at it. The developers make it extremely tedious to do anything without spending real money so that it's more tempting to pay for it. I'd rather buy the game for $60, $40 for each expansion, and pay a $15 monthly for it and have it take a REASONABLE amount of time to gather resources, currencies, and gear with everything unlocked for me (bag slots, classes, souls, areas, etc).
Playing this game, you'll end up spending far more money than buying the game out-right with a $15 monthly OR you'll spend 4x as much time doing anything.
Overall, I give this game a D-. It *can* be fun, but it just costs either too much money OR too much time to do anything. Neither of which I have in ample amounts. If you're either a teenager without a job giving you plenty of free time, or you're willing to throw hundreds of dollars away, then you'll enjoy this game. Otherwise, stay away from it, it's not worth your time and money.
P.S.
I did play WoW from the tail end of vanilla all the way to Cataclysm. If you want a comparison from WoW to Rift, this game is most like the Burning Crusade expansion of WoW (the best expansion in my opinion). Skills are semi-complicated, talent points give bonuses to skills, and dungeons require strategy. I could rant on for hours how Blizz ruined WoW, but I won't do that here.
I will say, if Rift ever goes from free-to-play to buy the game, removing all micro-transactions and rebalancing currencies, I'd come back to this game in a heart-beat. However, I *seriously* doubt they will. So as it stands, I do not recommend this game.

While the idea is intriguing and the art is nice, the gameplay excecution is very poor.  Many of the choices simply don't make sense.  Instant oatmeal is instant.  You add hot water, and it's done. In
you play as Samantha, a college student who lives alone in a dorm. She gets hungry and decides that the best thing is some oatmeal. However, she also has severe social anxiety that will encumber her trip to the kitchen and back. It is up to you to try to make the correct decisions and keep Samantha's anxiety level to a minimum.
This game is a visual novel meaning that it is mostly story-driven and much of the game is just reading. You make choices along the way that dictates Samantha's actions during the course of the story.
As I understand it, the main purpose of this game is to show what it is like for a person to have social anxiety. I admit that I am not an expert on this topic. Although I have certainly had times in my own past where I had difficulty interacting with others or getting nervous over relatively minor things, I have never been diagnosed with any sort of disorder.
To start off with the positive aspects of this game, I thought that the artwork was pretty good. Although not necessarily detailed, it looks good and helps to tell the story.
However, I thought the writing in this game was weak. As a shorter visual novel, there was not much room for any character development. As such, Samantha came off as a rather unlikable character who gets angry and apparently hates the few people she encounters for no real reason. There is a sort of implication that being spiteful is just part of having social anxiety, which I doubt to be true. There are ten or so endings in this game, but there is not a lot of variation between them. Even though you can achieve 100% completion in under an hour, it still felt like a chore to complete.
Despite the nice art, I thought the main character was rather unsympathetic. Since the story revolves around her, I feel that I cannot recommend this game. Still, it is short so if you are curious enough it might be worth a play.

While it does a good job of putting you in the shoes of someone with serious social anxiety, the game can be finished in minutes, and definitely lives up to the title of "Average, Everyday". With so many great VNs on Steam, even free ones, it's hard to recommend this game.

Samantha is what it feels like to have severe social anxiety. Mixed wityh a dose of depression, procrastination and motivation issues.
Short VN with a few choices and endings, amusing if your read through all of her thoughts and insightful to some degree, having experienced social anxiety before. That irrational thought chain is a very real thing, combined with depression can lead to very real over-evaluating, paranoia and make the simplest of tasks feel impossible. That is social anxiety. This VN hits it right on the head.

This game is exactly what the desciption says. You need to help a girl get oatmeal. How hard can that possibly be? For most people this is a very simple task but Samantha is a little different. I'd say she's more than just painfully introverted - I'd say she has Social Anxiety Disorder (SAD). This is a short game about how some seemingly simple everyday tasks can be incredibly difficult for people with SAD. Sam isn't representative of the whole group (particularly the scene when she leaves the kitchen) but it gives insight into the minds of those who deal with SAD.
The parts where you have to wait for timers is a little annoying because you can't skip them- especially if you're going for full achievements and have to replay it over and over. The animation is cute with the fonts being particularly aesthetically pleasing (for me anyway) as it isn't generic font. There isn't much music and the sound effects are mediocre.

I really liked this game, I think I will keep coming back occasionally to get the rest of the endings. As someone who suffers from social anxiety I can totally relate to the character and I liked the animation. It kind of reminded me of an old french cartoon.
I hope you bring another game out and hopefully a little longer.

is the first game in a 4-part series of VNs (the final entry is just now having its Japanese release, second one already have an English one planned). It’s a pretty expansive (
15 hours for full playthrough)
, that is a female/female romance without explicit sexual content (it never goes further than a kiss). It tells a story of a shy, insecure girl who enters an all-female boarding school to find friends and change her previously solitary life, but also comes to terms with her attraction to women and finds love.
, with beautiful sprites, backgrounds and CGs. From this point of view, it was definitely the most pleasing VN I’ve read to date. The music, while maybe lacks variety appropriate for such a long story, is very good and voice acting is most of the time phenomenal (and while protagonist’s VA maybe overdid the “shy girl” thing a bit, it’s really a somewhat minor complain). Even the menus and user interface are very aesthetic and thematically fitting.
. The characters are really good, being (apart maybe from the protagonist) hard to easily identify with typical amine clichés and having a lot of depth and backstory underneath their obvious characteristics. Most of them can’t really be criticised as one-dimensional or boring, they show both positive and negative traits and can surprise you, especially when strong emotion and romance is involved, while also never feeling inconsistent.
What people might dislike about this VN is that the pacing is pretty slow and some sections of the story goes on for much longer then you would expect. It’s hard to say it has any filler content or boring dialogues though, everything in there adds something meaningful to the game's world and details that seems unimportant at first may prove crucial later. The plot itself isn’t super-original, but also have enough twists and good ideas to keep you interested and emotionally engaged. More impatient people might get bored, but I was really enthralled for much of my playtime and didn’t mind the slower moments either. The romance itself is also pretty slow and timid, but feels deep and realistic enough to be satisfying. It also fits the characters, who are young and often unsure about their sexuality.
. While the game suggests that you have two separate romance options, only one of them is actually available from the start. Without a walkthrough, it’s really not that easy to understand what the game expects from you and what the UI is trying to communicate when reacting to your choices. There is also a few “puzzles” in the game, that asks you to deduce explanations of certain mysterious events at the school, but with some of them I’m not sure that the game gives you enough information to actually find the ansers yourself – if I didn’t use a walkthrough, I would probably have to do it through trial-and-error.
Also, apart from a few “you screwed up” bad endings (from failing said “puzzle” sections), the game have a canon “true ending” and an alternative ending that requires a second playthrough. And while the alternative ending is very sweet and IMO fits the protagonist’s character best, the “official” one, that is continued in the sequels, is a depressing cliff-hanger with some dodgy writing added to the mix. It wasn’t off-putting for me mostly because I knew there was an alternative path to explore and there’s most likely a happy ending coming with the fourth, final game (although we’ll most likely wait a few years for English release, if it ever happens).
Other minor things I have to mention are some editing and grammar mistakes in the game’s text, probably connected to the localization. At one time a bit of japanese text apprearing on the screen even lacked any subtitles. For the most part, the translation seemed very solid though.
