I'm a returning player.  Bought the game in 2011 and quickly leveled a rogue soul to 50 back then, maxed crafting to 300.  At some point, got bored and quit and went on to other games as happens in this industry.  And then it surfaced as a "free to play" MMO in my Steam queue.  I'm so glad that it did.  I decided to check it out and I'm hooked all over again.
Just a few bullet points for the returning players / original box set purchases on what you'll find:
- All my characters were on the trial server.  Easily transferred to a "real" server.
- If you purchased a box set back in the day, you've already unlocked some of stuff new players have to pay for.  Namely, a few extra character slots, auction house access, extra bag slots.  That was nice to find out.
-  Graphics have been much improved.  I logged in once before this and thought, no way, graphics are too dated.  Well, at some point along the line, they did a major overhaul.  It looks nice.  Could still use some optimization, won't lie.  I had to bring my settings down some and my machine is not a slouch.  But neverthless, still looks good.
Here's what they have added off the top of my head since I played:
-  Instant Adventures:  Think instant raids that level you quickly and give you quick coin.  If you don't relish the thought of leveling all over again, this is the way to level up quickly.  It's also a way to get a "dungeon group" of sorts since noone really does the dungeons actually in the game anymore.  Scales to your level starting from level 10.
-  Minions.  New collectibles that go out and run adventures for you and bring back loot.  Sort of a card game as well.
-  Costumes.  Unlock costume items as you find them and now make your character look how you want no matter what he/she is actually wearing (I love this, won't lie).
-  Diminsions - Housing essentially.  You get a personal house and your guild can purchase one.  You can purchase diminsion items to decorate and your minion can go on missions to find items as well.
-  Chronicles / Planar attunement - Honestly, no idea yet since this is all stuff you do with your character post level 50 and I actually started a new character to refresh my memory on how to play this game again. :P  I have looked it up and it seems as if it's a way of customizing your character even further however.
At any rate, yes, the standard "pay" features are in this game as any:
- Pay for extra soul walks or wait for a cool down.
- Pay for extra bags
- Pay for additional souls
And so forth.  But they are not as obtrusive as other games.  And frankly, I've already purchased the $24.00 add on pack and might consider others in the future.  I like the game that much again.

This game is amazing. I play very few of these narrative driven, little user input kind of games because the quality of them out there is little. This game however, is amazing. The visuals are very clean and polished and the detail that has been created is superb on the train itself, especially since it will be the only thing you are seeing in this game.
Gameplay mechanics are very interesting. There is one point where you have to change a "setting" on a character to get different responses, a logic puzzle (which has the option of using auto complete to do for you, which I would have done but I didn't have anything with me to suitably write out the notes for. I won't spoil the other puzzles but those are some really great moments in the game. The dialogue is also fantastically written. Each robot has a different personality and they all feel genuine.
There was also a reference to Thomas was alone which made me laugh and it was told in a really interesting manner.
The ultimate plot was great. Most of the other kinds of games like these that I've played have had plots that become predictable and I can accurately guess what is probably going to happen, but this game has a story that is so well crafted that I am amazed.
It is super short but it is one of those games that can have multiple different endings depending on actions that you perform even from the very start of the game. At just about 2 hours per run, this game is great and I highly recommend that people pick it up.

H2S2 is a neat little survival game that is more on the casual side. This can be it's saving point or it's downfall, depending on the type of player that you are. Indeed, the learning curve is much smoother here than in, let's say, Day-Z or Rust or the other throng of survival games out there.
You can get a gun after the first 3-4 hours of gameplay, which will make the start even easier. Don't worry, though. You can select the difficulty for missions in-game and things also get harrier the more players you have on your server.  Not too difficult however, as you will find yourself often saying "Bloody hell. That was -ALMOST- intense!".
By the way, this isn't open-world. Or a world in itself. There is a primary-zone with a quest hub and missions teleport you to small-sized maps with various objectives. Playing in Multiplayer means joining or creating a server. Not that it would matter much since the main-area where you build your camp is always the same. It also feels a bit like a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥since you can't cut down trees, which means your base might end up looking like a snake and. (pro-tip: build the base up north, near the train tracks).
It's also a pretty big grind. Your character will (of course) want food and water and X or Y resource to progress; some of these are only found in specific missions at first; meaning you have to do the same mission over and over until you get everything you need.
Shooting is also a bit console-y, with your guns automatically "homing" in on a target after a few seconds, doing more damage. Also, as it stands now, there is no "chat" function. Oh sure, you have a radial wheel chat option with various lines of dialogue, but none of those will say "Holy f*ckballs get over here!". Playing with friends and no Mic means you have to rely on steam chat service. Playing with strangers and no mic means you will relive the level of communication console people have.
But I -do- recommend it, at least when finding it at a discount. For the casual survivalist who has a friend playing it every now and then, it's a decent pick. You will find an ocassional bug (still early access ATM) and you will also find yourself saying "wtf?" a lot, but at a decent price the game isn't really bad and the grind will morth into a Diablo 3-like feeling soon enough, if you're into that sort of thing.

I was always sceptical about such "survival" type of games - probably because I don't have a group of friends that could play them with me. Nevertheless, one of my friends persuaded me to give this game a try, so I did. I have to admit that I bought it just because I thought we would be playing it together, but since my friend was busy at the time, I gave it a go at single player and I have to say I was pleasantly surprised. For an early access this game is just perfect - doesn't even feel like an early access (aside from the fact that character customization is too small and shallow). In 8 hours I haven't encountered a single bug or annoyance in the gameplay. However, I haven't tried the multiplayer yet, so I can't say that my review is about the whole game. Still, from what I've seen so far, this game is awesome - decent graphics, smooth controls, good optimization, fun gameplay, interesting and funny characters from the storyline, very well done cutscenes, perfect voice acting (well, for one character anyway). Tbh, I thought I'd get bored in this game in a few hours, but 8 hrs into it and I still need a lot of xp to finally reach higher lvl stuff, so my interest in this game is still very high.
Update: tried out the co-op multiplayer yesterday and I have to say that it requires polishing. I was playing with a friend from my country, closeby area and there was this delay sometimes (doesn't really affect the gameplay much, but you have to get used to it). For example, when you start a quest, you need to wait for all zombies to spawn - if you don't, you'll be hitting an air for a while). I don't know if the performance was worse if two players from different areas played this game, but it's a possiblity. Another thing that got me off-balance was the interface and how not intuitive the menu and UI when in co-op is. I was used to playing singleplayer and when I had to get to the game with my friend, it took us good 10 minutes to finally get into the same camp just because it's not really clear how or where to go to actually start playing with your friend, how to start quests together or how to give a friend more permissions in your camp, so you have to go through a trial&error process to finally figure everything out. Also, after we both left the camp, our own camp did not save in a separate tab or something similar - we had to go through the list of ALL possible camps until we found ours (it gets worse if you're not sure what was the name of your camp). My friend took like 5 minutes searching for our camp in the list of all camps. Sure, once you find it, you can favorite it and next time you don't need to search for it in the all camps list, but I think it could be a little bit more user-friendly.
Overall, I'd say this game still deserves a strong 8/10 score. The game lacks user-friendliness in some areas (mostly in multiplayer/co-op), sometimes it may feel a little dry (character customization, lack of ingame music) but I still enjoyed it a lot. After over 30hr into the game, I still have a lot to acomplish in it and want to continue playing it.

Despite the negative reviews I really enjoyed playing this game. I played through the game with a friend. Some may find it repetitive, but for me it did not seem that bad. Yes most missions are the same general idea, but how you approach each mission and plan your entry to each heavily guarded compound is where the fun comes from.
There are definitely flaws in the game. I played through on Extreme diffulty and the AI becomes a bit absurd. If they get suspicious of any kind of action the whole base seems to gravitate toward you position whether they saw/heard you or not. We go used to how to play the game and developed our own unique strategies each time.
Where the game really shines is the environment. It features this abosolutely gorgeous landscape with a failry large map where each area is fairly unique (or as much as it can be when its the same country). The game is very demanding on your hardware, but it definitely pays off if you can afford a very powerful PC. The jump from "Very High" to "Ultra" was the most difficult. The incredible amount of vegitation along with the evironmental effects (which cause vegitation to respond to the weather and so on), are where the real performance hits are.
Overall not a super exciting plot, but playing this game with friends can be a blast. Esspecially with some of the goofy driving and bugs you'll see along the way.

This is a highly enjoyable game, but unfortunately not worth its hefty price tag of $24.99 (or $22.49 on sale). They have a great concept and the game flows well, but it lacks content. There are only six units in the entire game and about five or so zombies. The number of buildings and technologies is equally as limiting. This would not be an issue if the game was $10, at which I would highly recommend it.
After the first few games (or many as you screw up early on), the game becomes extremely repetitive. The exact same strategies are employed, the only real difference is how fast you manage to get all technologies researched and how far you manage to expand by endgame. The other critical point is how much oil you have, as that determines how many endgame units you can field. It then becomes a matter of stacking up as many walls and turrets as you can and hoping you didn’t leave any weak points.
I put ten hours into this, and I feel like I have seen all there is to see. I will probably wait a year and get another few hours out of it with more content, but at this point I would hold onto your money. Similarly priced indie games like Rimworld and Factorio have heaps more content in their early access that it isn’t even fair to compare them.

This is a game I want to love. Your first few play throughs are going to be losses as you learn the ropes. Yet with each defeat you reemerge stronger and stronger with an ever increasing experience. Truly this is the pure joy that comes from being a gamer.
When then don’t I love it? The balance is abysmal. After learning the ropes you’ll start surviving longer and longer and you’ll being running into the games hordes. Massive waves of Zerg…I mean zombies that take the shortest route to your command center in such high numbers you’ll often find yourself lacking the military power to fight them if you didn’t start with the perfect randomization.
As the game goes on, smaller spam groups will be added to the zombie hordes from different directions. For a RTS this would be a simple solution, but this is a game with a town management mindset facing RTS odds. Most of the time you’ll crumble fast, the times you manage to hold out will end in disappointment as any small thing goes wrong jamming up your production.
The game has a great potential that I hope it realizes, but right now I can’t recommend it.
fantastically realized world, visually pleasing, decent town management, troops don’t need to be babysat,
Horrible balance, your start determines if you are going to win, Hordes don’t act like zombie hordes, but instead act like a zerg rush, game is not designed around defending against zerg rushes, frustrating
special zombies don’t fit the setting or game, lower difficulties are passable but problems persist
Many claim the game is hard or difficult, but the truth is it suffers from balance issues that make winning nigh impossible. These balance issues are so bad that if you do not have the optimum start you should immediately wipe and restart. Even then with a good start if the native zombies prove to much of a problem you’ll end up losing anyway as soon as the first horde hits because the game isn’t about surviving the zombies it’s surviving the hordes.
The hordes do not behave like zombies in the slightest. You will be informed what direction they are coming from and you can track them on the minimap as they approach. Problem is if you have two eastern walls close together, but a long distance to transfer your soldiers because of topography, you’ll find out which wall is going to be hit with to little time to react.
When the hordes hit they always seek the shortest route to your command center. Yes they have all seeing eye, so they know how to reach there and what hazards await them. If the horde is coming from the south and you are playing on an easier difficulty and have two defense zones set up, get ready for the horde to know that one area of you walls that they will skip over both defense zones to hit your inner region.
In an RTS this would be an easy problem to solve, but They Are Billions is first and foremost a town light town management game that is supposed to be the fuel for your warmachine. More often the town management gets in the way of footing a large enough defense force to survive one of the incoming waves. Military production has to be unlocked with resources you don’t have at your disposal right away.
Once unlocked military needs and town needs to be able to build a large enough military will continue to but heads. Soldiers and buildings both cost money to product. You’ll either find yourself with not enough for soldiers or not enough for buildings. While you sort through this, the hordes will be sent in, bee line it straight for your walls, break through a single wall, destroy your towers, then proceed to wipe your colony out.
Resources will be very important to your success. If you don’t start with the optimum map layout you should just immediately wipe. Not enough wood, resource lock, wipe. Iron not within two to three tesla towers of your command center, military lock, wipe. You see a necropolis, wipe immediately no matter the difficulty, you’ve lost. Not enough space to start with? Wipe. Too much space to defend? Wipe.
Setting balance aside there is an extremely fun game underneath the issues. Units have enough intelligence not to need to be babysat freeing you up to actually manage your campaign of survival. Of course if you leave them to their devices they are soldiers and will stand their ground until the bitter end, but you can pause the action and issue them orders at any time. Of my numerous attempts I’ve only had one issue of pathfinding that required me to micromanage their movement and I would assume it to have been a bug.
The underlying game is good to the point I wish I had more to say about it, when the balance is resolved, if it is resolved you’d be a fool not to try this game. If you love RTS game or town management games it satisfies both, but don’t expect Banished with rts features. I look forward to the issues being addressed, and when they are my review will change to recommend. Till then I’d recommend holding off on this title.

Well now. With all the upset this game is receiving at the moment, here's a game I certainly wasn't expecting to enjoy as much as I did. Granted, it isn't unjustified: from what I've seen of the company, Paradox Interactive seems open to the idea of charging their players nickel and dime for DLC that should really be present in the game, which is a pretty poor decision on their part. That, and the AI is pretty stupid.
But regardless, I can't help but
enjoy this game. Maybe it's because it's literally my first ever Hearts of Iron game, or maybe it's because I'm seduced by the romantic ideal of small Denmark repelling the German hordes and being the driving force of WW2 that appeals to me, a la Gallia from Valkyria Chronicles, But regardless, though it has several flaws regarding it's questionable business decisions and poor AI, it still manages to be an EXTREMELY fun game for me.
Hearts of Iron 4 is basically what Dwarf Fortress' endgame yearns to be: if you didn't know, the game Dwarf Fortress
to be is a fantasy world simulator spanning across thousands of years of history allowing you to assume anyone or any body of government at any time. Hearts of Iron 4 basically runs with this concept during World War 2, arguably
most bloody conflict in human history. Allowing you to assume any nation at any given time - even the theoretical nations, a la civil war and revolution - the amount of nations you can play and change history with is staggering, and the game not only promotes this as an advertisement feature, but
it by letting you choose the nation you like the most and changing world history during humanity's darkest hour.
What
makes me adore this game, however, is the sheer flexibility involved. There's very few things you can't play as: democratic Hungary, communist Tibet, fascist France, and with the Historical Focus system being the only system roughly linking together human history in one straight fashion, every game feels different and unique. Personally, I'm an Allies nerd, being that one goody two-shoes who cannot feasibly side with some genocidal♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ but even then, there's a lot of fun to play any nation at any given time. Add this with the amazing mod support and cheats that give you tons of freedom, and you have a game that succeeds at two things for me: it gets my imagination running wild, and it's just damn fun to play as.
True, the AI is dumb as bricks, and the DLC is pretty stupid. But the base game is so fun that I really don't mind, unless Paradox pulls something monumentally stupid such as removing the playability of several nations that were originally available as DLC. That will be something to be concerned over, but for something like new focus trees for minor nations? I really, honestly don't mind, as long as the game itself is good.
As a whole, Hearts of Iron 4 manages to be a
fun game that I legit cannot get enough of. Given how divisive this game is, I won't be surprised if I'm in the minority, but as far as history simulation is, Hearts of Iron 4 is easily one of the best games I've had the pleasure of playing so far. After all, with the world and hundreds of nations at your fingertips, I certainly can't complain with forging my own story.
10/10 would invade every country on the planet again.

A compelling, one-room, sci fi detective story.
Calling the game a text-based adventure game seems unfair to Subsurface Circular's beautifully rendered transit system of the same name and the Teks that pass through it. Paired with wonderfully subtle sound design and a great soundtrack, Subsurface pulls you in from the moment the intro movie starts.
As the story progresses, the chapters will offer different & unique puzzles to keep things fresh. The 'focus points' dialog choices that help move the story along also provide some unexpected and humorous interactions with the other characters. Like any good detective story Subsurface Cicular offers enough red herrings and mcguffins to keep you guessing and engaged. Fans of Bithell's earlier games will also appreciate the cute references to those titles hidden within some of the dialog trees.
While I only played through chapter 2 with the unlockable ‘BithellBot’, the developer commentary seems to offer enough insight into the game's creation to warrant a 2nd playthrough.

Excellent story and writing. The world and characters feel very alive. Fans of sci-fi and mysteries will definitely find a lot to like here. As for value, even at 2 hours, the $5 price point is a steal.
I sincerely hope this project is a success for Bithell and his team and they create more experiences like this in the future.

This game is a Visual Novel with an insane level of polish. I do think though that this game is so well executed that it will have appeal to people who are not normally interested in the genre.
Subsurface Circular takes place entierly on a subway car for robots. You are a robot detective that is attempting to solve a mystery by questioning other robots in the car. Through questioning other robots, you unravel bits of the mystery as well as discover more about the personal lives of the robots and even attempt to solve some of their problems (aka: problem solving you can do with dialogue trees while sitting down).
It's worth noting that the problem solving aspect of the game is the most, well, "game like" thing you do in Subsurface Circular. Solving problems will involve you quickly looking through maps for travel answers, looking through dialogue for hidden clues, as well as other puzzles that may require you to pull out the pencil and notepad. The problem solving is never too hard, but I enjoyed the process of doing it whenever possible anyways. It's a neat way to add a "game like" element to sitting down and talking to some robots on the subway.
But this game excels in the parts where you are just talking to the robots, chipping away at the overarching mystery and learning more about their world. The robots range from amusing conversationalists to downright hilarious and then all the way to wise. The robots you meet on the subway lead to conversations that at a minimum are enjoyable and at their best made me reconsider some thoughts and belifs that I hold. I'm not saying that this game is life altering or anything, but it makes some decent points about some issues that I haven't thought about in a lot of detail.
Finally, I want to mention that this games art direction is killer and the soundtrack is well written and presented in a way that suprised me.
I recommend this game to those that want to experience a cool story in weird future. While the game will probably take you only around 2 hours, I think it is time that is very well spent, and very much worth the price tag. Even if story games aren't usually your thing, I think you should give it a shot. It is so well done that I think any person who likes games as a hobby will at least appreciate it for telling a good story and showing how conversations in games can be done very well.
Also, I recommend playing this in one sitting, so get a drink and a snack and please, play this game.

I may not have played this game for a long time yet, but I can say in my experience at least ( playing solo in single player ) it is an absolutely incredible game. It may have some bugs and some things that don't work out so evenly or fair, but that is too be expected with an Early Access Game. I have had several on-edge heart-pumping moments in this game in only 10 hours, which is definitely saying something, and I am going to tell you about the most recent, most on the line, most risky one.
I had just died from a long journey to a cave in order to get diamonds and some more lithium to build myself a hover-bike. I had no guns or anything to fight with left. So what did I do you may ask? I gathered those resources, I captured that gas, and I made myself! a pistol...
I had no way of making myself an assault rifle as it required diamonds, which was one of the resources I was trying to get in the first place.
This was my final gun. I did not have enough lithium to make another one if I messed up and the nearest lithium source that was not a cave was over two and a half kilometers away; a journey in which there is bound to be the greatest monsters. After this I did not know what to do, I made a post on the discussions section of the steam community section for Osiris: New Dawn asking if anyone had any suggestions. One lad gave me information that there was a cave entrance much closer to my base that the original entrance I took, I might be able to make it.
I started the journey towards the cave entrance and carefully, silently ( to avoid detection from a nearby monster ) plopped down my inflatable dome kit next to the entrance and saved my spawn point there in case I died. Next, I hopped down the hole into the cave...
I followed the cave to an opening into a larger cavern, there it was, diamonds! I started mining them but then I heard the noise. Most players of Osiris probably know the noise I am talking about. It was the noise, of a monster. I used my jetpack and in a complex order of left mouse button and space bar I was able to take it out! After that moment I was in the zone. Two more monsters came after me but I easily popped em' with my pistol. I managed to get two nodes of diamond and two nodes of lithium. I started to head back towards the entrance praying that I would not fall into the same fate as my prior journey, which was monsters guarding the cave entrance on my way out. I heard some, but I blasted out of that cave and ran into my inflatable dome as fast as I could! Monsters of all shapes and sizes were attacking my temporary housing unit, but I took them all out, every last one of them. one. by. one.
I had done it I thought, all I had to do was make it back to my base ( heh, should've been wiser ). I started back to my base when suddenly two crab monsters, one young, and one adult, started charging at me. I was dead in less than half a minute. I spawned back in my inflatable dome only to come face to face with the adult crab monster. I just stood there, waiting for my death. 1, 2, 3, 4-
BUT WAIT, my memory was blurry but I thought I had read somewhere that if you die in succession your first body will disappear. My last gun was on that body. I could NOT let that happen. I ran, I RAN as fast as my little legs could push me on a planet with much heavier gravity than on earth. I took my stuff back, and I continued running. I was one hit away from dying, yet, in some stunning incredible extreme max clutch moment, I somehow managed to get myself up onto a rock and slowly, yet surely take both of the crab monsters out with my pistol. It was nighttime now, if I tried to make the short journey back to my base I would have a large chance of being ambushed my monsters, yet same true if I stayed. I ran back to my base even faster than before, monsters approached from all sides! I threw myself into my airlock and screamed, I MADE IT! I safely stored away the diamonds and lithium and shot all the monsters down from the safety of my base. I remade my guns and also made the hover-bike I had wanted!
TL;DR: Died on resource run in order to build certain item, Lost guns, could only make one more gun. Built gun and clutched a resource run with it, died once, almost twice taking resources back to base but clutched it and survived. Built back guns and original goal item.
10/10 Would die on a long journey in order to get diamonds and lithium to build a hoverbike but die and lose their only guns again.

I'll start off with saying that this is my first review here on steam, so bear with me.
Flowers, Spring chapter, is neither my first visual novel nor the first yuri one. That said, I'm not such huge VN fan, so I can miss some things. The genral first impression has been very much positive for me, though I've been waiting for the game to get localised pretty much since I saw the CGs, which would be not too long after release in Japan. I was quite hyped and I was't disappointed when I finally got to play it.
One might or might not like the OP, but I think it's decent enough, Haruka Shimotsuki does good job with singing, only thing is you might not like the spoilers of sorts.
While in the game, there are plenty of settings, also character-based, so this is all nice. BGM is actually quite immersive and I think it goes especially well with the flow of the story.
Character designs are.. yeah, what can I say, they are really nicely done. CGs are as good as they say. They are not overly simplistic and have this certain watercolor look that I personally like quite a lot.
Novel features two main routes but there are lots of choices to be made. I'm playing it without reading too much not to get the spoilers, so from my point of view it seems as some of them are short-branching and others will either push you furhter down your main route or stall the progress a bit. Personally I found the puzzles encountered rather hard to figure out, especially if your knowledge of japanese is limited. I had to do quite a bit of research on what is called 'Hanakotoba' before I got the first major one. If you're not googling walkthroughs, you'll have a bit of fun. I guess this comes with the territory, so I'm not really counting this as a flaw, maybe even the opposite for some.
It all sounds too good, right ? To be honest, there are things I didn't like. The translation does seem a bit weird at times. There are certian parts where I thought the lines were copy-pasted or inappropriately repeated. Not sure if it follows original text, but this seemed wrong. Might update the review later if I see this continues.
All in all this isn't such a major problem to really impact the game or the way the story is told. BGMs and CGs are top-notch and the way you will feel about the game depends mostly on attitude towards such stories. I'd certainly recommend it to most VN fans and a must-have for yuri fans out there !

I was always sceptical about such "survival" type of games - probably because I don't have a group of friends that could play them with me. Nevertheless, one of my friends persuaded me to give this game a try, so I did. I have to admit that I bought it just because I thought we would be playing it together, but since my friend was busy at the time, I gave it a go at single player and I have to say I was pleasantly surprised. For an early access this game is just perfect - doesn't even feel like an early access (aside from the fact that character customization is too small and shallow). In 8 hours I haven't encountered a single bug or annoyance in the gameplay. However, I haven't tried the multiplayer yet, so I can't say that my review is about the whole game. Still, from what I've seen so far, this game is awesome - decent graphics, smooth controls, good optimization, fun gameplay, interesting and funny characters from the storyline, very well done cutscenes, perfect voice acting (well, for one character anyway). Tbh, I thought I'd get bored in this game in a few hours, but 8 hrs into it and I still need a lot of xp to finally reach higher lvl stuff, so my interest in this game is still very high.
Update: tried out the co-op multiplayer yesterday and I have to say that it requires polishing. I was playing with a friend from my country, closeby area and there was this delay sometimes (doesn't really affect the gameplay much, but you have to get used to it). For example, when you start a quest, you need to wait for all zombies to spawn - if you don't, you'll be hitting an air for a while). I don't know if the performance was worse if two players from different areas played this game, but it's a possiblity. Another thing that got me off-balance was the interface and how not intuitive the menu and UI when in co-op is. I was used to playing singleplayer and when I had to get to the game with my friend, it took us good 10 minutes to finally get into the same camp just because it's not really clear how or where to go to actually start playing with your friend, how to start quests together or how to give a friend more permissions in your camp, so you have to go through a trial&error process to finally figure everything out. Also, after we both left the camp, our own camp did not save in a separate tab or something similar - we had to go through the list of ALL possible camps until we found ours (it gets worse if you're not sure what was the name of your camp). My friend took like 5 minutes searching for our camp in the list of all camps. Sure, once you find it, you can favorite it and next time you don't need to search for it in the all camps list, but I think it could be a little bit more user-friendly.
Overall, I'd say this game still deserves a strong 8/10 score. The game lacks user-friendliness in some areas (mostly in multiplayer/co-op), sometimes it may feel a little dry (character customization, lack of ingame music) but I still enjoyed it a lot. After over 30hr into the game, I still have a lot to acomplish in it and want to continue playing it.
Definitely recommended, much more to do than the first game. Story could do with some work, find it hard to care what's going on. But local couch co op is awesome and addictive.

They Are Billions is a refreshing take on the RTS genre offering a very challenging, yet rewarding experience. Currently the game features no tutorial, but anyone familiar with similiar games in the genre should be able to pick up mechanics as you go.
The game’s horde system makes this game stand out. The zombies will react to sound made my your troops in addition to line of sight. Silent units like Archers are perfect for thinning down the horde without attracting attention; Soldiers are more powerful, but group too many together and you might find yourself attracting too much heat to deal with. And the first time I tested the Thanos unit, I was not prepared for the explosive weapon attack nor the now enraged zombie horde.
They are Billions is a difficult game punishing the slightest oversight with often overwhelming consequences. You’ll learn important lessons from your mistakes, like the importance of keeping well armed patrols and defending choke points, because a single zombie can raise an army if they shamble past your watch It can be disheartening to watch what you consider your best colony go up in flames because a single zombie stumbled into your town; but there is a spectacle to witness when you watch the infection burn through your towns and a moment to reflect on what areas you could have improved on, if any.
The tools are there to survive including the standard base making affair. Stuff like walls, farms, training centers, lumber mills, houses, walls, turrets, and specialized buildings to unlock new tech and it all works well with the idea of surviving hordes of the undead. And the amount of zombies on screen is not only impressive, but encourages the careful planning of where to place everything.
I highly recommend this game to anyone who’s willing to watch hundreds of innocents die because of their poor decision making.

They Are Billions is an RTS/ Colony Sim/ Tower defence hybrid with elements of managment games aswell. The main aim of the game [Currently only survival mode, the planned campaign is going to be the main feature of the game], is to survive for  a set amount of days againts not quite billions but 1000's of zombies (average kill count on brutal is 30-50,000 zombies).
Each zombie has its own AI with sight, sound and smell being there primary directives for finding you. Troops with guns will attract further zombies with the noise they make. The core gameplay loop is to expend, defend and gather resources untill the last days of the game, at which point you are assulted from all sides by 1000's of zombies. You will have to manage food, power and resourse (stone, wood, gold ect) as well as worker populatiuons to produce troops and defences in preperation for them final days.
After 250+ hours of plying this game i can honestly say, im not even remotely bored of it or itis core gameplay loop. Alot of people have complained about how hard the game is. Most of these people will have under 20 hours in the game and say that while they understand the mechanics of the game its just too hard. Too these people i would say you havent played enough to understand the mechanics if you find it hard. The game is well balanced in its current state, and the challange of a forced iron man mode is exactly what this game needs. The fun of this game is knowing that when you commit too a decicsion there is no going back. This means you will always be learning from your mistakes, this does make the inital learning curve of the game steep, but once you "get it" the game suddenly opens up into more of a managment game rather than survival. You will only survive by managing your coloney well and planning ahead.
Overall i found this game to be vastley enjoyable, there hasnt been a game like this that has gripped me and made me want to invest time into learning it and i find that rare in games nowerdays. Over all the arbitary score i would give this game is 9/10. (it loses 1 point on its current voice overs for the troops... they need work...)

Many reviewers are complaining, quite rightly, about the atrocious DLC and pricing policy - but if you're considering buying Hearts of Iron 4 (Hoi4),
. It's complexity means that by the time you've worked out how to play and realised how deeply broken it is, you won't be able to get your refund.
Hoi4 is a gimmicky (cartoon generals and flashy day/night graphics) and shallow (divisions have no more value than plastic soldiers in a game of risk) WW2 game, topped with one of the worst combat AIs around.
One of the main features, 'focus trees' for the main nations, is railroady, forcing you to take action at fixed times or promoting silly alternate history paths without any sense of depth (click a few buttons, make the UK be communist).
Hoi3 suffered from too much tedious micromanagement, and the developers' "solution" was to remove the Order of Battle (OOB) system, which separated your military into divisions, corps, armies and army groups - and was the game's strongest point. Not only the OOB add realism and immersion, it allowed the AI to cope with large fronts at once and for the player to take control of one area of fighting. Now this is gone, divisions have no real meaning at all - they can be produced in the hundreds and thrown away at will because you can always pump out more, making the game feel arcadey.
The Ai is beyond bad. Seriously. It is totally inept at maintaining a front line, which was bad enough at release - and it has hardly improved at all. There's no reward at all in encircling and wiping out the static and unresponsive AI, which still can't prioritise what it needs to defend properly. Hoi3's AI was more fun to play against.
The balance is horrific and a year after release, gameplay feels unpolished and like a beta. You
mods to add content and bring the game experience to a decent standard.
Hearts of Iron 4 (Hoi4) could've been fantastic - taking the complexity and depth of its predecessor, Hoi3, and making it beautiful and accessible by toning down the most tedious aspects of that game. Hoi4 was released late and so full of bugs it was essentially unplayable. It quickly became apparent that it wasn't going to be fixed with free updates. I used to think it would reach its potential after 3/4 years of successive, espensive DLC - which was a pretty low expectation anyway.
It's now becoming clearer that it will probably never reach its potential, as glaring problems with balance and the AI remain unadressed and the developers release tiny DLCs ('expansions' they call them) at extortinate prices which add little more than a couple of silly 'focus trees' full of in-jokes and nods to memes. They aren't even taking this game seriously, and they certainly don't respect their customers.

Have been a fan of the Hearts of Iron series but this is the worst one yet. AI performance is so poor its laughable. Rather than fix the problems that have existed since it was released Paradox instead focus on releasing DLC that adds little or nothing to the game. Would avoid this game until they fix the AI which is truly hopeless.

The Average Everyday Adventures of Samantha Browne is a fine visual novel with a quirky theme (social anxiety), has different endings (more than Mass Effect 3) and they make sense (more than Tiberium Twilight), has content for about a hour, which is my only turn off.
Props to the devs of the game.

I am a veteran of Hoi 3 (with all expansions) and I just bought HOI part 4 for testing.
Positive:
-Overall the game comes in good shape. The handling is good, the graphics fit.
-The AI for armies and the system for its use was overhauled. It takes some time to get used to it, but then it works just fine, and takes lots of work from the player.
-The battle system for air combat and navy combat was completley redone - in a nice good way.
-The (even with all expansions, there was a focus in the last expansion as far as i remember) former more or less useless spy system was removed :).
-New is a national focus tree; its different from EU4 - its more linear and lets you decide the fate of the country, providing historical and a-historical paths. The focus tree lets you quite easily change your government, something that was very hard in HOI3.
-You can now justify wargoals, similar to EU4. (and you have to justify even for your not owned cores) That in turn generates world tension.
-The World Tension system was overhauled and gives more insight now.
Negative:
-I miss my division icons. To get a good view at your frontlines you have to zoom quite alot into the map, that can be irritating. <- As I saw they come back in the expansion packs.
-The AI seems to have certain problems, especially when it comes to fighting around islands like in the mediterreanean (turkey/greece).
-The fleet options seem to have some issues too. The buttons for immediate repair don't work for me.
-The political party system was simplified, you have now the 3 ideologies with just 1 party+1 non aligned party. I can see the meaning behind this simplification, but (as a historian) it takes a lot of quality and depth away.
-All ideologies have the same ministers(if you change your ideology), and of them there are very few to choose from. That degrades the game experience.
-The map modes have somehow degraded, giving less overview and less modes.

It is more than true that casual interactions of everyday life and trivial anecdotes of one random conversation end up being tremendous tests of courage and regulation for some people. Nowadays, it is called as Social Anxiety Disorder. I have never been one of those, yet I had my mood swings, my antisocial moments and most invested "me-times" as any other introvert. I most prefer reading a book, watching a movie or sipping a glass of drink all by my lonesome to thrilling adventures of a social butterfly. I can - to a degree, relate to this.
features a young university student living on a remote dorm - who isn't also only an introvert, but one that suffers from SAD most assuredly. This short, relatable visual novel is Samantha's challenge to make herself a cup of oatmeal porridge in the middle of the night at her dorm's commune kitchen. She first has to gather courage to get out of her bed and leave her room, still her drumming heart to walk down the hallway, brave all possible social encounters around and manage to cook herself a cup of oatmeal before returning victorious to the safety of her room. It is a quest nonetheless.
Visuals are all hand-drawn in a humorous graphic novel style, with cheesy anecdotes scattered, carrying proper exaggerations to illuminate Samantha's own train of thought better. I must say sound effects are another well done detail to enhance the mood. As a character, Samantha isn't impressive or even remotely interesting but she is real. She is a girl who lives in a dorm and has genuine hardship to get herself a cup of oatmeal only. She fears of judgment and suffers from constant social insecurity, constantly trying to plan what to do, how to react, what to say or not to avoid any kind of awkwardness. It is there. It is very real, even though it is not logical at all, and this game manages to enact a trivial errand as a perilous quest most successfully.
For the gameplay mechanics, it is mostly a visual novel with some choice options. You are to watch for Samantha's anxiety meter and manage to lead her through her quest and back to her room with a cup of edible oatmeal. That's all. I'll present a clue to help your heroine: sometimes not making a choice and waiting things out is a choice.
The game is free here on Steam for your enjoyment, and it also carries some humorous anecdotes just as it has its contemplative nature. Look around, you'll notice Samantha's kindred all around you in your daily life; waiting on the bus line, sitting at your desk at school or the workplace, at the movies... They are the people that would sweat and blush before asking you directions to a place. Treat them with kindness, and you may get surprised by them.

Great, short and concice experience. If you've enjoyed games such as Journey, and find the discussion of sentient robots place in society fascinating, this game is definitely a must have for you.
The story is enganging and the characters feel like they have personality, even though they're literally robots and there's no voice over, Mike has once again managed to breathe life into nearly inanimate characters.
Dialogue is also engaging since it doesn't just contain question and answer sequences, but implements something called 'Focus Points' which adds a level of depth and puzzle to conversations you otherwise wouldn't get.
While I won't spoil any details regarding the ending, I'm very impressed with how Mike & Co. managed to create an engaging decision, that I had to sit and think about for a minute or two, considering the game is only a short 2 hours long. It reminds me of the ending to Life Is Strange, in the sense that the decision felt like it carried weight.
Any criticism I have of the game, such as an unfortunate lack of void actors, can be wholely attributed to it being a short, and not a fully fledged product like Thomas Was Alone. With that said, I definitely feel like I got my moneys worth of entertainment, and hope Bithell Games will expand upon this concept by turning it into a fully fledged experience.

I found the story to be structured in a very interesting way - small pseudo-choices leading to a very big, difficult and subversive final choice.
I won't spoil the ending, of course, but I have to say I have seen very few games that built up to a single, potentially quite emotional and philosophical player choice in such a way or to that degree.
It's like a condensed "Life is Strange" where one and a half hours are all about world building and allowing you to understand the potential consequences of the choice to be made far before the choice is signaled in any way.
The fact that the game gripped me till the end is proof enough that it's good since I'm very picky with finishing anything these days - even 2-hour propositions.
One thing I may have liked is voice-over - after all it was one of the highlights of "Thomas Was Alone" but I guess it would have required a much bigger budget and a higher price for a game that could get its message across without it anyways.
Looking forward to other shorts by Mike Bithell & Co. They seem to be just the right format for me to enjoy.

So, here it is, the most anticipated Yuri Visual Novel developed by Innocent Grey is finally on steam, Flowers -Le volume sur printemps- .
I finished the game several days ago, before we get into the review, you might also want to skip the entire review and read the pros and cons at the end of the review... just in case you guys can't understand my english.
Alright let's not prolong my boring chat and go straight to review shall we?
CHANGELOG :
4 Nov, 2016 - First time Posted
24 Nov, 2016 - Error Check
29 Jan, 2017 - 100% Completion (Both Route finished)
==========================================
Story : 9/10
==========================================
Flowers -Le volume sur printemps- or Flowers -The volume of Spring- is an School Romance/Yuri Visual Novel where the reader will experience the love story of Suoh Shirahane (A girl with stunning beauty but also an quiet, anxious, timid girl) in a Japanese Catholic School.
Story Presentation in Flowers is in Episodic Format or separated into few Chapter, there's 8 Chapter total (7 in non-canon route) where most of the chapter focused on character getting themself into certain conflict and there's minigame where you need to solve those conflict.
The Story is well written each chapter where the character build their romance through action bit by bit not because the director said so, not only that but this Visual Novel also have good melodrama inside, so expect the feels train.
Now let's talk about the route, there's 2 route/heroine to choose one canon/Mayuri Kousaka and one non-canon/Hanabishi Rikka, remember how Suoh personalities i mention earlier? quiet, anxious, timid girl, the route you choose will determine Suoh personalities in the future, if you choose canon route Suoh will be more confident person meanwhile in non-canon route, Suoh will remain... well, same as before.
I already finish both route. First, here's my though about the canon route, it's amazing but ended with "disapointment" and the chapter 7 is kinda dumb, it feel forced to resolve the conflict at that time.
Meanwhile, the non-canon route is also ended up disappointing, why? because the story went down same as the canon route, the only differences is there's 5-6 new scene that doesn't really matter or significant with the heroine you pick in non-canon route/Rikka Hanabishi, if you're expecting her route to be fully written chapter only for Rikka, then guess what, you didn't get what you want.
Character : 10/10
==========================================
Now here's the first good part of the character in this Visual Novel, This visual novel introduce you Suoh Shirahane as the main character alongside the two main heroine and several side character, with the small cast character the writer could use every character potetial to maximum and yeah they manage to do that, every character is well written and developed really well include the side character, they feel realistic (not plot-device and not "2D character in term of story), you never knew what stuff they going to pull, everyone is unexpected in this Visual Novel. That's what the make the character here realistic and interesting, you also might find the character is annoying/un-likeable but that's what make the character them a good character.
==========================================
Art/Grapich : 10/10
==========================================
Second good part of the visual novel, The artstyle is gorgeous (thanks Sugina Miki), the character sprites is amazing, the CG is beautiful and tempting
There's a lot of Visual Novel where you fap to H-Scene or Character, however this one... you can fap to it's artstyle.
==========================================
Music/Sound : 10/10
==========================================
Third good part of this Visual Novel.
You love piano? then you'll love the soundtrack in this Visual Novel
Too bad they didn't sell the OST as DLC :(
==========================================
Enjoyment : 10/10
==========================================
I really enjoy this Visual Novel, Great Story, Solid Character, Amazing Art, Beautiful and Calming Soundtrack
What else not to enjoy?
==========================================
CONCLUSION
==========================================
+ Great Story
+ Each Character is developed really well, include the side character
+ Likeable and Interesting Character
+ Melodrama
+ Stunning Artstyle
+ Beautiful Soundtrack
+ Rikka Hanabishi
- ♥♥♥♥♥♥ Minigame
- Non-canon route is locked, you need to finish the game on canon route first before unlocking it
- Sequel is not yet released
I recommended this Visual Novel, doesn't matter you love Yuri or not, you have to read it.
What are you waiting for, READ IT!!
I hope JAST USA release the sequel ASAP

First of all, let me stop you there by saying that my playtime isn't representative of the number of hours I surrendered to this game. There were a lot, because this thing just would not wrap it up. The transition between the second and third acts felt like a freaking Cousteau expedition. Digging my way out of the epilogue in particular was a physical triumph. It felt a lot like getting through the last books of
, if
were as bad as it is long. There are some spoilers below. I don't care, and I don't think that you should care either. Buckle up.
Buddy,
starts out like Scooby Doo Yamayurikai and then goes full Yandere Nice Boat. I'm no yuri dilettante and this isn't my first rodeo, so I made sure to do my homework before jumping in. I browsed the Steam reviews and looked at the pretty screenshots and thought I was gonna get some cute girls doing cute things. Well, I got hardcore stunted on, lemme tell you.
The first hour is a real Pied Piper. Droopy Dog has a couple of unctuous meet-cutes with Tweedledumb and Tweedlemegane-chan before the narrative gets capped like Bambi’s mom and everybody starts throwing down and having PTSD flashbacks. These kids need a safe space and some anti-psychotics, because nobody in this game does anything but screw up a perfectly good yuri. The last chapter gets a bit cheeky and trots out an ill-timed piece of Joseph Conrad and then the whole cast absconds to a cathedral in the middle of the night to have a Wangst competition and compare pathologies. It’s like Dueling Banjos but with mental illness. Tweedledumb had me fooled for a couple of minutes but that cow with the glasses was a real piece of work from day one.
You’d think that being romantically and psychologically victimized by the moe equivalents of Casper’s Ghostly Trio would make the protagonist the most likable character in the game by default, but you’d be wrong. Droopy Dog is among the worst and droopiest romantic leads I’ve ever seen in a visual novel. She gets chucked around by the rest of the cast like an old ventriloquist dummy who's just been lobbed off the stage. It’s all huffs and puffs and a persistently creepy internal monologue that made me feel really concerned for her fictional peers and the fictional adult who's failed them. It should be noted that the game is less than forthcoming about the fact that its main characters are literally fourteen years old; whether or not that's a turn-on for you is between you and your probation officer. I’m a grown woman and this crap made me feel like an accessory to a crime. I finished Tweedledumb’s route and spent the duration of the end credits wondering if I should throw my PC into the bathtub with a toaster. There's no sex or nudity, but Droopy Dog's protracted appraisals of her classmates' pubescent bodies are frequent and gratuitous enough that I'm just waiting for the FBI to show up and confiscate my harddrive.

I absolutly love this game. It is addicting with a steep learning curve but fun from start to the wee hours of the night. I can see where it can get frustrating but it is beatable, you just gotta find the way and try harder.

SHORT REVIEW
This is a challenging and insanely addicting base-builder where you survive a zombie apocalypse, it has a fairly interesting steampunk apocalyptic setting.
LONG REVIEW
Gameplay: A base-builder that is simple on the surface, but rapidly becomes difficult as you have to manage a multitude of resources, unit management, and the knowledge that buildings overrun present you with ever more undead.
Sound Design: Not memorable, but not bad. Some of the voice-acting curiously sounds a lot like people from Futurama to the point I wouldn't be surprised if they were involved in the game somehow. Also, what accent is the solider supposed to have? At times he sounds canadian, other times sort-of Eastern-European, I figured this was to represent the fact soldiers come from a multitude of backgrounds but I'm really not sure.
Music: Not bad at all! Some good dark, driving orchestral music that's very fitting with the game's aethetic, somehow managing to be both ominous and encouraging. And trust me, you'll need that encouragement if you're on the harder difficulties.
Graphics: A very old-school mock-3d look that's reminescent of old RTS games, like Red Alert 2. Not bad, it really grew on me.
Difficulty: Holy f*** is this game ruthless! If you have a hole in your permieter, or have a failing strategy, this game will punch you in the gut, take your lunch money, use that money to buy a steaming hot pot of stew to then throw in your face and laugh at you as you scream in agony... Joke's aside, this game can be unforgiving. I've often lost bases or half a base to an oversight that led to the zombies-killing-people-and-turning-them-into-ever-more-zombies snowball effect. This game really does deserve that title when you get into the harder waves... it really feels like you're facing down billions of zombies, to the point that you need virtually an entire wall of gattling guns to even hope of possibly surviving the massive, insatiable tide of undead that is going to descend upon you like some infernal tsunami from the depths of hell! And yes, it's that brutal. You'd better be ready for it because those zombos are coming, they don't pull punches, and they will make the WWII Japanese banzai charge look like it's just the little-league.
Overall thoughts: This game was a gamble, I must admit, but you know what? It's a gamble that really surprised me in a good way. So here's to you, makers of "They Are Billions", you guys made a good game, keep up the good work. I'd love to see more from you someday. I'm an avid fan of zombie survival, steampunk, and base builders and this game was something I always needed but never knew I needed. It's hard, but fun as hell. I have a feeling I'm going to sink way more hours into this title than I'd ever dare admit to.

idk what to say here so ima write a recipe on how to make cannabis cookies
Ingredients:
1 1/3 cup of flour
1/3 cup of sugar
2/3 cup of brown sugar
1/2 cup of cannabutter
1 1/3 cup of chocolate chips
1/4 tsp of baking soda
1/4 tps of salt
2 tsp of vanilla extract
1 egg
The first step is to pre-heat your oven to 325 degrees and grease the baking sheet that you will be using. Grab a medium sized bowl and combine the 1 1/3 cups of all purpose natural flour, 1/4 tablespoon of baking soda and 1/4 tablespoon of salt. Whisk this mixture until everything is combined and the set it aside for the time being. Grab another medium sized bowl and mix the 1/2 cup of cannabutter, 1/3 cup of granulated sugar and 2/3 cups of packed brown sugar. For the best results, I like to use a mixer.Continue mixing until the contents in this bowl are creamy.
Once the mixture is all set, add in the 2 tablespoons of vanilla extract and egg. Continue mixing with your hand mixture until the butter/sugar/brown sugar combination has a light consistency, and then add in the chocolate chips. Once the chocolate chips are added, gently stir in the flower mixture from the first bowl into the second. It may take awhile, but continue mixing until you have decent looking and firm cookie dough.
Once the dough is ready, you will then spoon the mixture out into 1/4 cup cookies on a sheet and spread them out accordinly. Place them into the preheated oven at 325 degrees and let the cookies bake for 18-25 minutes. Remove the sheet from the oven when the cookies are a crisp golden brown and let them cool for approximately 10-15 minutes before removing from the sheet.

I decided I would play and try The District to the fullest extent that I could. At one in the morning in a dark room with a headset audio output I cringed when listening to the loud crunches of stepping in the snow. However after the first night I found myself hearing murmurs in the air. I was standing at the Hungarian prisoner of war momument (Google translating the Hungarian and Russian text) when I noticed this new sound. Along with that I heard birds chirping. Interesting I thought. In investigating the murmurs I approached the small settlement and realized it was the radio I had seen before that was mute. It was playing (assumingly) Russian army?... Marching?..music... It suddenly played this on repeat. By my second night I found there was a specific tree type I could cut down. Woo! After hauling logs into the settlement it started getting dark, For fear of change I tried climbing into the attic of a house. I glitched up the ladder somehow and sat there for a bit. Then I heard the howling... I heard the chants of wolves over the mountain tops. I may have crapped my pants at that point. After listening to holws over and over along with Russian chants I was freaked out. On day three I found the construction site and made it my goal to build my house. Mac users: You'll have to opt-in for Mac Beta access at the moment to get the proper download, otherwise you'll end up with an empty folder. Opt-in : Go to Steam Library, right click Pixel Piracy ; Properties and you'll find it.
Too early to tell whether it will become a truly great game as content and features are still being added, but I definitely like it a lot so far. Plenty of replayability which in itself is excellent. The UI still has a few rough edges here and there (and seems a bit too mouse focused to my likings), but it's very functional already. The game has a fairly low entry level when it comes to it's simple controls, but can be difficult when taking more risk than makes sense. At times it has a similar flair to games like FTL. It can be a bit brutal early on, but gets ever more rewarding the further along you get. Not many games get that part right, but this one certainly does.
I think so far the main problem I'd have is the fact that the game needs a bit more content and variation in the content.  Every island or town I've seen so far seems to have a flat surface. Why not add a few random slopes and hills or even mountains? Shouldn't be too difficult to randomise that part.
The art style is great and the animations suit this style perfectly. It's the typical pixel art, but it's a bit more mature in how it also shows (a bit but decent amount of) gore. Definitely good looking. The sound FX and music fits right in with the art as well. It's a tiny bit low-fi, as in 8bit old school, and that definitely works here.
At this point in time it's of course still early access, but having bought this game at a discount myself I've already gotten great value. With the discount still going til 30th of june it's not difficult to recommend buying now.
With the developer promising updates for many months to come, but more importantly the current state of the game itself I do think it's a fairly save buy. I'd definitely like to see a variety in weapons, bombs, pirate guns, hooks and so on.
One last thing to mention, for an early access game it seems to (currently) be rather bug free which is of course quite awesome in and of itself. Most other early access games I own have bugs plentiful and constantly 'need' this early access qualification as excuse. Pixel Piracy seems to suffer less from this problem (so far).
It plays a bit slow, and is definitely much more of a grind than a skill based game. It does have solid RPG progression though.

Many reviewers are complaining, quite rightly, about the atrocious DLC and pricing policy - but if you're considering buying Hearts of Iron 4 (Hoi4),
. It's complexity means that by the time you've worked out how to play and realised how deeply broken it is, you won't be able to get your refund.
Hoi4 is a gimmicky (cartoon generals and flashy day/night graphics) and shallow (divisions have no more value than plastic soldiers in a game of risk) WW2 game, topped with one of the worst combat AIs around.
One of the main features, 'focus trees' for the main nations, is railroady, forcing you to take action at fixed times or promoting silly alternate history paths without any sense of depth (click a few buttons, make the UK be communist).
Hoi3 suffered from too much tedious micromanagement, and the developers' "solution" was to remove the Order of Battle (OOB) system, which separated your military into divisions, corps, armies and army groups - and was the game's strongest point. Not only the OOB add realism and immersion, it allowed the AI to cope with large fronts at once and for the player to take control of one area of fighting. Now this is gone, divisions have no real meaning at all - they can be produced in the hundreds and thrown away at will because you can always pump out more, making the game feel arcadey.
The Ai is beyond bad. Seriously. It is totally inept at maintaining a front line, which was bad enough at release - and it has hardly improved at all. There's no reward at all in encircling and wiping out the static and unresponsive AI, which still can't prioritise what it needs to defend properly. Hoi3's AI was more fun to play against.
The balance is horrific and a year after release, gameplay feels unpolished and like a beta. You
mods to add content and bring the game experience to a decent standard.
Hearts of Iron 4 (Hoi4) could've been fantastic - taking the complexity and depth of its predecessor, Hoi3, and making it beautiful and accessible by toning down the most tedious aspects of that game. Hoi4 was released late and so full of bugs it was essentially unplayable. It quickly became apparent that it wasn't going to be fixed with free updates. I used to think it would reach its potential after 3/4 years of successive, espensive DLC - which was a pretty low expectation anyway.
It's now becoming clearer that it will probably never reach its potential, as glaring problems with balance and the AI remain unadressed and the developers release tiny DLCs ('expansions' they call them) at extortinate prices which add little more than a couple of silly 'focus trees' full of in-jokes and nods to memes. They aren't even taking this game seriously, and they certainly don't respect their customers.

I picked this game up for £2.99 during the summer sale, and I have to say, it isn't bad considering what I paid for it.
While it certainly doesn't live up to the X-Com name, it still manages to be a reasonable shooter. It's main problem is the name. With the word 'X-Com', there are certain expectations, and this game meets none of them. There isn't much management, and the tactical elements becom annoying to manage during the combat, or maybe that's just me. It wants to be a shooted, but can't quite bring itself to let go of the turn-based elements, which are slightly awkwardly transferred into real-time.
The characters hold water, and it felt good to be able to explore the base in person, a feature that, looking back, would've been a nice addition to Enemy Unknown.
In short, if it had just called itself 'The Bureau', and been about fighting aliens in an age when fedoras weren't a sign of a man to be avoided, it would've been a decent, if not especially great, shooter.
But it didn't, so it manages to deliver a lot less than it promises.
Still, worth picking up if you can get it at a big enough discount.

A consolified (read: dumbed down) entry in the XCOM series.
Can only recommend for fans of the series who want to get in on the "XCOM Origins" Storyline and don't mind slogging through a wastelane of not giving a damn on the way.
Levels are Final Fantasy 13-esque strings of corridors, an illusion of choice-of-action never really develops, and thus neither does immersion. I found myself far too often just holding sprint to reach the next blue marked button or yellow outlined door  (aka. plot point) without caring for my surroundings/the actual level at all.
And even using the sprinting feature reaching the end of a corridor took far too long, making the game feel like a marathon simulator interspersed with interesting cutscenes. IMHO: Bad leveldesign.
The controls and covermechanic also doesn't work half as well in third person as than it did in isometric, leading to some very frustrating deaths.
Lastly, the main story was pretty slipshod, even measured against the other XCOM installments. There are several (read: too many) facepalming moments in the story, where the player has to wonder if this mankind is actually worth saving. The main character seems to suffer from severe mood swings, and the highly decorated woman-playing-a-man's-game turns out to be an unintentional comic relief character.
If it weren't for the interesting backstory about the origins of XCOM I would've give 2/5, but even for a longtime fan of the series this game barely clears "meh" status.

Unlike Life is Strange, there are more than two endings. It's pretty strange to see a game as heavy on player choices while retaining engaging gameplay like this without ever recieving praise for it, which is strange because when a game that only has player choice and story going for it is praised for it; despite only having two endings determined by ONE (1) single choice made at the last 2 minutes of the game. I don't understand how anyone can call that choiced based, which is especially hindered in the mediocre episodic release of the game which will never work for games as a medium.
There aren't really many downsides to the game specific to the series. The open level design occasionally makes it look like it's possible to go one way when it's either useless or impossible to, I guess? Really though only super linear games (or half life/bioshock) have really made it hard to mistake paths. There are also more than a few reoccuring small bugs such as the blink sound and pistol sound randomly not working and animation mixups where you attack a person lying on the floor you knocked away and slash their invisible head hitbox off. The biggest downside is probably the lack of usefulnes in some of the rune powers like seeing in the dark or the ridiculously high cap on health/mana potions, which is present in practically every singleplayer game with a mana/health potion system anyway. Also the fov by default is like 60 but that's changed quickly so whatever.
Virtually everything else about the game is good though. It runs very smoothly on my dated computer, has a creative, balanced variety of the rune powers (in the useful ones at least), and a working difficulty system that doesn't only change damage and health. The visuals are also decent for 2012 and the animations are smooth, especially incorperating a motion blur trail behind the sword which looks great (for some reason Left 4 Dead is the only other series I've seen do this in melees). The story is also coherent and quickly paced, with characters actually responding to how you approach your missions. Surprise surprise if you kill 400 guards, 100 civillians, and kill someone an optional quest has you save your team is more than a little unhappy. It's ok though because you can just kill them later on. Another good thing is that mana costs for everything aren't ridiculously high so you'll never use them even with 7 mana potion because it feels like a waste  and they have a system for balanced mana regeneration
And, about the endings, there are 4 distinct different endings that actually depend on what you do and aren't only extremist endings. If you kill 1 guard not everyone will betray you after 3 seconds and even if you directly kill nobody, you aren't treated like a saint. The game really gets across the feeling of lingering suspicion, even as you help the "Loyalist Conspiracy" group.
Either way the game is easily worth $10, especially during on a sale for a couple bucks as a must buy.

A rather difficult RTS game, rewarding you with progression and relief of survival. A unique theme of steampunk/ zombie survival based on 5 different maps. The art style is very well detailed and beautiful, yet dark and eary. The aim of the game is to beat each map, unlocking the next. The game has no real goal besides surviving to the last wave, although a story mode is comming in the near future.
The difficulty of the game is one of its many charms, you will try a map (including the first one) multiple times, before being able to succeed, getting closer and closer before reaching day 100, you see yourself progress closer and closer towards the goal, however with this sense of joy comes great anxiety of the unknown capacity of the next zombie hoard.
The games difficulty really comes from the fact that every 15 days or so, a zombie hoard comes, the hoard becomes bigger and includes more challanging zombies the higher the day. The days in between feel like a constant preperation for the next wave, which never leaves a time period where you don't know what to do.
The maps themselves are always randomly generated so you can't just figure out the "best strategy" for each one, however they are also the biggest asset and flaw of the game. Some maps are just unpleyable, meanwhile other are much easier with obvious choke points and large pieces of land between them. This making some maps impossible, or close to imposible to actually succeed on, whilst others are less challanging. This creates a small problem of having to spawn into a map, scout it out and see if its actually playable before each game, however i believe theirs not much they can do with computer generated maps.
Overall the game is extremely frustrating (in a good way) but also extremely satisfying at the same time.
If you like RTS games or would like to try one, this is definately a great pick up, which is worth the $20 pricetag.

I never write reviews despite spending a good chunk of my life playing video games, but I beleive that right now Hearts of Iron deserves it. Roughly 99% of these reviews are angry at the whopping ten whole dollars for something that you can easily download a mod for. God forbid paradox is at least offering official DLC. Why complain about it if A: It's pretty cheap and B: You can easily get a free mod for the skill trees. Almost every new core feature that's added with the DLC's such as impassable areas (great addition IE The saharah) and the new air force system are patched in for free. I personally only bought the first dlc and later refunded it due only to lack of interest in playing the colony countries to start with, but after spending so much time in HOI I later went back and gladly rebought it. I believe that even at $15 it's still a great value if you have the money to spare for the true way Paradox wants the trees to be, This is a fantastic game that's a dream come true for history fans. Any focus tree you feel is missing (including fantasy joke ones such as Hundland, pupper empires) is almost certainly a free mod. I'd like to thank Paradox for being so supporting of what in my opinion is the best modding community of any game rivaling Skyrim especially for is much smaller player base and age. People my compain about stupid AI, but imo it only seems slightly dumb sometimes and even then it's when you've spent a lifetime, like me, playing this game. It first appears to have a steep learning curve, but in reality is quite simple. It's a game best learned by tiny reddit tips, and watching youtubers just have fun like Isorrowproductions and the Yogscast. I'm not without minor complaints, such as the fastest speed slugging down later in the game during long battles such as against the Soviets, but even then my minor complaints are just that, minor. I love this game, and would easily give it a 9 or 10/10.

Between bizarre game mechanic choices/bugs (like the monster being able to instant-pounce after a normal melee swing, or the game not properly assigning players to preferences) and server instability/lack of punishment for people who bail either in character select or mid-game (the game doesn't actually break win streaks if you bail; I've tested it) I can't really recommend the game in its present state.
Which is a shame because I want to like this game. The concept is sound, the characters are (usually) fun to play as regardless of class, and it costs nothing but your time to play now.
That time just feels incredibly wasted if you corner a stage 2 monster and the host disconnects, making the game not count for anything at all. Or if you fight a monster and he instant-pounces mid-fight (multiple times) after using all his abilities and clearly being in the open while domed of all things. The most ridiculous of errors in the game was when they broke preference assigning in the game lobby; I had a game where each player preferred a different class, so naturally the game should've assigned each one to their preferred role. Instead, it assigned me (preference assault) as monster, put the monster as medic, and more or less ignored the preferences of each player to shuffle them into classes. Yes, you can hit "back" and pick what you want in cases like this - so long as each player does the same - but the point is that the game itself was broken to the point of preferences meaning literally nothing. That is extremely shoddy work that still hasn't been fixed. I'm not sure how they managed to break it considering the game has been out for well over a year.
The overall feeling of the game presently is one with a lot of potential, but incredibly frustrating to play more often than not. Here's hoping they patch a lot of these issues to make the game as enjoyable as it honestly should be.
